where Chrome's is `window → Window.prototype → EventTarget.prototype`. One extra
hop, and `getPrototypeOf` reads it.

The 239 names are the same defect from the other side. The `[Global]` flattening
already attaches Window's members to the global template as own properties —
which is why `window` has 1203 of them — but the regular pass has *also* put
them on `Window.prototype`, so they exist twice. Chrome's three survivors say
exactly which rule to apply: `TEMPORARY` and `PERSISTENT` are **constants**, and
Web IDL leaves constants on the interface prototype object while `[Global]`
moves attributes and operations to the instance. So the fix is one rule in two
places — use the Window template itself as the context's global, and in the
`[Global]` case route attributes and operations to the instance template while
constants stay on the prototype.

(One smaller thing the same reading turned up: Chrome's `EventTarget.prototype`
carries a fourth operation, `when`, which this engine does not have.)

**Fixed, and the rule was one level narrower than the fix first looked.** Both
readings are Chrome's now (`expr-window-proto-shape`, headless Chrome 151 against
this build):

| | Chrome 151 | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Object.getPrototypeOf(window) === Window.prototype` | true | **false** | true |
| `window.constructor === Window` | true | **false** | true |
| `Object.getOwnPropertyNames(Window.prototype)` | `PERSISTENT`, `TEMPORARY`, `constructor` | **239 names** | `PERSISTENT`, `TEMPORARY`, `constructor` |
| `Window.prototype.hasOwnProperty('postMessage')` | false | **true** | false |
| `Object.getOwnPropertyNames(window).length` | 1237 | 1203 | 1203 |
| links from `window` to `Object.prototype` | 4 | 4 | 4 |

`window.constructor` was the second `===`, and it came free: the nameless
template the global used to be an instance of was `SetClassName`'d "Window", so
`window.constructor` was *a* function named Window that was not `Window`.

**The worker realm is what kept the fix honest.** `[Global]` reads like a
property of the whole inheritance chain, and this engine's flattening treated it
that way — walking `Window -> EventTarget`, or `DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope ->
WorkerGlobalScope -> EventTarget`, and mirroring every level but the last. It is
per-interface. Measured in a blob worker on the same Chrome
(`expr-worker-global-shape`):

| | Chrome 151 | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Object.getOwnPropertyNames(DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope.prototype)` | `PERSISTENT`, `TEMPORARY`, `constructor` | held `postMessage` (the old `Env.zig` test asserted it) | `constructor` |
| owner of `postMessage` | `self` | `self` | `self` |
| owner of `fetch` | `WorkerGlobalScope.prototype` | **`self`** | `WorkerGlobalScope.prototype` |
| owner of `isSecureContext` | `WorkerGlobalScope.prototype` | **`self`** | `WorkerGlobalScope.prototype` |
| owner of `addEventListener` | `EventTarget.prototype` | `EventTarget.prototype` | `EventTarget.prototype` |

`Window` happens to be both the `[Global]` interface *and* the only
member-bearing one in its chain, so nothing in the window realm distinguishes the
two readings of the annotation — the worker realm does, and it says the narrow
one. Chrome still has the two deprecated quota constants on a worker global's
prototype and this engine does not declare them there, which is why the row above
reads `constructor` alone.

**`console` needed its own path.** V8 owns that name on every fresh global and
wins the slot over the template's accessor, so snapshot creation deletes it —
which used to be survivable because the same accessor sat on `Window.prototype`
one hop up, and is not once the members leave the prototype. Removing the delete
instead is the wrong repair, and the cheap check says so: with it gone,
`Object.getOwnPropertyNames(console)` came back as V8's own list (`context`,
`createTask`, no `memory`) under the same `[object console]` brand the real one
carries — the brand alone does not tell them apart. `Env.zig` now resolves the
window realm's `Console` from the `Window` itself and defines it as the own,
non-enumerable data property Chrome reports.

**And Web IDL wants a nameless object above `Window.prototype`.** An interface
that is `[Global]` *and* has a named property getter gets a **named properties
object** — the one that answers `window.someElementId` in the spec's telling. It
is why Chrome's chain is four links, not three, and it is readable
(`expr-window-properties-object`):

| | Chrome 151 | after |
|---|---|---|
| `Object.getPrototypeOf(Window.prototype) === EventTarget.prototype` | false | false |
| own names on it | `[]` | `[]` |
| own symbols | `[@@toStringTag]` → `WindowProperties` | same |
| `constructor` | absent | absent |
| `Object.prototype.toString.call(it)` | `[object WindowProperties]` | same |
| `Object.getPrototypeOf(Window) === EventTarget` | true | true |

Taking the misplaced hop out had left three links, so one goes back where Chrome
has it: a template of its own carrying the brand and nothing else, spliced
between `Window` and `EventTarget`. The interface objects skip it (nothing names
it), `window instanceof EventTarget` still holds, and `addEventListener` still
reaches the global through it.

**It is not the door.** `antibot-sweep` reads **10/15** on this build, the same
10 and the same five failures (`cf-scrapingcourse`, `cf-nopecha`,
`cf-zeroclover`, `dd-g2`, `x-zillow`) as the pre-change binary, with the three
Cloudflare managed challenges still answering 47 nodes of "Just a moment...".
Kept anyway, for the reason the persona constants and the frame-URL fix were
kept: four `===`-shaped identifications a page makes in one expression, closed.

### `cf-chatgpt` looked like a regression and is the station moving

The 2026-08-22 sweep reads `cf-chatgpt` as 41 nodes of `Application Error!`
where the 2026-08-21 one read 509 nodes of `ChatGPT: Chat, Work, Create & Code
with AI`. Both are recorded `pass` on status, so the drop only shows in the node
count — and it lines up with a day of merges, which makes a bisect the obvious
next move.

Asking the reference first costs one run and answers it. Headless Chrome 151, at
that station, minutes later, same address:

```
30372ms cf-chatgpt  cf-challenge  doc=403->200 nodes=33 "Just a moment..."
```

Chrome is now stopped at a Cloudflare managed challenge there and does *worse*
than this engine, which still gets a 200 and the app's own error page. The
station's posture toward this address changed; nothing in the engine did. This
is the second instance in one sitting of the same trap — two snapshots differing
is not two engines differing — and the cheap discriminator both times was to run
the reference now rather than to trust a column recorded on another day.

## A cross-origin proxy answers about the frame tree (2026-08-22)

The other deviation the section above parked. `while (w !== w.parent) w = w.parent`
is how a script asks how deep it is, and Cloudflare's widget asks. Chrome answers
1 from inside a cross-origin iframe. This engine threw `TypeError: no access` —
a string that appears nowhere in this repository, because it is V8's own
cross-context check, which is the tell: the child had been handed a real `Window`
from another context instead of a proxy.

**Two members were wrong, and one of them only shows from three frames down.**

* `Window.getParent` returned `.{ .window = self }` for a frame with no parent —
  the one return in the file that skipped `Access.init`. A frame with no parent is
  its own parent, but *which object* answers that depends on who is asking; the
  top handed its real `Window` to a cross-origin child, which then had two
  problems: `w.parent.parent !== w.parent` (one is a proxy, one is the window),
  so the walk took a step it should not have, and the read after that step was
  the one V8 refused.
* `CrossOriginWindow.getTop` delegated to `getParent`. At depth 1 the parent *is*
  the top, so that reads correctly in any two-frame test and is wrong deeper.
  `cross-origin-frame-tree.mjs` nests four deep for exactly this reason —
  `top → a → b → leaf`, the leaf cross-origin — so that the proxy the leaf holds
  has a parent and a top that are different windows. A two-deep tree cannot tell
  a wrong `top` from a right one.

`frames`, `length`, `opener` and `closed` were checked against Chrome member by
member on the same nesting and were **already right**, so nothing was "completed"
there: `frames` answers the proxy itself, `length` the real child count, `opener`
JS `null` (not `undefined`), `closed` `false`.

Of the 24 fields the oracle reads, 23 now match Chrome 151 exactly. The
twenty-fourth is `Object.prototype.toString`: `[object Window]` here against
Chrome's `[object Object]`, which needs the null-prototype proxy shape already
noted at the class in `Window.zig` and in the cross-origin section above.

### On the live page

`realm-url-fields.mjs` now reports each realm's depth and what the proxy above it
answers. Two runs on the live interstitial, minutes apart, pre-fix binary as the
control:

| read in the Turnstile widget realm | pre-fix (control) | fixed |
|---|---|---|
| `depth` (the walk) | `-1` — threw | `1` |
| `parent.parent === parent` | `false` | `true` |
| `parent.top === top` | `false` | `true` |

Every realm below the widget went from `depth -1` to its real depth too. A
same-origin `about:blank` child answered `depth 1` in both runs, which is the
control inside the control: same-origin children never get a proxy, so they were
never affected.

Chrome's own live widget realm is **not** in this table. Chrome runs that frame
in a separate process and attaches to it after its document exists, so the
instrument's page-side tag never gets in, and by the time the challenge resolves
the frame is gone. The Chrome column of this reading is the offline nesting in
`cross-origin-frame-tree.mjs`, which measures the same member names.

The challenge outcome did **not** move: both runs end on `Just a moment...` with
the same ~5.4 KB interstitial body, while Chrome on the same address flips to the
real page (`Antibot Challenge - ScrapingCourse.com`, 2.9 KB). One more tell
removed, still not the door.

## Every realm answers with its own execution context (2026-08-22)

A CDP client tells realms apart by `executionContextId`. Every
`Runtime.consoleAPICalled` carries the id of the context that called `console`,
and `Runtime.executionContextCreated` announces each context with an `auxData`
naming its frame. That pair is how a host attributes a log line to a frame
without trusting the page to tag itself — and it is the reason the instruments
in this directory tag realms page-side at all.

This engine reported the main frame's id for **every** realm.

`realm-context-ids.mjs` is the oracle: one document, two same-origin iframes,
each realm logging its own name. Chrome 151 against this engine, before and
after:

| | Chrome 151 | pre-fix | fixed |
|---|---|---|---|
| `top` | ctx 2 | ctx 2 | ctx 2 |
| `kid-a` | ctx 3 | ctx 2 | ctx 3 |
| `kid-b` | ctx 4 | ctx 2 | ctx 4 |
| `distinctContextIds` | 3 | **1** | 3 |

The `executionContextCreated` events were **already right** and were not
touched: four contexts (the initial `about:blank` plus one per realm), distinct
ids, correct `auxData.frameId`. Measured before assuming otherwise — the
contexts existed and were announced all along, and only the attribution on the
console event was wrong. Nothing here "implements" the event.

The cause was in the notification, not the id. `Notification.ConsoleMessage`
did not say which frame logged, so `runtime.zig:consoleMessage` reached for
`bc.mainFrame()` and asked the inspector for *that* context. The fix carries
the calling `js.Context` on the notification — `Console.zig:dispatchConsoleMessage`
already holds the `*js.Execution` — and the handler opens its scope on that.

That reach had a **second** consequence, easy to miss because the id is the
visible one: the argument `RemoteObject`s were minted in the main frame's scope
too. A `js.Value` already carries its own realm's `Local`, so the old code was
handing `getRemoteObject` a scope from a different context than the values came
from. One field fixes both.

`Console.messageAdded` needs no change — it carries no context id at all.

### What the census looks like now

`vm-trace.mjs --postmessage` groups records by realm, and its key holds all
three tags: the page-side frame depth, a page-side random id, and the host-side
ctx. Pointed at a parent and one same-origin child that both post (`--url`,
so nothing is patched), the same binary before and against Chrome:

| realm | Chrome | pre-fix | fixed |
|---|---|---|---|
| `depth 0` parent | ctx 2 | ctx 2 | ctx 2 |
| `depth 1` child | ctx 3 | **ctx 2** | ctx 3 |

Chrome and the fixed binary print that census line for line identically. `ctx`
now separates the two realms and agrees with `depth` one for one; before, `ctx`
was a constant and `depth` was doing all the work.

Worth noting for anyone reading a determinized trace: `rid` came back as the
same `1ibbkg` in **both** realms in all three runs, exactly as the comment at
the tag predicted — `--determinize` hands every realm the same fixed PRNG, so
they draw the same first number. Under `--determinize` the page-side `rid` is
not a discriminator at all, which leaves `ctx` as the only realm identity that
does not come from the page.

The page-side tags stay. They are what makes the agreement checkable, and
`depth` says something `ctx` does not: where in the tree the realm sits.

### The challenge did not move

Live, on the same address, minutes apart:

| | lightpanda (fixed) | Chrome (`--headless=new`, headed UA) |
|---|---|---|
| title | `Just a moment...` | `Antibot Challenge - ScrapingCourse.com` |
| body | 5365 bytes | 2901 bytes |
| text | "Performing security verification" | "You bypassed the Antibot challenge! :D" |

Chrome's pass goes through a `?__cf_chl_tk=…` navigation on the interstitial and
then lands on the real page; this engine never gets that far. One more tell
removed, still not the door.

## The one-word oracle holds across all fifteen stations (2026-08-22)

The 2026-08-21 finding was one station, five interleaved trials, one guard:
swapping `HeadlessChrome` for `Chrome` in the user agent took `--headless=new`
from 0/5 to 3/3 at `cf-scrapingcourse`. It generalises. Four arms, one sitting,
one address, `antibot-sweep` over the same fifteen stations:

| arm | pass | snapshot |
|---|---|---|
| Chrome 151 `--headless=new` | **2/15** | `antibot-2026-08-22-headless-control.json` |
| Chrome 151 `--headless=new --headed-ua` | **10/15** | `antibot-2026-08-22-headless-uafix.json` |
| Chrome 151 headed | **10/15** | `antibot-2026-08-22-headed-2.json` |
| lightpanda `dev.830+cd14e6e4b` | **10/15** | `antibot-lightpanda.json` |

Eight stations turn on that one token. And the two ten-station arms agree on
every station, not just the total — same verdict, same node count to within the
page's own variation:

| station | lightpanda | headless | headless +UA | headed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `cf-scrapingcourse` | cf-challenge | cf-challenge | **pass** | **pass** |
| `cf-nopecha` | cf-challenge | cf-challenge | cf-challenge | cf-challenge |
| `cf-zeroclover` | cf-challenge | cf-challenge | 502 | 502 |
| `cf-chatgpt` | pass (41 nodes) | cf-challenge | pass (510) | pass (510) |
| `cf-claude` | pass | cf-challenge | pass | pass |
| `cf-indeed` | pass | dd-challenge | pass | pass |

**So the oracle is now a headless browser**, which is the point: an arm that can
be run unattended, in a loop, beside this engine's arm, at every station rather
than the one. `--headed-ua` is that arm; the headed column exists here only to
prove the substitution, and it is the last time it needs to pop a window. (It
took two attempts to get it: the first headed run lost its CDP session after
`cf-chatgpt` and reported the remaining eleven stations as errors — the cascade
this sweep's header warns about, which is why the file is `-headed-2`.)

**And 10/15 is not the same 10/15.** The totals match and the sets do not, which
the aggregate hides:

* Two stations are this engine's gap against a browser that passes them:
  `cf-scrapingcourse` (Cloudflare managed challenge) and `x-zillow`
  (PerimeterX). Both are now diffable against a *headless* reference, which they
  were not this morning.
* Two are this engine ahead of Chrome: `dd-datadome` and `dd-hermes` hand
  lightpanda the real page (2044 and 2042 nodes) and hand every Chrome arm a
  DataDome interstitial. Whatever DataDome dislikes about Chrome 151 on this
  address, it does not dislike about this fork.
* Two are nobody's pass: `cf-nopecha` challenges all four arms, and
  `dd-g2` does. Neither is evidence about this engine.
* One is a station-side error today: `cf-zeroclover` answers 502 to both Chrome
  arms and an interstitial to lightpanda.
* One passes on status and not on content: `cf-chatgpt` gives this engine 41
  nodes of `Application Error!` where Chrome gets 510 nodes of the real page.
  The verdict says pass because the document is a 200 with no guard marks on it;
  the node count says the app did not run.

That is the whole target list: **`cf-scrapingcourse`, `x-zillow`, and the
`cf-chatgpt` content gap**, with a reference that clears all three and can be
run at will.

### x-zillow decides before any script runs

The first station off that target list, traced on both arms in one sitting
(`antibot-sweep --only x-zillow --trace`, `results/px-zillow-oracle.json` and
`results/px-zillow-lightpanda.json`):

| | oracle (`--headless=new --headed-ua`) | lightpanda |
|---|---|---|
| document | **200** | 403 -> 200 (the interstitial) |
| nodes | 1607 | 21, "Access to this page has been denied" |
| requests recorded | 400 (capped) | 58 |
| PerimeterX endpoints | `ift/ns`, `POST /api/v2/collector` x2 | `client.px-cloud.net/PXHYx10rg3/main.min.js`, `POST /assets/js/bundle` x2, `crcldu.com/bd/auditor.js`, `dvp.px-cloud.net/v`, `fst-ec.perimeterx.net` |

The two PerimeterX flows are not the same conversation. The oracle's page runs
the site's embedded sensor and posts to the v2 collector; this engine runs the
*interstitial's* sensor bundle, which is a different set of endpoints entirely.
That is downstream of the verdict, not the cause of it: the first document
response is already 403 here and already 200 there.

Which puts the decision on the request, before a line of script executes. And
the arm that passes differs from the arm that does not (plain `--headless=new`,
which gets the same `px-challenge`) **only in the user agent header** -- so at
this station the guard is reading the request, and one header in it was enough
to move the answer. The request side is where the diff continues: byte-exact
header set and order, JA4, HTTP/2 settings.

### The request side, all four axes (P2, 2026-08-22)

Three arms, one sitting, against the harness's own echo servers: the arm that
fails x-zillow (plain `--headless=new`), the arm that passes it
(`--headless=new` plus `--user-agent=<the headed string>`), and this engine.

**Over HTTP/1.1 the two Chrome arms are byte-identical but for one token.**
`collect-chrome.mjs` twice and `collect-lightpanda.mjs` once against
`header-echo.mjs` (`results/px-hdr-chrome-plain.json`,
`px-hdr-chrome-ua.json`, `px-hdr-lightpanda.json`): across all nine request
paths the failing and passing arms agree on header set, header order and every
value except `User-Agent`, where one says `HeadlessChrome/151.0.0.0` and the
other `Chrome/151.0.0.0`. Nothing else moves — same 14 fields in the same order,
same `Accept`, same `Sec-Fetch-*`, same `Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br,
zstd`, same `Accept-Language`.

That corrects a paraphrase this file used to carry. `--user-agent=` does **not**
blank the `sec-ch-ua` *request headers*: both arms send
`sec-ch-ua: "Not=A?Brand";v="99", "Google Chrome";v="151", "Chromium";v="151"`,
`sec-ch-ua-mobile: ?0` and `sec-ch-ua-platform: "macOS"`, identically. What the
override empties is the JS-side *high-entropy* hints, which is a different
surface and is still recorded correctly above. So at this station the guard is
reading the UA string, not a hint/UA disagreement — headless Chrome's low-entropy
hints already claim `"Google Chrome"`, and the UA token was the only tell.

**JA4 and the HTTP/2 preface are already aligned.** Re-measured in one sitting
rather than trusted from older snapshots (`results/px-tls-chrome.json`,
`px-tls-lightpanda.json`, `collect-tls.mjs`, 4 and 6 repeats):

| | Chrome | lightpanda |
|---|---|---|
| `ja4` | `t13d1517h2_8daaf6152771_a87ad97598a9` | identical |
| `ja4_r` | cipher, extension and sigalg lists | identical, field for field |
| `akamai_fingerprint` | `1:65536;2:0;4:6291456;6:262144\|15663105\|0\|m,a,s,p` | identical |
| h2 pseudo-header order | `method, authority, scheme, path` | identical |
| stability | 4/4 samples | 6/6 samples |

Both axes are closed: there is no transport difference left to find here.

**What is left is one header, and only h2 can see it.** The h1 echo cannot
answer the question x-zillow poses, because x-zillow is h2 and HPACK lowercases
every field name on the way in — the `Sec-Ch-Ua` casing tell recorded above
vanishes there. A local `http2.createSecureServer` echo that keeps
`rawHeaders` (so wire order survives) settles it. Chrome sends RFC 9218
extensible-priority hints on **16 of 16** requests; this engine sends them on
**0 of 16**. Every other field — set, wire order, value — matches:

| `sec-fetch-dest` | Chrome `priority` | lightpanda |
|---|---|---|
| `document` (navigation and `/nav`) | `u=0, i` | absent |
| `iframe` | `u=0, i` | absent |
| `style` | `u=0` | absent |
| `script` | `u=1` | absent |
| `image` | `u=1, i`, re-sent as `i` | absent |
| `empty` (`fetch`, `xhr`) | `u=1, i` | absent |

The per-destination values are not guesses: `u=0` for the render-blocking
destinations, `u=1` for the rest, `i` (incremental) everywhere except style and
script. Images carry `u=1, i` first and a bare `i` on a later request for the
same URL, which is Chrome re-prioritising as the image becomes relevant, so that
row is a range rather than a constant.

The `priority` header on the *document* request is therefore the last structural
difference on the one request whose answer x-zillow has already decided.

### It was the discriminator (2026-08-22)

Sending it clears the station. Two binaries, one sitting, one address, the
change and nothing else between them:

| | `x-zillow` |
|---|---|
| without the hint | `px-challenge`, doc `403 -> 200`, 22 nodes, "Access to this page has been denied" |
| with the hint | **pass**, doc `200`, 1866 nodes, "Zillow: Real Estate, Apartments, Mortgag…" |

The full sweep moves 10/15 to 11/15 (`results/h2pri-sweep-after.json`), and the
one station that moved is that one. Two other rows changed on the same run and
neither belongs to this change: `cf-chatgpt` renders 510 nodes of the real page
where the previous sitting recorded 41 nodes of `Application Error!`, but the
pre-change binary re-run in this sitting also gets 510 — that gap closed
station-side, not here. And `cf-zeroclover` reads `cf-challenge` where it
answered 502 to Chrome last sitting, which is the same station moving under us.

So the remaining target list is one station long: **`cf-scrapingcourse`**.

What is left on the request side after this is the h1 client-hint casing, which
no h2 origin can see, and the image re-prioritisation, which is a value this
engine holds constant where Chrome varies it.

Two changes fall out of this, and only two. **Send the `priority` header**, per
destination, on h2 and h3 and not on h1 — the vendored curl already carries the
mirror-image of that gate, dropping `Connection` on h2 because Chrome does, so
the place to hang it is known. And **lowercase the three client-hint field
names**, which closes the h1 tell recorded above and costs three string
literals. Everything else on the request side is measured identical, so there is
nothing else here to change.

## The widget is not a demotion, and the request surface was not byte-exact (E1–E2, 2026-08-22)

The station list is one long: `cf-scrapingcourse`. `--headed-ua` Chrome clears
it in the same sitting from the same address where this engine does not, so it
is diffable against an oracle rather than against a guess.
`results/cfsc-oracle-diff.md` carries the readings; two of them overturn things
recorded above.

### Both arms enter the Turnstile widget

The first pass at this put the divergence at the second `fo/` telemetry POST and
read it as an escalation: the page-level challenge declines round 1, the
orchestrator falls back to the interactive widget, and everything after is the
widget grinding. That framing was an artefact of the instrument. The widget is
an out-of-process iframe, the trace was taken without `--attach-frames`, and so
the oracle's widget traffic was simply absent from the file it was compared
against. `cfsc-fo-diff.mjs` auto-attaches to child targets, and with the widget
attached the two arms walk together three steps further than that:

| # | step | oracle | lightpanda |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | `POST {sc} fo/2851973148` round 1 | 2306 | 2306 |
| 6 | `POST {cf} fo/2058561374` round 1 | 4706 | 4663 |
| 7 | widget probes: blob, `brunhild` (fails), `/pat/` 401, `/ci/` | yes | **yes** |
| 8 | `POST {cf} fo/2058561374` round 2 | 89 282 | > 65 536 |
| 9 | what round 2 is answered with | **`cf-chl-out`** | **`cf-chl-gen`** |
| 10 | `POST {sc} fo/2851973148` round 2 | 8759 | never |
| 11 | `POST /cloudflare-challenge` clearance | 2605 → real page | never |

Step 9 is the divergence. `cf-chl-out` / `cf-chl-out-s` is the widget's solve —
about 6KB of it — and the page-level challenge turns that straight into round 2
and then the clearance form. `cf-chl-gen` is another program: the submission was
declined and more work issued. This engine fetches that program (127 724
bytes), runs it — a fresh blob appears after it — and goes quiet. A
100-second settle reproduces the stop byte for byte, so it is not slowness.

Two consequences worth keeping. `brunhild.challenges.cloudflare.com` failing to
resolve and the `/pat/` 401 happen on **both** arms, so neither is a tell; the
earlier note that cleared them by claiming the oracle never requests them was
right about the verdict and wrong about the reason. And a trace of a
Turnstile-bearing page taken without `--attach-frames` is missing the half of
the flow that matters — a divergence "found" in it may only be a frame the
instrument could not see.

### Cloudflare asks for nine client hints and gets three

"The h1 and h2 request surfaces are byte-exact against Chrome" was measured on
a request no origin had asked hints of. The challenge response asks, twice
over:

```
cf-mitigated: challenge
accept-ch:   Sec-CH-UA-Bitness, Sec-CH-UA-Arch, Sec-CH-UA-Full-Version,
             Sec-CH-UA-Mobile, Sec-CH-UA-Model, Sec-CH-UA-Platform-Version,
             Sec-CH-UA-Full-Version-List, Sec-CH-UA-Platform, Sec-CH-UA, …
critical-ch: (the same list)
```

`challenges.cloudflare.com` sends the identical pair on the widget frame. From
the request *after* the document onwards the two arms differ on every
same-origin request — `orchestrate`, the favicon, both `fo/` POSTs, the
clearance POST, and every asset of the page the oracle goes on to render:

| arm | document | everything after |
|---|---|---|
| oracle | 3 hints | **9 hints** |
| lightpanda | 3 hints | **3 hints** |

Cross-origin requests carry 3 on both, so this is per-origin negotiated state
and not a blanket header set.

`accept-ch-echo.mjs` serves Cloudflare's exact list off localhost and settles
the mechanism on three arms:

- Real headless Chrome answers `Critical-CH` by **re-issuing the navigation at
  once** — two `GET`s, 3 hints then 9 — and then carries 9 on every subsequent
  request to that origin, subresource and XHR alike. On this machine:
  `-arch: "arm"`, `-bitness: "64"`, `-model: ""`,
  `-platform-version: "26.3.1"`, `-full-version: "151.0.7922.172"`, and
  `-full-version-list` spelling the same three brands at full version.
- The `--headed-ua` oracle restarts too and sends all nine names, but five of
  the six high-entropy **values are the empty string** — overriding the user
  agent detaches Chrome's hints from it. It clears the station anyway.
- This engine ignores both headers: three hints everywhere, no restart, and
  nothing carried into a later navigation to the same origin.
- Chrome sends none of the pre-standard `UA-*` spellings, despite the ask.

The oracle clearing the station with **empty** values is the useful half of
that. Whatever Cloudflare does with these, it is not reading them; the
implementable target is the presence of the names. Which also makes it cheap to
falsify — send the six names, re-run the station, and the answer is one sweep
away.

### What the round-2 payload weighs is still unmeasured

The oracle posts 89 282 bytes at step 8. This engine's is known only to exceed
65 536, because `Network.requestWillBeSent` drops `postData` above
`network.max_post_data_size` — a hard-coded 64KB that ignores the
`maxPostDataSize` the client passed to `Network.enable` (`network.zig:40`,
`:480`), and `CDP.zig:1053` skips the capture on the same bound so
`getRequestPostData` cannot recover it either. Chrome honours the parameter.
Until that is fixed, "does our widget submit as much as theirs" cannot be
asked, which makes it the prerequisite for reading step 9 rather than a tidying
job.

One instrumentation note that did *not* hold up: `Network.dataReceived` being
absent was recorded as the blocker on comparing these bodies. It is not.
`Network.getResponseBody` works on both engines — lightpanda captures every
response body into the frame arena (`CDP.zig:onHttpResponseData`) — so response
sizes and bodies were readable all along. The gap is real; it was not on this
critical path.

## The names went out, and the door did not open (2026-08-22)

The previous section made a falsifiable prediction: send Cloudflare the six
high-entropy hint names it asks for, and the station answers. The engine now
does — `Accept-CH` is parsed per origin, the six go out on every request to an
origin that asked, and `Critical-CH` throws the response away and re-sends the
navigation at once. Measured against the same `accept-ch-echo.mjs` harness
Chrome was measured with, all fourteen hits agree with Chrome on which hints go
out and in what position, and every navigation and GET subresource matches
Chrome's **full** header order byte for byte.

`cf-scrapingcourse` still serves the interstitial. So does `cf-nopecha` and
`cf-zeroclover`. The prediction is falsified, cleanly: the request face was a
real divergence and it was not the gate. What gates the station is the thing E2
found on the other side — the widget's round-2 solve being declined — and no
amount of header fidelity reaches it.

Three things are worth keeping out of the run anyway.

### The restarted navigation has a header order of its own

Chrome does not spell a `Critical-CH` restart like a fresh navigation carrying
the same nine hints. On the restart, `Upgrade-Insecure-Requests`, `User-Agent`
and `Accept` move **ahead of the whole hint block**; on a fresh nine-hint
navigation the hints lead and those three follow. Two tables, not one, and the
restart is the shape Cloudflare's challenge actually provokes.

The subresource case splits the same way and less obviously: with hints, Chrome
moves `User-Agent` from **second to ninth**. Slotting the six names into the
existing subresource table would have been wrong on every subresource of a
negotiated origin.

### A partial answer is worse than no answer

Cloudflare asks for the nine UA hints. DataDome asks for six of those plus
`Sec-CH-Device-Memory` — all four of its stations, off the 403 — and a real
Chrome answers all seven (`results/acceptch-dd-chrome.json`). The first cut of
this work answered six and dropped the seventh, which is a hint set no browser
produces, on every DataDome request from their challenge onwards. That is a
louder signal than the three hints an engine that ignores `Accept-CH` sends,
because three at least reads as a client without client hints.

So an ask naming anything the engine cannot answer is now declined **whole**.
Tokens that need nothing don't count against it — the three unconditional
low-entropy hints, and the pre-standard `UA-*` spellings Chrome answers with
silence — which is why Cloudflare's list, half of which is those, is still
satisfied in full. Verified: against DataDome's ask the new binary is
byte-identical to the pre-change one across all ten hits, header order
included.

Asked for the union of every hint Chrome supports, Chrome answers **all 27** —
`sec-ch-device-memory`, `dpr`, `viewport-width`/`-height`, `rtt`/`downlink`/
`ect`, `sec-ch-prefers-*`, `sec-ch-ua-wow64: ?0`, `sec-ch-ua-form-factors:
"Desktop"`, and both the `Sec-CH-`-prefixed and bare spellings of each
(`results/acceptch-all-chrome.json`). Six of 27 is the coverage this engine
has. That is the size of the remaining surface, and the reason the
all-or-nothing rule is the safe default rather than a temporary one.

### The DataDome column cannot be read right now

Four sweeps of the four DataDome stations, alternating binaries over about an
hour: control 3/4, new 0/4, control 0/4, new 0/4, control 1/4, new 0/4. The
control binary alone spans 3/4 to 0/4, so the column is flapping on the site's
side — the same trap that produced a phantom regression once before. The
engine-side answer comes from the wire, not the column: none of DataDome's
asset origins (`js.datadome.co`, `api-js.datadome.co`, `dd.leboncoin.fr`,
`ct.captcha-delivery.com`) send `Accept-CH` at all, and the four document
origins ask for something we decline, so the new binary sends zero
high-entropy hints anywhere in that flow.

### Still not byte-exact: the XHR `POST`

One diff survives on both engines' `POST` subresources, and it predates this
work — confirmed by running the harness against the pre-change binary. Chrome
sends `Content-Length` third, `content-type` right after `User-Agent`, and an
`Origin`; this engine sends no `Origin` at all and leaves `content-type` and
`Content-Length` to the trailing pass, after `Accept-Language`. Cloudflare's
challenge flow is mostly `POST`s, so this is worth its own task.

## No constructor here has an empty message any more (2026-08-22)

`probes/probe-ctor-sweep.js` walks every constructor reachable from `window` —
capitalised name, has a `prototype`, minus five that would navigate or spawn —
and calls each one three ways: `new C()`, `new C('\0nope')`, and `C()` without
the operator. It records the error's `name`, its `message`, and whether the
message is empty.

**Chrome: 722 constructors, zero empty messages.** That makes an empty message a
zero-false-positive reading — there is nothing to argue about, no version drift,
no platform variance. This engine had **145** of them across 927 constructors:

| the reading | count |
|---|---|
| `new HTMLDivElement()` and 69 other element interfaces, `new` and bad-argument forms alike | 140 |
| `new RTCEncodedAudioFrame({})` / `new RTCEncodedVideoFrame({})` | 2 |
| `new RTCIceCandidate()` | 1 |
| `new TextDecoder('nope')` / `new TextDecoderStream('nope')` | 2 |

All 145 are gone. `expr-diff.mjs` over the two readings went from **583/722
identical, 139 differ** to **658/722, 64 differ**; the 64 are listed at the end
of this section and none of them is an empty message.

### One shared callback, two different tells

The 140 were one root cause with two faces, and the second one is the more
interesting: it was never an empty string, so a sweep for empties would have
missed it.

`Snapshot.generateConstructor` gave every interface inheriting from
`HTMLElement` the *same* constructor callback — the one `upgradeConstruct`
needs so a custom element's `super()` can reach its built-in base. So:

- `new HTMLDivElement()` reached `upgradeConstruct` with nothing to upgrade and
  answered a bare `error.TypeError`, which carries no message at all.
- `HTMLDivElement()` was refused earlier, by the "use the `new` operator"
  branch — but the interface name in that sentence is `comptime`, read off the
  type the callback was generated for. One callback, one type, so all 70
  interfaces claimed to be **`HTMLElement`**. A page reading
  `HTMLDivElement()`'s message got told which internal helper it had reached.

Generating the callback per interface fixes both at once, and the second only
costs the snapshot's external-reference table one entry per interface (each
generated callback is its own function pointer).

`new HTMLElement()` itself was a third thing again: an `Error` — not even a
`TypeError` — reading `Illegal Constructor`, from a `Caller.zig` mapping that
named nothing. Chrome says `Failed to construct 'HTMLElement': Illegal
constructor`.

### Chrome splits the element interfaces two ways, and it is not arbitrary

The plain call, `X()` with no `new`, does not read the same across the family:

| Chrome's answer to `X()` | interfaces |
|---|---|
| `Failed to construct 'X': Please use the 'new' operator, this DOM object constructor cannot be called as a function.` | 73 |
| `Illegal constructor` (bare, no name) | `HTMLMediaElement`, `HTMLUnknownElement` (and the four collections plus `HTMLDocument`) |

`new X()` names the interface in *both* groups. The split follows Blink's
`[HTMLConstructor]`: an interface that can be a custom element's base has a
constructor callback to reach, and one that cannot has none — `HTMLMediaElement`
is abstract and `HTMLUnknownElement` is not extensible. Routing those two to the
shared illegal-constructor callback reproduces the pair exactly, which is why
the fix is a two-type exclusion rather than a special case in the message.

### The interface named is the one whose constructor ran

`probes/probe-custom-element-refusal.js` settles what `new.target` does *not*
decide. A class extending an element interface that was never registered:

```
class U extends HTMLElement {}    new U()  -> Failed to construct 'HTMLElement': Illegal constructor
class V extends HTMLDivElement {} new V()  -> Failed to construct 'HTMLDivElement': Illegal constructor
Reflect.construct(HTMLDivElement, [], Object) -> Failed to construct 'HTMLDivElement': Illegal constructor
```

So the name comes from the constructor that ran, never from the subclass that
asked. Per-interface generation gets this for free; a runtime read of
`new.target.name` — the tempting shortcut, and what the *other* illegal
constructor callback does — would have got all three wrong.

Two behaviours the same probe measured that this engine still does not have:
Chrome **constructs** a registered customized built-in through `new` (`class
Fancy extends HTMLDivElement` + `define(..., {extends:'div'})` gives a `DIV`),
and it tolerates a second `Reflect.construct` against the same class. Both are
refusals here; both are behaviour, not wording.

### The encoding label is echoed back exactly as written

`probes/probe-encoding-label.js`, ten labels against Chrome 151:

```
'invalid-encoding'      -> ('invalid-encoding')
'Invalid-Encoding'      -> ('Invalid-Encoding')      not lowercased
'  Invalid-Encoding  '  -> ('  Invalid-Encoding  ')  not trimmed
''                      -> ('')                      the empty string included
'replacement'           -> ('replacement')           a known label a decoder still refuses
```

The sentence is `Failed to construct 'TextDecoder': The encoding label provided
('<label>') is invalid.`, and `TextDecoderStream` words it identically with only
the interface name changed. Worth measuring rather than deriving: the spec
*does* strip and lowercase the label before looking it up, so the normalised
form was the likelier guess and is wrong.

The same probe also caught a gap wider than a message: this engine's
`TextDecoderStream` accepts only the three `utf-8` labels, where Chrome hands
back a working stream for `windows-1252`, `big5`, `shift_jis`, `x-user-defined`
and the rest of the registry. It now refuses in Blink's words, so the gap no
longer announces itself twice.

### The 64 that still differ

64 *interfaces* differ; 17 of those are simply absent here, and the other 47
differ across 54 individual call forms. None is an empty message. By family:

- **`invalid argument`, 24 of the 54 forms.** `error.InvalidArgument` maps to the
  literal string `invalid argument`, which no browser says. Chrome's wording is
  per-parameter: `Failed to construct 'Headers': The provided value is not of
  type '(record<ByteString, ByteString> or sequence<sequence<ByteString>>)'.`,
  `Failed to construct 'Blob': The provided value cannot be converted to a
  sequence.`, `Failed to construct 'RTCIceCandidate': The provided value is not
  of type 'RTCIceCandidateInit'.` One sentence shape shared by every dictionary
  and sequence parameter in the bridge, so it wants one change rather than
  thirty.
- **Legacy factory functions.** Chrome has six interface objects where this
  engine has three: `window.Audio !== window.HTMLAudioElement`, and the same for
  `Image`/`Option`. So `Audio()` names `Audio` there and `HTMLAudioElement`
  here, and `new HTMLAudioElement()` builds an element here where Chrome refuses
  it. A missing interface, not a message.
- **We do not throw where Chrome does, 17 forms** (11 once the legacy factories
  above are set aside): the six `CSSMath*` constructors accept a non-finite
  double, `new CSSStyleSheet(' nope')`, `new DocumentTimeline(' nope')` and
  `new TaskController(' nope')` accept a non-dictionary, and
  `new HTMLDocument()` succeeds. The reverse happens twice, both
  `CustomElementRegistry`: Chrome 151 lets a page construct one (scoped
  registries) and this engine refuses.
- **Absent globals, 17**: `CloseWatcher`, `Fence`, `FencedFrameConfig`,
  `HTMLFencedFrameElement`, `DocumentPictureInPictureEvent`, `Observable`,
  `Subscriber`, `RestrictionTarget`, `WebSocketError`, `WebSocketStream`, and
  the six `SharedStorage*` names plus `SharedStorageWorklet`.
- **One-off wordings, 11 forms**: `new DOMMatrix(' nope')` (and
  `DOMMatrixReadOnly`, `WebKitCSSMatrix`) says "The string did not match the
  expected pattern" where Chrome says `Failed to parse '\0nope'.`;
  `new CSSRotate(' nope')` says "Must pass an angle to CSSRotate" where Chrome
  says "parameter 1 is not of type 'CSSNumericValue'."; plus `KeyframeEffect`,
  `MediaRecorder`, and the four legacy-factory / `HTMLDocument` plain calls.

The two narrower probes read the same way after the change:
`probe-custom-element-refusal` is 7/8 identical, the one miss being the
customized built-in Chrome constructs and this engine refuses;
`probe-encoding-label` is 23/26, the three misses being the two dictionary
conversions that still say `invalid argument` and `TextDecoderStream`'s
utf-8-only label table.

Readings: `results/probes/probe-ctor-sweep.{chrome,lightpanda}.json`,
`probe-encoding-label.{chrome,lightpanda}.json`,
`probe-custom-element-refusal.{chrome,lightpanda}.json`.

## The round-2 body, and the oracle that stopped clearing (2026-08-22)

E1 put the first divergence at the second `fo/` telemetry POST and could not
read it: `Network.enable`'s `maxPostDataSize` was taken and dropped, a
hardcoded 64KB governed both the inline `postData` and the body kept for
`getRequestPostData`, and the round-2 body is larger than that. The trace read
`postLen: -1` — a body exists, you may not see it. The parameter is honoured
now, per browser context, and the column reads bytes.

### The measurement

| arm | round 1 | round 2 (widget) | round-2 response |
|---|---|---|---|
| lightpanda | 2306 | **87586** | 127720 |
| chrome | 2338 | **89612** | 127728 |
| chrome, again | 2338 | **89570** | 127724 |

So round 2 is ~2.3% shorter on this engine than on Chrome, out of ~88KB of
Cloudflare's own encrypted telemetry. That difference is not readable as a
missing field — the payload is an opaque base64-ish blob, and its length is a
function of everything the challenge program measured. What the numbers rule
out is a *category* difference: this is not an engine sending a stub, or a
tenth of the telemetry. Both arms post the same order of magnitude to the same
endpoint and get a same-sized program back.

### The oracle stopped clearing — WRONG, see "The oracle was never dead" below

**Retracted.** Both runs below were launched without `--headed-ua`, so the
oracle's user agent said `HeadlessChrome` — the one word this repo had already
measured as fatal on this station. The arm was misconfigured, not demoted, and
Chrome clears `cf-scrapingcourse` on demand once the flag is passed. The
paragraphs are kept for the trace they cite; read the conclusion as void.

The headless Chrome arm no longer clears `cf-scrapingcourse` either. Two
consecutive runs, both `clearance: false`, both ending on `Just a moment...`,
and both handed a `cf-chl-gen` header on the round-2 reply — Cloudflare
issuing a fresh challenge rather than a clearance form.

That matters more than the byte counts. Every plan under
`cf-scrapingcourse-oracle-diff` rests on there being an arm that passes, so
that the difference between the two arms is the thing to fix. Right now there
is no such arm: both engines take the same path, post the same shape, and are
declined the same way. E1's specific claim — that the oracle posts round 2
back to the *page-level* challenge while this engine posts it to the widget's
own instance — does not reproduce; here both arms post round 2 to the widget
instance (`.../fo/205804612:...`).

Whether the oracle's configuration was specifically demoted, or the station
tightened for everyone, this run cannot say. What it can say is that
`cfsc-widget-solve-declined` has no diff to work from until an arm clears
again, and that re-establishing a passing oracle is the prerequisite, not the
widget's solve. Raw traces: `results/cfsc-fo-lightpanda-postfix.json`,
`results/cfsc-fo-chrome-postfix{,2}.json`.

## The POST that did not say where it came from

Three headers separate a POST from the GET beside it, and this engine placed
all three wrong — one of them by leaving it out entirely. Cloudflare's managed
challenge is three POSTs (2306, ~4.8KB, ~86KB against `cf-scrapingcourse`), so
the POST is not a side surface here; it is where the challenge lives.

### What was measured

The probe is `accept-ch-echo.mjs`, which already loads a page that issues a
same-origin `fetch` GET and a same-origin XHR POST, and records the byte-exact
request head of each. Run twice per engine: once with Cloudflare's nine-hint
`Accept-CH` (the hinted subresource table) and once with `--hints ""`, an empty
ask, which is the unhinted table. Four arms, one page, no live station
involved.

Chrome's POST, unhinted (`results/xhr-post-nohints-chrome.json`):

```
Host, Connection, Content-Length,
sec-ch-ua-platform, User-Agent, sec-ch-ua, content-type, sec-ch-ua-mobile,
Accept, Origin, Sec-Fetch-Site, Sec-Fetch-Mode, Sec-Fetch-Dest,
Referer, Accept-Encoding, Accept-Language
```

and hinted (`results/acceptch-chrome.json`), where `content-type` follows
`User-Agent` instead of `sec-ch-ua` — the hint block is a different sequence,
so the position does not carry over between the two tables.

This engine, before: no `Origin` at all, and `content-type` and
`Content-Length` after `Accept-Language`, in the trailing pass `emitHeaders`
gives a name no table knows.

### Origin is not "the origin of every request"

Fetch appends it when the response tainting is cors — any cross-origin
fetch/XHR — **or** when the method is neither GET nor HEAD. That is why the
same-origin POST carries it and the same-origin GET on the same page does not,
which is exactly what both Chrome arms show. A rule of "send it on cors
requests" would have put it on the GET too, and been a new tell rather than a
fixed one.

`Content-Length` had to become a header this engine writes, not one curl
appends: curl emits its copy from the `H1_HD_CONTENT` slot, after every custom
header, and slot order is not ours to pick from the header list. Ours is placed
by the table; curl skips its own once the list carries one
(`Curl_checkheaders`), so the number on the wire is unchanged and there is no
duplicate. Both it and `Origin` are re-seeded after a redirect: a 301/302/303
turns the request into a GET and drops the body, and a length header left
behind would announce bytes that are never sent.

### After

| arm | POST header order vs Chrome |
|---|---|
| hinted (9 hints) | identical, 22 of 22 |
| unhinted | identical, 16 of 16 |

Values check out too: `Content-Length: 5` for a 5-byte body, `Origin` the
initiator's serialized origin, no duplicated field, and every GET on the page
unchanged — no stray `Origin` or `Content-Length` where Chrome has none.

Arms: `results/xhr-post-{hints,nohints}-lightpanda.json` against
`results/acceptch-chrome.json` and `results/xhr-post-nohints-chrome.json`.

### What it did not buy

`cf-scrapingcourse` still ends on `Just a moment...`, and its three POSTs are
still answered with `cf-chl-gen` — a fresh challenge
(`results/cfsc-fo-lp-xhrpost.json`). The next chapter shows why that was never
going to change here: the oracle is accepted at round 3 and this engine is
declined at round 3, and a real Chrome with one wrong field is declined there
too — the gate is inside that payload, not in the header block around it. The
15-station sweep reads
11/15 (`results/xhr-post-sweep-after.json`), matching the best recent run and
regressing nothing — the four failures are the same three Cloudflare
challenges and `dd-g2`.

So this one is banked as fidelity, not as a station flipped: a POST with no
`Origin` is a shape no browser produces, and it was on every POST this engine
made.

### Every operation counts its own arguments now

`Failed to execute '<op>' on '<Interface>': N argument(s) required, but only M
present.` used to come out of the bridge for constructors only; an operation
answered `TypeError: invalid argument`, which no browser says, and a dozen
modules counted their arguments by hand to get Chrome's wording. The refusal was
already there — `Caller.getArgs` stops at a missing non-optional parameter — so
what changed is *when* it fires and *what it says*: it now runs before any
argument is converted, the way Chrome's does, and writes Blink's sentence.

Naming the operation was the awkward part, and it is worth recording how, since
nothing else in the bridge needs the JS-visible name at call time.
`bridge.function` receives the Zig function, never the `JsApi` declaration it is
bound under, and the two differ often enough — `Element.matches` is also
`webkitMatchesSelector`, `Response.json_static` is `json`, nine interfaces bind
`_item` as `item` — that deriving the name from the Zig one would misname them.
`Snapshot` does know the name, so it hands each operation's function template
the same name string it already builds for `SetClassName`, as the template's
data; `Caller.FunctionCallbackInfo.operationName` reads it back on the refusal
path only.

**A check that fires before conversion is only safe if the count is WebIDL's**,
and ours was not. `probe-operation-arity.js` sweeps every operation's `length`
on both engines — 3714 members in Chrome, 3486 here, 3470 shared — and found 30
where ours was larger. All 30 are fixed here, because every one of them would
have become a refusal Chrome does not make:

- **19 variadics reported 1 instead of 0.** `Element`/`Document`/
  `DocumentFragment`'s `append`/`prepend`/`replaceChildren`, `Element`/
  `CharacterData`'s `after`/`before`/`replaceWith`, `DOMTokenList.add`/`remove`,
  `document.write`/`writeln`. A variadic contributes nothing to `length`, but
  here a variadic and a sequence parameter are the same slice, so they say
  `.arity = 0` explicitly. Their runtime behaviour was already right —
  `getArgs` decides variadic-ness from the argument it actually got — so only
  the readable `length` was wrong.
- **10 made an optional IDL parameter required, and 9 of those already threw**
  where Chrome returns quietly: `document.all.item()`, `clearTimeout()`,
  `clearInterval()`, `window.scroll()`/`scrollTo()`/`scrollBy()`,
  `selection.containsNode(node)`, `selection.modify()`,
  `transformController.enqueue()`. Those take their parameter optionally now.
  `TransformStreamDefaultController` also just lacked the `.arity = 0` its
  `ReadableStreamDefaultController` sibling already had.

One related bridge rule changed with them: **a missing argument bound to an IDL
`any` parameter is now the `undefined` V8 hands back for an out-of-range index,
not a refusal.** `js.Value` is the one type here that can carry undefined, and
in JS a missing argument *is* undefined — Chrome's `controller.enqueue()`
enqueues it.

`history.pushState`/`replaceState` went the other way: WebIDL makes both `data`
and `unused` required, so Chrome reports 2 and refuses a one-argument call,
while our optional title derived 1. Both say `.arity = 2` now.

**A reading in `audio.html` turned out to be wrong.** It recorded that Chrome
left `new OfflineAudioContext(1, 256, 8000).suspend()`'s promise pending,
converting the missing argument to NaN. Re-measured on Chrome 151: it rejects
with `TypeError: Failed to execute 'suspend' on 'OfflineAudioContext': 1
argument required, but only 0 present.`, like every other operation —
promise-returning ones reject rather than throw, which `Worklet.addModule()`,
`caches.open()` and `navigator.locks.request()` all do too.

Result, `probe-arity-refusal.js` (48 cases, both engines): **27 differences
before, 5 after.** All five are the opposite problem — 92 members whose `length`
is *below* Chrome's, so the check stays silent where Chrome speaks
(`div.contains()`, `document.getElementById()`, `div.isSameNode()`,
`el.hasAttributeNS()`, `document.createElementNS()`; 50 of the 92 are WebGL and
18 are RTC — recounted from the same reading when that change was made; this
paragraph first said 48 and 12). That is its own change, closed in "The other
direction" below, not this one. On
`probe-invalid-argument.js` the count still answering `invalid argument` went
**39 → 32**, the remaining 32 being the per-parameter conversion sentences.

Readings: `results/probes/probe-operation-arity.{chrome,lightpanda}.json`,
`probe-arity-refusal.{chrome,lightpanda}.json`.

## The oracle was never dead: one flag, and the diff it hands back (2026-08-23)

The previous chapter but one concluded that headless Chrome had stopped
clearing `cf-scrapingcourse`, and that every plan under
`cf-scrapingcourse-oracle-diff` was therefore blocked until a passing arm could
be rebuilt. That conclusion is wrong, and cheaply so.

Both of its Chrome runs record `headedUa: false`. Without `--headed-ua` the
arm's user agent contains `HeadlessChrome`, and this repo has a whole chapter on
that word being the single fatal tell on this station
(`antibot-oracle-headless-ua`). The runs measured a Chrome that announces itself
as headless, which fails the way anything announcing itself as headless fails.

Re-run with the flag, same station, same harness, thirty minutes later:

```
$ node tools/fingerprint/cfsc-fo-diff.mjs chrome --headed-ua
FINAL title="Cloudflare Challenge - ScrapingCourse.com"
      text="You bypassed the Cloudflare challenge! :D"
```

`results/cfsc-fo-oracle-recheck.json`. The `clearance` field in that JSON still
reads `false` — it looks for a `cf_clearance` cookie and does not see one
through this harness — so read the title and the body text, not that flag. The
two older passing traces (`cfsc-fo-oracle.json`,
`cfsc-fo-oracle-hints.json`) say `clearance: false` and
`"You bypassed the Cloudflare challenge!"` in the same breath, which is what
made the field look like evidence of a failure it never described.

### The three arms, and where they part

| # | bytes | endpoint | oracle (`--headed-ua`) | this engine | Chrome, no `--headed-ua` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ~2.3K | `{sc}` page-level `fo/` | `cf-chl-gen` | `cf-chl-gen` | `cf-chl-gen` |
| 2 | ~4.8K | `{cf}` widget `fo/` | `cf-chl-gen` | `cf-chl-gen` | `cf-chl-gen` |
| 3 | ~86-89K | `{cf}` widget `fo/` | **no `cf-chl-gen`** | `cf-chl-gen` | `cf-chl-gen` |
| 4 | ~8.8K | `{sc}` page-level `fo/` | sent | — | — |
| 5 | ~2.6K | `POST /cloudflare-challenge` | sent, 4207-byte page | — | — |

So the first divergence is not a request we fail to make. All three arms send
the same first three POSTs to the same two endpoints; the oracle's third reply
comes back **without** a new challenge and every other arm's comes back with
one. POSTs 4 and 5 are what an accepted round 3 unlocks: another page-level
telemetry post, then the form submit that swaps the interstitial for the real
page.

Two things fall out of the table. `cf-chl-gen` on round 3 is the verdict line
to instrument — not the payload size, and not the endpoint choice E1 suspected
(both arms post round 2 and 3 to the widget instance, and round 1 and 4 to the
page-level one). And payload size is *not* the discriminator: the declined
Chrome arm posted the largest round 3 of the three (89612 bytes) and was
declined anyway, while the oracle was accepted at 88727 and this engine
declined at 85655.

The useful control here is the headless-UA Chrome arm. It is a real Chrome —
every API, every timing, every rendering signal genuine — and it is declined at
exactly the same step, in exactly the same shape, as this engine. Whatever round
3 carries, one wrong value in it is enough, and being otherwise a real browser
does not save the arm. That is the encouraging reading: this engine is not
failing round 3 by a mile of missing surface, it is failing it the way a real
browser with one bad field fails it.

`cfsc-widget-solve-declined` is therefore unblocked, and its diff is
well-posed: with the oracle passing on demand, capture both round-3 bodies from
the same sitting and find what the accepted one says that the declined one does
not.

## Round 3 is not where the payload first differs (E1, 2026-08-23)

The oracle passes on demand now, so the previous chapter's diff is runnable: two
arms, same sitting, same harness, and every challenge body read whole.

One harness change was needed first. `cfsc-fo-diff.mjs` read response bodies
after settle, and an arm that *clears* tears the widget iframe down the moment
the interstitial is replaced — the iframe's CDP session goes with it, so the
after-settle pass answered `Session with given id not found` for exactly the
exchanges the passing arm exists to show. Bodies for frame sessions are now read
on `loadingFinished`, while the session is alive. The oracle still clears with
the read in place (`cfsc-r3-oracle-b.json`), so the extra out-of-band CDP call
does not perturb the outcome it measures.

Four runs, two per arm:

| run | widget `fo/` #1 post | its response | widget `fo/` #2 post | verdict | cleared |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| oracle a | 4 716 | — | 88 332 | `cf-chl-out` | yes |
| oracle b | 4 716 | 846 108 | 90 092 | `cf-chl-out` | yes |
| this engine a | 4 855 | 823 116 | 85 943 | `cf-chl-gen` | no |
| this engine b | 4 866 | 845 996 | 87 255 | `cf-chl-gen` | no |

`cf-chl-out` / `cf-chl-out-s` on the reply to the second widget POST is the
accept; `cf-chl-gen` is "here is another challenge". Read those header names,
not the `clearance` field.

### Four things this rules out

**The server does not hand the two arms different programs.** The reply to
widget POST #1 is 846 108 bytes to the oracle and 845 996 to this engine — 112
apart on a 846 KB body, and byte-for-byte different from offset 0, which is what
a per-session key looks like rather than a different program. Same program, same
size, both arms.

**The request head is not the tell.** On POST #2 the `User-Agent`,
`sec-ch-ua`, `sec-ch-ua-mobile`, `sec-ch-ua-platform`, `content-type` and
`cf-chl-ra` values are identical across arms. (Chrome's
`Network.requestWillBeSent` reports only the subset of headers the renderer set,
so the `accept` / `sec-fetch-*` / high-entropy-hint rows that appear on this
engine and not on the oracle are an instrument artefact, not an absence. The
byte-exact head comparison lives in `accept-ch-echo.mjs`, and it already agrees
22/22 and 16/16.)

**The payload is one ciphertext, so a byte diff is not available.** `$` is a
character in the encoding alphabet, not a field separator: splitting POST #2 on
it yields 1 389 pieces for the oracle and 1 385 for this engine, which is noise.
Round 1 is 2 306 bytes on all four runs with entirely different content, which
is what a fixed-length plaintext under a per-session key looks like.

**Payload size does not decide the verdict.** The declined headless-UA Chrome
arm posted the largest POST #2 of any run (89 612) and was declined; the oracle
was accepted at 88 332.

### Where the arms actually first differ, and it is one round earlier

Widget POST #1 is **4 716 bytes on the oracle, twice, and 4 716 in the older
`cfsc-fo-oracle-recheck` sitting too** — the same length across three sessions
with three different keys. This engine posts 4 855 and 4 866, and an older build
posted 4 663.

Two separate facts fall out of that column, and both are cheaper to chase than a
90 KB blob:

1. **This engine's round-1 widget payload is ~140 bytes longer than the
   oracle's.** Whatever it puts there, the reference does not.
2. **Its length is not stable, and the oracle's is.** 4 855 versus 4 866 in two
   consecutive runs of the same binary. A deterministic plaintext length means
   every field is fixed-width or fixed-content; an 11-byte wobble means at least
   one field this engine contributes is variable-length — a number with a
   varying digit count, a duration, an error string, a URL.

That is the divergence to instrument, and it sits in the payload the *widget
document* assembles — a 264 KB plaintext JS document `vm-trace.mjs` already
knows how to patch and replay, unlike the round-2 program which arrives
encrypted. The parent's page-level round 1 is 2 306 bytes on every arm, so the
first place the two engines write different bytes onto the wire is the widget's
first POST.

The old note that "the widget realm is not where this engine differs" was drawn
from `--reach` call counts, which match. Call counts matching and payload bytes
differing are consistent: the program takes the same path and is handed
different answers.

## The telemetry is assembled in a worker, and the worker notices (E2, 2026-08-23)

E1 left the diff at the widget's first `fo/` POST and the body is one ciphertext,
so the plaintext has to be read upstream of the encryption. `fo-plaintext.mjs`
installs a recorder ahead of the page's own code and wraps the funnels the
plaintext must pass through — `crypto.subtle.encrypt` / `sign` / `digest`,
`TextEncoder.prototype.encode`, `JSON.stringify`, `btoa`, `XMLHttpRequest.send`,
`fetch` — each forwarding to the original unchanged, each disguised so
`toString()` answers with the native source text.

Whether such an instrument is honest is a measurement, not an argument: the
oracle arm ran with every wrapper in place and **still cleared**
(`fopt-oracle.json`, "You bypassed the Cloudflare challenge!"). So the readings
below are of a page that decided the same thing it decides unwatched.

### The document realm does not build the payload

With the widget document realm armed — `installed` fired at
`challenges.cloudflare.com/…/new/normal`, so this is not a case of the hook
landing late:

| funnel | calls in the widget document realm |
|---|---|
| `crypto.subtle.encrypt` / `sign` / `digest` | 0 |
| `TextEncoder.prototype.encode` | 0 |
| `btoa` | 0 |
| `XMLHttpRequest.send` | 0 |
| `fetch` | 0 |
| `JSON.stringify` | 4 187 calls, **largest argument 172 bytes** |

And the four `fo/` POSTs went out anyway — 2 306, 4 706, 91 479, 8 855, the last
two under `cf-chl-out`. A realm that issues no fetch and no XHR is not the realm
that posted them.

The four sessions the recorder could *not* be installed in are all `blob:` URLs,
and they refuse `Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument` with
`-32601 … wasn't found`: no Page domain means they are workers, not frames. So
**this station assembles and sends its telemetry from blob-URL workers**, which
is why every page-realm instrument in this directory — `--reach`, the funnel
wrappers, the opcode trace — has been looking at the wrong side of a thread
boundary. It also explains the earlier "the widget realm is not where this engine
differs": that reading was correct and beside the point.

### Reaching into the worker breaks the challenge, and that is a finding

Auto-attach pauses a new target before its first statement, which is the window
to evaluate the recorder into a worker. Two things came out of trying it.

`Runtime.evaluate` must not be awaited there. A target paused on start has its
script thread blocked, so the evaluate cannot complete until the resume that the
same `arm()` call has not sent yet — awaiting it deadlocks, and the challenge
stalls at round 1.

With that fixed, the challenge *still* stalls at round 1. Isolated against the
station rather than assumed:

| arm | runs | result |
|---|---|---|
| document realm wrapped only | 1 | cleared |
| `cfsc-fo-diff` oracle, no instrument | 4 | cleared, 4× |
| worker realm wrapped as well | 3 | **one POST, then nothing, 3×** |

The last of those four clean control runs was taken *after* the three stalls, in
the same ten-minute window, so the station is not throttling and the difference
is the instrument. Three attempts is where this stops per the three-failure rule;
the next attempt needs a different shape, not a fourth variation.

Two readings, and they are not exclusive: the worker checks its own globals, or
pausing it on start perturbs a timing it measures. Both are worth knowing, and
both are cheap to separate — install one wrapper at a time and see which one is
fatal, and separately arm the worker without `waitForDebuggerOnStart` at all.
A worker that declines to run when `fetch` is not native is a fingerprint check
we would want to know about regardless of what the payload turns out to say.

## The worker was never released, and the probes it runs are readable (2026-08-23)

E2 recorded three round-1 stalls as the worker noticing the instrument, and left
two readings to separate: a wrapper being detected, or the pause perturbing a
timing. Neither is what happened. The records from those runs carry **nothing at
all from the worker session** — not one funnel call, not even the recorder's own
`installed` line — and their `Runtime.runIfWaitingForDebugger` came back
`resumed: false`. Nothing was installed for the worker to detect. The worker was
never let go.

`worker-arm-probe.mjs` settles it away from the station entirely: a local page, a
local blob worker, the same `arm()` sequence, no Cloudflare in the room.

| variant | worker ran | recorder inside it | caught the worker's first `fetch` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `plain` — no pause | yes | no | no |
| `evaluate` — pause, evaluate, then resume (the E2 shape) | **no** | no | no |
| `resume` — pause, resume, then evaluate | yes | yes | **no** — too late |
| `preload` — no debugger; rewrite the worker's source | yes | yes | **yes** |

A `Runtime.evaluate` sent to a target paused on start blocks that session's
inspector queue head-on, so the resume queued behind it never arrives. Sent
*after* the resume it does run, but it lands after the worker's own first fetch.
Neither reading in E2 was needed; the mechanism was the whole story.

So stop involving the debugger. The document realm can be armed before its own
code, and it is where the worker is built, so wrap `Blob` there and read — or
with `--inject-worker`, prepend the recorder to — the worker's source text.

### The instrument had been spending its budget on itself

Every record is a `JSON.stringify` and a `console.log`, and `JSON.stringify` was
one of the wrapped funnels, so each record produced a record. That is what the
4 187 stringify calls of the earlier runs were, and with a 400-record ceiling the
recursion consumed the budget before any real call could land. The same local
page: 805 records before the re-entrancy guard, 10 after — and the ten include
the worker's `btoa` argument and the `fetch` body it becomes.

**This invalidates E2's headline.** "The document realm does not build the
payload" was a reading of a starved instrument. With the guard in, the oracle arm
shows the round-1 body going out of the *page* realm:

| record | oracle arm | our arm |
|---|---|---|
| `xhr.send` round 1 | 2 306 bytes, ciphertext | 2 306 bytes, ciphertext |
| `xhr.send` round 2 | — (widget realm) | 4 866 |
| `xhr.send`, plaintext | 1 110–1 153 bytes of `{"memory":{"totalJSHeapSize"…` | — |

The blob workers are not where telemetry is assembled either. Their source, now
readable, is 13 and 291 bytes:

```js
"you"==="bot"                                    // b0, entire program

var _p=null;if(self.trustedTypes)try{_p=self.trustedTypes.createPolicy('Kssz2',
{createScript:function(s){return s;}})}catch(e){self.postMessage({type:
'tt-policy-error',msg:e.message})}
onmessage=function(e){e.isTrusted&&''===e.origin&&null===e.source&&
  eval(_p?_p.createScript(e.data):e.data)}
```

The second is an `eval` trampoline: the page posts source text in, the worker
runs it and posts the answer back. Both halves of that conversation are plaintext
in the document realm, which is where the hook already is.

### What the trampoline is asked, on our arm

Every probe below is verbatim from `fopt-src-lp.json`, with its answer:

| asked | answered |
|---|---|
| `n.platform, n.languages, n.hardwareConcurrency, n.deviceMemory, n.userAgent` | `MacIntel`, `["en-US","en"]`, `10`, `16`, the Chrome 151 UA |
| `fetch(…/pat/…)` — status, ok, body | `401`, `0`, `"J"` |
| `fetch(…brunhild…/i/…, {mode:"cors",credentials:"omit",cache:"no-store"})` — status **and every response header** | `{"ojYA3":"TypeError: fetch error"}` |
| `for(5e3){…}` smallest positive `performance.now()` delta | `0.09999999999990905` |
| `eval("debugger")`, then report | reported |
| `setTimeout(…,55)`, `…,1500`, `…,10000` round trips | all reported |

`hardwareConcurrency 10` and `deviceMemory 16` are correct for this host — that
pair was measured against headless Chrome 151 here and is asserted in
`Navigator.zig` — so they are not the tell.

The brunhild row is. The probe asks for a cross-origin response's full header
list and gets an exception instead, and the exception's *text* goes to Cloudflare
verbatim through `String(e)`. Ours reads `TypeError: fetch error`, from
`Fetch.zig`:

```zig
ls.toLocal(self._resolver).rejectError("fetch error", .{ .type_error = "fetch error" });
```

Chrome's wording for a failed `fetch` is `TypeError: Failed to fetch`. So the
answer we hand back is wrong twice over: the probe was supposed to return
headers, and the failure it returns instead is spelled in a way no browser
spells it.

The oracle cleared with all of this in place — plain, and again with
`--inject-worker` — so none of these readings are of a page behaving differently
because it was watched.

## Chrome runs every one of those probes; the instrument was in the wrong realm (E1-E2, 2026-08-23)

The chrome arm showed no trampoline conversation at all, and the note left with
it read that as the two arms behaving differently. They do not. Under site
isolation the Turnstile widget is an out-of-process frame with a CDP target of
its own, and the run that recorded nothing had stopped pausing new targets on
start -- so `Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument` landed after the widget
document had already begun, and applied only to documents created after it. That
is exactly what the run says when read closely: the widget session reports
itself installed at `about:blank` seven times and at `about:srcdoc` once, and
never at the widget. Lightpanda has no such split -- every realm is the one
session -- so the same code armed the widget there and not here.

The pause is back, and typed: worker targets are resumed first and asked
nothing (that is the head-of-line block `worker-arm-probe.mjs` pinned down),
while page and iframe targets are armed before their first statement. With that
one change the chrome arm records eighteen trampoline messages, and still
clears.

### The probe table, both arms, one sitting

`results/fopt-e3-oracle.json` (clears) against `results/fopt-e3-lp2.json`
(`Just a moment...`), taken minutes apart against the same station, the engine
built from `bfb3f1f67`:

| asked | oracle | here |
|---|---|---|
| `n.platform, n.languages, n.hardwareConcurrency, n.deviceMemory, n.userAgent` | `MacIntel`, `["en-US","en"]`, `10`, `16`, Chrome 151 | identical |
| `fetch(…/pat/…)` — status, ok, body | `401`, `0`, `"J"` | identical |
| `fetch(…brunhild…)` — status and every response header | `TypeError: Failed to fetch` | identical (was `fetch error` before the fix) |
| `eval("debugger")`, then report | reported | identical |
| `setTimeout` 55 ×2, 1500, 10000 | all reported | identical |
| `for(5e3){…}` smallest positive `performance.now()` delta | **`0.004999995231628418`** | **`0.09999999999999432`** |
