Two rows, and both of them are one fact.

### The challenge page is cross-origin isolated, and we are not

The recorder now reports four realm facts alongside its own arrival. On the
oracle arm every realm of the challenge — the interstitial, its `about:blank`
and `about:srcdoc` children, and the widget document — answers
`crossOriginIsolated: true`, with `SharedArrayBuffer` a function. The last
realm of the run, the real page that replaces the interstitial once it clears,
answers `false` and `undefined`: the isolation belongs to the challenge, not to
the site. Here it is `false` in all four, because `Window.getCrossOriginIsolated`
returns a literal `false` and `Env.zig` deletes `SharedArrayBuffer` outright.
Nothing in this engine reads `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy` or
`Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` at all.

That is where the clock row comes from. Chrome clamps `performance.now()` to
100 μs, and to 5 μs in a cross-origin isolated realm; the oracle's
`0.004999995` is the isolated clamp, and our `0.0999999` is the number Chrome
would give a realm that is *not* isolated. `Performance.zig` hardcodes
`clock_resolution_micros = 100` with a comment saying 5 μs is Firefox's number
— which was right for an ordinary page and is wrong for this one. The probe
does not have to reason about any of it: it reads the clamp off a loop and
sends the double.

The OPFS row is the third face of the same absence. `navigator.storage` here
carries `estimate()` and nothing else — no `getDirectory`, no
`FileSystemDirectoryHandle`, no `createSyncAccessHandle` (the legacy
`webkitRequestFileSystem` tree in `filesystem.zig` is a different API). The
widget feature-detects before it asks, so on our arm the probe is never posted
and the answer field never exists. `probes/expr-trampoline.js` replays the
whole list offline against both engines and shows the gate directly:
`getDirectory` is `true` in Chrome on a loopback origin and `false` here, and
the same probe posted anyway produces no answer at all, not even the `Tltp4`
error the station's own `catch` would have sent — the throw is synchronous and
lands before the promise chain exists.

Everything else in the table matches. The three divergences are
`crossOriginIsolated`/`SharedArrayBuffer`, the clock clamp that follows from
it, and OPFS.


### The other half of the sentence: which argument, and what it wanted

Counting an operation's arguments left the *conversion* refusals untouched, and
those were the larger half — 32 of `probe-invalid-argument.js`'s 55 cases still
answered `TypeError: invalid argument`. Blink's wording is two independent
halves, and only the prefix was in place. The detail comes in four shapes, and
which one you get depends on how the conversion failed, not on where the call
came from:

| failure | detail |
|---|---|
| interface or callback parameter, wrong brand | `parameter <N> is not of type '<Type>'.` |
| dictionary or union, wrong shape | `The provided value is not of type '<Name>'.` |
| sequence, not iterable | `The provided value cannot be converted to a sequence.` |
| dictionary member, enum out of range | `Failed to read the '<member>' property from '<Dict>': The provided value '<v>' is not a valid enum value of type <Enum>.` |

**Only the first carries a position.** A dictionary is named, not counted, and
the sequence refusal names nothing at all. Getting that backwards — adding
`parameter 1` everywhere — would be its own tell.

`Caller.getArgs` already knew the position: the loop over parameters is an
`inline for`, so the index is comptime and `parameter <N>` is `i + 1`. What it
lacked was a type name, and where one is derivable it now derives it: an
interface pointer names its `JsApi`, a `js.Function` is `'Function'`. The
callback-interface case is the one worth recording — `EventListener` and
`NodeFilter` are modelled here as a union of a function and an object, and Blink
names **neither** of them: `el.addEventListener('x', 1)` and
`document.createNodeIterator(el, 1, 1)` both say `'Object'`. Not the interface,
not `'Function'`.

**A bare `js.Object` parameter is deliberately not `'Object'`.** It is what a
parameter whose IDL type this bridge does not model looks like, and the two the
probe covers are both named after the interface they wanted — `new Animation(1)`
is `'AnimationEffect'`, `crypto.getRandomValues(1)` is `'ArrayBufferView'`. They
keep the generic refusal rather than a confident wrong name.

Dictionaries and unions cannot be derived at all — `Blob.InitOptions` is a
`BlobPropertyBag`, `DOMQuad`'s corners are `DOMPointInit`, and an IDL union's
name is its whole spelling (`new Headers(1)` wants
`'(record<ByteString, ByteString> or sequence<sequence<ByteString>>)'`). Each
type declares its own `js_idl_name`. That sentence had to be told apart from the
one a bad *member* gets, so the conversion layer now distinguishes them: a value
that was never the right shape answers `NotOfType`, while a member's own
conversion returns whatever it returns. Naming the dictionary when it was a
member that failed would point at the wrong thing.

The nested enum sentence went the other way — by hand, in the modules. The
bridge's enum conversion knows neither the member's name, nor the dictionary's,
nor the enum type's, and the sentence needs all three, so `RequestInit`'s
`cache`, `credentials` and `redirect` stopped being typed enums and became
strings the constructor reads itself. `duplex` already worked that way and
already wrote the sentence; the four with an enum behind them now share one
helper. `attachShadow`'s `mode` is the same sentence with the execute prefix.

Two refusals came from the bridge reading a sequence as something else.
`CSSTransformValue` was bound with a slice parameter, which makes a non-array
first argument look like the start of a variadic list, so the message came from
converting that one element instead of from the parameter as a whole; it takes
the raw value now. `CSSUnparsedValue` only had to check before converting.

Result on `probe-invalid-argument.js` (55 cases): **13 identical to Chrome
before, 42 after** — 43 once the setter pass below landed — and the count
answering `invalid argument` went **39 → 32 → 3**. What is left, and none of it
is wording:

- **7 cases Chrome refuses and we do not.** `new CSSStyleSheet(1)`,
  `new DocumentTimeline(1)`, `new TaskController(1)`,
  `new Request(u, {mode:'nope'})` (there is no `mode` member here at all),
  `new Response('x', {status:99})`, `crypto.getRandomValues([])`,
  `el.animate(1)`.
- **1 we refuse and Chrome does not**: `new URLSearchParams(1)`.
- **2 whose IDL type the bridge does not model**, described above:
  `new Animation(1)` and `crypto.getRandomValues(1)`.
- **2 self-invented messages**: `new CSSRotate(1)` says "Must pass an angle to
  CSSRotate" where Chrome says `parameter 1 is not of type 'CSSNumericValue'.`,
  and `el.insertAdjacentHTML('nope', 'x')` says "The string did not match the
  expected pattern" where Chrome lists all four legal values.
- **1 setter**: `url.href = 'nope'` is still an empty message. The prefix
  pipeline does not reach accessors — `Snapshot` sets no data on getter/setter
  templates — so no setter can name itself yet. Fixed in the next section,
  which is about setters and nothing else.

Readings: `results/probes/probe-invalid-argument.{chrome,lightpanda}.json`.

### The third lead-in: what a setter says when it refuses

The last item on that list — `url.href = 'nope'` answering an empty message —
was left for its own pass because it is not one bug. Blink has three lead-ins,
not two, and the third belongs to attributes:

```
Failed to construct 'URL': Invalid URL              <- constructor
Failed to execute 'createElement' on 'Document': …  <- operation
Failed to set the 'href' property on 'URL': …       <- attribute
```

`probe-setter-refusal.js` walks 61 assignments across every mechanism a setter
can refuse with. **24 agreed with a headed Chrome 151 before this pass and 37
after.** The readings are in
`results/probes/probe-setter-refusal.{chrome,lightpanda}.json`.

The property named is the attribute's own spelling — `href`, not the `set href`
the accessor function goes by — and the interface is the one that *declares* the
attribute, not the receiver's class. `input.maxLength` and `textarea.maxLength`
name `HTMLInputElement` and `HTMLTextAreaElement` respectively; `audio.volume`
names `HTMLMediaElement` and not `HTMLAudioElement`.

**The setter's brand sentence is not the operation's.** This is the reading
worth keeping, because it is exactly the kind of detail a shared code path gets
wrong by being shared:

| where the value came from | Blink's detail |
|---|---|
| an operation's parameter | `parameter <N> is not of type '<Type>'.` |
| an attribute | `Failed to convert value to '<Type>'.` |

No position, because an attribute takes one value and there is nothing to
number. A union and a sequence keep the sentences they already had — `The
provided value is not of type '(MediaSourceHandle or MediaStream)'.` and `The
provided value cannot be converted to a sequence.` — so only the brand case
forks.

The same lead-in also fronts the DOMExceptions a setter's own steps raise, which
is where most of this engine's readings were wrong: it answered the stock
DOMException text and Blink answers a written detail.

| assignment | Chrome 151 |
|---|---|
| `input.size = 'x'` | `IndexSizeError: … 'size' … : The value provided is 0, which is an invalid size.` |
| `input.maxLength = -1` | `IndexSizeError: … 'maxLength' … : The value provided (-1) is not positive or 0.` |
| `input.selectionStart = 1` on `type=number` | `InvalidStateError: … : The input element's type ('number') does not support selection.` |
| `document.domain = 'evil.test'` | `SecurityError: … : 'evil.test' is not a suffix of '127.0.0.1'.` |
| `document.domain = ''` | `SecurityError: … : '' is an empty domain.` |
| `document.documentElement.outerHTML = 'x'` | `NoModificationAllowedError: … : This element's parent is a Document, which may not be modified.` |

Two of those are worth stating as negatives, since guessing them the obvious way
gets them wrong: `input.size = -1` does **not** throw (WebIDL wraps it to
4294967295 and Chrome takes it — only a value that converts to 0 is refused),
and `document.domain = 'com'` gets the plain suffix sentence, not a
top-level-domain one.

Where the sentence lives now follows what the engine already did. Roughly forty
setters in `webapi/` were already writing their own full sentence, with
`dictionary.SetterReader` as the comptime helper for it, so the six that were
not now do the same. Only one refusal cannot work that way — the value failed to
convert, so the bridge refused before the Zig setter ran and there is no site to
hold the sentence — and that one the bridge writes, the way it already writes an
operation's. `Snapshot.attachAccessorProperty` set no data on either accessor
template; the setter half now carries the attribute's name, which is what
`Caller.setterPrefix` reads back.

#### A read-only attribute picks V8's other sentence

Writing a read-only attribute in strict mode is refused by V8, not Blink, and
V8 has two sentences for it:

```
Cannot set property userAgent of #<Navigator> which has only a getter   <- Chrome
Cannot assign to read only property 'userAgent' of object '#<Navigator>' <- was here
```

The second is V8's sentence for a non-writable **data** property. Both engines'
descriptors for `Navigator.prototype.userAgent` are identical — `get` a
function, `set` undefined, enumerable, configurable — so nothing you can read
tells the two apart. What differed was invisible from JS: this engine passed
v8's `ReadOnly` attribute bit alongside the getter-only accessor, and V8 checks
that bit before it looks inside the accessor pair. WebIDL makes a read-only
attribute an accessor whose setter is *absent*; the bit is a different claim.

Dropping it fixes the object name as well as the sentence. V8's accessor path
names the **holder** — the prototype the accessor lives on — so `document.URL`
reads `#<Document>` and not `#<HTMLDocument>`, and `el.tagName` reads
`#<Element>` and not `#<HTMLBodyElement>`. Every read-only attribute in the
engine was carrying this.

#### What is left, and none of it is wording

The remaining differences are cases where this engine does not refuse at all,
which is a coverage question rather than a wording one:

- **No brand check on an interface-typed attribute**: `document.body`,
  `table.tHead`/`tFoot`/`caption`, `media.srcObject`, `input.valueAsDate`.
  `document.body` is the loud one — its setter here takes an HTML *string*, so
  `document.body = 1` does not throw and replaces the body with one containing
  "1", where the IDL says `attribute HTMLElement body`.
- **No range or finiteness guard**: `audio.volume = 5`, `video.currentTime = 'x'`,
  `audio.playbackRate = 'x'`, `input.valueAsNumber` on a `type=text`.
- **An enum attribute that does not fall back**: `img.loading = 'nope'` keeps
  `'nope'` where Chrome reports `'auto'`. (The engine gets the others right —
  `xhr.responseType`, `history.scrollRestoration`, `img.crossOrigin` and
  `input.type` all ignore a bad value silently, which is what WebIDL requires of
  an enum-typed attribute. Turning any of those into a throw would be a new
  tell, not a fix.)
- **`document.adoptedStyleSheets = 1`** stays generic: the setter takes a bare
  `js.Object`, so the bridge cannot tell it was meant to be a sequence. It is
  the only one of the 24 remaining differences that is still about wording; the
  other 23 are all assignments this engine simply takes.

One note for whoever writes the next one of these: a formatted refusal has to go
on `call_arena`, not `local_arena`. `document.domain` first shipped on the local
one and came back through CDP as `SecurityError:` followed by a run of blanks —
the arena is reset before `handleError` reads the message. The html test did not
catch it and the probe did, which is the whole argument for taking a reading
after the tests go green.

### And the third row: OPFS answers now (2026-08-23)

`navigator.storage.getDirectory()` exists, and everything behind it works:
`getFileHandle({create:true})`, `createSyncAccessHandle()`, and a sync access
handle whose `write` / `read` / `getSize` / `truncate` / `flush` / `close` are
all real and all synchronous. The tree is `filesystem.zig`'s `Node` — the same
in-memory per-origin tree the legacy `webkitRequestFileSystem` entries walk,
shared rather than duplicated — anchored on the Page and keyed by origin, so a
page and the workers it starts reach the same entries the way Chrome's do.

Four of the five interfaces are `Exposed=(Window,Worker)` and now go on the
worker realm too, which takes that realm's own-name count from 207 to 212.
`FileSystemSyncAccessHandle` is `Exposed=DedicatedWorker` and is registered for
that realm alone.

Both arms, offline, one sitting, the station's own probe list replayed by
`probes/expr-trampoline.js` against a loopback page (`results/p3-tramp-chrome.json`,
`results/p3-tramp-lp.json`):

| asked | chrome | here |
|---|---|---|
| `gates.getDirectory` | `true` | `true` (was `false`) |
| `vZBc4` — time a `createSyncAccessHandle().flush()` | `0.5999999940395355` | `1.1999999999999993` (was absent) |

The number is not supposed to match. Three oracle sittings against the real
station answered `0.4000000059604645`, `0.4949999749660492` and
`4.144999980926514` (`results/fopt-e1-oracle.json`, `fopt-e3-oracle.json`,
`p4-oracle.json`) — Chrome is timing a real fsync and the spread is an order of
magnitude wide, so no particular value is expected. What *is* expected is a
number, and not zero. The first implementation answered a flat `0`, because
there is nothing here to sync; a timed operation that costs exactly nothing is
not a plausible reading from any machine with a disk, so `flush()` spends a
jittered 250 μs–1.27 ms of real time inside the measured band. Jittered rather
than fixed: a constant repeated across samples would be its own tell.

#### Two tooling notes from taking that reading

`run-expr.mjs` cannot take this probe on our arm, and neither can `run-probe.mjs`:
this engine runs no scheduled tasks while a CDP `Runtime.evaluate` with
`awaitPromise` is outstanding, so a probe that awaits a `setTimeout` never
resolves and the call times out at 30 s. Microtasks do resolve — a
`Promise.resolve().then()` comes back fine — which is what makes the failure
look like a hang rather than an error. Both tools already say so in their header
comments; this is the confirmation, and it applies to every arm of this probe,
not just the OPFS question. `run-page-probe.mjs` is the tool, and Chrome takes
either.

`run-page-probe.mjs` had drifted out of sync with the CLI and reported success
while measuring nothing: it passed a bare `--dump` (which now takes a mode, so
the url was being eaten as its value) and did not wait, so `fetch` serialized an
empty `#out` after 14 ms and the driver decoded the marker text out of the
script source. It passes `--dump html` and a guarded `--wait-script` now, and
`WAIT_MS` (default 30 s) sets the ceiling.

#### And on the station (2026-08-23)

Both arms rerun in one sitting (`results/p4b-oracle.json` clears,
`results/p4b-lp.json` gets `Just a moment...`). Every realm on our arm now
answers `opfs: true`, matching the oracle realm for realm — the third and last
row of the E3 table. And the probe is not just permitted, it is asked and
answered: the widget posted the `~function(){navigator.storage.getDirectory()…}`
source into its blob worker on both arms and got a number back, `0.455` on the
oracle and `1.245` here. Both are multiples of their realm's clamp (91 and 249
steps of 5 μs), which is the isolation bit and the clock clamp from the two
previous plans showing up in a third place.

The challenge still refuses (`cf-chl-gen`). All three rows of the E3 table are
closed now and none of them was the deciding property.

What the same sitting shows still differing, as leads rather than findings —
none of these was chased:

- The oracle arm records two `fetch` calls from the widget's realms; our arm
  records none.
- `subtle.digest` is called 66 times on our arm against the oracle's 15, and its

  oracle passes an ArrayBuffer view. The offline `typedarray` probe in
  `probes/expr-trampoline.js` says both engines agree on `ArrayBuffer.isView`,

- The largest thing the oracle hands to `JSON.stringify` is a 30 902-character
  CSS property enumeration (`{"0":"accent-color","1":"align-content",…}`) and the
  string it then encodes is 15 361 characters. Ours encodes 1 999. That is an

#### Reading the same two files record by record (2026-08-23)

The three leads above were chased against `results/p4b-oracle.json` and
`results/p4b-lp.json` — no new site visit, the sitting already on disk. Two of
the three turned out to be worth less than they looked and one turned out to be
four separate holes.

Sizes are `a.n` on each record, not `r.n` (which does not exist).

| oracle | ours | what the payload is | verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 15 361 ×2 | 1 999 ×2 | 1 000 `\|`-joined floats — an audio render | ours is 1 000 zeros |
| 30 902 | 27 142 | a `getComputedStyle` dump | 720 of 736 values are `""` here |
| 9 216 | 9 216 | RGBA pixel readback | all zero here, 8 005 non-zero bytes there |
| 8 624 ×3 | 8 624 ×1 | RGBA pixel readback | all zero here, and two of the three reads never happen |
| 1 024 | — | 16×16 of solid `d7 8a 74 ff` | never read here |
| 4 096 | — | 32×32 RGBA | never read here |
| 20 696 | 20 367 | the page's `@keyframes` text | 329 characters short |

So "we collect an order of magnitude less" was the wrong reading. The widget
asks us the same questions; we answer four of them with zeros.

**The 15 361 string is an audio fingerprint and ours is silence.** Both arms
send exactly 1 000 values. The oracle's first 265 are zero and the remaining 735
run to ±0.3386. Ours are 1 000 zeros. 265 is the number `chrome_audio.zig`
already documents as the compressor's 6 ms pre-delay at 44 100 Hz, so the
widget's graph is fingerprintjs-shaped and the recorded render is the right kind
of answer — but it is not *this* answer. Compared against
`chrome_audio_macos.bin` over the same 1 000 frames the oracle diverges from the
first non-zero sample: same 333 zero crossings (so same waveform and frequency),
amplitude ratio around 1.044 and not constant (so not a gain node — a
non-linearity, which points at the compressor's settings). `canonical_render`
refuses to replay for a graph it cannot match, by design, and falls back to
silence. Which predicate rejects it is not knowable from this file; it needs the
widget's actual construction traced. → `cfsc-audio-graph-mismatch`.

**The 30 902 object is `getComputedStyle` and the names were never the
problem.** Both arms enumerate the same 1 211 indexed property names and the
same 736 camelCase keys, in the same order. What differs is the values behind
them: the oracle fills 702 of 736, we fill 16. Reproduced offline on a bare
`<div>`, no site involved:

|  | ours | Chrome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| indexed names | 475 | 475 |
| camelCase keys | 738 | 738 |
| empty values | **722** | 35 |
| `getPropertyValue` empty, first 40 | **39** | 0 |
| `fontSize` | `""` | `16px` |
| `writingMode` | `""` | `horizontal-tb` |
| `widows` | `""` | `2` |

`CSSStyleDeclaration.getDefaultPropertyValue` covers sixteen properties by hand
and returns `""` for everything else, so every longhand nobody declared reads
empty. The two we do answer and get wrong are `width` and `height`: the site's
element measures `0px` in Chrome and `1920px` / `100000000px` here.
→ `cfsc-computed-style-initials`.

**`subtle.digest` 66 times is the recorder counting itself, and the plain object
is a cross-realm read.** The 66 records are 15 real calls with a fixed multiple
of 7 records each — six of them reporting `t:"obj"` and one `t:"view"`. Both
arms install the recorder in the same ten realms, so the multiplication is not
extra calls: it is one `crypto.subtle` object wrapped seven times, once per
realm, and `describe()` in six of those closures then tests `v.buffer instanceof
ArrayBuffer` against a *different* realm's `ArrayBuffer` and falls through to the
object branch. Confirmed offline, both arms, same probe:

|  | ours | Chrome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `crypto` | distinct | distinct |
| `crypto.subtle` | **SHARED** | distinct |
| `crypto.subtle.digest` | **SHARED** | distinct |
| `localStorage` | **SHARED** | distinct |
| patch in iframe reaches parent | **true** | false |

`JSON`, `ArrayBuffer`, `TextEncoder`, `navigator`, `performance`, `fetch`,
`Math` and `Promise` are all per-realm here, which is why only `digest` shows
the multiplication. So the lead was real but pointed the wrong way: nothing
upstream produces a plain object, and the finding is that an iframe can patch
its parent's `crypto.subtle`. → `cfsc-realm-crypto-subtle`.

**The zero pixels are a no-op and a rect-only rasteriser.**
`WebGLRenderingContext.readPixels` is declared `.noop = true` and its body is
`{}`, so it leaves the destination buffer untouched — which is how a 9 216-byte
read comes back as 9 216 zeros. `canvas/raster.zig` implements `fillRect`,
`clearRect` and `strokeRect` and nothing else, so a 2D fingerprint canvas that
draws text or paths reads back blank too. → `cfsc-canvas-pixel-readback`.

The `fetch` lead (2 there, 0 here) is the smallest of the four and stays
unchased; it is plausibly downstream of one of the above.

## The other direction: the ninety-two operations that were counting too few (2026-08-23)

The arity pass above closed the over-reported side — 30 members whose `length`
was *larger* than Chrome's, which would have made this engine refuse calls
Chrome accepts — and left the mirror image open: **92 members whose `length` was
smaller**, where Chrome refuses and this engine answers. That side is the one a
detector can use, because it does not need to guess a wording. It calls
`div.contains()` and reads whether anything came back.

Ninety-two is what `probe-operation-arity.js` counts; eighty-five distinct
bindings, because `webkitRTCPeerConnection` is an alias and its seven show up
twice. `probe-arity-gaps.js` reads the consequence rather than the symptom:
every one of the eighty-five called with no arguments, plus eighteen called
short by one, on both engines.

### One cause, and it is not a mistake

All ninety-two are the same shape. `getArity` walks the Zig parameters and
**stops at the first optional one**, so a signature like

```zig
pub fn getElementsByTagNameNS(self: *Element, namespace: ?[]const u8, local_name: []const u8, frame: *Frame)
```

counts zero, even though `local_name` after it is required. The `?` is doing two
jobs that WebIDL keeps apart: *nullable* (`DOMString? namespace` — `null` is a
legal value that means "no namespace") and *optional* (the argument may be
omitted). Chrome reports 2 here and refuses a one-argument call.

That distinction decides the fix. Removing the `?` would make the count right
and the behaviour wrong: `div.contains(null)`, `gl.isBuffer(null)` and
`sender.replaceTrack(null)` are all legal calls that must keep answering. So the
count is *declared*, with the `.arity` override the bridge already had for
variadics, and the signature keeps its nullability. `bridge.Function.init` feeds
`.arity` to both the reported `length` and the `required_args` check, so the two
cannot drift apart.

Where the ninety-two sit, and what each was doing instead of refusing:

| interface | n | before |
|---|---|---|
| WebGL2 33, WebGL 17 | 50 | half threw `invalid argument`; half read the missing object as null, so `gl.isBuffer()` said `false` and `gl.getShaderSource()` said `""` |
| RTCPeerConnection ×2 aliases | 14 | `InvalidStateError` from a body Chrome never reaches — except `addStream`/`removeStream`, which returned `undefined` |
| Element | 10 | the NS five threw `invalid argument`; `animate()` returned an Animation, and the pointer-capture three returned quietly |
| Node | 5 | `contains()` → `false`, `lookupNamespaceURI()` → the XHTML namespace |
| Document | 4 | `getElementById()` → `null`; `evaluate('x')` → an XPathResult |
| RTCRtpSender 2, RTCRtpTransceiver 2 | 4 | unreachable in this engine; `length` only |
| Selection 2, DOMImplementation, DataTransferItem, DocumentFragment | 5 | all returned rather than refused |

Three of them were already refusing and refusing *wrongly*, which is worse than
silence because the sentence carries a number: `document.evaluate()` asked for
one argument where Chrome asks for two, and `impl.createDocumentType()` asked
for one where Chrome asks for three. A refusal with the wrong count is as
readable as no refusal.

### Two shapes that a zero-argument throw test would have missed

**A promise-returning operation does not throw its refusal, it rejects with it.**
`pc.setRemoteDescription()` has `length === 1` in Chrome and returns a rejected
promise; nothing is thrown. The bridge already routed a promise-returning
operation's error to a rejection, so declaring the arity moved it from an
`InvalidStateError` rejection to the `TypeError` one — but a test written as
`expectError` would have called this member fine and moved on.

**The count is checked after the receiver, not before.** The refusal fires
inside `Caller.Function._call`, which is upstream of every conversion — but V8
checks the function template's signature before the callback runs at all, so a
borrowed receiver never gets there. `Node.prototype.contains.call({})` is
`TypeError: Illegal invocation` in Chrome 151 **and** here, both before and
after this change. That is why the four RTP members assert `length` only: an
`RTCRtpSender` and an `RTCRtpTransceiver` are unreachable in this engine
(`getSenders()` answers empty, `addTransceiver()` refuses), and borrowing a
receiver does not reach the operation.

### Reading

`probe-operation-arity.js` (3714 members in Chrome, 3486 here, 3470 shared):
**92 smaller before, 0 after.** The over-reported side stays at 0, so this did
not trade one direction for the other.

`probe-arity-refusal.js` (48 cases): **5 differences before, 0 after** — the
five were `node.contains()`, `node.isSameNode()`, `document.getElementById()`,
`document.createElementNS()` and `el.hasAttributeNS()`, named in the section
above as the leftovers of the first pass.

`probe-arity-gaps.js` (188 readings): **0 identical before, 184 after.** The
four that remain are not arity at all — they are the RTP receivers this engine
cannot produce, so the probe cannot reach the operation to hear it refuse.
Their `length` is among the 184.

`probe-invalid-argument.js` is unchanged at 12 differences, which is the point:
those are per-parameter conversion sentences, a different half of the wording.

Readings: `results/probes/probe-arity-gaps.{chrome,lightpanda}.json`,
`probe-operation-arity.{chrome,lightpanda}.json`,
`probe-arity-refusal.{chrome,lightpanda}.json`.

#### Objects two realms were sharing (2026-08-23)

Chased from the `subtle.digest` reading above. The sweep walks 34 objects
reachable from the global and compares each against the same path on a
same-origin iframe. Chrome shares none of them; we shared five.

| | before | after | Chrome |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| shared with a same-origin iframe | 5 | **2** | 0 |

`crypto.subtle` had two causes stacked, and fixing only the first made it worse
rather than better — worth writing down, because the second is a hazard the rest
of the tree shares.

`Crypto` carried `empty_with_no_proto`, the marker that says a type is stateless
enough to skip its internal field. `TaggedOpaque.fromJS` answers such a type with
`@constCast(@as(*const T, &.{}))` — one comptime instance for the whole process.
`Crypto` is not stateless: it owns `_subtle`, and `&self._subtle` off that single
instance is one address, so the identity map handed every realm the same
`SubtleCrypto`. Dropping the marker alone then made `crypto.subtle` come back as
`[object Crypto]` with no `digest` on it, because `_subtle` was the *first* field
and `&self._subtle == &self`: the identity map is keyed on the address alone, so
it found the `Crypto` entry already sitting there. A padding field ahead of
`_subtle` separates the two. Any embedded struct handed to JS from offset zero
has the same collision waiting.

`localStorage` and `sessionStorage` were a different shape of the same problem
and not a bug in the storage code: the store really is per-origin and really is
shared with every same-origin frame. It is the `Storage` *object* Chrome makes
per-realm. So `storage.View` is now the per-Window handle and `storage.Lookup`
stays the per-origin state, which is one wrapper per realm because the identity
map keys on the address it is handed.

`screen` and `visualViewport` are still shared. Both are EventTargets with their
own listener lists, so splitting them per realm is not a handle over shared
state the way `Storage` was — it is a second instance with its own dispatch, and
that is its own plan (`cfsc-realm-screen-viewport`), not a line in this one.

#### Both arms again, after the two fixes (2026-08-23)

`results/p5-oracle.json` / `p5-lp.json`, one sitting. Neither arm cleared this
time — the oracle got `Just a moment...` too, so this reading says nothing about
pass or fail. What it does say is what the widget now collects, and two of the
four holes from the reading above are closed or nearly so.

| | before | now | oracle |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `subtle.digest` records | 66 (55 `obj`) | **11, all `view`** | 15, all `view` |
| `getComputedStyle` dump | 27 142 chars | **30 972** | 30 902 |
| values differing from the oracle | 720 | **26** | — |
| `installed` / `worker` realms | 10 / 7 | 10 / 7 | 10 / 7 |
| the audio vector | 1 000 zeros | 1 000 zeros | 265 zeros + 735 floats |
| the 9 216-byte pixel read | all zero | all zero | 8 005 non-zero bytes |

The digest count landing on 1:1 with `TextEncoder.encode` is the realm fix
showing up where it was first noticed: the recorder is no longer wrapping one
shared object seven times.

The 26 values still differing are not 26 separate problems. They are three:

- **thirteen `margin*` spellings** read `0px` where Chrome reads `8px`. The
  recorded table is flat and was measured on a `<div>`; the element here has the
  UA sheet's body margin. Same shape as `display`, which already has a per-tag
  path.
- **`unicode-bidi`** reads `isolate` where Chrome reads `normal` — again a
  per-tag UA default that a flat table cannot carry.
- **twelve layout names** (`width`, `height`, the logical and `-webkit-`
