→ `cfsc-computed-style-per-tag`.

## The eighteen pixel readbacks, and the one return value that stops five of them (2026-08-23)

`fo-plaintext` established that the widget hashes pixels, and that this engine
hands it the wrong ones. Four readbacks passed through `TextEncoder.encode` in
the widget's realm, and the two arms disagreed about all four:

| chars | arm that clears | this fork |
|---|---|---|
| 9216 | 1211 of them zero | 9216 zero |
| 1024 | none zero, one solid colour | never happens |
| 8624 | 1725 zero | 8624 zero |
| 4096 | 3744 zero | never happens |

Two arrive the right *size* and the wrong *content*, so the readback path itself
is wired up and it is the drawing underneath that is missing. Two do not arrive
at all, which is a different question: some branch upstream is not taken here.

Neither observation says *which* drawing calls to implement. A readback is the
end of a sequence, so `canvas-draw-trace.mjs` records the sequence: every method
and every settable accessor on `CanvasRenderingContext2D`,
`OffscreenCanvasRenderingContext2D`, `WebGLRenderingContext` and
`WebGL2RenderingContext`, held in a per-context log and flushed when a readback
happens, with the readback's own result attached. What comes out is one record
per readback saying *these fifty-seven calls produced these 9216 bytes*.

The prototypes are wrapped rather than the instances: the widget hands its
context around, and a per-instance wrapper would have to be re-applied at every
entry point that can hand one back. Accessors are wrapped alongside methods,
because `fillStyle`, `font` and `globalCompositeOperation` are assignments
rather than calls and a trace with the fills but not the colours cannot be
replayed. `CanvasGradient.prototype.addColorStop` is wrapped too, and the stops
ride along on the gradient to the point it is assigned to `fillStyle` — a
gradient without its stops is not reproducible either.

Whether the instrument is honest is a measurement, not an argument. Three
separate oracle runs with all four prototypes wrapped ended at *You bypassed the
Cloudflare challenge! :D*, so the wrappers did not change what the page decided.

    node tools/fingerprint/canvas-draw-trace.mjs chrome --headed-ua --out results/cdt-oracle.json
    node tools/fingerprint/canvas-draw-trace.mjs lightpanda --out results/cdt-lp.json

### What the two big readbacks are

**9216 is a 48×48 OffscreenCanvas 2D**, 57 calls. Six `createRadialGradient`
calls, each assigned to `fillStyle` with two colour stops; `shadowBlur` and
`shadowColor` set and cleared around each shape; paths built from `moveTo`,
`quadraticCurveTo`, `bezierCurveTo` and `ellipse`, each both `stroke`n and
`fill`ed; a `scale(0.384, 0.384)` over the lot; and text in a font that does not
exist (`27.77777777777778px aanotafontaa`) through `fillText` and `strokeText`.

**8624 is a 49×44 OffscreenCanvas 2D**, 36 calls. Ten `measureText` calls on
emoji at `16px sans-serif`, then `scale(0.4, 0.4)`, then three filled `arc`
circles in `#f2f`, `#2ff` and `#ff2` with `globalCompositeOperation` switched to
`multiply` between them, and finally a `#fff` two-`arc` path filled with the
`evenodd` rule — a ring.

`raster.zig` rasterises `fillRect`, `clearRect` and `strokeRect`. Not one call
in either sequence is one of those three, which is why both come back as zeroes
at exactly the right length.

### The WebGL readbacks stop at `getShaderParameter`

The 1024-byte readback is not 2D at all. It is `readPixels` on a 16×16 WebGL
context, and the sequence is thirteen calls this fork executes identically:
three `createShader`/`shaderSource`/`compileShader` triples, a `createBuffer`
with 32 bytes of clip-space quad, and then `getShaderParameter(shader,
COMPILE_STATUS)`.

There the arms part. Chrome answers `true` and the widget goes on to
`createProgram`, `linkProgram`, `getProgramParameter(LINK_STATUS)`,
`useProgram`, `vertexAttribPointer`, `viewport(0,0,16,16)`,
`drawArrays(TRIANGLE_FAN,0,4)` and `readPixels`. This fork answers `false` —
`WebGLRenderingContext.getShaderParameter` returns `.{ .boolean = false }` for
`DELETE_STATUS` and `COMPILE_STATUS`, and `getProgramParameter` does the same
for `LINK_STATUS` — and the widget tears the whole attempt down:
`deleteShader` three times, `deleteBuffer`, done. Both WebGL readbacks die on
that one return value.

The colour it would have read back is not a GPU's opinion. The fragment shader
is `gl_FragColor = vec4(sin(1.0), cos(1.0), sin(1.0)*cos(1.0), 1.0)`, and
quantising those three constants to 8 bits gives `d7 8a 74 ff` — byte for byte
the 1024 bytes Chrome returns, all 256 pixels of them.

What follows the teardown is worth recording separately, because it only exists
on the failing arm: 70 further calls on the WebGL1 context and 122 on the WebGL2
one — `getParameter` sweeps, `getShaderPrecisionFormat` for six precisions in
both shader stages, `getSupportedExtensions`, and 35 `getInternalformatParameter`
probes followed by seven `renderbufferStorage`/`checkFramebufferStatus` rounds.
The oracle arm makes **none** of those calls. They are the widget's fallback for
a context that would not compile a shader, so the sweep is not a second thing to
match — it is a symptom of the first.

Finding them at all needed a change to the instrument. Flush-on-readback was the
only exit, so a sequence that never reached a readback was collected and then
thrown away — and the arm that needed explaining was precisely the one that
reported nothing. The recorder now drains idle logs on a timer as well.

### The eighteen, side by side

Eighteen readbacks on the oracle arm, thirteen here. Eleven pair up by call
sequence, and **two of those eleven are byte-identical** — both of them
`fillRect(0,0,16,16)` followed by a one-pixel read, which is the one shape
`raster.zig` covers.

| produced by | oracle | lightpanda |
|---|---|---|
| `font` + `fillText` on a flag emoji, 1×1 | `00000029` | `00000000` |
| radial gradients, paths, shadows, text — 48×48 | 9216 B, 1211 zero | 9216 B, **all zero** |
| shader compile → `drawArrays` → `readPixels`, 16×16 | 1024 B, `d78a74ff` | **absent** |
| second shader program, `readPixels` 4×1 | 16 B | **absent** |
| `fillRect` + `arc` + `fill`, 2×2 | `ffffffff c0c0c0ff f4f4f4ff 353535ff` | `000000ff` ×4 |
| `fillStyle = color(display-p3 …)`, 2×2, four attribute sets | `ff1b7fff` / `ff407fff` / 8 B `5b3cc92e…` / 8 B `003c0034…` | `000000ff` four times, always 4 B |
| emoji `measureText` + composite arcs + evenodd ring — 49×44 | 8624 B, 1725 zero | 8624 B, **all zero** |
| `drawImage(ImageBitmap)`, 49×44, twice | 8624 B, same hash as above | **absent** |
| text at 80×24 downscaled into 1×1 by `drawImage`, then read | 4 B | reads the **80×24** instead, 7680 B all white |
| `fillRect` + `arc` + `fillText`, 16×16 | 1024 B, 90 zero | 1024 B, 2 zero |
| `filter: grayscale(1)` + `difference` composite via `drawImage`, 16×16 | 1024 B, 90 zero | `drawImage` absent from the log entirely |
| `fillRect(0,0,16,16)` then a 1×1 read, twice | `f06d06ff` | `f06d06ff` — **match** |

The four `display-p3` rows are a separate reading: the widget passes
`getImageData` an options bag, and the byte counts on the oracle arm (4, 4, 8,
8) say two of the four asked for `float16` storage. This fork returns four bytes
every time and the same `000000ff` for a fill it cannot parse.

The `drawImage` rows are the same missing primitive seen three ways: an
`ImageBitmap` source, an `OffscreenCanvas` source, and a downscaling
nine-argument form. It is a no-op here, so the two readbacks that only read what
`drawImage` deposited never happen, and the downscale case reads the source
canvas at full size instead.

→ `cfsc-canvas-pixel-readback` P2 (drawing), P3 (the branches that never run).

## What a path rasteriser is worth, and the two bugs only the live trace found (2026-08-23)

`raster.zig` covered `fillRect`, `clearRect` and `strokeRect`, and neither of
the widget's two big readbacks contains one of those three. So the geometry
went in: `path.zig` holds the current transformation matrix and a path
flattened under it as it is built, and `raster.zig` fills that path by sampling
a 4x4 grid per pixel against its edge list under either winding rule, and
strokes it by filling the quad each segment sweeps plus a disc at every join.
Both context types share it through `context_draw.zig` rather than carrying two
copies of the same code.

| readback | before | after | arm that clears |
|---|---|---|---|
| 9216, 48×48 | 9216 zero | 8536 zero | 1211 zero |
| 8624, 49×44 | 8624 zero | **1720 zero** | 1725 zero |
| 7680, 80×24 | 7488 zero | 0 zero | (reads 1×1 there) |
| 1024, 16×16 | 1022 zero | 138 zero | 90 zero |

The 49×44 lands within five zero bytes of the reference. It is still not
byte-identical — `multiply` compositing is not implemented and our coverage
edges are not Chrome's — but the shape is the right shape. The 48×48 is only
part-way because its ink is six radial gradients and two runs of text, and
neither gradients nor glyphs exist here yet.

Two bugs turned up that no offline test would have produced, and both were
settled by measuring Chrome rather than reasoning about the spec.

**A resize resets the context, not just the bitmap.** The widget reuses one
`OffscreenCanvas` at half a dozen sizes and never clears the transform itself —
it relies on the resize between them. Assigning to `width` cleared the bitmap
here and nothing else, so the `scale(0.384)` from the 48×48 readback was still
in force for the next canvas and then multiplied by that one's own `scale(0.4)`;
everything after the first readback came out shrunk into a corner. Chrome, for
an assignment of the value the canvas already has:

    transform → identity   fillStyle → #000000   lineWidth → 1
    font → 10px sans-serif   globalAlpha → 1   path → empty   save() stack → empty

**A counterclockwise turn of exactly `2π` is a whole circle.** Every arc the
widget draws passes `counterclockwise = true`, and every one is a full turn:
`arc(x, y, r, 0, 2 * Math.PI, true)`. Subtracting a turn from a sweep of
exactly a turn gives zero, so all three composited circles and the even-odd
ring drew nothing at all — which is why the 8624 readback did not move on the
first pass even though the path rasteriser was in. Ten readings on a 64×64
canvas at r=25, ink pixels:

| call | clockwise | counterclockwise |
|---|---|---|
| `arc(0, 2π)` | 2032 | 2032 |
| `arc(0, 2π + π/2)` | 2032 | 1843 |
| `arc(0, −π)` | 1012 | 1012 |
| `arc(0, ∓3π)` | 1012 | 1012 |
| `arc(0, π/2)` | 206 | 1843 |

A sweep against the requested direction wraps by whole turns rather than
clamping; a sweep of exactly one turn against it becomes a whole turn rather
than nothing; only two exactly equal angles draw nothing.

## The five that still do not happen, and what each is waiting on (2026-08-23)

The two readbacks P3 names are `1024` and `4096`. They turned out to be
different kinds of thing.

**The 1024 is WebGL, and it is stable.** It appeared in all four fresh oracle
sessions, always as `readPixels` on a 16×16 context, always `d78a74ff` — the
constant fragment shader quantised. Its cause is the one return value P1 found:
`getShaderParameter(shader, COMPILE_STATUS)` answers `false` here, so the widget
deletes its shaders and never reaches `drawArrays`. Making the readback happen
means answering `true`, and answering `true` without executing the shader would
put 1024 zero bytes where Chrome puts a colour — a wrong value in place of a
missing one. The colour itself is computable without a GPU (both of the
widget's programs are small), but that is a GLSL evaluator, and it is its own
plan.

**The 4096 did not recur.** Four fresh oracle sessions produced no 4096-byte
readback of any kind, while producing the 1024 every time. Its recorded shape,
from the session that did produce it: 1024 pixels — 224 opaque black, 32 of one
colour, 768 transparent — so a 32×32 image with a block drawn in it. It is not
part of the canvas work the widget does today; whoever meets it again has the
shape.

### drawImage was not a no-op, it was absent

The op logs read as though five oracle-only readbacks depended on a `drawImage`
that quietly did nothing here. Measuring both engines said otherwise:

    chrome      drawImage(canvas)  [255,0,0,255]   drawImage(canvas,0,0,4,4,0,0,1,1)  [255,0,0,255]
    lightpanda  threw: dctx.drawImage is not a function

On `OffscreenCanvasRenderingContext2D` the member did not exist. The element
context had it as a declared no-op; the offscreen one, a near-identical file,
had never been given the line — the classic cost of two parallel copies. A
`TypeError` takes the rest of the caller's function with it, which is why the
readbacks *around* those calls vanished too, and why the 80×24 canvas was read
at full size here where Chrome reads the 1×1 it had been downscaled into.

With a real blit behind it (canvas and `OffscreenCanvas` sources, inverse-mapped
so a rotated destination needs no separate path), the arms line up:

|  | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| readbacks here | 13 | 13 |
| pairing with an oracle readback by call sequence | 11 | **13** |
| readbacks only this arm makes | 2 | **0** |
| readbacks only the oracle makes | 7 | **5** |

The five that remain: two WebGL `readPixels`, waiting on shader execution; two
`drawImage(ImageBitmap)` reads, waiting on `ImageBitmap` carrying pixels rather
than only its dimensions; and one bare `getImageData` that follows the second of
those.

→ `cfsc-webgl-shader-readback`, `cfsc-imagebitmap-pixels`.
#### The 26 values, closed and checked against the oracle's own bytes (2026-08-23)

`cfsc-computed-style-per-tag`. All 26 are gone, and the check is stronger than
the sitting that would have measured it: the widget's whole computed-style
payload now comes back **byte-identical** to the 30 902 characters recorded in
`results/p5-oracle.json`.

The three shapes turned out to be two causes.

**The UA stylesheet is per tag and the table was not.**
`chrome_initial_values.zig` holds one value per longhand, measured off a bare
`<div>`, so every element answered a div's answer. That is the `margin*`
spellings (a `<body>` takes `8px`, a div `0px`) and `unicode-bidi` (a div takes
`isolate`, everything inline `normal`). `dump-css-initial-values.mjs` now walks
every HTML tag through the same two differently-sized hosts the two divs go
through and writes `chrome_per_tag_values.zig`: 1 147 values over 125 tags.
Three things the measurement decided rather than a list did:

- The fallback for a tag with no rules is **not** the div. A div is itself
  styled by the UA sheet, so an element the sheet says nothing about answers
  `unicode-bidi: normal` where a div answers `isolate`. A tag that measured
  identical to the div still gets a key with an empty row, so a miss can only
  mean "not an HTML tag" and reaches `unknown_tag`.
- `html`, `body` and `head` are read out of two about:blank iframes rather than
  from `createElement`. A synthetic `<html>` does carry the sheet's rules, but
  not `view-transition-name: root`, which only a document's real root gets.
- `display` is deliberately never stored. `resolvedDisplay` blockifies a flex or
  grid parent's children and honours a cascaded `display: none`; a stored
  per-tag string can express neither, and would shadow both.

**`100000000px` was a root-container constant, not a table entry.**
`getElementDimensions` sized every `<html>` and `<body>` at any depth from two
numbers — 1920 wide and 100_000_000 tall, so `calculateDocumentPosition`'s
100px-per-level stacking always had room — and both went out through
`getComputedStyle`. A document's root containers fill its *viewport*, and a
child document's viewport is the iframe element's box. Measured on Chrome 151:
the `<html>` of a 300x150 iframe reports 300x150 and its `<body>` 284x134 — the
viewport less the body's own 8px UA margins — while a 0x0 iframe reports `0px`
throughout.

That 0x0 case is what the widget reads, and it is how the element was
identified at all: `width: 0px` and `transform-origin: 0px 0px` is neither a
`display:none` iframe (`auto` and `50% 50%`) nor a default-sized one (`284px`).
A body filling its viewport is the *quirks* rendering, and an about:blank
document is in quirks mode — `compatMode` reads `BackCompat`, measured, and it
reads that for an iframe's document whether or not a `srcdoc` carries a doctype.
So the viewport is the right answer for exactly the documents these iframes
hold. For the top-level document Chrome is in standards mode and sizes a body to
its content, which this faux layout cannot compute; the viewport is the wrong
half of a real browser's two answers there, but it is one of them, which the
sentinel never was.

`probes/computed-style-iframe-body.js` reproduces the widget's read offline and
carries the one-liner that diffs it against the recording.

| | before | after | oracle |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `getComputedStyle` dump | 30 972 chars | **30 902** | 30 902 |
| values differing from the oracle | 26 | **0** | — |

**The sitting itself measured nothing, and a control says why.**
`results/p6-oracle.json` / `p6-lp.json`, one sitting, and the station was in a
heavier mood than it was for p5: the oracle got `Just a moment...` again, and
this arm stopped after 6 records with 2 realms armed where p5 reached 10. That
reads like a regression until the control is run — `p6-lp-baseline.json` is the
same sitting with the *pre-change* binary, and its record tally is identical,
six records and two realms. So the shallow reach is the station, not the change,
and this sitting says nothing about pass or fail either way. The byte comparison
above is what stands in for it: it checks the same payload against the same
oracle bytes without needing the station to answer at all.

### The 1 000 floats: the widget's audio graph is not fingerprintjs's (2026-08-23)

The other half of the E1 table was the audio vector — 15 361 characters of
`|`-joined floats on the oracle arm, 1 999 here, because ours are 1 000 zeros.
`canonical_render.zig` replays a recorded render only for the graph it
recognises and falls back to silence for anything else, by design. Which of its
predicates refused was the open question.

**It can be answered without the station, up to a point.** Three sittings on
disk (`p4b`, `p5`, `p6`) carry the same vector byte for byte, so the widget's
render is deterministic and is a fixed target. `audio-graph-solve.mjs` searches
real Chrome for the graph that produces it, scoring candidates inside the page
so only a number per candidate crosses CDP, and it carries a control:
fingerprintjs's graph against `chrome_audio_macos.bin` must score exactly zero
or the harness is measuring something other than what was recorded.

Walking the five compressor settings moved the error by less than a thousandth —
which said the difference was not the compressor. Fitting a sinusoid to both
renders said what it was instead:

| | ours | oracle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| leading zeros | 265 | 265 |
| zero crossings in 1 000 frames | 333, at the same indices | 333, at the same indices |
| best-fit tone | 10 000.000 000 Hz | **9 998.125 Hz** |
| phase over frames 270..910 | flat | drifts +0.171 rad, linearly |

A phase that drifts linearly apart from an identical waveform is a frequency
difference and nothing else. Correcting it cut the error 4.5×, and re-walking
the compressor from there cut it another 26×. The search then stalled at a
4.8e-5 residual with parameters that had stopped being plausible numbers
(threshold −49.998, gain 1.0001), which is what a structural gap looks like from
inside a search — and in any case `matches()` compares exact doubles, so an
approximation buys nothing.

**So watch the construction.** `audio-graph-trace.mjs` wraps every funnel a
graph has to pass through — the context constructors, `create*`, `connect`,
`AudioParam.value` and its ramp methods, `OscillatorNode.type`, `start`/`stop`,
`startRendering` and `getChannelData` — in the widget's own realm, ahead of its
own code. The installation is fo-plaintext's, now shared as `fo-harness.mjs`:
arming a cross-origin child before its document runs, resuming worker sessions
before asking them anything, and collecting records over the console are the
same fight whatever the question. The report reads back as the source that
produced it (`results/a1-oracle.json`, and the arm cleared):

```
OfflineAudioContext(1, 1000, 44100)
osc.type = 'triangle'
osc.frequency.value = 9998.123456
comp.threshold.value = -52
comp.knee.value = 40
comp.ratio.value = 12
comp.attack.value = 0.0001
comp.release.value = 0.25
osc -> comp -> destination
osc.start(0)
```

Rendered in Chrome, that graph reproduces `p4b-oracle.json`'s 1 000 floats with
a **maximum difference of zero** — a different sitting, weeks apart. So the
identification is not a fit, it is the bytes.

Three of `matches()`'s predicates refused it: `threshold` (−50), `attack` (0)
and `frequency` (10000). The numeric solve had the frequency right to five
figures and the compressor wrong, which is the argument for having run both.

Two smaller things the same trace shows, neither chased here:

- The widget builds the graph **three** times per visit — twice as above, which
  is why the oracle's payload carries the vector twice, and once more as
  `createBuffer(1, 1000, 44100)` → `createBufferSource()` → destination with the
  buffer filled by the page itself. That third render is a pure passthrough with
  no DSP in it, so unlike these two it could be computed rather than recorded.
- `AudioBufferSourceNode.prototype.start` is its own overload in Blink rather
  than inherited from `AudioScheduledSourceNode`, so a recorder that wraps only
  the base class sees an oscillator start and never a buffer source's.

**And it closes.** `chrome_audio.zig` now carries a `Graph` enum with a
recording per graph per platform, and `canonical_render`'s `matches()` became
`which()`: the structure every recorded graph shares — a started triangle
oscillator into a compressor into a mono destination — is checked once, and the
six numbers are then checked against each candidate in turn, so half of one
graph and half of another is neither and still gets silence. Regenerating both
recordings reproduced the existing fingerprintjs tail sums exactly on both
platforms, which is the control that says the second graph did not disturb the
first.

Asked the widget's graph on a loopback page (`results/a2-lp-turnstile.json`),
this engine now answers:

| | before | after | oracle |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| the audio vector | 1 000 zeros | **265 zeros + 735 floats** | 265 zeros + 735 floats |
| samples differing from the station's | 735 | **0** | — |
| the string the widget then encodes | 1 999 chars | **15 361** | 15 361 |

The tail sums the recordings hash to, for whoever regenerates them next: macOS
`112.4458671315806`, Linux `112.46367831656244`.

#### The same sitting, both arms, after the audio row closed (2026-08-23)

`results/a3-oracle.json` / `a3-lp.json`, one sitting, and this one is worth
trusting: the oracle cleared (`cf-chl-out`, "You bypassed the Cloudflare
challenge! :D") while this engine got `cf-chl-gen` at round 2, so the station
was willing and the two arms are genuinely being told apart.

Payloads of 1 000 bytes or more, counted by size:

| size | oracle | ours | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 30 902 | 3 | 3 | the `getComputedStyle` dump — **closed** |
| 15 361 | 4 | 4 | the audio vector — **closed this round** |
| 20 696 / 20 367 | 2 / 0 | 0 / 2 | the page's `@keyframes` text, 329 characters short |
| 13 468 ×3 / 14 007 / 4 416 / 1 792 | 1 each | 0 | *not payloads* — see below |
| 9 216 | 1 | 2 | RGBA pixel readback |
| 8 624 | 3 | 2 | RGBA pixel readback |
| 4 096 / 1 168 ×2 / 1 024 / 1 009 | 1 each | 0 | never produced here |
| round 2 POST | 4 716 | 4 866 | 150 bytes wider than the arm that clears |

**Half of those rows were the same payload counted twice (2026-08-23).** Every
`subtle.digest` in `a3-oracle.json` is handed the UTF-8 encoding of the string
the `TextEncoder.encode` immediately before it was given, and the funnel records
*both*, so one collection shows up under two sizes whenever the string is not
plain ASCII. It is arithmetic, not a second surface — `Buffer.byteLength(v)` of
each encode input reproduces the digest size exactly:

| encode (chars) | digest (bytes) | which |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 8 624 | 13 468 | RGBA pixel readback, three times over |
| 9 216 | 14 007 | RGBA pixel readback |
| 4 096 | 4 416 | never produced here |
| 1 024 | 1 792 | never produced here |
| 15 361 | 15 361 | the audio vector — ASCII, so the two agree |

So the 13 468 row was never "the biggest payload this engine never produces".
It is the digest of the 8 624-byte pixel readback, and it appears three times
because that readback does — which puts it inside `cfsc-canvas-pixel-readback`
rather than in a plan of its own. Reading the records directly, the `lp` arm
emits *no* readback digest at all in this sitting: its only encode/digest pairs
above 1 000 bytes are 30 902 (computed style) and 20 367 (`@keyframes`).

Which leaves the genuinely unclaimed list shorter than it looked: the pixel
readbacks, the `@keyframes` shortfall, and 4 096 / 1 168 ×2 / 1 024 / 1 009.

The widget's **third** OfflineAudioContext — `createBuffer(1, 1000, 44100)`
filled by the page, through `createBufferSource()` to the destination — is now
closed. Chrome hands that buffer straight back and this engine used to render
1 000 zeros; `buffer_render.zig` computes the passthrough instead. Traced
through `audio-graph-trace.mjs` on a loopback page, both engines report the
graph record for record and the render comes back sample for sample identical
(1 000/1 000, maximum difference zero). → `cfsc-audio-buffer-passthrough`, done.

## The `@keyframes` shortfall is a selector serialiser, not a missing rule (2026-08-23)

The 329-character gap in the page's `@keyframes` payload (`a3-oracle.json`
records[67], 20 696 chars; `a3-lp.json` records[26], 20 367) is not a rule we
fail to produce. Both arms emit the same 183 rules in the same order. Split on
`|` and diffed entry by entry, 120 are already byte-identical and every
remaining one is a *serialisation* difference in how a rule's `cssText` is
written back.

Three normalisations account for two thirds of the gap, applied to our own
payload and re-measured:

| applied to our text | chars recovered | entries now identical |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `,` → `, ` in selector and value lists | 190 | |
| `~` → ` ~ ` | 26 | |
| `grid-area: 1/1` → `1 / 1` | 2 | 168 of 183 |

The remaining 111 characters are in 15 entries and are value-level, listed
here largest first so whoever picks them up knows the size of each:

| what | example: oracle vs ours | net |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `animation` shorthand order | `0.3s cubic-bezier(…) 0s 1 normal both running scale-up-center` vs `scale-up-center 0.3s cubic-bezier(…) both` | +90 |
| `box-shadow` order and units | `rgb(34, 139, 73) 0px 0px 0px inset` vs `inset 0 0 0 rgb(34, 139, 73)` | +42 |
| `transform` dropped entirely | `transform: rotate(0deg) scale(1)` vs absent | +34 |
| `border-image` kept as longhands | `border-image: none` vs five `border-image-*` plus a spurious `border-top-width` | −98 |
| `transform-origin` order | `center bottom` vs `bottom center` | +2 |
| `stroke-dasharray` separator | `32, 32` vs `32 32` | +1 |

One structural leftover: our payload has a 184th element, the single character
`2`, where the oracle's list ends at 183. Both end the last rule with a bare
`0` appended after the closing brace, so the collector concatenates something
beyond the joined `cssText` list; what our extra `|2` is has not been run down.

### What Chrome actually does to a selector, measured

`probes/expr-selector-serialize.js` puts 38 selectors through
`new CSSStyleSheet().replaceSync()` and reads `selectorText` back. Chrome never
returns the author's bytes — it re-serialises the parsed selector. We return
the source, trimmed, so 32 of the 38 disagree:

| written | Chrome | ours |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `a,b` | `a, b` | `a,b` |
| `  a  ,  b  ` | `a, b` | `a  ,  b` |
| `a~b` / `a>b` / `a+b` | `a ~ b` / `a > b` / `a + b` | unchanged |
| `a   b` | `a b` | unchanged |
| `:not(a,b)` | `:not(a, b)` | unchanged |
| `:not(a~b)` | `:not(a ~ b)` | unchanged |
| `a:has(+b)` | `a:has(+ b)` | unchanged |
| `DIV.Foo#Bar` | `div.Foo#Bar` | unchanged |
| `A:HOVER` | `a:hover` | unchanged |
| `[HREF]` | `[href]` | unchanged |
| `a:before` | `a::before` | unchanged |
| `[a=b]` / `[a='b']` | `[a="b"]` | unchanged |
| `*\|a` | `a` | unchanged |

And the things Chrome leaves alone, which a normaliser must not touch:
`[class~="x"]` and `[class\|="x"]` keep their matchers unspaced, `a[href~="b,c"]`
keeps the comma inside the string, `a:nth-child(2n+1)` keeps its `+` unspaced,
`.\31 23` keeps its escape, and class and id names keep their case.

### What the selector serialiser recovered, on the payload itself

`selector_text.zig` rewrites a parsed selector the way Blink does, at the one
point both the stylesheet parser and `rule.selectorText = ...` go through.
Re-measured on the 38-case probe, this engine now agrees with Chrome on 36 of
38, up from 6. The two left are deliberate: Chrome rejects the column
combinator `a||b` outright, which is a parser-acceptance difference rather than
a serialisation one, and `*|a` needs namespace elision.

Replayed against the sitting's own bytes — our 183 rules fed back through a
fresh `CSSStyleSheet` and joined the way the collector joins them — the
shortfall against the oracle's text:

| | chars | gap | rules byte-identical |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| oracle | 20 695 | — | — |
| before | 20 364 | 331 | 120 / 183 |
| after | **20 556** | **139** | **164 / 183** |

Every one of the 19 rules still differing differs in a *declaration*, not a
selector. Ranked, that residue is: the `animation` shorthand written name-last
in Chrome's eight-longhand order rather than as the author wrote it; the
`box-shadow` colour written first with `0px` rather than `0`; `font-family` and
`stroke-dasharray` lists needing `, ` where we join with `,`; `grid-area: 1 / 1`
for our `1/1`; a `transform` declaration we drop entirely; and `border-image`
which Chrome folds back into one shorthand where we emit five longhands plus a
`border-top-width` Chrome does not. → `cfsc-keyframes-shortfall`, done; the
declaration side is its own plan.

Noticed while pinning the cascade side of this and not chased: a `color`
declared by a stylesheet rule does not reach `getComputedStyle().color` here at
all — it reads `rgb(0, 0, 0)` whatever the selector, while `display` from the
same sheet cascades correctly. That is not a selector bug (a bare `.class` rule
misses it too) and Chrome answers with the cascaded colour.

Swept afterwards (`results/kf-selector-sweep-after.json`): 11 of 15 stations
open, the same eleven as before the change and the same four shut
(cf-scrapingcourse, cf-nopecha, cf-zeroclover, dd-g2). No door moved, which is
what a 139-character residue on one payload predicts; the reading that matters
here is the absence of a regression, since the normalised text is what the
cascade re-parses.

### Measuring the rest without a sitting

`keyframes-roundtrip.mjs` feeds our own recorded payload back through a fresh
`CSSStyleSheet` and diffs the re-read against the oracle's text. Because both
arms recorded the same 183 rules, that re-runs the whole serialiser over real
CSS in about three seconds, with no station and no challenge:

```
node tools/fingerprint/keyframes-roundtrip.mjs [--verbose]
```

Where it stands after the value-punctuation pass, which writes every comma as
`, ` and every slash as ` / ` (and every `stroke-dasharray` separator as `, `):

| | gap | rules byte-identical |
| --- | --- | --- |
| before the selector serialiser | 331 | 120 / 183 |
| after it | 139 | 164 / 183 |
| after value punctuation | **112** | **169 / 183** |

## The round-1 wobble belongs to both arms; only the surplus is ours (P1, 2026-08-23)

`cfsc-r1-payload-length` was opened on two readings taken from four runs: the
widget's first `fo/` POST is 4 716 bytes on the oracle in every sitting it had
been seen in, and 4 855 / 4 866 here — a ~140-byte surplus *and* a run-to-run
wobble the reference did not have. The second of those readings does not
survive more samples.

Six runs in one sitting, `dev.973+946e2ad02`, `cfsc-fo-diff.mjs`, alternating
arms (`results/r1len-{lp-1..4,oracle-1,oracle-2}.json`):

| arm | page `fo/` #1 | widget `fo/` #1 | widget `fo/` #2 | cleared |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| here a | 2 316 | 4 866 | 85 570 | no |
| here b | 2 306 | 4 866 | 85 687 | no |
| here c | 2 306 | 4 876 | 85 548 | no |
| here d | 2 306 | 4 866 | 85 996 | no |
| oracle a | 2 306 | **4 706** | 88 535 | yes |
| oracle b | 2 306 | **4 727** | 88 716 | yes |

The oracle's widget round 1 is 4 706 in one run and 4 727 in the next. Read
together with the three earlier sittings (4 716, 4 716, 4 706) its range is
4 706–4 727, spread **21**; ours across seven runs is 4 855–4 876, spread
**21**. The two arms wobble by the same amount. "4 716 three times" was three
samples of a distribution, not a constant, and the earlier note that a
deterministic length means every field is fixed-width was drawn from it.

The page-level POST says the same thing from the other side: it is 2 306 on
every run of either arm except one of ours, which is 2 316 — one step of the
same size, on the arm and the payload that otherwise agree exactly.

Both observed step sizes are 10 or 11, and the spread is 21 = 10 + 11 rather
than a multiple of either. That is what a base-64-shaped encoding does to a
plaintext that moved by 8 bytes: 8 × 4/3 = 10.67, which lands alternately on 10
and 11. So the wobble is ~8 plaintext bytes on both arms — a timestamp digit, a
duration, one number — and it is not a tell.

What survives is the surplus, and it is far steadier than either arm's wobble:

| | oracle | here | gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| min | 4 706 | 4 855 | 149 |
| median | 4 716 | 4 866 | 150 |
| max | 4 727 | 4 876 | 149 |

**~150 encoded characters, every run, ≈ 112 plaintext bytes at 4/3.** That is
the thing to localise, and P2/P3 are re-aimed at it: not "find the
variable-length field" — both arms have one and it is the same size — but "find
the ~112 bytes this engine puts in the round-1 telemetry that the reference does
not."

## What the widget reads before round 1, and where it is told something else (P2, 2026-08-23)

The round-1 body is one ciphertext and `fo-plaintext.mjs` already showed the
plaintext never passes a funnel — no WebCrypto, no `btoa`, nothing over two
bytes through `JSON.stringify` in the widget realm before the POST goes out. So
the last place the payload is readable in the clear is one property getter at a
time, which is what `fo-reads.mjs` records: every configurable accessor on the
standard prototypes forwards to its original and writes down what it answered,
disguised the same way the funnel wrappers are, cut at the realm's first
`XMLHttpRequest.send`.

The honesty check is the same one and it passes: **the oracle cleared with the
tracer installed, twice** — "You bypassed the Cloudflare challenge! :D" in both
`results/r1reads-oracle-{1,2}.json`.

| run | widget realm reads | before first send | round-1 POST | cleared |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| oracle 1 | 797 | 124 | 4 727 | yes |
| oracle 2 | 797 | 124 | 4 716 | yes |
| here 1 | 889 | 171 | 4 887 | no |
| here 2 | 889 | 171 | 4 887 | no |

Two things to read off that table before the diff. The reads are *stable* per
arm — identical counts across runs on both — and the widget makes essentially
the same ones on each: 47 of our 51-read surplus is `window.window`, which
Chrome refuses to let the tracer wrap at all (see below), so it is reads the
instrument cannot see rather than reads Chrome does not make. And our round-1
POST was 4 887 both times with the tracer in, against 4 866–4 876 without it:
the recorder costs about 20 bytes of its own, which is inside the wobble and
does not move the ~150-byte gap.

`fo-reads-diff.mjs` puts two runs side by side, either two arms or two runs of
one arm. Same arm, twice, only three keys move — `Date.now()`, `Math.random()`
and `performance.now()` — which is the 8-byte wobble P1 measured and nothing
else. Across arms, six keys differ for a reason that is not a clock.

### The six, re-measured off the station

`probes/expr-r1-reads.js` asks both engines directly, so none of these rests on
a reading taken through a challenge:

| read | Chrome | here |
|---|---|---|
| `performance.timeOrigin` | `1787494938199.7` — epoch ms | `244508796.7` — boot-relative |
| `timeOrigin + now() - Date.now()` | **1 ms** | **-1 787 250 459 740** |
| `<style>.innerText` | its text | `""` |
| `JSON.stringify(el.classList)` | `{"0":"main-wrapper","1":".tOHY4"}` | `{}` |
| `Object.getOwnPropertyNames(el.classList)` | `0 1` | *(empty)* |
| `window.window` descriptor | `configurable: false` | `configurable: true` |
| `window.top` descriptor | `configurable: false` | `configurable: true` |
| `window.frameElement`, cross-origin child | `null` | the `<iframe>` element |

`self`, `parent`, `frameElement` and `location` already carry Chrome's exact
descriptor shape; `window` and `top` are the two that do not, and the tracer
found them by being *able* to replace them here and not there. The
`display: none` fallback for `innerText` is already right — a hidden `<div>`
answers with its text on both — so the `<style>` case is its own bug and not
that one.

`frameElement` is the odd one out: its descriptor matches, its value does not,
and only on the station, because it needs a cross-origin embedder to differ at
all. A widget that can reach the `<iframe>` element embedding it can read the
embedder's attributes; Chrome hands it `null`. This engine already denies
`document`, `navigator` and the rest of the must-deny list on an outbound
cross-origin `contentWindow` (`results/probes/probe-cross-origin-surface.*`) —
the inbound direction is what was never closed.

None of these can be attributed to a byte count from here: the payload is
encrypted and there is no field boundary to attribute against. They are the set
of things the widget was told and was told wrong, and the round-1 length is the
instrument that says whether closing them moves it. That is P3.

## Five of the six are closed, and the payload did not move (P3, 2026-08-23)

Every difference P2 found is fixed and re-measured, and none of them was the
150 bytes.

| what | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `performance.timeOrigin` | `244508796.7`, boot-relative | `1787495569894.4`, epoch ms |
| `timeOrigin + now() - Date.now()` | `-1 787 250 459 740` | **1**, Chrome's answer exactly |
| `window.window` / `window.top` descriptor | `configurable: true` | `false`, like `location` and `document` |
| `<style>.innerText` | `""` | its CSS |
| `display:none` div's `innerText` | `"one\n\ntwo"` | `"onetwo"` |
| `JSON.stringify(el.classList)` | `{}` | `{"0":"one","1":"two"}` |
| cross-origin child's `frameElement` | the `<iframe>` | `null` |

The last one is the only one that needs a frame boundary to show, and it is
also the only one with a plausible story about *volume*: a widget that can
reach the element embedding it can read the embedder's attributes. It reads
`null` now, the way Chrome's does.

Three runs afterwards, `dev.979+9cd217ce7`, with an oracle control in the same
sitting (`results/r1len-after-*.json`):

| arm | page `fo/` #1 | widget `fo/` #1 |
|---|---|---|
| here a | 2 306 | 4 855 |
| here b | 2 316 | 4 866 |
| here c | 2 306 | 4 876 |
| oracle | 2 306 | **4 716** |

That is the same distribution as before the change, wobble and all. **The
surplus is not made of the values the widget reads.**

### What the tracer can now see, and what it cannot

Rerun with the fixes in and an enumeration pass added — `Object.keys`,
`getOwnPropertyNames`, `getOwnPropertySymbols`, `values`, `entries`,
`getOwnPropertyDescriptors`, `getPrototypeOf`, `Reflect.ownKeys` and
`Function.prototype.toString`, each keyed by the brand of its argument
(`results/r1enum-{lp,oracle}-1.json`) — five keys differ across the arms and
four of them are a clock or a `Math.random()`. `window.window`, `window.top`,
`innerText` and `classList` have all dropped out of the diff, which is the
station confirming the fixes from the other side.

The enumeration pass is a clean negative and it rules out the biggest
outstanding suspect. In the widget realm, before the round-1 POST, this engine
makes **three** enumeration calls: `Function.prototype.toString` twice (both
`function eval() { [native code] }`) and one `Object.keys` returning
`["window"]`. Nothing walks `window`. So the ~112 plaintext bytes are not a
list of globals, which was the obvious candidate given this engine carries 237
own names on `window` that Chrome does not.

Stack strings are ruled out too, off the station:
`probes/expr-error-stack-shape.js` reads byte-identical on both engines for a
bare `Error`, one with a message, a nested call, and a native `TypeError` —
same length, same line count, same wording, same `Error.stackTraceLimit`.

Two named leads survive, neither of which explains the volume on its own:

- **`window.parent` from the widget.** Chrome's cross-origin WindowProxy makes
  `JSON.stringify` of it throw, so the tracer records `[object Object]`; ours
  returns `{}`, meaning the stringify walked it. Something on the must-deny
  list — `toJSON` at least — is reachable through the inbound proxy here.
- **`performance.timing.secureConnectionStart`** is `0` here on an https load
  and a real stamp in Chrome. That one makes Chrome's payload *longer*, not
  ours, so it is a parity bug rather than a candidate for the surplus.

### Where the next attempt should look

The page-level round 1 is 2 306 bytes on both arms, exactly, run after run —
assembled by the same Cloudflare code family, in the page realm, and it agrees.
The widget's is 150 longer here. Whatever the surplus is, it is specific to the
*widget* realm, and it is not a property value, not an enumeration and not a
stack. What is left that the widget has and the page does not: the DOM it builds
for itself (an iframe with its own shadow tree and styles) and reads back, and
the challenge parameters it is handed over `postMessage`. Both are readable with
the instruments already in this directory — `fo-plaintext.mjs` records the
trampoline conversation, and the widget's own subtree can be serialised from the
document realm the recorder is already installed in.

## The assembly step, and what it is not (P3 again, 2026-08-23)

The previous attempt wrapped the values and found six differences, fixed five,
and did not move the length. This one wrapped the step after the values: the
one that turns what was collected into a string.

`fo-join.mjs` is that instrument. Its lead came out of `fo-plaintext.mjs`'s own
records: every block of the widget's later rounds arrives pipe-joined —
`"0|0|0|..."`, `"@keyframes spin { ... }|@keyframes scale..."` — which is
`Array.prototype.join`, a funnel nobody had wrapped. So it wraps `join` (keyed
by separator), `Array.prototype.toString`, `String.fromCharCode`,
`encodeURIComponent`, `btoa`, `JSON.stringify` and `XMLSerializer`, and it adds
a `message` listener, which answers the other half of the README's open lead —
the challenge parameters the parent hands the widget — in the same run. Records
stop at each realm's first `XMLHttpRequest.send`, because only what was built
before the send can be in the body it carried.

The lead was right about the mechanism. `join("")` in the widget realm returns
**the round-1 ciphertext exactly**: 4 855 characters here, 4 716 on the oracle,
byte-for-byte the body of the send that follows it. The payload is assembled by
joining an array of encoded characters, and that is the last place it exists as
one object.

Honesty check, same as its two predecessors: the oracle cleared with the
wrappers in — "You bypassed the Cloudflare challenge! :D".

### Both arms build the same things, in the same order

| # | here | oracle |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `split<-` 15 469 — the program's `;` string table | `split<-` 16 359 |
| 2 | `charCodeAt<-` 318 | `charCodeAt<-` 318 (identical) |
| 3 | `message` 67 — `{"event":"init",...}` | same |
| 4 | `message` 3 297 — the `managed` parameters | `message` 4 378 |
| 5 | — | `split<-` 629 — a permutation of 0..184 |
| 6 | `join("")` ×3 — the three widget link labels | same |
| 7 | `split<-` 4 542 — the Cloudflare logo path | same |
| 8 | `message` 1 439 — `cs`, a list of captured stacks | `message` 1 441 |
| 9 | `charCodeAt<-` 5 206 | **identical string** |
| 10 | `charCodeAt<-` 1 663 / 575 — cf tokens | 1 514 / 575 |
| 11 | `join("")` **4 855** = the send | `join("")` **4 716** = the send |

Two negatives worth keeping, because both were live suspects:

- **The inbound parameters are not the surplus.** The `cs` message — the one
  that carries `Error` stacks captured in the page realm, and the obvious way a
  stack difference could reach a payload it is not thrown in — is 1 439 bytes
  here against 1 441 there. It corroborates `expr-error-stack-shape.js` from the
  other side rather than contradicting it.
- **The one parameter that does differ pushes the wrong way.**
  `apiJsResourceTiming` is a 1 035-byte entry on the oracle and `undefined`
  here, so the oracle's inbound is 1 081 bytes *longer* while its payload is
  139 shorter. Whatever the widget does with it, it is not echoing it.

The string table and the two cf tokens differ in length between arms, but those
are per-session server-issued values: the tables are made of random five-character
identifiers (`shiZs;NEQqF;hrYYt4…` against `OFPbR;plKjc;ySGNg…`), so a run-to-run
difference there is noise, not a tell. The 629-character permutation the oracle
splits and we never do sits inside that same per-session table, so it cannot be
attributed either.

So the assembly step is understood and the surplus is still not attributed. Four
routes are now closed by measurement — property values, enumeration, stack
strings, and now the assembly funnels and the inbound parameters. The plaintext
itself is reachable by no funnel: it is handed to nothing and read by nothing
until it is already encoded.

## What the run did find: the resource timing buffer never fills

`apiJsResourceTiming` arriving as `undefined` is not a missing field. It is an
empty buffer, and it is an engine-level gap rather than a challenge-specific one.

`probes/expr-resource-timing.js` asks both engines directly — fetch something,
then look:

| | here | Chrome |
|---|---|---|
| `typeof PerformanceResourceTiming` | `function` | `function` |
| `"resource"` in `supportedEntryTypes` | **yes** | yes |
| `getEntriesByType('resource')` after a `fetch` | **0** | 1 |
| `performance.getEntries()` entry types | `navigation`, `visibility-state`, `paint`, `paint` | …, `resource` |

`Performance.zig` says so itself, at the `onresourcetimingbufferfull` handler:
"Nothing fires it — the resource buffer never fills because nothing fills it."
Every subresource a page loads — every script, stylesheet, image, XHR and
`fetch` — leaves no entry behind.

That surface contradicts itself, which is the part that matters. Advertising
`resource` in `supportedEntryTypes` and then answering every query with an empty
list is not a browser with a feature missing; it is a browser whose own
self-description is wrong. And it is read on the station: Cloudflare's api.js
reads the resource timing of *itself* and the page posts it to the widget, which
is how the gap turned up here at all.

That is `perf-resource-timing`, and it is worth more than the 139 bytes this
plan was chasing.

## The buffer fills now, and the station reads it

`perf-resource-timing` wired the producer and every load that reaches it. The
ground truth for what a load should be filed under is
`resource-timing-initiators.mjs`: it serves its own origin carrying one of every
load kind — a classic `<script src>`, a `defer`, an `async`, a module and the
module it imports, a `<link rel=stylesheet>`, a sheet that stylesheet
`@import`s, a `<link rel=preload as=script>` with a `<script src>` that consumes
it, an `<img>`, an XHR, and the favicon — navigates both engines to it, and
reads the buffer back with every field a fingerprinter can see.

What Chrome 151 answers, and what this engine now answers identically for every
row but the last:

| load | `initiatorType` | `renderBlockingStatus` |
|---|---|---|
| `<script src>` (no async/defer) | `script` | `blocking` |
| `<script defer>` / `async` / `type=module` / static import | `script` | `non-blocking` |
| `<link rel=preload as=script>` | `link` | `non-blocking` |
| `<link rel=stylesheet>` | `link` | `blocking` |
| `@import`ed sheet | `css` | `blocking` | ← **not produced here** |
| `<img>` | `img` | `non-blocking` |
| favicon | `other` | `non-blocking` |
| XHR | `xmlhttprequest` | `non-blocking` |

Two of those took measuring rather than guessing. The prescan starts a fetch for
every `<script src>` it finds in the raw HTML before parsing; that head start is
internal, and Chrome files such a load under the script, not under a `<link>`
the page never wrote — so a preload with no hint element records `script`. And
because the prescan sees the whole document first, a URL that both a
`<link rel=preload>` and a `<script src>` name was already registered by the time
the link was parsed, which made the link's own registration a no-op and cost the
entry its `link` attribution. The link adopts the in-flight fetch now, which
also gives it the `load` event it had been silently missing.

The eleventh row is the one still missing: an `@import`ed sheet leaves no entry
here because no `@import` is followed at all. That is a missing request, not a
missing entry, and it belongs to CSS rather than to this.

### On the station

`apiJsResourceTiming` is no longer `undefined`. The page-level challenge now
posts a 33-key, 836-byte entry for api.js, with `initiatorType: "script"` and
`nextHopProtocol: "h2"` — the protocol plumbing reporting a real negotiated
version off the live connection. The capture is
`results/r1join-lp-after-resource-timing.json`; the oracle column below is
`results/r1join-oracle-2.json`.

Against the oracle's 1 065 bytes, the residue is named rather than a length:

| field | oracle | here |
|---|---|---|
| `navigationId` | `9894` | *absent* — 33 keys against 34 |
| `contentType` / `contentEncoding` | `text/javascript` / `br` | `""` / `""` |
| `domainLookupStart` … `finalResponseHeadersStart` (9 milestones) | real | all `0` |
| `serverTiming` | one `cfExtPri` entry | `[]` |
| `encodedBodySize` | 27 124 | 84 236 |
| `nextHopProtocol` | `h3` | `h2` |

`serverTiming` is the server's own header and cannot be invented. The rest can:
the entry carries no content type or encoding, none of the nine connection
milestones, and an `encodedBodySize` that is the *decoded* size — api.js arrives
brotli-compressed and this reports what it decompressed to, which says the
response was not compressed at all. That is the next plan, not this one.

### The response fields, filled

That plan ran. The entry is 34 keys now, the same count as the oracle's, and
the six named rows above are five closed and one reclassified. Recapture:
`results/r1join-lp-response-fields-2.json`.

| field | oracle | here | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `navigationId` | `9894` | `8784` | a per-navigation number, shared by the buffer |
| `contentType` | `text/javascript` | `text/javascript` | |
| `contentEncoding` | `br` | `br` | |
| nine milestones | real | real | seven filled, two zero, same two as Chrome |
| `encodedBodySize` | 27 124 | 27 073 | the compressed body, not the decoded one |
| `nextHopProtocol` | `h3` | `h2` | open |
| `serverTiming` | one `cfExtPri` | `[]` | open, and the same cause |

The last two are one thing, not two. Cloudflare sends **no** `Server-Timing`
header on the HTTP/2 path — verified by requesting the same api.js URL with
curl over h2, which returns `content-type`, `content-encoding` and nothing
else. `cfExtPri` is Cloudflare's extensible-priorities signal, and the oracle
sees it because the oracle negotiated QUIC. So the residue is not "two missing
fields", it is "this engine does not speak HTTP/3", and closing it is that
plan rather than this one.

Worth writing down separately: Chrome *does* parse `Server-Timing` into the
entry — a response carrying `cfExtPri;dur=0, db;dur=53;desc="lookup"` files two
PerformanceServerTiming entries with the names, durations and descriptions
parsed out (measured). Nothing here parses it, so any site that sends the
header reads an empty array where a browser reads entries. No station in the
sweep sends one, which is why it is a note rather than a task.

#### What is measured about the cross-origin rules

`resource-timing-response-fields.mjs` serves the same script four ways off a
second origin. Chrome 151 gates these fields behind two independent doors:

| gate | fields it opens |
|---|---|
| same-origin, **or** `Timing-Allow-Origin` matches | the nine milestones, `encodedBodySize`, `decodedBodySize`, `transferSize` |
| same-origin, **or** the response was fetched in CORS mode and allows it | `contentType`, `contentEncoding`, `responseStatus` |

A cross-origin response with neither reads as all zeros and empty strings.

This engine opens both doors unconditionally, which is a deliberate choice and
not an oversight. The api.js this plan exists to match carries no
`Timing-Allow-Origin` at all (verified with curl) and the oracle still reports
every milestone for it — so it must have been fetched in CORS mode, and a gate
keyed on TAO alone would zero the exact reading being chased. Modelling the
second door needs the request's CORS mode threaded through four fetch paths;
until that exists, the honest failure is to over-report rather than to break
the match. A detector that loads a cross-origin resource with neither header
and reads a non-zero `encodedBodySize` separates this engine from Chrome, and
that is the shape of the next move here if one is ever seen doing it.

Same-origin, there is nothing left to separate them: every response-derived
field of every row — plain, gzip, brotli, a parameterised `text/CSS`, a 404
favicon — reads identically on both engines, including the seven non-zero
milestones and the two Chrome leaves at zero over plain HTTP.

#### The sweep, and what a moving station looks like

`results/antibot-2026-08-23-response-fields.json` reads 8/15 against the 11/15
of `results/r1-fixes-sweep-after.json`. The eleven Cloudflare and `x-` stations
are verdict-for-verdict identical; all three of the differences are DataDome
sites flipping from `pass` to `datadome-challenge`.

That is not this change. The binary the 11/15 was measured on is still on disk
(`dev.990+10ed7882c`, this branch's merge base), so the control is exact: run
`--only dd-` on it, then on this build, minutes apart from the same address.
The merge base scored **0/4**; this build scored **1/4**
(`results/dd-control-base.json`, `results/dd-control-mine.json`). DataDome had
moved under both. A sweep number is only a regression signal when the station
holds still, and the way to find out whether it did is to re-run the old binary
rather than to reason about the new one.

One other thing the sweep taught, worth knowing before reading one: a run whose
rows all say `CRASHED exit 1` is usually not a crash in the engine. It is the
CDP port still held by a previous run — the `engineLog` in the output file says
`address already in use` in plain text, and every station in that run is
meaningless. Check that field before believing a bad sweep.

The sweep says nothing moved that should not have:
`results/antibot-2026-08-23-perf-resource-timing.json` against
`results/r1-fixes-sweep-after.json` is verdict-for-verdict identical across all
fifteen stations, 11/15 either way. Filling a buffer that was empty is a change
in what every page can read about itself, so the reading that matters here is
the absence of a regression rather than a number going up.

## The two WebGL readbacks are arithmetic, and both now happen (2026-08-23)

`cfsc-webgl-shader-readback`. The previous round left five oracle readbacks we
never made, and named the first two: `readPixels` on 16×16 and on 4×1, blocked
behind `getShaderParameter(shader, COMPILE_STATUS)` answering `false`. It also
named the trap — answering `true` without executing the shader would put 1024
zero bytes where Chrome puts a colour, which is a wrong value in place of a
missing one.

So the shaders are executed. The point worth keeping is **why that was
affordable**: a WebGL readback of this kind is arithmetic, not graphics.

    precision mediump float;
    void main(){gl_FragColor=vec4(sin(1.0),cos(1.0),sin(1.0)*cos(1.0),1.0);}

Chrome answers `d78a74ff` for all 256 pixels. Those are `sin(1)`, `cos(1)` and
their product quantised to eight bits. No GPU decided any of it. The second
shader is 413 characters and per-pixel, but it reads only `gl_FragCoord`, so it
is the same statement with a coordinate in it — two loops, four
transcendentals, a `fract`, and Chrome's sixteen bytes come out.

Both were checked in JavaScript before a line of Zig was written: fp32
arithmetic, transcendentals at double rounded once to fp32, and the bytes
matched. That is the reading the interpreter is built to, and getting the
rounding the other way round would have produced numbers that look right and
are not.

`canvas/glsl.zig` is the interpreter (lexer, precedence-climbing parser,
tree-walking evaluator over one-to-four-component values).
`canvas/webgl_state.zig` is the state both contexts delegate to, with a
perspective divide, a viewport transform and a point-in-triangle test on pixel
centres between the two interpreter runs.

### The row order the widget would never have caught

The widget reads `gl_FragCoord.x` only, so nothing in either readback notices
if the rows come back upside down. A 3×3 viewport whose shader reads both
components does, and Chrome says:

    202000ff 602000ff 9f2000ff   <- returned first
    206000ff 606000ff 9f6000ff
    209f00ff 609f00ff 9f9f00ff

Green climbs down the returned buffer while red climbs across it: GL's window
origin is the bottom-left and `readPixels` hands back the bottom row first. The
surface underneath stores rows top-down like every other surface in the tree,
so the flip lives where window coordinates become row indices.

### Refusing is part of the answer

Every call in a shader is resolved at compile time, not when a fragment runs.
A shader reaching a builtin this interpreter does not have fails
`COMPILE_STATUS` instead of reporting success and then drawing nothing — a page
told its shader compiled and handed an empty readback has been misled twice,
where a page told it did not compile is in a state real drivers put it in. The
same holds for a draw with no linked program, an unsupported primitive or a
short attribute buffer: the destination keeps whatever the caller put there.

### Five neighbours, all measured rather than assumed

Reading the spec would have got one of these wrong. `getActiveAttrib` reports
the **declared** type — `FLOAT_VEC2` for `attribute vec2 p`, not the `vec4` the
value is padded to on the way in, which is what had been written before the
measurement contradicted it.

| reading | before | Chrome 151 |
|---|---|---|
| `ATTACHED_SHADERS` | 0 | 2 |
| `ACTIVE_ATTRIBUTES` | 0 | 1 |
| `getAttribLocation(p, "p")` | -1 | 0 |
| `getShaderSource` | `""` | the source it was given |
| `getActiveAttrib(p, 0).type` | (null record) | 35664 = `FLOAT_VEC2` |

Two existing assertions were wrong in the same direction: a context cleared to
opaque black reads an alpha of **255**, not 0, and the degenerate triangle in
`#doesNotThrow` (`gl_Position = vec4(0.0)`, so `w` is zero) puts nothing on
screen, which means what comes back there is the clear colour.

Twenty-two operations also stopped being registered as literal no-ops, which
makes them throw for a missing argument the way Chrome does. Each arity was
measured, because an optional object parameter does not count towards WebIDL
`length` and would have silently dropped it — the same cause as the seventeen
in `#missing_argument`.

Both arms, 90 s settle, `canvas-draw-trace.mjs` (35 s is no longer enough for
our arm: reaching the WebGL branch is *more* work than failing out of it, and

of wall clock, so the wait is the page's, not ours):

|  | oracle | here |

| readbacks | 18 | 16 |
| WebGL `readPixels` | 2 | **2** |
| ... `[16,16]` | `zeros=0/1024` | `zeros=0/1024`, fnv `1785938531` both |
| ... `[4,1]` | `zeros=0/16` | `zeros=0/16`, fnv `1065983184` both |

What still differs is what the other plans hold. The two `[2,2] n=8` reads are

## An ImageBitmap carries a snapshot, and the read that used it stops coming back empty (2026-08-23)

`ImageBitmap` held its width and its height and nothing else. `drawImage(bmp)`
therefore had no source to blit, so the widget's readback of the canvas it had
just drawn a bitmap into came back 8624 zero bytes where Chrome has an image.

`createImageBitmap()` now copies the source's pixels into a surface of the
bitmap's own — a *snapshot*, taken there and then, so repainting the source
afterwards does not reach through it — and `close()` releases that copy.

### The half the existing test did not cover, measured rather than reasoned

`src/browser/tests/window/image_bitmap.html` already carried ten expectations
off Chrome 151. Four things it did not settle would each have been guessed
wrong or guessed thinly, so `probes/expr-imagebitmap-pixels.js` measured them:

| case | Chrome |
|---|---|
| `drawImage` of a closed bitmap, element context | `InvalidStateError: Failed to execute 'drawImage' on 'CanvasRenderingContext2D': The image source is detached` |
| the same on an `OffscreenCanvas` context | same sentence, but **`OffscreenCanvasRenderingContext2D`** |
| an `ImageData` source | carries its bytes; bitmap is the ImageData's size |
| crop `sx=3, sw=2` on a 4-wide source | one column of source pixels, one **transparent** — the rect is not clipped |
| crop `sx=-1, sw=2` | leading column transparent, then the source's |
| crop `sx=4, sy=2, sw=-2, sh=-2` | the same rect read forwards |
| a canvas whose only context was WebGL | the cleared colour, `ff0000ff` |

The detached wording naming the *receiver's* interface is the one that matters
for the implementation: the message is built from `T.JsApi.Meta.name` in the
shared mixin rather than hardcoded, and that is measured, not inferred.

Both arms now agree on eight of the probe's nine cases. The ninth is the WebGL
one: `Canvas.pixels()` rasterises nothing for a WebGL canvas, so our bitmap of
one is transparent where Chrome's holds the clear colour. `webgl_state.zig`
does keep a top-down RGBA8 surface now, so closing it is cheap — but the same
accessor feeds `toDataURL` and `convertToBlob`, and what those should answer
for a WebGL canvas is unmeasured. Left as its own question.

### On the live trace, the read changes content and not count

Both arms, 90 s settle, `canvas-draw-trace.mjs`. The readback whose entire op
log is a single `drawImage(ImageBitmap, 0, 0)`:

|  | before | after | oracle |
|---|---|---|---|
| bytes | 8624 | 8624 | 8624 |
| zero bytes | **8624** | **1720** | 1725 |
| fnv | 1883974240 | 2159546272 | 931458320 |

`2159546272` is not an arbitrary improvement: it is byte-identical to *our own*
readback of the 36-op render the bitmap was made from. The oracle has exactly
that relationship — all three of its `[49,44]` reads carry `931458320`, the
hash of its render. What still separates the two hashes is the render, not the
bitmap: radial gradients and glyphs, which is the 48×48 work.

**The readback count did not move: 16 here, 18 on the oracle.** That is worth
stating plainly, because the plan was written expecting it to. The two absent
readbacks turn out not to be waiting on `drawImage` at all — the context lists
say so:

    oracle   x9 [49,44]   x10 [49,44]   x11 canvas/2d [1,1]   x12 [49,44]
    here    x10 [49,44]   x11 [49,44]                          — never created

The oracle builds **three** 49×44 offscreen contexts and we build two, so the
third's readback has no canvas to happen on. And the `canvas/2d [1,1]` context
is the oracle's twelfth, created late in the run; here it is the *first* one
