## The trace said every streamed response weighed nothing (2026-08-23)

`Network.loadingFinished` carries an `encodedDataLength`, and so does the
response object that `Network.responseReceived` carries. This engine answered the
`Content-Length` header in both places. A response that never sends that header
— a chunked h1 reply, anything an h2 origin streams — was therefore announced
as zero bytes long, while the same transfer's Resource Timing entry reported its
real weight. The comment at the second site said as much and left it.

That is not a cosmetic gap: the `fo/` response on a Cloudflare challenge **is**
the VM program the client then runs, and its size is the one number that says
how much work the challenge asked for. `antibot-sweep --trace` records it off
`loadingFinished` precisely so it can be read without patching a prototype in
front of a guard that is deciding whether this is a browser. Every one of those
readings was zero.

### What Chrome puts in the two fields

`cdp-encoded-data-length.mjs` writes each response byte-for-byte over a raw
socket, so the header bytes and the body bytes are separately known and the two
CDP numbers can be checked against them rather than guessed at. Chrome 151,
headless, over CDP:

| response | header bytes | body bytes | `responseReceived` | `loadingFinished` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| plain, `Content-Length` | 129 | 7 046 | 129 | 7 175 |
| gzip | 152 | 105 | 152 | 257 |
| brotli | 149 | 65 | 149 | 214 |
| chunked, no `Content-Length` | 135 | 7 059 | 135 | 7 194 |
| chunked + gzip | 159 | 116 | 159 | 275 |
| 204, empty | 103 | 0 | 103 | — |

So `responseReceived` reports the response head alone — which is all that has
arrived when it fires — and `loadingFinished` reports the head plus the body as
it sat on the wire, before any content-encoding was undone. The chunked rows
count the chunk framing: 7 059 is a 7 046-byte body plus its chunk headers.

A redirect settles the last question. curl accumulates its header-byte counter
across a chain it follows itself, so the reading would be wrong if this engine
let it: it does not, `setFollowLocation(false)`, one transfer per response.
Chrome puts the 302's own 124 bytes on `redirectResponse.encodedDataLength` and
counts only the final hop at `loadingFinished`, and the row matches.

### What this engine answers now

Two curl readings that were already there for the taking: `CURLINFO_HEADER_SIZE`
for the head, and the `CURLINFO_SIZE_DOWNLOAD_T` that `perf-resource-timing`
added for the encoded body. Same probe, same server, both engines:

| response | Chrome `responseReceived` / `loadingFinished` | here |
|---|---|---|
| navigation document | 105 / 438 | 105 / 438 |
| plain | 129 / 7 175 | 129 / 7 175 |
| gzip | 152 / 257 | 152 / 257 |
| brotli | 149 / 214 | 149 / 214 |
| 404 favicon | 45 / 54 | 45 / 54 |
| after a redirect | 129 / 7 175 | 129 / 7 175 |
| chunked | 135 / 7 194 | 135 / **7 181** |
| chunked + gzip | 159 / 275 | 159 / **264** |

Identical everywhere but the chunked rows, which read 13 and 11 bytes low —
exactly the chunk framing, which curl strips before anything here can count it.
Nothing this engine can reach counts those bytes, and no origin worth
disguising against speaks h1 chunked anyway.

### The `fo/` responses, on the real station

`program-origin.mjs` measures both ends of the same load at once: the CDP byte
count off the wire, and the string the page hands to `runProgram`. Same station,
same page, old binary then new:

| `fo/` response | before | after | Chrome |
|---|---|---|---|
| parent realm | 0 | 33 576 | 33 346 |
| widget realm | 0 | 419 957 | — |
| widget, round 2 | 0 | 47 493 | — |
| whole page, all requests | 2 814 (19 req) | 739 618 (19 req) | 153 867 (9 req) |

Chrome's column records only the parent realm's `fo/`: the widget is an
out-of-process iframe, and `program-origin.mjs` attaches to the page target
only, which is also why its request count is half. So the cross-engine
comparison is the one row both arms have: 33 346 against 33 576, 0.7 % apart,
for a body the page measured at 113 584 characters against 113 576. The `fo/` responses are compressed, so the CDP number
is the *wire* weight and the page-side length is the decompressed text — the two
are related by the content-encoding, not by a constant, which is precisely why
the wire number could not be inferred from the page before.

The arithmetic that ties them together still holds, and now both halves of it
can be read off one run:

| where | `fo/` body | ×3/4 | `runProgram` arg | delta |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| here, parent | 113 576 | 85 182 | 85 180 | −2 |
| here, widget | 823 120 | 617 340 | 617 340 | 0 |
| here, widget #2 | 127 724 | 95 793 | 95 792 | −1 |
| chrome, parent | 113 584 | 85 188 | 85 188 | 0 |

Deltas of 0…−2 are base64 padding, which reproduces the twelve-measurement table
further up this file exactly.

And the instrument the plan named, `antibot-sweep --trace` against
`cf-scrapingcourse`, before and after:

    before   0 0 0 0 0 291 0 0 0 291 291 1 291 768 0 291
    after    6003 83028 27513 32348 291 104540 5880 5893 419554 291 291 291 2794 6155 48131 291

Twelve of sixteen `done` events used to report nothing, including all three
`fo/` replies. The station's verdict is unchanged — `cf-challenge`, doc
`403->200`, "Just a moment…" — which is the expected shape: this fixes what the
instrument could see, not what the challenge decides.

### What is still missing from the Network domain

`Network.dataReceived` is not emitted at all. Chrome sends one per body chunk,
carrying the decoded length in `dataLength` and the wire length in
`encodedDataLength`, and a client that sums them arrives at the same total
`loadingFinished` reports. Nothing here needs it — the totals are right without
it — but a trace consumer that watches a transfer progress rather than complete
sees nothing until it ends. Recorded as a gap, not scheduled as work.

## The last three objects two realms were sharing (2026-08-23)

The sweep in "Objects two realms were sharing" left `screen` and
`visualViewport` behind on purpose: both are EventTargets, so splitting them is
not a handle over shared state the way `Storage` was, it is a second instance
with its own listener list. That is this section.

The sweep is now a committed probe rather than an ad-hoc paste,
`probes/expr-realm-shared-objects.js`: 34 paths reachable from the global, each
read in the page and again on a same-origin iframe's `contentWindow`, plus a
`stable` guard so a path that mints a fresh object per read cannot be mistaken
for per-realm identity.

| | before | after | Chrome |
|---|---|---|---|
| paths compared | 34 | 34 | 34 |
| **same object in both realms** | **3** | **0** | **0** |
| unstable within one realm | 0 | 0 | 1 |

The three were `screen`, `screen.orientation` and `visualViewport` — the earlier
count of two did not walk `screen.orientation`, which was shared for the same
reason and by inheritance from it: the `ScreenOrientation` is created lazily on
first read and cached on the `Screen`, so one `Screen` was one orientation
object as well. Every frame now mints its own `Screen` and `VisualViewport` and
all three fall out together. The numbers they report are unchanged, and asserted
unchanged: both types read `frame._page.getViewport()`, so the measurements stay
page-level and only the object identity is per-realm. Pins in
`src/browser/tests/frames/realm_object_identity.html`.

`antibot-sweep --only cf-scrapingcourse` after the change reads exactly as
before it: `cf-challenge`, doc `403->200`, 47 nodes, "Just a moment…". Closing
the last three shared objects did not move that station's verdict.

Readings: `results/probes/expr-realm-shared-objects.{chrome,lightpanda,lightpanda-before}.json`.
The probe needs a real origin — served over loopback, not the bare `about:blank`
target, where a child frame is cross-origin to its parent here and every read
comes back `SecurityError`.

### There is no resize or orientation event to fan out

The plan expected this change to also split an existing dispatch across the new
instances. There is none to split: nothing in this engine fires `resize`,
`orientationchange` or the orientation's `change` at all (`grep` over `src` for
each; every `resize` hit is `ResizeObserver`, the CSS property, an allocator
vtable's `resize` or a comment about the terminal, and `onorientationchange`
occurs only in the two attribute-name tables that spell every `on*` name — the
`Screen`'s `onchange` and the orientation's listener list have no dispatcher
behind them). The viewport can move — `Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride` writes
`browser.viewport_override` and every reader goes through `Page.getViewport` —
but no event follows it, before this change or after. So the per-realm instances
are per-realm listener lists that nothing in-engine dispatches to yet, and a
page that installs a resize handler hears nothing in either arm of a headless
run. Recorded as a gap, not scheduled as work: adding an event Chrome only fires
when metrics change would be new behaviour, not a divergence anyone measured.

### One the sweep did find: `navigator.userAgentData` is stable here

The `stable` column is not decoration. Chrome answers a **fresh
`NavigatorUAData` on every read** — `navigator.userAgentData ===
navigator.userAgentData` is `false` there and `true` here, and `.brands` is
`false` in both arms because that one already builds a new array per read.

    chrome        { uaData: false, brands: false, plugins: true }
    lightpanda    { uaData: true,  brands: false, plugins: true }

One `===` reads it, with no iframe and no realm involved. Out of scope for this
plan — noting it where it was measured.

## The other ten indexed collections (2026-08-23)

`classList` was fixed first because the Turnstile widget stringifies it, and
the commit that fixed it named the ten collections with the same hole and left
them for a plan of their own. This is that plan. An indexed property getter
makes the indices *own* properties in Web IDL; an implementation that answers
`list[0]` but registers no enumerator leaves them reachable and invisible, so
`Object.getOwnPropertyNames(list)` is empty and `JSON.stringify(list)` reads
`{}`.

`probes/expr-indexed-own-names.js` grew four readings for this (the keyframes
rule, a radio node list, a form's controls collection, `document.all`, plus
`document.styleSheets` re-read once it has entries, and `window`'s own numeric
names with the descriptor behind index 0). Twenty readings against Chrome 151:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| readings identical to Chrome | 7 | **13** |
| own-name lists identical to Chrome | 9 | **16** |

Ten enumerators, in three commits: CSSRuleList, StyleSheetList, MediaList and
CSSKeyframesRule; RadioNodeList, HTMLFormControlsCollection,
HTMLOptionsCollection, HTMLAllCollection and DOMStringList; and `window`
itself. The loop is copied per JsApi rather than shared, because the fourteen
collections that already carried an enumerator each carry their own copy.

`window` needed more than the enumerator, and every flag below is measured, not
inferred:

| reading | before | after | Chrome |
|---|---|---|---|
| `getOwnPropertyNames`, numeric | — | `0 1` | `0 1` |
| `Object.keys`, numeric | — | `0 1` | `0 1` |
| descriptor of `0` | `{e:false, c:true, w:true}` | `{e:true, c:true, w:false}` | `{e:true, c:true, w:false}` |
| `window[0] = 5`, strict | silently allowed | `TypeError` | `TypeError` |
| `delete window[0]` | `true` | `false` | `false` |
| `window[99] = x` then read | dropped | dropped | dropped |

The indices are *enumerable*, which is the one place they differ from a
collection's named entries: `HTMLCollection` is
`[LegacyUnenumerableNamedProperties]` and `window`'s frame indices are not.
`window[99]` is refused in all three columns because `window`'s
[[DefineOwnProperty]] rejects every array index, in range or not — that one was
measured on Chrome before it was pinned, and it happened to already hold here.

Pins: `src/browser/tests/css/indexed_own_names.html`,
`collections/indexed_own_names.html`, `frames/window_frame_indices.html`.
Readings: `results/probes/expr-indexed-own-names.{chrome,lightpanda,lightpanda-before}.json`.
`antibot-sweep --only cf-scrapingcourse` after the change: `cf-challenge`, doc
`403->200`, 47 nodes, "Just a moment…" — unchanged.

### What the sweep still reads differently, and none of it is an index

Seven of the twenty readings still differ, and the four that belong to this
family are all about *named* properties rather than indices:

- **`form.elements` and `select.options`** own their supported names in Chrome
  (`0 1 a b`) and *enumerably* — unlike `HTMLCollection`, whose named entries
  are own but skipped by `Object.keys`. Neither is wired up here: only
  `HTMLCollection` carries the `getNames`/`queryByName`/`describeByName` trio.
- **`document.all`** owns its ids the `HTMLCollection` way (own, not
  enumerable). Same missing machinery.
- **`element.attributes`** is the mirror image: our named entries are own *and*
  enumerable, where Chrome's `class`/`id` are own and not. So
  `JSON.stringify(el.attributes)` reads `{"0":{},"1":{},"class":{},"id":{}}`
  here against Chrome's `{"0":{},"1":{}}` — a divergence in the direction
  nobody added on purpose.
- **`window.fa`**, a frame reached by its name, is `undefined` here. `window`
  has no named-property handler at all, and adding one to the global object is
  not a line in this plan.

The remaining three are not this family: `getClientRects` is layout numbers,
`inlineStyle` is the CSS property list, and `document.all` counts 20 elements
here against Chrome's 21 on the same page. One more thing fell out of the
window probe and is worth writing down where it was measured: removing an
`<iframe>` element leaves `window.length` at its old value here and drops it
immediately in Chrome, so the frame is not detached from `child_frames` when
its element goes.

## Seven sentences behind one exception name (2026-08-23)

`js-error-message-text` measured 28 deliberate throws in both engines and found
one shape of divergence: `name`, `code`, the constructor and whether the call
throws at all already matched Chrome everywhere, and only `message` differed.
Two sibling plans closed `atob`/`btoa` and the constructor `TypeError`s. This
one takes the rest — the DOM throwers a page reaches in one line, plus
`getRandomValues` and `structuredClone`.

The mechanism was never the obstacle. `Context.fail` already stores a message
that `domExceptionToJs` puts on the exception, leaving the spec's generic table
as the fallback. What each site needed was to be handed the sentence, and the
sentences are not one per exception name — they are one per *branch*:

| exception | Chrome's sentences |
|---|---|
| `HierarchyRequestError` | 7 |
| `NotFoundError` (node mutation) | 3 |
| `InvalidCharacterError` (attribute names) | 4 |
| `InvalidCharacterError` (element names) | 5 |
| `SyntaxError` (selectors) | 2 × interface |

So `e.message` tells a page which of seven pre-insert branches rejected its
`appendChild`, and one generic description for all seven is the tell.

### The parts that are interpolated

A single case per family would have missed all of these, so the probe reads
several per family:

- **The tag name and the selector are echoed back**, quoted:
  `The tag name provided ('1x') is not a valid name.`,
  `'###' is not a valid selector.`
- **The interface follows the receiver.** `document.querySelector('###')` says
  `'Document'`, `div.querySelector('###')` says `'Element'`, and a
  `DocumentFragment` names itself. Same rejection, three sentences.
- **`createElementNS` names the first character the production tripped over**
  (`contains the invalid character '1'`), not the whole name — so knowing
  *that* a name is invalid is not enough to write the message.
- **Node mutation echoes both node names**, the child's then the parent's, and
  an element's is its `nodeName`: upper case in an HTML document.
  `Nodes of type '#document' may not be inserted inside nodes of type 'DIV'.`
- **`getRandomValues` quotes the byte length, not the element count.** A
  `Uint16Array` of 65536 elements reports `131072`.
- **`structuredClone` names the interface of a host object it cannot clone**:
  `HTMLDivElement object could not be cloned.`

### Two of these were behaviour, not wording

The sweep that produced the sentences also caught two divergences that no
amount of message text would have fixed:

- **`closest` never went through the DOMException mapping** its three
  neighbours share, so `div.closest('###')` threw `Error: InvalidIDSelector` —
  the raw Zig error name, which no browser produces and which is a louder
  reading than any wording. It goes through the same funnel now.
- **Attribute names were held to the XML `Name` production.** Blink is not:
  walking every code point `0x00`-`0xFF` through `setAttribute` in Chrome 151,
  in first and in middle position, the entire rejected set is *empty name* plus
  NUL, tab, LF, FF, CR, space, `/`, `=` and `>`. Nine characters, position
  independent. So `setAttribute('0abc')`, `'.foo'`, `'@'`, `'!'` and `'~'` all
  worked in Chrome and threw here. Vertical tab is *not* in Blink's set even
  though it is whitespace, which is why the check cannot be
  `std.ascii.isWhitespace`. The same relaxed rule covers `toggleAttribute`,
  `createAttribute` and `setAttributeNS` — one rule, four different sentences.

The existing `invalidAttributeNames` test block asserted our stricter rule, so
it was rewritten against the measurement rather than kept.

### Readings

`probes/expr-error-message-dom-crypto.js`, 34 cases, three arms in
`results/probes/expr-error-message-dom-crypto.{chrome,lightpanda,lightpanda-before}.json`:
**2/34 identical to Chrome before, 34/34 after.** The parent plan's 28-case
sweep, which had been at 27/28 with `structuredClone` the last one out, is now
**28/28**.

`make test` 1429/1429, `zig fmt --check` clean.

### What was measured and deliberately not built

- **`shadowRoot.querySelector` says `'DocumentFragment'` here.** Chrome says
  `'ShadowRoot'`. `ShadowRoot` reuses `DocumentFragment`'s methods, so telling
  them apart means giving `ShadowRoot` its own pair rather than passing a
  different string. Not read out of Chrome either, so it is a gap, not a fix.
- **`postMessage` and `BroadcastChannel` still send the bare sentence.** They
  share the serializer with `structuredClone` and Blink gives each its own
  prefix (`Failed to execute 'postMessage' on 'Worker': `), but none of those
  were measured — the prefix is threaded through as an optional argument and
  those callers pass `null` rather than a guessed string.
- **`document.appendChild(div)` does not throw here** on an `about:blank` page
  where Chrome says `Only one element on document allowed.`; the check exists
  and fires on a `createDocument` tree, so what differs is whether the blank
  document has an element child at all. Separate from the wording.

## The worker realm is a hand-picked subset, and it is 124 names short (P1–P2, 2026-08-23)

Every surface reading above this line was taken in a Window realm. The station
this fork is measured against does not ask its questions there: it builds a
blob worker whose entire program is an `eval` trampoline, posts source text in,
and reads the answer back out. Whatever it asks is answered by a
`DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope`, and nobody had ever read one.

`probes/expr-worker-surface.js` reads the same reader twice in one page — once
inside the worker, once in the page that built it — so a worker-only difference
can be told from a difference this engine has in both realms. Readings:
`results/probes/expr-worker-surface.{chrome,lightpanda}.json`, headless Chrome
151 against the engine built from `efcc66db3`, both arms on a loopback http
origin.

**The two arms need different drivers, and that is not a detail.** This engine
does not run scheduled tasks while an `awaitPromise` evaluate is outstanding —
already recorded at the top of `run-page-probe.mjs` — so a probe that awaits a
worker's message never returns under `run-expr.mjs` or `run-probe.mjs`; it hangs
until the CDP client's own 30 s timeout. The lightpanda arm goes through
`run-page-probe.mjs` (page load), the Chrome arm through
`run-probe.mjs chrome <probe> http://127.0.0.1:<port>/`. `about:blank` is the
one URL not to compare across engines, because the secure-context gate reads it
differently on the two.

### The size of it

| level | Chrome 151 | here |
|---|---|---|
| `self` | 336 | **212** |
| `DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope.prototype` | 3 | 1 |
| `WorkerGlobalScope.prototype` | 30 | 25 |
| `EventTarget.prototype` | 5 | 4 |
| `Object.prototype` | 12 | 12 |

The chain has the same shape and the same length. What differs is what is on
it. For scale, the **window** realm of the same sitting is 1237 against 1203 —
34 names apart, and every one of those 34 is a feature this engine does not
implement. The worker realm is 124 apart **in names this engine already has**.

`bridge.zig`'s `worker_common_apis` is a hand-written list of about ninety
modules with a `TODO: Expand this list to include all worker-appropriate APIs.`
above it. That TODO is the whole finding.

### (A) 124 names we implement, in a realm we did not name them in

Chrome's worker carries them and so does *our own window realm*; only our
worker does not. In rough families: the whole WebGPU surface (45), WebUSB (13),
WebHID (4), WebCodecs (11), Background Fetch (3), Push (3), Media Source (4),
`Cache`/`CacheStorage`, `FontFace`/`FontFaceSet`, `ImageBitmap` +
`ImageBitmapRenderingContext` + `createImageBitmap`, `ImageDecoder`/`ImageTrack`/
`ImageTrackList`, `Lock`/`LockManager`, `Scheduler`/`TaskController`/`TaskSignal`/
`TaskPriorityChangeEvent`, `TrustedHTML`/`TrustedScript`/`TrustedScriptURL`/
`TrustedTypePolicy`/`TrustedTypePolicyFactory` + `trustedTypes`,
`PerformanceResourceTiming`/`PerformanceServerTiming`, `Serial`/`SerialPort`,
`ServiceWorkerRegistration`, `StorageBucket`/`StorageBucketManager`,
`SyncManager`/`PeriodicSyncManager`, `NavigationPreloadManager`,
`NetworkInformation`, `MediaCapabilities`, `UserActivation`, `CSSSkewX`/
`CSSSkewY`, `Worker` itself, and the members `caches`, `crossOriginIsolated`,
`name`, `onlanguagechange`, `origin`, plus `PERSISTENT`/`TEMPORARY`.

`trustedTypes` is worth naming on its own, because the station reads it
directly. Its trampoline worker's entire preamble is
`var _p=null;if(self.trustedTypes)try{_p=self.trustedTypes.createPolicy('Kssz2',…)}`
— a feature detect that takes the other branch here, every time.

### (B) 17 names Chrome's worker has that we have in neither realm

`BarcodeDetector`, `CreateMonitor`, `FileSystemObserver`, `Observable`,
`PressureObserver`, `PressureRecord`, `RestrictionTarget`, `Subscriber`,
`Temporal`, `WebSocketError`, `WebSocketStream`, `WorkerNavigator`, `fonts`,
`onrtctransform`, `webkitRequestFileSystemSync`,
`webkitResolveLocalFileSystemSyncURL`, and `EventTarget.prototype.when`. All but
`WorkerNavigator` are also missing from our window realm, so they are not
worker-realm findings; they belong to whatever plan closes the window shortfall.

### (C) 8 names our worker carries that a Chrome worker does not

Window-only in Chrome, and every one of them a leak:

| name | how it got in |
|---|---|
| `Navigator` | `worker_common_apis` names `Navigator.zig` — see below |
| `CookieStore`, `CookieChangeEvent`, `cookieStore` | named outright; `cookieStore` is Window and ServiceWorker, not DedicatedWorker |
| `PerformanceNavigation`, `PerformanceTiming` | flattened in with `Performance.zig`'s type list |
| `WebKitCSSMatrix`, `webkitURL` | `constructor_aliases` of `DOMMatrix` and `URL`, which are worker-exposed while the aliases are not |

### The worker-only readings, which is what this plan is actually for

Sorted by how loudly each answers a fingerprinter:

1. **`navigator` here is a `Navigator`, and in a worker it is a
   `WorkerNavigator`.** `Object.prototype.toString.call(navigator)` answers
   `[object Navigator]` against Chrome's `[object WorkerNavigator]`, and
   `navigator.constructor.name` says the same. The brand is the small half. The
   large half is that nine window-only members come with it: `webdriver`,
   `vendor`, `vendorSub`, `productSub`, `doNotTrack`, `cookieEnabled`,
   `pdfViewerEnabled`, `javaEnabled`, `maxTouchPoints`. **`navigator.webdriver`
   does not exist at all in a Chrome worker** — not `false`, absent — and a
   worker that answers `false` has answered a question no browser was asked.
2. **`self.origin` is `undefined`** where Chrome answers the owner's origin
   (`http://127.0.0.1:9701`). Ours is not a wrong string; the property is not
   there.
3. **`self.crossOriginIsolated` is `undefined`.** It was fixed in the window
   realm and the worker never got it, so a challenge that is cross-origin
   isolated reads `true` in the page and `undefined` one thread over.
4. **`self.name` is `undefined`** where Chrome answers `""` for an unnamed
   worker.
5. **A blob URL is parsed as though the scheme were not there.**

   | | Chrome 151 | here |
   |---|---|---|
   | `location.origin` | `http://127.0.0.1:9701` | `"null"` |
   | `location.host` | `""` | `127.0.0.1:58749` |
   | `location.hostname` | `""` | `127.0.0.1` |
   | `location.port` | `""` | `58749` |
   | `location.pathname` | `http://127.0.0.1:9701/<uuid>` | `/<uuid>` |

   `blob:http://host/uuid` has one opaque path — the whole `http://host/uuid` —
   and no host of its own; the origin comes from the inner URL. We parse the
   inner URL as if it were the outer one and then hand back `"null"` for the
   origin we did have.
6. **`console` sits on `WorkerGlobalScope.prototype` as well as on `self`.**
   Chrome has it own on `self` and nowhere else. `cookieStore` is on that
   prototype too and should not exist at all (C above).
7. **`DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope.prototype` is missing `PERSISTENT` and
   `TEMPORARY`** — the same two deprecated quota constants already recorded as
   missing from `Window.prototype`.

Two rows in that list are *not* worker findings and are recorded so nobody
chases them here: `performance` lacks the three `EventTarget` methods in both
realms (this engine's `Performance` does not inherit `EventTarget`), and the
`HeadlessChrome`/`Chrome` split in the user agent is this fork's deliberate
disguise, not a gap.

### What the seven cost, and the one that could not be paid (P3, 2026-08-23)

All seven are closed. Rerun of the same probe against the engine built from this
branch, worker realm, both arms in one sitting:

| | before | after | Chrome 151 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `self` own names | 212 | 211 | 336 |
| `DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope.prototype` | 1 | **3** | 3 |
| names our worker has and Chrome's does not | 8 | **4** | — |
| `navigator` brand | `[object Navigator]` | `[object WorkerNavigator]` | `[object WorkerNavigator]` |
| window-only members on `navigator` | 9 | **0** | 0 |
| `self.origin` / `self.name` / `self.crossOriginIsolated` | all `undefined` | the owner's origin / `""` / `false` | same |
| `location.origin` in a blob worker | `"null"` | the inner origin | the inner origin |
| `location.host` / `port` / `pathname` | inner URL's | `""` / `""` / whole inner URL | same |

`self` going *down* by one while all of that was added is the leak count paying
for it: `Navigator`, `CookieStore` and `CookieChangeEvent` left, `WorkerNavigator`
arrived, `cookieStore` came off the global, and `name` went on.

The four names still ours alone are the two that ride in on a flattened type
list (`PerformanceNavigation`, `PerformanceTiming`, behind `Performance.zig`) and
the two `constructor_aliases` (`WebKitCSSMatrix`, `webkitURL`). Neither
mechanism has a realm gate, which is a bridge change rather than a list edit.

#### A worker realm cannot borrow its owner's Frame

Trusted Types was going to come with this pass, because the station's own
trampoline worker feature-detects `self.trustedTypes` in its first statement.
It cannot, and the reason is worth recording as a rule rather than a note.

`Caller.getGlobalArg` answers `unreachable` when a bound member wants a `*Frame`
and the realm is a worker. A worker *has* a frame — the one that created it, the
same one its origin, secure-context bit and cross-origin isolation already come
from — so returning it looks like the obvious repair, and it behaves: the engine
builds, all 1433 tests pass, and a local page whose blob worker calls
`trustedTypes.createPolicy('Kssz2', {createScript: …})` gets a policy back.

Against the live station it aborts. With that one line changed and
`trustedTypes`/`caches` exposed on top of it, `antibot-sweep --only
cf-scrapingcourse` went from `cf-challenge / 47 nodes / "Just a moment…"` to
**`CRASHED SIGABRT`**, twice, with the stack ending in the trampoline worker's
own `onmessage` dispatch. Reverting the line — and only that line, plus the two
accessors that needed it — restored the control reading exactly: `cf-challenge`,
`doc=403->200`, 47 nodes. The frame's factory and arenas belong to the page
thread, and a worker running on its own thread reaching through them is a race
that a local single-page probe does not provoke.

So: **a member that takes a `*Frame` stays out of the worker realm.** That is
also the ceiling on the 122-name shortfall — the families in it that resolve
through a Frame (`gpu`, `usb`, `hid`, `serial`, `locks`, `connection`,
`mediaCapabilities`, `storageBuckets`, and Trusted Types) need worker-owned state
before they can be named, not a line in a list.

The challenge still refuses (`cf-challenge`, same verdict as the control), so
none of this was the deciding property. The realm it asks its questions in now
answers as a worker rather than as a borrowed window.

### The last four leaks, and 57 of the names (cfsc-worker-surface-rest, 2026-08-23)

The worker realm's own-name diff against Chrome is now **0 extra, 72 short**,
against 4 extra and 129 short at the end of the pass above. Same probe, same two
drivers, engine built from this branch; reading refreshed in place at
`results/probes/expr-worker-surface.lightpanda.json`.

| | before | after | Chrome 151 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `self` own names | 211 | **264** | 336 |
| names our worker has and Chrome's does not | 4 | **0** | — |
| names Chrome's worker has and ours does not | 129 | **72** | — |

The window realm is untouched at 1203 against 1237 — the same two deliberate
extras (`ModelContext`, `ModelContextClient`) and the same 36 short.

#### An interface object needed its own `[Exposed]`

All four leaks got in by riding along with something else, and neither carrier
had a realm gate:

- `PerformanceTiming` and `PerformanceNavigation` are in `Performance.zig`'s
  `registerTypes()`, and `worker_common_apis` names the file. Their only
  reference is `performance.timing` / `.navigation`, both already
  `.exposed = .window`, so the interface object was the whole of their presence
  in a worker.
- `WebKitCSSMatrix` and `webkitURL` are `constructor_aliases` on `DOMMatrix` and
  `URL`, and a worker has both of those interfaces.

`[Exposed]` was a member-level annotation only; it now has an interface-level
half. `Meta.exposed` gates the one place in `Snapshot.zig` where a name reaches
a global — the type still goes in both realms' lists, because they share one
`JsApiLookup` and the template and class id are not optional.

The aliases needed no annotation at all, because there is nothing to decide per
interface. Chrome's Window carries 14 webkit-prefixed names and its dedicated
worker carries four, and the four are `WorkerGlobalScope` *operations*
(`webkitRequestFileSystem` and friends) rather than interface objects. Not one
legacy alias crosses, so the whole block is window-only.

#### 57 of the 129 were already built, just never named here

Of the 129 missing names, 115 are interfaces this engine already implements for
the page realm. What decides which of those can be named is not judgement, it is
the Frame rule from the section above: **57 have no member that wants the owner's
Frame, and they all go on.** WebCodecs whole (the reason media work moves off the
page in the first place), `ImageBitmap` and its canvas context, the prioritised
scheduler behind the `self.scheduler` that was already exposed, cache storage,
`NetworkInformation`, resource and server timing, the USB/HID/Serial families
whole, ten of `service_worker.zig`'s twelve, and five of
`navigator/services.zig`'s seventeen.

Two exclusions inside otherwise-eligible files are worth naming, since the audit
that finds them is per *type*, not per file:

- `service_worker.zig` also registers `ServiceWorker` itself and
  `CookieStoreManager`, neither of which a dedicated worker carries — the cookie
  store is Window and ServiceWorker only, which is the same reason `CookieStore`
  came out in the pass above.
- `navigator/services.zig` fails the Frame rule twice, differently. `GPU` has
  `wgslLanguageFeatures`, which takes a `*Frame` outright. `StorageBucket` has
  `indexedDB`, which reaches `global.frame` *through the Execution* — the member
  signature is clean and the hazard is inside the body, on a stated assumption
  ("Window-only, so the global is always a Frame") that naming the type in a
  worker list would quietly falsify. So its bucket manager stays out with it.

#### What the remaining 72 are

| | count | why |
|---|---|---|
| Frame-bound families we implement | 58 | WebGPU (40 incl. `WGSLLanguageFeatures`' owner), Trusted Types (5), MediaSource (4), Trusted-Types-adjacent `FontFace`/`FontFaceSet` (2), `CSSSkewX`/`CSSSkewY` (2, through `CSSStyleValue.toString`), `StorageBucket`/`StorageBucketManager` (2), nested `Worker` (1), the two `webkit*FileSystem*` operations (2) |
| not implemented in either realm | 14 | `BarcodeDetector`, `CreateMonitor`, `FileSystemObserver`, `Observable`, `PressureObserver`, `PressureRecord`, `RestrictionTarget`, `Subscriber`, `Temporal`, `WebSocketError`, `WebSocketStream`, `onrtctransform`, `webkitRequestFileSystemSync`, `webkitResolveLocalFileSystemSyncURL` |

So the shortfall is no longer a list to expand. Every remaining name needs either
worker-owned state to replace the borrowed Frame, or the feature itself.

`trustedTypes` is still the one that stings, because the station's trampoline
worker feature-detects it in its first statement — and it is squarely in the
first row.

#### The A/B

`antibot-sweep --only cf-scrapingcourse` after each of the two batches:
`cf-challenge`, `doc=403->200`, 47 nodes, `"Just a moment..."` — the control
reading, unchanged, no abort. `make test` 1433/1433 for both. The challenge
still refuses, so the 57 names were not the deciding property either; the realm
it is asked in is now 264 names wide against Chrome's 336, with nothing in it
that Chrome does not have.

### The Frame was never the requirement — Trusted Types in a worker (worker-trusted-types-state, 2026-08-23)

The section above closed with Trusted Types in the "needs worker-owned state
before it can be named" row, and that row was wrong about what the obstacle was.
It is now live in the worker realm, `createPolicy` and all, and the fix touched
no state at all.

`trusted_types.zig` took a `*Frame` in seven places and wanted exactly four
things from it: a factory to create branded objects in, an arena to dupe a
policy name into, the isolate to throw on, and the local handle to call the
page's callback through. **All four are on `*Execution`, and `Env.zig` builds one
per context out of that context's own global** — `._factory = global._factory`,
`.arena = global.arena`. So a worker's Execution already *is* worker-owned
state; the file was reaching past it to the frame that happened to be more
familiar. One of the file's own members, `getTypeMapping`, already took an
`*Execution`.

Seven signatures changed from `frame: *Frame` to `exec: *Execution`, the file's
`Frame` import came out, `WorkerGlobalScope` got a `_trusted_types` factory of
its own next to its scheduler and crypto, and the module went on
`worker_common_apis`.

**The A/B, which is the whole point.** The previous attempt at this — handing the
worker realm `worker._frame` out of `getGlobalArg` — turned `cf-scrapingcourse`
into `CRASHED SIGABRT`, twice. Through an Execution instead: `cf-challenge`,
`doc=403->200`, 47 nodes, `"Just a moment..."`, **three consecutive runs**, which
is the control reading exactly. `make test` 1435/1435. So the abort was never
"Trusted Types in a worker" — it was the borrowed Frame, and nothing else.

| | before | after | Chrome 151 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `self` own names | 264 | **269** | 336 |
| `WorkerGlobalScope.prototype` | 25 | **26** | 30 |
| names Chrome's worker has and ours does not | 72 | **67** | — |
| `self.trustedTypes` | `undefined` | `[object TrustedTypePolicyFactory]` | same |
| `createPolicy('Kssz2', {createScript}).createScript('x')` | — | `[object TrustedScript]`, `"x/ok"` | same |

The station's trampoline worker opens with
`var _p=null;if(self.trustedTypes)try{_p=self.trustedTypes.createPolicy('Kssz2',…)}`,
and that branch is now the one it takes. The verdict is still `cf-challenge`, so
the feature detect was not the deciding property either — but it was the one
place in the whole worker realm where the station's own code was demonstrably
reading us and getting `undefined`.

**The rule this replaces.** "A member that takes a `*Frame` stays out of the
worker realm" still holds as written — you may not hand a worker its owner's
Frame. What does not follow, and what the section above assumed, is that such a
member is therefore *stuck*. Check what it actually wants from the Frame first:
if it is a factory, an arena, a scheduler, the isolate or the local handle, an
`*Execution` has all of them per-realm and the conversion is mechanical. Only a
member that wants something genuinely page-scoped — the DOM, the frame's URL, the
navigation state — is really blocked.

By that test the remaining 67 divide differently than the table above suggests,
and the next pass should re-audit rather than trust it: WebGPU wants one Frame
for one accessor, `StorageBucket.indexedDB` reaches `global.frame.window`, and
the MediaSource and font families want a Page. Those are three different
distances from possible.

### The re-audit, and what a `*Frame` actually costs (worker-frame-to-execution, 2026-08-23)

The section above ended by asking for a re-audit of the remaining 67 names
rather than trusting its own table. Here it is. Of the 53 that this engine had
in the window realm and not the worker, **50 were reachable** and are now
exposed; 3 stay out. The worker realm's own-name count went 269 → **319**
against Chrome 151's 336, the names Chrome's worker has and ours does not went
67 → **17**, and the names we have and Chrome does not stayed at **0**. The
window realm did not move (1203 vs 1237, the same two deliberate `ModelContext`
extras).

| | before | after | Chrome 151 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `self` own names | 269 | **319** | 336 |
| `WorkerGlobalScope.prototype` | 26 | **27** | 30 |
| names Chrome's worker has and ours does not | 67 | **17** | — |
| names ours has and Chrome's does not | 0 | **0** | — |

**The question that did the work.** Not "does this member take a `*Frame`" but
"what is it reaching through the Frame *for*". Every answer that came back was
per-realm state the Execution already carries:

| what it wanted | where it is on `*Execution` | families |
|---|---|---|
| object factory | `exec._factory` | WebGPU (40 names), the storage buckets, the fonts, MSE |
| pooled arena | `exec.getArena` | FontFace, FontFaceSet |
| local handle / isolate | `exec.js.local`, `exec.js` | all of them |
| the realm's IDB factory | `switch (exec.js.global)` | `StorageBucket.indexedDB` |
| the realm's listener list | `switch (exec.js.global)` | `FontFaceSet.load` |
| the realm's own slots | `switch (exec.js.global)` | the two sandboxed filesystems |

The last three are the interesting ones, because they are not a signature change
— they are a member that had hard-coded *which* realm it belonged to.
`StorageBucket.indexedDB` read `exec.js.global.frame.window`, with a comment
saying "Window-only, so the global is always a Frame". Both arms of that union
answer `getIndexedDB`. `FontFaceSet.load` dispatched into the frame's event
manager; a FontFaceSet is an EventTarget, and an EventTarget exposed in two
realms has to dispatch into the asking realm's list. `filesystem.forKind` kept
its two DOMFileSystem objects on `window._filesystems` and read the origin off
the frame — both per-realm, and the filesystem *name* is built from the origin,
so a worker borrowing the window's would have been observably wrong rather than
merely borrowed.

**One trap worth naming: `*Page` is not safer than `*Frame`.** MSE's two list
accessors took `page: *Page`, and `getGlobalArg` *does* answer `ctx.page` in a
worker realm — so they looked exposable as they stood. They were not:
`page.factory` is the owner's, so the SourceBufferList would have come back
branded in the wrong realm. That is the same bug the Frame rule exists to
prevent, arriving through a type the rule does not mention. The rule is about
per-realm state, not about the word `Frame`.

**Where the ground truth had to be read rather than reasoned.** Three readings
changed the implementation:

- `MediaSource.canConstructInDedicatedWorker` is a static that exists to say a
  dedicated worker is the only realm Chrome constructs a MediaSource in. Ours
  answered true in a realm with no MediaSource — the surface contradicting its
  own static.
- Five of the 40 WebGPU names (`GPUBufferUsage`, `GPUColorWrite`, `GPUMapMode`,
  `GPUShaderStage`, `GPUTextureUsage`) are namespace objects, not interface
  objects, on Chrome as much as here. A `typeof === 'function'` check over the
  family fails on exactly those five.
- `webkitRequestFileSystem` and `webkitResolveLocalFileSystemURL` are **own
  properties of the worker global**, not `WorkerGlobalScope.prototype` members.
  Only a `[Global]` interface's own members land there, so they belong on
  `DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope` — next to the `TEMPORARY`/`PERSISTENT` constants
  they take, which were already there. Chrome also reports arity **2** for the
  request operation in a worker where its Window reports **3**, with the same
  optional error callback in both. That is Chrome's inconsistency; both numbers
  are mirrored where they were read.

**What stays out, and the two reasons are different.** Of the 17 remaining, 11
are interfaces neither realm implements (`BarcodeDetector`, `CreateMonitor`,
`FileSystemObserver`, `Observable`, `PressureObserver`, `PressureRecord`,
`RestrictionTarget`, `Subscriber`, `Temporal`, `WebSocketError`,
`WebSocketStream`), 2 are the sync filesystem operations, 1 is `onrtctransform`,
and 3 are the audit's leftovers:

- **`Worker` (nested workers)** is genuinely frame-scoped. `Worker.init` takes
  the session off the frame, resolves against the frame's base URL, fetches
  through `frame.newRequest` and registers with `frame.trackWorker`. This is
  what the rule's exception actually looks like: it needs a worker-side spawn
  path, not an argument change.
- **`CSSSkewX`/`CSSSkewY`** are not blocked at all. typed_om.zig's 112
  `frame: *Frame` signatures want `js`, `local_arena`, `_factory`,
  `dupeString`, `arena`, `call_arena` and `_page` — every one on the Execution.
  What stops them is the other end: Chrome exposes exactly those two of the
  whole typed-OM family in a worker and *none of their prototype chain*
  (`CSSTransformComponent`, `CSSStyleValue`). Matching that is not the
  mechanical conversion the rest of the audit was.

**The A/B, three batches deep.** `cf-scrapingcourse` after WebGPU, after
MSE+buckets+fonts, and after the filesystem: `cf-challenge`, `doc=403->200`,
47 nodes, `"Just a moment..."` — **two consecutive runs at each of the three
checkpoints, six in total**, which is the control reading exactly. `make test`
1435/1435 at each. The verdict has not moved; the surface it is reading has.

## Twelve of nineteen colour notations painted the previous colour (2026-08-23)

`ctx.fillStyle = 'rgb(255, 0, 0)'; ctx.fillRect(...)` filled **blue**, because
the fill before it was blue. So did `hsl()`, `hwb()`, `lab()`, `lch()`,
`oklab()`, `oklch()`, `color()` and `currentColor`: `RGBA.parse` read a hex form
and a name and nothing else, and the setter's `catch self._fill_style` turned
every other notation into silence. Only hex, the named colours and
`transparent` worked. A page that fills red and reads back blue is a tell one
line of JS finds, and it does not need a canvas hash to find it.

**The measurement had to come first, because the notations do not all behave the
same way.** `probes/canvas-color-notation.js` puts 86 notations through a 2D
context on headed Chrome and records three things for each: the string
`fillStyle` answers, the bytes `fillRect` leaves in each of four
canvas-space × readback-space combinations, and what the context says about
itself. Readings in `results/canvas-color-notation.chrome.json`, this engine's
arm in `results/canvas-color-notation.lightpanda.json`.

What that turned up, none of it derivable from the spec text:

- **The notations split in two, by what comes back rather than by how they are
  computed.** Hex, a name, `rgb()`, `hsl()` and `hwb()` all collapse to a hex
  string, or to `rgba()` when translucent. `lab()`, `lch()`, `oklab()`,
  `oklch()` and `color()` are answered back as *themselves*, canonicalised:
  `lab(50% 40 30)` → `lab(50 40 30)`, `color(xyz 0.5 0.25 0.1)` →
  `color(xyz-d65 0.5 0.25 0.1)`, `color(display-p3 50% 25% 50%)` →
  `color(display-p3 0.5 0.25 0.5)`. So a context cannot keep only the bytes it
  paints with. `color.Wide` is the source of those five — plain data, no slices,
  so the save/restore stack copies it and no arena is involved.
- **The canonicalisation has its own rules, all measured.** `none` is kept as
  `none`; an alpha of exactly one, or one that clamps to it, is dropped from the
  string entirely; a lightness clamps ([0,100] for lab/lch, [0,1] for
  oklab/oklch) and the clamped value is what is written back; a chroma clamps at
  zero; a hue wraps ( `lch(50 40 400)` → `lch(50 40 40)`, `-30` → `330`) and
  loses its unit; a percentage is worth 125 on lab's a and b, 150 on lch's
  chroma, 0.4 on the oklab family's, and 1 everywhere in `color()`; and
  `color()`'s channels are *not* clamped, so `color(srgb 1.5 -0.5 0.5)` comes
  back whole. The comma grammar is rejected for all five.
- **a98-rgb uses a plain 2.2, not CSS Color 4's 563/256.** Four of the five a98
  readings cannot tell the two exponents apart. The one that can —
  `color(a98-rgb 1 0.25 0.5)`, which Chrome answers `ff3d82` — puts the green
  channel at 61.5017 under the spec exponent, a thousandth of a byte over the
  rounding boundary, and at 61.4676 under 2.2.
- **The alpha a canvas writes back was two decimals and should be shortest.**
  `#ff000080` read `rgba(255, 0, 0, 0.50)` where Chrome says `0.5`, and
  `transparent` read `0.00` where Chrome says `0`. The correct serialiser
  already existed in `CSSStyleDeclaration.zig` and nowhere else; it, `hslToRgb`
  and `hwbToRgb` moved down into `color.zig`, which is where the canvas could
  reach them.

**Result: the `fillStyle` strings are 86/86 identical to Chrome, and the srgb /
rgba-unorm8 pixels 85/86.** The one miss is `color(display-p3 1 0.25 0.5 / 0.5)`
— with an alpha, Chrome's *colour* channels shift too (`ff1c7e` against the
opaque `ff1b7f`), which is its premultiplied 8-bit storage round trip, not its
parser. Two readings elsewhere in the set land within a twentieth of a rounding
boundary and answer one LSB away: Skia carries its gamut matrices as D50 fixed
point, so a knife-edge channel can fall either side of the boundary. Those two
were not knife-edge luck and they have since been chased — see "The srgb ↔
display-p3 transform is three layers of Skia" below, which closes them.

### What the same probe found next door, and why it is a different axis

The Turnstile widget's four canvases (`results/ibt2-oracle.json`) are not one
canvas read four ways — they are `{srgb, display-p3}` × `{unorm8, float16}`,
each built with `willReadFrequently: true` and read back with the *matching*
settings. An earlier note read the display-p3 row as a conversion applied at
readback time; it is not, it is a display-p3 **canvas**. That distinction
matters because it puts the row in a different place: `getContext('2d', …)`
discards its options here, `getContextAttributes()` answers a fixed struct
(so `willReadFrequently` reads `false` on a context created with `true`), and
`getImageData` has no fifth parameter at all. Three of the probe's four pixel
columns diverge for that one reason, and the fix is a different shape — a canvas
that has a colour space has to keep the source colour for `fillStyle` to answer
with *and* the converted bytes to paint with. It is `cfsc-canvas-color-space`,
with the measured targets already in it.

## globalCompositeOperation and filter were stored, echoed and never read (2026-08-24)

Both attributes existed as fingerprint surface only: the setters validated and
kept them, the getters answered, and the rasteriser painted source-over with an
unfiltered paint whatever they said. That made the widget's
grayscale-then-difference pass a no-op — the second `drawImage` overwrote the
first instead of differencing against it — so the 80×24 readback came back as
the text panel where Chrome hands over 1920 pixels of opaque black, and the 1×1
downscale taken from it reported white.

**1920 of 1920 pixels wrong: the largest single all-wrong block measured on
that program.**

### What Chrome actually does, measured before anything was written

`probes/expr-composite-blend.js` sweeps (backdrop alpha × source alpha ×
globalAlpha) for the two blend modes, because the informative cells are the
ones where either side is partly transparent — opaque-over-opaque is just the
blend function, and a naive "apply the blend function to the two colours" gets
it right by accident there and wrong everywhere else.

| case | Chrome 151 | what it pins down |
|---|---|---|
| `difference` opaque `#ff8000` ← `#4080c0` | `191,0,192,255` | `B(Cb,Cs) = \|Cb−Cs\|` |
| `multiply` same | `64,64,0,255` | `B(Cb,Cs) = Cb·Cs` |
| either, no backdrop | the source, opaque | nothing to blend with |
| `difference`, source α=0.5 | `223,64,96,255` | the blend governs only the overlap |
| `difference`, backdrop α=0.5 | `128,64,192,255` | the uncovered source stays itself |
| `difference`, both α=0.5 | `170,85,128,192` | all three terms of the spec formula |
| a path's half-covered edge pixel | `223,64,96,255` | coverage *is* the source alpha |

The last row is the one that decides where the arithmetic goes: a half-covered
path pixel reads exactly what a half-opaque fill reads, so coverage multiplies
into the source alpha and the blend needs no separate handling for edges.

`probes/expr-canvas-filter-grayscale.js` does the same for `filter`, and three
of its answers contradict what the plan assumed:

- **It reaches a plain fill, not only `drawImage`.** A `fillRect` of `#4080c0`
  under `grayscale(1)` reads `119,119,119`. So the filter belongs on the paint
  going into the rasteriser, where every entry point gets it at once, rather
  than inside `drawSurface`.
- **The coefficients are the sRGB luminance ones applied to the bytes.** A CSS
  filter does not linearise: 255 red reads 54, green 182, blue 18. And
  `grayscale(a)` is exactly an interpolation towards that luminance — all
  thirteen sampled amount/colour pairs land on Chrome's byte, percentages and
  the empty argument included.
- **It applies to the source and never to the backdrop.** `grayscale(1)` under
  `difference` reads `136,9,119,255`, which is `|backdrop − luminance(source)|`
  to the byte. Filtering the destination would have given something else
  entirely.

### Result: 46 of 53 sampled cells identical to Chrome

The seven that are not are each recorded next to their assertion rather than
chased, because five of them are not about blending at all:

| cell | Chrome | here | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `multiply`, both sides α=0.5 | `128,106,64,192` | `127,107,64,192` | both channels sit within half a unit of the rounding boundary; Chrome is the other side of it because its backdrop is premultiplied 8-bit, so what it un-premultiplies out of a half-alpha 128 is 127 |
| `grayscale(1)` on a translucent paint | `120,120,120,128` | `119,119,119,128` | same root: Chrome greys premultiplied bytes |
| `multiply` with `globalAlpha = 0.5` | `159,96,0,255` | `160,96,0,255` | see below — the alpha, not the blend |
| `grayscale(1) blur(2px)` | `128,128,128,8` | the colour unfiltered | deliberate: honouring only the half we implement lands *further* away than honouring none of it, since the blur is most of what happened |
| `filter = 'grayscale'` / `'notafilter(1)'` / `''` | keeps the previous filter | stores the string | the setter is `freeform`; refusing these needs the whole `<filter-value-list>` grammar, and a partial one would reject `blur(2px)` — which Chrome echoes back |

### A separate finding: globalAlpha is a byte in Chrome, and a double here

The `multiply`/`globalAlpha` row above is not about compositing, so
`probes/expr-globalalpha-quant.js` isolated it. Source-over of black over white
separates the two hypotheses, because `255·(1 − 0.5) = 127.5` rounds up and
`255·(1 − 128/255) = 127.0` does not:

| `globalAlpha` | Chrome | implies |
|---|---|---|
| `0.5` | `127` | the paint alpha is `round(a·255)`, i.e. 128 |
| `rgba(0,0,0,0.5)` at α=1 | `127` | identical — both are bytes |
| `0.502` | `127` | rounds to the same 128 |
| `0.498` | `128` | rounds to 127, a different byte |
| `1/3` | `170` | 85/255, not a third |

So Chrome quantises `globalAlpha` to eight bits before it reaches the
compositor and we carry a double all the way through. Only one of the probe's
eight cells actually diverges today, and the widget's program never touches
`globalAlpha` — so this cannot move any of its readbacks. **Left unfixed and
uncoupled from this work on purpose:** it is one line in the rasteriser, but it
shifts every antialiased pixel drawn under a fractional alpha, and it wants its
own before/after against the whole probe corpus rather than a ride along a
compositing change.

### On the widget's own program, per pixel against headed Chrome

`scratch/expr-widget-canvas-program.js`, every phase diffed pixel by pixel:

| phase | pixels | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| `p6.diff` 80×24 | 1920 | **1920 wrong** | **0** — and the hash is Chrome's exactly |
| `p7.1x1` (read twice) | 1 | 1 wrong | **0**, matching the live oracle |
| `p4.49x44` three multiplied discs | 2156 | 657 wrong | **362** |
| the other seven phases | — | — | untouched to the pixel |

Whole program: 5217 wrong pixels → 3000. Phases whose hash now equals Chrome's:
two → four of nine.

`p4` improving without being the target is the `multiply` in its own program —
three discs composited that way, which had been painting source-over. Its
remaining 362 are the arc antialiasing gap noted elsewhere, not the blend.

Reading `filter` moved no widget pixel, which is expected and worth stating:
the panel it greys is white, black and neutral grey text, and grayscale is the
identity on a neutral colour. The pass matters for what a page reads back from
a *coloured* fill, not for this program.

    lightpanda     cf-challenge doc=403->200 nodes=47  "Just a moment..."

## The srgb ↔ display-p3 transform is three layers of Skia (2026-08-24)

The canvas leg converted between the two colour spaces with CSS Color 4's exact
D65 product and a libm `powf`. `canvas-space-matrix.js` had already ruled that
out at byte precision — across 24 colours picked so that the two published
matrices disagree, Chrome sided with the D65 fractions 11 times, with Skia's D50
matrices 12 times, and with neither once. A third thing, unnamed.

What named it was widening the read. A `rgba-float32` `getImageData` hands back
the *encoded float* the transform produced, seven significant digits of it,
where a byte read can only pin a channel to 1/255. At that width the transform
comes apart into three layers, and each has a stimulus that isolates it.

**The matrix, from readings that never touch a powf.** The composed matrix's
blue column has two cells of order 5e-6 and 1e-5, so a blue-only fill lands the
red and green outputs inside the encode's *linear* segment, where the encode is
one multiply by 12.92 and exactly invertible. A grey fill does the same for the
row sums. Nine cells, read directly:

    srgb -> display-p3                    display-p3 -> srgb
     0.822547197  0.177678615 -0.000004828   1.224816442 -0.225114793 0.000004023
     0.033179868  0.966723800 -0.000010076  -0.042038292  1.042147279 0.000011312
     0.017070306  0.072381869  0.910398364  -0.019623475 -0.078635663 1.098419309

That is `skcms_Matrix3x3_concat(invert(dst->toXYZD50), src->toXYZD50)` over
`SkNamedGamut::kSRGB` and `kDisplayP3` — where `skcms_Matrix3x3_invert` works in
double and *stores f32*, and the concat is f32 throughout. Rounding the
composition twice is the whole of why it is neither published product; nothing
about the published D50 cells is wrong. Two structural marks fall out that no
exact D65 matrix has: the rows do not sum to one, so `#ffffff` reads
`1.0000992 0.9999619 0.9999466` rather than white, and the blue column's top
cells are not structural zeros, so an srgb blue reads with a faint negative red.

**The order it is applied in, from the greys alone.** Skia's `matrix_3x3` is a
chain of fused multiply-adds, innermost term first. A plain left-to-right f32
sum of the same nine cells is one ULP off on one channel of every grey reading —
and only a row whose three inputs are equal can see that, which is why the greys
carry this and the basis columns cannot.

**The curve, both halves.** `canvas-space-float-decode.js` inverts the linear
segment for all 256 bytes and finds the decode is the raster pipeline's
`approx_powf` — a polynomial over the float's own exponent and mantissa bits,
worth 1.6e-4 of the result, a hundred times the last bit. It is not skcms's own
`powf_` either: skcms truncates the cast where the pipeline rounds, and 26 of
those 512 readings say so. So this work is `SkRasterPipeline`'s, not
`skcms_Transform`'s — worth knowing on its own.

The encode was the layer that stayed open longest, and the answer was in the
*shape* of the residual rather than its size. Against the textbook
`1.055*y^(1/2.4) - 0.055` the miss is 3.022e-5 at every one of the 1470 samples
in the nonlinear segment — a reading of 0.043 and a reading of 1.0 are off by
the same amount — and exactly zero in the linear one. A pow that is wrong is
wrong proportionally; only a constant term is wrong by a constant. Solving for
that term gives one f32, `-0.05496978759765625`, which is
`1 - approx_powf(1.1372833, 1/2.4)`.

That is the last paragraph of `skcms_TransferFunction_invert`: after inverting
each coefficient it bends `e` so that "the valuable invariant
`inv(src(1.0f)) == 1.0f`" survives the approximation. **Chrome's encode is not
its decode inverted** — it is the inverse tilted by 3.02e-5 so that white stays
exactly white. Miss that and every reading in the nonlinear segment is short by
the same 0.009 of a byte, which is invisible until a channel sits near a
rounding boundary, and then it is a whole byte.

### What it moved

| probe | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `canvas-space-matrix` (24 colours chosen to discriminate) | 11/24 | **24/24** |
| `canvas-space-float-matrix` (46 float readings) | — | **46/46** |
| `canvas-space-float-sweep` (256-value grey sweep, both ways) | nonlinear segment all short | **512/512** |
| `canvas-space-float-decode` (512 byte readings) | — | **512/512** |
| `canvas-color-notation` | 411 same / 21 diff | 415 same / **17** diff |

The 17 that remain are a different axis and are not this transform: they are the
premultiplied 8-bit round trip an alpha forces (`color(display-p3 1 0.25 0.5 /
0.5)` shifts its colour channels too) and the wide-notation source channels
(`hsl(30 60% 40%)`, `lab(50 40 30)`), which is `canvas-float-source-channels`.
The earlier note here that two knife-edge readings "answer one LSB away …
recorded next to their assertions rather than chased" is no longer true of the
matrix — those were this residual, and they are exact now.

## `hsl()` and `hwb()` are floats; legacy `rgb()` is bytes (2026-08-24)

`canvas-color-notation` had 17 readings left after the transform above was
pinned. Four of them were one notation family, and the tell was that they only
appear on a display-p3 canvas: `hsl(30 60% 40%)` stored `9a6935` where Chrome
stores `9b6935`, and read back as srgb it was `a36628` against `a46628`. On an
srgb canvas the same notation agreed exactly. A conversion that is wrong is
wrong on both canvases; a *source* that is wrong only shows where the
conversion runs before the quantisation does.

So the source. `hsl(30 60% 40%)` answers `#a36629`, but its sRGB channels are
(0.64, 0.4, 0.16) — (163.2, 102, 40.8) — and a display-p3 canvas converts before
it rounds. Converting the float stores `9b`; converting the 163 the notation
answers back stores `9a`.

### The float16 read says it directly

Inferring the source from a converted byte is one inference too many, so the new
probe (`canvas-float-source-channels.js`) reads the paint back through a
`float16` context, which hands back the channel rather than a byte:

| notation | Chrome's stored red | half-precision neighbour of |
|---|---|---|
| `hsl(30 60% 40%)` | `0.64013671875` | **0.64**, not 163/255 (`0.6396484375`) |
| `hwb(200 10% 20%)` green | `0.56689453125` | **17/30**, not 145/255 (`0.568359375`) |
| `rgb(50% 0% 0%)` | `0.501953125` | **128/255**, not 0.5 |
| `rgb(10% 20% 30%)` | `0.10198974609375` | **26/255**, not 0.1 |

Two families, opposite answers. `hsl()`, `hsla()` and `hwb()` reach the canvas
unrounded. Legacy `rgb()` — number *and* percentage forms — is quantised by its
own parser, so 127.5 is a 128 before any conversion sees it. That is the bound
that keeps the fix from spreading: `rgb(50% 0% 0%)` on a p3 canvas is `75140c`
in both engines, and converting 127.5 would have made it `74140c`.

### The width, for free

`hwb(200 10% 20%)`'s green is 17/30 of a byte. In double that is
144.49999999999997 and rounds to 144; in float it is exactly 144.5 and rounds
to 145. Chrome stores 145, and the float16 read above says why. This row needs
no colour space conversion at all — it is an srgb canvas — so it isolates the
width from everything else, and it is one of the two readings a previous round
recorded as "one LSB away from Chrome, recorded rather than chased". It is exact
now. The other one, `color(display-p3 0.2 0.4 0.6)`, is a `color()` notation and
still ours.

Eleven more knife-edge notations were measured on headed Chrome for this, four
canvas-space × readback-space axes each, and all forty-four readings agree.

### What it moved

| probe | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `canvas-color-notation` (430 readings: 86 notations × 1 string + 4 pixel axes) | 413 same / 17 diff | 417 same / **13** diff |
| `canvas-float-source-channels` bytes (76 readings) | — | **75/76** |

The 13 that remain are two other axes, neither of them this one:

- **six** are the premultiplied 8-bit round trip an alpha forces — every
  `alpha=0x80` row read across spaces (`#ff000080`, `rgba(255,0,0,0.5)`,
  `lab(50 40 30 / 0.5)`), where Chrome premultiplies the float and we
  premultiply the byte;
- **four** are `color()` and `lab()` on the p3 leg, which still goes through CSS
  Color 4's naive f32 sum and an exact `srgbFromLinear` rather than the Skia
  spelling the canvas leg now uses — `color(display-p3 50% 25% 50%)` stores
  `80407f` against Chrome's `7f407f`;
- **three** are `color(display-p3 1 0.25 0.5 / 0.5)`, which is worse than one
  LSB (`ea3b7e80` against `fe407e80` on `srgb->display-p3`) and looks like a
  colour already in p3 being converted a second time.

### The float16 *canvas* is still byte-backed, and the widget builds four

The probe's float16 half was measured on both engines and only 6 of its 38
readings agree. That is not the source channels — it is that a
`colorType: 'float16'` context stores a byte bitmap here and expands it on read,
so every channel comes back as the half-precision neighbour of `n/255`. Chrome's
comes back as the neighbour of the colour itself. The readings above are exactly
that gap, and it is not a rounding argument: `hsl(30 60% 40%)` is
`0.64013671875` there and `0.63916015625` here.

This matters more than a byte. The Turnstile widget (`results/ibt2-oracle.json`)
builds four offscreen canvases — {srgb, display-p3} × {unorm8, float16} — fills
each with `color(display-p3 1 0.25 0.5)` and reads 1×1 back from each. Two of
its four rows are float16, and both of them read a quantised channel from this
engine. Readings in `results/canvas-float-source-channels.{chrome,lightpanda}
.json`.

## The float16 canvas is a float bitmap, and the paint reaches it in two legs (2026-08-24)

`colorType: 'float16'` and `pixelFormat: 'rgba-float16'` had been treated as one
axis. They are two. The pixel format is a finer *read* of whatever the bitmap
holds, so off an eight-bit bitmap every channel it answers is the half-precision
neighbour of some `n/255` — which is why the float16 rows measured before this
all agreed. The colour type is a finer *bitmap*: the paint goes in unquantised,
and stays that way.

`raster.Surface` now has two stores, picked by `colorType`: the premultiplied
RGBA8 it always had, and a premultiplied RGBA of half floats on the 0..1 scale.
Everything between them works in one currency — premultiplied 0..255 as f64,
alpha included — so the eight-bit arithmetic is unchanged to the byte and the
only difference is the quantisation at the end of it, which is the whole of what
a page can see.

Three things only the float bitmap shows, all measured on headed Chrome
(`probes/canvas-float-source-channels.js`):

- a channel that is not byte-valued stays that way — `hsl(30 60% 40%)` reads
  `0.64013671875`, the neighbour of 0.64, against `0.63916015625` for the
  neighbour of 163/255;
- the colour space conversion is not quantised **and not clipped**: the same
  `color(display-p3 1 0.25 0.5)` on an *srgb* float16 canvas keeps a red of
  `1.0888671875`, where the eight-bit canvas clamps it to 255;
- the premultiply round trip is lossless — `color(display-p3 1 0.25 0.5 / 0.5)`
  comes back as itself, where the eight-bit store moves two of its channels.

### Which is how the paint's own two legs became visible

A float16 reading answers the converted channel rather than a byte of it, so it
pins the conversion about ten times finer than a byte does. Against 42 of them
the pipeline is not one conversion but two, and they are not the same
arithmetic:

1. **Blink** resolves the CSS colour into *extended* sRGB — unclipped, exact
   transfer function, Skia's own composed gamut matrix. `color(display-p3 1 0.25
   0.5)` becomes `1.0885332783 0.1060315679 0.4972262487`.
2. **Skia** converts that into the bitmap's space, which is the leg this repo
   already had: `approx_powf` either side of the same matrix. It is the identity
   when the canvas is srgb.

Both legs are needed and neither one alone reproduces Chrome. Leg 1's exact
transfer function over leg 2's matrix is the only combination of the 27 tried
that lands on all three channels of that colour; and running leg 2 *after* leg 1
is what makes a display-p3 notation on a display-p3 canvas round trip — Chrome
stores `ff407f` there, not the `ff4080` `round(0.5 * 255)` would give.

`Wide.toPaint` used to go through CIE XYZ D50 with CSS Color 4's rationals for
the whole distance. That route puts `color(display-p3 1 0.25 0.5)`'s green at
0.10587 where Chrome has 0.10602 — two half-precision steps, invisible in an
opaque byte and a whole byte apart once the fill is translucent.

### What it moved

| probe | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `canvas-color-notation` (86 notations × 1 string + 4 pixel axes) | 417 same / 13 diff | 422 same / **10** diff |
| `canvas-float-source-channels`, all 126 readings | — | **123 same / 3 diff** |
| its 42 `colorType: 'float16'` readings | 6 of the 38 measured last round | **42 same** |

Two readings recorded in earlier rounds as "one LSB away from Chrome, recorded
rather than chased" were the same D50 route and are exact now:
`color(display-p3 0.2 0.4 0.6)` on an srgb canvas is `1a689d`, and
`color(display-p3 1 0.25 0.5 / 0.5)` is `ff1c7e80`.

### The ten that remain are one axis

Every one of them is a translucent pixel read *across* spaces:
`display-p3->srgb` `#ff000080` answers `fe050280` here against Chrome's
`fe040280`. The read rounds each channel to a byte before converting it, where
Chrome un-premultiplies in floating point, converts, and quantises once at the
end. Modelled offline against all ten, the float order lands on Chrome's byte in
every one.

### The widget's own four rows, against the live-site oracle

`results/ibt2-oracle.json` records what Turnstile actually read on
challenges.cloudflare.com: four offscreen 2×2 canvases, `{srgb, display-p3}` ×
`{unorm8, float16}`, each filled with `color(display-p3 1 0.25 0.5)` and read 1×1
back through the matching pixel format. Run against this engine, all four now
answer the oracle's bytes; two of them did not before.

| context | oracle | this engine |
|---|---|---|
| srgb / unorm8 | `ff1b7fff` | `ff1b7fff` |
| display-p3 / unorm8 | `ff407fff` | `ff407fff` |
| srgb / float16 | `5b3cc92ef537003c` | `5b3cc92ef537003c` |
| display-p3 / float16 | `003c00340038003c` | `003c00340038003c` |

The two float16 rows decode to `1.0888671875 0.10601806640625 0.497314453125 1`
and `1 0.25 0.5 1` — the out-of-gamut red and the lossless identity from the
section above, which is why both legs of the paint had to be right for either
row to land.

### Re-measured next door: fourteen canvas probes, one row worse

Every other canvas probe was re-run against this build and diffed twice — against
its committed lightpanda arm and against Chrome. Nine are bit-identical to
before, `canvas-space-{matrix,float-decode,float-matrix,float-sweep}` and
`expr-composite-blend` included (1354 readings between them, all still exact).
Two files had drifted and were stale rather than wrong: they predate the
`hsl()`-is-a-float commit, and refreshing them shows three readings that moved
onto Chrome (`canvas-premultiplied-encode`'s two p3 `hsl()` rows and
`canvas-image-data-construct`'s float32 p3 read) and one that moved off it.

The one that moved off is worth naming, because it is a live lead and not a
rounding shrug. On an **srgb unorm8** canvas, `hsl(30 60% 40% / 0.5)` reads
`a3662a80` on Chrome and `a3662880` here. The blue is 40.8, and it is the alpha
that separates the arms: premultiplying the float gives `round(40.8 × 128/255) =
20`, which reads back 40; premultiplying the *byte* the same colour rounds to
gives `round(41 × 128/255) = 21`, which reads back 42 — Chrome's answer. The
opaque row agrees either way (`a36629`), and a float16 canvas says the colour
itself is still 0.16 rather than 41/255, so this is not the source channel
coming back: it is the premultiply alone.

That would mean an eight-bit canvas quantises a *legacy* colour before it
premultiplies, while `color()`/`lab()`/`oklch()` keep the float — which the same
file's `color(display-p3 1 0.25 0.5 / 0.5)` demands, since premultiplying its
rounded byte would store `ff1c8080` and Chrome stores `ff1c7e80`. One reading is
not enough to build that split on; it needs a sweep of legacy notations at half
alpha on both engines before anything is written.

## A translucent pixel read across spaces: quantise once, clip at the store (2026-08-24)

The ten readings the float16 round left were one axis, and closing it turned out
to need two clips moved rather than one.

**The read.** `getImageData` into the other colour space rounded each channel to
a byte and converted that byte. The bitmap is premultiplied, so the read divides
the alpha back out first — and that quotient is not a byte. Worse, where it
lands *outside* the gamut, which is the whole reason the premultiply preserved
it, rounding first throws the excess away. The cross-space arm now reads through
`readUnitPixels`, converts unclipped, and quantises once at the end.

**The paint.** `Wide.toPaint` clipped the colour into the destination gamut
before the bitmap ever saw it. On an srgb canvas `color(display-p3 1 0.25 0.5 /
0.5)` has a red of 277.6; clipped to 255 it premultiplies to 128, unclipped to
139 — and 139 is what fits in the byte, because the alpha is what brought it back
into range. An eight-bit bitmap does clip, but at the *store*, after the
premultiply, which `RGBA.round255` was already doing. So the clip is gone from
the paint, and with it the paint's dependence on the bitmap's channel type:
`CanvasFormat` is removed and `Style.paint` takes a `CanvasSpace` again.

Read as display-p3, that pixel is `fe407e80` on Chrome; before this it was
`ea3b7e80` here, which is what the srgb red clamped to 255 converts to.

| `canvas-color-notation` (432 readings) | 10 diff | **0 diff** |
| `canvas-float-source-channels` (126 readings) | 3 diff | **0 diff** |
| `canvas-own-color-space` (40 readings) | 1 diff | **0 diff** |
| `canvas-premultiplied-encode` (25 readings) | 4 diff | 3 diff |

Ten other canvas probes are bit-identical to their committed readings —

`canvas-premultiplied-encode`'s remaining three are the legacy-notation
