`oklch()` row, and `globalAlpha 0.5` on a p3 canvas. None of them is this axis.

## A shadow is three box blurs, and the radius is device space (2026-08-24)

`shadowBlur` is stored here and reaches no pixel. It is the largest single
divergence left in the widget's 48×48 render — that scene sets five of them,
11, 16, 3, 4 and 14 — so `probes/canvas-shadow-blur.js` measured what Chrome
actually puts down before anything is implemented.

The shape is offset clear of its own shadow, so every reading is the shadow
alone. Two sweeps: a 4×4 square, whose centre row is the kernel *squared*
because a separable blur hands back the product of the two axes, and a
full-height 4-wide bar, whose centre row is the one-dimensional kernel itself.

**The radius is not transformed.** The same sweep under the widget's own
`scale(0.384, 0.384)`, with the shape's coordinates divided by the scale so the
device shape is identical, produces byte-identical profiles at every radius. A
`shadowOffsetX` is not transformed either, and that one is visible as an
absence: dividing the offset by 0.384 puts the shadow at device x=129 on a
96-wide bitmap and nothing is drawn at all.

**The kernel is Skia's three box passes.** With σ = `shadowBlur` / 2 and

    window = max(1, floor(σ · 3·√(2π) / 4 + 0.5))

three box convolutions reproduce Chrome's bytes exactly — every pixel, no
residual — at nine radii:

| σ ≥ 2 | window | passes (width, left offset) | error |
|---|---|---|---|
| blur 4 | 4 | (4,1) (4,2) (5,2) | **0** |
| blur 5 | 5 | (5,2) (5,2) (5,2) | **0** |
| blur 6 | 6 | (6,2) (6,3) (7,3) | **0** |
| blur 8 | 8 | (8,3) (8,4) (9,4) | **0** |
| blur 11 | 10 | (10,4) (10,5) (11,5) | **0** |
| blur 14 | 13 | (13,6) (13,6) (13,6) | **0** |
| blur 16 | 15 | (15,7) (15,7) (15,7) | **0** |
| blur 20 | 19 | (19,9) (19,9) (19,9) | **0** |
| blur 32 | 30 | (30,14) (30,15) (31,15) | **0** |

An odd window is three equal centred boxes; an even one is (w, w, w+1) with the
first box shifted one to the left, which is how Skia keeps an even box centred.

**Below σ = 2 it is not that.** Blur 3 (σ 1.5) is 28 off the best box triple,
blur 2 is 104 off and blur 1 is 100 off, so Skia takes its small-sigma path there
instead. Blur 1 fits an exact Gaussian at σ ≈ 0.39 and blur 2 and 3 fit neither
cleanly — the threshold sits exactly at σ = 2, and one of the widget's five
radii (3) is under it. That branch is still unnamed.

**The rest of the shadow state**, one reading each at blur 8:

| reading | Chrome | says |
|---|---|---|
| opaque shape, opaque shadow | `ff00000f ff00001f ff00000c` | the reference |
| `shadowColor` at α 0.5 | `ff000008 ff000010 ff000006` | the colour's alpha multiplies the coverage |
| shape at α 0.5 | `ff000008 ff000010 ff000006` | so does the shape's — identical to the row above |
| `shadowColor: transparent` | nothing | drawn at all |
| blur 0 with an offset | `ff0000ff` | the silhouette in `shadowColor`, no spread |
| no offset | shadow either side, shape on top | the shadow goes *under* the shape |
| a 2px stroke | `ff00001f ff00003a ff000017` | strokes cast one too, which is four of the widget's five |

This engine answers 39 of the probe's 40 readings differently: it draws no
shadow at all, and the one it matches is the transparent `shadowColor` that
draws nothing in either.

### The sigma < 2 branch is a discrete Gaussian (2026-08-24)

The box triple above stops being exact below sigma 2, which is where Skia
changes kernel. A bar *one* pixel wide reads the taps straight off — no
deconvolution — and `SkGaussFilter.cpp` names them: `gauss(n) = I_n(var) /
e^var` with `var = sigma^2`, the modified Bessel form of the discrete Gaussian
from "Scale-Space for Discrete Signals". Taps are expanded outward by the
recurrence `b[n+1] = b[n-1] - (2n/var)·b[n]` until one falls below 1/100, then
normalised to sum to one.

That model reproduces every tap Chrome answers, to the byte, first try:

| blur | sigma | Chrome's taps |
|---|---|---|
| 0.7 | 0.35 | `14,227,14` |
| 1 | 0.5 | `25,204,25` |
| 1.5 | 0.75 | `6,43,158,43,6` |
| 2 | 1 | `13,54,121,54,13` |
| 2.5 | 1.25 | `5,20,56,92,56,20,5` |
| 3 | 1.5 | `9,26,55,75,55,26,9` |
| 3.5 | 1.75 | `4,13,29,51,62,51,29,13,4` |
| 3.9 | 1.95 | `6,15,31,48,56,48,31,15,6` |

It is a *discrete* Gaussian rather than a sampled one, and the difference is
visible in the tails: an erf-integrated Gaussian fitted freely still misses
`13,54,121` by 23 across the row, and every box model misses by more.

Below the kernel there is one more line: `3·sigma <= 1`, Skia's `hasNoBlur`.
Sigma 0.3 draws the silhouette unblurred and 0.35 blurs, which brackets it
exactly. Fourteen kernels measured across all three regimes, none unexplained.

## A gradient's geometry is thrown away here (2026-08-24)

`createLinearGradient` and friends keep their stops and discard every
coordinate they were given, so a gradient fill paints whatever flat colour it
replaced. The widget's 48×48 scene builds seven of them, which makes this the
largest block of wrong pixels left in that render now that shadows draw.
`probes/canvas-gradient-paint.js` measures what Chrome does, ahead of the
`cfsc-gradient-paint-source` refactor: **26 readings, all 26 different here.**

**The transform is the one in effect when the gradient is *used*, not when it
is made.** Three rows say it together and they are byte-identical: a gradient
of 0→32 at the identity, a gradient of 0→16 created under `scale(2, 1)`, and a
gradient of 0→16 created at the identity and then painted under `scale(2, 1)`
all give `fb0004ff … 0400fbff`. A `translate(8, 0)` applied only for the fill
moves the ramp with it.

**The stops interpolate in straight alpha, not premultiplied.** Red opaque to
*blue* transparent reads `7900827c` in the middle — a blue channel of 130. A
premultiplied ramp would carry no blue at all there, because premultiplying the
transparent blue end zeroes it.

**The degenerate cases paint nothing rather than something.** A zero-length
linear axis, two identical circles, and a gradient with no stops at all are
each `00000000` all the way across; one stop is that colour everywhere.

Left for the implementation to settle, all of it measured in the probe: where
a conic gradient's zero angle points, the two-circle cone's extent, what a
`color(display-p3 …)` stop is kept as (it reads `ff2281`, which is not the
`ff1b7f` the same notation paints as a flat fill), and which colour wins on a
pixel that lands exactly on a repeated offset (the later one).

## Skia dithers a gradient, and that is half its bytes (2026-08-24)

The gradients paint now: 23 of the 26 readings above are byte-identical, where
before every one of them was wrong. What took the longest was not the geometry.

The exact interpolation is not what Chrome stores. `linear across` is red to
blue over 32 pixels, so pixel *i* wants a blue of `255 · (i + 0.5) / 32` — and
at i = 4 that is 35.859 while Chrome stores **35**, and at i = 27 it is 219.141
while Chrome stores **220**. Neither rounding nor truncation nor a 256-entry
ramp cache reaches both. What does is `SkRasterPipeline`'s `dither` stage: an
8x8 ordered Bayer matrix, indexed by interleaving and bit-reversing the low
three bits of *x* and *x^y*, scaled to one part in 255 and added to the
premultiplied channels before they are rounded. It fires on a gradient and not
on a flat fill, so it belongs to the paint source rather than to the store, and
it is worth roughly half the pixels of every ramp measured.

Alpha is not dithered — `alpha ramp same hue` is the exact interpolation to the
byte — and the offset lands on the premultiplied value, not the straight one:
`alpha ramp`'s pixel 0 stores a blue of 3 where the undithered premultiply
gives 3.92, and reads back as 3 rather than 4.

**`globalAlpha` is a byte for a flat fill and a float for a gradient.** A flat
fill reaches Skia as a premultiplied eight-bit colour, which is why black over
white at 0.5 reads 127 and only `128/255` explains it. A gradient is a shader
and the paint's alpha is scaled into its output in floating point: the same
ramp under `globalAlpha = 0.5` stores a premultiplied 125 where the byte gives
126. One measurement each way, and they disagree.

Three of the questions the chapter above left open are settled, all first try:

- **A conic gradient's zero points along +x and the sweep follows `atan2` with
  y downwards**, the angle subtracted rather than added.
- **The two-circle cone is Skia's two-point conical**: the larger root of the
  quadratic whose circle passes through the point, rejected when the radius
  there has gone negative — which is what makes the region outside the cone
  transparent rather than an extended end stop.
- **A `color(display-p3 …)` stop interpolates in Oklab.** That is the whole of
  why it reads `ff2281` where the same notation paints `ff1b7f` as a flat fill:
  the stop is not being kept in a wider gamut, the *ramp* is being taken
  somewhere else. Converting both ends to Oklab, interpolating there and
  converting back reproduces all 32 pixels of `wide stop` exactly, where no
  per-channel sRGB ramp reproduces even one — a solver over every start colour
  at quarter-byte resolution finds nothing that fits. This is CSS Color 4's
  default interpolation space, which applies to any pair that is not both
  legacy sRGB. It is not implemented yet; `cfsc-gradient-oklab-stops` is it.

### What is still off

Two rows and 16 pixels, both understood, neither a gradient problem. One of
the two has since been closed — see below:

- ~~**`alpha ramp`, 3 pixels.**~~ **Fixed (2026-08-24).** All three were an
  un-premultiply that lands on an exact half: 18 stored over an alpha of 68 is
  67.5, and Chrome answers 67 where this rounded half away from zero to 68. Two
  of the three come back under the half in f32 (`18 · (1/255) · (1/(68 ·
  (1/255)))` is 67.49999237), and the third is exactly 42.5 in f32 too and
  needs round-half-to-**even** — which is what `_mm_cvtps_epi32` and
  `vcvtnq_s32_f32` both do, and what Skia's `to_unorm` therefore does. So the
  readback is f32 and ties go to even. It was `readPixels` rather than the
  gradient, and the sweep it wanted first has now been run: all 23 canvas
  probes, six leaves moved, every one onto Chrome, and the set that still
  disagrees after is a strict subset of the set before. It also closed
  `hwb alpha ramp` and `legacy alpha ramp` in `canvas-gradient-stop-space` and
  the translucent grayscale fill in `expr-canvas-filter-grayscale`.
- **`shadow of a ramp`, 13 pixels**, all in the four columns nearest the
  shape's left edge and exact from x = 4 rightwards. So the blur kernel is
  right and the mask's left boundary is not. Modelling it as *blur the rect's
  flat coverage, then modulate by the ramp* gets to 2 rather than 13, which
  says Chrome is not simply blurring the alpha this engine draws — but 2 is not
  0, and one row is not enough to choose between them.

## The notation, not the colour, picks the ramp's space (2026-08-24)

`probes/canvas-gradient-stop-space.js` is the follow-up the chapter above asked
for: the same red-to-blue ramp written sixteen ways, so that a row either
matches the plain hex one or does not. Red to blue is where sRGB and Oklab part
company hardest, so no colour arithmetic is needed to read the answer.

**Six notations ramp in sRGB and five ramp in Oklab, and the split is not about
gamut.** `#ff0000`, `rgb(255 0 0)`, `rgb(255, 0, 0)`, `hsl(0 100% 50%)` and
`hwb(0 0% 0%)` all give the identical row. `color(srgb 1 0 0)` — *the same
colour, in sRGB, in gamut* — gives a different one, and it is byte-identical to
what `oklch(0.62796 0.25768 29.234)` and `lab(54.29 80.8 69.89)` give. So what
decides is which notation was written, not what colour it names or what gamut
it needs.

That set is exactly the one this engine's `color.Style.wide` already marks:
`color()`, `lab()`, `lch()`, `oklab()`, `oklch()`. Note `hwb()` is *not* in it,
even though CSS Color 4 does not call `hwb()` legacy and this engine already
tracks that elsewhere — `Style.alpha` exists precisely because `hwb()`'s alpha
stays a float. Whatever Blink is branching on, it is not that flag.

**One such stop takes the whole gradient, not just the segments it ends.** A
three-stop ramp whose *last* stop is `color(srgb 0 0 1)` differs from the
all-legacy one across its **first** sixteen pixels as well as its last — and the
mirror, with the wide stop first, differs across the last sixteen. Neither half
is left alone, so the space is chosen once for the gradient.

Interpolating in Oklab — sRGB to linear, to LMS, cube roots, to Oklab, lerp,
and back — reproduces every one of these rows to the byte: `color srgb`,
`oklch`, `lab`, both three-stop rows, and `wide stop` from the earlier probe.
Six rows, 192 pixels, no residual. The ordered dither still applies on top, and
alpha still interpolates straight and separately (`hwb alpha ramp` and
`legacy alpha ramp` are the same row, which also puts `hwb()` on the sRGB side
a second time).

`cfsc-gradient-oklab-stops` is the implementation.

### Implemented (2026-08-24)

Fourteen of the sixteen rows are byte-identical now. `color.srgbToOklab` and
`color.oklabToSrgb` are the two legs; `raster.Gradient.Interpolation` carries
which space a ramp is in and, for the Oklab arm, the bitmap space to convert
back into; `CanvasGradient.resolve` makes one pass over the stops and sends the
whole gradient to Oklab if any of them was written wide. Because the ramp is no
longer linear in the channels it interpolates, `ctx.filter` moved from the
stops to the mixed colour — the same result on the sRGB arm, since
`grayscale()` is affine, and the right one on this one.

Eight pixels of 512 are left, and six of them are not about stops at all:
`hwb alpha ramp` and `legacy alpha ramp` are the same three pixels of the
un-premultiply tie described in the chapter above, and they are the same three
pixel indices in both rows. Those six have since gone — the tie was `readPixels`
and it is fixed. The other two are in `legacy wide legacy`, at the
ends of the segments either side of a `color(display-p3 0 1 0)` stop, each one
byte. They are not the Oklab matrices: a reference model in Python drifts on
the same pixels with either the published inverse pair or this file's, and
misses one of the two by the same byte in either direction. Something about how
a display-p3 *stop* reaches sRGB before Oklab is a hair off the canvas
conversion leg this uses, which is one reading and not enough to move it.

## `run-expr` reads an insecure realm, and the two arms disagree there (2026-08-24)

Worth knowing before trusting any `expr-*` baseline that counts names:
`run-expr.mjs` evaluates on a freshly created `about:blank` target, and in
Chrome **that target is not a secure context** — measured, `isSecureContext` is
`false` on it, and with it go `navigator.xr`, `XRSystem`, `XRWebGLLayer` and
`WebGLRenderingContext.prototype.makeXRCompatible`. This engine answers
`isSecureContext: false` on the same target and keeps all of them.

So `expr-context-proto-members` shows one extra WebGL member on this side,
442 against 443, and that reading is **not** "Chrome has no
`makeXRCompatible`". Three other probes collected through a real page —
`probe-descriptor-kind`, `probe-operation-arity`, and `probe-win52`, which
actually calls it and records the rejection — all have it. Deleting it would
have been a regression dressed as a fix.

It is a harness artifact rather than a site tell. The [SecureContext] gate runs
from `Frame.commitSecureContext`, at the two points that commit a document, and
deliberately not at frame init — a root frame is born at `about:blank` and
navigates inside the same context, so gating at init would strip the surface
off every https page. A CDP target that never navigates therefore never gets
gated. Every path a real page takes does: an http origin commits and gates, and
a script-created `about:blank` iframe goes through the synthetic-navigation
branch, which calls it too.

## Akamai's sensor says how hard it worked, and we are 40x under (2026-08-24)

`ak-macys` reaches the end of the challenge now. Both arms, one sitting, two
pairs, `antibot-sweep.mjs --only ak-macys --trace`:

| | headed Chrome | lightpanda |
|---|---|---|
| sensor POSTs | 1918 → 5205 → 4652 (`?t=`) → clearance | 1915 → 5182 → 4627 (`?t=`) → **interstitial again** |
| verdict | pass, 8025-8026 nodes | empty-document, 32 nodes |

So the missing second and third rounds that this station was stuck on for six
sessions are gone; what is left is that Akamai reads our payload and re-serves
the door. Its own cleartext header says why it might:

    3;0;1;2048;<n>;<sitekey>;A,B,C,D,E,F;<ciphertext>

`A` is 627-664 from Chrome and 14-22 from us, four runs each, real site and
replay alike. It is not elapsed time since the sensor script loaded -- Chrome
POSTs 14ms after that response arrives -- it is CPU: `sensor-cpu-profile.mjs`
puts 652-664ms of self time in a single function of the sensor script (its name
is regenerated per session: `UVq`, `cRK`), running as one uninterrupted burn
right before the POST. We finish whatever that is in 14ms.

### The harness, and it lives in the repo this time

* `sensor-cpu-profile.mjs <url> --body-dir <dir>` — Chrome's sampling profile of
  a page up to its first POST, plus every response body off the wire. The bodies
  are the capture; the profile's `url:line:column` are offsets into them.
* `akamai-replay.mjs --bodies <dir> --port N [--inject probe.js]` — serves one
  capture back. Hermetic by construction: every `https://<host>/` in the
  document is rewritten to the local server, because the captured loader derives
  its module URLs from its own `src` and an earlier round of this work spent
  three sessions comparing two arms that were fetching *different* code from the
  live site. POSTs answer 201 `{"success":true}`, or 200 for the `?t=` endpoint
  the interstitial's inline poller watches. The capture in
  `results/b41-macys-bodies` replays indefinitely: the sensor never checks the
  reply.
* The replay reproduces the gap exactly — Chrome `664,0,0,0,1,0`, lightpanda
  `14,0,0,0,1,0` — which makes this the first local oracle this station has had.

### What the burn is not

Measured on the replay, both arms, same capture:

* **Not a different branch.** Marking the guard's flattened dispatcher with a
  counter (`case` id → calls) gives an identical map on both sides: `9:1, 26:1,
  39:1, 46:4, 54:1, 76:1, 262:1, 391:1, 559:1, 738:1, 749:2, 897:1, 958:1,
  969:1`. Same cases, same counts, 47x the time.
* **Not a deadline-polling loop.** `probes/probe-clock-calls.js`: `Date.now` 65
  vs 54, `Math.random` 62 vs 43, `performance.now` 2 vs 2. Nobody is watching a
  clock 600 times.
* **Not per-character hashing of its own source.** It does hash its own source —
  `probes/probe-hash-work.js` counts `charCodeAt` over a 496239-char string, and
  496256 is exactly the challenge script's size — but the count is the same on
  both sides: 635673 (Chrome) vs 650797 (us).

### Two instruments that do not work here

* **`Debugger.enable` stops the guard.** With the domain on, the sensor runs
  ~5900 statements and then nothing: no POST, in either engine.
  `Profiler.startPreciseCoverage` works fine *without* it — map scriptIds from
  the coverage result's own `url` instead of from `Debugger.scriptParsed`.
* **Rewriting the script's text kills it too.** See the note at the top of
  `akamai-replay.mjs`. Instrument from outside, with `--inject`.

### Also measured, in passing

* `Runtime.evaluate` with `awaitPromise` never resolves on this engine if the
  promise settles from a timer — already known (`run-page-probe.mjs` header
  says so), rediscovered the hard way. Load probes as a page.
* Chrome clamps `setInterval(f, 1)` to ~4ms: 129 ticks in 500ms, headed, on
  about:blank (`probes/expr-timer-cadence.js`).
* On the real site the sensor's `_bm/get_params` is never requested by either
  arm — an earlier suggestion to capture its response is moot.
* Our arm issues ~154 `chrome-extension://` HEAD requests (the sensor's
  extension probe list) and they surface as `UnsupportedProtocol` failures on
  the wire. Chrome shows none: the scheme is refused before the network service,
  so CDP never reports them. Not yet checked whether the two arms' *JS-visible*
  outcome for those probes matches.

### The burn is one-time, and nothing we can wrap is holding it (2026-08-24, same round)

Chrome's first load of a fresh profile reports 645-786 in that counter. Its
*second* cycle through the same interstitial reports 5. Ours reports 14-22 then
5-9. So the difference is entirely in the first pass over a cold browser, and
after that the two engines agree.

Wrapping candidates and charging each call, on the replay, both arms:

| wrapped | Chrome's total | counter still |
|---|---|---|
| `Date.now` / `performance.now` / `Math.random` (`probe-clock-calls.js`) | 65 + 2 + 62 calls | 667 |
| `charCodeAt` / `charAt` / `fromCharCode` / `fn.toString` (`probe-hash-work.js`) | 635673 charCodeAt over a 496239-char string | 645 |
| every string, regex and codec builtin (`probe-native-time.js`) | 1.7ms across all of them | 674 |
| layout, geometry, canvas entry points (`probe-layout-time.js`) | 8ms (ours: 30ms) | 660 |
| every method on WebGL / WebAudio / SubtleCrypto / Performance / Navigator / Storage / MediaDevices prototypes (`probe-device-time.js`) | nothing above noise; WebGL and audio are never touched at this stage | 698 |

And the raw work is not the engines' difference: 650k `charCodeAt` at random
offsets into a 496239-char string plus a 200k-iteration string build runs in
5/2/3ms on *both* engines (`probes/expr-charcode-cost.js` via `run-expr.mjs`). Creating
and reading 20k `Error().stack` is 19ms here against 13ms in Chrome
(`probes/expr-error-stack-cost.js`), so it is not stack capture either.

What is left is engine work inside the JS frame that no page-visible API
mediates, spent once and never again — V8's lazy compilation of a 578KB script's
inner functions is the shape that fits (it lands as self time in whichever frame
first calls each function, and a second load hits the code cache). Both engines
compile with `kNoCompileOptions` (`src/script/Runtime.zig:308`,
`src/browser/js/Local.zig:210`), so if that is the answer it is a real
difference in how much work the two V8s do on first call, and the next step is
to measure it directly: a synthetic ~500KB script of many large functions, timed
from inside the page, in both arms.

Also worth a look: on the replay Chrome sends a fourth POST per cycle, ~2.2KB
and binary (leading tab, NULs, replacement characters), that this engine never
sends. Not investigated.

### Not lazy compilation, and not a headed-browser cost either (2026-08-24, same round)

`probes/expr-lazy-compile-cost.js` builds a 469492-byte script out of 3000
distinct functions and separates compiling the outer script, declaring the inner
ones, calling each once, and calling them again:

| | compile | declare | first call | second call |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| headed Chrome | 5ms | 0ms | 10ms | 0ms |
| lightpanda | 6ms | 0ms | 13ms | 0ms |

Half a megabyte of first-call compilation is 10ms, not 650, and the two engines
agree — so V8's lazy compilation is not where a 578KB script's first pass goes.

And `sensor-cpu-profile.mjs --headless` on the same replay reports **654** in the
counter, against 645-698 headed. Whatever the work is, a headless Chrome does it
too; it is not the window system, the GPU, or a display-server font path.

So the counter's 47x remains unexplained by anything measurable from outside the
script. The next instrument that can answer it is the script itself: the
sampling profile's chain (`cRK` ← `H8Y` ← `g5Y` ← `HrY` ← `PUY` ← `cBK` ←
`RjY` ← anonymous@31999, offsets into `results/b41-macys-bodies/02-*`) is a map
into a capture that is now on disk and replayable, and the burn is one call deep
in a flattened dispatcher whose case ids both arms enter identically.

## The WebMCP surface went behind `--webmcp` (2026-08-25)

Three names this fork carried that no Chrome has: `ModelContext` and
`ModelContextClient` on the global, and `modelContext` on
`Navigator.prototype`. The G14 chapter above and the own-name table both record
them as kept on purpose. They were kept on a premise — that nobody was looking
at them — and the read log falsified it.

**Kasada reads `navigator.modelContext`.** In `results/prop-reads-hyatt.json`,
main realm, `seq: 369`, `occurrences: 2`, and it sits in the middle of the run
of 73 `Navigator.*` reads that walks the interface's own names in order. A guard
enumerating names and then reading one of them is comparing the *table*, so a
getter answering `undefined` would not have helped: the name has to be gone.

So the surface is opt-in now. `lightpanda mcp` carries it unconditionally —
that mode exists for it — and the CDP-only modes ask with `--webmcp`, which is
what keeps the CDP `WebMCP` domain usable from `serve`: a page cannot register a
tool through a surface it cannot see. `Env.createContext` runs the gate as a
third one next to [SecureContext] and cross-origin isolation, and it is
delete-only for the same reason theirs is — every context is rebuilt from the
V8 snapshot, so the gate runs again for each, in-place navigations included.

Three readings, all on the gated build:

| reading | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `fetch` / `serve`, the three names | present | absent (`--webmcp` restores all three) |
| `mcp --cdp-port`, the three names | crashed on connect | present, no flag |
| `Object.getOwnPropertyNames(window).length`, secure | 1203 | 1201 |
| x-hyatt read log, main realm | 508 members | 507, `Navigator.modelContext` gone |

The `prop-reads-diff` probe — the 352 members of x-hyatt's read log reachable
from a singleton — now differs on **27 of 352 between headed-UA Chrome and this
engine at `https://example.com/`, and not one of them is a name**: 14
`PerformanceTiming` stamps, 4 `Screen.*` and 5 `Window.screen*` plus
`innerHeight` / `VisualViewport.height` (headless Chrome's fixed 800x600 against
our viewport), 2 `MemoryInfo` heap sizes, and `NetworkInformation.rtt`.
`Navigator.modelContext` is `undefined` on both arms.

**x-hyatt did not flip.** Same sitting, `refused-429`, `doc=429`, 6 nodes. The
station's blocker is the one the chapter above isolated — `/tl` answers without
`x-kpsdk-r`, so there is no second navigation — and this was never going to be
it. What this closes is the one-expression identification, which was real
whether or not any single station was spending it.

`mcp --cdp-port` is in that table because it did not work at all: three of the
CDP limits `Connection.init` asks the config for answered for `serve` only, so
the first client to connect reached `unreachable`. Fixed alongside, since it is
the only way to read the mcp arm end to end.

## The log knew how often, never what about

The read log answers "which of our members did the page reach, in what order".
For an accessor that is the whole question — `navigator.webdriver` has nothing
else to say — but for an operation it is barely half of one. x-hyatt's log said
Kasada called `matchMedia` 431 times. Which 431 queries, the part a two-arm diff
could act on, was nowhere in it. Same for 152 `getParameter` enums, 36
`canPlayType` MIMEs, 17 `MediaRecorder.isTypeSupported` ones.

So the operation wrapper now keys its read on the call's first argument when
that argument is a string or a number, behind its own log scope (`prop_arg`,
`prop-reads.mjs --args`). Only the first: `matchMedia`, `getParameter` and
`canPlayType` each ask their whole question there, and a key that grew with the
argument list would stop being the one thing two arms can be lined up on. The
scope is separate from `prop_read` because the key set stops being bounded by
our surface and starts being bounded by whatever the page passes — past 8192
distinct keys a context falls back to the bare member.

One settle of `https://www.hyatt.com/`: 1023 keys over 508 members in 4 realms,
and the three counts come apart.

| member | calls | distinct arguments |
|---|---|---|
| `Window.matchMedia` | 431 | 227 |
| `HTMLCanvasElement.toDataURL` | 80 | 80 |
| `HTMLMediaElement.canPlayType` | 36 | 36 |
| `MediaRecorder.isTypeSupported` | 17 | 17 |
| `WebGLRenderingContext.getParameter` | 138 | **1** |
| `WebGL2RenderingContext.getParameter` | 13 | 10 |

The one `getParameter` enum asked 138 times is `37446`,
`UNMASKED_RENDERER_WEBGL`. The 80 `toDataURL` types are the IANA image
registry read end to end, `image/aces` to `image/wmf`. And 64 of the 227 media
queries are a **binary search for `devicePixelRatio`** — `(min-resolution:Ndppx)`
halved twenty-four times, then the same walk again in `dpi` and again in
`dpcm` — with the remaining 163 covering every media feature in the spec, one
query per keyword.

### Putting all 390 back to both arms

`probes/kasada-argument-answers.js` is generated from that log: every recorded
argument whose call has an answer worth comparing, asked of both arms on the
same page. **101 of 390 differ.** The wide probe uses Kasada's exact strings,
which turned out to matter — `probes/media-feature-forms.js` and
`probes/kasada-argument-followup.js` re-ask the differences under conditions
that separate the feature from the way it was written.

What survived that second pass, all confirmed on both arms at
`https://example.com/`:

| reading | Chrome | this engine |
|---|---|---|
| `matchMedia('(min-width:100px)').media` | `(min-width: 100px)` | `(min-width:100px)` |
| `matchMedia('(min-aspect-ratio: 1/2)').media` | `(min-aspect-ratio: 1 / 2)` | `(min-aspect-ratio: 1/2)` |
| `matchMedia('(max-aspect-ratio: 2.125)').media` | `(max-aspect-ratio: 2.125 / 1)` | `(max-aspect-ratio: 2.125)` |
| `(min-resolution: 0.625dppx)` | `true` | `false` |
| `(min-resolution: 50dpi)`, `(max-resolution: 256dpi)` | `true` | `false` |
| `(width > 100px)`, `(color = 8)`, `(resolution > 50dpi)` | `true` | `false` |
| `(max-color-index: 4)`, `(max-aspect-ratio: 2.125)` | `true` | `false` |
| `(device-posture: continuous)` | `true` | `false` |
| `gl.getParameter(37446)` before `getExtension('WEBGL_debug_renderer_info')` | `null` | the renderer string |
| `canvas.toDataURL('image/jpeg' \| 'image/webp')` | that type | `data:image/png` |
| `MediaRecorder.isTypeSupported('video/mp4;codecs=avc1.64003E,mp4a.40.2')` | `true` | `false` |
| `document.createEvent('TouchEvent')` | throws `NotSupportedError` | `[object TouchEvent]` |

The serialization row is the widest of these in principle — it is not a feature
we are missing, it is every query coming back in the form it was written rather
than the form the spec says to print — but **x-hyatt does not read it**. The log
settles that: `MediaQueryList.media` never appears, and `MediaQueryList.matches`
appears once with `occurrences: 431`, one read per query. Kasada asks and takes
the boolean.

Which puts the value grammar and the range forms ahead of it here, because
those are what `matches` answers with. Of the 227 booleans Kasada collected,
about 60 come back different from Chrome's, and ~55 of those are the resolution
walk alone: the binary search converges on a `devicePixelRatio` below
`5.96e-7dppx`, a number no browser reports. The remainder of the 81 matchMedia
differences are the viewport and screen readings the chapter above already
covers, plus `prefers-color-scheme`.

`(min-resolution: 1dppx)` and `(min-resolution: 2dppx)` both answer correctly,
which is why the plain read log never showed anything here — the gap is in the
value grammar (fractional `dppx`, the `dpi` and `dpcm` units, a bare number
where a ratio is expected) and in the range forms (`<`, `>`, `=`), not in the
features themselves.

Left out of the probe on purpose: `TextEncoder.encode`, `btoa` and
`SubtleCrypto.digest` are arithmetic, `rotate` and `translate` return nothing,
and `Storage` and `Performance.getEntriesByType` answer about the page rather
than about the browser. Not counted as differences either: `screen` (800x600 on
headless Chrome), `innerHeight`, and `prefers-color-scheme` (headless Chrome
defaults to dark) — those are readings of the harness, and the chapter above
already has them.

| `(max-monochrome: 4)` | true | false |
| `(max-aspect-ratio: 2.125)` | true | false |
| `(max-device-aspect-ratio: 2.125)` | true | false |
| `(min-aspect-ratio: 1.5/2.5)` | true | false |
| `(device-posture: continuous)` | true | false |
| `(device-posture)` | true | false |

Three separate causes, and only the first was the one the read log pointed at:

- **A resolution was an integer.** `dppx` and `x` took whole numbers only, `dpi`
  parsed only when it divided by 96, and `dpcm` was rejected outright. That is
  what makes a binary search wrong at *every* rung rather than at one bound —
  and why the ladder converged on `5.96e-7dppx`.
- **A `max-` bound was being equated, not compared.** `max-color-index` shared
  an `== 0` with the bare feature, and `max-monochrome` did the same one line
  below it. `color-index` is 0 here, which is *under* every bound, so the right
  answer is true for all of them. The plan only named `max-color-index`; the
  probe found `max-monochrome` because it went looking for the same shape.
- **A `<ratio>` term was an integer.** MQ4 widened both terms to `<number>`;
  Chrome serializes `2.125` back as `2.125 / 1`.

Two near-misses worth keeping: `(max-resolution: 30dpcm)` was false before and
is false now, but only because `dpcm` used to be rejected — it is false for the
right reason now (30dpcm is 0.79dppx, below 1). And `(max-grid: 0)` /
`(min-grid: 0)` are false in Chrome: `grid` is discrete and takes no range
prefix, so recognising them would have been the anomaly. Both are pinned by
tests so the next pass over this file does not "fix" them.

What is left on this probe is two other plans, not this one: the eight `<`, `>`
and `=` queries are `mq-range-syntax`, and sixteen `.media` values still echo the
input instead of the normalized form (`(min-resolution:0.625dppx)` and
`.625dppx` both print as written) — that is `mq-media-serialization`, which
x-hyatt does not read.

## The range form was answering false to all of it (2026-08-25)

The eight `<`, `>` and `=` queries the chapter above left to this plan now
answer, and the probe grew to 97 queries to pin down the half a "does it
evaluate" check cannot see: *which* shapes Chrome calls malformed.
`results/mq-range-syntax.json` has both arms. **Zero mismatches on the matches
column.**

What was wrong was not a value, it was that `evalFeature` only knew two shapes —
`name: value` and a bare `name`. An operator matched neither, so `(width >
100px)` fell through to the boolean branch, failed to find `width >` as a
feature name, and answered false. All eight, always.

The measurements that shaped the implementation, none of which the plan named:

| query | Chrome | why |
|---|---|---|
| `(100px < width)` | true | the value may sit on either side; the comparison flips |
| `(600px <= width <= 5000px)` | true | two-sided is two comparisons on one value |
| `(600px < width > 1200px)` | false | both operators must point the same way |
| `(600px <= width = 1200px)` | false | and neither may be `=` |
| `(width>100px)` | true | the operator needs no surrounding whitespace |
| `(orientation = landscape)` | false | discrete features have no ordering |
| `(hover = hover)` | false | ditto — the value being right does not help |
| `(grid = 0)` | false | ditto |
| `(min-width >= 600px)` | false | a prefix and an operator are mutually exclusive |

So the range form applies to exactly seven features — `width`, `height`,
`resolution`, `color`, `color-index`, `monochrome`, `aspect-ratio` and their
`device-` spellings. That whitelist is the reason the last four rows answer
false deliberately rather than by falling off the end of a chain of `if`s, and
they are pinned by tests.

**A trap for anyone re-running this probe:** `(height >= 1080px)` and
`(aspect-ratio = 16/9)` are *false* in the Chrome arm and *true* in ours. That
is not a gap. `(width = 1920px)` is true in both, so the width agrees — but the
headless harness viewport is not 1080 tall and its `screen` is 800x600, which is
the same viewport/screen axis the earlier chapters call out. Five rows are
excluded on that basis and the acceptance script names them.

## The GPU answered before anything asked for it (2026-08-25)

`getParameter(37446)` is the single most-read expression Kasada has: 138 of its
152 `getParameter` calls on x-hyatt asked for that one pname. We answered it
with the real string behind ANGLE every time. Chrome answers `null` until the
context has asked for `WEBGL_debug_renderer_info` — the extension whose two
constants those pnames *are*. Both arms now agree on all fourteen `webgl*` rows
of `probes/kasada-argument-followup.js`; before and after are in
`results/webgl-debug-renderer-gate.json`.

The gate turned out to have a shape worth measuring rather than guessing, so
`probes/webgl-debug-renderer-gate.js` pins it down:

| question | Chrome | so |
|---|---|---|
| enable on context A, read on context B | `null` | the gate is per-context, not per-page |
| `getSupportedExtensions()` then read | `null` | listing an extension is not asking for one |
| `getExtension('WEBGL_lose_context')` then read | `null` | a *different* extension does not open it |
| `getExtension('webgl_debug_renderer_info')` | opens it | the name is matched case-insensitively |
| `typeof` the gated read | `object` | it is `null`, not `undefined` |

A bool per context, set in `getExtension` and read in `getParameter`, on both
`WebGLRenderingContext` and `WebGL2RenderingContext` — the two are separate
types with separate prototypes, and a gate on only one of them is a gate a
detector walks around by asking the other.

**Two rows in that probe still differ, and neither is the gate.** They are their
own gaps, found while measuring this one:

- `gl.getExtension('OES_texture_float')` is **truthy in Chrome and falsy here**.
  Chrome hands back a named interface object — `[object OESTextureFloat]`,
  `[object EXTBlendMinMax]`, one per extension — where our WebGL 1 union carries
  a `void` payload that marshals to `undefined`. That is ~35 extensions which
  `getSupportedExtensions` advertises and `getExtension` then refuses, a
  self-contradiction in one expression, and any script that feature-detects with
  `if (gl.getExtension(name))` takes the other branch. WebGL 2 already models
  this correctly with `supported: struct {}`, though it answers
  `[object Object]` where Chrome names the interface.
- `getError()` after the gated read is **1280 (`INVALID_ENUM`) in Chrome and 0
  here**, because our `getError` is a constant `NO_ERROR`. The gated read is one
  way in; any invalid enum is another.

## The engine advertised 75 extensions and handed back 4 (2026-08-25)

`getSupportedExtensions()` listed 39 names on WebGL 1 and 36 on WebGL 2.
`getExtension()` then answered `undefined` for 37 of the 39 and `[object Object]`
for 34 of the 36. One expression — `if (gl.getExtension(name))` — took the wrong
branch on 71 of the 75, on a context that had just claimed all of them.

The two halves failed differently, which is why they read as one gap only after
being measured. WebGL 1's union carried a `void` payload: nothing to marshal, so
`undefined`. WebGL 2's carried a single anonymous `struct {}` standing in for 34
names at once, so every one of them branded as `[object Object]` — and its
prototype *was* `Object.prototype`, so a script reading the prototype got
`__defineGetter__`, `hasOwnProperty` and ten more members no WebGL extension has.

`probes/webgl-extension-brands.js` is the ground truth: every advertised name
put back through `getExtension`, and for each one the brand, the prototype's
member names, and each member's value — GLenums as the numbers the driver
reports, methods as `fn/<arity>`. 53 interfaces, 213 member slots.

The brands are why this had to be measured rather than derived from the extension
string. There is no rule that survives the list:

| extension | brand |
|---|---|
| `EXT_sRGB` | `EXTsRGB` |
| `EXT_shader_texture_lod` | `EXTShaderTextureLOD` |
| `OES_fbo_render_mipmap` | `OESFboRenderMipmap` |
| `WEBGL_compressed_texture_s3tc_srgb` | `WebGLCompressedTextureS3TCsRGB` |
| `EXT_disjoint_timer_query_webgl2` | `EXTDisjointTimerQueryWebGL2` |
| `NV_shader_noperspective_interpolation` | `NVShaderNoperspectiveInterpolation` |

So `webgl_extensions.zig` is generated — `tools/fingerprint/gen-webgl-extensions.mjs`
transcribes the results JSON — and both contexts construct from it with the same
four steps: check the advertised list, look the name up case-insensitively,
open the `WEBGL_debug_renderer_info` gate if that is the one asked for, construct.
Both arms now agree on all 77 keys of the probe with no difference in brand,
prototype member set, member value or arity.

**One name had no reading behind it, and it was not harmless.** `OVR_multiview2`
is SwiftShader-only: the macOS/Metal driver the reference run used never
advertises it, so the probe could not see it — while `gpu.zig`'s *linux* table
does advertise it. Under a linux claim the engine would have listed a name it
then refused, which is the exact contradiction this work removed. Guessing
`OVRMultiview2` from the string was available and, on this list, would have been
a coin flip. Forcing the same Chrome onto SwiftShader was not expensive:

```
--use-gl=angle --use-angle=swiftshader --enable-unsafe-swiftshader
```

It advertises the name, the brand *is* `[object OVRMultiview2]`, and the five
members and their GLenums are recorded under `chrome_swiftshader` in the results
JSON — its own key, because the rest of that run is a different GPU table. That
run also advertised `EXT_disjoint_timer_query_webgl2`, which the linux table says
SwiftShader lacks; a timer query is the host's to grant, so that is a host
difference and not a correction to the table.

**Still short of Chrome: the methods are no-ops.** Arity matches, so `fn.length`
does; the return value does not. `getSupportedProfiles`,
`getTranslatedShaderSource` and `isVertexArrayOES` answer something in Chrome and
`undefined` here. That needs its own two-arm measurement — which is why this
probe records arity and not return values.

## Ten of the 37 extension methods answer something (2026-08-25)

The extension interface objects match Chrome now, and every method on them had
Chrome's arity and Chrome's name and a no-op body. For 27 of the 37 that is
already right — `drawArraysInstancedANGLE`, `blendFunciOES`, `polygonModeWEBGL`
and the rest are commands, and Chrome returns `undefined` from all of them. The
other ten answered `undefined` where Chrome answers a value, which is the kind of
gap that cannot be found by reading method names: `getSupportedProfiles` looks
like a getter, and so does `getQueryEXT`, but `isVertexArrayOES` and
`createQueryEXT` do not, and two of those four were already suspected while the
other two were not.

So `probes/webgl-extension-method-returns.js` calls all 37 with arguments chosen
per method — a created query, a bound vertex array, a compiled shader — and
records what comes back. 18 of its 47 rows differed. What was behind them:

| method | Chrome |
|---|---|
| `OES_vertex_array_object.createVertexArrayOES` | `[object WebGLVertexArrayObjectOES]` |
| `OES_vertex_array_object.isVertexArrayOES` | `false` |
| `EXT_disjoint_timer_query.createQueryEXT` | `[object WebGLTimerQueryEXT]` |
| `EXT_disjoint_timer_query.isQueryEXT` | `false` |
| `EXT_disjoint_timer_query.getQueryEXT` | `null` |
| `EXT_disjoint_timer_query.getQueryObjectEXT` | `null` |
| `WEBGL_compressed_texture_astc.getSupportedProfiles` | `["ldr", "hdr"]` |
| `WEBGL_debug_shaders.getTranslatedShaderSource` | ~4KB of Metal Shading Language |

**Two of them are object types nobody had.** `WebGLVertexArrayObjectOES` is not
`WebGLVertexArrayObject`: same job, different type, and only the core one has an
interface object on the global. `WebGLTimerQueryEXT` is not `WebGLQuery` either.
Both are `WebGLObject`-rooted with an empty prototype — no `constructor` on it —
so the brand is the only thing that names them, which is why `LegacyHandle` in
`webgl_objects.zig` exists next to `Handle`.

**`getSupportedProfiles` is the driver's answer, not the browser's.** Metal
reports `["ldr", "hdr"]`; the same Chrome forced onto SwiftShader reports
`["ldr"]`. So it belongs in `gpu.zig` beside the other per-table readings, not as
a constant — a claimed-linux run answering `hdr` would contradict its own
renderer string.

10 of the 47 rows still differ, and both remaining categories are named rather
than left as a count:

- **`getTranslatedShaderSource` (2 rows).** Chrome answers ANGLE's translation of
  a *compiled* shader. We answer `""`, which is exactly what Chrome answers for
  an uncompiled one — the right type where `undefined` was the wrong one, and the
  content needs a shader translator this engine does not have.
- **`WEBGL_multi_draw`'s four methods (8 rows).** Chrome throws
  `TypeError: … The provided value cannot be converted to a sequence.` when the
  argument is not one. Ours accepts anything. That is argument conversion, which
  is its own gap and not a return value.

## createEvent knew a name no desktop browser knows (2026-08-25)

`probes/kasada-argument-followup.js` asks five event types of the legacy
`document.createEvent` factory, and four of them answered the same on both arms.
The fifth:

| | Chrome 150 | engine, before |
|---|---|---|
| `createEvent('TouchEvent')` | `NotSupportedError` | `[object TouchEvent]` |

The same Chrome has `typeof TouchEvent === 'function'` and builds
`new TouchEvent('touchstart')` without complaint. Both facts are true at once
because they come from different tables: the constructor is on the global
unconditionally, while the `createEvent` factory only carries an entry when the
build has touch event feature detection on, and a desktop build does not —
`navigator.maxTouchPoints` is 0 and `'ontouchstart' in window` is false on the
machine that answered. So the refusal is not "TouchEvent does not exist here",
it is "that string is not in this table", and Chrome says so with the same
message it gives any unknown name, original casing echoed:

```
Failed to execute 'createEvent' on 'Document': The provided event type ('TouchEvent') is invalid.
```

We had a `touchevent` branch, so one call to a factory nobody has used since
2015 reported a touch-enabled event table alongside a mouse-only
`maxTouchPoints: 0` — a contradiction cheaper to read than to fake. Deleting the
branch is the whole fix: the `invalidEventType` path already produced Chrome's
exact message, and `new TouchEvent(...)` still works, because it never went
through here.

The probe's 38 rows are now down to four differences, none of them this:
`toDataURL` for `image/jpeg` and `image/webp` still fall back to png (its own
plan), and `innerHeight` / `screen` differ because the two harnesses use
different viewports.

## `media` was the text we were handed, not the query we parsed (2026-08-25)

`matchMedia(q).media` is not an echo of `q`. Chrome parses the query and writes
the parse back out, so the property is a normal form and any deviation from it is
a spelling no browser produces. The engine echoed, and `probes/media-feature-forms.js`
put 22 of its 97 rows on the wrong side of that:

| input | Chrome 150 | engine, before |
|---|---|---|
| `(min-width:100px)` | `(min-width: 100px)` | `(min-width:100px)` |
| `(min-resolution: .625dppx)` | `(min-resolution: 0.625dppx)` | `(min-resolution: .625dppx)` |
| `(min-aspect-ratio: 1/2)` | `(min-aspect-ratio: 1 / 2)` | `(min-aspect-ratio: 1/2)` |
| `(max-aspect-ratio: 2.125)` | `(max-aspect-ratio: 2.125 / 1)` | `(max-aspect-ratio: 2.125)` |
| `(width>100px)` | `(width > 100px)` | `(width>100px)` |

The last two are the ones that cannot be reached by patching whitespace. A
`<ratio>` is always two numbers around ` / `, so a bare `2.125` grows the `/ 1`
the spec says it already means; and `1e2px` becomes `100px` because the number is
re-emitted from its value rather than copied. Kasada asked 227 media queries on
x-hyatt, which is 227 chances to read a normal form that is not one.

`probes/media-query-serialization.js` is the wider probe written to pin the rules
down before implementing them — 119 forms, all measured on a headed Chrome 150.
What it found:

- **Names, units and keywords lowercase; the colon takes one space; the parens
  take none.** `(  MIN-WIDTH  :  100PX  )` is `(min-width: 100px)`.
- **Numbers are CSS-serialised**: `0100` → `100`, `+100` → `100`, `.625` →
  `0.625`, `0.6250` → `0.625`, `100.50` → `100.5`, `1e-2` → `0.01`.
- **What does not parse is quoted byte for byte.** `(  min-bogus  :  1px  )`
  keeps every space. So does `(min-width: 100)`, `(orientation:bogus)`,
  `(color: 8.0)` and `(grid:2)` — and that last group is the useful one: a value
  outside a feature's own set is echoed rather than canonicalised, which is how
  Chrome distinguishes "false" from "not a value of this feature". `(pointer:
  coarse)` normalises and answers false; `(orientation:bogus)` does neither.
- **`all` disappears in front of a condition.** `all and (min-width:100px)` is
  `(min-width: 100px)`, while `not all and (min-width:100px)` keeps its type,
  because the negation needs something to negate.
- **A query with no valid reading at all is `not all`** — `screen and bogus`,
  `(min-width:100px) and bogus`, a bare `not`, a stray `)`, and an empty branch
  of a comma list. But an empty *query* is empty, not `not all`, and an
  unterminated `(` is quoted like any other unreadable text.

That last pair of rules is why the serialiser is organised the way it is: what
parses is rewritten, what does not is quoted, and the parser is therefore the
authority on both. A form this engine cannot read comes back verbatim instead of
guessed at — which is also what keeps the 22 rows above from becoming 22 new
wrong answers somewhere else.

Two of the 119 rows still differ, and both are the same gap seen twice:

| input | Chrome | ours |
|---|---|---|
| `(min-width: 1e2px)` | `true | (min-width: 100px)` | `false | (min-width: 1e2px)` |
| `(min-width: -0px)` | `true | (min-width: 0px)` | `false | (min-width: -0px)` |

Neither is a serialisation gap: the number scanner takes no exponent and rejects
a signed zero, so the length never parses and the condition is quoted. The wider
probe turned up eleven more rows where `matches` differs for the same kind of
reason — a fractional `em`, a nested `((…))`, an `or`, an empty query, a negated
unknown media type — all of them evaluator gaps this plan deliberately did not
touch, and all of them named in `results/media-query-serialization.json`.

## The serialiser was right and the evaluator was wrong, thirteen rows over (2026-08-25)

Writing `media` from the parse rather than the input left the wider probe with
two media rows differing and *thirteen* `matches` rows differing — the
serialisation had become the more accurate half of the same module. Every one of
the thirteen was a rule the evaluator never had, and they group into two:

**A media feature's number is a full CSS `<number>`, and a `<length>` is a
float.** The scanner took digits and an optional fraction and nothing else, so
five spellings of a perfectly ordinary bound answered backwards:

| query | Chrome 150 | engine, before |
|---|---|---|
| `(min-width: 1e2px)` | true | false |
| `(min-width: 100.5px)` | true | false |
| `(min-width: 6.25em)` | true | false |
| `(min-width: 1919.5px)` | true | false |
| `(min-width: -1px)` | true | false |

The last row is the one that had to be measured rather than reasoned about. A
negative `<length>` is *well-formed* — useless as a bound, but every viewport is
above it, and `(max-width: -1px)` is correspondingly false. A `<resolution>` and
a `<ratio>` are the two that reject a negative outright, so the rule lives with
each feature instead of in the scanner. `-0` passes all three, because `-0` is
zero: `(min-resolution: -0dppx)` matches and serialises as `0dppx`.

And the length is a **float32**. `(min-width: 1e400px)` clamps to
`3.40282e+38px` rather than going infinite, `1e-400px` collapses to `0px`, and
`119.9375em` serialises as `119.938em` — printf `%g`, six significant digits,
which is the routine `webapi/css/typed_om.zig` already had for Typed OM. It moved
to `css/units.zig` rather than being written twice. A ratio's terms are *not*
written that way: `(aspect-ratio:1000000/1)` answers `1000000 / 1` where
`(min-width:1000000px)` answers `1e+06px`, both measured.

**A media condition nests, takes `or`, and negates.** The evaluator scanned
tokens and ANDed every parenthesised feature it found, which is four wrong
answers wearing one coat:

| query | Chrome 150 | engine, before |
|---|---|---|
| `((min-width: 100px))` | true | false — read as a feature named `(min-width` |
| `(a) or (b)` | or | and — `or` was accepted as a no-op separator |
| `''` | true | false — an empty query is `all` |
| `not bogus` | true | false — the unknown type returned out of the parse |

That last one is the instructive one. An unknown media type answers false
because it is not this browser, but it is still a *well-formed* query, so
negating it answers true — and the old code returned out of the parse the moment
it saw an ident it did not know, throwing the negation away with it. `not tv` and
`not print` were false for the same reason.

`matches` now walks `tokenize`, the same token split the serialiser writes from,
so the two halves agree on what a query *is* by construction. After it, the
119-row probe is **identical on every media row** and down to three `matches`
rows, all three the two harnesses' viewports (`16 / 9` is true at 1920x1080 and
false at Chrome's 800x600).

One row moved on its own between two runs of the *same* Chrome:
`(prefers-color-scheme:dark)` answered true in the morning and false in the
afternoon. That is the host's appearance setting reaching into the browser, not a
gap in either engine — worth naming because a probe that reads it will disagree
with itself.

## The page was the whole world

`window.outerHeight - window.innerHeight` was **0** and `screenX`/`screenY` were
both **0**. Together those two readings describe a viewport with nothing around
it: no tab strip, no omnibox, no bookmarks bar, and no desktop for the window to
sit on. No browser reports that, and Kasada reads all four numbers — nine
`outerHeight`, nine `outerWidth`, six `screenX`, six `screenY`, five each of
`screenLeft`/`screenTop`, eleven `innerHeight`, four `availHeight`, two
`availWidth` — on a single x-hyatt load (`results/prop-reads-hyatt.json`).

The browser's height is a **constant 87 CSS pixels**, measured with
`scratch/expr-window-shell.js`:

| Chrome 151 | inner | outer | dh | screenX, screenY | screen |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| headed, macOS | 1512x862 | 1512x949 | **87** | 0, 33 | 1512x982 |
| `--headless=new`, `--window-size=1024,768` | 1024x681 | 1024x768 | **87** | 22, 22 | 800x600 |
| `--headless=new`, `--window-size=1280,720` | 1280x633 | 1280x720 | **87** | 22, 22 | 800x600 |
| `--headless=new`, `--window-size=1920,1080` | 1920x993 | 1920x1080 | **87** | 22, 22 | 800x600 |
| `--headless=new`, `--window-size=1920,1200` | 1920x1113 | 1920x1200 | **87** | 22, 22 | 800x600 |

87 in every row: it does not scale with the window, and it does not scale with
the device pixel ratio either (the headed row is a retina panel at dpr 2). Note
that `--window-size` sets the *outer* box and Chrome derives the page from it,
the opposite of the direction CDP's `Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride` works
in — that one sets the page, which is why the page stays the number a caller
owns here.

The headed row is the one worth copying, because every number in it agrees with
every other: the window is maximised into the usable area, so it starts exactly
at `(availLeft, availTop)` and is exactly `availWidth x availHeight`, and the
menu bar is the whole difference between the display and the usable area. The
headless row agrees with nothing — a 1920x1080 window at (22, 22) on an 800x600
screen — which is its own tell and not one to reproduce.

So `Viewport` now derives the arrangement from the page, in one place:

```
inner   = the viewport                          1920 x 1080   (unchanged)
outer   = inner + 87 tall, same width           1920 x 1167
window at (availLeft, availTop)                 (0, 33)
avail   = outer                                 1920 x 1167
screen  = avail + a 33px menu bar               1920 x 1200
```

1920x1200 is a display a Mac has, and the arrangement is the headed reading
scaled up. It also retires an impossibility that was already there and unrelated
to the window: `availHeight` was a hardcoded 1040 against an `innerHeight` of
1080 — a page taller than the screen it was drawn on.

One consequence worth naming: the `device-width` / `device-height` /
`device-aspect-ratio` media features read the **display**, which MQ4 §5 says
they are and which `screen.width`/`screen.height` now answer, so they stopped
being the same numbers as `width`/`height`. `(aspect-ratio: 16/9)` is the page
and still holds; `(device-aspect-ratio: 8/5)` is the display. CreepJS compares
the two families against `screen.*` to catch an iframe-shrunk window, so they
have to be told apart rather than aliased.

### The sweep says the door is unchanged

Two ReleaseFast arms, same IP, minutes apart (`results/b75-*.json`). On all
**21 non-DataDome stations the two arms agree station for station** — the same
16 passes, the same three Cloudflare challenges on scrapingcourse / nopecha /
zeroclover, the same `cf-blocked` on allopneus, the same empty document on
macys, the same 429 on hyatt. The window box moved nothing there, in either
direction.

The eight DataDome stations are not readable in this window, and the control
says so rather than the arms doing. The first patched run scored two fewer than
baseline; a `--fresh` rerun of the *same* patched binary then scored two fewer
again; and a third run of the **unmodified baseline** scored 0/8 — every station
challenged, including three it had passed forty minutes earlier. Individual
stations flipped both ways on both arms (`dd-leboncoin` challenge → pass → 
challenge on baseline alone). DataDome is rate-limiting the address, and a
column measured while that is happening prices the address, not the binary.

One other trap worth writing down, because it produced three convincing
failures: the first patched run ended with `px-wayfair` timing out on
`Runtime.evaluate` and `ks-canadagoose` / `x-hyatt` then timing out on
`Page.navigate`. All three passed on the `--fresh` rerun. That is the cascade
this file's own header warns about — one engine process serves the whole sweep
unless `--fresh` is passed, so a station that wedges the page takes every
station after it with it. Read a run's *tail* failures with that in mind.

## The last two window properties of the wrong kind

Walking every own property of `window` and recording what *kind* it is —
`scratch/expr-window-own-descriptor-kinds.js`, which prints
`kind/writable/enumerable/configurable` per name — leaves **1201 names shared
with Chrome 151 and exactly two disagreements**:

| name | lightpanda | Chrome 151 |
|---|---|---|
| `chrome` | getter, enumerable, configurable | **data**, writable, enumerable, *not* configurable |
| `CSS` | getter, enumerable, configurable | **data**, writable, *not* enumerable, configurable |

Both are one expression from being read (`Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(window,
'chrome').get` is a function here and `undefined` there), and `CSS`'s enumerable
bit is readable with a bare `for...in`. `CSS` is a WebIDL *namespace* object, and
WebIDL §3.2 hangs one off the global as a non-enumerable data property, which is
where its shape comes from; `chrome` is not a WebIDL anything, and Chrome pins
it down with DontDelete.

The bridge only declares accessors, which is what the note in `Window.zig` said
made this unfixable. It is the wrong reading of the constraint: the *realm
setup* has installed data properties with runtime-built values all along —
`Env.zig` does it for `console` and `Context.zig` for `SharedArrayBuffer`, both
through `Object.defineOwnProperty` with explicit V8 attributes. Both properties
moved there, `DontDelete` for `chrome` and `DontEnum` for `CSS`. Descriptor
diffs across the 1201 shared names: **2 → 0**, attributes included.

Identity comes free rather than from the accessor's per-instance cache slot: the
value is built once, when the realm is, so there is only ever one of it.

One thing did not improve. The names moved to the *end* of
`Object.getOwnPropertyNames(window)` — index 1199 and 1200, where they were 70
and 80, against Chrome's 892 and 643. Neither position was right, and the
enumeration order of the global is a separate and much larger disagreement (1201
names against 1237, in a different order throughout). Nothing here makes that
worse or better.

## The cross-origin WindowProxy has no prototype, and its refusals have sentences (2026-08-25)

The section *The cross-origin proxy answered undefined where Chrome throws* above
closed the throw. This closes the shape it left open, and corrects two readings
it left behind.

The fixture is `scratch/xo-server.mjs`: one process listening on 8872 and 8873,
serving `scratch/frame-probe/`. `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` are different origins
to a browser even when they are the same host, so `index.html` on the first port
holds a real cross-origin frame on the second without touching the network. The
reading is `scratch/expr-xo-proxy-detail.js` — 103 readings, name by name and
symbol by symbol: does `[[Get]]` throw, does `[[HasProperty]]` throw, and exactly
what does `[[GetOwnProperty]]` hand back.

**Two arms, 103 readings: sixty-odd differences before, eighteen after.**

### What Chrome's proxy is

Not an instance of anything. `Object.getPrototypeOf(w)` is `null`, so
`w instanceof Object` is false and there is no inherited `toString` to reach for.
The brand is an own `Symbol.toStringTag` whose **value is undefined** — the symbol
is there, the tag is not — which sends `Object.prototype.toString` past every
branded answer and back to `[object Object]`.

The own names are Blink's `CrossOriginProperties` table read top to bottom, nine
attributes then four operations, with `CrossOriginOwnPropertyKeys` appending a
tail:

```
window self location closed frames length top opener parent
blur close focus postMessage then
@@toStringTag @@hasInstance @@isConcatSpreadable
```

Every one is non-enumerable, so `Object.keys(w)` and a for-in are both empty
while `getOwnPropertyNames` answers fourteen — a detector that walks one and then
the other reads the *pair*, and neither alone. The nine attributes are accessor
pairs (`location` is the only one with a setter, and the setter is real:
assigning to another origin's `location` navigates that frame, which is how an
opener sends its popup somewhere). The four operations are data properties with
`writable: false`, not the writable ones an ordinary Web IDL operation gets,
because they are minted by `CrossOriginGetOwnPropertyHelper` rather than by the
member machinery. `then` and the two remaining symbols are data properties whose
value is `undefined`; the own `then` is what makes `await w` resolve instead of
reaching for a call on undefined.

### The sentence, not just the throw

A script that catches the `SecurityError` and reads `.message` gets one. Blink's
names both the property and the origin that was refused, and the line it draws is
**"is this a read of a named property"** — not "does it return a value":

| operation | message |
|---|---|
| `w.document`, `getOwnPropertyDescriptor(w, 'document')` | `Failed to read a named property 'document' from 'Window': Blocked a frame with origin "<o>" from accessing a cross-origin frame.` |
| `w.foo = 1` | `Failed to set a named property 'foo' on 'Window': Blocked …` |
| `'document' in w`, `delete w.document` | bare `Blocked a frame with origin "<o>" …` |

This engine answered DOMException's stock *"The operation is insecure"* for all
of them — a sentence no browser prints here, naming neither. All four now match
byte for byte, which needed the named handler's getter, setter, deleter, query
and **descriptor** callbacks to be separate functions. Not a definer: V8 runs
`Object.defineProperty` through the descriptor lookup first, so a definer
callback never sees it. That was measured, not assumed — one was written, changed
nothing, and is not in the tree.

### The eighteen that are left, and the one mechanism behind five of them

`JSON.stringify(w)` answers `"{}"` where Chrome throws. Be careful about how
strong that evidence is: the widget does read `window.parent` 44 times per
interstitial (that count is from the `prop_read` log, which records the key and
nothing else), and the `"{}"` was recorded in the r1 payload-length hunt above —
but by **our own tracer's** serializer, not by the widget's. So this is a real
divergence a detector could read, and there is no measurement of one doing it.
The stronger reason to want it is that it is the same mechanism as four other
divergences, not that it has a named consumer.

It is not reachable from an interceptor. V8's `JsonStringifier` looks `toJSON` up
with `PROTOTYPE_CHAIN_SKIP_INTERCEPTOR`, deliberately, to avoid the garbage a
full lookup would make. The evidence is decisive from the outside: `w.toJSON`,
`Reflect.get(w, 'toJSON')`, `'toJSON' in w` and
`getOwnPropertyDescriptor(w, 'toJSON')` all throw on this engine, and
`JSON.stringify(w)` still answers `"{}"`. The stringifier never asks.

Chrome's mechanism is not an interceptor at all. It is V8's **access check** —
`ObjectTemplate::SetAccessCheckCallbackAndHandler` plus a failed-access-check
callback — which runs *before* the own-property lookup and therefore catches
every entry point at once. That is why Chrome's `'then' in w` throws even though
`then` is in its own-key list, why `delete w.length` throws on an own property,
and why `Object.setPrototypeOf(w, null)` throws. Five of the eighteen are that
one mechanism. The zig-v8 fork's C binding exposes the handler-less
`SetAccessCheckCallback`, which denies the safelist too and is therefore useless
on its own; the way in is the same one `code_generation.cpp` already took for
`SetModifyCodeGenerationFromStringsCallback` — a repo-owned shim that restates
the declarations it needs. Plan: `cross-origin-access-check`.

The other thirteen, for the record. Six are symbols: `w[Symbol.toPrimitive]` and
`w[Symbol.iterator]` should throw and answer `undefined`, because the handler
carries `kOnlyInterceptStrings` (hardcoded in `Snapshot.zig` for every
`NamedIndexed`); a per-member opt would close it, and the three own symbols are
shielded by `kNonMasking` either way. Four are the property name inside the
sentence: `String(w)` gets Chrome's **nameless** *"Failed to read a named
property from 'Window'"* while this engine names `'toString'`, since ToPrimitive
walks @@toPrimitive → toString → valueOf and an interceptor knows which one it
was asked for where an access check does not. Three of those four are the probe's
own artefact — it calls `String(v)` on the returned proxy, so both arms throw and
only the sentence differs. The last is `w.location`, which answers a
`CrossOriginLocation` object in Chrome (own names `href replace then`) and
`undefined` here; that object is still unbuilt.

## A computed style now answers what the stylesheet said (2026-08-26)

`getComputedStyle` resolved exactly three things out of the author cascade:
`display`, `visibility`, and custom properties. Everything else fell through to
the element's inline `style=` attribute and then to the initial value, so a rule
saying `color:rgb(1,2,3)` read back `rgb(0, 0, 0)`. `Element.zig` said so at the
one place it mattered — *"the computed cascade resolves stylesheet rules for
`display:none` and `visibility` alone"* — so this was scope, not a regression.
Kasada's page reads `getComputedStyle` 126 times on x-hyatt
(`results/prop-reads-hyatt-args.json`; that count is off the `prop_read` log,
which records the call and not which property was then taken off the result).

### Sizing it before doing it

Two probes, four axes, because each axis is a different amount of work:
`scratch/expr-cascade-scope.js` declares each property in an author rule, and
`scratch/expr-cascade-inline-control.js` declares the same ones inline.

| group | agreed before | what it costs to fix |
|---|---|---|
| direct (longhand on the element's own rule) | **2/36** | keep the declaration |
| inherited (declared on an ancestor) | 4/10 | an inherited-property table + a parent walk |
| relative (em, %, calc) | 0/5 | a base value — the parent's font, the containing block |
| shorthand (longhand only exists once expanded) | 0/5 | run the expander on author rules |
| priority (later rule, specificity, !important vs inline) | 1/4 | free, it was already implemented |

**The inline control agreed on 33 of 36.** That is the number that decided the
plan: the values were already being computed and serialised correctly, and only
the cascade was not consulted. So the big slice was cheap, and the two expensive
axes were separable rather than prerequisites.

The machinery turned out to be built, too. `StyleManager.cascadedCustomDeclaration`
already did the whole job for custom properties — id/class/tag bucket walk,
packed specificity, importance ranked above specificity, last-declaration-wins
within a rule. Its only non-generic part was reading one hardcoded list.
`extractRuleProperties` hand-picked seven property names out of each rule and
dropped the rest; that was the actual limit. Widening the storage and
parameterising the walk over which list it reads is the whole change, and
`computedFontSize` already spelled out the ordering to reuse: an `!important`
rule, then the style attribute, then a normal rule, then the initial value.

Two smaller things fell out of it. Shorthands expand on the CSSOM path (whose
declarations went through the declaration parser) and did not on the raw path
(which reads the sheet's text), and which of the two runs depends on whether
anything has touched `.cssRules` — so `margin:11px` answered `margin-top` on one
path and not the other. And the raw path's values are the author's spelling, so
they had to go through `normalizePropertyValue` or a rule's `rgb(1,2,3)` read
back differently from the identical inline declaration's `rgb(1, 2, 3)`.

### The version of this that was worse than doing nothing

Wiring the cascade in fixed 34 readings and broke five in a new way, and the new
way was the more detectable one. `padding-top:2em` used to compute to `0px`; it
computed to `2em`. **A browser never prints a font-relative length, a percentage
or a `calc()` from `getComputedStyle`** — those resolve at computed-value time
and used-value time respectively. `0px` is a value Chrome does print here. `2em`
is a value it never prints, so a detector reading it learns strictly more.

So the cascade's answer is only reported when it is already in the shape a
computed value has; anything else falls through to what was reported before the
cascade was consulted at all, which cannot be worse than the status quo. The
shapes declined are what the two-arm probe surfaced — `calc()`, a percentage, a
font- or viewport-relative length, a bare multiplier for `line-height` — and not
a claim to have enumerated every unresolvable one.

**7/60 to 44/60, with no reading moved to a worse answer.** 1494/1494, and the
29-station sweep reads 19/29 both before and after, with all four station-level
differences traced to DataDome's rate limiting of this address, a 429, or the
tail-cascade effect (each re-checked with `--fresh`).

What is left is three plans, one per remaining axis: `computed-style-inheritance`
(6 readings), `computed-style-relative-units` (5), and
`computed-style-value-gaps` (3 — `border-radius`, `transform`'s `matrix()`, and
`white-space`, all three of which the *inline* control fails too, so they are
value bugs and not cascade ones). `font:` still does not expand, on either path.

## Which properties inherit, measured rather than remembered (2026-08-26)

The cascade change above asked the author sheet about the element and nowhere
above it, so a rule on a parent declaring `color:rgb(1,2,3)` still left the child
on `rgb(0, 0, 0)`. Six of the ten readings in `expr-cascade-scope.js`'s inherited
group disagreed with Chrome — and the four that agreed were the four that do not
inherit, which is the shape a "no ancestor walk at all" bug has.

Nothing in the DOM reports whether a property inherits. There is no
`CSSPropertyRule` for standard properties, no flag on the computed declaration,
and no trick with `inherit` / `initial` / `unset` that distinguishes the two
classes without already knowing a non-initial value. So
`dump-css-inherited.mjs` measures it:

```
initial  = the value on an element that declares nothing
took     = the parent is given candidate values until one of them moves the
           parent's *own* computed value off `initial`
inherits = the child, which declares nothing, now reads the parent's value
```

`child === parent && parent !== initial` has no false positive: a child only
leaves its initial value by inheriting. The "took" step is checked rather than
assumed because most candidates are invalid for most properties and an invalid
declaration is dropped silently — without that check, a property whose candidate
never applied would be classified off a comparison of two initial values.

**131 of Chrome 151's 475 computed longhands inherit, 339 do not, and 5 cannot be
classified this way.** The candidate list took three passes to get there, and
what each pass exposed is worth recording:

- 79 unclassified after the generic keyword list. The gaps were shapes no
  keyword reaches: a percentage (`font-stretch`), a string (`-webkit-locale`), a
  url (`list-style-image`), an image (`background-image`), a shadow
  (`text-shadow`), a font-feature tuple (`font-feature-settings`), an SVG path
  (`d`), a dashed-ident (`scroll-timeline-name`).
- 15 after adding those. Eight were the `border-*-width` family, and they are
  the interesting failure: **a border width is pinned to 0 while the border
  style is `none`**, so no value of `border-top-width` alone can move it off its
  initial. The auxiliary `border-style:solid` that fixes it goes on the child as
  well as the parent — otherwise the child could not have shown a width even if
  the property did inherit, and the test would be constructing its answer
  instead of measuring it.
- 5 after that: `overlay` and `-webkit-text-decorations-in-effect` are UA-only
  and an author cannot set them at all; `animation-trigger`, `rule-overlap` and
  `text-fit` are new enough that no candidate matched their grammar. They are
  left out of the table rather than guessed at, so a lookup answers "does not
  inherit" — which is exactly what the engine did before the table existed.

The walk itself stops at the first ancestor that declares the property, whether
or not the value can be reported. An ancestor declaring `letter-spacing:2em` is
the one that decides the answer even though this engine will not print `2em`, so
a grandparent's `3px` must not show through it — which is why the per-element
lookup answers `none` / `unreportable` / `value` and not an optional. No depth
cap: the chain terminates at the root, and capping it would stop inheriting in a
deep document, which is a wrong answer rather than a slow one.

**inherited 4/10 to 10/10; the probe's total is 50/60.** What is left is three
`direct` readings that the inline control fails too (`border-radius`,
`transform`, `white-space` — value bugs, not cascade ones), five `relative` ones,
and `font:`, which still does not expand on either path.

### ak-macys passes in windows, and the window is not the binary (2026-08-26)

The sweep that carried the inheritance change read `ak-macys` as **pass** —
10 137 nodes and the real title — for the first time in many sessions of
`empty-document`. It is not the change, and the way that was established is
worth keeping, because the station is a trap for exactly this kind of reading.

1. Seven `--fresh` runs on the patched binary: three passes, four
   `empty-document`. So the station is non-deterministic, which by itself
   already kills a one-sample A/B.
2. Four interleaved pairs against the previous main (the cascade work, no
   inheritance): the **control** passed twice. So it is not the inheritance
   change.
3. Five interleaved pairs against `99786a11b`, this session's starting commit,
   rebuilt ReleaseFast — neither the cross-origin nor the computed-style work in
   it. **Ten runs, ten `empty-document`, both arms.**

So the station let both binaries through for something under an hour and then
let neither through. Whatever decides it lives with the address, not with the
engine. **Any A/B run inside a good window reads as a win for whichever arm you
happened to run there**, and the only reading that means anything is interleaved
pairs repeated across windows. The DataDome stations have behaved the same way
all session (dd-datadome flipped challenge → pass → challenge → pass across four
sweeps of three different binaries).

### The burn is a per-character hash in the *challenge* script, and it sits between the GET and the POST (2026-08-24, same round)

`Profiler.takePreciseCoverage` resets its counters on every call, so the first
snapshot after a navigation is exactly the window that ends when the main thread
first yields — and on this page that is the end of the burn. Reading it instead
of diffing it puts the work in the challenge script, not the sensor:

| executions | function | offset |
|---|---|---|
| 5896530 | `MOm` (the `while` body) | 138027 |
| 496241 | `kTh` (`return a.length`) | 137757 |
| 496239 | `DTh`, `rOm`, `ENh`, `T4h`, `K8m` | 120754 … 495657 |

496239 is the length of the challenge script's own source (the file is 496256
bytes), and the code at offset 137986 is a hash over it driven by a state
machine that reassigns its own step function every iteration:

    function MOm(WLh, pDh) {
        var hTh = { WLh: WLh, Phh: pDh, nzh: 0, Gdh: 0, czh: DTh };
        while (!hTh.czh());
        return hTh['Phh'] >>> 0;
    }

That shape is not what makes Chrome slow: `probes/expr-state-machine-hash.js`
runs the same 5954867 steps over the same 496239 characters in **27ms in Chrome
and 28ms here**. So Chrome's 650ms is that loop plus whatever the real step
functions do per step, and the question is only whether we run it at all.

`probes/probe-hash-timeline.js` stamps every 50000th `charCodeAt` and every XHR
open/send, which lines the two arms up:

| | Chrome | lightpanda |
|---|---|---|
| chars 50k → 550k | 49ms → 95ms | 76ms → 231ms |
| `open GET …<sitekey>` | 104ms | 248ms |
| `send` first sensor POST | **783ms** | **295ms** |
| chars 600k | 796ms | 399ms |

Chrome spends **680ms between the GET and the POST with no character reads at
all**; we spend 46ms there. So the two arms do comparable `charCodeAt` work
(635673 vs 650797 over a run) but only one of them pays for the hash inside the
window the payload's counter covers — MOm reads its characters some other way
(indexing, or `codePointAt`), which is also why wrapping `charCodeAt` never
showed it.

Ruled out along the way: it is not script execution order. A page whose first
`<script src>` answers 400ms late and whose second answers immediately runs them
`slow, fast` in *both* engines, so a parser-inserted script is not being run out
