| `margin-block-start:7px;margin:8px` | `8px` / `8px` |

Reproducing that means one slot at *storage* time, which changes what `el.style`
hands back — the specified view, a different surface. `unreportable` is treated
as a declaration for the same reason: the page did set the property and this
engine merely cannot finish resolving the value, so letting the counterpart in
there would answer the wrong declaration.

### Where the computed view stands

`expr-computed-shorthands.js`, declaring arm, over the two plans:

| | agreeing of 261 |
|---|---|
| before the join | 162 |
| after the join | 199 |
| after the mapping | **241** |

The bare arm is 249/261, unchanged by the mapping — nothing there declares
anything for a counterpart to reach.

The 20 that remain are four small things and no large one: ten are the
shorthands `chrome_shorthands.zig` leaves `.unmodelled` and this engine keeps
whole, so they answer the author's own text (`columns:2 30px` reads back in the
author's order where Chrome writes `30px 2`, `font`'s `/1.5` stays a ratio where
Chrome prints the resolved `/21px`); four are the computed-vs-declared
serialisation split plus `timeline-trigger`; two are `background-position-x`/`-y`
computing to the literal `initial`, a hole in the initial-value table; and four
are layout (`-webkit-logical-width` and the two origins).

### The sweep, and what not to read into it

`results/b77-logical.json` reads **20/29** against `b77-patched.json`'s 17/29
from earlier the same day — same optimiser, same host, the join-only build as
the control. Four stations moved: `px-wayfair`, `ks-canadagoose` and
`dd-leboncoin` came back, and `x-hyatt` went from a timeout to `refused-429`.

**None of that is this change.** Three of the four were tail timeouts recovering
and the fourth is a rate limit; no station moved from `pass` to a detection
verdict, which is the only direction that would have mattered here. The +3 is
the same window effect that made the previous section's DataDome runs look like
a regression, running the other way — and twelve alternating runs against a
same-mode control were what it took to establish that. A computed-style value
fix that opens a station would show up as a challenge verdict turning into a
pass and *staying* there across a control, which this is not.

What the change is measured by is the probe: 199 → 241 of 261, zero regressions.

## A computed length is px, and this engine was printing `12pt` (2026-08-26)

Two failures with opposite shapes, both in `declaredValue`'s one binary guard.
`resolvesHere` decides whether a declaration is *already* in the shape a computed
style has; anything it refuses falls back to the initial value. So:

- **Font-relative lengths were refused**, and `padding-top:2em` on a 20px element
  read `0px` where every browser reads `40px`.
- **Absolute lengths were not refused at all.** `pt`, `cm`, `mm`, `in`, `pc` and
  `Q` are not in RELATIVE_UNITS, so they went straight through and
  `getComputedStyle(el).paddingTop` answered `12pt` — the one shape a computed
  style can never carry, and a single expression that separates the engine from
  every browser.

A declaration is now resolved token by token before the guard is reached: `em`
against the element's own computed font size (the parent's on `font-size`
itself), `rem` against the root's, the absolute units by the 96px-per-inch
factors, `vw`/`vh`/`vmin`/`vmax` against the viewport, and the two percentages
with no containing block in them — `font-size` against the parent's size,
`line-height` against the element's own — plus `line-height`'s bare multiplier.

**Nothing new had to be written to print the result.** `units.writeNumber` was
already `%g` at six significant digits with a two-digit exponent, and
`expr-length-format.js` confirms that is exactly Chrome's rule, down to
`1234567.89px → 1.23457e+06px` and `0.0000001px → 1e-07px`. `computedFontSize`
already resolved a font size through `inherit` and relative units.

### Where an inherited length resolves

At the element that *declared* it, not the one inheriting it — a computed px is
what crosses the inheritance boundary. `expr-inherited-em.js` measures it, and
the case that separates the two readings is the one where the child changes its
own font:

| | Chrome's `letter-spacing` on the child |
|---|---|
| ancestor `font-size:20px;letter-spacing:2em`, child bare | `40px` |
| …child `font-size:40px` | `40px` |
| …child `font-size:2em` | `40px` |

The ancestor walk hands each ancestor to `declaredValue` in turn, so this fell
out rather than needing arranging — but it is asserted now, because the two
readings only differ in a case no earlier test had.

### Three refusals, each measured rather than skipped

- **Percentages against a containing block.** `margin-left:50%` is `200px` of a
  400px block for Chrome. Nothing here models a containing block.
- **`ex` and `ch`.** `expr-ex-ch-ratio.js` over five families and three sizes:
  the ratio to the font size is *exactly* constant per family and different for
  every family — 0.44873 serif, 0.52295 sans-serif, 0.54688 monospace, 0.48145
  Georgia, 0.51855 Arial. That is font metrics. One ratio would be a guess
  wearing a measurement's clothes.
- **`calc()`**, which needs an evaluator.

### One leak closed on the way

The guard now runs on the *substituted* text rather than the declaration's.
`padding: var(--x)` where `--x` holds `2em` used to pass — it has no unit of its
own to see — and hand the substituted `2em` straight out.

The cascade probe reads **56/60**, from 53 before this and 7 at the start of the
month's computed-style work. The four left are the two refusals above and the
`font` shorthand, which the table leaves unmodelled and this engine keeps whole.
## The SVG family, filled in (B52, 2026-08-26)

B51 re-measured the four prototype tables against the merged main and found the
window realm at **887 of 923 byte-identical**, 158 names short over 36
interfaces, 21 of which would still be mis-ordered after the names were added.
This batch takes the eight SVG interfaces off that list -- 53 members, from
`SVGSVGElement`'s twenty down to `SVGMaskElement`'s two -- and the table moves
to **895 of 923, 105 missing over 28 interfaces, 16 mis-ordered**. The eight
went from differing to byte-identical, order included; nothing else moved.

| interface | was short by | also mis-ordered |
|---|---|---|
| `SVGSVGElement` | 20 | yes |
| `SVGAElement` | 8 | yes |
| `SVGImageElement` | 8 | no |
| `SVGTextContentElement` | 5 | yes |
| `SVGUseElement` | 4 | no |
| `SVGViewElement` | 4 | no |
| `SVGGeometryElement` | 2 | yes |
| `SVGMaskElement` | 2 | yes |

### Six answers the IDL would have got wrong

Every member was measured on a headed Chrome 151 before it was written, through
`probes/expr-svg-family-semantics.js` and `probes/expr-svg-family-edges.js`.
Six of them do not do what the specification text suggests, and each would have
been written the wrong way from the IDL alone:

- **`currentTranslate` is a fresh object every read and still writes through.**
  `svg.currentTranslate === svg.currentTranslate` is false, yet
  `svg.currentTranslate.x = 5` is readable from the *next* point. It is a
  tear-off; `SVGPoint`'s existing attachment hook -- the one a reflected point
  list uses -- is what makes ours behave the same way.
- **`zoomAndPan`'s setter does not write the attribute.** `svg.zoomAndPan = 1`
  leaves `getAttribute('zoomAndPan')` empty and wins over an attribute that is
  still there. The keywords are case-sensitive, an unrecognised one is
  `UNKNOWN` rather than the initial `MAGNIFY`, and *removing* the attribute
  leaves 0 rather than restoring 2 -- so a `<svg>` that never carried it reads
  2 and one that carried and lost it reads 0. See `svg/zoom_and_pan.zig`.
- **`SVGAElement.referrerPolicy` is not the limited-to-known-values reflection
  `HTMLAnchorElement` uses.** `<a referrerpolicy="bogus">` reads back `bogus`
  in SVG and `""` in HTML. All six of the anchor's string members read the
  lowercase attribute, which in a case-sensitive namespace is worth stating.
- **`SVGAElement.target` is read-only.** `a.target = '_blank'` silently does
  nothing: the descriptor has a getter and no setter, because the IDL type is
  `SVGAnimatedString`.
- **`suspendRedraw` returns 1 every time**, not an incrementing handle.
- **An empty query rect meets nothing.** `getIntersectionList(createSVGRect())`
  is length 0 even on a document whose shapes sit at the origin, which is
  Blink's `gfx::RectF::Intersects` refusing an empty rect. The *element's* box
  is not held to that rule: a `<image>` with no width or height is listed.

`isPointInFill()` and `isPointInStroke()` both report arity 0 and answer `true`
for a path whose first vertex is the origin, so the omitted point is (0,0) and a
point on the outline counts as inside -- a bare winding test would say false
there. `PathData` grew `containsPoint` and `strokeContainsPoint` over the
flattener it already had.

The refusals are two sentences, not one: `charnum > numberOfChars` is "greater
than the maximum bound", `charnum == numberOfChars` is "greater than or equal
to", and a negative index arrives as its unsigned wrap and is quoted back as
4294967295.

### The two readings that still differ, and why they are not this batch's

`getStartPositionOfChar` and `getEndPositionOfChar` disagree with Chrome by
~0.4px on `https://example.com/`, whose stylesheet sets `system-ui, sans-serif`.
The control says where that comes from: give the same `<text>` an explicit
`font-family="serif"` and **every** advance reading matches Chrome to the last
digit, the new ones included.

```
                                 chrome        this engine
text  (system-ui)  getSubStringLength(0,1)   11.5625        11.1875
serif (explicit)   getSubStringLength(0,1)   11.5546875     11.5546875
```

Two pre-existing gaps produce it, both older than this batch and shared with the
already-shipped `getSubStringLength` and `getExtentOfChar`: `system-ui` is not
in the font-metrics table, and an SVG presentation attribute (`font-family` on
`<text>`) does not reach computed style at all -- our serif answer above is the
fallback agreeing by luck, not the attribute being resolved. Neither is a
prototype-completeness gap, so neither is fixed here.

Across both probes, 226 of 230 readings are identical between the arms; those
two are the whole remainder.

## The HTML family, filled in (B52, 2026-08-26)

The same treatment for the ten HTML interfaces the window table still listed:
42 members, and the window realm goes from **895 of 923 byte-identical to 905,
63 missing over 18 interfaces, 9 mis-ordered**. Six of the ten needed their
whole declaration order rewritten, and two of them needed `constructor` moved
off the end.

| interface | was short by | also mis-ordered |
|---|---|---|
| `HTMLImageElement` | 8 | yes |
| `HTMLVideoElement` | 8 | yes |
| `HTMLMeterElement` | 6 | no |
| `HTMLSelectElement` | 5 | yes |
| `HTMLAnchorElement` | 3 | yes |
| `HTMLFormElement` | 3 | yes |
| `HTMLMarqueeElement` | 3 | no |
| `HTMLDialogElement` | 2 | yes |
| `HTMLProgressElement` | 2 | no |
| `HTMLTrackElement` | 2 | yes |

### `constructor` is not last on two of them

B47 recorded that Blink installs a partial interface's members *after* V8
appends `constructor`, so the slot lands mid-list. Two of this batch's
prototypes are in that state, and `Meta.constructor_after` is how they say so:

```
HTMLImageElement   … x, y, decode, constructor, browsingTopics, attributionSrc,
                     sharedStorageWritable
HTMLAnchorElement  … interestForElement, toString, constructor, hrefTranslate,
                     attributionSrc
```

Every one of the five late members is a privacy-sandbox or navigation
attribute Blink gates on a runtime flag. Adding them at the end of the JsApi
would have put them before `constructor` and left both prototypes wrong on a
byte-comparison, having just been made complete on names.

### Six more answers the IDL would have got wrong

- **`<meter>`'s six numbers are one chain, not six reflections.** Each is
  clamped by the ones before it: a bare `<meter>` reads 0/0/1/0/1/0.5 (low
  falls back to min, high to max, optimum to the midpoint) and one written
  `value=5 min=10 max=4 low=1 high=99 optimum=-2` reads **10 for all six**,
  because `max` is floored by `min` and everything else clamps into the
  collapsed range. `high` is the odd one: it is floored by `low`, not by `min`.
- **`<progress>`'s `position` is -1 for a bar carrying no `value` attribute** --
  not for one whose value is 0. `progress.max = 0` is dropped entirely,
  attribute included, because `max` is limited to positive numbers.
- **`select.remove()` is two methods.** With an index it drops that option;
  with no argument it is `ChildNode.remove` and takes the select itself out of
  the tree. Chrome reports arity 0 for both jobs.
- **`dialog.closedBy`'s missing-value default is not a fixed string.** An open
  *modal* dialog reads "closerequest"; every other state -- closed, or open
  non-modal -- reads "none", and so does an unrecognised keyword. That needs a
  modal flag on the element: it is not derivable from the `open` attribute.
- **`marquee.loop` refuses exactly one value.** 0 is an `IndexSizeError`
  ("The provided value (0) is neither positive nor -1."), -1 is accepted and
  written, and a missing or unparseable attribute reads -1.
- **`video.requestPictureInPicture()` rejects rather than throwing**, with an
  `InvalidStateError` naming the missing metadata -- not the user-gesture
  refusal the method is better known for. Measured directly rather than
  recalled.

`<track>` gained the `TextTrack` it owns, built from its own kind/label/srclang
and starting `showing` when the element carries `default`. Reading it also
registers the track with the owning media element, so a `<video>` with one
`<track>` child now reports `textTracks.length` 1 the way Chrome does.
`HTMLFormElement.reset()` is real: a cancelable `reset` event, then every
`<input>`, `<textarea>` and `<select>` back to what its attributes say.

### The two readings that still differ

147 of 150 readings across the probe match. The three that do not are two
findings, both wider than this batch:

- **`img.x` / `img.y` are not `offsetLeft` / `offsetTop`.** On a headed Chrome
  151 the image sat at `offsetLeft` 801 and `x` 1602 -- exactly twice -- so
  Blink is reporting an absolute box in device pixels while `offsetLeft` is in
  CSS pixels. This engine has one layout position and answers it for both,
  which at least keeps the four members consistent with each other.
- **`autocomplete` does not validate its token, on any of the three interfaces
  that carry it.** Chrome reads `<select autocomplete="zz">` back as `""`; so
  it does for `<input>` and `<textarea>`, and this engine answers `zz` for all
  three. The new `select.autocomplete` is the existing `reflect.string`, which
  keeps the three consistent; implementing the autofill field-name grammar is
  one change for all of them and is not a prototype-completeness gap.

## The last eighteen, and the two that are not worth faking (B52, 2026-08-26)

The remaining 63 names had nothing in common but being short. 61 of them are
in, over fifteen interfaces plus `Navigator`'s misplaced `constructor` slot,
and the window realm now reads **921 of 923 byte-identical, 2 missing, 0
mis-ordered, 0 order-only**.

| interface | was short by | | interface | was short by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Request` | 11 | | `NamedNodeMap` | 3 |
| `ProcessingInstruction` | 8 | | `VisualViewport` | 3 |
| `IntersectionObserver` | 6 | | `CustomElementRegistry` | 2 |
| `FontFace` | 5 | | `DOMMatrixReadOnly` | 2 |
| `Selection` | 5 | | `DataTransferItem` | 2 |
| `Navigation` | 4 | | `IDBVersionChangeEvent` | 2 |
| `DocumentType` | 3 | | `WebTransportDatagramDuplexStream` | 2 |
| `IDBDatabase` | 3 | | `Navigator` | 0, order only |

### The two left out, and why each is not one member

- **`EventTarget.when`** returns an `Observable`, and `Observable` is 19
  members with `Subscriber`'s 6 behind it -- two whole interfaces this engine
  does not have. Adding a `when` that answers anything else would put a wrong
  object on the most-walked prototype in the realm rather than a missing name.
  It is worth its own plan; the member list is in `b51-ch-protos.json`.
- **`Date.toTemporalInstant`** needs `Temporal`, and this V8 build has none:
  `--harmony-temporal`, `--js-temporal`, `--js-staging` and `--harmony` all
  leave `typeof Temporal` undefined. Installing the method alone would leave
  the global missing underneath it, which reads worse than the missing method:
  Chrome's `toTemporalInstant` is also the one non-enumerable member in this
  whole batch (`enum=false`), so a script that finds it and then finds no
  `Temporal` has learned more than one that finds neither.

### Six more measured answers

- **`Request`'s defaults are not all the empty string.** `referrer` is
  `about:client` -- the empty string is what an explicit `{referrer: ''}`
  produces -- while `destination` and `referrerPolicy` are empty,
  `targetAddressSpace` is `unknown`, and `duplex` is `half` whether or not the
  request carries a streaming body.
- **A processing instruction's `data` is a pseudo-attribute list**, and Chrome
  puts seven Element-shaped methods over it. Reading never rewrites it; the
  first write re-serialises the whole run with double quotes and single
  spaces. Its `toggleAttribute` answers **undefined**, unlike `Element`'s,
  which answers whether the attribute is now there. One thing was deliberately
  *not* copied: Chrome's member order is not source order (`href="…" type="…"`
  reads back `type,href`) because Blink iterates a `WTF::HashMap`, and a
  bucket order is not a rule.
- **`IntersectionObserver` stores a margin in its four-sided form.** A
  `rootMargin` of `5px` reads back `5px 5px 5px 5px` and `10px 20px` reads back
  `10px 20px 10px 20px`. A `root` of `document` reads back null.
- **`removeNamedItem` throws for a name that is not there** -- a `NotFoundError`
  quoting the name -- where `getNamedItem` answers null. This engine answered
  null from both, which is the one behaviour bug this batch fixed rather than
  filled in (test-first: the assertion failed on the old binary before the
  change). The namespaced form quotes `namespace::localName`, so an empty
  namespace prints as `'::gone'`.
- **`customElements.get` and `getName` disagree about the empty answer.** `get`
  is undefined for an unknown name; `getName` is null for an unknown
  constructor. Only one of the two carries the null-as-undefined flag.
- **`WebTransportDatagramDuplexStream`'s two buffered-datagram limits both
  default to 1**, read off `new WebTransport(...).datagrams` before the
  connection settles. `web_transport.html`'s recorded shape predated them; it
  is re-taken here.

Four interfaces needed `Meta.constructor_after` in this batch and the last
one: `Navigator` (after `vibrate` -- everything from
`deprecatedRunAdAuctionEnforcesKAnonymity` down is installed per context),
`HTMLImageElement` (after `decode`), `HTMLAnchorElement` (after `toString`) and
`DOMMatrixReadOnly` (after `translate`, where the Window-only stringifier
lands). All four are now asserted in `constructor_slot.html` alongside the
twenty that were already there.

163 of 170 readings across the probe match; the seven that do not are the two
deferred members and the `Temporal` global behind one of them.

### The worker realms came along for free

Nothing in these three batches was aimed at a worker, and both worker realms
moved anyway: the interfaces are the same objects, so filling a prototype fills
it everywhere it is exposed. Re-read with the same probes P1 used:

| realm | before (B51) | after |
|---|---|---|
| dedicated worker | 271 of 283 identical, 47 missing over 12, 5 mis-ordered | **277 of 283, 22 missing over 6, 1 mis-ordered** |
| shared worker | 231 of 241 identical, 45 missing over 10, 5 mis-ordered | **237 of 241, 20 missing over 4, 1 mis-ordered** |

What is left there is almost entirely *interfaces*, not members: 17 globals each
realm does not have (`Observable`/`Subscriber`, `Temporal`, `WebSocketStream`/
`WebSocketError`, `CSSSkewX`/`CSSSkewY`, `PressureObserver`/`PressureRecord`,
`BarcodeDetector`, `FileSystemObserver`, `CreateMonitor`, `RestrictionTarget`,
the webkit filesystem-sync pair), plus the same two names the window realm is
short. Only two single-member prototypes remain in a worker and nowhere else:
`FileSystemSyncAccessHandle.mode` and `MediaSource.handle`.

## Acceptance: what 921 of 923 bought at the door (B52 P5, 2026-08-26)

Six ReleaseFast antibot sweeps, alternating base and head across 70 minutes --
`control` is this branch's base (`6b5b27398`), `treatment` is its head, both
built ReleaseFast so a debug SIGABRT on x-sony cannot masquerade as a collapse,
and every run on its own `--port`. 29 stations, 87 station-runs per arm.

```
control:   56/87 station-runs passed (64.4%)   per round: 21, 18, 17
treatment: 54/87 station-runs passed (62.1%)   per round: 17, 20, 17
```

**25 of the 29 stations answered identically in all six runs.** The four that
did not are two findings, and neither is "the batch cost a station":

```
station          c1          t1          c2          t2          c3          t3
dd-datadome      pass        DD-chal     DD-chal     DD-chal     DD-chal     DD-chal
dd-hermes        pass        DD-chal     DD-chal     DD-chal     DD-chal     DD-chal
dd-leboncoin     pass        DD-chal     DD-chal     pass        DD-chal     DD-chal
dd-etsy          pass        pass        pass        pass        DD-chal     DD-chal
ks-canadagoose   error       error       error       pass        error       refused-400
x-hyatt          error       error       error       refused-429 error       refused-429
px-wayfair       pass        error       pass        pass        pass        pass
```

**The DataDome "difference" is a window, not an engine.** All four DataDome
stations were open on the first run of the session and shut between `c1` and
`t1` -- the very first arm switch -- and stayed shut for *both* arms after
that. `dd-datadome` and `dd-hermes` therefore read "control 1/3, treatment 0/3"
while the control's only pass at each is its first run, before the door closed.
Reading that as a regression is exactly the mistake the interleaving exists to
catch: `dd-leboncoin` and `dd-etsy` swung the same way with no rate difference
at all, because their swings happened to straddle an arm boundary differently.

**The one difference that does track the binary is an improvement.** The
control times out on `Page.navigate` at `ks-canadagoose` and `x-hyatt` in
*every* run -- c1, c2 and c3, with t1 and t2 interleaved between them -- while
the treatment completes the navigation in rounds 2 and 3, passing canadagoose
once and getting real 400/429 answers instead of no response at all. A clock
cannot produce that shape: `c2` sits between the treatment's failing t1 and its
succeeding t2 and still hung. All three of the treatment's timeouts, `px-wayfair`
included, are in round 1 and none recur.

### What this says about the lever

**No station moved from challenge to pass because of these 156 members**, and
none regressed. That is worth stating plainly rather than dressing up: the
prototype-completeness hypothesis that B50 proved on ak-macys -- by twelve
builds and 41 site runs -- is now essentially spent as a lever. The window realm
is 921 of 923 byte-identical with 0 mis-ordered prototypes, and the two names
left are two whole interfaces and a missing JS built-in, not a fidelity gap
anyone can close by declaring members.

The eight stations still closed to this engine are `cf-scrapingcourse`,
`cf-nopecha`, `cf-zeroclover` (Cloudflare's managed challenge), `dd-allopneus`
(CF edge, DataDome cookie), `dd-g2`, `dd-saks`, `dd-datadome`, `dd-hermes`
(DataDome), and `x-hyatt`. ak-macys, ak-kohls, ak-homedepot, ak-expedia,
x-sony, x-zillow, px-wayfair and every Cloudflare-fronted ordinary page pass
3 of 3 on both arms. Whatever those eight read, it is not the shape of a
prototype.

## Six of the nine closed doors are shut to Chrome too (B53 P2/P3, 2026-08-26)

B52 ended with nine stations this engine could not get into and no way to tell
which of them anybody gets into. That distinction is the whole difference
between a gap and a phantom, and B35 spent half a month on the wrong side of
it, so the arms here are the two browsers rather than two builds: headed Chrome
against main HEAD (`4c6bba162`, ReleaseFast), ten stations, three rounds, arm
order flipped inside each round, every station its own `--only` and its own
port, Chrome a fresh `--user-data-dir` every time. One sitting, one address,
07:22 to 07:49. Driver `b53-arm.sh`, snapshots `results/b53-{chrome,
lightpanda}-{1,2,3}.json`, rates via `sweep-rate.mjs`.

```
station            chrome    lightpanda
cf-scrapingcourse  3/3       0/3        <- gap
dd-saks            2/3       0/3        <- gap
x-hyatt            3/3       0/3        <- gap
ks-canadagoose     3/3       3/3
cf-nopecha         0/3       0/3        Chrome gets "Just a moment..." too
cf-zeroclover      0/3       0/3        Chrome gets 403 -> 502 Bad gateway
dd-allopneus       0/3       0/3        both arms: CF 403 "Attention Required!"
dd-g2              0/3       0/3
dd-datadome        0/3       0/3
dd-hermes          0/3       0/3
---
chrome: 11/30 (36.7%)   lightpanda: 3/30 (10.0%)
```

**Three of the nine are real; six are doors nobody walks through.** Reading the
six as engine gaps would have been six plans against nothing. `cf-zeroclover`
is not even guarding — it answers Chrome with its own origin's 502.

`dd-saks` is the one that could have been a window, and the interleaving says
it is not: in round 2 this engine went first and was challenged, Chrome
followed four and a half minutes later and passed; in round 3 the order was
reversed and the verdicts were not. Both directions, Chrome wins.

### What the three that are real were measured asking

The `prop_read` log (`prop-reads.mjs --args`, Debug build, target closed so the
context tears down) against one station per vendor —
`results/b53-reads-{x-hyatt,dd-saks,cf-scrapingcourse}.json`. Then every
distinct argument in those logs asked back to both arms on one https page:
`probes/expr-b53-guard-questions.js`, 469 readings, **343 identical, 126 not,
and the 126 are all one subject**.

**The media queries about the display, which both real gaps read.** `dd-saks`
asks eleven and this engine answers two of them the other way: `color-gamut:
p3` and `dynamic-range: high`. `x-hyatt` reads `devicePixelRatio` eight times,
`screen.width`/`height` six, `colorDepth` five, and binary-searches the ratio
to twenty bits with **314 `(min|max)-resolution` queries** — reading `.matches`
every time and `.media` never. Chrome here: DPR 2, screen 1512×982, colorDepth
30, P3, HDR. This engine: DPR 1, 1920×1200, colorDepth 24, sRGB only, SDR only.

That is not Chrome being right — a real Chrome on an sRGB SDR monitor answers
the way we do. It is that the user agent this engine sends says macOS, and no
Mac reports that combination. Whether a guard acts on it is an A/B nobody has
run; `display-capability-persona` and `device-pixel-ratio-persona` are that
A/B, and their acceptance is `b53-arm.sh` over these same ten stations.

**The engine also disagrees with itself near the boundary — but so does Chrome.**
With `devicePixelRatio` 1, this engine answers `min-resolution` *true* at
`1.0000038146972656dppx` and `1.0000044107437134dppx`, and *false* at
`37.795257568359375dpcm`, which is 0.99999995dppx. That was written up here as a
monotone predicate answered non-monotonically, i.e. a defect needing no
reference browser — **and that was wrong**. Driving the same halving ladder in
all three units against Chrome under `--force-device-scale-factor` produces
non-monotone pairs there too: Chrome's dpcm conversion is coarse enough that its
tie region is about 0.005dppx wide, five hundred times wider than this engine's.

What survives is smaller and has to be stated as a *difference*, not a defect.
Asked the three thresholds above, Chrome at ratio 1 answers false, false, true;
this engine answers true, true, false. All three. So the near-boundary answers
diverge in both directions, which matters here only because Kasada's 314 queries
are a binary search that spends its last twenty rungs inside exactly that
region.

The plan named for this is `resolution-query-monotonicity`; its premise is
corrected to "match Chrome's near-boundary answers", and asserting monotonicity
would now be asserting something the reference does not do.

**The negative result is worth as much.** Forty-five `canPlayType` strings,
nineteen `MediaSource.isTypeSupported`, seventeen
`MediaRecorder.isTypeSupported` and the ten WebGL2 `getParameter` pnames Kasada
pulled — **every one identical across the arms**. The media capability table is
not a gap and does not need looking at again.

### Two more differences the guard questions turned up in passing

Neither is evidence about a door; both are fidelity, recorded so nobody has to
find them twice.

**CSS numbers round the other way.** Chrome serialises to six significant
digits breaking ties **to even**; this engine breaks them **away from zero**.
`1.015625` → `1.01562` against `1.01563`, `1078.125` → `1078.12` against
`1078.13`, `1234565` → `1.23456e+06` against `1.23457e+06`. It is the same rule
everywhere a number leaves CSS: the media-query serialiser, `style.width` /
`opacity` / `rotate`, `cssText`, `getComputedStyle`, `CSSUnitValue.toString()`.
`probes/expr-b53-number-serialisation.js` puts 188 half-way cases through all
of them and 101 differ. `<ratio>` is worse than a tie-break: it is not rounded
at all, so `(min-aspect-ratio: 1.421875)` serialises as `1.421875 / 1` against
Chrome's `1.42188 / 1`.

Two smaller things fell out of the same probe. Chrome clamps `opacity` in the
*computed* value and not the specified one — `style.opacity` reads back
`1.01562` and `getComputedStyle(el).opacity` reads `1`; this engine clamps in
neither. And the `CSS` namespace object has three own properties here against
Chrome's sixty-nine: the entire numeric factory (`CSS.px`, `CSS.em`, `CSS.deg`
and sixty more), `registerProperty`, `paintWorklet`, `x` — and it is a
null-prototype object, where Chrome's inherits from `Object.prototype`. B52's
921-of-923 counts *interface prototypes*; a namespace object is not one, which
is exactly the kind of surface that survey could not reach.

## The panel was a contradiction; fixing it opened nothing (2026-08-26)

B53 found the only readings where this engine differs from the headed Chrome
that clears `dd-saks` and `x-hyatt` are the media queries about the display. Two
of the eleven `dd-saks` asks came back the other way — `color-gamut: p3` and
`dynamic-range: high` — and the reason was a persona decision written down in
`css/MediaQuery.zig`: `screen.colorDepth` 24, so eight bits a channel, so sRGB
and SDR. Internally consistent, and contradicted by something this fork says
elsewhere. Its WebGL renderer answers `ANGLE Metal Renderer: Apple M4`, and no
Mac an M4 ships in has an 8-bit sRGB panel.

So the four moved together — colorDepth and pixelDepth to 30, `color` to 10,
`color-gamut` to match `p3` as well as `srgb`, `dynamic-range` to match `high`
as well as `standard` — and one more thing came out of the same probe that is
not about the panel at all: Chrome answers the **boolean** `(dynamic-range)`
false on a display where `(dynamic-range: high)` matches, so it does not
implement that feature in boolean context. This engine answered true. It
answers false now. `(color-gamut)` in boolean context is true in both.

### The A/B

Control main, treatment the branch, both ReleaseFast, the same ten stations and
the same interleaving, 08:32 to 08:59.

```
control   5/30 station-runs passed
treatment 3/30
```

**Nine of the ten stations answered identically in all six runs, and the tenth
pair is the artefact B52 named.** `dd-datadome` and `dd-hermes` passed on `c1`
— the session's very first run — and were shut to both arms from the first arm
switch onward. Both are stations B53 measured headed Chrome failing 0 of 3, so
a pass there is the door's clock, not the binary's. `dd-saks` and `x-hyatt`, the
two this change was aimed at, did not move: 0 of 3 either way.

**The panel was not what those two are reading.** The change stays anyway — it
removes a measured divergence in the boolean form, it removes a self-contradiction
that needs no reference browser to see, and it costs nothing: thirty station-runs
with no regression and 1508 of 1508 tests green. But it is not a lever, and the
next one to try in the same family is the bigger one: `x-hyatt` binary-searches
`devicePixelRatio` with 314 queries, and that number is still 1 against Chrome's 2.

## The ratio moved 41 answers and no doors (2026-08-26)

The display-capability change closed two of the eleven media queries `dd-saks`
asks and opened nothing. The bigger reading in the same family is the one
`x-hyatt` spends 314 queries on, so it went next: `devicePixelRatio` 1 to 2.

What that costs was measured rather than reasoned about. The same headless
Chrome under `--force-device-scale-factor=1` and `=2`, same window, same page,
moves **eleven readings out of forty-two and no others**
(`probes/expr-device-pixel-ratio-blast.js`): the ratio itself, the resolution
media queries, `screen.width`/`height`/`avail*` — which halve *there* only
because that browser's physical panel is fixed while ours is a claim — and
`img.x`/`img.y`, the one place a device pixel reaches a DOM reading.
`innerWidth`, `outerWidth`, `getBoundingClientRect`, `offsetLeft`, computed
width, the canvas backing store, `drawingBufferWidth` and `srcset` selection all
stay put. `screen.*` is CSS pixels, so keeping 1920x1200 at ratio 2 names a
3840x2400 panel: a 16:10 4K monitor, which macOS drives at exactly this scale.

### The A/B

Control the branch's base, treatment its head, both ReleaseFast, fifteen
stations — the three real gaps plus twelve regression watches — three rounds,
arm order flipped inside each. 09:43 to 10:23.

```
control   32/45 station-runs passed
treatment 33/45
thirteen of the fifteen stations answered identically in all six runs
```

`x-hyatt` was `refused-429` six times out of six. `dd-saks` and
`cf-scrapingcourse` likewise never moved. Of the two stations that did,
`px-wayfair` degraded on *both* arms as the session went on — our own repeated
knocking — and `dd-leboncoin` came up 2/3 treatment against 0/3 control, which
is the station B52 already named as the most window-prone on the list and is
n=3. Neither is a result.

**Two changes into this family, no door has moved, and that is the finding.**
The panel and the pixel ratio are not what `dd-saks`, `x-hyatt` and
`cf-scrapingcourse` are reading. Worth keeping anyway, and worth being precise
about what "worth keeping" means: of the 314 media queries `x-hyatt` asks, the
number this engine answers differently from the Chrome that clears it went from
93 to 52, and the 72-rung resolution ladder went from 41 disagreements to none.
Every one of the 52 left is a `width` / `height` / `aspect-ratio` query — the
size of the display we claim, which a real Chrome on a 1920x1200 machine answers
our way too. Twelve regression watches held, 1509 of 1509 tests green.

One inconsistency this introduces, recorded rather than hidden: `img.x`/`img.y`
should now double, and does not. It is read off a layout that does not place
absolutely positioned boxes yet — `position:absolute; left:37px; top:53px`
reports 100,100 here against Chrome's 37,53 — so there is no correct value to
double. That belongs to the layout work, not here.

## x-hyatt: the missing reload is a symptom, not the cause (2026-08-26)

Two changes to the display persona moved nothing at `x-hyatt`, so the next
question was not about a JS surface at all: this engine is refused with a bare
429 and never recovers, while headed Chrome takes a 429 and then a 200. Trace
both (`--trace`, results/b53-hyatt-trace-{chrome,lp}.json) and the two runs are
**identical for four steps**:

```
GET /                      -> 429
GET .../ips.js             -> 200   (Kasada's challenge program, ~305KB)
run the challenge
POST .../tl                -> 200
```

and then diverge in one:

```
chrome   GET Document /    -> 200   <- same millisecond the /tl reply lands
lightpanda   (nothing)             <- sits until the settle expires
```

Chrome goes on to load the whole site, 258 wire entries against this engine's 18.

### Doing the missing step by hand

`--inject`, a cookie to stop it looping, one `location.reload()` after six
seconds. The trace confirms the navigation really went out at ms 6202 — and
Kasada answered **429 again** at ms 6369.

**So the reload is not the missing piece; it is the visible end of one.** Chrome
reloads into a 200 because clearance was granted at `/tl`. This engine does not
reload because the challenge program read its own `/tl` reply and concluded it
had not been cleared — `Location.reload`, `assign` and `replace` appear nowhere
in the `prop_read` log for this station, though `href`, `origin` and `pathname`
are read repeatedly. The script is behaving correctly. The POST is what was
declined.

Two supporting readings, both consistent with a decision that lands before any
of this: the `/tl` reply is 1372 bytes here and 1028 in Chrome, and the very
first 429 interstitial is 1882 bytes here and 1483 there.

**The target for whoever picks this up is "why is `/tl` declined", not "make the
engine navigate".** Cheapest first: compare the two arms' `POST /tl` request
head and h2 frames byte for byte with the tooling that already exists
(`h2-arms.mjs`, `header-echo.mjs`) and rule the protocol layer out before going
anywhere near the payload — B36 lost a stretch inside Akamai's `sensor_data`
doing it the other way round. One protocol difference is already visible in the
trace and is worth checking on its own: the `POST reporting.cdndex.io/error`
that both arms make is preceded by an `OPTIONS` preflight in Chrome and by
nothing here.

### A tooling correction that came out of this

`antibot-sweep.mjs` used to describe `--attach-frames` as the safe way to see an
out-of-process frame's traffic, with only `--same-process` changing the verdict.
That is wrong. Back to back in one sitting, headed Chrome clears `x-hyatt` with
plain `--trace` and is refused 429 with `--trace --attach-frames`. Kasada can
see the attachment. Neither flag is free; the comment now says so.

## The protocol layer is clean, and two of the three readings that said otherwise were the instrument (B53 P3, 2026-08-26)

B52 left the target as "why is `POST /tl` declined", with the protocol layer to
be ruled out first. It is now ruled out, and doing so cost three of the readings
that pointed at it.

### What Kasada actually answers

`antibot-sweep.mjs` grew `--trace-headers`, which records the header block of
every request and every response, and `--trace-body`, which pulls a matching
reply back with `Network.getResponseBody`. One sitting, both arms, `x-hyatt`
(`results/b54-hyatt-xi-chrome.json`, `results/b54-hyatt-hdr-lp.json`):

| `POST …/tl` reply | Chrome | this engine |
|---|---|---|
| status | 200 | 200 |
| `content-length` | 15 | 0 |
| `content-type` | `application/json; charset=utf-8` | `text/plain` |
| `x-kpsdk-r` | `1-B1RHfgQ` | *absent* |

That is the clearance, stated in the reply. B52's conclusion — the challenge
program read its own answer and correctly declined to reload — holds, and the
signal it read is this one.

### The request head is Chrome's, field for field

* `POST /tl` request headers: **every name matches**, and 14 of the 20 values
  match too. The six that differ are `content-length` and the three per-session
  `x-kpsdk-*` tokens — plus `cookie`, below.
* The first `GET /`: **identical, field for field.**
* Local h2 echo, five request shapes (navigation, subresource, XHR POST, JSON
  POST, fetch POST): `h2-cookie-order.mjs --diff` reports **0 differences**
  (`results/b54-h2-{chrome,lp}.json`).

**Nobody needs to re-run the header comparison.** What is left is the cookie
value (two findings below) and the payload itself.

### Three readings that were the instrument, not the guard

**`encodedDataLength` is not comparable across the two arms.** B52 read the
first 429 as 1882 bytes here and 1483 in Chrome and recorded it as the guard
serving two different interstitials. With `--trace-headers` on, the two
responses are the same response: same header set, gzip `content-length` 495
against 496, the one byte being the token, `x-kpsdk-r` on both. The 1882/1483
came from `Network.loadingFinished.encodedDataLength`, which each engine
accounts for in its own way. The same applies to "the `/tl` reply is 1372 bytes
here and 1028 there" — the real difference in that reply is the table above, not
its size. `antibot-sweep.mjs` now says so where the field is pushed.

**`connection: keep-alive` is not an extra header we send.** CDP shows it on
every request of ours and on none of Chrome's, which reads as a connection-
specific field forbidden by RFC 9113 going out on an h2 stream. Both halves are
false. Chrome's `requestWillBeSent` carries only what the renderer set — Cookie,
Accept-*, Sec-Fetch-*, Origin and Content-Length are added later by the network
service and appear only on `requestWillBeSentExtraInfo`, which the sweep now
records. And our `connection` never reaches the wire: curl strips it for h2, and
it is absent from the HPACK block the local echo receives. Comparing the two
arms on `requestWillBeSent` alone invents about a dozen headers Chrome does
send.

**`responseReceived` does carry headers on this engine.** The sweep's own header
comment said it did not, and used that to explain why `cf-mitigated` is unread.
`ResponseWriter` in `src/cdp/domains/network.zig` writes the map, and a traced
run gets 17 response headers off this engine — the same count Chrome reports.

### What survived: the cookie value

`h2-cookie-order.mjs` measured where the `cookie` field sits in the header block
and was blind to what is inside it, because its page set only ever one cookie
and with one cookie every ordering rule agrees. It now serves the shape
`hyatt.com` hands out — four cookies set at once, two of them re-set later — and
two differences come out, on 6 of 6 request shapes
(`results/b54-h2c-{chrome,lp}.json`).

**Chrome sends one `cookie` field per cookie.** Off the same `POST /sensor`,
node's unnormalised `rawHeaders`:

```
Chrome  cookie: source-country=US
        cookie: source-region=CA
        cookie: SENSOR-ID=abcdefghijklmnop
        cookie: a-ssn=2
        cookie: a=2
here    cookie: a-ssn=2; a=2; source-country=US; source-region=CA; SENSOR-ID=abcdefghijklmnop
```

RFC 9113 §8.2.3 allows the split so HPACK's dynamic table can hold one entry per
cookie, and Chrome always takes it. A receiver must join them again, so no
server sees a difference — only something reading the HPACK block does.

**And an overwritten cookie changes place.** Before the overwrite both arms send
`a-ssn a source-country source-region SENSOR-ID`. After `/refresh` re-sets
`a-ssn` and `a`, Chrome sends `source-country source-region SENSOR-ID a-ssn a`;
this engine never reorders.

The obvious explanation — Chrome refreshes a cookie's creation time on overwrite,
so RFC 6265's "path length descending, then creation time ascending" moves it to
the back — is contradicted by the same run. The second visit to `/` re-sets all
four (the following request carries `a-ssn=1; a=1`, so it took) and moves
nothing. Overwriting `a-ssn`/`a` reorders; overwriting `source-country`/
`source-region` does not. The two groups differ in `Max-Age`, `HttpOnly`,
`Secure; SameSite=None`, and in whether the overwrite arrived on a navigation or
a subresource. Which of those is the rule is unmeasured — the plan that
implements this has to isolate it rather than take the sentence above on trust.

### The payload deficit

`POST /tl` body length, three sittings: Chrome 19602 / 19602 / 19594, this
engine 19042 / 19002. **A stable shortfall of about 600 bytes, near 3%.** With
the protocol layer ruled out this is where the decision most likely lives, and
the way in that does not require deobfuscating anything is the read log B50/B52
already built: `results/b53-reads-x-hyatt.json` plus
`probes/expr-b53-guard-questions.js` ask the guard's own 469 questions back, so
the two arms' answers can be ranked by how much shorter ours serialise. A single
`--inject` that lengthens one answer, followed by watching `postLen` move by the
same amount, maps bytes to reads without touching the obfuscated code.

### The preflight, which is a real bug either way

Both arms send `POST https://reporting.cdndex.io/error` cross-origin with the
same `Content-Type: application/json;charset=UTF-8`. Chrome sends an `OPTIONS`
first, carrying `Access-Control-Request-Method: POST` and
`Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type`. This engine sends the POST
directly. `application/json` is not a CORS-safelisted content type, so Fetch
requires the preflight; this is a spec gap that happens to have been found here,
and it needs no anti-bot station to verify.

**None of the four is evidence that Kasada reads it.** They are what a clean
protocol-layer comparison turned up: places where the two arms differ and this
engine is the one that is wrong. A station that stays 429 after any one of them
is fixed is the expected outcome, not a reason to call the fix worthless.

## One cookie field per cookie (B53, 2026-08-26)

The h2 half of the finding above, fixed. `Curl_http_req_to_h2()` in
`deps/curl-patched/lib/http.c` now splits the `Cookie` header into one `cookie`
field per cookie, which is what RFC 9113 §8.2.3 allows the split for and what
Chrome always does. It sits there rather than in `HttpClient.zig` because the
split is legal over h2 and is not over HTTP/1.1, where RFC 6265 §5.4 allows
exactly one Cookie header and Chrome sends exactly one — and one header list is
reused across an h1 and an h2 attempt, with the negotiated version unknown while
it is built. Same division as the `priority` hint.

Before, `h2-cookie-order.mjs --diff` reported on all six shapes:

```
cookie fields carrying 5/5 cookies: left 5, right 1
```

After, the header **name sequence matches Chrome on all six**
(`results/b54-h2c-lp-after.json`). What the diff still reports is the order of
the cookies inside the value, which is a separate defect with its own plan.

`zig build` green, `zig fmt --check` 0, 1509/1509.

**Regression sweep, control against treatment, back to back on one address**
(`results/b54-sweep-{control,patched}.json`): **19 of 29 both arms.** Three
stations moved and none of them is this change:

| station | control (main, 1431) | patched (1433) |
|---|---|---|
| `dd-leboncoin` | pass | datadome-challenge |
| `ks-canadagoose` | error (nav timeout) | pass |
| `x-hyatt` | error (nav timeout) | refused-429 |

`dd-leboncoin` is the only one that looks like a loss, and it is not: three
alternating rounds on that station alone
(`results/b54-lebon-{patched,control}-{1,2,3}.json`) put **both** arms at
`datadome-challenge` 3/3, the unmodified binary included. The station shut
between the two sweeps. The other two moved out of a navigation timeout, which
is not a verdict.

**This is a fidelity fix and not a key.** No station opened, and none was
expected to — nothing here is evidence that any guard reads the cookie field
count.

## A flex row divides its line (B79, 2026-08-26)

Every flex item in this engine was shrink-to-fit. `<div style="display:flex">
<div style="flex:1">x</div></div>` came out 8px where Chrome says 1904, and the
ten-case probe `scratch/expr-flex-item-width.js` agreed with Chrome on 3 of 10.

Two things were in the way, and the first is not a layout question at all.

### `flex` reaches no longhand

`flex` is `.unmodelled` in `chrome_shorthands.zig`. That is the generator being
right: `flex: none` is `0 0 auto` while every other value fills the two numbers
and then the basis, and no single distribution rule reproduces both. So the
declaration is kept whole — and the three longhands had nothing declared at
all, which is why `getComputedStyle(el).flexGrow` on `flex: 1` read the initial
`0` here and reads `1` in Chrome. The layout asking "does this item grow" read
that same `0`.

Measured with `scratch/expr-flex-shorthand.js` against Chrome 151:

| `flex:` | grow | shrink | basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| `1` | 1 | 1 | `0%` |
| `0` | 0 | 1 | `0%` |
| `none` | 0 | 0 | `auto` |
| `auto`, `1 auto` | 1 | 1 | `auto` |
| `2 3` | 2 | 3 | `0%` |
| `200px`, `1 200px` | 1 | 1 | `200px` |
| `2 3 40px` | 2 | 3 | `40px` |
| `50%` | 1 | 1 | `50%` |
| `content` | 1 | 1 | `content` |
| anything that does not parse | 0 | 1 | `auto` |

A computed read of one of the three now derives it from the shorthand. The
declaration is still stored whole, so `style.length` answers 1 where Chrome
says 3, and `el.style.flexGrow` still answers `""` — only the computed view
changed. `flex-basis` also had to stop refusing a percentage: `50%` is what
Chrome computes there, not a length it resolves.

### The row

Each item starts at its flex base size — `flex-basis` when that is a length or
a percentage of the container, else whatever width the box would have had — and
every item whose `flex-grow` is above zero takes a share of what is left, in
proportion to its factor. Measured on the 1904px line:

| row | Chrome |
|---|---|
| two `flex: 1` | 952, 952 |
| `flex: 1` and `flex: 3` | 476, 1428 |
| `flex: 1` beside `width:300px; flex:none` | 1604, 300 |
| `flex: 1` beside a plain item | 1896, 8 |
| `flex-grow:1;flex-basis:100px` beside `…:500px` | 752, 1152 |
| `flex: 1; margin: 0 20px` in a 400px row | 360 |
| `flex: 1; width: 60px` | 1904 |

The last row is the one to keep: `flex: 1` sets the basis to `0%`, so the
declared width never enters the sizing, and Chrome reports a **used** width —
`getComputedStyle(el).width` is `1904px` there and not `60px`. A column
container puts the width on the cross axis instead, where the item stretches
unless `align-items` or its own `align-self` places it; that is the same shape
`justify-items` has on a grid. An out-of-flow or `display: none` child is not
an item and takes no share.

### The correction: `flex-basis: 0` is not a dropped declaration

The first reading of `flex-basis: 0` looked like an invalid value — Chrome laid
the item out at its content width, which is what a dropped declaration would
do, and CSS does require a unit on a `flex-basis` length. The control arm
killed it: **both engines compute `0px` for it**, so the declaration parsed
fine. What holds the item open is the automatic minimum size, and
`scratch/expr-flex-min-content.js` pins down which one:

| item | Chrome |
|---|---|
| twenty `x` (160px of one word), `flex-basis: 0` | 160 |
| a sentence of four-letter words, `flex-basis: 0` | 32 |
| the same sentence, plain | 363 |
| twenty `x`, `flex-basis: 50px` | 160 |
| the sentence, `flex-basis: 50px` | 50 |
| two `flex: 1` items of that word in a **200px** row | 160, 160 |

The floor is the longest **word**, not the whole run — min-content, not
max-content — and the last row overflows the row rather than honouring the 100
each item is entitled to. `min-width: 0` turns it off, which is the proof that
this is `min-width: auto` and nothing else. So an item is never sized below
`Element.minContentWidth`, and a declared `min-width` skips the floor entirely
because this engine models no value for it.

### Acceptance

`scratch/expr-flex-item-width.js`, both arms on one URL: **3/10 → 10/10 rows
identical**, every field of each row included. The 32-case
`expr-flex-shorthand.js` goes to 31/32; the one that stays is `flex-shrink`,
which is deliberately not modelled — two 300px items in a 200px row are 100
each in Chrome and 300 here.

`scratch/expr-layout-box-shapes.js` is unchanged at 14/25 shapes and 196/250
field readings: every remaining difference there is a height, a padding or a
border box part, and none of them is new. `zig build` green, `zig fmt --check`
0, **1509/1509**, and `WebApi: Document` — the 40-calls-over-800-elements
`elementFromPoint` budget — at 1191ms of its 1500.

**Regression sweep** (`results/b79-layout.json`, ReleaseFast, one arm): **22 of
29**, against 19–20 on the two previous sweeps. That is a no-regression
reading and not evidence of a gain — `ks-canadagoose` went 429→200 in this one,
and stations are known to open and shut in windows. Nothing here opened a door,
and nothing here was expected to.

## What moves a cookie in the jar (B53, 2026-08-26)

The other half of the cookie finding, and the one where the first rule that fit
was wrong.

`h2-cookie-order.mjs` showed Chrome moving an overwritten cookie to the back of
the `Cookie` header while this engine never reordered — and, in the same run, a
second visit re-setting all four cookies and moving nothing at all. "An
overwrite refreshes the creation time" explains the first and cannot produce the
second.

`cookie-jar-order.mjs` is the matrix that settles it: ten cases, each planting
`p1 p2 p3` and overwriting `p1`, one property varied at a time, each case in its
own process with its own profile because a jar carries state. Chrome 151
(`results/b54-jar-chrome.json`):

| case | | Chrome | this engine, before |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | baseline, three session cookies, subresource overwrite | `p2 p3 p1` | `p1 p2 p3` |
| B | all three persistent | `p2 p3 p1` | `p1 p2 p3` |
| C | only the overwritten one persistent | `p2 p3 p1` | `p1 p2 p3` |
| D | only the untouched ones persistent | `p2 p3 p1` | `p1 p2 p3` |
| E | the overwritten one is `HttpOnly` | `p2 p3 p1` | `p1 p2 p3` |
| F | the overwritten one is `Secure; SameSite=None` | `p2 p3 p1` | `p1 p2 p3` |
| G | overwrite arrives on a navigation | `p2 p3 p1` | `p1 p2 p3` |
| H | overwrite comes from `document.cookie` | `p2 p3 p1` | `p1 p2 p3` |
| I | **overwrite writes the same value back** | **`p1 p2 p3`** | `p1 p2 p3` |
| J | no overwrite; `p2` on a longer path | `p2 p1 p3` | `p1 p2 p3` |

So the rule is RFC 6265 §5.4's sort — path length descending, then creation
ascending — with one measured deviation from §5.3: **Chrome keeps the original
creation time only when the overwrite writes the same value, and stamps a fresh
one when the value differs.** Persistence, `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, and who did the
overwriting make no difference at all.

That turns the reading that looked like a counter-example into a confirmation.
The second visit re-set four cookies, but two of them (`source-country`,
`source-region`) were written back unchanged and so kept their place, while the
two that did change (`a-ssn`, `a`) were already at the back.

Case J is worth its own line: this engine did not sort by path length either,
and that half is the RFC rather than a Chrome habit.

After the fix, `cookie-jar-order.mjs --diff` goes from **9 differences to 0**
(`results/b54-jar-lp-after.json`), and `h2-cookie-order.mjs --diff` — field
sequence, cookie field count and cookie order together — reports **0 differences
on all six request shapes** (`results/b54-h2c-lp-final.json`). 1510/1510,
`zig fmt` 0.

**Regression sweep: 21 of 29, against 19 for the same main without this change**
(`results/b54-sweep-jar.json` against `results/b54-sweep-patched.json`). **The
two extra passes are not this change.** `dd-leboncoin` and `dd-hermes` were the
stations that moved, and three alternating rounds on each, treatment against a
main build carrying everything but this cut
(`results/b54-ab-dd-{hermes,leboncoin}-{treat,ctrl}-{1,2,3}.json`), put **both
arms at `datadome-challenge` 3/3**. The stations had reopened between the two
sweeps and shut again. `dd-hermes` is in any case one of the six B52 measured as
shut to headed Chrome too.

Read the sweep as "nothing broke". No door opened here either.

## One element, three boxes (B79, 2026-08-26)

`<div style="padding:10px">` on the 1904px line answered 1904 for computed
width, clientWidth and offsetWidth alike. Chrome answers 1884, 1904 and 1904:
one element has three boxes and this engine had one number behind all of them.

Measured with `scratch/expr-box-parts.js` and `expr-box-parts-flex.js` against
Chrome 151. Which reading takes which box:

| reading | box |
|---|---|
| computed `width` | content — **but the border box under `box-sizing: border-box`** |
| `clientWidth` | content + padding, border left out |
| `offsetWidth`, `getBoundingClientRect().width` | content + padding + border |
| `scrollWidth` | the content extent plus the padding |
| `transform-origin` | the centre of the border box |

Four things fall out of that, and each was a reading before it was a rule:

* **An auto-width block fills its containing block with its BORDER box**, so
  its own padding and border come out of its content: `padding:10px` is 1884 of
  content, `padding:10px;border:5px solid` is 1874. What its children fill is
  its content box — a `padding:20px;border:5px solid` parent leaves them 1854.
* **A shrink-to-fit box grows outward instead.** A float, an inline-block and
  an absolutely positioned box with `padding:10px;border:5px solid` are all
  8 / 28 / 38: the content stays at the text and the parts are added on.
* **`box-sizing: border-box` moves which box a declaration names.**
  `width:400px` with 10px of padding and 5px of border per side is 370 of
  content, 390 of clientWidth, 400 of offsetWidth — and its computed `width`
  answers the 400. Declare a width too small to hold its own parts
  (`width:20px` against 30px of them) and the content clamps to nothing while
  the computed width reports `30px`.
* **A percentage padding takes its share of the containing block's WIDTH on
  both axes.** `width:400px;padding:25%` is 476px per side, top and bottom
  included, so the box is 970 tall. This engine computed `0px` for it: every
  percentage but a width was refused.

In a flex row the two halves interlock. What the line hands out are **border
boxes** — `flex:1;padding:0 25px` in a 400px row is 350 of content and 400 of
offsetWidth — while **`flex-basis` stays in the box-sizing's own terms**:
`flex-basis:200px;padding:0 25px` is 200 of content and 250 of offsetWidth, and
the same with `box-sizing:border-box` is 150 and 200. So the free space is the
line less every item's base plus its padding, border and margin, and each
item's content is its base plus its share: two growers, one of them padded,
come out 175/225 and 175/175.

### The 1/64 grid is the one case left

`scratch/expr-box-parts.js` goes from **4 of 21 cases and 137 of 223 field
readings to 20 of 21 and 216 of 223**. The case that stays is `padding:10%` of
1904, where Chrome answers `190.391px` and this engine `190.4px` — Chrome lays
out on a 1/64px grid (190.390625, printed to six figures) and this does not.
That belongs to `layout-unit-64th-grid`, and the test here uses 25% instead,
which lands on the grid exactly.

`expr-box-parts-flex.js` is 8/8. `expr-flex-item-width.js` holds 10/10 and
`expr-flex-shorthand.js` holds 31/32. `expr-layout-box-shapes.js` goes from
14/25 cases and 196/250 readings to **17/25 and 212/250**, and every width
difference left in it belongs to `inline-box-has-no-width` or to a table cell.

`zig build` green, `zig fmt --check` 0, **1509/1509**, and `WebApi: Document` —
the `elementFromPoint` budget — at 1240ms of its 1500. The edges are read only
on the width-measuring path, so `getElementHeight`, the y-only walk that budget
is about, reads no more longhands than it did before.

**A fidelity fix, not a key.** No station opened.

## An inline box has no box (B79, 2026-08-26)

`width` and `height` do not apply to a non-replaced inline box. Chrome computes
`auto` for both and answers **0** for clientWidth, clientHeight, scrollWidth and
scrollHeight, while offsetWidth and `getBoundingClientRect` still report the ink
its line boxes take. This engine gave every `<span>` an 8px box and let a
declared width into it.

Measured with `scratch/expr-inline-box.js` against Chrome 151:

| case | computed w/h | client w/h | offset w/h | scroll w/h |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `<span>x</span>` | auto / auto | 0 / 0 | 8 / 18 | 0 / 0 |
| `<span></span>` | auto / auto | 0 / 0 | **0 / 0** | 0 / 0 |
| `<span style="width:300px">x</span>` | **300px** / auto | 0 / 0 | **8** / 18 | 0 / 0 |
| `<span style="padding:10px">x</span>` | auto / auto | 0 / 0 | 28 / 38 | 0 / 0 |
| `<span>xx<b>yy</b></span>` | auto / auto | 0 / 0 | **32** / 18 | 0 / 0 |
| `<span><div>x</div></span>` | auto / auto | 0 / 0 | **1904** / 18 | 0 / 0 |
| `<img width=40 height=30>` | 40px / 30px | 40 / 30 | 40 / 30 | 40 / 30 |

Three of those rows are the ones worth keeping:

* a declared width is **reported by getComputedStyle and ignored by the box**.
  Both halves matter — answering `auto` there would be as wrong as sizing to it.
* the ink is the whole line, this element's own text **plus its children's**,
  which is where the 32 comes from.
* a `<span>` holding a `<div>` is 1904, because **an inline box is not a
  containing block for a block-level child**. The block escapes to the block
  container the span sits in — which is also what keeps the span's ink from
  asking the div for a width the div would have asked back for.

### The correction: going out of flow gives you a box

An absolutely positioned `<span>` with a declared width kept dropping the width,
because it was still an inline box. It is not: `scratch/expr-abs-inline-display.js`
shows **`position:absolute`, `position:fixed` and `float:left` all compute
`display: block`** on an inline element, while `relative` and `sticky` leave it
`inline`. Blockifying those three is what makes the declared width apply again —
and it is a fidelity fix in its own right, since a computed `display` read of an
absolutely positioned span answered `inline` here and `block` in Chrome.

### Acceptance

`expr-inline-box.js` goes from **4 of 13 cases and 81 of 143 field readings to
16 of 16 and 176 of 176**. `expr-abs-inline-display.js` is 9/9.
`expr-layout-box-shapes.js` goes from 17/25 cases and 212/250 readings to
**18/25 and 217/250** — the inline span's five differences are gone, and the
only width difference left in that table is a table cell's. `expr-box-parts.js`
holds 20/21 and `expr-flex-item-width.js` holds 10/10.

`zig build` green, `zig fmt --check` 0, **1510/1510**, `WebApi: Document` at
1197ms of its 1500ms budget.

**A fidelity fix, not a key.** No station opened.

## The payload deficit: three shapes ruled out, and a bug found on the way (B53, 2026-08-26)

With the protocol layer at x-hyatt ruled out, the only place left for Kasada's
refusal was the `/tl` body, which is a stable ~600 bytes shorter here than in
Chrome (19042/19002 against 19602/19602/19594, three sittings). This is what
that shortfall is *not*.

**It is not an enumeration of the global.** Plant a hundred own properties with
six-character names on `window` -- six hundred bytes of names, chosen to match
the gap -- and `postLen` moves by **-16**, inside the run-to-run noise
(`probes/inject-b54-window-padding.js`, `results/b54-hyatt-{base,padded}.json`).
That matters beyond this station: it would have put the search back on B52's
prototype-completeness lever, which is recorded as spent.

**It is not a collection budget a faster engine fills further.** The Debug
build, a fifth slower to the POST (853ms against 732ms), posts 19034 -- the same
length (`results/b54-hyatt-debug.json`).

**It is not in the answers Kasada was measured taking.** 115 length-bearing
answers drawn from `results/b53-reads-x-hyatt.json` -- the identity block,
screen and viewport, WebGL including the `UNMASKED_RENDERER_WEBGL` the log asks
for 153 times, the media-capability triple, timing, computed style, Intl, the
`toDataURL` fan-out by length -- run on both arms on the same https page
(`probes/expr-b54-answer-lengths.js`, `results/b54-answers-{chrome,lp}.json`).
**19 differ and the total is -116 bytes, not -600**, and even that is mostly
noise: the largest entry was a `performance.now` sample that looked twelve bytes
short until a 4000-sample probe showed both arms have the same shape
(`probes/expr-b54-now-shape.js`, Chrome mean length 15.04 against 14.66 here),
and the ±1s are the headed window being one pixel taller.

So the payload is a fixed set of answers, and what makes it short is not among
the answers the read log names. Whoever picks this up should suspect that its
length is not a linear function of its content at all.

### `javascript:;` was being dropped about a third of the time

Found while looking for the above. Every x-hyatt run leaves two
`javascript-url compile CompilationError` lines in the engine log. Getting the
source took three attempts and two of them were the instrument:

* Planting candidate sources and seeing which warn measures the harness's
  settle, not the engine. The javascript: URL runs as a *scheduled task*, so its
  warning lands wherever the settle puts it -- with a shared engine it is
  charged to the following source, and with a fresh engine per source every
  source warns, including ones that cannot throw.
* Reporting from an injected script over `console` produces nothing, because
  `antibot-sweep` never sends `Runtime.enable` -- Kasada withholds clearance
  from a client that has -- so a station run has no console at all.

Reporting through `document.title` works, and the sweep records it. The answer:
five `<iframe src="javascript:;">` (`probes/inject-b54-jsurl-source.js`,
`results/b54-hyatt-jsurl3.json`). `;` is an empty statement — it compiles in
every JS engine there is, so a CompilationError for it is ours.

`URL.unescape` took an allocator and, for any input without a `%`, handed the
caller's own slice back instead of allocating. `runJavascriptUrl` unescapes into
a task arena and then *schedules* the task, and `javascript:;` has no `%` in it.
Same page, same engine, twenty navigations on ReleaseFast: **six answered
CompilationError before the fix, none after** (`scratch/b54-jsurl2.mjs`). It
hides in a Debug build, where the freed bytes are not reused as promptly — eight
of eight passed there beforehand, which nearly closed the file on it.

At x-hyatt the warnings go **2 → 0** and all five scripts now run
(`results/b54-hyatt-jsurlfix.json`). **The station is still refused-429 and the
body is still ~600 bytes short.** A real bug, not the key.

### The body's length does depend on its content, at about 2.2x

The three negatives above leave one possibility that would change the whole
search: that `postLen` barely depends on what went in, because what goes in is
hashed or packed to a fixed width. One value settles it, and it should be one
that is certainly collected — `navigator.userAgent`, which the read log has
Kasada taking here.

Lengthen it by 200 characters (`probes/inject-b54-ua-padding.js`) and the body
goes **18986 → 19426**, up 440 (`results/b54-hyatt-uapad.json` against
`results/b54-hyatt-jsurlfix.json`). So the length *is* a function of the
content, and the encoding inflates it by roughly 2.2×.

**Which means the target is not six hundred bytes of answers; it is about two
hundred and seventy.** The 600 was measured on the body, and the body is not
where the answers are.

The method generalises and is much cheaper than deobfuscating anything: to ask
whether a value is in a guard's payload and how much of it there is, lengthen it
by a known amount and read `postLen`.

### A sweep whose tail is all timeouts is one crash, not twenty stations

Two runs on one afternoon produced the same shape: normal verdicts for the first
stretch of stations and then `timeout: Page.navigate` for every one after. The
sweep drives 29 stations through a single `serve`, so a process that dies
partway leaves the scanner talking to a corpse, and the printed pass count reads
as a collapse in the guards' behaviour.

**Re-run the affected stations individually before concluding anything.** Doing
that here recovered four of five (`results/b54-solo-*.json`); the fifth,
`ak-kohls`, times out on the control binary too (2/2,
`results/b54-kohls-{ctrl,treat}-*.json`) and is the known intermittent hang that
already has its own plan.

## What the /tl payload is actually short of, asked at the funnels (B55, 2026-08-26)

B54 left this plan a method — lengthen a known answer, watch `postLen` — and a
number: the body inflates content by about 2.2x, so the ~600-byte shortfall was
~270 bytes of answers. The method holds. **The number was wrong, and so was the
frame.**

### The padding table: what the body carries, and what it does not

One station run per candidate, one binary held fixed across all of them, two
baselines taken either side of the set (19018 and 19010, so the sitting drifted
8 bytes). Each family's accessors were lengthened by a fixed amount from
`Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument`, and each probe reports how many times
its override fired through a beacon five seconds in — long after the `/tl` POST,
which goes out at 861ms.

| padded | pad chars | postLen | Δ | probe |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `navigator.userAgent` | 200 | 19426 | **+412** | `inject-b55-ua-pad.js` |
| `getPropertyValue` | 93 × 50 | 22626 | **+3612** | `inject-b55-cssvalue-pad.js` |
| `Plugin`/`MimeType` strings | 65 × 30 | 20826 | **+1812** | `inject-b55-plugins-pad.js` |
| `DOMRect`/offset/client | 212 × ~15 | 20042 | **+1028** | `inject-b55-rect-pad.js` |
| `canPlayType` | 41 × 20 | 19722 | **+708** | `inject-b55-canplaytype-pad.js` |
| `getParameter` strings | 166 × 100 | 19338 | **+324** | `inject-b55-glparam-pad.js` |
| `toDataURL` | 80 × 20 | 19050 | **+36** | `inject-b55-todataurl-pad.js` |

`toDataURL` is the control the set needed: eighty answers lengthened by sixteen
hundred characters move the body by nothing. The canvas bytes are hashed, not
carried. `getParameter` carries about one and a half copies of the renderer
string out of 166 lengthened answers, which is what a guard that asks 153 times
and stores once looks like from outside.

### `--inject` was a no-op on the Chrome arm

Chrome answers `Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument` with an identifier
whether or not the Page domain is on, and runs the script only if it is.
`antibot-sweep` never sent `Page.enable`, so every `--inject` run against Chrome
measured stock Chrome while reporting itself as patched. Verified both ways at
`scratch/b55-inject-check.mjs`: the window marker is `MISSING` without the
enable and present with it. Now sent for both engines whenever `--inject` is
used, so the arms keep the same domains.

Nothing already in the repo is invalidated — B54's injections were all
single-arm — but a two-arm injected reading taken before this was one-armed.

### Hooking the funnels instead of guessing the answers

`TextEncoder.encode`, `btoa`, `crypto.subtle.digest` and `XMLHttpRequest.send`
are where every value has to pass on its way into the body, and the read log
already showed Kasada using all four. Hooking them (`inject-b55-funnels.js`)
gives the payload's sections in plaintext on **both** arms, which is what the
b53 read log could not do.

The Kasada realm, side by side:

| section | lightpanda | Chrome |
|---|---|---|
| timezone / date / GMT string | 21 / 57 / 32 | identical |
| `MediaRecorder` codec list | 522 | 522 |
| a four-value style readback | `0px,0px,0px,0px` | `100075px,155556px,165464px,305134px` |
| **the serialised payload** | **18945–18990** | **19514–19552** |
| `speechSynthesis.getVoices()` | `""` | 9619 |
| `navigator.keyboard.getLayoutMap()` | `{}` | 596 |

**The body is `TextEncoder.encode(payload)`** — 18990 characters against a
postLen of 19002 — so content and body are one to one, not 2.2 to one. The
target is not 270 bytes. It is **524 to 607 characters**, and it can now be read
straight off the payload instead of inferred from the body.

The payload is a JSON array of `<n>:<base64>` tokens, and **both arms emit
exactly 449 of them**. Nothing is missing wholesale; the shortfall is spread
inside about 47 tokens, and the array's order is shuffled per run, so index
alignment across the arms is meaningless (`inject-b55-funnels.js` reports the
per-token lengths; `difflib` on them produces nonsense, which is how the shuffle
was found).

### The voice list is a race this engine loses by being fast

Kasada joins `getVoices()` into `name,voiceURI,lang,localService,default;`
records and hashes the result. Chrome hands it 9619 characters of macOS voices;
this engine hands it the empty string.

This engine *has* the list — 199 entries in `webapi/speech/voices.zig` — and
withholds it for a measured 665ms after first access because that is what Chrome
does. An independent poll (`inject-b55-voices-time.js`) returns 0 at 500ms and
199 at 700ms **on both arms**. What differs is when the guard asks:

* Chrome: `voices@1400=199`, POST at 1670ms.
* here: `voices@555=0`, POST at 858ms.

Same latency, and this engine reaches the guard's collection in a third of the
time. B53 tested this idea with a Debug build and called it settled — but a
fifth slower (853ms against 732ms) does not cross a threshold missed by 145ms.

Spinning the main thread 900ms at document start (`inject-b55-slow-start.js`)
moves the read to `voices@4197=199`: **the list fills, and `postLen` goes to
19026 against a 19014 baseline.** So the voice list is worth *zero* payload
bytes — it is hashed — and the station is still refused. The same is true of the
keyboard layout map. **Two of the three biggest readable differences cannot be
part of the 524.**

### Kasada plants a control colour, and this engine falls for it

Capturing the answers themselves on the live station (`inject-b55-answers.js`)
found what the ninety-three `getPropertyValue` calls are for. Kasada sets
`color` to each of about ninety keywords and reads the computed value back.

Reproduced away from the station, both arms on the same https page
(`probes/expr-b55-system-colors.js`, `results/b55-syscolor-{lp,chrome}.json`),
**53 of 53 differ**:

* 42 CSS system colours — Chrome resolves `accentcolor` to `rgb(0, 117, 255)`,
  `buttonface` to `rgb(239, 239, 239)`, `highlight` to `rgba(128, 188, 254,
  0.6)`. This engine answers with the keyword it was handed.
* 10 `-moz-` names, which only Firefox ever supported, and **`FakeColor`** —
  Kasada's own control, chosen because no browser resolves it. Chrome rejects
  all eleven and `color` keeps its previous value. This engine accepts and
  echoes all eleven.

A computed `color` of `FakeColor` is one expression that no browser on earth
answers. It has its own plan (`css-system-color-keywords`).

### What is attributed, and what is not

Of the 524-character shortfall, measured directly off the payload string:

* **~169 characters** of element geometry — 202 readings answering 985
  characters in Chrome against 208 readings answering 816 here, because Chrome
  answers on its 1/64px grid where this engine answers whole numbers. Feeds the
  existing `layout-unit-64th-grid` plan.
* **20 characters** in the style readback section above.
* **0** from the voice list and **0** from the keyboard map, both proven hashed.

**That leaves roughly 335 characters unaccounted for**, inside tokens that
cannot be aligned across the arms because the array order is randomised. Saying
so is the point: the padding table says which families are carried, but a family
being carried is not evidence that *its* bytes are the missing ones. The next
person should either find an anchor that survives the shuffle — padding one
family and watching which token length moves would do it — or accept that the
byte count is the wrong question, since the two loudest divergences found here
are worth nothing in bytes and everything in value.

## Two ways to measure the same box forever (B79, 2026-08-26)

A regression sweep found this, not a test. Nine stations in, `x-sony` died with
`CRASHED SIGBUS ERR timeout: Runtime.enable`, and the nineteen stations after it
timed out against a process that was already gone. `lldb` on the same page:
`EXC_BAD_ACCESS (code=2)` — a write to the guard page, which is a stack
overflow. Bisecting three merged branches put it in `inline-box-has-no-width`,
and a spike that made the inline ink measurement return zero confirmed it.

The minimal reproduction is five lines:

```html
<span><div style="width:50%">x</div></span>
```

**The loop.** A percentage width resolves through the computed-value machinery,
which reaches back for the containing block's box — and it asked the *parent*.
An inline box is not a containing block, so the `<div>` asked the `<span>`,
whose own ink is that div's box, which asked the span again. Neither call
carried a depth that grew, because `getElementDimensions` starts a fresh
measurement at zero. It resolves against the containing block now, which is
also Chrome's answer: the div takes half of the block the SPAN sits in — 952 on
the 1904px line — and the span is 1904, because a block-level child breaks an
inline in two and what is left spans the line whatever width the child took.

**The fan-out.** The same width is what a percentage padding needs, and an
element has four of those — each measuring the parent from scratch, on top of
the measurement the fill branch already makes. Five of the parent's box per
element is 5^n down a chain:

| nested `padding: 1%` | before | after | Chrome |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8 deep | 626ms | 1ms | 1653 |
| 12 deep | never returned | 1ms | 1525 |
| 16 deep | never returned | 1ms | 1406 |
| 20 deep | never returned | 1ms | 1297 |

The measurement is made once per element and shared with the fill branch, which
makes the chain linear and the widths Chrome's to the pixel.

**The backstop.** `Frame._layout_depth` counts every measurement in flight
whatever route it came in by. A `depth` parameter cannot do that job on its own
— the percentage path above proves it, and there is no reason to think it is
the last route into the layout that drops one.

### What the repro pages exposed on the way past

Two differences that had nothing to do with the crash, both measured on the
same fractional box:

* **clientWidth, offsetWidth and scrollWidth are integers.** They are a `long`
  in the IDL and Chrome rounds the box to reach one: a 1652.911px padding box
  reads **1653** for all three. `getBoundingClientRect` keeps the fraction.
* **A computed `width` is written to six significant figures**, like every
  other computed length. `{d}` printed `1619.8527949957197px` where Chrome
  prints `1619.85px` — seventeen digits is a number no browser has ever
  answered, so that one was a tell on its own.

### Acceptance

`x-sony` passes again. `expr-box-parts.js` goes from 216 to **221 of 223 field
readings** (the two left are the 1/64px grid); `expr-inline-box.js` holds 16/16,
`expr-flex-item-width.js` 10/10, `expr-box-parts-flex.js` 8/8,
`expr-abs-inline-display.js` 9/9, `expr-layout-box-shapes.js` 18/25 cases and
217/250 readings. 1510/1510.

**The reading discipline this cost us**, since it has now bitten twice in one
day: a sweep log where the first N stations look normal and everything after is
`CRASHED … timeout` is **one** crash, not N failures. Only the first line is
signal, the trailing `N/29` is void, and the way to tell a station that shut
from an engine that died is to re-run the suspects one at a time.

### What was fixed from this, and what it cost

`css-system-color-keywords` (merge `f86cb92b0`): the forty-two system colours
resolve to the measured `rgb()`, and `color` is graded against the value classes
