it was measured as taking, so `FakeColor` and the `-moz-` names are refused the
way Chrome refuses them. **53 of 53 readings differed before, 0 of 53 after**;
1510/1510.

`colour-fold-needs-colour-property` (merge `0f5e1ebcb`): the first change had a
regression the tests did not cover. The system colours are words other
properties take as keywords — `menu`, `caption`, `field`, `window`, `mark`,
`background` — and `font` takes six of them, so `getComputedStyle(el).font`
answered `rgb(255, 255, 255)` for `font: menu`. It was caught by *measuring*
the six system font keywords on both arms rather than by a test, which is the
lesson: a fold that reaches every property outside one gate reaches more than
the properties it was written for. `currentcolor` is now the gate, and it is
exact — all sixty colour-valued properties in the measured tables list it and no
other property does.

Neither opens the station: x-hyatt was in a refusing window by the time both
landed, with a clean headed Chrome control answering 429 as well
(`results/b55-chrome-control.json`), so no verdict was measurable either way.

### The six system font keywords, measured (P1 of system-font-shorthand-readback)

Kasada writes all six in one burst at x-hyatt —
`setAttribute('style', 'font: caption !important')` through `status-bar`,
recorded on both arms in `results/b55-voices-{lp,chrome}.json` — and reads four
numbers back.

Chrome expands every one of them identically, and headed and headless agree
exactly (`probes/expr-b55-system-fonts.js`,
`results/b55-sysfont-chrome{,-headed}.json`):

```
font-style=normal|font-variant=normal|font-weight=400|font-stretch=100%
font-size=16px|line-height=normal|font-family=Arial
getPropertyValue('font') -> "16px Arial"
```

This engine keeps `font-family: system-ui, sans-serif` and answers the keyword
itself for `font` — `getComputedStyle(el).font === 'caption'`, which no browser
produces. A thousand-character string measures 13328.125 there and 14227 here.

**One thing this does *not* explain.** The station readback is
`0px,0px,0px,0px` here against `100075px,155556px,165464px,305134px` in Chrome,
and this engine measures a non-zero width for a system-font element locally.
So the zeros on the station come from something else — the element Kasada
measures is laid out with no width there, not merely with the wrong font.
Whoever takes `system-font-shorthand-readback` P2 should fix the expansion on
its own merits and expect the station's four zeros to survive it.

### The voice race, read again: this engine is not wrong, it is early

Worth being precise about, because the first reading above invites the wrong
fix. The independent poll in `inject-b55-voices-time.js` starts at document
start on both arms and answers 0 at 500ms and 199 at 700ms **on both**. So the
665ms this engine models is not out of step with Chrome at all — the timer runs
the same on each. What differs is only when the guard gets round to asking:
555ms here, 1400ms there.

There is no engine bug in that. A Chrome driven this fast would hand Kasada the
same empty list.

Which leaves a real trade-off rather than a defect, and it is the whole of
`speech-voice-warmup-race` P1:

* **Shorten or drop the latency.** The guard then reads what every real browser
  it meets on this page hands it — a full list. Costs the CreepJS row that
  `webapi/speech/SpeechSynthesis.zig`'s header documents: with nothing warming
  it, a headed Chrome renders all three speech hashes blocked, and so does this
  engine today. Zero latency would put us on the other side of that.
* **Leave it.** Faithful in the timing dimension, and wrong in the dimension
  Kasada actually reads.

Do not decide this from the desk. It wants a station measurement, and x-hyatt
was refusing every client by the time this was found — so it waits for a window
where a headed Chrome control passes.

### The 665ms is a per-browser cost, not a per-document one

The paragraph above says not to decide the voice race from the desk. It was
half right: the *station* half still wants a window where a headed Chrome
control passes, but the question it framed — shorten the latency, or leave it —
turns out to be the wrong pair, and one local measurement settles which end
moves. `voice-warmup-timeline.mjs` drives one browser through several
navigations of a loopback page that touches nothing before its `--delay`
elapses, and records when `getVoices()` stops answering empty.

Headed Chrome 151, `--delay 200` so the first ask is separable from document
start, three navigations in one process (`b56-voice-chrome-d200.json`):

| navigation | first ask | length | list complete | after the ask |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1st (cold process) | 200ms | 0 | 902ms | **702ms** |
| 2nd | 201ms | 0 | 226ms | **26ms** |
| 3rd | 200ms | 0 | 227ms | **27ms** |

Two `--delay 0` runs of three navigations each agree: 727/751ms on the first
document, 26/27ms on every one after (`b56-voice-chrome-d0-run{1,2}.json`).

So Chrome pays the ~700ms **once per browser process**, and every later
document gets the list one task tick after it asks. Two things do *not* change
with warmth:

* The first synchronous call is always empty. At `--delay 3000`, on the second
  navigation of a warm process, the ask at 3002ms still answers 0 and fills at
  3028ms (`b56-voice-chrome-d3000.json`). The renderer never has the list ready
  before the page asks for it, however old the document.
* The ask is what starts the load. Same file, first navigation: a cold process
  left alone for three seconds has loaded nothing, and the ask at 3001ms waits
  the full 700ms. Nothing warms this at browser start.

This engine pays it every time. Same page, `--delay 200`, three navigations
(`b56-voice-lp-d200-baseline.json`): complete at 875 / 870 / 865ms — 665ms
after the ask, every document, forever.

That kills both options P1 was written around. Shortening the latency is wrong
for the first document, which is exactly where Chrome is slowest. Moving the
start to document creation is wrong too, and the `--delay 3000` cold arm is why:
Chrome demonstrably has not started when the document is created, or at 3000ms
either. The divergence is neither the length of the wait nor when its clock
starts — it is that ours restarts for every document and Chrome's does not.

Which makes the fix the third option: keep the measured 665ms for the first ask
in the process, and hand every document after it the list on the next task tick
(26ms, measured). That is Chrome, and it also happens to be what a sweep sees —
`antibot-sweep.mjs` drives all 29 stations through one browser, so on any run
where x-hyatt is not the first station, a real Chrome has been warm since
whichever earlier station asked first, and hands Kasada the list ~26ms in while
this engine hands it an empty array for the first 665ms of the page.

It does not resolve the CreepJS trade-off by fiat, it relocates it: the row
depends on whether anything warmed the browser earlier, in this engine exactly
as much as in Chrome. P2 is where that gets checked rather than assumed.

### What the per-browser wait changed, and what it did not

`Browser.voices_asked_at_micros` replaces the per-document countdown: the first
`getVoices()` anywhere in a browser stamps it and waits the measured 665ms, and
every ask after that either finds the stamp older than 665ms (26ms, the round
trip) or waits out the rest of that one run. A stamp rather than a flag, because
Chrome's enumeration runs in the *browser* process and finishes whether or not
the document that asked is still there — measured below, by accident: the
`--warm` arm asks and navigates away within milliseconds, and Chrome still
reaches CreepJS warm. A flag set when the list arrived did not, which is what
the first attempt at this did and why it is not what shipped.

Patched engine against the same page, `--delay 200`
(`b56-voice-lp-d200-patched.json`): 867 / 252 / 251ms complete, i.e. 666ms after
the first document's ask and ~51ms after each later one. Chrome's numbers are
702 / 26 / 27. The residual is a sampling artifact, not a difference: the poll
ticks every 25ms, so a 26ms fill is first seen at 51ms unless the tick lands
past it, as Chrome's did. The iframe arm agrees — 51ms here, 27ms there
(`b56-voice-lp-iframe-patched.json`).

Then the check the plan was written for: does the CreepJS reasoning in
`SpeechSynthesis.zig`'s header survive? It does, but it moves. `creep-speech-row.mjs`
loads creepjs in one browser, optionally after one earlier site (`--warm`), and
reports the speech row:

| | cold browser | an earlier document asked |
|---|---|---|
| headed Chrome 151 | all three `blocked` | `local (180): a158dc36 / remote (19): 036f6dce / lang (51): c4951b20` |
| this engine, before | all three `blocked` | **all three `blocked`** |
| this engine, after | all three `blocked` | the same three hashes, byte for byte, down to the section hash `a8c32496` and `default: Samantha [en-US]` |

So the header's claim — with nothing warming it, a headed Chrome renders the row
blocked and so does this engine — still holds, and is still measured, both rows
of the cold column above. What was wrong was the other column, and the reason it
was wrong is that the wait was scoped to the document. A run that reaches a
guard through several sites, which is every sweep, spends nearly all of its time
in that second column.

Files: `b56-creep-{chrome,lp}-{cold,warm}*.json`.

### Cross-origin: no preflight, and no check on the answer either

`cors-preflight-nonsimple` P1. B53 found the headline case on x-hyatt — the same
`POST application/json` to a third-party origin draws an `OPTIONS` from Chrome
and none from this engine — and the plan asked for the whole shape of it,
measured on loopback rather than on a station. `cors-preflight-echo.mjs` serves a
page on `http://localhost:<a>` and an API on `http://127.0.0.1:<b>` (different
port, therefore a different origin, and both trustworthy), runs eighteen
cross-origin requests, and reports both halves of each: the methods the API
origin actually saw, and what the page's promise did.

| case | Chrome 151 (headed) | this engine |
|---|---|---|
| `GET`, no author headers | `GET` | `GET` |
| `POST text/plain` | `POST` | `POST` |
| `POST application/x-www-form-urlencoded` | `POST` | `POST` |
| `POST application/json` | **`OPTIONS` → `POST`** | `POST` |
| `POST application/json;charset=UTF-8` | **`OPTIONS` → `POST`** | `POST` |
| `GET` with `X-Probe: 1` | **`OPTIONS` → `GET`** | `GET` |
| `PUT` / `DELETE` / `PATCH` | **`OPTIONS` → the method** | the method alone |
| XHR `POST application/json` | **`OPTIONS` → `POST`** | `POST` |
| `credentials: 'include'` + json | **`OPTIONS` → `POST`** | `POST` |

Both engines send `Origin` on every one of them, so that half is already right.

The preflights Chrome sends carry `Access-Control-Request-Method` and, where an
author header is involved, `Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type` or
`x-probe` — the same pair B53 read off x-hyatt.

Chrome also *acts* on the answer, and this is the half the plan's title does not
say out loud:

| case | Chrome | this engine |
|---|---|---|
| preflight allows `GET` only, request is `POST` | `OPTIONS` → `POST`, resolves | same |
| preflight allows `GET` only, request is `PUT` | `OPTIONS`, then **rejects** | `PUT` goes out, resolves |
| preflight omits `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` | `OPTIONS`, then **rejects** | `GET` goes out, resolves |
| preflight names another origin | `OPTIONS`, then **rejects** | `POST` goes out, resolves |
| simple `GET`, response has no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` | **rejects** | resolves, body readable |
| preflight fine, actual response has no ACAO | `OPTIONS` → `POST`, **rejects** | resolves, body readable |
| same request twice, `Access-Control-Max-Age: 600` | `OPTIONS` → `POST` → `POST` | `POST` → `POST` |

The first row is not a bug in either engine: `POST` is a CORS-safelisted method,
so leaving it out of `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` does not block it. `PUT` is
the row that separates them.

So there are two divergences here, not one. The missing `OPTIONS` is the visible
one. The other is that a page in this engine can read *any* cross-origin
response — the check that every real browser applies is not applied at all, which
one expression distinguishes from every browser a guard has ever met.

That is wider than this plan's P2, which is scoped to the preflight and its
answer, and it is deliberately left to its own decision rather than folded in:
this engine exists to fetch pages, and refusing cross-origin reads is a change
with users on the other side of it.

Where an implementation would hook, found while measuring: `Transfer.HeaderSource`
in `network/HttpClient.zig` already separates `.author` (script-set) headers from
the ones the engine adds, which is exactly the set that decides
`Access-Control-Request-Headers`; and `EventSource.corsAllowed` in
`browser/webapi/net/EventSource.zig` is already a working
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin` / `-Allow-Credentials` check, written for the
EventSource WPTs, with a comment saying the general stack does not model CORS.
`Fetch.zig:215` marks the same gap in one line: `assume CORS passed`.

Readings: `b56-cors-chrome.json`, `b56-cors-lp-baseline.json`; `--diff` prints
the per-case comparison.

### The preflight, sent — and what the OPTIONS itself has to look like

`cors-preflight-nonsimple` P2. The gap above is closed: `network/PreflightGate.zig`
sits at the end of the request pipeline, one step behind the robots gate and
shaped like it — a cross-origin `fetch()`/XHR outside the CORS safelist parks,
an internal `OPTIONS` goes out, and the parked transfer either resumes or fails
with the `TypeError: Failed to fetch` that Chrome rejects with. Concurrent
requests behind the same question share one preflight through `SingleFlight`,
and a successful answer is cached for its `Access-Control-Max-Age` (capped at
600s, as Chrome caps it).

Re-measured with the same tool, two cases added: 18 of 20 now agree with Chrome
151. The two that do not are the *other* divergence above — `no-acao-simple` and
`no-acao-after-preflight`, where the preflight half is byte-identical and only
the unapplied check on the actual response separates them.

Sending an `OPTIONS` is not enough on its own: a preflight of the wrong shape is
a fingerprint as surely as no preflight at all. Chrome's, read off the wire:

```
Host | Connection | Accept | Access-Control-Request-Method |
Access-Control-Request-Headers | Origin | User-Agent | Sec-Fetch-Mode |
Sec-Fetch-Site | Sec-Fetch-Dest | Referer | Accept-Encoding | Accept-Language
```

Three things in there are not carried over from any other request shape:

- **No client hints at all.** The `POST` behind the preflight carries
  `sec-ch-ua`, `sec-ch-ua-mobile` and `sec-ch-ua-platform`; the `OPTIONS` carries
  none of the three, and none of the negotiated high-entropy ones either.
- **`Sec-Fetch-Mode` before `Sec-Fetch-Site`.** Every other shape in
  `emitHeaders` writes Site first. The preflight is the one that inverts them.
- **Never credentialed.** `credentials: 'include'` still sends the `OPTIONS`
  without a `Cookie`; only the answer is read more strictly (no `*` wildcard).

`Access-Control-Request-Headers` is lowercased, sorted and joined with a bare
comma — a page setting `X-Zeta` then `X-Alpha` announces `x-alpha,x-zeta` — and
a safelisted `Content-Type` beside an unsafe header does *not* join the list.
`Access-Control-Request-Headers` is omitted entirely when the preflight is
caused by the method alone.

15 of our 16 `OPTIONS` now match Chrome's field order byte for byte. The
sixteenth is XHR's, and it differs for a reason that has nothing to do with
preflight: an uncredentialed cross-origin XHR in this engine sends no `Referer`
at all (`XMLHttpRequest.zig:308` only calls `headersForRequest` when cookies are
in play), so the preflight faithfully copies a header that is not there.

Two more pre-existing gaps the wire dump surfaced, both on the *actual* request
and both outside this plan:

- **On HTTP/1.1**, a script-set `Content-Type` reaches the wire lowercased where
  Chrome sends `Content-Type`; same for `X-Probe` vs `x-probe`. Only on h1: HPACK
  requires lowercase field names, so over h2 curl lowercases the whole set and
  the casing is not ours to pick either way (the same caveat `baselineHeaders`
  already carries for the client hints). Both arms here were measured over h1 —
  the harness's API is a bare `node:http` server — so the difference is real, but
  it is an h1-only one.
- A custom author header lands last for us; Chrome slots it into the client-hint
  block, right after `User-Agent`. Field *order* survives h2, so this one is not
  protocol-limited the way the casing is.

Readings: `b57-cors-chrome.json`, `b57-cors-lp.json`; `--diff` prints the
per-case comparison, and each request in `requestLog` now carries the full
`rawHeaders` it arrived with.
## Chrome lays out on a 1/64px grid (B79, 2026-08-26)

`33.3%` of 400px is 133.2 in arithmetic and **`133.188px`** in Chrome — 8524/64.
Blink's LayoutUnit is a fixed-point number with six fractional bits, and it is
reached by **flooring**: 133.2 x 64 is 8524.8 and the .8 is dropped, not rounded.
This engine answered the arithmetic, and that is worth more than tidiness:
element geometry is the largest attributable block of the `/tl` payload deficit
at x-hyatt, and what the other arm's byte-level read showed missing was
*decimal places* — 202 geometry readings coming to 985 characters in Chrome and
816 here.

### What snaps is a used value, not every length

Measured property by property with `scratch/expr-grid-props.js`, every case
declaring a value deliberately off the grid:

| declared | Chrome computes | on the grid? |
|---|---|---|
| `width: 133.2px` | `133.188px` | **yes** |
| `width: 33.3%` | `133.188px` | **yes** |
| `height: 33.3px` | `33.2969px` | **yes** |
| `padding-left: 33.3%` | `133.188px` | **yes** |
| `padding-left: 10.1px` | `10.1px` | no |
| `margin-left: 10.1px` | `10.1px` | no |
| `font-size: 13.3px` | `13.3px` | no |
| `padding-left: 0.5em` of it | `6.65px` | no |
| `letter-spacing: 0.7px` | `0.7px` | no |
| `border-left: 2.7px solid` | `2px` | whole px, not 1/64 |

`width` and `height` report the **used** value — the box the layout built — so
they snap whatever unit was written. A percentage resolves against a used
length, so it snaps too, wherever it appears. Everything else reports the
**computed** value, which is the length the author wrote.

### The layout had to stop reading its own numbers back out of text

A computed length is written to six significant figures. Snap `33.328125`, write
it, parse it back as `33.3281`, and it is now a hair BELOW its own grid step —
the next floor drops it to the step beneath, and `33.3333%` of 100px comes out
`33.3125` where Chrome says `33.3281`. **No tolerance fixes that**: a value
genuinely 0.0002 below a step and a printed one 0.0002 below the same step are
the same two digits. (Two tolerances were tried before this was understood; both
fixed some rows and broke others, which is what a guess looks like.)
`cascadedComputedLength` hands the layout the number instead of the text.

### The residue, with its diagnosis

An author value with **more than six significant figures** still comes out one
grid step high: `width:465.5466592px` computes `465.546875` here and
`465.53125` in Chrome. Both engines serialise `el.style.width` to `465.547px`
— the difference is that Chrome keeps the number behind it and this engine
keeps only what it serialised. That is a storage defect, not a grid one, and it
has its own plan.

### Acceptance

`expr-layout-grid.js` goes from 2/12 cases to **10/12**; the two that stay
belong to the two neighbouring plans (`266.812` vs `266.813` is six figures
rounded half to **even**, and a percentage margin still reads the initial
`0px`). `expr-box-parts.js` reaches **223 of 223 field readings** — all of it.
`expr-inline-box.js` holds 16/16, `expr-flex-item-width.js` 10/10,
`expr-box-parts-flex.js` 8/8, `expr-abs-inline-display.js` 9/9,
`expr-layout-box-shapes.js` 217/250. 1510/1510.

On a 40-row page of fractional percentages, the measure the payload analysis
uses — total characters of element-geometry readings — is **1790 here against
Chrome's 1783**, over 280 reads. Before this it was short by an order more than
that gap, and short in the direction that mattered.

### The regression sweep, and the two stations that were a window rather than a change

`cors-preflight-nonsimple` P3. Both arms ReleaseFast at the same commit
(`da66d8dd3` = main, against it plus the preflight change), same egress IP
(108.211.179.124, colo SJC), 34 minutes apart. The patched sweep printed
**15/29** and the baseline's had printed 18/29; neither number is the reading.
Both runs hung at station 27 (`ak-kohls`, `timeout: Runtime.enable`, ~56s) and
both dragged the four stations behind it into `timeout: Page.navigate` — the
tail is one hang, not four failures, and the trailing `N/29` is void. Re-run
individually, all four came back the way the baseline has them:
`ak-expedia` pass, `px-wayfair` pass, `ks-canadagoose` pass (429→200),
`x-hyatt` refused-429.

Three DataDome stations did read differently — `dd-datadome`, `dd-leboncoin`,
`dd-hermes` passed for the baseline and drew a challenge here. `dd-leboncoin`
came back on its own re-run. The other two were settled by alternating the two
binaries at the same station, three rounds each, six pairs in all:

| round | `dd-datadome` | `dd-hermes` |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | baseline challenge / patched challenge | baseline challenge / patched challenge |
| 2 | baseline challenge / patched challenge | baseline challenge / patched challenge |
| 3 | baseline challenge / patched challenge | baseline challenge / patched challenge |

The baseline binary that had passed them 34 minutes earlier now fails them too.
That is the window, not the change — which is why a single-sample A/B at a
DataDome station cannot be read at all, and why the alternation is the only
thing that answers it.

`ak-kohls` was alternated the same way: the baseline errored 3 of 3, the patched
arm 2 of 3. It is the pre-existing intermittent hang (`ak-kohls-evaluate-hang`),
it bites both arms, and it is not this change's account.

Net: **zero regressions.** Every station compared inside the same window agrees
between the two arms.

Readings: `b57-sweep-patched.json`, `b57-only-<station>.json`,
`b57-ab/ab-{base,patch}-<station>-<round>.json`.

## A percentage margin is a share of the width, on all four sides (B80, 2026-08-26)

`margin-left: 33.3%` in a 400px line is `133.188px` in Chrome and was `0px`
here: the percentage had no containing block to take a share of, so the whole
declaration fell through to the initial value. The box beside it kept the whole
400 where Chrome gives it 266.8125, so one declaration was wrong in two
readings at once.

Measured with `scratch/expr-margin-pct.js`, seventeen shapes on the 1904px body.
The reading worth writing down is the vertical pair:

| declared, in a 400px line | Chrome `margin-*` | Chrome computed `width` |
|---|---|---|
| `margin-left: 33.3%` | 133.188px | 266.812px |
| `margin-left: 10%` | 40px | 360px |
| `margin-left: 10%; margin-right: 10%` | 40px / 40px | 320px |
| `margin-top: 10%` | 40px | **400px** |
| `margin: 10%` | 40px × 4 | 320px |
| `margin-left: -10%` | -40px | **440px** |
| `margin-inline-start: 10%` | 40px on the LEFT | 360px |

**A percentage margin never looks at a height.** `margin-top: 10%` of a 400px
line is 40px — the same width a percentage padding takes its share of, which is
already why a `padding: 10%` box has a clientHeight of 399 and not 18. And a
margin may be **negative**, which a padding may not: the box gets 440 of a 400px
line, so the resolver had to stay signed where `paddingPx` clamps at zero.

### The width is measured once, because two margins asking is the shape that crashed

This is the third property family to want the containing block's width from
inside the measurement that is already computing it. The rule from the padding
crash applies unchanged: **the same parent width is measured once per element
and shared** (`CSSStyleDeclaration.containingWidth`, a `*?f64` threaded through).
Letting each of the two horizontal margins ask for itself would have put the
same multiplier back on the chain that `boxEdgesSharing` exists to keep off it,
and routing them through the computed-value path would be worse — that path
starts a fresh measurement at depth 0, which is the loop that took `x-sony` out.

Two places already hold the number and now hand it over: the fill branch in
`dimensionsAt`, and the flex line in `flexItemWidth` — every item on a line has
the same containing block, and `container` is already its content width, so the
flex case costs nothing at all.

Measured with `scratch/expr-deep-margin.js` on `named-probe/pctmargin-*.html`:

| nested `margin: 1%` | one clientWidth | width here | Chrome |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8 deep | 3ms | 1619.97px | 1619.97px |
| 12 deep | 1ms | 1494.28px | 1494.28px |
| 20 deep | 1ms | 1271.34px | 1271.34px |
| 60 deep | 2ms | 567.063px | 567.062px |

Linear, and identical to Chrome sixty levels down but for one digit — and that
digit is the six-figure tie, not the layout: 567.0625 rounds half to **even** in
Chrome and half **up** here, which is `css-number-round-half-even`'s task.
`inline-pct-margin.html`, the `<span><div style="margin-left:50%">` shape that
was the crash's other half, answers 952px on both engines.

### What is still not a margin here

`margin: auto` centres the box in Chrome and it reports the used value it
computed — **150px a side** for a 100px box on a 400px line. This engine reports
the keyword `auto`. That is a used value for a keyword rather than a percentage
against a width, so it is a different task and has no plan yet.

Found on the way, and also not this: a `<p>`'s initial top margin is `1em` of
its own font, so Chrome answers **20px** inside a `font-size: 20px` parent where
this engine answers a fixed 16px.

### Acceptance

`expr-margin-pct.js` goes from 1 of 17 shapes to **16 of 17** (the 17th is
`margin: auto`), and every field but one matches Chrome exactly — that one being
the six-figure tie above. `expr-layout-grid.js` goes 81/88 field readings to
**86/88**, and the two left are both that same tie. No regression anywhere else:
`expr-box-parts.js` holds 223/223, `expr-inline-box.js` 176/176,
`expr-flex-item-width.js` 60/60, `expr-box-parts-flex.js` 8/8,
`expr-layout-box-shapes.js` 221/257 (its residue is the height family, which
still has no plan). 1511/1511.

Three assertions that pinned the refusal now carry Chrome's own numbers: 40px in
`percentage_width.html`, 200px twice in `computed_relative_units.html` — the
vertical one included — and 952px in `computed_author_longhands.html`.

### The sweep, and the two stations that looked like a regression

Compared against a sweep from earlier in the day the patched run printed
**17/29** where that one printed 22/29, with two DataDome stations gone from
pass to `datadome-challenge` and a four-station tail of `timeout: Page.navigate`.
Read off the summary line, that is a regression. It is not one, and neither half
of it survives a second look:

* **The tail is one hung process, not four failures.** Re-run each station on
  its own with `--only`, both binaries: `ak-expedia` pass/pass, `px-wayfair`
  pass/pass, `ks-canadagoose` pass/pass, `x-hyatt` refused-429 on both. The
  baseline sweep has the same tail in the same place, and its own head of it is
  `ak-kohls` hanging 55s on `Runtime.enable` -- a known intermittent that is on
  the control arm too.
* **The two DataDome stations are a time window, not the patch.** The first
  paired run had the baseline going first and passing, then the patched arm
  seconds later getting challenged -- which reads exactly like a regression.
  With the order **reversed** and repeated three times, **all twelve runs on
  both arms were challenged**: 6 patched, 6 baseline, no exceptions. Then a
  full baseline sweep in the same band as the patched one came back with
  `dd-leboncoin` and `dd-hermes` challenged as well. The door was open for
  whoever knocked first that hour and shut for everyone after it.

Two full sweeps in the same time band, with every `error` replaced by its paired
`--only` re-run: **baseline 20/29, patched 20/29, and one printed difference in
29 stations** -- `ak-kohls`, which is the intermittent hang and re-runs to pass
on both.

A single A/B on a DataDome station cannot tell the engine from the hour. The
only reading that can is an alternation whose order is flipped, and the claim it
supports is deliberately narrow: **the two arms are indistinguishable at every
station**, which is all a fidelity change should be asked to show. No door opened
here, the same as every layout task before it on this line.

## The layout was reading its own print back (B80, 2026-08-26)

A computed length is written to six significant figures. That print is measured
and correct — Chrome answers `465.547px` for `width:465.5466592px` and so does
this engine — but it was also the only copy of the number the layout had, and
six figures is not enough to lay a box out with.

| declared width | Chrome lays out | this engine laid out |
|---|---|---|
| `465.5466592px` | 465.53125 | 465.546875 (a step high) |
| `465.53125px` — already on the grid | 465.53125 | 465.515625 (a step **low**) |
| `1.9999999px` | 1.984375 | 2 |
| `199.9843751px` | 199.984375 | 199.96875 |

The second row is the one that says this is not a rounding preference. An author
value sitting exactly on the grid came out a step below it, because `465.531` —
its own print — floors to the step beneath. The rounding runs both ways and
neither direction is recoverable from the text.

### What Chrome keeps is a float, not the double the author wrote

Three models were put to twenty-one widths chosen because their 1/64 floors
separate them (`scratch/expr-precision-model.js`): the author's double, that
value narrowed to a **32-bit float**, and the six-figure print.

| model | matches Chrome |
|---|---|
| f32 of the author's number | **21 / 21** |
| the author's f64 | 15 / 21 |
| the six-figure print | 14 / 21 |

`width:100.0156249px` is the cleanest of them: as a double it is a hair under a
grid step and floors to 100, and as a float it **is** the step — 100.015625,
which is Chrome's answer. So keeping full f64 precision would have been the
wrong fix twice over: it fails six rows, and it fails rows this engine was
getting right by accident.

That is Blink's own shape — a CSS length is parsed into a float and LayoutUnit
floors it — and `Element.layoutUnit` narrows there now. It is also what the
`1e-9` epsilon that used to sit in that expression was standing in for: a product
that lands 1e-13 under an exact step is that step once it is a float, and the
epsilon was a guess at the same thing.

### One string cannot be both

The print has to stay six figures and the layout needs more, so the number is
carried beside the text: `Declaration.specified` and `NamedDeclaration.specified`,
filled from the RAW value at both routes into the cascade — a stylesheet rule and
the style attribute — and null whenever `var()` substitution changed the text,
because then the number belongs to what was stored rather than to what came out.
It costs nothing at read time, which matters: a Cloudflare challenge sweeps 736
property names off one element, and re-serialising at every read would have paid
for this on the hottest path in the engine.

### A box's parts are grid units before they are added

Found on the way, and measured: `padding-left:465.5466592px` inside a 1000px line
leaves 534.46875 of content and a border box of exactly **1000**. Subtracting the
unsnapped 465.546646 leaves 534.453125 and a border box of 999.99978 — a number
no browser reports, and a tell on its own. Each part snaps on the way in, not
after the arithmetic.

### Acceptance

`expr-precision-model.js` goes from 14/21 rows to **21/21** on geometry, and
62/63 field readings; the one left is `7.015625` printed to six figures, a tie
Chrome breaks to even and this engine breaks up — `css-number-round-half-even`'s
task, not this one. Nothing else moved: `expr-box-parts.js` holds 223/223,
`expr-inline-box.js` 176/176, `expr-flex-item-width.js` 60/60,
`expr-margin-pct.js` 133/136, `expr-layout-grid.js` 86/88,
`expr-layout-box-shapes.js` 221/257. 1518/1518.

**And the byte gap the payload analysis was left with closes exactly.** On the
40-row fractional-percentage page, the element-geometry character count over 280
reads was 1790 here against Chrome's 1783. It is now **1783**, and all 40 rows
read identically — 4 of them differed before, each by one grid step in a width
whose percentage had eight significant figures. That was the last named item in
the `/tl` payload deficit.

### The sweep pair, read the way the last one had to be

Both arms ReleaseFast, both based on `9e1a31366`, same egress address, run
back to back: `1.0.0-dev.1488+9e1a31366` as the control and
`1.0.0-dev.1491+23d22093e` as the patched one. Zero `CRASHED` on either.

The two full sweeps printed **17/29 patched against the control's own count**,
with two verdict differences — and the differences pointed in **opposite
directions**, which is the shape noise has and a change does not:
`dd-datadome` challenged the control and passed the patched arm, `dd-leboncoin`
did the reverse. Neither survived contact with an alternation whose order flips
between rounds: twelve runs, three rounds, both stations, **both arms
challenged every single time**.

The four-station `timeout: Page.navigate` tail was on both arms in the same
place. Re-run one station at a time against both binaries: `ak-expedia`
pass/pass, `px-wayfair` pass/pass, `ks-canadagoose` pass/pass, `x-hyatt`
refused-429 on both. One hung process, as it was last time.

Resolved, with every `error` and every noisy DataDome verdict replaced by its
paired per-station reading: **base 19/29, patched 19/29, and zero
station-by-station differences across all 29.** The ten that stay shut are
identical on both arms — the three Cloudflare challenges, five DataDome, the
Cloudflare block at `dd-allopneus`, and `x-hyatt`'s refused-429.

**Two discipline notes, both earned tonight and both of the same family:** the
`N/29` summary line is never the reading (17/29 became 19/29 twice this evening),
and a log that prints an arm's *label* can claim a comparison it never made. A
sibling session wrote `arms="patched baseline"; for arm in $arms` — bash reflex
in a zsh shell, which does not word-split an unquoted scalar — and ran nine
comparisons of one binary against itself while the log said "patched" for half of
them. Print the binary's `version` string on every row, not the label: two
commits cannot share eight characters, and a label can.

## Every empty element is 5px tall here (B80, 2026-08-26, in progress)

`block-height-from-content` was opened for a narrower thing — an empty `<div>`
is 0px tall in Chrome and 5px here, the placeholder `dimensionsAt` starts every
measurement at. Measuring the tag space first (`scratch/expr-empty-intrinsic.js`)
showed the leak is not about blocks: **eighteen of twenty empty elements report
5px**, and one expression over any of them separates this engine from a browser.

Chrome's answers are not one number either. They fall into four groups, and a
blanket 0 would be wrong for eleven of the twenty:

| empty element | Chrome computed / client / offset / rect | here |
|---|---|---|
| `div`, `p`, `section`, `ul` | `0px` / 0 / 0 / 0 | 5px throughout |
| `table` | `0px` / 0 / 0 / 0 | 5px |
| `img` (no src) | `0px` / 0 / 0 / 0 | 5px |
| `canvas`, `video`, `object`, `svg` | `150px` / 150 / 150 / 150 | 5px |
| `iframe` | `150px` / 150 / **154** / 154 | 150 / 150 / 150 — offset misses the border |
| `input` | `15px` / 17 / **21** / 21 | 5px |
| `textarea` | `30px` / 34 / **36** / 36 | 5px |
| `select` | `19px` / 17 / 19 / 19 | 5px |
| `button` | `6px` / 2 / **6** / 6 | 5px |
| `progress`, `meter` | `16px` / 16 / 16 / 16 | 5px |
| `hr` | `0px` / 0 / **2** / 2 | 5px |
| `br` | `auto` / 0 / 0 / **18** | auto / 0 / 0 / **0** |
| `span` (inline) | `auto` / 0 / 0 / 0 | already correct |

Three readings worth pulling out, because they are the ones a single constant
cannot reproduce:

* **the replaced default is 150px**, not 0 — `canvas`, `video`, `object` and
  `svg` all answer it with no attributes at all, and `iframe` answers 150 of
  content with 154 of offset because its 2px default border is outside the
  client box. This engine already has the 300x150 pair for `iframe` and nothing
  for the other four.
* **a form control's height is intrinsic and each one is different** — 21, 36,
  19, 6, 16. `button` is the odd one: 6px of offset off 2px of client, which is
  padding and border around an empty line.
* **an `<img>` with no src is 0**, which is the opposite of the broken-image
  icon this engine already models. The icon is for an `src` that failed, not for
  an absent one.

The `<div>` case has a failing test (`css/block_height.html`, six of eight
shapes red). The rest of this table has none yet, and the remaining plan tasks —
a block's height as the sum of its line boxes, and the stack of its in-flow
children — are measured but unstarted. Readings for those:
`scratch/expr-block-height.js`.

*Closed in B81: that table is now 33 of 34 readings against Chrome, from 3. The
chapter below is what it took.*

## The placeholder was a question the layout asked itself (B81, 2026-08-27)

`dimensionsAt` started every measurement at `{width: 5, height: 5}` and then
asked `dims.height == 5.0` to mean "nothing has sized this yet". That is two
defects wearing one number, and only the first was known.

The known one: 5px leaked out of eighteen of twenty empty elements, and 5px is
not a number a browser reports for an empty box.

The other one: **a length an author may write was a magic value.** Seven readings
across four shapes had their declaration mistaken for the absence of one
(`scratch/expr-five-sentinel.js`). `<div style="height:5px">x</div>` answered the
text's 18 four times over. And `<div style="width:5px">` came out reporting a
computed `width` of **5px beside a clientWidth of 400** — getComputedStyle reads
the declaration, and the fill branch had overwritten the box. No browser produces
a 5px-wide box that is 400px wide, and a guard reading both at once sees it.

"Undetermined" is `null` now, and whatever is still null at the end is 0.

### One rule found three defects

The placeholder fix turned up a pattern that then explained two more, and it is
worth stating on its own because it is a way of looking rather than a fact:

> **When one half of a pair consults a table and the other half does not, the
> wrong half is invisible for exactly as long as nobody compares them.**

* `usedBorderWidth` asked the AUTHOR cascade for `border-top-width` and answered
  `medium` — 3px — when it found nothing. The `border-top-style` read two lines
  away *did* consult the per-tag UA table and came back `inset`. Six tags
  reported a border they draw at 1px or 2px as 3px, and the style half looking
  right is why nobody noticed. Measured: input, button, iframe and fieldset draw
  2px; textarea, select and hr 1px.
* the same asymmetry ran through `paddingPx`, `borderPx` and `usesBorderBox`:
  **the layout box had never seen the UA stylesheet at all**, while the computed
  style beside it always had, through `getDefaultPropertyValue`. A `<ul>` kept
  its 40px `padding-inline-start` inside the content box. An `<iframe>` and an
  `<hr>` drew no default border. A `<button>`, whose entire 16x6 box *is* UA
  padding and border around a 0x0 content box, came out 0 by 0. A `<select>`
  declared `width:100px` reported a clientWidth of 100 against Chrome's 98.
* and the first commit of this plan did it to itself. Collapsible whitespace
  correctly stopped making a line box, with an escape hatch for
  `white-space: pre` beside it — which asked the cascade for a longhand called
  `white-space`. There is no such longhand: `white-space` is a **shorthand**,
  expanded to `white-space-collapse` and `text-wrap-mode`, and
  `chrome_shorthands.zig` had carried that measured table all along. So the
  hatch never fired, `<div style="white-space:pre"> </div>` was 0 tall against
  Chrome's 18, and a lone space measured 0 where Chrome makes it 4. The commit's
  own test asserted only the collapsing cases and went green over the half that
  did not work.

### The empty-element table, and why a blanket 0 is wrong for eleven of twenty

| what | Chrome | how it is reached here now |
|---|---|---|
| `div`, `p`, `section`, `table`, `img` (no src), empty float / absolute / inline-block | 0 | nothing sized it |
| `ul` | 360 of content, 400 of client | UA `padding-inline-start: 40px`, now visible to the layout |
| `canvas`, `video`, `object`, `svg`, `iframe` | 300x150 | intrinsic content box |
| `iframe` offset | 304x154 | UA 2px border, now visible |
| `input` | 145x15 / 149x17 / 153x21 | intrinsic 145x15 + UA `1px 2px` padding + 2px border |
| `textarea` | 177x30 / 181x34 / 183x36 | intrinsic 177x30 + 2px padding + 1px border |
| `select` | 22x19 computed, 20x17 client | intrinsic 20x17 + 1px border, reported as the BORDER box |
| `button` | 16x6 / 12x2 | **no** intrinsic box — the whole thing is UA padding and border |
| `progress`, `meter` | 160x16, 80x16 | intrinsic content box |
| `hr` | 398 of content, 400x2 of offset | fills the line as a border box, less its UA 1px border |
| `br` | rect 0x18, offset 0 | the one element whose rect is not offsetHeight's box |
| `svg` offsetWidth | `undefined` | SVGElement has none; already correct |

Two of those a rule would get backwards:

* **`select` and `button` report the BORDER box as their computed width**, which
  is not the content box the spec names. Checked against a plain div rather than
  assumed: `<div style="box-sizing:border-box;width:100px;padding:3px;border:5px
  solid">` computes `100px` beside a clientWidth of 90 in Chrome, and this engine
  already agreed. So an empty `<select>` reporting 22px of computed width beside
  20 of clientWidth is one box read two ways, not a contradiction. Forcing either
  tag back to `content-box` gives the intrinsic content box directly — 20x17 for
  select and **0x0** for button (`scratch/expr-border-box-resolved.js`).
* **a `<canvas>` has an intrinsic ratio and it comes from the buffer.** Its
  width/height attributes are the buffer's size, not presentational hints for the
  CSS properties the way `<img>` and `<iframe>` take them — so a declared width
  scales the other axis and does *not* leave the height attribute standing.
  `<canvas width=400 height=100 style="width:600px">` is 600x150 in Chrome, the
  4-to-1 buffer applied to the declared width, not the 600x100 an
  attribute-as-hint model gives. `video`, `object` and `svg` have no ratio at
  all: each keeps its 300 or its 150, and an `<svg viewBox="0 0 40 10">` at 600px
  wide is still 150 tall.

### A line box is worth its line-height, and text wraps

The computed `line-height` was already right — `30px`, `32px`, `24px` for every
form. Only the layout was not asking, so a block holding one character was always
the font's own box. Thirteen forms measured (`scratch/expr-line-box.js`): a
length, a bare number, a percentage and an em, each against two font sizes, and
inherited from a wrapper.

A fractional line-height lands on the layout grid like any other used length:
`line-height:1.1` at 16px is 17.6 in arithmetic and **17.59375** on the page,
printing as `17.5938px`, rounding to 18 for clientHeight while the rect keeps the
fraction. Two lines of it are 35.1875 — each line snapped and then summed, the
same "parts snap on the way in" the box edges follow.

And `line-height` does **not** reach a non-replaced inline box's offsetHeight: a
`<span style="line-height:30px">` is 18 tall where an `inline-block` with the
same declaration is 30.

Wrapping is greedy, and the useful finding is that this engine's advances are
already within half a pixel of Chrome's — enough to land on the same line *count*
rather than merely close. Forty `word`s in a 100px box are twenty lines in both,
in 200px eight, in 400px four. A word wider than the box overflows instead of
breaking (twenty-four `a` in 50px is one line), which falls out of never
splitting one.

Two axes decide it and they are separate longhands:

* `text-wrap-mode: nowrap`, which `white-space: pre` expands to — those same
  forty words are one line.
* `white-space-collapse` anything but `collapse` keeps a newline as a break, and
  the count there is measured rather than derived: **one more line than there are
  newlines, less one when the text ends with one.** A lone newline is one line,
  `\na` is two, `a\nb\n` is two, `a\n\n` is two, `a\n\nb` is three,
  `a\n\n\nb` is four.

### The line COUNT is right at either device scale; the line's height is not

Worth separating, because it decides which plan owns which half. Re-measured on
headed Chrome at `--force-device-scale-factor=1` and `=2`:

| reading | dsf1 | dsf2 | here |
|---|---|---|---|
| `line-height: normal` at 16px | 18 | **18.5** | 18 |
| forty words in 100px | 360 | **370** | 360 |
| forty words in 200px | 144 | **148** | 144 |
| `line-height:30px` | 30 | 30 | 30 |
| `line-height:1.1` | 17.59375 | 17.59375 | 17.59375 |

370 / 18.5 is twenty and 148 / 18.5 is eight, so **the wrap counts are identical
at both scales** — what moves is the value of one line, which is
`font_metrics.boundingBox` and not this plan. Every explicit line-height is
identical at both scales, because those are not font metrics. Headed at dsf1 is
byte-identical to headless over all 29 readings, so "headed changes it" is really
"dsf2 changes it".

### The rect was not the box offsetHeight is

`offsetHeight` goes through `clientHeight`, which falls back to the sum of the
children when the box has no height of its own. `getBoundingClientRect` used the
raw dimensions and skipped that fallback, so a div holding three lines of text
reported **54 of computed height, 54 of clientHeight, 54 of offsetHeight and 0 of
rect height**. With padding and a border, 66 against 30. Another pair no browser
produces.

And every visible child counted toward the stack, including the ones that are not
in it. A floated, `absolute` or `fixed` child does not contribute — a block
holding only one of those is 0 tall — while `relative`, `sticky`, `inline` and
`inline-block` children do, which is the half a "position is not static" test
would get wrong.

The float is why that is three states and not two: **a float is out of its
parent's height and still inside the parent's scrollable overflow**, so a block
holding one reads 0 of clientHeight and 18 of scrollHeight. An `absolute` child is
out of both (`scratch/expr-out-of-flow-stack.js`).

### What this did not close

The verification pass measured a block whose children are *inline*, and that is a
whole formatting context rather than a loose end — **fourteen of twenty shapes
disagree** (`scratch/expr-inline-content-lines.js`), so it is recorded here as
the next thing to build rather than folded in:

| shape | Chrome | here |
|---|---|---|
| `a<br>b` | 36 | 0 |
| `a<br>b<br>c` | 54 | 0 |
| `<br>` alone | 18 | 0 |
| `<span>a</span><span>b</span>` | 18 (one line) | 36 (stacked) |
| `<span style="line-height:30px">a</span>` | 30 | 18 |
| `a<div>b</div>` | 36 | 18 |
| `a<div>b</div>c` | 54 | 18 |
| a `<span>` of forty words in 100px | 360 | 18 |
| `a<img width=40 height=30>b` | 34 | 30 |

`textLayout` bails on any element child, so a `<br>` — two lines in every browser
— had no text height at all and fell back to the child stack, which for a `<br>`
is nothing. The two directions in that table are the point: we stack two spans
that Chrome puts on one line, and we put on one line the wrapped span Chrome
gives 360. Neither is a patch to the other.

Four smaller ones, each measured and each needing its own decision:

* **scrollWidth sums the children as a ROW.** `contentWidth` says so in its own
  comment, so a stack of three 400px children answers 1200 where Chrome answers
  400 (and 760 against 390 for a padded one). The row sum is what lets a page
  that appends nodes until a width threshold terminate, so changing it needs
  measurements of what that sum is actually for.
* **adjacent sibling margins collapse.** Two 18px children with `margin:10px 0`
  put their parent at 46 in Chrome and 36 here: 36 of content plus the one
  collapsed 10 between them, the outer two collapsing out of the parent.
* **`display:none` keeps `transform-origin: 50% 50%`** rather than resolving
  against a box. Chrome answers the percentages verbatim; this engine answers
  `0px 0px`.
* **an `<img>` whose src 404s** is 0 in this build of Chrome, where this engine
  draws the 16px broken-image icon that bot.sannysoft.com's "Broken Image
  Dimensions" row reads. Left alone rather than traded for the other.

### The sweep, and the three-station drop that was not one

Both arms ReleaseFast, 29 stations, same route, thirteen minutes apart:

| | base `dev.1502+6d316fafb` | patched `dev.1513+4e519df7e` |
|---|---|---|
| stations open | 22 | 19 |

The three that differ are all DataDome — `dd-datadome`, `dd-leboncoin`,
`dd-hermes`, each `pass` on the base column and `datadome-challenge` on the
patched one. The other 26 are identical station by station, including the three
real gaps (`cf-scrapingcourse`, `dd-saks`, `x-hyatt`), which stayed shut on both.

That is the shape a regression has, and it is also the shape this station group's
hourly window has, so the two were separated with a symmetric control rather than
an argument: **six alternating rounds over the eight `dd-` stations, both arms,
sharing the same hour, printing each binary's version string on every row.**

Every one of the six came out 2 of 8, station for station. `dd-datadome`,
`dd-leboncoin` and `dd-hermes` were challenged on the **base** binary in all
three of its rounds — the same binary that had served all three forty minutes
earlier — while `dd-etsy` and `dd-seloger` passed on both arms throughout. So the
drop is the hour and not the diff.

Three things about the apparatus that are the reusable part:

* the log prints each binary's `version`, never the arm's label. A previous baton
  wrote `for arm in $arms` in **zsh**, which does not word-split an unquoted
  scalar, and ran nine "comparisons" on one binary while the log said "patched"
  for half of them. A label can lie; `dev.1502+6d316fafb` cannot.
* the alternation is what makes the control symmetric. Running base then patched
  once each cannot distinguish the engine from the hour, however many stations it
  covers, because the two columns are never in the same hour.
* the patched binary's version changed between round 1 and round 2 (a rebuild
  landed mid-run: `dev.1513+4e519df7e` then `dev.1514+82a1875c9`). Both are the
  patched arm and both read 2 of 8, so it costs nothing here — but it is visible
  in the log precisely because the version is printed, which is the point.

No station opened. Six of the seven closed doors on the base column are ones
headed Chrome cannot open either; the three that are real gaps were unmoved. This
plan closed 33 of 34 readings on the empty-element probe, took layout-box-shapes
from 221 of 257 to 243, and left the door count where it found it.
## The layout grid is a device pixel's, and text reaches it by ceiling (B81, 2026-08-27)

> **On what this was worth.** This change closed 120 of the 208-character
> geometry gap on the page the `/tl` attribution was built from, and that number
> is a PROXY -- a synthetic 40-row page, not the payload. A later reading of the
> real `/tl` length across seven alternating samples found the remaining 88
> characters worth **zero** bytes (see "The /tl payload does not weigh the
> geometry" above). Read the section below for what it made *correct* -- the used
> lengths this engine reports are Chrome's now, on the grid Chrome uses -- and
> not as bytes recovered. B55's own note applies: the byte count is the wrong
> question.

Two rules, measured together because the first one is why the second was
findable. The grid this engine floors onto is **half the size Chrome's is** on
the display this engine claims to have, and a width that comes from measuring
text does not floor at all.

### The grid is 1/64 of a *device* pixel, not of a CSS pixel

`Chrome lays out on a 1/64px grid` above is a reading of a **1x** Chrome. Run
the same cases under `--chrome-arg --force-device-scale-factor=2` and every step
halves:

| declared | Chrome at dsf 1 | Chrome at dsf 2 | this engine |
|---|---|---|---|
| `width: 33.3%` of 400px | 133.1875 | **133.1953125** | 133.1875 |
| `width: 133.2px` | 133.1875 | **133.1953125** | 133.1875 |
| `width: 100.0078125px` | 100 | **100.0078125** | 100 |
| `width: 100.012px` | 100 | **100.0078125** | 100 |
| `width: 33.35%` of 400px | 133.390625 | **133.3984375** | 133.390625 |
| `padding-left: 33.3%` | `133.188px` | **`133.195px`** | `133.188px` |
| `transform-origin` of that box | `66.5938px 9px` | **`66.5977px 9.25px`** | `66.5938px 9px` |

Read with `probes/expr-b81-specified-grid-dpr.js` and
`expr-b81-grid-test-cases.js`, the second of which builds the markup
`tests/element/layout_unit_grid.html` asserts rather than a paraphrase of it, so
the dsf-1 column reproduces the assertions in the file today and the dsf-2 column
is what they become. The floor and the 32-bit narrowing are both unchanged —
twelve widths chosen to sit a hair under a 1/128 step by less than half a float
step give the float model **11/11** and the double model **0/11**
(`expr-b81-precision-at-128.js`). Only the step size moves.

**This engine answers the dsf-1 column while telling every page its
`devicePixelRatio` is 2.** That is not a rounding difference, it is the persona
disagreeing with itself, and `Window.zig`'s own note on why the ratio is 2 says
what reads it: Kasada takes eight reads of `devicePixelRatio` on one x-hyatt load
and then spends 314 media queries binary-searching it to twenty bits.

### A text advance ceils onto the same grid, once per text node

The plan that found this was named for the wrong rule. Its first reading — seven
strings, all seven on the 1/64 grid — was taken at a device scale factor of 1,
and four of the same seven are not on the 1/64 grid at the factor this engine
claims:

| string at 16px serif | dsf 1 | dsf 2 | on 1/64? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `aaa` | 21.3125 | **21.3046875** | no |
| `word` | 32.890625 | **32.8828125** | no |
| `aaa bbb` | 49.3125 | **49.3046875** | no |
| `aaa bbb ccc` | 74.609375 | 74.609375 | yes |

**Say `--force-device-scale-factor` explicitly; do not infer it from
`--headed`.** The first version of this section blamed headlessness, because the
original reading was headless and the reading that corrected it was headed. That
was a coincidence of this host: run the 2x2 and the factor is the whole story
(`results/b81-2x2-{headless,headed}-dsf{1,2}.json`) —

- `headless/dsf1` and `headed/dsf1` are **byte-identical** over all ten strings,
- so are `headless/dsf2` and `headed/dsf2`,
- and headed with no factor named equals `dsf2` here, because this display is 2x
  while headless defaults to 1x.

So `serif` resolved to the same metrics either way, and `--headed` fixed the
reading by accident. It may still be the right flag for a question about which
family a name resolves to; it is not what this one turned on, and a machine whose
display is 1x would reproduce none of this from `--headed` alone.

Every headed reading is a multiple of 1/128, and the rule that fits all of them
is `ceil(advance * 64 * dpr) / (64 * dpr)`:

- **the grid is the device pixel's**, same as above. One 30-case probe answers
  `ceil(x*64)/64` at dsf 1 and `ceil(x*128)/128` at dsf 2, and 14 of the 30
  differ, so it is not a coincidence of 16px (`expr-b81-grid-128.js`,
  `expr-b81-grid-vs-dpr.js`);
- **it is a ceil.** At dsf 2, `aaa bbb ccc` at 12px, at 14px and `aaa` at
  13.25px are cases where floor and round both land one step low and only ceil
  lands on Chrome's answer;
- **once per text node, not once per box.** Three text nodes holding one `a`
  each are 17.3203125 at 13px where one node holding `aaa` is 17.3125 — three
  ceils against one. `aa` + `aaa` in two nodes is 28.859375 where `aaaaa` in one
  is 28.8515625. Both hold at both scale factors.

Where 16px hid it: a 2048-unit font at 16px puts every advance on a multiple of
`16/2048` = 1/128 already, so the ceil has nothing to do and the grid is
invisible. 13px, 19.5px and 11px separate them.

The advance itself is already right. Over 30 strings and sizes this engine's
`measureText` matches headed Chrome's to the last bit 29 times, and the one miss
(21.3px, differing in the 11th digit) ceils onto the same step. **What is wrong
is only the last step**: this engine rounds the advance to a whole pixel and then
reports that integer as the length, so `getBoundingClientRect().width` and
computed `width` lose the fraction while `offsetWidth` — which is `round()` of
the box in Chrome too — was right all along.

### Scoring the model, and what is left over

`sum over text nodes of ceil(f32(advance) * 128) / 128` reproduces **100 of 107**
headed-Chrome readings across four probes. Narrowing the sum to a 32-bit float
before the ceil is worth 2 of those (25/26 against 23/26 on a 200-glyph run over
26 sizes); accumulating per glyph in a float instead, which is what Blink looks
like it does, scores 17/26 and is wrong.

All seven residuals are the advance, not the grid, and none of them is this
plan's:

- `AV` is 21.046875 in Chrome and 23.109375 here — **no kerning**. `five words
  in a row` misses for the same reason.
- 8.4px and 9.9px have a per-glyph advance **0.00444px under** the linear one,
  the same absolute offset at both sizes, while the 24 other sizes swept are
  linear to within float noise (`expr-b81-small-sizes.js`,
  `expr-b81-nondyadic-sizes.js`). Whatever Chrome does there, it is not
  `units * size / upem`.

### Found on the way: the `font` shorthand never reaches the box

The size sweep only worked once it stopped using the `font` shorthand. With
`style="font:<n>px serif"` this engine answers **the same width for every size** —
the default font's — while its own `measureText` answers each size correctly, so
the shorthand reaches the canvas and not the cascade. `font` is `.unmodelled` in
`chrome_shorthands.zig`, so the declaration is kept whole and the nineteen
longhands are never set:

| declared | read | Chrome | this engine |
|---|---|---|---|
| `font:13px serif` | computed `font-size` | 13px | **16px** |
| `font:13px serif` | computed `font-family` | serif | **Times** |
| `font:13px serif` | rect width | 60.625 | **75** |
| `font:13px monospace` | rect width | 86.09375 | **75** |
| `font-weight:bold` | computed `font-weight` | 700 | **bold** |
| `font-stretch:condensed` | computed `font-stretch` | 75% | **100%** |
| `font-family:monospace` | computed `font-size` | **13px** | 16px |
| `<b>aa</b>` | rect width | 16 | **14** |

The longhands are fine — `font-size:13px` gives 61 here against Chrome's 60.625,
which is this section's grid and nothing else. Chrome's own expansion is read
directly off `style.length` and the indexed names in
`probes/expr-b81-font-expansion.js`: nineteen entries, in an order that is **not**
the one a CSS-wide keyword produces, holding the specified tokens (`font-weight`
is stored as `bold`, not 700) with the twelve the grammar never names reset to
their initials. `font: 13px`, `font: 1001 16px serif` and `font: bold inherit
serif` all leave **zero** entries — an invalid `font` is refused outright, where
this engine keeps one. That is the `font-shorthand-cascade` plan.

### The sweep says 22 against 19, and the baseline says why not to believe it

One sweep per arm, both ReleaseFast off the same base, separate ports, the
engine's `version` recorded in each reading rather than a label: base
(`dev.1526+7b3d9b485`) 22/29, patched (`dev.1533+8cad43eda`) 19/29. Three
stations differ and all three are DataDome — dd-datadome, dd-leboncoin,
dd-hermes, each `pass` on base and `datadome-challenge` on patched.

That is the shape a regression makes, and it is not one. Eight more runs at
`--only dd-`, alternating the arms in both orders:

| run | arm (by version) | dd-datadome | dd-leboncoin | dd-hermes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| first sweep | base | pass | pass | pass |
| r1 | base | challenge | challenge | challenge |
| r1 | patched | challenge | empty-document | challenge |
| r1b | patched | challenge | challenge | challenge |
| r1b | base | challenge | challenge | challenge |
| r2 | base | challenge | challenge | challenge |
| r2 | patched | challenge | **pass** | challenge |
| r2b | patched | challenge | challenge | challenge |
| r2b | base | challenge | challenge | challenge |

Two readings settle it. **The base binary — byte-identical, unchanged code —
passed all three in the first sweep and then failed all three in four
consecutive later runs.** And the patched binary *passed* dd-leboncoin in a
later round, which a regression cannot do. The window closed between the first
sweep and the second, and it closed on both arms.

This is the third independent confirmation of the same station behaviour: the
session working on `block-height-from-content` measured base 22/29 and patched
19/29 for a completely unrelated change (vertical line boxes) at a different
hour, and lost the same three stations in the same direction. Two unrelated
changes cannot both break exactly dd-datadome, dd-leboncoin and dd-hermes and
nothing else.

So the discipline that matters is the one that produced the table, not the
verdict: a single-sample A/B across these three stations will manufacture a
regression or a win on demand, and the only reading that means anything is the
one where **the control arm is re-run inside the same window**. Print the
binary's `version` on every row — a label will happily say "base" while running
the other binary.

## A line box is not the canvas font box

`line-height: normal` was worth `round(fontBoundingBoxAscent +
fontBoundingBoxDescent)` from the generated canvas table. Re-measured against
headed Chrome at `--force-device-scale-factor=1` and `=2` over six families and
ten sizes (`scratch/expr-font-box-dsf.js`, readings in
`scratch/b82-fontbox-ch-dsf{1,2}.json`), that sum is exactly the laid-out line at
scale 1 — sixty of sixty — and it is the line at scale 2 for twenty-six of the
same sixty:

| family, size | ascent + descent | line box at dpr 2 |
|---|---|---|
| serif 16px | 18 | **18.5** |
| serif 10px | 13 | **11.5** |
| monospace 20px | 24 | **23** |
| monospace 8px | 9 | **9.5** |
| system-ui 12px | 15 | **14** |
| fantasy 32px | 49 | **49.5** |

The `serif 10px` row is why this is measured rather than modelled. Half-pixel
rounding of each half onto the device pixel can move a sum by at most one; that
row moves by one and a half.

**The canvas font box does not move with the device scale at all, and neither
does anything else in `font_metrics.zig`.** That is not an inference from the
sixty pairs — the whole file was regenerated at scale 1 and at scale 2 and the
two outputs are byte-identical, 182 faces of glyph advances, ink bearings,
ascents, descents, last-resort seeds and fallback overrides. So the canvas half
was right where it is read, and only the layout half was wrong.

### Three boxes, not two

`dump-fonts.mjs` now measures three per family, and the third exists because the
second was still wrong for faces with a line gap:

* `ascents` / `descents` — what the canvas reports. Unchanged.
* `layout_ascents` / `layout_descents` — what a line box is built from. Read off
  a laid-out block with a zero-height `display:inline-block` marking the
  baseline: a box 0 tall cannot raise the line, so the distance from the block's
  top to that mark's bottom edge is the ascent and the rest of the block is the
  descent. Checked at every size of every family against a plain block beside it.
* `svg_ascents` / `svg_descents` — what an SVG `<text>` stands on, which is the
  layout box **less the face's leading**. Arial at 16px lays a line out 18 tall
  and draws its `<text>` box 17; Times, Menlo and the rest have no gap and answer
  the same two numbers twice.

An SVG `<text>` shows the split in one reading, which is why it was the first
thing tried for the layout pair — and it is the wrong reading for that pair
twice over. `getBBox` is the union of the font box and the glyph **ink**, so
`Hxg` in Arial answers a descent of 3.3671875, which is the tail of the `g`.
Measuring it with a full stop is clean for 181 of the 182 faces and not for
Webdings, whose `.` is a symbol reaching 3.203125 past a descent of 3. U+00A0 is
the character with an advance and no ink; a plain space collapses and `getBBox`
comes back empty.

Two faces of 182 keep an SVG box **wider** than their line box at every size —
Myanmar Sangam MN (14.5 / 10.5 against 12.5 / 9 at 16px) and Tamil Sangam MN.
That is Chrome's answer, not contamination: it survives the switch from `.` to
U+00A0.

### What reads the line box

Four readings, each measured at both scales before it was moved
(`scratch/expr-inline-ink-line-box.js`, `scratch/expr-br-and-svg-text-dsf.js`):

* a block's `line-height: normal` line;
* a non-replaced inline box's ink — a `<span>` in 20px monospace is 24 tall at
  scale 1 and 23 at scale 2, and a declared `line-height` does not reach it in
  either;
* a `<br>`'s rect, which is the line it breaks and the only reading that sees it;
* the SVG text extents, on the third table.

And one that had been quietly truncating. `DOM.getBoxModel` answers an integer
`width` and `height` beside a quad that keeps its fraction, and Chrome **rounds**
where this engine cast: 19 for a rect 18.5 tall, 41 for one 40.6953125 tall, 40
for one 40.1953125 tall (`scratch/cdp-box-model.mjs`, one CDP round trip against
real Chrome). While every box was a whole pixel that cast was invisible; a
fractional line box makes it a reading no browser produces — a box model a pixel
shorter than its own content quad.

### The gap it was opened to close

The Kasada `/tl` payload's element geometry over forty percentage-sized rows,
field by field, against Chrome at dpr 2:

| field | Chrome | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| computed height | 240 chars | 160 | **240** |
| rect height | 328 chars | 320 | **328** |
| everything else | 1423 | 1423 | 1423 |
| **total** | **1991** | 1903 | **1991** |

Every field matches now, and the 88 characters the previous session attributed
to the line's height were the whole of the residual.

## A block's inline content is a line box, not a stack

`textLayout` returned null the moment it saw an element child, and
`contentHeight` then stacked those children as if each were a block. Nineteen
shapes measured against Chrome at dpr 2
(`scratch/expr-inline-content-lines.js`); four agreed.

| shape | Chrome | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| `a<br>b` | 37 | 0 | **37** |
| `<br>` alone | 18.5 | 0 | **18.5** |
| `<span>a</span><span>b</span>` | 18.5 | 37 | **18.5** |
| `<span style="line-height:30px">a</span>` | 30 | 18.5 | **30** |
| a `<span>` of forty words in 100px | 370 | 18.5 | **370** |
| `a<div>b</div>` | 37 | 18.5 | **37** |
| `a<div>b</div>c` | 55.5 | 18.5 | **55.5** |
| `a<img width=40 height=30>b` | 34 | 30 | **34** |

Three things had to be right at once, and each is a measurement rather than a
rule that sounded plausible.

### A line is an ascent over a descent, not a tallest line-height

Both models say a taller inline box raises the line and a shorter one does not
lower it — `line-height:5px` inside a plain block is still 18.5, because the
block's own strut is on every line. They part company as soon as one box has a
baseline offset the others do not, and the case that separates them is a big
font in a small line. `font-size:32px; line-height:20px` is a 37px font box in a
20px line, so its half-leading is **negative**: 20.5 above the baseline and -0.5
below. Beside plain 16px text, whose strut is 14.5 over 4:

* tallest line-height says `max(18.5, 20)` = 20;
* tallest ascent over deepest descent says `max(14.5, 20.5) + max(4, -0.5)` =
  **24.5**.

Chrome says 24.5 (`scratch/expr-line-halves.js`). The same reading also settles
that the maximum is per LINE and not per run:
`<span style="line-height:30px">a</span><br><span>b</span>` is 48.5, which is 30
and then 18.5 — a count times one height would say 60 or 37.

font_metrics already had the two halves for this: `layout_ascents` and
`layout_descents` are separate arrays because the device scale moves them
independently, and the same split is what a line box is assembled from.

### An atomic inline brings its own baseline, or stands on the block's

An `<img>`, an `inline-block`, an `inline-flex` is a box ON the line rather than
a box the line is made of, and where its baseline sits is not one answer:

| on the line | Chrome | why |
|---|---|---|
| `a<img width=40 height=30>b` | 34 | stands on the baseline: 30 above, the strut's 4 below |
| `a<img width=40 height=10>b` | 18.5 | shorter than the strut, so the strut wins |
| `a<div style="display:inline-block">b</div>` | 18.5 | brings its own line's baseline: 14.5 above, 4 below |
| the same, two lines tall | 37 | still its LAST line's baseline |
| the same, `height:50px` with text | 50 | 46 above, its own 4 below |
| the same, `height:50px` and EMPTY | 54 | no line inside, so no baseline to bring — it stands on ours |

### The hit test does not place inline boxes

Knowing whether a child is inline costs a cascade read, and a cascade read is a
selector match against every rule that could reach the element. The suite
budgets `elementFromPoint` at forty calls over eight hundred elements in 1.5s;
with a read per child it took **six seconds**, and the page it is measured on —
four hundred rows of `.cN .dM span{display:block}` — is exactly the shape that
makes the read expensive.

So `getElementDimensions` places inline boxes and `getElementHeight` does not.
Every reading a page can make goes through the first. The second is
`document.elementFromPoint`, which rejects thousands of elements on their y
alone and does it against a y model that is synthetic anyway — the same trade
the wrapped-text path already made.

The cheap half of the question is free and is asked first: a child the UA sheet
calls block-level hands the box straight back to the child stack with no cascade
read at all, which is what the walk did for every element child before there was
an inline flow.

### What it cost the nets

box-parts 223/223, inline-box 176/176, flex-item-width 61/61, layout-grid 83/84
unchanged, layout-box-shapes **240/250 → 245/250**. The five that moved are the
`a<br>b` block and nothing else.

## The /tl payload does not weigh the geometry (B82, 2026-08-27)

B55 measured Kasada's `/tl` payload at x-hyatt as **524 to 607 characters** short
of Chrome's, and attributed **~169 of them to element geometry** — "202 readings
answering 985 characters in Chrome against 208 readings answering 816 here,
because Chrome answers on its 1/64px grid where this engine answers whole
numbers".

Three plans have since put that geometry on the grid: `text-advance-64th-grid`
(advances on the 1/128 grid of a dpr-2 device pixel), `font-box-at-device-scale`
(the line box is 18.5 and not 18), and `inline-content-line-boxes`. On the page
the attribution was measured from — forty percentage-sized rows, seven readings
each — the engine now answers **1991 characters against Chrome's 1991, field for
field** (`scratch/expr-geom-fields.js`, `scratch/b82-geomfields-lp-linebox.json`
against `results/b81-geomfields-chrome.json`), where it answered 1903 before.

**The real payload did not move.** Same station, same hour, the two binaries
alternated, the payload string read off the `TextEncoder.encode` funnel:

| binary | payload characters |
|---|---|
| base `dev.1543+31216a1e9` | 18811, 18836 |
| patched `dev.1550+d6ce8a97a` | 18836, 18838, 18804, 18803, 18813 |

Two arms, seven samples, one distribution. The 88 characters of geometry that
the synthetic page gained are worth **zero** characters of `/tl`.

And the ~140 the payload is below B55's 18945–18990 is not the diff either — the
**base** binary, byte for byte the code B55 measured plus two unrelated merges,
posts the same 18811 as the patched one. That is the station or the script
moving between one day and the next, which is the same lesson the DataDome trio
teaches about verdicts, now told about payload lengths.

So the byte-count model of the shortfall is finished, and it was the last thing
holding the geometry line to the goal. B55 said it first — "the byte count is
the wrong question, since the two loudest divergences found here are worth
nothing in bytes and everything in value" — and this is the confirming
experiment: the one family whose bytes were *attributed* was made to match
exactly, and the payload did not notice.

x-hyatt answers `refused-429` on both arms, as it has for every reading in this
file. Chrome answered `refused-403` to the injected runs taken in the same
window, so no same-window Chrome payload is available to compare against; the
19514–19552 above is B55's, a day older.

### The DataDome trio, a fifth time, and this time with the arms swapped

Two full 29-station sweeps, both ReleaseFast, alternating in one window:

| run order | binary | stations open |
|---|---|---|
| first, morning | base `31216a1e9` | 22/29 |
| second, morning | patched `cef44ea19` | 20/29 |
| first, afternoon | patched `d6ce8a97a` | 22/29 |
| second, afternoon | base `31216a1e9` | 19/29 |

The three that move are `dd-datadome`, `dd-leboncoin` and `dd-hermes` every
time, and **which arm loses them is decided by which arm runs second**, not by
which binary it is. In the morning that made the patched arm look like a
regression; in the afternoon the same three stations made the base arm look like
one. Four `--only dd-` rounds in between, alternating, are identical station for
station on both binaries.

Every other station is identical across all four sweeps, including the three
real gaps.
## The font shorthand never reached the cascade (B83, 2026-08-27)

`font` was one of the shorthands `chrome_shorthands.zig` calls `.unmodelled`, so
the declaration was kept whole and its nineteen longhands were never set. What
that cost is one reading: over eighteen sizes with `style="font:<n>px serif"`
this engine answered **the same box width for every one of them** — the default
font's — while its own `measureText` answered each size correctly. The shorthand
reached the canvas font and nothing else.

| declared | read | Chrome | this engine, before |
|---|---|---|---|
| `font:13px serif` | computed `font-size` | 13px | **16px** |
| `font:13px serif` | computed `font-family` | serif | **Times** |
| `font:13px serif` | box width | 60.625 | **75** |
| `font:13px monospace` | box width | 86.09375 | **75** |
| a parent's `font`, on the child | everything | inherited | **nothing to inherit** |

### The expansion is read off the browser, not derived from the grammar

Chrome keeps no shorthand in a declaration, so `style.length` and the indexed
names ARE its expansion (`probes/expr-b81-font-expansion.js`). Nineteen names, in
an order that is **not** the one a CSS-wide keyword produces — the two differ
from the third name on — holding the specified tokens, with the twelve the
grammar never names reset to their own initials, which is why `font-size-adjust`
is `none` and two others are `auto`.

### The refusal boundary, one shape at a time

Refusing what Chrome accepts loses a page a style it was written with, so the
grammar's edges were measured rather than recalled
(`probes/expr-b83-font-refusals.js`, 29 cases):

- the leading parts are a `||` group; each may appear once — `bold bold 16px
  serif` and `italic oblique 16px serif` are both refused — except that `normal`
  repeats freely, since four of them in a row is accepted;
- **everything after the size is the family, whatever it looks like.**
  `16px bold serif` is accepted with a family of `bold serif`;
- the weight range is 1 to 1000 **inclusive** and takes fractions: 1, 1000 and
  350.5 in, 0 and -1 and 1001 out;
- a size of `0` is legal and a negative one is not;
- `oblique 20deg` is one part in two tokens, and both are stored.

`0 16px serif` is refused where `0 serif` is accepted, which looks arbitrary
until the family explains it: taking the `0` as the size leaves `16px serif` as
the family, and `16px` is a dimension rather than an identifier.

**`font` is also the one shorthand Chrome does not keep whole when it is
invalid** — it drops the declaration, leaving `style.length` at 0 where this
engine left one entry. That is a third outcome no other shorthand needs.

### Three more gaps the same reading turned up

- **computed `font-weight` is a number and `font-stretch` a percentage.** This
  engine echoed the keyword on both sides, so `getComputedStyle` answered `bold`
  and `condensed` — values no browser computes. The arms agreed on 7 of 31
  readings before and 31 of 31 after. Two things a spec-from-memory version gets
  wrong: `bolder`/`lighter` are **ranges**, not CSS 2.1's nine-step table (an
  inherited 1000 gives `bolder` = 1000, and an inherited 350 gives 700 — eleven
  rows read, all eleven fit the ranges); and `<b>` takes its 700 from the UA
  stylesheet, so a resolver that walks from "nothing declared here" straight to
  the parent answers 400 for every `<b>` on every page.
- **the computed `font` is a different join from the specified one**: weight
  numeric with 400 left out, line height in px, and the stretch written **back**
  as a keyword even though computed `font-stretch` is a percentage — so that one
  part maps both ways. It answers `""` in four measured states the shorthand
  cannot express. 1 of 27 before, 27 of 27 after.
- **both paths have to expand.** `StyleManager`'s own comment says why — "the
  expansion happens here rather than being missing on whichever of the two paths
  a page happens to take" — and `font` was expanding on one of them. A rule
  `.x{font:13px serif}` left computed font-size at 16px. The six system keywords
  had the same hole and predate this.

### Left alone, with the reading that says whose it is

- a value carrying `var()`, a function or a comment is **kept whole** rather than
  expanded. Chrome expands all three, and reorders the arithmetic inside
  `calc(1px + 1em)` to `calc(1em + 1px)` while it is there — exactly the detail a
  guess gets wrong.
- a multi-identifier family reads back **unquoted**. Chrome writes
  `16px "bold serif"`; so does its `font-family` longhand, and this engine's
  longhand writes `bold serif` there too, so the gap is `font-family`'s
  serialisation (`probes/expr-b83-font-family-quoting.js`).
- `font: inherit` now stores nineteen `inherit`s, and this engine's computed path
  answers the literal keyword for them. That gap is **general and predates
  this**: `margin: inherit` computes to `inherit` here too, and so does the
  `font-size: inherit` longhand (`probes/expr-b83-wide-keyword-computed.js`).
  Expanding is what every modelled shorthand already does, so `font` is
  consistent rather than special-cased; resolving CSS-wide keywords in computed
  styles is its own plan and a wider win than this one.
- **the layout's font still ignores stylesheets.** A rule `.x{font-size:13px}`
  computes 13px and leaves the box 16px wide — and so does the plain longhand,
