  measured side by side, so it is not the shorthand's
  (`probes/expr-b83-sheet-font-layout.js`). `Element.resolveFont` walks inline
  style declarations instead of the cascade. Real pages put their fonts in
  stylesheets, so on a real page **every text width is computed at the default
  16px serif whatever the page declared** — which is why this is filed as
  `resolve-font-ignores-stylesheets` and is probably larger than everything
  above it.

Across six probes the arms agree on **340 of 371** readings, and every one of the
31 that remain is named above.

## A stylesheet's font never reached the box (B82, 2026-08-27)

`Element.resolveFont` walked the ancestors itself and read each one's
`getStyle`, which is that element's **inline declaration** and nothing else. So
a font declared by a stylesheet rule never got near the layout, while the
cascade beside it knew all about it. Ten routes to the same 13px, box and
computed value read together so "the cascade knows" and "the layout knows"
separate (`scratch/expr-sheet-font-layout.js`, at dpr 2):

| how the 13px arrives | Chrome box | computed | before | now |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| a rule's longhands | 171.148 | 13px ✓ | 210.64 | **171.148** |
| a rule on the parent | 171.148 | 13px ✓ | 210.64 | **171.148** |
| a rule's `font` shorthand | 171.148 | 13px ✓ | 210.64 | **171.148** |
| the style attribute | 171.148 | 13px ✓ | 171.148 | 171.148 |
| an inline `font` shorthand | 171.148 | 13px ✓ | 210.64 | **171.148** |
| `font-family:monospace` alone | 234.805 | **13px** | 210.64 | 288.98 |
| `<font size=1>` | 131.656 | **10px** | 210.64 | 210.64 |
| nothing declared | 210.640 | 16px ✓ | 210.64 | 210.64 |

**Real pages do not write inline fonts.** So this was every text box on every
real page measured at the default 16px Times, whatever the page declared — and
it is invisible in every geometry reading in this file, because the probes here
all write inline styles. It was found from the other end, by
`font-shorthand-cascade` fixing the computed value and noticing that the box did
not move.

`StyleManager` already answers both properties properly — rule against inline
declaration with the `!important` ordering, the legacy presentational
attributes, inheritance up the chain with the same depth cap the hand-rolled
walk had. Asking it is the whole fix.

The `font` shorthand needed the second half of the same bug fixed one collection
further along: its expansion filled the longhand list a *computed style* is
answered from and not `RuleProperties`, which is what `cascadedDeclaration`
answers the *layout* from.

Two routes still differ and neither is about reaching the box: Chrome's default
size for `font-family: monospace` is **13px** (this engine says 16 — the family
does reach the box now, and 288.98 is monospace at 16px, exactly 16/13 of
Chrome's 234.80), and `<font size="1">` is a legacy presentational attribute
this engine does not map at all.

## The keyboard layout map was the empty one (B83, 2026-08-27)

`navigator.keyboard.getLayoutMap()` resolved a `KeyboardLayoutMap` with `size`
0: right brand, right prototype, no entries. The reference Chrome resolves
**48**, and three runs of `scratch/expr-keyboard-layout-map.js` returned the
same 48 pairs in the same order and the same 401-character join
(`scratch/b82-kbmap-ch-{1,2,3}.json`). The map is one of the values B55 caught
being hashed rather than sent, so it weighs nothing in the payload — which is
exactly why it was still worth sending after
[the /tl payload does not weigh the geometry](#the-tl-payload-does-not-weigh-the-geometry-b82-2026-08-27):
a hash that does not match is a lever the byte count never touched.

The standing argument against it was in the source: baking one machine's layout
in would hand every deployment a shared, wrong keyboard. That reasoning
contradicts its own neighbours — this navigator already hands out one machine's
182 font faces, 199 voices, GPU strings, screen size and device pixel ratio —
and it trades a *shared and plausible* answer for a *unique and impossible* one.
No desktop Chrome resolves an empty layout map. The 48 entries now ship
verbatim, order included, because a collector joins the pairs before hashing
them.

The order is Chrome's own and is not alphabetical: `KeyK, KeyG, Digit2, Digit0,
KeyV, KeyA, Backquote, …`. It also carries `IntlBackslash` → `§`, which is the
reference machine's ISO key; that is the layout that was measured, so that is
the layout that ships.

### An empty struct cannot be its own forEach argument

Writing the test surfaced a second, smaller gap. Chrome's maplike `forEach`
hands the callback `(value, key, map)` and the third argument **is** the map;
ours was a different object. `KeyboardLayoutMap` declared
`empty_with_no_proto`, and that path deliberately stores no tagged opaque
(`TaggedOpaque.fromJS` returns a pointer to one shared static instance instead),
so `self` inside any method is never the pointer the caller's wrapper was
created from. Dropping the flag for this one type restores identity.

**Every other `empty_with_no_proto` maplike has the same gap** —
`WGSLLanguageFeatures` next door passes `self` to its callback the same way.
They were left alone: nothing has measured a collector reading that argument,
and this one only came up because the map stopped being empty.

## The audio fingerprint was silent on the one station that reads it (B83, 2026-08-27)

B82 proved the `/tl` byte count is not the lock. What that leaves is the class
of readings that weigh nothing and are compared as values — hashes — and the
audio fingerprint is the largest of them.

First, a check that there was anything else left. `prop-reads-diff.mjs` turns
`results/prop-reads-hyatt.json` into a probe asking both arms for exactly the
members Kasada reached on x-hyatt, and `run-expr.mjs` ran it on both against
the same https page: **322 of the 352 singleton-reachable members are
identical**. All 30 that differ are the harness rather than the engine — the
Chrome arm's default 800×600 / dsf 1 / colorDepth 24 against the persona's
1920×1200 / dsf 2 / 30, `PerformanceTiming`'s absolute epoch stamps, and
`MemoryInfo`'s heap sizes. **There is no value lever left in what that log can
reach from a singleton.** The 229 reads it cannot reach need an instance, and
one group of them is a whole graph.

### One render, and we answered it with silence

Seq 479–494 of that log is a single offline render and it is the canonical
audio fingerprint: `createOscillator`, `OscillatorNode.frequency`,
`createDynamicsCompressor` and its five parameters, two `connect`s, `start`,
`startRendering`, `renderedBuffer`, `getChannelData`. G21 already replays that
graph — `canonical_render.zig` hands back a buffer recorded off real Chrome —
and the tail sum matches Chrome to the last digit when the graph is built the
way fingerprintjs builds it.

Kasada does not build it that way. Seq 482 is **`AudioParam.setValueAtTime`**:
the oscillator's frequency is scheduled onto the automation timeline, not
assigned to `frequency.value`. Both arms, same page
(`scratch/expr-audio-setvalueattime.js`):

| how 10 kHz arrives | `frequency.value` read back | Chrome tail sum | here |
|---|---|---|---|
| `osc.frequency.value = 10000` | 10000 / 10000 | 124.04347624466754 | 124.04347624466754 |
| `osc.frequency.setValueAtTime(10000, 0)` | 440 / 440 | 124.04347624466754 | **0** |

The read-back is the trap. `param.value` does not move for a scheduled event
until a render has walked the timeline — **Chrome's does not move either**, and
this engine copies that deliberately, with a measurement in the comment. So the
getter agreed on both arms while the render disagreed completely, and
`canonical_render.which()` compared the graph's 10 000 against a `_value` still
sitting at the oscillator's default 440 and fell through to silence. On the one
station that has been closed for ten sessions, the guard's audio fingerprint
read a buffer of zeros.

### Where the timeline stops being a constant

`AudioParam` now carries what a render would hold it at, separately from what
the getter answers: a `setValueAtTime` landing at the start of the render, and
a flag for a timeline that does anything else. `param.value = x` and
`setValueAtTime(x, 0)` are the same event at the same instant, so the last one
written wins — which is Chrome's answer both ways round.

Everything past the start refuses the replay, and the reason is one reading
rather than caution (`scratch/expr-audio-scheduled-params.js`, both arms):

| the canonical graph, plus… | Chrome | before | now |
|---|---|---|---|
| frequency scheduled at 0 | 124.04347624466754 | 0 | **124.04347624466754** |
| every parameter scheduled at 0 | 124.04347624466754 | 0 | **124.04347624466754** |
| scheduled at 0 to 1 kHz | 101.4564685229434 | 0 | 0 |
| assigned 10 kHz, then scheduled 1 kHz at 0 | 101.4564685229434 | **124.043** | **0** |
| scheduled 10 kHz at 0, then assigned 1 kHz | 101.4564685229434 | 0 | 0 |
| scheduled, then a ramp | 101.40662774103566 | 0 | 0 |
| assigned, then an event mid-render | 101.45745121572327 | **124.043** | **0** |
| assigned, then an event *past* the render | **124.04346760431508** | **124.043** | **0** |

The last row is why the rule is "any event at all", not "any event inside the
window". An event a full second past the end of a 0.1134 s render still moves
Chrome's answer — by 8.6e-9, which is nothing to a listener and a different
string to a hash. A timeline that exists is walked. And the three rows in bold
under *before* are the failure this file has always warned about running the
other way: the engine was handing back a recorded buffer for graphs Chrome
renders differently, which is louder than silence.

`buffer_render.zig`, the sibling matcher for the widget's buffer-source graph,
reads its three parameters the same way now. It was not measured failing —
nothing has been seen scheduling a playback rate — but it is the same matcher
against the same field, and leaving one of two on the old reading is how a fix
half-lands.

### The recording was shorter than the render

Fixing the scheduled parameter turned the guard's buffer from zeros into a real
render, and the live trace showed the next thing wrong with it in the same
line:

```
setValueAtTime:10000|0
render:rate:44100,len:44100
len:44100,rate:44100,ch:1,first:265,tail:0,all:1085.3711197695307
```

`first:265` is the compressor's pre-delay, so the replay fired. `all` is
1085.3711197695307 — the whole of the recorded 5 000 frames, and nothing after
them. **Kasada renders 44 100 frames, a full second.** fingerprintjs takes
5 000 and the Turnstile widget 1 000, so 5 000 was what G21 recorded, and every
frame past it came back zero. `tail:0` in that line is the last 500 frames of
the second, 39 100 frames into the silence.

`dump-audio-buffer.mjs` was already parameterised by length, so the fix is the
constant and a re-record on both platforms. 176 400 bytes per graph per
platform, and the generator's own prefix check still holds — a 1 000-frame
render is frame-for-frame identical to the 44 100-frame one.

| graph | platform | whole-buffer sum | frame 44099 |
|---|---|---|---|
| fingerprintjs | macos | 10748.964784431235 | -0.21189409494400024 |
| fingerprintjs | linux | 10748.964801543829 | -0.21189410984516144 |
| turnstile | macos | 9988.088666068505 | 0.09531436860561371 |
| turnstile | linux | 9989.601845444764 | 0.09532961249351501 |

The macOS row was measured off this machine's Chrome before the re-record
(`scratch/expr-audio-44100.js`) and reproduced by summing the recorded bytes
afterwards, to the last digit — the two arrive by different routes and agree,
which is what says the recording is the render and not a transcription of it.

## The ticket is `x-kpsdk-r`, and the station was never the question (B83, 2026-08-27)

Ten sessions have measured x-hyatt by asking whether the station served the
page. That is the *end* of a chain — guard verdict, then rate limit, then the
widget's reload — and the middle of it moves on its own, which is what the
alternating-arms section above is about. One step earlier there is an answer
that does not move.

Both arms POST the collected payload to `/tl` and both get a 200. What comes
back is not the same thing (`kasada-verdict.mjs`, same route, same sitting,
three runs each):

| | Chrome | this engine |
|---|---|---|
| `/tl` status | 200 | 200 |
| content type | `application/json; charset=utf-8` | **`text/plain`** |
| content length | 15 | **0** |
| `x-kpsdk-cr` | `true` | `true` |
| **`x-kpsdk-r`** | `1-B1V4Al4` / `1-B1JkT1k` / `1-B1IEBWM` | **absent, 3/3** |
| `set-cookie` | absent | present |
| what follows | navigates, 200 | sits on the 429 |

**`x-kpsdk-cr: true` is not clearance.** Both arms get it, on every run, and
this engine is refused anyway — so ten sessions' worth of "the fingerprint must
still be wrong somewhere" was being checked against a header that says yes to
everyone. The ticket is `x-kpsdk-r`, and it is handed out with a fifteen-byte
JSON body to one arm and not the other, deterministically.

Two explanations died on the way to that table.

**It is not the cookie.** The clearance cookies (`tkrm_alpekz_s1.3` and
`tkrm_alpekz_s1.3-ssn`, both `HttpOnly`, one of them `Secure; SameSite=None` and
the other neither) do reach the jar — `Storage.getCookies` lists all four
cookies with the values the `/tl` response set, not the ones the 429 document
set. And a second navigation carries all four: a 426-byte `Cookie` header, sent
on the document request, answered 429.

**It is not that the widget never reloads.** It does not, and that had looked
like the whole gap: Chrome's wire shows a second `Document` request after the
POST and ours does not. But navigating a second time by hand is refused too. The
missing reload is a *consequence* — the widget did not get a ticket, so it has
nothing to reload with.

### What this buys

A verdict in eleven seconds, per run, with no station window in the way. That
matters more than any single finding: `antibot-stations-pass-in-windows` exists
because a station's answer to one binary in one hour is not evidence, so every
claim has had to be paid for with alternating full sweeps. `x-kpsdk-r` is the
guard's own answer to "is this a browser", read off the response to the request
that asks it.

```
node tools/fingerprint/kasada-verdict.mjs lightpanda --runs 3
node tools/fingerprint/kasada-verdict.mjs chrome     --runs 3
```

Nothing is injected and `Runtime.enable` is never sent, so the reading is taken
under the same conditions the sweep takes its own.

### What the request looks like on each side

From `--trace --trace-headers`, the `/tl` POST. Chrome's list is the renderer's
own view and omits what the network process adds (`Cookie`, `Accept`,
`Sec-Fetch-*`), which is the asymmetry the encoded-data-length section warns
about — so this compares what is *there*, not what is missing:

| header | Chrome | this engine |
|---|---|---|
| `x-kpsdk-ct` | 178 chars | 178 chars |
| `x-kpsdk-im` | 148 chars | 148 chars |
| `x-kpsdk-dt` | 53 chars | **51 chars** |
| `content-type` | `application/octet-stream` | `application/octet-stream` |
| `Referer` | `https://www.hyatt.com/` | `https://www.hyatt.com/` |
| body | ~19.5 kB (B55) | 18 930 bytes |

The two tokens the widget computes from the collected values are the same
length on both arms; the device token is not. That is where the next session
should point the oracle.

### Two controls, and what they leave

The oracle is cheap enough to spend on controls, which is the first thing it was
spent on.

**The same engine gets a ticket from Kasada — just not from this deployment.**
Pointed at ks-canadagoose, the station this engine already passes:

```
lightpanda run 1: doc=429->200->200->200->400->200  tl=200 cr=true r=1-B1NOV3w
lightpanda run 2: doc=429->200->200->200->400->200  tl=200 cr=true r=1-B1R1UWQ
chrome     run 1: doc=429->200->200->400->200       tl=200 cr=true r=1-B1NuAQM
chrome     run 2: doc=429->200->200->400->200->200  tl=200 cr=true r=1-B1J5ZXI
```

Both arms are ticketed there, and both are served. So the payload this engine
builds is not categorically unacceptable to Kasada, and `x-kpsdk-r` is not a
header only real Chrome ever sees. **x-hyatt refuses this engine specifically**,
while its sibling deployment does not.

**And it is not headlessness.** Chrome with `--headless=new` and the same user
agent is ticketed on x-hyatt too:

```
chrome (headless) run 1: doc=429->200  tl=200 application/json len=15 cr=true r=1-B1NFXVM
chrome (headless) run 2: doc=429->200  tl=200 application/json len=15 cr=true r=1-B1JOf0Q
```

So the gap is between this engine and Chrome, on this one deployment, with a
verdict that costs eleven seconds to read. The obvious next move is the
difference between what the two deployments' collectors *read*:
`results/prop-reads-hyatt.json` exists and its canadagoose counterpart does not,
and the members x-hyatt reaches that canadagoose does not are a much shorter
list than everything a browser has.

### The two deployments ask the same questions

If one Kasada deployment tickets this engine and another does not, the cheap
explanation is that the second one asks something the first does not. It does
not. `prop-reads.mjs` against both, and the comparison taken inside each
guard's own realm — the interstitial's origin, before the site's own code gets
a realm of its own:

| | members read in the guard's realm |
|---|---|
| x-hyatt | 505 |
| ks-canadagoose | 536 |
| **read by x-hyatt and not by ks-canadagoose** | **4** |

The four are `Document.title`, `HTMLCollection.length`,
`OffscreenCanvas.getContext` and
`OffscreenCanvasRenderingContext2D.getContextAttributes`. The last two are the
interesting-looking pair, and this engine answers both exactly as Chrome does
(`scratch/expr-offscreen-context.js`: same prototype, same
`{alpha, colorSpace, desynchronized, willReadFrequently}`, same answer with
options passed). One unrelated difference turned up beside them —
`OffscreenCanvas.getContext('bitmaprenderer')` is `null` here and an
`ImageBitmapRenderingContext` in Chrome — but x-hyatt never asks for that
context: with `--args`, its only call is `getContext("2d")`.

**So both deployments ask the same questions and one of them accepts the
answers.** What is left is the answers themselves, on a customer that grades
them harder.

### What x-hyatt actually does with a canvas

`prop-reads.mjs --args` on x-hyatt, the canvas portion of the guard's own
realm, which is the largest block of answers this engine is known to get wrong:

* `getContext("2d")` ×4, `getContext("webgl2")` ×3, `getContext("webgl")` ×1,
  and one `OffscreenCanvas.getContext("2d")`.
* twelve `save` / `translate(16)` / `rotate(k·2π/10)` / `fillText(…)` /
  `restore` cycles — a rotated glyph raster, not a flat one.
* `getImageData` ×3 and `putImageData` ×2.
* `toDataURL` over **about ninety MIME types**, from `image/png` through
  `image/vnd.zbrush.pcx` — a support probe, not a pixel probe.
* `measureText` of `""`, `" "`, `"m"` and `"mm"`.

The rotated `fillText` block is the part with no honest answer here: this engine
has no glyph outlines to raster (`cfsc-glyph-outline-raster`, still 0/3). That
is the obvious suspect, and the next reading takes it away.

### …and the deployment that tickets us reads the canvas too

The same log for ks-canadagoose, restricted the same way to the guard's own
realm, lists 27 canvas and WebGL members: `fillText`, `rotate`, `save`,
`restore`, `translate`, `scale`, `transform`, the path builders, **and both
readbacks — `getImageData` and `toDataURL`** — plus `getParameter` and
`getExtension` on both WebGL versions.

So the deployment that hands this engine a ticket rasters glyphs and reads the
pixels back, on the same engine, in the same hour x-hyatt refuses one. **Canvas
raster fidelity is not what separates the two.** That is worth more than it
sounds: it is the one reading that keeps the next session out of
`cfsc-glyph-outline-raster`, which is the most expensive plan in the queue —
there are no glyph outlines in this repo at all — and which the paragraph above
points straight at.

What is left is quantitative: the same questions, the same kinds of wrong
answers, and one customer grading them harder. Finding the weight means
pointing the oracle at differences one at a time, which is now cheap enough to
do — eleven seconds a verdict, deterministic, no station window.

## The station weighs one answer, and it is the input's box (B84, 2026-08-27)

B83 handed over a verdict oracle and three leads. Two of the three are now dead
and the third was never on the list.

**`x-kpsdk-dt` is a random token, not a measurement.** The lead was a length
difference, Chrome's 53 characters against our 51. Taken across stations it does
not survive: this engine sent a 50-character `dt` to x-hyatt and was refused,
sent a 52-character one to ks-canadagoose and was ticketed, and Chrome's own
runs range over 53 and 54. The value carries no structure that lines up across
runs. Nothing to fix here.

**An injected script does reach the challenge document, on both arms.** B83
recorded the opposite -- that Chrome's `--inject` cannot enter the 429 -- and
built the oracle around never injecting. The blocker was ordering, not policy:
`Page.enable`, then `Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument`, then
`Page.navigate`, and the script runs in the 429 itself and in every
`about:blank` iframe the guard opens under it. Chrome keeps its ticket while
hooked, so the injection costs nothing to use. That is the whole instrument
below: `kasada-knob.mjs` with `kasada-knobs.mjs`.

### The knob, and the two controls it needs

A knob rewrites one payload section on its way into `TextEncoder.encode`, which
is where the guard hands each section over as plaintext. Two controls make a
"still ticketed" reading mean anything:

  * `break-encoder` removes `TextEncoder` and the POST disappears entirely. The
    hook is on the payload's critical path.
  * `webdriver-true` sets `navigator.webdriver` and Chrome **posts and is
    refused** -- `postLen` 19634, `x-kpsdk-cr: true`, no `x-kpsdk-r`, stuck on
    429, 3 for 3. That is the zero point. Without it every negative below would
    only say the oracle cannot read a refusal. (This engine reports
    `webdriver: false` from a native-looking getter on `Navigator.prototype`, so
    it is not our tell.)

### What the payload's content turned out not to decide

Reading the funnels on both arms, at last with each section tagged by the
document it was read in, gave two real content gaps:

| section | Chrome | this engine |
|---|---|---|
| four lengths | `100075px,155556px,165464px,305134px` | `0px,0px,0px,0px` |
| speech voices | 9619 characters | the empty string |

Both are genuine defects. Neither is what x-hyatt is judging. Chrome sending
ours for either keeps its ticket, and so does `all-ours`, which at once gives
Chrome the zeroed lengths, the empty voice list, an empty codec list and a
timezone of `Olympus Mons Time` -- ticketed twice out of twice. The tamper
control `px-nudge` (same rewrite path, values one larger) is also ticketed, so
the rewrites are not being caught as rewrites.

**Section content does not even set the body's size.** `px-inflate` appends
twenty thousand characters to a section and `postLen` stays inside its baseline
range. The guard folds each section to a fixed width, which is why our body is
short by a flat ~750 bytes no matter what is in it. Both arms emit exactly 449
tokens. The B55 note that content and body are 1:1 does not hold.

### The one answer it does weigh

With content ruled out, the structure is where the arms part, and they part in
one place. The payload carries tokens keyed by an element size. Chrome's eight
land on six distinct sizes; ours land on two, `153x21` and `149x17`, and the two
sets do not overlap at all. Fifteen measurements collapsing into two buckets is
a measurement that cannot tell its inputs apart.

Tracing the boxes the guard asks for (`--knob dims`) names it: the guard sizes
font-metric probes as `<input>` elements at `font-size: 100px` and reads
`clientWidth`/`clientHeight`. Off the station, same page, both arms:

| probe | this engine | Chrome |
|---|---|---|
| `input` default | 153x21 | 153x21 |
| `input` `font-size:100px` | **153x21** | 1049x121 |
| `input` `font-size:100px` monospace | **153x21** | 1245x123 |
| `input` `font-size:100px` serif | **153x21** | 1048x121 |
| `input` `font-size:8px` | **153x21** | 91x15 |
| `span` `font-size:100px` (control) | 803x118 | 803x118 |

The span control matches Chrome exactly, so the font metrics and the font-size
cascade are both fine. `intrinsicBox` in `src/browser/webapi/Element.zig` simply
returns a constant `145x15` of content for `.input`, measured once at the
default font, and every form control in that table has the same shape.

**And x-hyatt withholds the ticket for exactly this.** `input-box-frozen` gives
Chrome our frozen box:

| knob | runs | ticket |
|---|---|---|
| none | many | yes |
| `input-box-passthru` -- same five accessors replaced, real values returned | 2/2 | yes |
| `input-box-frozen` -- our values | 3/3 | **no** |

The pass-through control matters: it replaces the same four size getters and
`getBoundingClientRect` through the same `defineProperty` calls and hands back a
script-built `DOMRect`, and it is ticketed. So the refusal is about the sizes,
not about the hooking.

The asymmetry ten sessions have been chasing falls out of the same knob:
frozen-box Chrome is **refused by x-hyatt and ticketed by ks-canadagoose**. Same
defect, weighed by one deployment and shrugged off by the other -- which is why
this engine passes canadagoose while x-hyatt holds it on the 429.

Chrome's own numbers give the model to fix it against. The height is the line
box of the computed font, `round(font-size x 1.15)` -- 13.333px is Chrome's UA
font-size for `input`, and 13.333, 100 and 8 give 15, 115 and 9 of content
against measured 15, 115 and 9. The width goes with the font's advance and the
`size` attribute rather than staying constant: 1041 of content at 100px in the
default font, 1237 in monospace.

## The input box is fixed, the door is still shut, and the next tell is named (B84, 2026-08-27)

The box now tracks the font, and Chrome's own numbers are reproduced almost
exactly off the station -- `input` at 100px is 1045x117 of client box against
Chrome's 1045x117, at 8px 87x11 against 87x11, in serif 1044x117 against
1044x117, with the `<span>` control matching as it always did. The full suite is
green at 1535 and `zig fmt` is clean.

**x-hyatt still withholds the ticket, 3 runs of 3.** That is not a
contradiction: the frozen box is enough to be refused -- Chrome loses its token
for it -- without being the only thing we are refused for.

The fix did reach the guard, and the payload says so:

| | Chrome | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| tokens keyed `149x17` | none | 5 | **none** |
| unkeyed tokens | 415 | 410 | **415** |
| tokens keyed `153x21` | none | 10 | 10 |

Our token count now matches Chrome's exactly, and one of the two degenerate
buckets is gone. So the remaining refusal is downstream of this, not evidence
against it.

**What is still collapsed, precisely.** Tracing the boxes the guard asks for
(`kasada-knob.mjs --knob dims`) shows what its font probe actually is: an
`<input>` at `font-size: 100px` per font family, whose **width it holds constant
at 112** while the **height carries the fingerprint** -- Chrome answers 134, 152,
117 and 124 across the families it probes. This engine answers `1045x117` ten
times over, identically.

What is left is not about the font at all -- see the next chapter, which read
the probes' own attributes and found they never name a family.

## The probe is not a font probe, it is an input-type probe (B84, 2026-08-27)

The previous chapter guessed the remaining collapse was font-family resolution.
It is not. Reading the probes' own attributes -- `getAttribute('style')`, which
touches no layout, unlike the `getComputedStyle` call that cost the report --
shows every one of them carrying the same declaration and nothing else:

```
clientW:62x0 @input|style=font-size: 100px; margin: -9999px;
clientH:0x117@input|style=font-size: 100px; margin: -9999px;
clientW:112x0@input|style=font-size: 100px; margin: -9999px;
clientH:0x134@input|style=font-size: 100px; margin: -9999px;
```

Ten inputs, one identical style, no `font-family`, no `size`, no width -- and
Chrome answers four different boxes for them. Hooking every path that can
declare a font (the `font-family`, `font` and `cssText` accessors,
`setProperty`, `setAttribute`, `insertRule`, a `<style>`'s `textContent`,
`innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, `insertAdjacentHTML` and `document.write`) caught 22
writes on the whole page, and the only ones the guard makes are six system-font
keywords, one `-apple-system-body` and one `font-family: monospace`. **It never
names a font face.**

The thing that varies is the `type` attribute. Measured on Chrome 151 at the
device scale factor 2 this engine's persona claims -- explicitly, with
`--chrome-arg --force-device-scale-factor=2`, which is the switch that decides
these numbers. Not `--headed`: a 2x2 of headed against headless at each scale
came out byte-identical per scale, so on a Retina machine `--headed` only
happens to coincide with scale 2 and would not reproduce on a 1x display:

| type | @100px | default | | type | @100px | default |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| text / search / tel / url / email / password / number | 1045x117 | 143x18 | | color | 48x25 | 48x25 |
| date | 834x119 | 121x18 | | checkbox / radio | 13x13 | 13x13 |
| datetime-local | 1442x119 | 207x18 | | range | 129x16 | 129x16 |
| month | 1073x119 | 151x18 | | file | 1891x121 | 253x22 |
| week | 1013x119 | 143x18 | | submit | 323x117 | 53x18 |
| time | 608x119 | 100x20 | | reset | 273x117 | 47x18 |
| image / hidden | 0x0 | 0x0 | | button | 12x117 | 12x18 |

**Fourteen distinct shapes. This engine has one**, because `intrinsicBox` keys
on the tag and never looks at `type` -- every input is the text box, and only
`hidden` comes out right, by accident, because `display: none` gets there first.

That the guard is enumerating types rather than fonts is not an inference. Its
second group of ten reads on x-hyatt is, in order, `48x25`, `13x13`, `129x16`,
`253x22`, `100x20`, `53x18`, `47x18`, `143x18`, `143x18`, `143x18` -- **ten for
ten** the colour, checkbox, range, file, time, submit, reset and text boxes from
the table above. This engine answers `149x17` to all ten.

Three notes for whoever implements it:

  * `color`, `checkbox`, `radio` and `range` do **not** move with the font --
    they are the same box at 100px as at the default. The others do.
  * the widths of `date` and its relatives are not the text-box formula: they
    are the rendered width of the field's segments, so each needs its own
    measurement rather than a shared model.
  * the first group of ten reads, the ones at `font-size: 100px`, come back
    `62x117`, `112x134`, `112x152` and `81x124` on the station and do not match
    the table above, so something on the challenge page constrains them. The
    second group is unambiguous, and that is the one worth implementing against.

## Cloudflare's ticket is `cf-chl-out`, and round 2 is posted to the wrong instance (B85, 2026-08-27)

`kasada-verdict.mjs` changed the Kasada line by replacing "did the station serve
the page" with a header read off the wire. `cf-scrapingcourse` needed the same
thing more badly, because **the document status does not even separate the arms**
— both answer `doc=403->200`. What separated them was the page *title*, which is
the last link in the chain and costs a `Runtime.evaluate` to read.

**First, the arm.** A README section retracted earlier claimed no arm clears this
station any more. It was a misconfigured run (no `--headed-ua`, so the product
token said `HeadlessChrome`, which this repo had already measured as fatal here).
Re-checked: `antibot-sweep --only cf-scrapingcourse --headed --headed-ua` clears
it on demand — `doc=403->200`, 34 nodes, the real title — while this engine ends
on `Just a moment...` with 47. So there is a passing arm, and every plan under
`cf-scrapingcourse-oracle-diff` is unblocked.

### The ticket

`cf-verdict.mjs` dumps every `/cdn-cgi/challenge-platform/` and
`challenges.cloudflare.com` exchange rather than guessing which header matters.
One header separates the arms, 2 runs for 2 on each:

| | Chrome | this engine |
|---|---|---|
| round 1 `fo/` POST | 2306B → instance `221752136` → `cf-chl-gen` | **identical** |
| round 2 `fo/` POST | **8770B → the SAME instance → `cf-chl-out`** | 4930B → instance `2506670658` → `cf-chl-gen` again |
| distinct instances | **1** | **2** |
| a `pat/` GET | never requested | **401** |
| after | `cf_clearance`, then a third document | blobs, another POST to the second instance, nothing |

**`cf-chl-out` on the second `fo/` POST's response is the ticket.** It arrives
about four seconds before the clearance cookie and the re-navigation that follow
from it, which is what makes it the oracle rather than the consequence.

Why not the cookie, which is the more obvious candidate: **this engine reports no
`Set-Cookie` to CDP at all** — not on the response headers and not in
`responseReceivedExtraInfo` — so `cf_clearance` cannot be read symmetrically, and
a cookie-based verdict reads "refused" for instrumentation reasons on a run that
passed. That is `cdp-fields-arent-symmetric` in the one place it would have cost
a whole session. `cf-chl-out` is a plain response header and both arms report
those fine (both carry `cf-chl-gen`, `cf-ray`, `content-type`, `server-timing`).

### Corrected: both arms use two instances, and the divergence is round 3

The first version of this section claimed Chrome used one challenge instance and
this engine opened a second, said E1's retracted claim therefore reproduced, and
named a `pat/` 401 that only this engine made. **All three were the instrument,
and all three are withdrawn.** What they were:

- **the instance count.** Chrome puts the Turnstile widget, which is
  cross-origin on `challenges.cloudflare.com`, in its OWN target. A listener on
  the page's session sees the page-level challenge and nothing the widget does.
  This engine does not isolate that frame, so its widget traffic arrives on the
  page session — and the two arms then look structurally different for a reason
  that is entirely the tool. With `Target.setAutoAttach` on every target, **both
  arms use two instances**, 2 runs for 2.
- **the `pat/` 401.** Chrome makes it too, and gets 401 too.
- **the round-2 size comparison** (4930 against 8770) compared our widget POST
  against Chrome's page-level POST — two different rounds.

A fourth field was lying and is fixed rather than withdrawn: `postData` is
omitted from `Network.requestWillBeSent` for a large body, only `hasPostData` is
set, and the round that matters most is ~90KB. The tool reported `0B` for it.
It now asks `Network.getRequestPostData` and prints `?` when even that cannot
answer — which is what this engine does, since it sets `hasPostData` and then
has no body to hand over.

### What the exchange actually is

Four `fo/` POSTs, two instances, 2 runs for 2 on each arm:

| round | instance | Chrome | this engine |
|---|---|---|---|
| r1 | page-level `221752136` | 2316B → `cf-chl-gen` | 2306B → `cf-chl-gen` |
| r2 | widget `2506670658` | 4716B → `cf-chl-gen` | 4898B → `cf-chl-gen` |
| r3 | widget `2506670658` | **~90KB → `cf-chl-out`** | ~89KB → `cf-chl-gen` |
| r4 | page-level `221752136` | **8834B → `cf-chl-out`** | **never sent** |

(r3's size for this engine is 88695B, read with `cfsc-fo-diff.mjs`, which
captures bodies; the oracle prints `?` there for the reason above. So the bodies
are the same order of magnitude — this is not a short-payload story.)

**One divergence, and everything else follows from it.** The widget's big POST is
answered `cf-chl-out` with `text/html` for Chrome and `cf-chl-gen` with
`text/plain` for this engine — a clearance instead of yet another challenge. r4
is the page-level round that hands over the page's own ticket, and it is never
sent here because r3 never gave the go-ahead.

So the target is named and it is narrow: **the ~90KB body of the widget's third
POST**, and what in it makes Cloudflare answer `chl-gen` rather than `chl-out`.
That is what a knob bisection should now be pointed at, on the arm that passes.

## The dpr-2 ground truth for the intrinsic boxes (B84, 2026-08-27)

Measured with `--chrome-arg --force-device-scale-factor=2`, which is the switch
that decides these numbers -- not `--headed`, which only coincides with scale 2
on a Retina machine.

**The height is the line box, exactly, with no rounding at all.** Checked across
three families and five sizes, the input's content height and a plain block's
`line-height: normal` box are the same number every time: Arial 9, 15.5, 18.5,
37, 115; monospace 9.5, 15.5, 19, 37, 116.5; serif 9, 15.5, 18.5, 37, 115. That
is cleaner than the scale-1 basis, where the same table needs a floor to land.

**The width ceils onto the device pixel**, which is the convention this engine
already states for text-derived lengths -- a text advance ceils where a
specified length floors. With Arial's scale-2 basis (avgCharWidth 50,
maxCharWidth **90.5**, against 91 at scale 1), `size * avg + (max - avg)` at the
UA's 13.333px predicts and Chrome answers:

| `size` | predicted | Chrome | | `size` | predicted | Chrome |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 12.000 | 12 | | 10 | 72.000 | 72 |
| 2 | 18.667 | 19 | | 20 | 138.667 | 139 |
| 3 | 25.333 | 25.5 | | 40 | 272.000 | 272 |
| 5 | 38.667 | 39 | | | | |

Seven of seven under `ceil(w * 2) / 2`. At 100px the basis is already on the
half-pixel grid -- `50 * size + 40.5` gives 90.5, 540.5, 1040.5, 2040.5 -- so
the ceil is the identity there and the model is exact at both ends.

The whole 204-family basis has been re-measured at scale 2 into
`scratch/b84-charwidth-dpr2.json`. Two traps cost a pass each and are worth
knowing: `offsetWidth` is an integer and cannot see a half pixel, so a sweep
reading it comes back with the scale-1 numbers unchanged; and the sweep
evaluates before its navigation settles, so the document is still `about:blank`,
where `box-sizing` reads border-box and `cs.width` is the border box. Take the
content box from the rect less the computed edges and neither applies.

The rest of the table at scale 2, for whoever does the re-basing: `textarea`
177x31 of content (181x35 client, 183x37 offset), `select` 22x19 computed with a
20x17 client, `progress` 160x16 and `meter` 80x16 unchanged, `button` 16x6
unchanged, and the replaced elements still 300x150.

One thing that does NOT fall out of this and needs its own measurement: the
swept line-box table holds integer sizes only, and 13.333px is not one, so it is
scaled from the top of the table. That gives monospace 15.556 where Chrome's is
15.5, while Arial's 15.333 rounds to the right answer by luck. Chrome answers
15.5 at 13.333px for Arial, monospace and serif alike, so the UA's own size
wants to be a swept entry rather than an extrapolation.

## Nine of the guard's ten readings, and the door is still shut (B84, 2026-08-27)

The re-basing is in. The guard's second group of ten box readings on x-hyatt:

| # | Chrome | before types | after types | after dpr 2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 48x25 | 149x17 | **48x25** | **48x25** |
| 1 | 13x13 | 149x17 | **13x13** | **13x13** |
| 2 | 129x16 | 149x17 | **129x16** | **129x16** |
| 3 | 253x22 | 149x17 | 253x21 | **253x22** |
| 4 | 100x20 | 149x17 | **100x20** | **100x20** |
| 5 | 53x18 | 149x17 | 54x17 | 54x18 |
| 6 | 47x18 | 149x17 | 47x17 | **47x18** |
| 7-9 | 143x18 | 149x17 | 149x17 | **143x18** |

**Nought, then four, then nine of ten.** The one still out is the `submit`
button at 54 against 53, and it is not the box table: our button's content box
agrees with our own `<span>` of the same label exactly, which is what Chrome's
do too. It is the text advance, which runs a 1/64th step high on some strings --
"Submit" and "Hello" by one, "XXXXXXXXXX" by three, "X" not at all -- and 41.5
against Chrome's 41.4921875 is just enough to carry the client box over a
rounding boundary. That is the advance model's own residual, which the README
already records as reproducing 100 of 107 readings.

**x-hyatt still withholds the ticket, 3 of 3.**

That is worth stating plainly, because it is the second time this box has been
made right and the door has not moved. The measurement line is now close to
exhausted: nine of the ten numbers the guard reads off these elements are
Chrome's to the pixel, the payload carries the same 449 tokens, and the refusal
is unchanged. Whatever x-hyatt is holding against this engine is not in the
boxes it measures, and the next session should look somewhere other than
layout -- `webdriver-true` remains the only knob ever seen to cost Chrome the
ticket, so a capability-shaped tell rather than a value-shaped one is still the
best-supported theory.
## console's formatter is a fingerprint, and it was worth 80% of the payload gap (B85, 2026-08-27)

`console.log('%d', obj)` prints somewhere a page cannot read. But `%d` has to
turn its argument into a number, and that conversion calls the object's own
`Symbol.toPrimitive` and `toString` — so an object with recording accessors
learns whether the conversion happened. **The formatter is observable with no
devtools open at all**, and this engine performed no conversion anywhere.

Cloudflare's cf-scrapingcourse challenge collects exactly it: a sweep of `%c%d`
across every console method, twice each. It showed up in the guard's own debug
output, captured by `cfsc-fo-diff.mjs`, where Chrome logged `a` and `NaN` for the
probes this engine logged `object` and `Error` for — one defect behind four of
the five console divergences on that station. (The fifth was the instrument:
Chrome emits `groupCollapsed` / `count` / `table` CDP events this engine does
not, and off-station both arms have all 25 console methods with identical
descriptors, so that one is invisible to a page and is not a tell.)

### The rules, measured rather than read off the standard

Four of these are what a from-the-spec implementation gets wrong
(`probes/expr-b85-console-probe.js`, `expr-b85-console-format-edges.js`,
`expr-b85-console-throwing-arg.js` — 43 readings):

| | Chrome |
|---|---|
| `%s` `%d` `%i` `%f` | convert, footprint `toPrimitive` → `toString` |
| the hint | **string**, so `%d` never reaches `valueOf` the way `Number(x)` would |
| `%o` `%O` | consume, convert nothing |
| **`%c`** | consumes its style argument and **does not convert it** |
| `%%` | literal, consumes nothing — and a specifier after it still converts |
| `%q` `%j` `%S`, or no argument left | convert nothing |
| a non-string first argument | no formatting at all, that argument not converted either |
| `group`, `assert` | **format** |
| **`dir`, `table`** | **do not format** |
| a `toString` that throws | **propagates**, out of the converting specifiers only |

That last one is the one only a live reading could settle — swallowing it is the
intuitive choice and is wrong. It also dictated the shape of the fix: capturing a
stack trace *clears* v8's pending exception, so `console.error` and
`console.trace` were swallowing the throw Chrome propagates until the formatter
started reporting the failure and its callers started returning on it.

All 43 readings match now, against 24 before.

### It reached the guard, and it did not open the door

Both halves are worth stating, because the first is the evidence the change is
real and the second is the evidence it is not the lock:

| | Chrome | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| r3 payload (the widget's big POST) | 90988B | 88695B | **90540B** |
| `cf-chl-out` | present | absent | **absent, 3/3** |

**The payload shortfall closed by 80%** — 1845 of the 2293 bytes — which says the
guard does record the console sweep and that our answers now largely match its
expectations. The verdict did not move.

That is the same shape the input box had on x-hyatt: a real defect, fixed, the
payload demonstrably moved, and the station still refusing. Being refused *for*
something does not make it the only thing being refused for. What it does mean is
that the ~448 bytes left in r3 are now a much smaller haystack than the 2293 that
were there this morning.

## A knob for Cloudflare, and the console formatter is weighed (B85, 2026-08-27)

`cf-verdict.mjs` answers "does this engine get a ticket". `cf-knob.mjs` answers
the more useful question — "does THIS ONE CHANGE cost a ticket" — by injecting
into the challenge on the arm that passes and reading the same `cf-chl-out`. That
is a different question from "where do the two engines differ", and the x-hyatt
work is what taught the difference: Chrome sent a fake timezone, an empty codec
list, zeroed geometry and an empty voice list all at once and kept its ticket.

Two things this had to get right that the Kasada version did not:

- **the widget is a separate target.** Chrome isolates
  `challenges.cloudflare.com`, so `Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument` on the
  page's session never reaches the frame that builds the ~90KB payload. The knob
  installs on every auto-attached target.
- `Network.enable` needs `maxPostDataSize`, or the round that matters reports no
  body at all.

### Calibration, which is what makes the rest readable

| knob | runs | ticket | what it establishes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `none` | 3/3 | **yes** | the station is handing out tickets in this window |
| `alive` | 1/1 | **yes** | the knob arrives in BOTH documents — `alive=www.scrapingcourse.com/top` and `alive=/frame` — and costs nothing |
| `webdriver-true` | 2/2 | **no** | the zero point: the oracle can read a knob-induced refusal |

The zero point matters twice over, because `navigator.webdriver` reproduces **our
engine's exact failure signature**: three rounds, r3 answered `cf-chl-gen`, no r4,
no ticket. Whatever we are being refused for puts us in the same state a
declared automation flag does.

### The console formatter is weighed, and the control says so

| knob | what it changes | runs | ticket |
|---|---|---|---|
| `console-no-format` | console hooked, **conversion removed** | 2/2 | **no** |
| `console-passthru` | console hooked the same way, **conversion still happens** | 2/2 | **yes** |

The two knobs replace the same nine methods through the same `defineProperty`
calls. The only difference is whether the argument gets converted — so **the
refusal is about the conversion, not about console being hooked.** That is the
`input-box-frozen` / `input-box-passthru` pattern, and it is the only way a
"still ticketed" reading means anything.

So the formatter this session implemented is something Cloudflare genuinely
weighs. It was **necessary and not sufficient**: fixing it closed 80% of the r3
payload gap and the ticket is still withheld, 3 runs of 3 on a ReleaseFast build.

(A third knob, `console-defang-format`, left the methods calling through and only
mangled the format string so no specifier could match. It came back 1 of 2 and is
**not** reported as a result — it changes the string's own content, so it is not
a clean isolation of the conversion. The two knobs above are.)

### What this leaves

r3 is now 448 bytes short of Chrome rather than 2293, and one of the two probes
known to live in it is answered correctly. The instrument is built and
calibrated, so the next family costs two runs to test rather than a session to
argue about.

### The family map, against a 7/7 baseline

Every row is two runs of `cf-knob.mjs chrome`, and the baseline was re-run
between the batches: `none` is ticketed **7 for 7**, so the station was not
wobbling and a lost ticket below means something.

| family removed from Chrome | ticket | reading |
|---|---|---|
| `none` (baseline) | **7/7** | the station is stable in this window |
| `webdriver-true` | 0/2 | **fatal** — the zero point |
| `console-no-format` | 0/2 | **fatal**, and controlled: `console-passthru` is 2/2 |
| `no-plugins` | 1/2 | marginal |
| `coarse-performance` | 1/2 | marginal |
| `no-error-stack` | 2/2 | **not weighed** |
| `no-canvas-readback` | 2/2 | **not weighed** |
| `no-webgl` | 2/2 | **not weighed** |
| `no-timezone` | 2/2 | **not weighed** |
| `detached-computed-values` | 2/2 | **not weighed** |
| `native-tostring` | 0/2 | **invalid** — see below |

`native-tostring` is not a result. It came back with **one round instead of four**
— the challenge never got past r1 — so the knob broke the guard's own code rather
than being judged by it. A knob that stops the exchange is not a knob that failed
it, and the round count is what tells the two apart.

**What this buys is mostly negative, and that is the point.** Five families are
ruled out for this door, and each of them is a direction someone could have spent
a session on:

- **canvas readback and WebGL are not weighed.** That is the second independent
  confirmation, after ks-canadagoose's guard running the whole canvas surface and
  ticketing this engine anyway — and it rules out `cfsc-glyph-outline-raster`,
  the most expensive plan in the queue, for this door.
- **a detached element's computed style is not weighed**, so the 36-of-36 gap in
  `detached-computed-style-empty` will not open it either.
- **the timezone is not weighed**, matching x-hyatt exactly.
- **`Error.prototype.stack` is not weighed.**

The two marginal rows are worth exactly what they say: `plugins` and a coarsened
`performance.now` each cost the ticket once in two. Cloudflare appears to score
them rather than gate on them, and neither is a place to spend a session on the
strength of one run in two.

Which leaves the honest summary. The only family this sweep found that Cloudflare
hard-gates on, apart from a declared automation flag, is the console formatter —
and this engine now implements it, 43 readings out of 43, with the r3 payload gap
closed by 80%. **The ticket is still withheld**, so what refuses us is something
this sweep did not cover. The instrument is the deliverable: the next family is
two runs, and a family ruled out stays ruled out.

## The `h:` tokens are a Proxy trap log, and they read the engine's WebIDL layer (B84, 2026-08-27)

The payload's `h:` tokens were the last structural difference left after the box
work: both arms emit 449 tokens and the keys otherwise line up, but Chrome sends
ONE `h:` token of 7 characters and this engine sends FOUR totalling 396.

They are not error reports. They are a **Proxy trap log**: the guard hands a
Proxy to Web API constructors and records which traps fire, in order --
`g:` get, `h:` has, `s:` set, `gpd:` getOwnPropertyDescriptor, `dfp:` define,
`a:` the apply result. Chrome's only `h:` token is `h:cause`, from an Error
construction, and this engine emits that one too. The other three are ours
alone, and each is a dictionary being converted:

```
RequestInit
  Chrome  g:adAuctionHeaders,g:attributionReporting,h:attributionReporting,g:body,
          g:browsingTopics,g:cache,g:credentials,g:duplex,g:headers,g:integrity,
          g:keepalive,g:method,g:mode,g:priority,g:privateToken,g:redirect,
          g:referrer,g:referrerPolicy,g:sharedStorageWritable,g:signal,
          g:targetAddressSpace
  ours    h:method,h:headers,h:body,h:cache,h:credentials,h:redirect,h:signal,
          h:priority,h:duplex,h:mode,h:referrer,h:referrerPolicy,h:integrity,
          h:keepalive

InputEventInit
  Chrome  g:bubbles,g:cancelable,g:composed,g:detail,g:sourceCapabilities,g:view,
          g:data,g:dataTransfer,g:inputType,g:isComposing,g:targetRanges
  ours    h:bubbles,h:cancelable,h:composed,h:detail,h:view,h:data,h:dataTransfer,
          h:inputType,h:isComposing
```

Three separate tells, in one mechanism:

  * **the trap itself.** Chrome reads a dictionary member with `[[Get]]`; this
    engine asks `[[Has]]` first. WebIDL says Get -- the conversion is "let value
    be Get(V, key)", with no HasProperty anywhere in it -- so this is a spec
    deviation and not a taste, and it shows up on **every** dictionary the page
    can reach, not just these two;
  * **the order.** Chrome walks the inherited dictionaries outermost-first and
    each one's own members in lexicographical order, which is what WebIDL
    requires. `InputEventInit` shows the shape plainly -- EventInit's bubbles,
    cancelable, composed, then UIEventInit's detail, sourceCapabilities, view,
    then InputEventInit's data, dataTransfer, inputType, isComposing,
    targetRanges. Ours has that shape here but reads `RequestInit` in the IDL
    file's declaration order instead;
  * **the member set.** `RequestInit` is 21 members in Chrome and 14 here, and
    `InputEventInit` 11 against 9. A missing member is a missing read, and the
    log shows exactly which.

This is the first thing found on x-hyatt that is shaped like the one knob ever
seen to cost Chrome its ticket. `navigator.webdriver` is a capability tell, not
a value tell, and so is this: no amount of getting numbers right reaches it,
because what the guard is reading is *how the engine's binding layer behaves*.
Every value-shaped chapter above came back negative; this one has not been tried.

### ...and the trap log is not the lock either (B84, 2026-08-27)

Tested with the knob, one direction. Chrome's binding layer cannot be changed
from a page, so `has-probe` replays this engine's exact `[[Has]]` sequence over
the same object before handing it to the real `Request` and `InputEvent`
constructors -- additive, so Chrome's own `[[Get]]` reads still happen and our
tell simply appears alongside them.

| knob | runs | ticket |
|---|---|---|
| `has-probe-passthru` -- same constructors replaced, replaying nothing | 1/1 | yes |
| `has-probe` -- our `[[Has]]` sequence added | 2/2 | **yes** |

The control matters and so does the body size: `postLen` goes from ~19610 to
19834 and 19842 under the probe, so the extra reads demonstrably reached the
payload rather than being dropped on the way.

**What this rules out:** the mere presence of `[[Has]]` reads on a converted
dictionary. **What it does not:** the absence of Chrome's `[[Get]]` reads, the
short member sets, and the wrong order -- none of which can be produced in
Chrome from script, because they are what its own binding layer does. So the
dictionary conversion is still worth fixing, and it is a genuine WebIDL
deviation either way, but it should be booked as fidelity rather than as a
door-opener until something tests the other direction.

## The widget reads one property of its parent, and it is `postMessage` (B85, 2026-08-27)

The Turnstile widget runs cross-origin, and it is the document that builds the
~90KB payload — so the cross-origin boundary looked like a promising place for
the remaining refusal, especially with `cross-origin-access-check` already open
on the claim that `JSON.stringify(crossOriginWindow)` answers `"{}"` here where
Chrome throws.

**Two real differences are there.** `cf-knob.mjs --knob report-crossorigin`
reports from every document it lands in, and in the widget's own frame:

| reaching across an origin | Chrome | this engine |
|---|---|---|
| `top.location.origin` | **`SecurityError`** | **`TypeError`** |
| `JSON.stringify(crossOriginWindow)` | throws `TypeError` | **`"{}"`** |
| `Object.keys(crossOriginWindow).length` | — | 0 |

The error *type* is a new finding; the `"{}"` is that plan's headline, confirmed
from the frame that matters rather than from a synthetic page.

### And the guard never looks at either

Before proposing the engine change — which is a V8 access-check shim, not a
page-level patch — one run answers whether the widget reaches across the
boundary at all. `--knob count-parent-reads` wraps `window.parent` in a counting
proxy and beacons each distinct property the first time it is read. Over a whole
challenge, in the widget's cross-origin frame, the count is **one**:

```
parent-read=postMessage  cross=true
```

No `location`, no `origin`, no `document`, no enumeration. So the boundary's
error type and its `JSON.stringify` behaviour are on properties this guard does
not touch, and **`cross-origin-access-check` will not open this door** — worth
knowing before spending a session exporting
`SetAccessCheckCallbackAndHandler` from V8.

**The limitation, stated rather than buried:** `window.top` is
**non-configurable** in this engine ("Cannot redefine property: top"), so only
`parent` reads were counted. In this frame tree `top` and `parent` are the same
window, but a read written as `top.x` would not pass through the proxy and would
not be seen. What is ruled out is reads via `parent`; reads via `top` are
unmeasured.

That non-configurability also made the first attempt at the inverse experiment
**void rather than negative**: a knob that hands this engine a Chrome-shaped
boundary could not redefine `top`, and a single try/catch around the loop aborted
before `parent` was reached, so it reported nothing wrapped at all. Per-name
handling fixed the knob; `wrapped=parent` then appears and the ticket still does
not — which tests `parent` and not the property that actually differs.

## The capability hunt comes up empty too, and it was tested the right way round (B84, 2026-08-27)

With values, boxes and the trap log all ruled out, the remaining theory was a
missing capability -- something shaped like `navigator.webdriver`, which is
still the only knob ever seen to cost Chrome its ticket.

**The unknown-property log names nothing.** `unknown-props.mjs` on x-hyatt
catches 107 reads across 94 interfaces that this engine could not answer. Nearly
all are sentinels no browser has -- `navigator.brave`, `navigator.duckduckgo`,
`navigator.wirelessDevices`, `screen.innerWidth`, `then` on half a dozen
interfaces -- where being absent IS the right answer. Every candidate Chrome
actually has was checked on both arms and comes back **identical**: `window.CSS`,
`window.console`, `window.chrome`, `globalPrivacyControl`, `onscrollstart`,
`onscrollend`. Not one real gap in the list.

**The realm diff names 36, and none of them is it.** An about:blank iframe --
which is where the guard runs -- has 1237 own names in Chrome and 1201 here,
with **none the other way round**. The 36 are the newest platform surfaces:

```
BarcodeDetector, CloseWatcher, CreateMonitor, DigitalCredential,
DocumentPictureInPicture, DocumentPictureInPictureEvent, Fence,
FencedFrameConfig, FetchLaterResult, FileSystemObserver, HTMLFencedFrameElement,
IdentityCredentialError, IdentityProvider, LanguageDetector, LanguageModel,
Observable, PressureObserver, PressureRecord, RestrictionTarget, SharedStorage,
SharedStorageAppendMethod, SharedStorageClearMethod, SharedStorageDeleteMethod,
SharedStorageModifierMethod, SharedStorageSetMethod, SharedStorageWorklet,
Subscriber, Summarizer, Temporal, Translator, WebSocketError, WebSocketStream,
documentPictureInPicture, fence, fetchLater, sharedStorage
```

`drop-36-globals` deletes all thirty-six from Chrome -- `dropped=36 of 36` on
the wire -- and **Chrome keeps its ticket, 2 of 2**. This is the first of these
negatives tested in the right direction: unlike the binding layer's `[[Get]]`
behaviour, a global CAN be removed from a page, so this reproduces our deficit
exactly rather than adding our tell alongside Chrome's.

### Where that leaves it

Four theories, four causal tests, four negatives:

| theory | test | ticket |
|---|---|---|
| the values are wrong | Chrome sends ours | kept |
| the boxes are wrong | ours fixed to 9/10 | still refused |
| the trap log is wrong | our `[[Has]]` added to Chrome | kept |
| a capability is missing | 36 globals removed from Chrome | kept |

Everything reachable from inside the page has now been tried. What has **not**
been tested is the other half of what the server sees: the `/tl` request's own
envelope -- the TLS handshake, the HTTP/2 settings and priority frames, the
header order on the wire. The verdict is issued by the server on that response,
and a page-side knob cannot reach any of it. `collect-tls.mjs` and `h2-arms.mjs`
already exist for exactly this comparison, and B53's "the protocol layer is
clean" was measured thirty sessions and one fork of work ago.

## The envelope is clean too (B84, 2026-08-27)

The last surface a page-side knob cannot reach: the `/tl` request's own wire
shape. Measured on both arms, and it is the same shape.

**TLS and the HTTP/2 preface**, off tls.peet.ws, three connections each:

| | Chrome | this engine |
|---|---|---|
| JA4 | `t13d1517h2_8daaf6152771_a87ad97598a9` | **identical** |
| Akamai h2 | `1:65536;2:0;4:6291456;6:262144\|15663105\|0\|m,a,s,p` | **identical** |
| SETTINGS | table 65536, push 0, window 6291456, list 262144 | **identical** |
| pseudo-header order | `method,authority,scheme,path` | **identical** |
| ciphers / extensions / groups / versions / sigalgs / alpn | 16 / 18 / 5 / 3 / 11 / 2 | **same sets** |

The raw JA3 hash differs and the cipher, extension, group and version *orders*
differ between single samples -- both arms permute their ClientHello per
connection and randomise GREASE, which is why JA4 exists and why it matches.
Comparing one sample's order here is comparing the noise; the sets are what
survive, and they are equal.

**Header order and values on the wire**, over a local h2 echo, 68 requests per
arm: 37 reported differences, 36 of which are the instrument -- 35 are
`HeadlessChrome` against `Chrome` in the user agent because the Chrome arm was
not given `--headed-ua`, and one is the echo's own ephemeral port in `origin`.

That leaves exactly one real difference in 35 paths:

```
GET /asset.png    chrome  priority: i
                  ours    priority: u=1, i
```

An image asks for the default urgency in Chrome, which omits `u=`, and urgency 1
here. **The POSTs match** -- `POST /hdr/post-ct` shows no priority difference --
and the verdict rides on a POST, so this is not on the path that matters. Worth
fixing as fidelity; not a candidate for the lock.

So B53's reading still holds thirty sessions later: the protocol layer is clean.

## The error reports are not a tell either, and Chrome makes them too (B84, 2026-08-27)

Carried forward from B83: "this engine reaches `reporting.cdndex.io/error` on
about half its runs, Chrome never does". The second half is **wrong**.

Counting the requests directly, three runs each:

| | run 1 | run 2 | run 3 | ticket |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| this engine | 2 | 0 | 4 | none, 3 of 3 |
| Chrome | 0 | 0 | 3 | **yes, 3 of 3** |

Chrome's third run reported three errors to Kasada's own endpoint and was
ticketed anyway (`r=1-B1JyAUc`). So the reports happen on both arms, they are
intermittent on both, and they do not decide the verdict.

Worth recording how the guard hides them, because it explains why this took a
direct count to settle: an `errors` knob that listens on `window.onerror`,
`unhandledrejection` and the console's error and warn channels, armed in all
five frames, catches **nothing** on a run that does report. The guard wraps its
own code in try/catch and reports through its own channel, so nothing reaches
any handler a page can install. The only sign from outside is the request.

The original note was not careless so much as under-powered -- it reasoned "both
of our runs are 429 anyway, so the errors are not the gate", which is true of
*our* runs and says nothing about the comparison with Chrome. Counting both arms
is what closed it.

## The verdict is a RATE, not a decision, and that weakens several readings above (B84, 2026-08-27)

The timing question answered itself and then took a much bigger claim down with it.

**The timing gap is real.** On x-hyatt the `/tl` POST goes out at 916, 1093 and
1478ms after the navigation here, and at 1932, 2000 and 3016ms in Chrome. The
ranges do not overlap. The 429 document arrives at the same moment on both arms
(~300-440ms), so it is the guard's own work that runs twice as fast here.

**Delaying the POST is not what earns a ticket.** A knob holding the send back
by 1100ms lands it at 1980-4437ms, inside Chrome's window, and the first such run
came back with `r=1-B1VncEQ` -- the first ticket this engine has ever taken from
x-hyatt. Alternating A/B is what stopped that from being reported as a win:

```
pair 1  BASE  840ms  (absent)     DELAY 2614ms  (absent)
pair 2  BASE  894ms  1-B1N5BgI    DELAY 1980ms  (absent)     <-- the BASE arm
pair 3  BASE  803ms  (absent)     DELAY 2537ms  (absent)
pair 4  BASE  958ms  (absent)     DELAY 2098ms  (absent)
pair 5  BASE  1110ms (absent)     DELAY 3458ms  (absent)
```

A ticket at 894ms on the **undelayed** arm. Across everything: roughly one
ticket in nine baseline runs and one in eight delayed ones. The delay does
nothing; x-hyatt simply issues a ticket now and then.

**So the oracle is not deterministic.** Counted directly, ten runs each:

| | tickets |
|---|---|
| Chrome | **9 / 10** |
| this engine | 0 / 10, and 0 / 10 again -- but 2 seen across ~17 runs earlier |

Chrome is about 90%, this engine about 5%. Not 100 and 0. B83 recorded the
oracle as deterministic on three runs per arm, and three runs at a 90% base rate
agree with each other 73% of the time by luck alone.

### What that does to the negatives in this file

Every "Chrome kept its ticket" above -- the falsified values, the `[[Has]]`
signature, the 36 dropped globals -- was one or two runs against a base rate of
90%. A knob that **halved** Chrome's ticket rate would still show two of two
about one time in five. Those readings are therefore **weak evidence, not
proof**: they rule out a knob that destroys the ticket outright, the way
`navigator.webdriver` does at 3 of 3, and they do not rule out one that merely
shifts the odds.

The webdriver zero point survives -- 0 of 3 against a 90% base is a real signal.
So does the direction of travel: this engine passes rarely and Chrome passes
usually. But anything measured here from now on needs a run count chosen against
a 90% base rate, and the cheap two-run knob reading that this file leaned on for
four chapters is not strong enough to close a question.

## Re-run at power: the negatives hold, and the guard has hard tells (B84, 2026-08-27)

The previous chapter warned that this file's knob readings were one or two runs
against a high base rate. Re-counted at ten runs each, on x-hyatt:

| knob | tickets |
|---|---|
| `none` (baseline) | **10 / 10** |
| `all-ours` -- fake timezone, empty codecs, empty voices, zeroed geometry | 10 / 10 |
| `drop-36-globals` -- every global Chrome has and we lack | 10 / 10 |
| `has-probe` -- our `[[Has]]` signature added to the trap log | 10 / 10 |
| all three of the above at once | 10 / 10 |
| `submit-off-by-one` -- one input box a pixel wide | 10 / 10 |
| `webdriver-true` | **0 / 10** |
| `input-box-frozen` -- every input box frozen | **0 / 10** |

Three things follow, and the first is a correction of the correction:

**The negatives hold.** Every one of them survives at ten runs. The worry that a
two-run reading had missed a knob which merely shifted the odds turns out to be
unfounded here -- these knobs do not shift the odds at all. The instrument is
also sharper than the previous chapter feared: baseline is 10 of 10, not 9.

**The guard does not score, it gates.** Combining three individually harmless
knobs is still 10 of 10, and one wrong input box out of ten readings is 10 of 10
while all ten wrong is 0 of 10. That is not an accumulating penalty crossing a
threshold; it is a small number of specific checks, each of which passes or
fails on its own. `input-box-frozen` fails because it makes the font probe
*degenerate* -- ten measurements landing on one value -- not because ten values
are individually wrong.

**And that leaves a third tell.** This engine does not trip `webdriver`, and its
input boxes now match Chrome on nine of the guard's ten readings, which
`submit-off-by-one` shows is comfortably enough. Yet the baseline rate here is
0 of 20 against Chrome's 10 of 10. Something else is being checked, it behaves
like the two known tells rather than like a score, and no knob written so far
reproduces it.

## cf-scrapingcourse: the poll was lying, and the split happens at r1

The previous chapter left one unexplained quantity -- the widget's first POST is
larger here than in Chrome -- and a list of four payload spans that disagree.
This one closes the list, corrects three readings that were instrument
artefacts, and moves the open question a long way upstream.

### Two instrument bugs, both of which had produced findings

**The stash was polled every two seconds, and the widget outlives the poll by
less than that.** On a passing run the challenge tears its own frame down the
moment the ticket arrives, and `Runtime.evaluate` against a detached frame
returns nothing, so everything still in that frame's global is lost. Chrome's
frame reported 8 spans; this engine's, which reports over the wire, reported 26.
The gap was read as "the arms collect different things". At a 250ms cadence
Chrome's frame reports 23 spans and the two lists line up.

**Identical lines were deduplicated on one arm and not on the other.** The
harness drops a line it has already seen -- it re-reads a growing array, so it
must -- while the wire channel used by the lightpanda arm keeps every repeat.
"We encode the 8624-byte buffer three times and Chrome encodes it once" was that
asymmetry: with a sequence number in front of every line, both arms encode it
three times. `report-payload`'s spans now carry `n=`, and that is what makes the
order and the multiplicity comparable at all.

Two further readings from the previous chapter fall with these. The 85-byte
shadow-root probe -- `[null,"closed","<body></body>","",4,4,N,...]` -- was read
as `N=37` in Chrome and `N=33` here; on a `ReleaseFast` binary both arms answer
37, every run. And the first widget POST does not jitter by 416 bytes here: on
`ReleaseFast` it is the same length in every run of a batch, against Chrome's
±22. The 416 was a Debug build, as the harness's default `zig-out/bin` still is.

### The one structural absence, attributed and tested

With the poll fixed, the arms differ in exactly one span rather than in a list of
them: Chrome encodes 4096 bytes of opaque black that this engine never encodes.
`report-pixels` accounts for every other buffer -- 9216 is an offscreen 2D
`getImageData` at 48x48, 1024 is a WebGL `readPixels` at 16x16, 8624 is 49x44 --
and none of them produces 4096.

`report-gpu` finds it. The widget takes a WebGPU adapter and device, configures
a canvas context, renders into a texture, copies the texture into a buffer, maps
it, and reads it. This engine walks the whole pipeline and then hands back
nothing from `GPUBuffer.getMappedRange()`, so 32x32 pixels never reach the
payload. It is a real defect and it is not the door: `gpu-mapped-undefined`,
which makes Chrome's `getMappedRange` return `undefined` exactly as this engine
does, is **3 / 3 ticketed**, against `gpu-mapped-passthru` 3 / 3 and `none` 3 / 3.

### The same question from the other side, which is new

Every knob before this one perturbs Chrome. That method can only test
differences Chrome can be made to imitate, and after sixteen negatives it was
worth asking the question in the direction that would matter: repair this
engine's answers and see whether it is ticketed.

`lp-chrome-values` does three repairs at once -- rejects `FontFace.load` for
families Chrome does not have, reports every permission as `denied`, and filters
the closed-shadow-root style element out of `document.styleSheets`. All three
land: paired with `report-payload` the font span is 69 bytes hashing to `mt6m58`
and the permission span is 167 bytes hashing to `1xcv2yu`, both byte-identical
to Chrome's, and the stylesheet span drops from 41393 to 20696. The arm is still
refused, twice. The collected values are closed from the productive side too.

### r2, and why it is not the question

`report-plain` shows the body of r2 leaving as `join("")` over 4716 single
characters, so it is assembled character by character and no encoder hook can
see the plaintext. `report-charsrc` gets it anyway, by recording the receiver of
`charCodeAt` once per distinct long string. What goes into the payload includes
an `Error` stack, a DOM description, and -- the largest single content
difference on this door -- a `createOffer` SDP: 8398 characters in Chrome, 7186
here.

`probes/expr-sdp-offer.js` reproduces both numbers off-site. The gap is a codec
list: this engine's canned offer predates H265 and the High-profile H264 payload
types, so nine payload numbers and all their `rtpmap`, `fmtp` and `rtcp-fb`
lines are missing. The same probe turns up a second defect on the way --
`addTransceiver()` throws `InvalidStateError` here unconditionally, which is why
the widget's offer has to come through the legacy `offerToReceiveAudio` route.

Neither is the door. `sdp-stale-codecs`, which cuts those nine payload types out
of Chrome's offer (8398 -> 7454), is **3 / 3 ticketed**; `sdp-passthru` is 2 / 3
and `none` 3 / 3 in the same window.

One more correction belongs here. `run-expr --headed-ua` and `cf-knob`'s
`--user-agent` switch do not only replace the header: Chrome empties the
high-entropy client-hint metadata that goes with it, so `getHighEntropyValues()`
answers `""` for architecture, bitness, platformVersion and uaFullVersion and
`[]` for fullVersionList and formFactors. Measured that way the Chrome arm looks
179 bytes shorter than this engine on exactly the fields the widget reads. With
the switch off -- `cf-knob --real-ua` -- Chrome's answer is 477 bytes, the same
length as ours. It did not change r2's size, which is how we know r2 does not
carry it, but it would have poisoned any comparison of those fields.

### A fourth artefact, caught before it became a lead

Capturing the response bodies of the `/fo/` posts looked at first like the
finding of the session. The r1 request is 2306 bytes on both arms and its
headers agree on everything but a client-hint patch version, and yet
`Network.getResponseBody` handed back 113 584 bytes for Chrome and 151 440 for
this engine, stably, with no overlap. A different program, before the widget has
run a line.

It is the same program. `getResponseBody` also returns `base64Encoded`, and this
engine sets it where Chrome does not, so the two lengths stand in a 4:3 ratio:
`4 * ceil(113584 / 3)` is 151 448, which is the number the first run produced to
the byte. Decoded, r1 is 113 580 here against 113 584 there and r2 is 846 192
against 846 284 -- run-to-run noise. The harness now decodes before it measures,
and records the flag, because the same trap is waiting for anyone who compares a
length across these two arms.

What survives the correction is the last row of the exchange:

| round | request | Chrome | this engine |
|---|---|---|---|
| r1 (page) | 2306 B both | 113 584 B | 113 580 B |
| r2 (widget) | 4716-4738 / 4898-4951 | 846 284 B | 846 192 B |
| r3 (widget) | ~90 000 both | 6936 B + **ticket** | 127 720 B + another `cf-chl-gen` |

That 127 720 is worth writing down: `webdriver-true`, the one knob that costs
Chrome its ticket, is answered with 127 724 bytes. The refusal this engine
receives is byte-for-byte the shape of the refusal a `navigator.webdriver`
browser receives, down to the follow-up challenge neither of them ever posts.
So "we never send an r4" is not a separate defect -- a refused Chrome does not
send one either.

`report-errors`, which listens for uncaught errors, rejections and
`console.error` in every document, finds nothing at that moment on this arm
beyond the console format-specifier probe. The exchange does not break; it is
turned away.

### The two edge readings, retested, and what they turned out to be

B58 left `no-plugins` and `coarse-performance` at 1 of 2 -- "edge, not a
conclusion" -- and both were measured before the widget's frame was reachable.
Retested with widget coverage, three runs each against `none` 3 of 3 in the same
window: `coarse-performance` is 3 of 3 and `no-plugins` is **0 of 3**, with the
same three-round, no-r4 signature as `webdriver-true`.

It is not the plugin list. `no-plugins` hands back
`Object.create(PluginArray.prototype)`, and every accessor on that prototype
throws `Illegal invocation` on a receiver that is not a real `PluginArray` --
so it does not present an empty plugin list, it presents a `navigator.plugins`
whose `.length` throws. Two knobs separate the claim, and the second settles it:

| knob | what it does | result |
|---|---|---|
| `no-plugins` | `.length` throws | 0 / 3 |
| `plugins-empty` | well-formed empty list, own `length` 0 | 0 / 3 |
| `plugins-passthru` | **reinstalls the getter, returns the real value** | **0 / 3** |
| `none` | -- | 3 / 3 |

A getter that changes nothing costs the ticket. What is judged is the accessor,
not the plugins behind it -- the same shape as `performance.memory`, where
`heap-passthru` also cost it. The family cannot be knob-tested at all, and
`no-plugins` was never a finding.

It is also not a gap here. `probes/expr-plugin-array.js` walks the whole surface
-- the array object, indexed and named access, `item`/`namedItem`/`refresh`, the
five plugins, their mime types, and the four prototypes behind them -- and the
two arms agree on **26 readings out of 26**. `probes/expr-accessor-nativeness.js`
then asks the question that check implies, dumping the descriptor flags, name,
arity and source text of the 95 native accessors and methods the widget reads:
**95 of 95 identical**, including `Function.prototype.toString` on a bound
function and on a `Proxy`.

### What the challenge asked for and did not get

Every comparison above starts from a list somebody chose -- the read-set knob
wraps a curated set of names, so a property the widget reads that is on nobody's
list is invisible to it. The engine can answer that from its own side:
`js/Context.zig` keeps an `unknown_properties` log in Debug builds, and
`unknown-props.mjs` dumps it when the context is torn down.

On the interstitial it lists **75 names**. Most are sentinels no browser has --
`_phantom`, `angular`, `pyimport`, `runProgram`, `global`, `module` -- or the
challenge's own scrambled globals (`qJByo6`, read 69 times). Sixteen looked like
they might be real, and `probes/expr-cf-unknown-members.js` checks them against
Chrome: `TextMetrics.emHeightAscent`, `NetworkInformation.type` and
`downlinkMax`, `GPUSupportedLimits.minSubgroupSize`,
`GPUAdapter.isFallbackAdapter`, `KHR_parallel_shader_compile`'s thread-count
constant, `document.lang`, `ontouchstart`, `SharedArrayBuffer` -- **Chrome does
not have any of them either**, and `window.CSS`, `console` and `chrome` are
present on both arms (`chrome` with the same three keys).

That leaves exactly one: `Summarizer`, Chrome 151's built-in AI summariser,
which the challenge reads twice and this engine does not have. Deleting it from
Chrome is 2 of 3, and deleting it together with `LanguageModel`, `Translator`
and `LanguageDetector` is 3 of 3, against `no-newer-globals` 3 of 3 and `none`
3 of 3 in the same window. Not weighed.

So the last "something they read that we lack" is closed too.

### The first worker dies here, and Chrome does not notice when it dies there

`report-workers` records every `createObjectURL`, every `Worker` construction
and every message or error on one. The challenge makes the same two blob workers
on both arms, in the same order: a **13-byte** `text/javascript` blob first, then
a 291-byte one that does the actual work.

The 13-byte one runs silently in Chrome. Here it fires `error` with the message
