**`Abort`**, in the top document and in the widget's frame, every run. That is a
real defect and the first difference in this chapter that is behavioural rather
than a value.

It is also, as far as six runs can say, not the door.
`first-worker-aborts` -- the knob that has stood since B59 -- turns out not to
model it: pointing worker #1 at a revoked blob URL makes Chrome produce nothing
at all, and the error listener added to that knob never fires, so its 6 of 6 was
about a silent worker rather than a failing one. `first-worker-throws`, which
gives worker #1 a script that throws at the top, does produce the error event in
Chrome, and it is **4 of 6** against `none` at **5 of 6** in the same window.

That baseline is the other thing to take away. This door refuses a clean Chrome
about one run in six, so a 3-of-3 negative is a weaker statement than it reads
as, and the only readings here that carry real weight are the zeros --
`webdriver-true` and the three plugins knobs.

### The timeline, which was different, and then was not

Timestamping the rounds put the arms on a timeline for the first time, and they
were not on the same one:

| | r1 | r2 | r3 | r4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Chrome | 0.25s | 1.22s | 2.06s | 2.13s |
| this engine | 0.26s | 0.53s | 1.66s | -- |

Chrome spends about **0.96s** between the interstitial's post and the widget's
first, to a hundredth of a second across runs; this engine spends 0.27s. Three
and a half times sooner, every run.

`fast-timers` cannot test it from Chrome's side: clamping every `setTimeout`
under two seconds to zero clamps **nothing** -- the counter reports zero
clampings and the run is 6 of 6 -- so that gap is work, not a timer.

`lp-delay-r2` tests it from ours, and it is one line: hold the widget frame's
first XHR back by 700ms. The timeline lands on Chrome's -- r1 at 0.16s, r2 at
1.13s, r3 at 2.1s -- and the arm is refused **4 of 4**. When the arms leave at
the same moment they are still judged differently.

### The widget's own frame, and a focus tell that is not the door either

Everything above measures what the widget *reads*. `report-widget-box` measures
what it *is* -- the iframe in the interstitial and the viewport inside it. The
frame is laid out on both arms and at the same size: `inner=300x65`,
`visualViewport=300x65`, `visibilityState=visible`, `hidden=false`,
`frameElement=undefined` (cross-origin, correctly). Two things differ:

- `document.body` inside the frame is `300x65` in Chrome and `300x49` here.
- **`document.hasFocus()` inside the frame is `false` in Chrome and `true`
  here.** The top document holds the focus and a cross-origin child does not;
  this engine says yes in both documents. Always-focused is a classic headless
  tell and it is a boolean, which is the shape of the only thing this door has
  ever been seen to judge.

`frame-has-focus`, which makes Chrome's widget frame answer `true` (and reports
that the real answer was `false`), is **6 of 6**. A real fidelity defect, worth
fixing, and not this lock.

### The tally so far

Knobs that keep Chrome's ticket, and so name something this door does not weigh:
canvas readback, WebGL, `Error.prototype.stack`, timezone, detached computed
style, the cross-origin boundary, the two newer globals, voices, the first
worker, the font list, the stylesheet rule count, the permission states, the
WebGPU readback, the SDP codec list, a 100ms `performance.now`.

Knobs that cost it, all of which are the knob's own machinery being seen rather
than a reading being judged: anything that redefines `navigator.plugins` or
`navigator.mimeTypes`, anything that touches `performance.memory`, and
`report-reads`, which wraps about two hundred accessors at once.

Knobs that cost it and are not artefacts: `webdriver-true`. Still one, after
twenty-odd families.

And the surfaces that are now closed from this engine's side, each measured
rather than argued: the read set (92 names, same on both arms bar the two
globals already cleared), the read values (104 readings, 9 differing, 7 of them
the measuring rig's geometry), the payload spans (same multiset, same order for
the first nine, one absent buffer that is not weighed), the plugin surface (26
of 26), native accessor shape (95 of 95), the unknown-property log (one name,
not weighed), TLS and the HTTP/2 preface (B53's reading, still holding), and the
header set on the wire. The door refuses this engine on something no instrument
in this harness has yet been pointed at.

## The degeneracy scan comes back nearly clean (B84, 2026-08-27)

`input-box-frozen` fails at 0 of 10 by making a probe family *degenerate* --
many measurements landing on one value -- so the way to hunt the third tell is
to scan for families where this engine collapses and Chrome spreads, rather than
for values that are merely wrong.

Run over the guard's own geometry reads on x-hyatt, counting distinct values per
family:

| family | Chrome (reads, distinct) | ours |
|---|---|---|
| `rect @div` | 16, 5 | **16, 5** |
| `offsetW @div` | 15, 4 | **15, 4** |
| `offsetH @div` | 17, 5 | **17, 5** |
| `clientW @input` | 20, 11 | 20, 10 |
| `clientH @input` | 20, 10 | 20, 7 |

Nothing collapses any more -- the old family that landed on a single value is
gone. The one remaining deficit is three missing distinct input *heights*, and
it traces to exactly the part `intrinsicBox` deliberately does not model: the
date family and the file picker keep their measured default box here and do not
follow the font, so at the guard's `font-size: 100px` probe they stay at 18, 18,
18, 18, 20 and 22 while Chrome's move to 119 and 121.

`freeze-date-file` gives Chrome that same deficit and nothing else -- and it is
**10 of 10**. So the missing variance is not what is judged either.

The payload has moved a long way in the meantime, which is worth recording
because it is the sum of this session's fixes: the four-length section is now 35
characters here as in Chrome (it was 15), the voice list is 9619 as in Chrome
(it was 0), and the posted body is 19578 against Chrome's 19618 -- the ~750-byte
deficit that opened this session is essentially closed.

None of which has moved the verdict. The geometry-shaped search is now as
exhausted as the value-shaped one.

## The guard does the same things on both arms (B84, 2026-08-27)

Seven candidate-shaped searches were spent guessing a difference and then
testing it. This one inverts that: record what the guard actually *calls* on
each arm and let the divergence name the candidate.

`kasada-knobs.mjs --knob calls` wraps about sixty APIs -- canvas 2D, WebGL,
audio, subtle crypto, the encoders, geometry accessors, navigator and screen
getters, `getComputedStyle` -- and beacons the call sequence out. Counted per
name:

```
canvas.toDataURL        80 / 80      crypto.getRandomValues  30 / 30
css.getPropertyValue    93 / 93      geo.clientWidth         22 / 22
getComputedStyle       128 / 128     geo.clientHeight        22 / 22
ctx.fillText            12 / 12      rect                    18 / 18
ctx.rotate              12 / 12      subtle.digest            3 / 3
ctx.translate           12 / 12      audio.startRendering     1 / 1
ctx.getImageData         3 / 3       speech.getVoices         1 / 1
nav.plugins             12 / 12      screen.colorDepth        4 / 4
```

Equal, name for name, count for count, across everything the guard touches.

Two apparent exceptions came up and **both were artifacts**:

  * `xhr.send` looked like 0 in Chrome against 2 here, which would have meant
    the guard picked a different transport. Hooking `open`/`send` and `fetch`
    directly shows **both arms POST `/tl` over XHR**, and both report the same
    capabilities (`fetch`, `sendBeacon` and `Request.keepalive` all present);
  * `gl.getParameter` looked like 160 against 136, and the whole difference sat
    on one enum, 37446 -- `UNMASKED_RENDERER_WEBGL`. Both arms return the *same
    66-character string* for it, both expose the `WebGL2RenderingContext` global
    and neither returns a `webgl2` context. Repeated, the count is simply
    unstable: **104, 173, 178 here and 152, 226, 125 in Chrome** -- overlapping
    ranges, no signal.

The rest of the gap -- `perf.now`, `Date.now`, `createElement` -- is Chrome
loading the real page after it clears, which this engine never gets to do.

So the guard makes the same calls, in the same numbers, and gets the same
answers to everything reachable from script -- and still tickets one arm and not
the other. That is worth stating as a finding rather than a failure: it says the
remaining tell is not something the page can observe about itself.

## The guard's own source, and what it turns out to check

The previous chapter ended on "the remaining tell is not something the page can
observe about itself". That is a statement about the page. It is not a statement
about the guard, and the guard ships its source to us on every request.

### The program is the same program on both arms

`kasada-fetch-guard.mjs` pulls every script the challenge document loads, on
either arm, grabbing bodies at `Network.loadingFinished` rather than after the
run: the 429 document and the program it inlines live in the navigation the
ticket then replaces, and asking afterwards answers `No resource with given
identifier found` -- which reads as a station that served nothing rather than a
harness that asked too late.

The 429 document is 690 bytes and identical in shape on both arms: a `KPSDK`
clock, then one `<script src=".../ips.js?tkrm_alpekz_s1.3=...&x-kpsdk-im=...">`.
`ips.js` came back **578106 bytes for Chrome, 581496 for this engine**, with
different SHA-256s -- which looks like the station serving us a different
program until Chrome is asked twice and answers **572729 bytes**, different
again. The program is re-obfuscated per request: constants, variable names and
length all move.

`kasada-program-shape.mjs` normalises to a token-kind stream (identifiers,
numbers, strings and keywords, in order) and compares 8-gram sets, so the only
baseline that means anything -- the same browser twice -- is on the table:

```
pairwise 8-gram Jaccard over token kinds
  0.9616   chrome #1  vs  chrome #2
  0.9676   chrome #1  vs  lightpanda
  0.9715   chrome #2  vs  lightpanda
```

**Cross-arm similarity is not lower than same-arm similarity.** Both arms get
the same program template. The verdict is not the station handing us a stricter
script.

### The constant pool decodes without running the guard

576KB of `ips.js` is 4746 tokens and **zero string literals**. The mass is one
base-44 string assigned to `H`, and a prelude that turns it into an integer
array: `var t=A(H,"TV9|3Z~USIds8...",44)`. That prelude is pure -- `Math`, `Map`,
`TextEncoder`, `Date` and nothing else -- so `kasada-decode-pool.mjs` lifts it
out and runs it here. **282567 integers.**

Almost no string is stored inline. The operand decoder `g(u,f,a,h)` takes an
accessor whose `.x(len, off)` slices out of one packed heap, so a string operand
is the triple `[tag, len, off]` and the interpreter never holds a table of
names. The heap is built a few statements further down and is equally
DOM-free, so extending the lifted region through it yields **the heap itself:
32705 characters, 3087 distinct string operands, 1078 of them identifier-shaped.**

The prelude self-checks against `Math.round(+new Date/18000081)` and bails on a
CRC mismatch, so a pool decodes only within roughly five hours of the fetch that
produced it. An empty result on an old file is that window closing, not a broken
decoder.

### What the heap says the guard looks for

Named outright: `webdriver`, `^__playwright`, `__pw_recorderRecordAction`,
`PhantomJS/`, `HeadlessChrome/`, `runHeadlessFixes`, `SwiftShader`,
`fakeShadowRoot`, `Automation`, `masking-agent`, `Lite Browser`, `Mint Browser`,
`HAL-9000`, `dragon://`, `AppleSetupDone`, `procursus_strapped`, `Sileo`. One
string is XOR-0x2a: `uuZ_ZZO^OOXuO\KF_K^CEDuYIXCZ^uu` is
`__puppeteer_evaluation_script__`. **Neither `lightpanda` nor `Panda` appears
anywhere in the heap.**

A whole family checks whether functions have been patched: `\[native code\]`,
`\[native code\]|\[Command Line API\]`, `Function.__proto__.toString.call()`,
`^[a-z]+\s*\(\)\s*\{\s*[a-z]+\s*'?[a-zA-Z0-9]+'?;?\s*\}`, `patchedFuncStringErrMsg`,
`patchedErrStringErrMsg`, and three class-extension probes -- `class kekko
extends Function.toString {}`, `class kek extends JSON.stringify {}`, `class lel
extends navigator.plugins {}` -- whose value is the exact `TypeError` text. Next
to them sit the source texts of common stealth patches, which only make sense as
`toString` comparands: `() => ['en-US', 'en']`, `() => [language]`,
`()=>['en-GB','en-US','en']`, `() => languages || ['en-US', 'en']`,
`()=>o.preferences[e]`, `opts.languages`, `e.srcdoc = v;`. And CDP binding
leaks: `const me = window[bindingName]`, `const me = globalThis[bindingName]`,
`Object.ErrorInInvocation`, `Object.getDetails`.

### Every one of those checks, run on both arms

`probes/expr-b85-guard-strings.js` quotes the recovered literals and applies the
guard's own regexes to the results. Over twelve native functions by kind
(plain builtins, DOM methods, prototype accessors), fourteen error texts, ten
plain tells and nine forbidden global names, **both arms agree on every single
reading**. Every native `toString` is `function name() { [native code] }` on
both; no forbidden global exists on either.

The only family that differed was unit conversion:

| declared | Chrome | this engine |
|---|---|---|
| `1pt` | 1.32812px | 1.32813px |
| `1cm` | 37.7812px | 37.7891px |
| `1mm` | 3.76562px | 3.77344px |
| `1ex` | 7.17188px | **0px** |
| `1ch` | 8px | **0px** |

which looked decisive, because the heap carries thirteen absolute-unit
constants -- `1.0521in`, `1.03in`, `0.9948in`, `1.0050in` through `1.0054in`,
`1.0078in`, `1.0104in`, `74.16pt`, `2.6162cm` -- and `1.03in`, `74.16pt` and
`2.6162cm` are all the same 98.88px, i.e. one length in three unit systems.

### It is not the units either

`units-scan` shows no absolute-unit string reaches the wire, so the constants
can only be a set-then-read-back. `units-set-log` logs style writes on the live
station, read-only, and the guard writes exactly three:

```
position:absolute;width:1.03in;height:1.03in
position:absolute;width:2.6162cm;height:2.6162cm
position:absolute;width:74.16pt;height:74.16pt
```

`probes/expr-b85-unit-triple.js` runs those three verbatim. **Both arms answer
98.875px to all three.** The `cm`/`mm` grid difference is real but does not
reach the inputs the guard actually uses; `ex` and `ch` are a real defect but the
guard never writes them here.

### Nor the OPFS timer

Five heap fragments reassemble into a worker body: `(async()=>{try{`, `const
d=await navigator.storage.getDirectory(),`, `b=new Uint8Array(1);let
m=1/0,s,i=0;`, `f.close();postMessage(m<.1)`, `}catch{postMessage(false)}})()`.
So: open the origin-private file system, take a sync access handle, time the
tightest write, report whether the floor is under 0.1ms -- and an engine without
OPFS takes the catch and answers `false`, a *different* answer rather than a
missing one. This is the first check found so far that a page-realm knob cannot
see at all.

`probes/expr-b85-opfs-worker.js` runs it where the guard runs it. On the page
thread both arms lack `createSyncAccessHandle`, which is correct -- it is
worker-only by spec. Inside a worker:

```
chrome      {"hasCreateSyncAccessHandle":"function","minWriteMs":0,"verdict":true}
lightpanda  {"hasCreateSyncAccessHandle":"function","minWriteMs":0,"verdict":true}
```

Identical.

### Where that leaves it

Ten families now have a causal reading behind them, and the two added here are
the first taken from the guard's own source rather than from a guess. The static
route did not close x-hyatt, but it changed what the next attempt costs: the
question is no longer "what might it check" but "which of these 1078 names does
it weigh", and that is a list rather than an imagination. What is still missing
is the instruction dispatch -- the pool, the heap, the type tags and the operand
decoder are all in hand, so a disassembler over the same integer array would
give the payload's field construction directly, and that is the one thing this
chapter could not read off the strings alone.

## The interpreter decrypts too, and the payload is readable without it

The previous chapter ended with "the payload's field construction is a
disassembler away". It is not, and finding out why took less work than the
disassembler would have.

### 187 handlers, two keys

There is no dispatch switch in `ips.js`. The second pool is a
`"...".split("C")` array behind a `Proxy` whose `get` trap decrypts one entry,
wraps it in `new Function`, and caches the result -- so the opcode table does
not exist until the interpreter asks for an opcode. `kasada-dump-handlers.mjs`
ends the lifted region after the `new Proxy(...)` statement instead of after the
string heap and asks for all of them: **187 handlers, 16726 bytes.**

77 come out clean and 110 come out as line noise, because `var C = a ? E : 49`
picks between a constant and `E`, and `E` is reset at runtime through the same
trap (`if (Number.isNaN(C) && a !== v) return function (V) { E = V }`). The
plaintext is JavaScript though, so the runtime key is recoverable without the
program: the cipher is `ch = n ^ (key + i % 11)`, the body must be printable, and
one key in the range makes all 110 bodies printable at once. **E=154, 110/110.**

What they show is that the disassembler was the wrong tool:

```js
op001  function(n,e,a,v,i,r){var v=e(n),i=e(n);a(n,v==i)}
op002  function(n,e,a,v,i,r){a(n,!e(n))}
op008  function(n,e,a,v,i,r){a(n,e(n)*e(n))}
op090  ... else n.u[2]=l.apply(o,_)
```

`e(n)` reads an operand, `a(n,v)` stores one, `v(n)` walks the scope chain. It
is a general-purpose JavaScript runtime -- scope-chain lookup, `obj[prop]`,
`fn.apply` -- with **no instruction that names a Web API**. The field list is
not in the bytecode; it only exists once the program has run.

### The payload in plain text, split by document

Every section goes through `TextEncoder.encode` before it goes on the wire, so
one interception point catches all of them. `payload-plain` chunks each into
beacon URLs; `kasada-payload-diff.mjs` reassembles and compares.

The first reading was wrong and the way it was wrong is worth keeping: the two
arms appeared to run *different probes* -- Chrome encoding voices and a
`KeyboardLayoutMap`, this engine encoding `Date` strings and a codec list. They
were the same probes. The passing arm navigates into the site once it clears,
the injected script runs again in the second document, and the two documents'
sections interleave on the wire. Tagging every beacon with a per-document id
separates them.

Split by document, the main collection realm (`about:blank`) is:

| sec | Chrome | this engine |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `Pacific Daylight Time` | same |
| 1 | `Sun Aug 05 1945 16:16:00 GMT-0700 (...)` | same |
| 2 | `GMT-0700 (Pacific Daylight Time)` | same |
| 3 | 522-char codec list | same |
| 4 | `100075px,155556px,165464px,305134px` | `0px,0px,0px,0px` |
| 5 | assembled body, 19528 | assembled body, 18869 |

**Four of the five collected sections are byte-identical.** The one that is not
is the geometry section, and `px-zero` -- handing Chrome our four zeroes through
the same encode hook -- was already run at ten runs and kept the ticket every
time.

In the challenge document itself the sections are a number-pair list, the
`KeyboardLayoutMap`, a storage figure and (in Chrome) the voice list. The pair
list looked like a structural difference at 7 pairs against our 10, until
Chrome's own second document in the same run produced 10: **it varies within
Chrome, so the count is noise.** The storage figure is `10737418240` here every
time and `10737418240` or `10737418391` in Chrome -- ours is exactly 10 GiB.

### Where that leaves it

The payload is now readable on both arms, section by section, in plain text,
with the document ambiguity removed. That is the thing eleven chapters of
guessing were trying to approximate. What it says is that the collection agrees
almost everywhere, and where it disagrees the disagreement has already been
cleared causally. The remaining candidates are narrow and named: the storage
quota that never varies, and the voice list the challenge realm does not
produce here.

### The 659 bytes, and px-zero re-run

Four collected sections identical and one geometry section 20 bytes shorter does
not account for an assembled body 659 bytes shorter, so the difference had to be
somewhere the encode hook does not look. Parsing section 5 -- the assembled body
is itself plaintext -- answers it. **Both arms post 449 elements.** The order is
shuffled per run, but the multiset is comparable, and two things differ:

  * the `<w>x<h>` token keys. Chrome's are six distinct sizes (`50x27`,
    `62x117`, `112x152`, `13x13`, `81x124`, `129x16`); ours are four, with
    `65x117` repeated five times. Chrome repeats too (`112x152` appears three
    times), so repetition is not the tell -- the missing spread is what is left
    of the probe-family degeneracy, already down from fifteen-into-two;
  * the `h:` and `g:` elements, which are the Proxy trap log. Chrome carries one
    `h:` element of seven characters; we carry four, at 7, 101, 146 and 150.
    Read out with `htokens` they are exactly what earlier work named: we probe
    `RequestInit` and the event dictionaries with `[[Has]]` where Chrome uses
    `[[Get]]`, so our log is longer.

Both are known families with a causal reading already against them -- `has-probe`
put our `[[Has]]` signature into Chrome and Chrome kept the ticket ten times out
of ten.

`px-zero` was re-run here rather than inherited, since it is the single
load-bearing negative for the payload route: **ten runs, ten tickets**, with
`beacons=1` on every run confirming the rewrite fired. And the storage quota
that looked like a candidate -- ours a flat 10737418240 where Chrome was seen at
10737418391 -- is not one: asked three times in a row on a fresh page, both arms
answer exactly 10 GiB and never vary. Chrome's other figure came from the second
document, where usage is no longer zero.

## The door count, re-measured

Two full sweeps, both arms, same route, minutes apart.

The first Chrome column read **3/29** against this engine's 22/29 -- Chrome
refused at ak-macys, ak-kohls, x-hyatt, ks-canadagoose and every DataDome
station. That is not this engine outperforming Chrome; it is the Chrome arm run
without `--headed-ua`, so its user agent still said `HeadlessChrome` while this
engine's says Chrome. Two arms with different product tokens is not a
comparison, and the sweep's own flag comment says so. Re-run with `--headed-ua`,
Chrome reads **19/29**.

Against that column, the closed doors sort into two piles:

| station | this engine | Chrome |
|---|---|---|
| **cf-scrapingcourse** | cf-challenge | **pass** |
| **x-hyatt** | refused-429 | **pass** |
| cf-nopecha | cf-challenge | cf-challenge |
| cf-zeroclover | cf-challenge | cf-blocked (502) |
| dd-g2 | datadome-challenge | datadome-challenge |
| dd-saks | datadome-challenge | datadome-challenge |
| dd-allopneus | cf-blocked | cf-blocked |

**Two real gaps.** The other five are shut to headed-UA Chrome as well, so
nothing about this engine is keeping them shut -- including `dd-saks`, which
earlier work had listed as a real gap and which is now a phantom on this route.

The five DataDome stations this engine passed and Chrome did not
(dd-datadome, dd-leboncoin, dd-hermes, dd-etsy, dd-seloger) are the throttling
this repo has recorded before: the Chrome column was the third pass over those
hosts from one address inside an hour. It is not a lead.

### Cloudflare serves both arms the same program too

The same question that closed off "the station hands us a stricter script" at
x-hyatt, asked at cf-scrapingcourse with the same tool. `orchestrate/chl_page/v1`
comes back 228236 bytes for Chrome and 232089 for this engine, different hashes
-- and 231750 for Chrome asked a second time. Token-kind 8-gram Jaccard:

```
  0.5376   chrome #1  vs  chrome #2
  0.5650   chrome #1  vs  lightpanda
  0.5537   chrome #2  vs  lightpanda
```

Cloudflare re-obfuscates far harder than Kasada -- same-arm similarity is 0.54
where Kasada's is 0.96 -- but the relation is what matters and it is the same
one: **cross-arm is not lower than same-arm.** Both arms get the same program.

Turnstile's `api.js` is stronger still: **byte-identical across both arms and
across requests**, 84236 bytes at `6212b8bf7b8f` every time. It is not
per-request obfuscated at all.

The `turnstile/f/av0/rch/...` document -- 274KB, and the widget's actual
program -- looked at first like something only this engine is served. It is not:
Chrome fetches it too. The widget frame is cross-origin and therefore its own
target, so a page-session listener never sees what it loads, and "Chrome does
not fetch it" was the instrument rather than the station. `--frames` attaches to
the child targets and Chrome's copy appears immediately. Both arms get the
widget program, as both arms get the orchestrate program.

### The static route does not transfer to Cloudflare

At x-hyatt the win was that the guard tables its names: one packed heap, one
pure decoder, 1078 identifiers recovered without running anything. The same
question at cf-scrapingcourse has a clean negative answer.

Three programs are reachable and all three were scanned. `orchestrate/chl_page`
uses the obfuscator's string-array form, and its accessor turns out to be a bare
offset lookup --

```js
function Y(G,E,v,u){ return G = G - 453, v = D(), u = v[G], u }
function D(AW){ return AW = "…31623 chars…".split("!"), D = function(){ return AW }, D() }
```

-- so no decoder needs lifting at all; splitting the literal *is* the name table.
Turnstile's `api.js` is not obfuscated. The 274KB `rch` widget document carries
one 256KB inline script whose array is `;`-delimited and equally readable.

Between them that is **1838 + 497 + 5909 entries**, and the number of
fingerprinting API names among them is **zero**. Not `webdriver`, not `plugins`,
not `screen`, `userAgent`, `canvas`, `getParameter`, `hardwareConcurrency`,
`deviceMemory`, `hasFocus` or `permissions`. The only match anywhere is the
string `[native code]`.

They are not hidden in an encoded pool the way Kasada's are -- there is no pool.
They are **computed**, which this harness already knew from the other end:
`report-charsrc` exists because r2's body leaves as `join("")` over 4716 single
characters, so no encoder hook can see it and names are assembled per character.
A program that never spells a name cannot be read for the names it uses.

So the instrument that closed x-hyatt's read set does not point at this door.
What did come out of pointing it: both arms get the same orchestrate program
(same-arm Jaccard 0.5376 against cross-arm 0.5650/0.5537), Turnstile's `api.js`
is byte-identical always, and Chrome fetches the `rch` document too once the
harness attaches to child targets.

### One of the two real defects on that door is fixed

`document.hasFocus()` returned `true` for every document here. Chrome's answer
is a chain: the top document has focus, a child frame has none until something
inside it is focused, both have it after that, the child keeps it when that
element is blurred, and a document with no browsing context never had it.
`probes/expr-b85-has-focus.js` takes all nine readings rather than the one the
widget happened to expose.

The Page now records the deepest focused frame and the chain to the root is
walked when the question is asked. Eight of the nine readings matched
immediately; the ninth was `activeElement`, and it is fixed too.

`probes/expr-b85-active-element.js` takes the parent and the child together
through six states. Chrome's rule: while the chain runs through a child frame,
the parent's `activeElement` is the iframe hosting it -- it stays the iframe
after the element inside the child is blurred, and goes back to real content the
moment top-level content is focused. Writing that test found a second defect it
had to fix to pass: removing an iframe that held the focus left the pointer on
the detached frame, so the parent kept answering `IFRAME` for an element no
longer in the document.

**All nine readings of the focus probe and all twenty-four of the activeElement
probe now match Chrome.**

Not expected to open the door: `frame-has-focus`, which makes Chrome's widget
frame answer `true`, was 6 of 6 against a baseline that refuses a clean Chrome
about one run in six. It is fidelity debt of exactly the shape this door has
been seen to judge -- a boolean, always the wrong way -- and it is now paid.
## cf-scrapingcourse: the last unpointed-at surface is the same on both arms

B60 left one面 untouched on this door: the plaintext the **top** document reads
on its way into r1. `report-charsrc` hooks `String.prototype.charCodeAt` and
`charAt` and reports any receiver at least `MIN` characters long, and its MIN
was 1000 — so the seven long strings it had already compared were the only ones
anyone had looked at, and they were byte-for-byte the same. Anything shorter
had never been read.

`report-charsrc-top` is the same hook with the floor dropped to **120**, the cap
raised to 90, and the install restricted to the top document — the widget's own
reads are already accounted for and at that floor they drown everything else.

**One trap, worth writing down because it looks exactly like a knob that changed
nothing:** the first version put `hash(s)` in the dedup key. At MIN 1000 that is
paid once per long string; at MIN 120 it is paid on *every character read of
every string over 120 characters*, which is quadratic. The challenge never
finished a single round — `rounds=[]`, no ticket, one beacon saying the hook
installed. The key has to be cheap (`length` plus the first and last character
codes) with the hash computed only on first sight. And the hook has to keep a
reference to the *unhooked* `charCodeAt` to build that key, or it recurses.

**The comparison has to be against a REFUSED Chrome run.** A Chrome that gets
its ticket walks to r4 and reads eleven more strings; a Chrome that is refused
stops at r3, which is the shape our arm always has. Clean Chrome is refused
about one run in six on this door (B60), so the control is one of those.

Nine receivers on each arm, and the same nine lengths:

| length | Chrome (refused) | this engine | what it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| 258 | `1ge6tsu` | `prtlx7` | carries a `-1787977…-` session token |
| **318** | **`1m5rw90`** | **`1m5rw90`** | **identical** |
| 1026 | `gwutlw` | `59ttki` | session token |
| 1279 | `vmzlif` | `1y302u9` | session token |
| 2050 | `11xuykz` | `n56fuw` | session token |
| 4098 | `ek6fdb` | `ld6ixl` | session token |
| **4520** | **`1242xzp`** | **`1242xzp`** | **identical** |
| ~63.9k | `50zzwr` (63883) | `exzzw7` (63889) | the challenge program |
| ~85.2k | `6y0mve` (85180) | `7ejm6j` (85188) | the challenge program |

The two strings that carry no per-session token hash identically. The other
seven cannot match across sessions by construction — they all hold a timestamp
— and their lengths do match exactly. The last two are the challenge's own text,
which moves between Chrome's own runs too (63890/85188 on one, 63883/85180 on
the next), and ours falls inside that spread.

So r1 holds nothing either, and the list of surfaces on this door that nobody
has pointed an instrument at is now empty.

One measurable difference is left over and still unattributed: the **r2 request
body**. Six ReleaseFast runs in one sitting gave 4898 / 4908 / 4919 / 4898 /
4898 / 4898 against Chrome's 4716 / 4716 / 4716 — a span of 21 bytes, not the
416 B60 saw, so that jitter really was the Debug build. The **~180-byte excess
itself did not move**, and it is now the only quantifiable, stable,
unattributed difference left on this door.

And the acceptance run for the whole batch: with all ten fidelity fixes in
(hasFocus, the terminated worker, addTransceiver, the platform's codec table,
getMappedRange, the shadow stylesheet scope, FontFace's local(), unitless
line-height, quoted family names, the full version), this engine is **0 for 6**
in a window where Chrome is 3 for 3. The door judges neither the values the
widget collects — which B60 closed from the breaking direction and this closes
from the repairing one — nor these ten.

(These readings are from the Debug binary — a ReleaseFast link was still running
when they were taken. It is a content comparison and both arms stop at r3, so
the build mode does not bear on the conclusion, but a re-check should use
`zig-out-rel`.)

## The number probe, end to end: 101 differences down to 4

`probes/expr-b53-number-serialisation.js` takes 188 readings across media
queries, style declarations, `cssText`, computed values, `CSSUnitValue` and
`CSS.px`. It started this stretch with **101 differing**. Three changes closed
97 of them:

  * **round half to even.** Chrome breaks the sixth-significant-digit tie to
    even and this engine broke it away from zero. The tie it breaks is the one
    in the shortest round-trip decimal, not in the double's exact value --
    `12345.65` is really `12345.650000000000090949`, which correct rounding
    takes up, and Chrome's media query answers `12345.6`. `<ratio>` needed its
    own writer: six significant digits like a dimension, but never the exponent
    form, and an integer written out in full.
  * **the alpha family clamps.** `opacity`, `fill-opacity`, `stroke-opacity`,
    `stop-opacity`, `flood-opacity` and `shape-image-threshold` are brought into
    [0,1] on the computed view and nowhere else. Which six is measured, over
    twenty-two properties with a range in their grammar; the near neighbours do
    not clamp and the test says so.
  * **`CSS.px` exists.** The namespace carried three own names against Chrome's
    69; it now carries 67, in Chrome's IDL order, matching every descriptor
    flag, name and arity.

The four that remain are attributed rather than outstanding:

| reading | Chrome | here | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mq min-width 12345.65` | 12345.6px | 12345.7px | pre-existing, same input as below |
| `style width 0.9765625` | 0.976563px | 0.976562px | the specified-value path is float32 and rounds half UP where the computed one rounds to even -- two rules in Chrome, and `specified_precision.html` owns that one |
| `style width 0.000101562500001` | 0.0001015px | 0.000101563px | same path |
| `computed letter-spacing 12345.65` | 12345.7px | 12345.6px | the one regression: Chrome's media query and computed style disagree with each other on this single input, and one rule in `writeNumber` cannot satisfy both |

## Four more computed-style defects, and the trap log closes

Continuing the fidelity sweep after the number probe. Each started by measuring
what Chrome does across the whole family rather than the one reading that
prompted the plan, and twice that changed the fix.

**A computed style out of a browsing context is empty.** `getComputedStyle` on
an element not in a document with a browsing context answers `length` 0,
`item(0)` "" and every property "" -- including `display` and custom properties.
This engine answered full values, so one expression told the arms apart. The
predicate is not "has no box": a `display: none` element is in the document,
has no box, and keeps a complete 475-longhand style, and so does
`visibility: hidden`. Four shapes count as out, and the fourth is the one worth
naming -- an element CONNECTED to a `createHTMLDocument` is connected, its root
being a Document, but that document has no browsing context, and this engine
answered `width: 1152px` there: the viewport's width, for a document with no
viewport. The declaration is live, too, so the same object empties the moment
its element is removed.

**A declared origin resolves against the border box.** `transform-origin` and
`perspective-origin` threw the declaration away entirely -- a percentage fell
through to the box-centre path and a keyword was echoed back, so `25% 75%` on a
240x24 border box answered `120px 12px` where Chrome answers `60px 18px`, and
`left top` answered `left top`. Fifteen of twenty-one forms differed; all
twenty-one match now. The test's box has content 200x10, padding 220x14 and
border 240x24 on purpose, so picking the wrong box is visible rather than a
coincidence.

**The alpha family clamps, and only it.** Six properties are brought into [0,1]
on the computed view: `opacity`, `fill-opacity`, `stroke-opacity`,
`stop-opacity`, `flood-opacity`, `shape-image-threshold`. Which six is measured
over twenty-two properties with a range in their grammar, and the near
neighbours are asserted too, because a wider clamp would be wrong:
`flex-grow: 1.015625` computes to `1.01562` with no upper bound at all, and a
negative one is rejected at parse rather than clamped.

**A dictionary is read with one `Get`.** This is the trap log the guard keeps.
WebIDL reads each member with `[[Get]]` and treats `undefined` as absent; this
engine probed with `[[Has]]` first, so a Proxy handed to a constructor saw `has`
and never a `get` -- which is exactly why our payload carried four `h:` entries
where Chrome's carries one. Members are also read one level at a time, base
first, alphabetically within a level, and this engine used IDL declaration order
and was missing nine members outright.

Six of the seven dictionaries now produce a **byte-identical trap sequence** to
Chrome's. The seventh differs by one trap: Chrome follows its
`get:attributionReporting` with a `has` on the same member, a quirk of that
member alone.

One trap of the fix is worth writing down. Applying "undefined means absent" to
*every* struct conversion hangs `pipeTo`: `{done, value}` is destructured out of
the engine's own reader, the last read is `{done: true, value: undefined}`, and
treating that as an absent member fails the whole conversion so the pipe never
settles. The rule belongs to fields that are optional or defaulted -- which
every real dictionary member is -- so what a page can observe is still a single
`Get`.

## Ten defects later, the door count is unchanged

The whole point of asking. Both arms re-swept after the fixes, same route,
ReleaseFast against Chrome with `--headed-ua`, no crash on either side.

```
                      before      after
  this engine         22 / 29     22 / 29
  Chrome (headed-ua)  19 / 29     21 / 29
```

Station by station the two real gaps are the same two: **cf-scrapingcourse** and
**x-hyatt**. The five phantoms are the same five, shut to Chrome as well
(`cf-zeroclover` answered `cf-blocked` to Chrome this time and `cf-challenge`
before -- that host is unstable, not discriminating). The three DataDome
stations this engine passes and Chrome does not are the address-reputation
throttling already recorded here; the Chrome column ran second again.

So the ten defects closed in this sweep -- the focus chain and `activeElement`,
`ex`/`ch`, the number tie-break and `<ratio>`, the alpha clamp, the CSS
namespace's 64 factories, the empty computed style, the declared origin, and the
dictionary's single `Get` -- moved nothing at the door. Each was real, each was
measured against Chrome and each now matches it; none of them is what either
station weighs.

That is worth stating plainly rather than leaving implied: **fidelity debt paid
one item at a time has not accumulated into a door**. Every one of these was
found by measuring a family Chrome differs on, not by evidence that a guard
reads it, and the two that a guard demonstrably does read -- the box-probe
family and the Proxy trap log -- were both already knob-cleared before the fix.
The next attempt on either door needs a new observation channel, not another
value made to match.

## The margin is not in the box model

`sibling-margin-collapse` asked for one reading -- three blocks whose parent
should be taller than the sum of their heights -- and the plan cited two files
in `scratch/`, which is gone. So it was measured again, wider than asked:
`probes/expr-b86-margin-collapse.js`, ten shapes, both arms on
`https://example.com/` so the page under the boxes is the same one.

Seven of the ten disagree, and the parent's height is the reading that carries
it:

| shape | Chrome | this engine |
|---|---|---|
| three siblings, `margin:10px 0` each | **56** | 36 |
| `margin-bottom:30px` against `margin-top:10px` | **54** | 24 |
| `margin-bottom:30px` against `margin-top:-10px` | **44** | 24 |
| first child `margin-top:20px`, bare parent | 12 | 12 |
| the same with `border:1px` | **34** | 14 |
| the same with `padding-top:1px` | **33** | 13 |
| last child `margin-bottom:20px`, bare parent | 12 | 12 |
| empty block between two blocks | **34** | 24 |
| parent whose only child is an empty margin | 0 | 0 |
| `overflow:hidden` parent, child `margin-top:20px` | **32** | 12 |

The cause is one line. `Element.contentHeight` walks the children and adds
`el.getElementDimensions(frame).height`; `Dimensions` carries `padding_x/y` and
`border_x/y` and no margin at all, so a margin contributes nothing anywhere.

The three that already agree agree by accident, and they are worth naming
because they are what stops "just add the margins" from being the fix: in all
three the correct answer is that the margin contributes **nothing to this
parent**, which is also what an engine that has never heard of margins says.
They are the escape cases, and they are the reason the rule set has to be
measured rather than generalised from the sibling case:

* adjoining sibling margins collapse to `max(positives) + min(negatives)` -- 30
  against 10 is 30 and not 40, and 30 against -10 is 20 and not 20-by-luck;
* a first child's top margin and a last child's bottom margin **escape** a
  parent that has no border and no padding on that side: the parent moves and
  does not grow. `escapeTop` reads 12 of height and 20 of offset from the host;
* a border or a padding on that side stops the escape, which is why the same
  markup answers 34 and 33 -- and note that those two also prove the margin is
  *counted* once contained, so the escape is not "margins never count";
* an empty block collapses through itself: its own two margins become one gap,
  so the two blocks around it are 10 apart and the parent is 34, not 44;
* none of it crosses a block formatting context. `overflow:hidden` contains the
  child's margin and answers 32.

Only heights are asserted in `css/margin_collapse.html`. Chrome's child
positions in this markup are real -- `0,22,44` for the three siblings -- and
this engine answers `5,10,15`, a placeholder; positioning every box is a
different piece of work and the height is what a guard reads.

## The other half of the child's box needs the subtree remembered, not recursed

`content-height-child-box` split cleanly into a term that was free and a term
that is not.

The free one landed: `contentHeight` added `dims.height` per child, which is
the child's CONTENT box, so every parent lost every child's padding and border.
The child already knew about both -- its own `offsetHeight` is
`height + padding_y + border_y` -- so the engine disagreed with itself: a
`padding:5px` child answered 22 for itself inside a parent that answered 12.
Seven of the ten shapes in `css/child_box_height.html` turn over on that one
term, with no extra traversal, and the full suite is unchanged.

The other one is **reverted and stays open**. What a parent still loses is what
the child's own children put in the child: a wrapper holding a 12px box is 0
here and 12 in Chrome, two levels down is 0 against 12, and a child that is its
own formatting context is 10 against 22.

The obvious fix was written and measured:

```zig
var inner = box.height;
if (!box.explicit_height) {
    inner = @max(inner, el.contentHeight(frame, visibility_cache, .in_flow, box.width));
}
```

It makes all ten shapes right and takes `WebApi: Element` to
**ExecutionTerminated**. A `frame._layout_depth` backstop around
`contentHeight` does not save it, and that is the diagnosis rather than a
missing guard: the counter stops a *cycle*, and this is not a cycle. A child
measured from inside its parent's walk reaches back UP for its containing
block, that measurement walks DOWN again, and the work multiplies with depth
instead of recursing forever. `element/box_measure_loops.html` is the test that
exists for this shape, written after www.sony.com took the engine out with a
stack-overflow SIGBUS.

So the term is not wrong, the traversal is. A correct version measures each
subtree once and remembers it for the duration of one top-level measurement --
the same "share one measurement" idiom `containing: *?f64` already uses for the
containing block, one level up in cost. That is a design task with its own
performance acceptance test, not a field on the existing walk, and it is filed
as its own plan rather than left as a comment.

## Three shapes of the same fix, all measured, all reverted

`content-height-memoised-subtree` was opened to finish what
`content-height-child-box` left: a parent counting what its children's children
put in them. A wrapper holding a 12px box is 0 here and 12 in Chrome, at every
depth — `probes/expr-b86-nested-depth.js` reads 12 at every level of a 1, 2, 4,
16 and 64-deep chain, and 480 for a parent of 40 such wrappers.

The term is one expression and it is not in doubt. What the plan actually found
is that **this engine cannot afford to ask the question the way it is
currently asked**, and it found it three times:

1. **Recurse into `el.contentHeight` per child.** Every measured shape becomes
   right. `WebApi: Element` ends in **ExecutionTerminated**.
2. **The same, wrapped in the `frame._layout_depth` backstop.** No change. That
   is the diagnosis rather than a missing guard: the counter stops a *cycle*,
   and this is not a cycle — a child measured from inside its parent's walk
   reaches back UP for its containing block and that walk goes down again, so
   the work multiplies with depth instead of repeating forever.
3. **A per-measurement memo**, `AutoHashMapUnmanaged(*Element, f64)` carried
   exactly the way `VisibilityCache` is, with a sentinel written before the
   walk so a re-entrant ask is answered rather than recursed. The nested test
   passes — 64 deep and 40 wide, every level — and the suite is **worse**: 373
   `ExecutionTerminated`, spread across pages that have nothing to do with
   layout (`cookie_store`, `indexeddb`, `url`, `media_devices`).

Reading 3 is the one that closes the plan. The memo is created inside
`clientHeightOf`, so a *nested* `clientHeight` — reached through
`getElementDimensions` and the computed-value machinery — starts over with an
empty one and the memo never sees the repeat it exists to stop. Sharing it
across those calls means hanging it on the Frame, and the arena it would have
to live in (`call_arena`, which is what the visibility cache uses) is released
between JS calls: a map kept across that boundary and then
`clearRetainingCapacity`'d is a use-after-free, which is a worse bug than the
one being fixed.

So the honest shape of the remaining work is not a field on the existing walk
and not a cache beside it. It is a measurement context that spans one document
pass — the same thing `containing: *?f64` is for the containing block, one
level up in scope — and that is an architecture change with its own budget.

**Nothing is asserted for it.** A test for something nothing implements is a
permanently red test rather than a specification, so `css/child_box_height.html`
still lists the three shapes in a comment, the probe carries the readings, and
the third attempt's patch is kept verbatim at
`probes/b86-memoise-attempt.patch` rather than half-merged as dead code.

## The door map, re-read after the layout work

Both arms re-swept on today's main (`1364be567`, ReleaseFast), Chrome with
`--headed-ua`, minutes apart on the same address. The raw counts moved and the
map did not:

```
                      B85 (08-29 07:34)   B86 (08-29 11:00)
  this engine              22 / 29             19 / 29
  Chrome (headed-ua)       21 / 29             21 / 29
```

**The two doors are the same two.** `cf-scrapingcourse` and `x-hyatt`: Chrome
walks in, this engine does not. Every other station either lets both in (19) or
shuts both out.

The three that fell out of this engine's column are `dd-datadome`,
`dd-leboncoin` and `dd-hermes` — the exact set B85 recorded as "we pass and
Chrome does not". That set is now empty, and its loss looks at first like a
regression from the day's two merges, because Chrome fails those stations in
*both* sittings and so cannot serve as the control.

### It is not a regression, and this is how that was established

Chrome being the wrong control means the attribution has to be made on our own
side, with two binaries. `df8e6a36e` — the commit before the margin-collapse
and child-box merges — was rebuilt ReleaseFast into its own worktree and
alternated against today's `main` over the whole DataDome family, four cycles,
32 runs. Alternating rather than block-against-block, because this family
passes in windows and a block of runs on one binary measures the hour.

```
  station          before today   today
  dd-datadome        0/4 ....     0/4 ....
  dd-hermes          0/4 ....     0/4 ....
  dd-leboncoin       1/4 P...     0/4 ....
  dd-etsy            4/4 PPPP     4/4 PPPP     <- control
  dd-seloger         4/4 PPPP     4/4 PPPP     <- control
  dd-g2              0/4 ....     0/4 ....     <- control
  dd-saks            0/4 ....     0/4 ....     <- control
  dd-allopneus       0/4 ....     0/4 ....     <- control
```

The pre-merge binary loses `dd-datadome` and `dd-hermes` just as completely as
today's does, and `dd-leboncoin`'s single pass out of four is the flicker this
family is known for rather than a difference. Meanwhile the two stations that
pass are 4 for 4 on both arms, so the instrument was working and the hour was
not hostile to everything — which is what makes the zeros mean something.

So the DataDome column tracks the address, not the build, exactly as
`antibot-stations-pass-in-windows` says. What it costs is the *comparison*: on
a day when those three are open, this engine reads 22 and Chrome 21 and the
engine looks ahead; on a day when they are shut, it reads 19 against 21. Both
readings describe the same two doors. **The count is the wrong headline and the
map is the right one.**

### What that leaves

Nothing about the map moved on the day the engine grew margin collapsing and a
correct child box — which is the third time in two sessions that a measured,
Chrome-exact fidelity fix has left the door count alone. The two doors are
where they have been: `cf-scrapingcourse`, where the live lead is
`cfsc-burst-mechanism`'s finding that a burst of long-query requests inside the
widget's frame flips the verdict, and `x-hyatt`, which is exhausted from the
page, the transport, the guard's source and the payload plaintext alike.

## It was never the subframe — it was the initiator

`subframe-resource-milestones` was written as "a resource entry's nine
connection milestones are all zero inside a cross-origin subframe, while the
top document fills them". Both halves of that are wrong, and the measurement
that says so is `probes/expr-b86-subframe-milestones.js` against
`probes/b86-subframe-fixture.mjs` — parent on `127.0.0.1`, child on
`localhost`, **each frame fetching its own origin** so that the
Timing-Allow-Origin rule (which zeroes these fields by spec for a cross-origin
resource) is not what gets measured. Four initiator types per frame, because
they do not share a code path here.

Chrome 151, plain HTTP, every one of the eight readings:
`secureConnectionStart` alone at zero. This engine, before:

```
  top   xmlhttprequest   domainLookupStart,domainLookupEnd,connectStart,
                         connectEnd,secureConnectionStart,requestStart,responseStart
  top   fetch            (the same seven)
  top   img              secureConnectionStart      <- already right
  top   script           secureConnectionStart      <- already right
  child (all four)       the same four answers as the top
```

So the top document is **equally** broken and the subframe is **not** special —
and two of the four initiators were already exact. The split is
`Frame.recordResourceTiming`, which calls `setConnectionMilestones` and says in
its own comment who skips it: script, link and img go through the Frame, while
"XHR and fetch call Performance directly". Those two built their
`timing.Timing` literal by hand and the connection walk was never in it.

The fix is the walk they were missing: `_perf_times`, captured off the transfer
beside `_perf_labels` and `_perf_next_hop_protocol` (the transfer is freed
before the done callback runs, which is why those are copied out at all), and
one `t.setConnectionMilestones(...)` call each. After it, all eight readings are
`secureConnectionStart` — Chrome's answer — and an XHR entry has the same shape
as the script entry beside it:

```
  fetchStart=2267.4 domainLookupStart=2267.4 domainLookupEnd=2267.4
  connectStart=2267.4 connectEnd=2267.4 secureConnectionStart=0
  requestStart=2269.1 responseStart=2270.5 responseEnd=2285.8
```

The lookup and connect fields collapsing onto `fetchStart` is not the bug
coming back: the fixture is keep-alive over loopback, the connection was
reused, and `http.ResponseTimes` documents that a reused connection answers
zero for the first three — which is what a browser reports too.

**Two things this does NOT establish, stated so nobody reads them in.** The TLS
branch of `setConnectionMilestones` (`app_connect > 0` →
`secureConnectionStart`) is exercised by neither measurement: the fixture has no
TLS, and the one https reading reused the connection the navigation had already
opened, so it correctly answered 0 there as well. And on that https page Chrome
opened a *fresh* connection for its XHR where this engine reused one — a
connection-pooling difference, not a milestone one, and not something this plan
touched.

### And the reason it is filed as fidelity, not as a door

The plan was picked because B64 measured Cloudflare's guard doing a
resource-timing census inside the widget's own frame — a cross-origin subframe
— which made this look like the rare fidelity item with evidence a guard reads
it. B64 then closed that off directly: a knob handing the guard 128 synthetic
entries **with the nine milestones forced to zero** is ticketed 3/3, same window,
strict alternation. The guard reads `requestStart` / `responseStart` /
`responseEnd` off every entry (prop_read log, widget realm) and does not refuse
over their values. So this is a correctness fix and is scoped as one.

## A reused https connection still negotiated TLS once

Chasing the pooling difference noticed while fixing the XHR milestones turned
up a sharper thing beside it. `probes/expr-b86-connection-reuse.js` fires six
**sequential** same-origin XHRs (sequential because parallel requests force
extra connections in any browser, which would manufacture the difference) and
reads reuse off the entry, the only place a page can see it:

```
                      fresh connections   secureConnectionStart on a reused one
  Chrome                    2 / 6              == fetchStart   (non-zero)
  this engine, before       0 / 6              0
  this engine, after        0 / 6              == fetchStart
```

The first column is real and unfixed: Chrome opens two sockets over that burst
and this engine opens none, riding the navigation's connection for all six.
That is connection pooling, it is an architectural difference, and B64's dose
sweep says it points nowhere for cf-scrapingcourse — the lever there is the
total byte-length of resource entry *names*, and connection count does not move
that number at all.

The second column is a value error on **every entry of every https page**, and
it is one expression to read. `setConnectionMilestones` branched on
`app_connect > 0`, which is curl's TLS handshake timer — and a reused https
connection reports 0 for it exactly like a plain http one. So the two schemes
were given the same answer, and reporting 0 said every https resource this
engine loaded had negotiated no TLS at all.

`http.ResponseTimes` grew a `secure` flag rather than the call sites growing a
parameter: it is a property of the connection the response arrived over, the
same as the five timers beside it, and one of the five call sites (the
navigation) does not have a URL in hand. It is read off `CURLINFO_EFFECTIVE_URL`,
so a redirect that left https for http is reported as what it landed on.

**Caveat kept from the previous chapter, still true:** the *fresh* TLS branch
(`app_connect > 0` → a real handshake timestamp between connectStart and
connectEnd) is exercised by neither measurement. This engine opened no fresh
connection in any run here, and the local fixture has no TLS. What is verified
is the reused branch and that plain http still answers 0 — eight readings on the
two-origin fixture, unchanged, plus 1546/1546.

### Why this is not filed under the door

Same reason as the milestones it came from. B64 measured the cf-scrapingcourse
lever to be Σ(name bytes) of the widget document's resource entries, bracketed
between 33KB (0/3) and 52KB (3/3) — while **Chrome's own widget document carries
1–3 entries and 278–1465 bytes**, thirty times under the threshold, and passes
anyway. Nothing in the resource-timing family is going to walk this engine up to
40KB of entry names, and nothing in it should be scoped as opening that station.

## The iframe was the missing entry, and the order is still not

`iframe-element-resource-entry`, measured on a fixture with one of every
subresource kind (`probes/b86-initiator-fixture.mjs` +
`probes/expr-b86-initiator-set.js`) rather than on the station, so it is
reproducible:

```
                 entries  byInitiator                                            nameBytes
  Chrome            7     fetch:1 iframe:1 img:1 link:1 other:1 script:1 xhr:1      215
  before            6     fetch:1        img:1 link:1 other:1 script:1 xhr:1      183
  after             7     fetch:1 iframe:1 img:1 link:1 other:1 script:1 xhr:1      215
```

The 32 bytes are that one URL. B64's live census says the same thing off the
station: Chrome's pre-ticket top document on cf-scrapingcourse is
`script:2 img:1 xhr:1 other:1 iframe:1` and this engine's was the same minus
the iframe.

An `<iframe>` reaches this engine as a *navigation* — the child frame runs
`Frame.navigate` and its own Performance records navigation timing — so nothing
was ever filed in the **parent's** resource buffer. What Chrome puts there is
one entry per framed document carrying that document's own fetch and connection
walk, which is precisely what the child's navigation timing already holds. So
the entry is not reconstructed: `Performance.navigationTiming()` hands the
child's own record over, `initiator_type` becomes `"iframe"`, and the parent
records it. Filed in `frameDoneCallback` rather than where the request goes out,
because the entry needs a body size and a response end and only a completed
navigation has both — the rule the image path already follows.

**The buffer ORDER is not settled by this and must not be read as settled.**
`resource-entry-buffer-order` is a separate open plan, both arms disagreed
before this change, and they still do:

```
  Chrome   link, script, img, iframe, xmlhttprequest, fetch, other
  after    iframe, script, link, img, xmlhttprequest, other, fetch
```

The new entry lands *first* here and fourth in Chrome, which is one more input
for that plan rather than a regression from this one — before the change our
order was already `script, link, img, …` against Chrome's `link, script, img, …`.

## The buffer was never sorted wrong — three numbers in it were

`resource-entry-buffer-order` was opened on one reading: our
`getEntriesByType('resource')` came back
`iframe,script,link,img,…` where Chrome's read `link,script,img,iframe,…`. The
plan's own P2 named the cause — "entries are queued by responseEnd, not by
start" — and that was backwards. Both arms already do the same thing, and this
engine's sort was already right.

The separator is `probes/b87-order-fixture.mjs`: three `<img>` whose server
delays them 600 / 300 / 0ms, so "the order they started" and "the order they
finished" are exact reverses of each other. Initiator is held constant on
purpose — a mixed-initiator page cannot tell a completion-ordered buffer from
one that happens to group by kind. `probes/expr-b87-order.js` reads the buffer
*and* the arrival order seen by a `PerformanceObserver` the fixture page
registers before the images, since an observer added afterwards sees either
nothing or the buffer's own order, and neither is arrival order.

```
                 observer (arrival)   getEntriesByType   sorted by responseEnd   sorted by startTime
  Chrome            c, b, a              a, c, b              c, b, a               a, c, b
  this engine       c, b, a              a, b, c              c, b, a               a, b, c
```

Both arms **queue at completion and read back sorted by startTime**. Ours was
already doing it (`Performance.zig:626`, `std.sort.block` on `_start_time`);
`sortedByStart` and `startEqualsFetch` are true on both. Had P2 been
implemented as written it would have broken a read path that was correct.

So the order divergence is entirely in the **values** the sort runs over.
`probes/expr-b87-initiator-times.js` prints them beside the order on the b86
mixed fixture, and three runs agree exactly:

```
  Chrome   sheet.css=66.5 head.js=66.5 pic.gif=66.6 frame.html=70.7 data.txt=70.9 data2.txt=71.8 favicon=117.6
  before   frame.html=1.8 head.js=6.8 sheet.css=7.7 pic.gif=8.9 data.txt=12.6 favicon=14.1 data2.txt=14.7
```

Three separate defects, of which one belonged to this plan.

**The iframe entry was stated in the child's time origin.** Our parent entry
read `end=5.7` and the child's own navigation read `responseEnd=5.7` — byte for
byte — while the two documents' `timeOrigin` were 10.9ms apart
(`probes/expr-b87-iframe-timebase.js`). Chrome's parent entry read
`start=55.6 end=69.4` against a child of `0.0 / 14.0` and a gap of `55.5`: the
child's numbers plus the gap. Ours therefore claimed a `startTime` of 2.4
against a nearest sibling of 8.3 — a subresource that began loading before the
elements *above* it in its own document were parsed. B86 handed the record over
without restating it. Fixed: `navigationTiming` becomes
`navigationTimingOn(host)`, which shifts by the origin difference and re-snaps
onto the host's lattice, walking the `f64` fields by reflection because "every
`f64` here is milliseconds since the owning document's time origin" is the
struct's stated invariant. A zero is left alone — it means the milestone did not
happen. Order after:

```
  Chrome   link, script, img, iframe, xmlhttprequest, fetch, other
  before   iframe, script, link, img, xmlhttprequest, other, fetch
  after    script, link, img, iframe, xmlhttprequest, other, fetch
```

**`<script src>` always goes out before a `<link rel=stylesheet>` above it.**
Not a timestamp: the *wire* says so too. `b87-order-fixture.mjs` logs arrival
order server-side and serves the same two elements in both source orders.
Chrome follows the document (`link-first` → `link,script`; `script-first` →
`script,link`); we answer `script,link` to both, and delaying the sheet by 250ms
does not change it. The cause is `frame/preload.zig:77` — the prescan reads the
raw HTML before parsing and its callback handles `.script` / `.module` /
`.base` and nothing else, so scripts leave before the parser has reached the
link. Chrome's preload scanner covers stylesheets, which is why its order is the
document's. That is a fetch-scheduling change, not a resource-entry one, and it
is now `stylesheet-prescan-order` — **priced as debt, not as a door**: cf's
lever is the *name-byte total* (33–52KB) and Chrome passes that station on
278–1465 bytes, so nothing in this family walks to it.

**The favicon is not misordered at all.** On the mixed fixture ours goes out at
14.1 with `fetch` at 14.7 and Chrome's at 117.6 with `fetch` at 71.8, which
reads like a rule difference. `/slow-chain.html` separates rule from race: its
only JS-initiated load is an XHR delayed 500ms, and **both arms ask for the
favicon while that XHR is still in flight** — Chrome issues the XHR at 40.1 and
the favicon at 67.0, ours 7.9 and 8.3. Chrome's rule is "after the load event",
not "after every other subresource", and an in-flight fetch does not hold it
back. `Frame.requestFavicon` already sits at the end of the load event
(`Frame.zig:1620`). The position gap is engine speed — our load event fires at
~14ms and Chrome's at ~117ms — and closing it would mean adding an artificial
delay to buy a position that is not a tell. Left alone.

## Another origin's bytes were the page's to count

`cross-origin-entry-opacity`. Resource Timing makes a cross-origin entry opaque
unless the response opts in with `Timing-Allow-Origin`. This engine opted every
response in: every cross-origin entry carried its real byte count, its real
protocol and its real connection walk, TAO or no TAO. On cf-scrapingcourse that
handed the page the Turnstile widget document's exact size — B66 measured
`encodedBodySize` 100804 and `transferSize` 101104 there against Chrome's zero.

The plan opened on B66's station reading, which also carried two conclusions
that the fixture overturned: that `Timing-Allow-Origin` is *not* the
discriminator, and that Chrome masks only cross-origin **iframe documents**
rather than cross-origin resources generally. Both are wrong, and the reason is
worth keeping: B66 read the header with a bare `curl -sI`, and Cloudflare only
echoes `timing-allow-origin` when the request carries an `Origin` header. A
header read off a request shape the browser never makes was then used to explain
the browser's behaviour.

`probes/b87-crossorigin-fixture.mjs` asks it on ground we control — two ports,
so two real origins — crossing the axes that could matter: framed document vs
plain subresource, opted-in vs not, and (added after the first cut was wrong)
no-cors vs CORS request mode. Chrome:

```
  load        origin   mode      TAO   sizes/proto/walk   status   contentType
  <img>       same     --        --    real               200      real
  <img>       cross    no-cors   no    0                  0        ''
  <img>       cross    no-cors   yes   real               0        ''
  <iframe>    cross    no-cors   no    0                  0        ''
  <iframe>    cross    no-cors   yes   real               0        ''
  fetch()     cross    cors      no    0                  200      real
  fetch()     cross    cors      yes   real               200      real
```

**Two gates, governed by different things.** `Timing-Allow-Origin` governs the
timing and the sizes, and nothing else. The status and the content type ride on
the response **type**: a CORS-mode request that came back is not an opaque
response, and its status is the page's to read however the response feels about
being timed. Reading the status gate off the `<img>` rows alone — "cross-origin
means status 0" — is the mistake this made first, and it hides the status of
every cross-origin fetch and XHR. The live station says so independently:
Chrome reports cf-scrapingcourse's cross-origin `api.js` with
`responseStatus: 200`, 3/3.

A third thing worth not getting wrong: an opaque milestone is a **true zero**,
not "collapsed onto `fetchStart`". Collapsing is what a *reused connection*
reports; confusing the two would say every cross-origin load rode a warm socket.
What survives either gate is `fetchStart`, `responseEnd`, and therefore
`startTime` and `duration` — a page may always know that it loaded something and
how long it took.

The mask is applied in `Performance.resourceLoaded`, which already existed as
the one place the five recorders funnel through (it is where the response labels
are duped for the same reason). `Timing-Allow-Origin` rides in on
`ResponseLabels` beside the two labels it already carries; the `<iframe>` entry
needs the *child* document's header, so the frame keeps its own on the frame
arena. `transferSize` stops keying on `response_status == 0` and gets an
explicit `responded` flag, because the mask zeroes the status of an entry that
did respond and Chrome still reports its bytes.

After: all eight fixture rows answer as Chrome does, and the live station reads
`leakedBytes=0`.

**One thing this deliberately does not fix, because it is not this entry's.**
Our `api.js` entry stays opaque where Chrome's is transparent. That is not the
mask being too eager — Cloudflare gives *us* no `Timing-Allow-Origin` at all,
because we do not send an `Origin` header on that request, because this engine
has no `crossorigin` attribute support on script, image or link elements. A
missing `Origin` on a `crossorigin` subresource is a wire-visible defect of its
own and wants its own plan; papering over it at the entry would report a
permission the response never granted.

**Priced as debt, not as a door.** cf's lever is the entry-name byte total
(33–52KB) and Chrome passes that station on 278–1465 bytes — see the chapter
above. What this closes is a leak: the page could read another origin's exact
response sizes, which one expression separates from Chrome.

## crossorigin was a property we reflected and never obeyed

`crossorigin-attribute-sends-origin`. `crossorigin` on a `<script>`, `<img>` or
`<link>` puts the load into CORS mode: the request announces an `Origin` and
says `cors` in `Sec-Fetch-Mode` where a bare one says `no-cors` and names
nobody. This engine reflected the attribute as an IDL property
(`Script.zig:111`, a `reflect.enumerated` and nothing else) and no part of the
fetch path ever read it, so every subresource went out identically whatever the
markup said.

It surfaced from the other end. After the cross-origin masking landed, our
`api.js` entry on cf-scrapingcourse stayed fully opaque where Chrome's is fully
transparent — which looked like the new mask being too eager, and was not.
Cloudflare only echoes `Timing-Allow-Origin` **when the request carries an
`Origin`**: `curl -sI` gets none, `curl -sI -H 'Referer: …'` gets none, and
`curl -sI -H 'Origin: https://www.scrapingcourse.com'` gets
`timing-allow-origin: https://www.scrapingcourse.com`. The header we were not
sending was changing what the server sent back.

`probes/b87-crossorigin-request-fixture.mjs` puts it on ground we control: the
page on `127.0.0.1`, the subresources on `localhost`, so the loads are
cross-**site** and not merely cross-origin, and the far server prints the
headers that arrived. Twenty rows over two rounds:

```
  load                        Chrome                     this engine (before)
  <script src>                origin=(none) no-cors      same
  <script crossorigin src>    origin=<page> cors         origin=(none) no-cors
  <script type=module src>    origin=<page> cors         origin=(none) no-cors
  <img src>                   origin=(none) no-cors      same
  <img crossorigin src>       origin=<page> cors         origin=(none) no-cors
  <link rel=stylesheet>       origin=(none) no-cors      same
  <link crossorigin …>        origin=<page> cors         origin=(none) no-cors
```

Two things the fixture settled that guessing would have got wrong. A **module**
script is CORS mode with no attribute at all, so `crossorigin` is not the only
thing that flips the mode. And a **same-origin** `crossorigin` subresource still
carries the `Origin` — which is where these part company with `fetch()`, whose
same-origin GET carries none, and why the header could not just reuse the
existing tainting-cors rule.

`Sec-Fetch-Dest` and `Sec-Fetch-Site` are unaffected by the attribute on both
arms. `anonymous` and `use-credentials` are **not** distinguished: separating
them needs a cross-site cookie, which needs `SameSite=None; Secure`, which needs
https, which no fixture here speaks. Both spellings read as "CORS mode" until
someone can measure the difference.

The prescan learns about it as its own kind (`KIND_SCRIPT_CORS`) rather than by
folding: it reads the raw HTML before parsing and starts script fetches from
there, so a speculative fetch for a `<script crossorigin src>` would otherwise
go out with a plain one's headers — which is the exact thing being fixed. No
module counterpart is needed, since modules are CORS either way.

The entry half needed wiring too, and was missed on the first pass: the element
recorders were still declaring themselves no-cors to `resourceLoaded` after
their requests had stopped being no-cors, so `responseStatus` stayed 0. Caught
by the live station rather than by the fixture, and then red-lighted properly —
forcing the script recorder back to `cors_response = false` turns the new test
block from `crossorigin: status=200 / plain: status=0` into `status=0` twice.

**After, on the live station** (`probes/expr-b87-station-opacity.js`, 3/3 each):

```
              enc      xfer     proto   walk      status
  Chrome      27124    27424    h3      nonzero   200
  before      27124    27424    h2      nonzero   200   (nothing masked at all)
  masked      0        0        (empty) zero      0     (no Origin -> no TAO)
  after       27124    27424    h2      nonzero   200
```

Every field matches Chrome now except `proto`, which is QUIC and a separate
axis — and one a neighbouring session has already shown is causally irrelevant
here: Chrome holds its cf ticket 6/6 with `--disable-quic`.

**The door did not move.** `cf-verdict.mjs`, six runs on the head binary:
`ticket=(absent)` 6/6, every round `chl-gen`, exactly as before. That is the
expected outcome — cf's lever is the entry-name byte total and Chrome passes on
278–1465 bytes — but it is worth stating plainly, because this was the strongest
signal found in a while: unlike every other defect closed on this codebase
lately, it was visible in the server's own request log without the page running
a line of JavaScript, and it demonstrably changed what Cloudflare sent back.
Closing it did not open anything.

## A preload link is a request, not a declaration

`preload-link-fetches-resource`. `<link rel=preload as=X>` fetches what it names
and warms the cache; the destination of that request is the `as` value. This
engine handled `as=script` and nothing else — every other `as` fired a synthetic
load event and asked for nothing — so a page preloading its hero image made one
fewer request than Chrome, in the site's own log, with no script running.

`probes/b87-preload-as-fixture.mjs` puts all eight `as` values on one page:

```
  as=       Chrome fetches?  dest    mode      Origin   this engine (before)
  image     yes              image   no-cors   no       no request
  style     yes              style   no-cors   no       no request
  script    yes              script  no-cors   no       fetched (the only one)
  font      yes              font    cors      yes      no request
  fetch     yes              empty   no-cors   no       no request
  document  no               --      --        --       no request
  audio     no               --      --        --       no request
  video     no               --      --        --       no request
```

Chrome files all five under `initiatorType: "link"`.

Two of them needed something the request layer could not express, and both are
the same shape of surprise — a destination whose header is *not* what the
destination usually implies:

* **`as=fetch` is no-cors.** Its destination is `empty`, the same as a real
  `fetch()`, but Chrome sends it no-cors where a real `fetch()` is always cors.
  So `Request` grows a `mode` override, null everywhere else.
* **A preloaded image is `priority: i`, where a displayed `<img>` is
  `u=1, i`.** Same destination, different urgency: the preload is not on screen,
  so it never gets the boost. Hence a `priority` override too.

That second one could only be seen over h2 — Chrome sends the RFC 9218 hint on
h2/h3 and nothing at all on h1, and every fixture here is node's `http`. So
there is a small h2 fixture now (`probes/b87-preload-priority-h2.mjs`), reusing
`h2-echo.mjs`'s throwaway-certificate helper rather than editing the shared page
set it serves. Both arms, all six rows, after:

```
  /p-image.gif   dest=image   prio=i
  /p-style.css   dest=style   prio=u=0
  /p-script.js   dest=script  prio=u=1
  /p-font.bin    dest=font    prio=u=1
  /p-fetch.bin   dest=empty   prio=u=1, i
  /favicon.ico   dest=image   prio=u=1, i
```

`as=font` brought a `font` destination with it — the first one this engine has,
since nothing here loads a font face.

**A use-after-free the html test passed straight through, worth remembering.**
The first cut resolved the href onto a scoped arena and released it on return,
but the transfer stores that slice and the entry quotes it back long after. The
buffer came back naming two preloads `favicon.ico` and a third a run of NUL
bytes — while the requests themselves went out perfectly well, so the wire log
looked right. The test passed because it looked entries up *by* name, and a
freed name reports as "(no entry)", which reads like the request never going
out. It now asserts the names the entries actually carry, so the same corruption
returns as a wrong string rather than a missing row.

**Priced as debt.** Nothing in this family has moved a door: see the two
chapters above and `only-two-real-doors-left`.

## The cap said what to inline; we heard "what to remember"

`cdp-post-data-beyond-the-cap`. `Network.getRequestPostData` answered
`RequestNotFound` for every body over `maxPostDataSize`, because the capture was
discarded at the same threshold. Those are two different questions — the
parameter governs how much rides along in the `requestWillBeSent` notification,
and this method exists *precisely* for the bodies that did not ride along.

It surfaced from a side-by-side that had been printing a `?` for months.
`cf-verdict.mjs`'s rounds line, this arm against Chrome:

```
  chrome   r1:2306B  r2:4716-4727B  r3:88311-90167B=TICKET  r4:8748-8855B=TICKET
  before   r1:2306B  r2:4898-4908B  r3:?B=chl-gen
```

The `?` means "the tool asked `getRequestPostData` because the body was not
inlined, and got nothing back". Chrome's fallback returned 90167 bytes; ours
returned an error, so the biggest exchange in the challenge was unreadable on
the arm that fails it.

`probes/b87-post-data-cap.mjs` isolates it — one 90KB POST, a bare
`Network.enable {}`, the same script driving both engines:

```
  chrome      bodyLen=92160  inlined=92160  getRequestPostData=92160
  before      bodyLen=92160  inlined=0      getRequestPostData=RequestNotFound
  after       bodyLen=92160  inlined=92160  getRequestPostData=92160
```

Note the middle column on the Chrome row. **The documented 64KB default is not
what Chrome does**: under a bare `Network.enable {}` it inlined the 90KB body,
and a 1MB one, and an 8MB one, in full. So the figure in the protocol docs
describes nothing anyone ships, and a 64KB default made this the only arm that
withheld a challenge payload from its own driver. Retention now has its own
fixed ceiling instead of following the client's parameter, since the memory is
ours and the protocol gives the client no way to ask for it.

**And then the negative that fell out of it.** With r3 readable:

```
  chrome   r1:2306B  r2:4716-4727B  r3:88311-90167B=TICKET
```
