```
  after    r1:2306B  r2:4908B       r3:87660-88460B=chl-gen
```

The third round is **not short, not missing and not truncated** — it is the same
~88KB Chrome sends, and Cloudflare answers `chl-gen` to it anyway. `r1` is
byte-identical between the arms and the instance ids match exactly
(`2417424015`, `2001508894`), on both. So "our r3 never gets built" is dead as
an explanation, and what is left is r2's extra ~185 bytes or r3's *contents*.
The body is now readable on this arm, which is what `cf-r3-payload-segments`
needs to look at those contents at all.

## Kasada's payload has a size it will not take, and a list it will not read (B88, 2026-08-29)

`hyatt-collector-overload`. A peer session had just opened cf-scrapingcourse by
overloading Turnstile: put enough text on the widget realm's global and the
guard fails open. The same instrument aimed at Kasada moved the `/tl` payload by
zero bytes and won nothing in twenty runs, which says Kasada does not enumerate
globals — it does not say Kasada cannot be overloaded. `x-hyatt-is-exhausted`
asks for a new observation channel before this station is reopened, and
"overload until it fails open" had never been swept here. This is that sweep.

Everything below is read off the wire by `kasada-knob.mjs`: the size of the
`/tl` POST and the `x-kpsdk-r` header on its response. `Runtime.enable` is never
sent. The knobs live in `scratch/b88/` and every one of them was checked against
a live page first (`scratch/b88/knob-alive.mjs`) — the harness wraps knobs in
`try/catch`, so a knob that throws on a surface this engine lacks is
indistinguishable from a knob that ran and changed nothing, and the second reads
as "the guard does not collect this". Two knobs were dead on the first try
(`document.cookie`'s accessor is not on document's immediate prototype; `stack`
is an own property of each error instance, not an accessor on `Error.prototype`),
and both would have printed a clean, wrong negative.

### The verdict header has three states, not two

`kasada-verdict-is-x-kpsdk-r` records two: Chrome gets `x-kpsdk-r: 1-B1VvW1U`,
this engine gets no header. There is a third, and it is easy to mistake for a
win. Hooking `TextEncoder.prototype.encode` and appending 64KB to the assembled
body produces:

```
  lightpanda  none      postLen 19186-19194  r=(absent)   docs=429
  lightpanda  pad-64k   postLen 84674-84706  r=1-AQ       docs=429
  chrome      none      postLen 19602-19618  r=1-B1JufVU  docs=429->200
  chrome      pad-64k   postLen 85106-85154  r=1-AQ       docs=429
```

A first tally counted any present header as a ticket and read `pad-64k` as 2/2 —
this arm's first `x-kpsdk-r` in the whole chain. The Chrome control killed it in
the next run: the same pad takes Chrome from cleared 2/2 to cleared 0/2, with
exactly that token. So:

| `x-kpsdk-r` | meaning | how it was pinned |
|---|---|---|
| `1-B1…` | cleared | Chrome baseline, `429->200` follows |
| `1-AQ` | body did not decrypt or verify | pad the encoded body; both arms, both lose clearance |
| absent | decrypted, scored, refused | **this engine's baseline** |

Our baseline is the *third* state. The guard's POST is well-formed and the
server reads it; it simply does not like the answer.

### The POST has a ceiling, and it is not where the tell is

Inflating the surfaces the guard's own decoded string heap names — voices,
plugins/mimeTypes, languages, `performance.getEntries`, cookies — gives a clean
staircase, and then a wall:

```
  lightpanda  none        postLen  19178-19194   200
  lightpanda  surf-2k     postLen  26434-26458   200
  lightpanda  surf-8k     postLen  49682-49706   200
  lightpanda  surf-32k    postLen 142026         200
  chrome      surf-64k    postLen 266738-266778  413
  chrome      surf-128k   postLen 515250-515258  413
  lightpanda  surf-200k   postLen 794202-794218  413
```

Between 142KB and 267KB the server stops taking it. Under the ceiling the POST
is accepted with `cr=true` and no `1-AQ` — and still no ticket, at any dose. On
the Chrome arm the same dose *costs* the ticket. **Volume never helps and
eventually hurts**, in both directions, which closes the overload class here.
Cloudflare's lever does not exist on this station.

### What Kasada actually collects

The staircase above is the useful part: `postLen` answers "is this surface in
the payload at all" for about twenty seconds' work. One family per arm, same
32KB dose, Chrome arm:

| surface | postLen | in the payload | tampering costs the ticket |
|---|---|---|---|
| `navigator.plugins` / `mimeTypes` | 142442 | yes | **yes** |
| `userAgent` / `appVersion` / `platform` / `vendor` | 216202 | yes (413) | — |
| WebGL `getParameter` + `getSupportedExtensions` | 117914 | yes | no |
| `Error` stacks | 85122 | yes | no |
| timezone + `Date.prototype.toString` | 52394 | yes | no |
| `speechSynthesis.getVoices` | 19626 | **no** | — |
| `navigator.languages` | 19586 | **no** | — |
| `performance.getEntries` / `getEntriesByType` | 19618 | **no** | — |
| `document.cookie` | 19602 | **no** | — |
| `mediaDevices.enumerateDevices` | 19618 | **no** | — |
| `canvas.toDataURL` | 19586 | **no** | — |
| `localStorage` | 19610 | **no** | — |
| document element attributes | 19594 | **no** | — |
| `userAgentData.getHighEntropyValues` | 19594 | **no** | — |

Baseline is 19546–19634 across every run of the day, so ±50 is noise and every
"yes" above is between +33KB and +196KB. The *collected* column is safe on one
sample each; the *ticket* column is not, and only the plugins row was measured
in a complete interleaved run of its own (0/2 against 2/2). The second round of
the map run returned no POST on all ten arms at once — that is one rate-limit,
not ten readings, and it is why the pace dropped after it.

Two entries are worth naming. Kasada does not read `performance` entries at all,
which is the exact surface Cloudflare's guard walks character by character —
these two collectors are not the same family, and a fix aimed at one says
nothing about the other. And `canvas.toDataURL` is not read either, though only
that one entry point was patched, so `toBlob`/`getImageData` remain untested.

### Every collected surface is already identical

That map turns the door question into a much smaller one: only a surface the
guard reads can be the thing it refuses us for. There are five. `plugins` /
`mimeTypes` was dumped in full — items, prototype chain, own names, `for..in`
order, the plugin↔mimeType cross-links, `String(collection)`,
`pdfViewerEnabled` — and is **byte-identical**. The other four were dumped
together (`scratch/b88/expr-collected-four.js`, both arms on the same https
page, the Chrome arm carrying this fork's user agent): the whole navigator
identity family, 83 WebGL parameters and 39 extensions on both `webgl` and
`webgl2` including `WEBGL_debug_renderer_info`, four flavours of `Error.stack`
with their descriptors, and the timezone/`Date` surface across a summer and a
winter date. **Identical, to the byte** — and not vacuously so: the ANGLE
renderer strings are real, the stacks carry matching line and column numbers,
83 parameters came back on each side.

So the paradox now has a measured floor under it rather than an assumed one:
*every surface this station is shown to collect, this engine already answers
exactly as Chrome does.*

### A real tell, found and priced at zero

Walking every function reachable from `globalThis` and asking
`Function.prototype.toString` about it (`scratch/b88/expr-native-tostring.js`,
11120 functions here, 11574 on Chrome) turns up four non-native entries on this
arm and none on Chrome — two functions counted twice:

```
  WebAssembly.compileStreaming       function compileStreaming(source) {
                                       return bytesOf(source, 'compileStreaming').then(...)
  WebAssembly.instantiateStreaming   function instantiateStreaming(source, imports = undefined) {
```

They are written in JavaScript here, and that shows three separate ways —
readable source text, a `prototype` own property, and `new` on them not
throwing:

```
                        toString      own names                    new fn()
  lightpanda            source        length,name,prototype        no-throw
  chrome                [native code] length,name                  TypeError: fn is not a constructor
  WebAssembly.compile   (identical on both arms — the control)
```

Kasada's decoded heap greps for precisely this family: `\[native code\]`,
`patchedFuncStringErrMsg`, `^[a-z]+\s*\(\)\s*\{...\}`,
`Function.__proto__.toString.call()`. So it looked like the door.

It is not. Giving Chrome the identical shape (`wasm-js`), alongside a knob
carrying only the `prototype` tell (`wasm-proto-only`) and a null control that
deletes the slot and puts the same native function back (`wasm-redefine`):

```
  none             ticket 2/2  cleared 2/2  postLen 19546,19594
  wasm-js          ticket 2/2  cleared 2/2  postLen 19586,19586
  wasm-proto-only  ticket 2/2  cleared 2/2  postLen 19626,19594
  wasm-redefine    ticket 2/2  cleared 2/2  postLen 19634,19570
```

`postLen` does not move either — the guard never reaches these two names.
`WebAssembly` appears once in its 3087-line name table and neither streaming
function appears at all. **A genuine fidelity defect, and causally not this
door.** It is worth fixing on its own terms; it is not worth pricing as a door.

### What this leaves

The overload class is closed here, in both directions and with the sibling
guard's mechanism explicitly tried. The collected-surface intersection is empty.
Combined with the four causal negatives already on record and the guard's own
source and payload plaintext, x-hyatt has now been refused an explanation on
every channel that can be reached from inside the page.

What the map does leave open is its own blind spot: `postLen` can only answer
for surfaces that can be made *bigger*. Numbers cannot. Screen and window
geometry, `hardwareConcurrency`, `deviceMemory`, storage quota and timing values
are invisible to this oracle — though the geometry segment specifically is
already excluded by `px-zero` taking 10/10 tickets on Chrome.

### The POST is early, and being early is not why it is refused (B88)

One difference survives every dump: the two arms put `/tl` on the wire in
windows that do not overlap. Across ~40 runs this engine posts at 790–1378ms
after navigation and Chrome at 1646–2323ms. The guard uses XHR for it on both
arms, so deferring that one `send` moves us into Chrome's window without
touching a single thing the guard collects.

It does nothing. With a Chrome arm interleaved as a window anchor:

```
  lightpanda none            tl@1077-3306ms   ticket 0/3
  lightpanda tl-delay-0      tl@1082-2229ms   ticket 0/3   (patch, no delay -- the control)
  lightpanda tl-delay-800    tl@1796-2558ms   ticket 0/3
  lightpanda tl-delay-1200   tl@2198-2641ms   ticket 0/3
  chrome     none            tl@1795-2107ms   ticket 3/3, cleared 3/3
```

The dosed arms sit inside and past Chrome's window; one `none` run drifted to
3306ms on its own and was refused too.

**And a caution about how nearly this went the other way.** The first pass at
this ran without the Chrome anchor, and the `none` arm came back **2/3 with real
`429->200` clearances** — on the same pinned binary that had read 0/2, 0/2 and
0/3 earlier in the afternoon. Five of that run's twelve runs won tickets, spread
evenly across all four arms. Twenty minutes later, interleaved and anchored:

```
  lightpanda none  ticket 0/5   postLen 19154-19202
  chrome     none  ticket 5/5   postLen 19618-19682
```

That is `antibot-stations-pass-in-windows` at full amplitude, inside one
afternoon, on an engine that did not change. Any x-hyatt arm read without a
same-window anchor is worth nothing — including the "no ticket at any dose"
columns on this engine earlier in this chapter, which is why the overload
argument rests on the Chrome arm *losing* clearance rather than on this arm
failing to gain it.

## The last 440 bytes are 34 global names, and the guard does not read them (B89, 2026-08-29)

The one quantified difference x-hyatt still had was the `/tl` POST length: this
engine 19114-19234, Chrome 19546-19690, two distributions that never overlap.
Re-measured on a ReleaseFast binary built from today's main (`cfb3e9ed6`, which
carries both the Cloudflare collector pad and the wasm-streaming fix), anchored
and interleaved:

```
  lightpanda none  ticket 0/4   postLen 19178-19234  mean 19206
  chrome     none  ticket 4/4   postLen 19570-19682  mean 19646
```

**440 bytes, and the window was open the whole time.**

### Decomposing it

`payload-plain` was run three times per arm, interleaved, and every element of
the assembled body bucketed by class — not by index, since the array is shuffled
per run, and not one run against one run, since a large part of the body is
per-run random material. Because every element lands in exactly one bucket the
class deltas sum to the body delta by construction, so nothing hides in a
residual:

| class | Chrome − us | note |
|---|---|---|
| **34 sampled global names** | **+330** | the whole story |
| trap log `h:` / `g:` | +72 | already negated by `has-probe`, 10/10 |
| non-global collected enums | +33 | `dark`/`light`, `running`/`idle`, `srgb`, `standard` |
| numbers | +30 | geometry and timing figures |
| `performance` member list | +7 | 34 names against our 33 |
| Intl `resolvedOptions` lists | ~−5 | within per-run spread |
| geometry `<w>x<h>:` | −11 | already negated by `px-zero`, 10/10 |

Sum of class deltas: 416, against a mean body delta of 416.

### The 330 bytes are an enumeration order, not a missing capability

Both arms emit **exactly 34** global names — same count, different bytes: 720
against 390. They are not a name list the guard carries. None of
`webkitRequestFileSystem`, `ongamepadconnected`, `onscrollsnapchanging` or
`__moduleCache` appears anywhere in the guard's own 3086-name table, but
`getOwnPropertyNames` does; and each arm omits names the other emitted although
both engines have them. The draws sit at contiguous index runs in each arm's own
list, and five of them are the **last five names**:

```
  chrome  1232..1236  webkitSpeechRecognition, ...Error, ...Event,
                      webkitRequestFileSystem, webkitResolveLocalFileSystemURL
  this    1197..1201  WebAssembly, __moduleCache, console, chrome, CSS
```

132 characters against 40. And we **have** all five of Chrome's — at indices
263, 264, 1059, 1065 and 1067. So this is not the missing-capability theory
`drop-36-globals` already tested; own string keys enumerate in creation order,
and this is the **order the engine defines its globals in**. Our tail is the
post-snapshot fixup block in `Env.zig` — the collector pad, the re-added
`console` — landing exactly where the guard samples.

Injection confirms the mechanism: five properties defined at the end of Chrome's
list appear in the payload at the tail multiplicities (`x1,x2,x2,x2,x2`) and
push Chrome's `webkit*` draws from `x4` down to `x2`.

### Both directions, both negative

`names-like-ours` deletes the eight long legacy names from Chrome and appends
five at our own name lengths — removal, the direction that reproduces a deficit
rather than adding our tell alongside Chrome's. `dropped=8/8` on the wire, and
277 of the 440 bytes gone:

```
  chrome none             ticket 8/8   postLen mean 19639
  chrome names-like-ours  ticket 8/8   postLen mean 19362
```

`names-like-chrome` is the mirror on this engine: it deletes and reinstates
Chrome's five tail names with their own descriptors so they move to the end, and
drops `__moduleCache`. `moved=5/5 padGone=1`, tail identical to Chrome's:

```
  lightpanda none              ticket 0/6   postLen mean 19162
  lightpanda names-like-chrome ticket 0/6   postLen mean 19434
  chrome     none              ticket 6/6   postLen mean 19629
```

Chrome keeps the ticket carrying our names; we do not win one carrying Chrome's.
The anchor is 6/6 in the same rounds, so the second reading is not a shut window.

### Where that leaves x-hyatt

Every term of the 440 bytes now has a causal negative against it, and the
largest one — 79% of the gap — was negated in both directions in the same
afternoon. The `performance` list is the only term that is a real defect rather
than a negated one: the missing name is **`when`**, `EventTarget.prototype.when`
from the Observable integration, which is already P3 of `observable-event-target-when`.

No exec sub-plan comes out of this. The payload route is closed the way the
page-side, transport and guard-source routes were closed before it.

**One thing worth carrying to the other station.** `__moduleCache` — the 268KB
Cloudflare collector pad merged into main today — is the **only** own global name
this engine has that Chrome does not, and it sits at index 1198, inside the
window Kasada samples. It costs nothing here (`padGone=1` was in the mirror arm,
still 0/6). But it is a name no browser sends, now default-on in every realm, and
at least one guard is known to sample global names positionally.

**Corrected the same evening:** the pad was reverted out of main (`0ede8ffb8`,
`76e2795d8`) while this was being measured, so `__moduleCache` is no longer a
name this engine sends and that last paragraph now describes a risk that has
been taken back rather than a live one. Every reading above was taken on a
binary that still had it. Nothing in the attribution moves: the pad was one of
five names in the sampled tail and worth about fifteen bytes of the 330, and the
mirror arm deleted it explicitly (`padGone=1`) and still read 0/6.

## Chrome is not a usable reference on DataDome, and dd-saks was never shown to be a door (B89, 2026-08-29)

The door map has carried three real gaps: cf-scrapingcourse, x-hyatt and
dd-saks. With the first two accounted for, dd-saks was the one nobody was on.
It is not clear it is a gap at all.

`dd-saks`, interleaved, three rounds each, same window:

```
  lightpanda  datadome-challenge  doc=403->200  nodes=9   3/3
  chrome      datadome-challenge  doc=403->200  nodes=9   3/3
  chrome --headed                 doc=403->200  nodes=9   3/3
```

Identical shape on every arm. But a station that refuses both arms says nothing
until you know what the reference arm does when it *should* pass, so the whole
vendor was swept:

```
              lightpanda                    chrome (headless)
  dd-g2       datadome-challenge            datadome-challenge
  dd-leboncoin  pass  200, 1486 nodes       datadome-challenge
  dd-hermes     pass  200, 2037 nodes       datadome-challenge
  dd-etsy       pass  200, 1829 nodes       datadome-challenge
  dd-seloger    pass  200, 1484 nodes       datadome-challenge
  dd-saks     datadome-challenge            datadome-challenge
  dd-allopneus  cf-blocked                  cf-blocked
              5/8 passed                    0/8 passed
```

**This engine passes five DataDome stations; Chrome passes none.** And headed
Chrome is challenged on `dd-leboncoin` and `dd-hermes` too — the two this engine
passes in the same window — first with `--headed-ua` and then again without it,
since `--headed-ua` passes `--user-agent=` and that blanks the high-entropy
client hints DataDome reads (memory `ua-override-blanks-client-hints`); a headed
browser needs no override in the first place. Same verdict both ways.

So on this vendor, from this address, a fresh-profile Chrome is challenged
everywhere regardless of head or user agent. Whatever DataDome is keying on —
cookie age, session history, address reputation — Chrome-with-a-scratch-profile
does not have it, and **the Chrome column cannot separate "this engine is
detected" from "this profile is".** dd-saks being refused is not evidence of an
engine gap; the arm that was supposed to prove it is refused on stations we walk
straight into.

Counts are honest: one round per station for the vendor sweep, three for dd-saks
per arm, one per station for each headed control. The passes are unambiguous
(200 with 1500–2000 nodes against an interstitial's nine).

**What this does to the door map:** of the three gaps that survived
`six-of-nine-closed-doors-are-phantoms`, x-hyatt is now exhausted on all four
routes, cf-scrapingcourse's ticket turned out not to be a pass, and dd-saks rests
on a control that does not hold. Re-deriving the map needs a reference arm that
actually passes — an aged profile, or a residential address — not another
scratch-profile Chrome.

## The door map, re-derived against a reference arm that can open doors (B89, 2026-08-29)

The previous chapter ended with the Chrome column refusing stations this engine
walks into, which makes every "station X is a door" reading in the map suspect.
So the reference arm was fixed first.

### What a reference arm needs

Two things, and neither alone is enough. Measured on `dd-leboncoin` and
`dd-hermes`, the two DataDome stations this engine passes:

```
         | headless  | headed
   fresh | challenge | challenge
   warm  | challenge | pass        <- 1436 and 2014 nodes
```

*Warm* is `--profile-dir` plus `warm-profile.mjs`: sixteen ordinary pages
(Wikipedia, BBC, HN, gov.uk, MDN, NYT, Stack Overflow, IMDb), no guarded site
among them, leaving 125 cookies and 11 history entries. The profile never
visited leboncoin or hermes before the run that passed them, so the pass comes
from the profile having a past at all, not from a cookie for the target.

Two things had to be fixed to get there. `--profile-dir` did nothing at first
because teardown sends `SIGKILL`, and Chrome writes its cookie store on
graceful shutdown -- the first warmed run persisted **0 cookies** into a
correctly created sqlite file, which reads exactly like a station that set none.
And the first headed control was run with `--headed-ua`, which passes
`--user-agent=` and blanks the high-entropy client hints DataDome reads; a
headed browser needs no override. Both are now handled.

### The map

29 stations, both arms back to back per station rather than two serial sweeps,
`--fresh` so one wedged station cannot report the rest as timeouts. The
disagreements re-run three more rounds:

| | stations |
|---|---|
| **real door** (reference passes, we do not) | **cf-scrapingcourse, x-hyatt** — 3/3 each |
| both pass | 19, including all four Akamai, px-wayfair, ks-canadagoose, x-sony, x-zillow |
| both refused | cf-nopecha, cf-zeroclover, dd-g2, dd-allopneus |
| **undetermined** | dd-datadome, dd-leboncoin, dd-hermes, dd-saks |

**dd-saks is not a door, and it is not a phantom either — it is undetermined.**
The claim that it was one of three real gaps rested on the old Chrome column.
With the fixed arm the question was put properly: five rounds gated on a canary,
`dd-leboncoin` first and `dd-saks` immediately after, and the canary never came
back `pass` in any of them. A reference arm that cannot open *any* DataDome
station in the window cannot referee one. There was one round where this engine
passed `dd-leboncoin` while the reference arm did not.

The whole DataDome column moved during the session — leboncoin, hermes, etsy and
seloger all passed for this engine early and were refused later, and the warmed
reference passed leboncoin and hermes at 22:30 and nothing after. Whether that is
the vendor's window closing for everyone or ~30 automated visits spending the
profile's reputation is not separated here; both arms degraded together, which
is what a vendor-wide window looks like. Either way **a warmed profile is a
consumable, not a fixture** — treat DataDome readings as valid only when a canary
station is passing in the same minute.

### Where that leaves the count

Two doors, both confirmed against an arm that demonstrably opens doors:
`cf-scrapingcourse` and `x-hyatt`. x-hyatt's four routes are closed (previous
chapter). cf-scrapingcourse is the one live gap.

## Two things Cloudflare scores, both of which this engine already does (B68, 2026-08-29)

Every knob in `cf-knobs.mjs` works by `defineProperty`, and `cf-what-is-scored`
found that six of its seven screen hits were the patch rather than the family —
this station refuses arms whose natives look rewritten. So the subtraction was
redone with **launch switches**: the capability is removed inside Chrome, and
there is nothing left for a native-integrity check to find. The wrappers go
through the `CHROME` environment variable (`scratch/b67/flags/*.sh`), so no
shared tool changed.

Seven switches, one run each, `none` interleaved and true 7/7. Three came back
`served=false`: `--disable-reading-from-canvas`, `--blink-settings=imagesEnabled=false`
and `--disable-notifications`. The permission family was measured first and is
identical on both engines — `Notification.permission` is `default` on both and
all seven `permissions.query` states are `prompt` on both — so that third one is
a family we are already on the passing side of, and the note in the
`lp-chrome-values` knob claiming otherwise is stale.

### `served=false` does not say which kind of failure it was

A scored arm and an arm whose challenge could not run produce the same column.
**The `rounds=` column separates them**, and that is the instrument this chapter
leaves behind. Three runs each, `none` before and after every group
(`scratch/b68/f2-confirm.sh`):

| arm | served | r1 | r2 | r3 | r4 | targets |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `none` ×3 | true 3/3 | 2306–2316B | 4716–4727B | 88.2–89.5KB **=TICKET** | 8.8KB | 8 |
| `--disable-reading-from-canvas` ×3 | **false 3/3** | 2306–2316B | 4716–4727B | 88.0–88.1KB **=gen** | — | 9 |
| `imagesEnabled=false` ×3 | **false 3/3** | 2306B | 4706–4727B | 88.1–90.1KB **=gen** | — | 9 |

All three arms post the same three rounds at the same sizes — the failing arms'
r3 is not short, and `imagesEnabled=false` posts a *longer* r3 than the control.
The guard collected everything and sent it; Cloudflare read it and answered
`cf-chl-gen` instead of `cf-chl-out`. A challenge that cannot run stops at r1 or
r2, and neither arm ever did. The extra target is the re-challenge.

So these are the first clean "Cloudflare weighs this" readings on this station:
hook-free, capability verifiably gone, challenge verifiably finished, 3/3.

### Both of them, measured on this side, come out passing

**Canvas readback: what is scored is whether it completes, not what it returns.**
The switch does not make readback noisy — it marks every canvas tainted, so
`getImageData` throws `SecurityError` (`scratch/b68/expr-caps.js`; WebGL
`readPixels` is unaffected). Against that, the `no-canvas-readback` knob returns
an all-zero `ImageData` and `data:,` from `toDataURL` and is served true 3/3.
Hooks produce false negatives, not false positives, so that pass stands. This
engine's `getImageData` returns exactly the pixel that was drawn and throws
nothing. Pixel *fidelity* is a different question and already has a plan tree
(`cfsc-glyph-raster` and its children); this is not it.

**Images: the state that is scored is not the state we are in.** A valid 2×2 PNG,
same URL on both arms (`scratch/b68/expr-image-family.js`):

| | Chrome | lightpanda |
|---|---|---|
| `onload` / `complete` | load / true | load / true |
| `naturalWidth` / `naturalHeight` | 2 | **0** |
| `width` / `offsetWidth` / rect | 2 / 2 / 2×2 | **16 / 16 / 16×16** (the broken icon) |
| `decode()` | resolved | resolved |
| `createImageBitmap(blob)` | `[2,2]` | **`InvalidStateError`** |
| `drawImage` then read back | `[200,100,50,255]` | **`[0,0,0,0]`** |

The cause is in the source, not inferred: `Image.getComplete`'s comment says the
bytes are fetched and never decoded, so images stay in the broken state. That is
a real divergence — but it is *not* the switch's state. `imagesEnabled=false`
stops `load` from firing at all and leaves `complete` false, while here `load`
fires and only the picture is missing. Filing a raster-pipeline plan off the
switch alone would have been writing an unverified causal claim into a
requirement.

So the state was put on Chrome directly (`scratch/b68/knobs-b68.mjs`, each knob
verified through `run-expr` before it was spent on the station): `lp-image-state`
forces `naturalWidth`/`naturalHeight` to 0, makes `drawImage` of an
`HTMLImageElement` a no-op and rejects `createImageBitmap(Blob)` with
`InvalidStateError`; `image-passthru` installs the same three hooks and returns
the true values.

| arm | served |
|---|---|
| `none` ×4 | true 4/4 |
| `image-passthru` ×3 | true 3/3 — the hooks alone cost nothing |
| **`lp-image-state` ×6** | **true 5/6** |

5/6 is this station's own floor; a clean Chrome drops about one page in six.
**Negative: Cloudflare weighs whether an image loads at all, not whether it
became pixels.** This engine fetches the bytes, fires `load`, and emits the image
subresource requests, so it is on the passing side of that too. Do not open a
decoder plan off this reading.

What this chapter actually leaves is the method: switch-based subtraction with a
`none` control on both sides, `rounds=` to classify the hit, and a passthru twin
before any knob-based reading is believed. Twenty more switches are two runs each.

## Twenty more switches, one survivor, and it is CORS (B68, 2026-08-30)

The method from the previous chapter, run wide: twenty launch switches, one run
each, `none` every fifth run, the whole line kept (`scratch/b68/gen-flags.sh`
generates the wrappers from a name→switch table, `w2-screen.sh` runs them).

Twenty-five runs, twenty-one served. **One of the five `none` controls was
refused**, which is the documented floor showing up on cue — and with twenty arms
against a floor of about one page in six, three false hits is what chance
predicts. The screen produced exactly three: `--blink-settings=defaultFontSize=32`,
`--blink-settings=forceDarkModeEnabled=true`, `--disable-web-security`.

So the screen decided nothing. Three more runs each did:

| arm | screen | +3 runs | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `defaultFontSize=32` (verified: 16px → 32px) | false | **true 3/3** | floor |
| `forceDarkModeEnabled=true` | false | **true 3/3** | floor |
| **`--disable-web-security`** (verified: cross-origin fetch 200) | false | **false 3/3** | **scored** |

`no-web-security`'s three runs post `r1:2306B r2:4706–4716B r3:88.2–89.6KB=gen` —
the same sizes the served control posts. The guard finished; Cloudflare read it
and re-challenged.

### What that switch actually removes is CORS, and nothing else

The obvious reading — "Cloudflare notices the same-origin policy is off" — is
wrong, and one probe says so. A cross-origin iframe on a real page, thirteen
readings, three arms (`scratch/b68/expr-xo.js`):

| | Chrome | `--disable-web-security` | lightpanda |
|---|---|---|---|
| `w.document`, `w.foo`, `w.foo = 1`, `String(w)` | SecurityError | **SecurityError — unchanged** | SecurityError |
| `JSON.stringify(w)` | SecurityError | SecurityError | **`"{}"`** |
| `'then' in w` / `delete w.length` / `setPrototypeOf(w, null)` | SecurityError ×3 | SecurityError ×3 | **true / true / ok** |
| `w.location.href` | SecurityError | SecurityError | **TypeError** (`w.location` is undefined) |
| `Reflect.ownKeys(w).length` | 17 | 17 | **16** |
| cross-origin `fetch` | TypeError | **200** | **TypeError** |

In Chrome 151 the switch leaves every frame-boundary check standing. The single
observable it moves is the CORS one — and this engine enforces CORS, so it is on
the served side of the only thing that switch subtracts.

The right-hand column is still a real divergence: it is six of the eighteen
readings `cross-origin-proxy-shape` left open, reproduced unchanged. The exec
plan that closes four of them in one mechanism (`cross-origin-access-check`, V8
access checks) is still unstarted. **What changed today is its justification** —
this switch shows Cloudflare is not weighing that family, so that plan is
fidelity work, not door work.

### Where the flag lever stands

Three families are now confirmed scored on cf-scrapingcourse — canvas readback
completing, images loading, CORS being enforced — and this engine is on the
served side of all three. Seventeen more families came back served=true.

One caveat on those seventeen, and it is the reason this chapter does not claim
them as closed: **only the hits were checked for whether the switch landed.** A
switch Chrome ignores also produces `served=true`, and that is an empty arm, not
a cleared family. Measured by stealth-a9 in the same window:
`--font-render-hinting=none`, `--blink-settings=standardFontFamily=Courier` and
`--force-color-profile=display-p3` leave the headless canvas hash bit-identical
to bare Chrome. Anyone quoting the served=true column has to verify the switch
first.

### Nine of the twenty arms were empty, and the two engines agree on nineteen families

The caveat the previous section ended on was worth acting on rather than
recording. One `run-expr` per arm over the same twenty-family probe, diffed
against `none` (`scratch/b68/v1-verify-arms.sh`, readings in `v1-*.json`):

**Eleven switches landed** — `minimumFontSize=24` (16px → 24px),
`defaultFontSize=32`, `localStorageEnabled=false` (now throws), `preferredColorScheme=1`
(prefers-dark true → false), `--disable-presentation-api`, `--disable-file-system`,
`--disable-shared-workers`, `--disable-webgl2` (context → null),
`--force-color-profile=generic-rgb` (p3 → false), `--disable-speech-api`, and
`--disable-web-security`.

**Nine were empty**, for four different reasons, and only one of them is a gap in
the method:

* `hide-scrollbars` and `databasesEnabled=false` remove something Chrome does not
  have here — macOS overlay scrollbars reserve no gutter, and `openDatabase` is
  already `undefined` in both engines. Nothing to subtract.
* `force-dark`, `--disable-accelerated-2d-canvas`, `--disable-lcd-text` and
  `--disable-smooth-scrolling` act below script. Nothing reads them, which means
  the guard cannot read them either.
* `--js-flags=--noexpose-wasm` and `--disable-permissions-api` are simply ignored;
  V8's own spelling `--no-expose-wasm` is ignored too, so **WebAssembly cannot be
  subtracted with a switch at all** — that family needs a knob and a passthru twin.
* `--disable-remote-fonts` is undecided: the probe page carries no webfont.

Which leaves the reading that closes the lever. The same probe run on this
engine: **nineteen of the twenty families are byte-identical to Chrome** —
`WebAssembly`, `document.fonts` (`loaded/0` on both), `FontFace`, the scrollbar
numbers, default font sizes, `localStorage`, `openDatabase`, `indexedDB`,
`navigator.permissions`, `navigator.presentation`, the three filesystem entry
points, `SharedWorker`, the WebGL2 `VERSION` string, every field of
`getContextAttributes()`, color-gamut and colorDepth, `speechSynthesis` (**zero
voices on both**), `scrollBehavior`, `document.domain`, and `measureText` at
143.9453125 to the last digit.

The one difference is `prefers-color-scheme`: Chrome answers dark on this host,
this engine answers light. `dark-scheme` is the arm that puts Chrome in our
answer, and it is **served true 4/4**. Not a door either.

So the capability-presence lever is measured out on cf-scrapingcourse: ten
clean "this family is not weighed" readings, one weighed family we already
satisfy, and the single surviving divergence confirmed harmless. The next
reading has to come from a different channel — not from a twenty-first switch.

## Loaded, and no size — the one image reading no browser gives (B90, 2026-08-30)

An `<img>` on this engine used to answer, for a picture that had genuinely
arrived:

    load fired · complete === true · naturalWidth 0 · box 16x16

Each of those three is a state some browser reaches. The *combination* is not.
Chrome with images switched off (`--blink-settings=imagesEnabled=false`) leaves
`complete` at **false** and fires nothing at all — measured, three arms on one
URL, `scratch/b90/expr-flag-capability.js`. Chrome with images on fires `load`
and answers a real size. "Settled, and no size" was a shape only this engine
had, and it was one expression away from any guard that looks at an image at
all. It also reached layout: every picture on every page was rendered as the
broken-image icon, so a collector reading geometry saw a page of 16x16 boxes.

The root cause was written down in the source the whole time — `Image.zig`'s
`getComplete`: *"We fetch the bytes but never decode them, so images stay in
the broken state."* The fetch is deliberate (a client that never requests an
image is separable from the server logs alone). Throwing the bytes away is what
left the contradiction.

Nothing decodes now either. The two numbers come out of the header the sniffer
already had to read to tell `load` from `error`, and the parsers were already
in the repo: `webcodecs/images.zig` has carried PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, AVIF and
BMP geometry since `ImageDecoder` needed it. What was missing was a way in for a
caller with no declared type (`Kind.fromSignature` — an `<img>` sniffs, because
the header a server sends gets no say) and a way to stop at the geometry
(`readSize`, so a PNG does not take the pixel path and its
width-times-height-times-four arena allocation). The kept head grew from 14
bytes to 4KB because two of the six scan for their size: JPEG walks segments to
its SOF marker, AVIF walks boxes to `ispe`.

SVG needed its own reader — no signature, no samples, its size is three
attributes of the root element. Chrome 151 was measured against eleven roots
(`scratch/b90/fixture-server.mjs`, rows `svg*`):

| root `<svg>` | naturalW×H | box |
|---|---|---|
| `width=4 height=6` | 4×6 | 4×6 |
| `width=40px height=12px` | 40×12 | 40×12 |
| `width=7.5 height=2.25` | **8×2** (the IDL rounds) | 8×2 |
| `width=40` alone | **40×150** | 40×150 |
| `height=12` alone | **300×12** | 300×12 |
| `width=40 viewBox="0 0 20 5"` | **40×10** | 40×10 |
| `viewBox="0 0 20 5"` alone | **300×75** | **1904×476** |
| nothing | 300×150 | 300×150 |
| `width=50% height=25%` | **300×150** | 300×150 |
| `width=2em height=3em` | 32×48 | 32×48 |
| `width=0 height=0` | 0×0 | 0×0 |

A percentage is not an intrinsic size — that is the row worth keeping, because
it is the one a reimplementation guesses wrong. The viewBox-only row is the
other: it is the only case where Chrome's intrinsic size and its box are
different numbers, because a replaced element with a ratio and no size
stretches to its containing block.

Eighteen `<img>` rows on the fixture page, both arms on the same http URL:
**sixteen are byte-identical**, including all six raster formats, both negative
controls (200-with-HTML-bytes and 404 still read `0x0` and `16x16`), and nine of
the eleven SVG roots. The two that remain differ only in the box — the
viewBox-only stretch, which needs replaced-element layout this engine does not
have, and `width="0"`, which reads as *no* size and so falls back to the icon.
Both are written into `svgSize`'s own comment rather than left to be
rediscovered.

**This is a fidelity fix and it is not a cf door.** `cf-flag-subtraction` F3
had already closed that question from the other side: a knob that puts Chrome
into exactly this engine's image state — `naturalWidth` 0, `drawImage` of an
`<img>` a no-op, `createImageBitmap(Blob)` throwing — keeps its page **5/6**,
against a passthru control at 3/3 and `none` at 4/4. Cloudflare weighs whether
images *load*, not whether they became pixels. The reason to fix it anyway is
that every other station is unmeasured, and a self-contradiction is a cheaper
thing for a guard to read than any value mismatch.

### Painting no glyphs does not cost cf-scrapingcourse the page either

The same round priced the most expensive open plan in the tree. This engine's
canvas readback is not broken — corner pixels and `gl.readPixels` match Chrome
byte for byte — but it paints **zero ink pixels** where Chrome paints 2348
(`scratch/b90/expr-text-pixels.js`; `toDataURL` 342 bytes against 10162).
`text-noop` reproduces exactly that on the arm that passes, by making
`fillText`/`strokeText` no-ops on both 2d prototypes and touching nothing else:

| arm | served |
|---|---|
| `none` | true 13/13 |
| `text-passthru` (same two wrappers, calling through) | true 11/11 |
| `text-noop` | true 15, false 3 (18 runs) |

Nothing like the 3/3 the real flags give. So `cfsc-glyph-outline-raster` — the
plan with no outline data in the repo at all — is not a cf door.

### A switch that changes nothing is an arm that proves nothing

Four candidate value-only canvas arms turned out to be null:
`--font-render-hinting=none`, `--blink-settings=standardFontFamily=Courier`,
`--blink-settings=defaultFontSize=30` and `--force-color-profile=display-p3` all
leave the canvas hash **bit-identical** to plain headless Chrome. A `served=true`
read off any of them is a reading of a flag that never landed. `--disable-gpu`
is the one that does move the hash (`a2a7da68` against `4d1fd0a7`) while leaving
readback intact. Before a switch arm is scored, it needs a probe showing the
capability actually moved — the same discipline `cf-flag-subtraction` F2 applies
to the arms that hit.

### A harness note that cost an hour

On this engine a `setTimeout` scheduled inside a
`Runtime.evaluate(awaitPromise: true)` never fires: the evaluate times out at
the CDP layer and the whole probe returns nothing, which reads exactly like a
hung page. `fetch` does resolve, so a few data-URL round trips are the usable
pump. Every async probe in `scratch/b90/` is written without timers for that
reason.

## Reading the guard's plaintext from inside the engine (B69, 2026-08-30)

Cloudflare's telemetry leaves the page as ciphertext in a 64-character custom
base64 (`+`, `$` and `-` are in the alphabet; r2 and r3 share their first ~166
characters, which is the session prefix). So every wire diff on this door has
been a diff of ciphertext. `cf-r3-payload-segments` was opened to read those
contents and could not.

The plaintext does exist, for one instant, as the argument to the encoder — and
the challenge program names `TextEncoder` twice. `prop-reads.mjs` against a
Debug binary confirms it is not dead code: **`TextEncoder.encode`, occurrences
15**, all of them in the `challenges.cloudflare.com` realm.

**This engine owns that encoder.** `Context.recordTextEncode`, called from
`TextEncoder.encode` and gated on the `text_encode` log scope, keeps the length,
a hash, and 512 characters of each end, and `Context.deinit` dumps them the way
`unknown_properties` is dumped. Nothing lands in the realm: no wrapped native,
no extra own property, no changed `Function.prototype.toString`. The driver is
`scratch/b69/encode-log.mjs`.

The hash is deliberately **djb2 over UTF-16 code units** rather than anything
Zig would reach for first, and the length is in code units too, because the
number it has to line up with is what a JS-side hook on Chrome reports. The
first version recorded UTF-8 byte lengths and every pixel buffer looked
thousands of characters longer than Chrome's — 9216 against 13753 — which is
one byte per non-ASCII character and not a difference at all.

Chrome's half is `report-encodes` in `scratch/b69/knobs-b69.mjs` (the beacon
prelude is copied, not imported: `beacon` is private to `cf-knobs.mjs` and a
knob referencing an undefined `__send` reads exactly like a knob that did
nothing). It does **not** cost Chrome its ticket — `served=true`, r3 and r4 both
ticketed — so the comparison is against a passing arm.

### Fifteen calls each, and what is in them

> ⚠️ **This table is superseded. Do not repair anything off it.** It was taken
> against a Chrome arm on neither of the persona's axes -- `fo-harness.mjs`
> pinned no device scale factor until B104, and nothing pinned the theme until
> B105 -- so its "this engine" column contains phantoms. Re-measured with both
> pinned, four of its rows are byte-identical (the computed style, the
> `0|0|0|…` pair, `readPixels`, and the font probe list, whose "41" here is
> flatly wrong -- both arms answer the same 69-byte string). What survives is
> below in "The same fifteen, with both axes pinned". Two sessions have now
> spent time repairing entries from this table that were never defects.

| what | Chrome | this engine |
|---|---|---|
| `getImageData` 48x48 | 9216 `1ly97t5` | 9216 `1xof2yz` |
| `readPixels` 16x16 | 1024 `ard9mt` | **1024 `ard9mt`** |
| 49x44 buffer, three times | 8624 `1m3v0nt` | 8624 `101c16` |
| WebGPU 32x32 | 4096 `sq54p1` | 4096 `e4lqd` |
| `JSON.stringify(getComputedStyle(el))` | 30918 `t3o0bu` | 30902 `15ewidm` |
| `0\|0\|0\|…`, twice | 15361 `3coxr6` | **15361 `3coxr6`** |
| the widget's own CSS rules | 20696 `ug2ibx` | 20696 `a5zc6l` |
| font probe list | 69 `mt6m58` | 41 `1iwivuo` |
| four timings/randoms | 17, 1, 18, 16 | 13, 2, 2, 14 |

Two are byte-identical. Every pixel buffer is the right *length* and the wrong
content, which was already known and already knob-tested as not weighed. The
two that are new and small enough to name:

**The font list.** Chrome reports
`Apple Symbols|Galvji|Geneva|InaiMathi Bold|Luminari|PingFang HK Light`; this
engine reports `Apple Symbols|Galvji|Geneva|Luminari|Skia`. Two families the
guard's probe finds here are absent, and one it does not find is present.

**The computed style is 16 characters short**, with the first and last 190
identical. `scratch/b69/computed-fixture.mjs` reproduces the same string on a
page whose every box is pinned, so nothing in the diff is layout: **41 of the
736 values disagree**, and none of them is a rounding difference. They fall into
five groups:

- **A shorthand set in author CSS does not reach its longhands.** `background`
  leaves all eight `background*` longhands answering the literal string
  `"initial"` — which is not a computed value in any browser — and
  `background-color` transparent. `list-style` leaves its three longhands at
  their defaults, `grid-area` leaves all four grid longhands `auto`, `columns`
  leaves `column-count`/`column-width` `auto`, and `font` leaves `font-variant`
  `normal`.
- **`url()` in a computed value is not absolutised.** Chrome answers
  `url("http://127.0.0.1:38689/none.png")` where this engine echoes
  `url("/none.png")`, for `list-style-image`, `mask-image` and the `mask` and
  `list-style` shorthands.
- **`-webkit-` aliases are not aliases.** `webkitFlex`, `webkitColumns` and
  `webkitAnimation` answer their initial values while the unprefixed property
  answers correctly.
- **Serialisation.** `columns` is `3 100px` here and `100px 3` in Chrome;
  `mask-position: center center` is `center center` here and `50% 50%` there;
  `timelineTrigger` is `none` here and the empty string there.
- **`animation` is not applied at all**, so a running keyframe's `transform`
  reads `none` where Chrome reports the matrix.

None of this is filed as the door. `cfsc-does-not-judge-collected-values` closed
the value question from both directions, and `lp-chrome-values` — the knob that
repaired three of these values on the arm that passes — was refused. It is filed
as what it is: a list of 41 named, reproducible, off-site-testable defects on
the single largest surface any guard in this file reads, obtained by an
instrument the guard cannot see.

### The same fifteen, with both axes pinned (B105, 2026-09-04)

Both arms on `devicePixelRatio` 2 and `prefers-color-scheme: light`, asserted in
the run rather than assumed (`assertPersonaParity`), oracle cleared and this
engine refused in the same sitting:

| what | verdict |
|---|---|
| `JSON.stringify(getComputedStyle(el))`, 30918 | **byte-identical** |
| `0\|0\|0\|…`, 15361, twice | **byte-identical** |
| `readPixels` 16x16, 1024 | **byte-identical** |
| font probe list, 69 | **byte-identical** |
| the widget's own CSS rules, 22972 / 22963 | 9 bytes, four `@keyframes` zeros |
| `getImageData` 48x48 / 49x44 x3 / WebGPU 32x32 | right length, wrong content |
| the four short values | 17/16/1/18 against 13/2/2/14 |

So the "41 defects on the largest surface" line above is spent: at matched
scale that surface agrees to the byte, and the earlier 41 were the scale. The
font list's "41 bytes against 69" was never a defect at all.

**The nine bytes are real and this repo cannot yet reproduce them.** All four
are `rotate(0deg)`→`rotate(0)` and `translateY(0px)`→`translateY(0)` inside
`@keyframes`. Three shapes were tried in
`tests/css/declaration_serialize.html` and all three pass: a zero followed by a
zero, the live shapes (a zero followed by a non-zero, and a lone zero
translate), and the live rule verbatim including its negative first step,
asserted whole against Chrome's `cssText`. The station's stylesheet lives in a
cross-origin child document and the runner's page is not one, so the next
reading has to come off the live document -- this engine's own `cssText` for
that rule beside what the guard encoded -- and not off a fourth guessed shape.

⚠️ A local test passing is not grounds to retract a difference measured on the
station. It was used that way here, and it retracted a real defect for half a
session.
## The channel nobody had pointed an instrument at is the access log (B69, 2026-08-30)

Seven sessions closed cf-scrapingcourse from inside the page: the read set, the
read values, the payload spans, the plugin surface, native accessor shape, the
unknown-property log, the transport layer, twenty launch-flag families. B68
ended with "what is left must be an observation channel we do not have, not
another candidate value". This is one, and it was sitting in the trace the whole
time: **how many times the server was asked.**

### The `ci` PNG, asked for twice

`cfsc-fo-diff.mjs` prints one line per challenge request. Read as a sequence
rather than as a set, one row is doubled on this engine and single on Chrome:

```
  lightpanda   GET 200 body=1994  {cf}/…/ci/a33295e729d0f31f/…
               GET 200 body=1994  {cf}/…/ci/a33295e729d0f31f/…   <- same URL, again
  chrome       GET 200 body=3050  {cf}/…/ci/a332985619af2734/…
```

`ci` is a greyscale PNG the challenge loads as an `Image` (`type: "Image"` on
both arms, identical request headers on both of ours). Three runs of three, and
it is 2 every time here and 1 every time there. The two `cf-ray` values differ,
so these are two real requests and not one record printed twice.

Nothing in the page can see this. Both loads fire `load`, both report the same
size, `complete` is true either way. It is only visible to whoever keeps the
access log — which is to say, to Cloudflare.

### What Chrome's rule actually is

`scratch/b69/img-cache-fixture.mjs` serves one PNG and loads it nine ways,
counting requests at the server and `PerformanceResourceTiming` entries in the
page. The two columns agree row for row on both engines, which is worth saying
first: a reused resource files no second entry either.

| shape | Chrome | this engine, before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| two `Image`s in sequence | 1 | 2 | 1 |
| two `Image`s in one task | 1 | 2 | 1 |
| one element, `src` assigned twice | 1 | 2 | 1 |
| markup `<img>` plus a scripted `Image` | 1 | 2 | 1 |
| three loads of one URL | 1 | 2 | 1 |
| response carries `Cache-Control: no-store` | 1 | 2 | 1 |
| 404 both times | 2 | 2 | 2 |
| 200 whose bytes are not a picture | 2 | 2 | 2 |
| second load in CORS mode | 2 | 2 | 2 |

The right-hand rows are the ones that pin the rule down, and they rule out the
two obvious guesses. It is not cacheability — `no-store` is reused. It is not
the status — a 200 carrying a page is not. **What is reused is a resource that
became a picture**, which is the question `ImageRequest.arrived` already answers
for the event. So `Frame` keeps one slot per resolved URL (prefixed for CORS,
which is a separate key in Chrome too): a load that finds an open slot attaches
to it and takes the outcome when the transfer lands, one that finds a settled
slot replays the `load` and the intrinsic size, and a transfer that failed or
whose bytes were not an image drops its slot so the next load asks again.

After the fix all nine rows match Chrome on both columns, and on the live
station the `ci` row is asked for once.

### And it is not the door

Six alternating rounds, the fixed binary against a headed Chrome with a Chrome
user agent, same sitting:

```
  chrome   5 / 5   "Cloudflare Challenge - ScrapingCourse.com"
  fixed    0 / 5   "Just a moment..."      ci asked for once, r2 still ~180B long
```

A real defect, fixed and measured, and the door did not move. Which is the
twenty-somethingth negative on this station, but the *channel* is new, so the
rest of it was worth walking.

### The rest of the channel: 26 kinds of request against 11

`scratch/b69/wire-census-fixture.mjs` is one page that names a subresource
every way a page can, and a server that counts. Duplicates are one half of
"what the server sees"; absence is the other, and nothing here had ever
enumerated it.

Chrome asks for 26 of them. This engine asks for 11. It never requests:

- from CSS: `@import`, `@font-face` `src` (for a family a rendered element
  uses), `background-image`, `list-style-image`, `border-image-source`,
  `cursor`, `-webkit-mask-image`
- from markup: `<object data>`, `<embed src>`, `<input type=image>`,
  `<video poster>`, `<audio preload=metadata>`, SVG `<image href>`,
  `<link rel=manifest>`, `<link rel=prefetch>`

and for `srcset`, `sizes` and `<picture>` it requests the **fallback** where
Chrome requests the candidate it selected — `srcset-fallback.png` against
`srcset-2x.png`, `sizes-fallback.png` against `sizes-800.png`,
`picture-fallback.png` against `picture-webp.png`. Both engines correctly skip
a `background-image` on a selector nothing matches.

The stylesheet itself is fetched — `Config.enableExternalStylesheets` is on
unless `--disable-external-stylesheets` says otherwise, and the census shows
`sheet.css` requested on both arms. What is never fetched is anything the
stylesheet *references*. `Frame.loadImage` already carries the argument for why
that matters — "never fetching images at all is a server-visible tell" — and
the same sentence applies to every row above. It was never extended past
`<img>`.

*(Every row in that list has since been closed — `frame/style_resources.zig`
and `frame/markup_resources.zig`, plus the `srcset`/`sizes`/`<picture>`
selection. The list is kept as the measurement that named them.)*

The same duplicate defect is there for the other two kinds:
`scratch/b69/sub-cache-fixture.mjs` measures a second `<script src>` and a
second `<link rel=stylesheet>` for one URL at 2 requests here and 1 in Chrome,
while two `fetch()`es are 2 on both and an `<img>` followed by a `fetch()` is 2
on both (a different destination is a different key).

**What the census reads today**, with this chapter's image cache in and the
absent-request work that followed it merged: `tools/fingerprint/wire-census.mjs`
has 26 of 27 paths agreeing. The one that does not is `tail.js` — the script
path, which runs through ScriptManager's async machinery rather than one
synchronous fetch and has its own plan.

The stylesheet half needed one more fix than it looked like. `_stylesheet_bodies`
keyed on the resolved URL, and that string was allocated from the pooled session
arena `loadExternalStylesheet` releases on the way out, so the map pointed at
memory the next pooled fetch takes back. Two adjacent `<link>`s hit anyway;
put a `<script src>` between them and the third misses, because the script's own
fetch takes the block the key was living in. That is exactly the shape the
census page has, and it is why the census still said `sheet.css 1 against 2`
after the cache shipped. Duping the key moves it to 1
(`stylesheet_cache_key_outlives_the_fetch`).

### Where the census does *not* fire, which is why it is filed as fidelity

On an interstitial there is nothing to miss. `scratch/b69/wire-net.mjs` lists
every request off `Network.requestWillBeSent` with **only** the Network domain
enabled — no `Runtime`, no `Page`, no `Target.setAutoAttach`, all three of which
are measured detectable on Kasada — and run against x-hyatt the pre-verdict
sequence is the same seven requests on both arms, in the same order, with the
same methods:

```
  GET  document   hyatt.com/
  GET  script     …/ips.js
  POST xhr        reporting.cdndex.io/error
  OPTIONS         reporting.cdndex.io/error      <- the CORS preflight, on both
  GET  script     blob:…
  GET              favicon.ico
  POST xhr        …/tl
```

Chrome's list then runs to 91 requests and ours stops at 7 — but that is the
consequence of the verdict, not its cause: request 9 on Chrome is a second
`Document` for `hyatt.com/`, the interstitial reloading the real page after it
passed. Everything before the verdict matches. Same on cf-scrapingcourse once
the `ci` row is single: fifteen requests each, in the same order.

Two differences survive there and neither is on the wire. Chrome loads a
`data:image/svg+xml` from the interstitial's markup and this engine issues no
request record for it (a data URL never reaches a server, so it is a CDP and
resource-timing difference, not a traffic one), and every `initiator.type` this
engine reports is `other` where Chrome distinguishes `parser`, `script` and
`preflight`.

One more small thing fell out of the same reading: on `example.com`, whose
markup carries `<link rel="icon" href="data:,">`, this engine's resource-timing
buffer holds an entry named `data:,` and Chrome's holds nothing — while a
`data:image/png` load *does* get an entry on both. An empty data URL is not a
load Chrome files.

### The blob worker's `Abort`, still unreproduced

B60 measured the challenge's 13-byte blob worker firing `error` with the message
`Abort` here and running silently in Chrome, and the live trace still shows the
first blob request ending `Abort` on this arm. It does not reproduce off-site.
`probes/expr-blob-worker-abort.js` covers four revoke timings on a plain page
and `scratch/b69/blob-worker-fixture.mjs` adds the same three worker shapes in
the top document, in a same-origin iframe and in a cross-origin one: **silent in
all nine**. Whatever the challenge does to it is not the source, not the revoke,
and not the frame.

## Three device pixels, and a table generated on the wrong arm (B69, 2026-08-30)

The last non-`animation` row of the computed-style diff was
`column-rule-width`: an element declaring no column rule reads `1.5px` in
Chrome and read `3px` here. B93 left it with a note saying not to guess the
rule from two points, and it was right not to — the two points were
confounded.

### The matrix

`scratch/b69/rule-width-fixture.mjs` puts 22 declaration sets on one page and
`scratch/b69/expr-width-keywords.js` puts nine more on one element, across every
width property that takes `thin`/`medium`/`thick`. Chrome 151:

| | undeclared | `thin` | `medium` | `thick` | style `none` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `border-top-width` | 0px | 1px | 3px | 5px | **collapses to 0px** |
| `outline-width` | 3px | 1px | 3px | 5px | no effect |
| `column-rule-width` | **1.5px** | 1px | 3px | 5px | no effect |
| `row-rule-width` | **1.5px** | 1px | 3px | 5px | no effect |
| `-webkit-column-rule-width` | **1.5px** | 1px | 3px | 5px | no effect |
| `-webkit-text-stroke-width` | 0px | **0.666667px** | **2px** | **3.33333px** | no effect |

Two things fall out of it that neither of the original two points could say.
The style beside these widths has no say at all — a `column-rule-style: none`
with `column-rule-width: medium` is 3px, where the same shape on a border is
0px, so the border's used-value path is the wrong model to copy. And
`-webkit-text-stroke-width` has a scale of its own, two thirds of the others.

This engine echoed the keyword back on all five non-border names —
`outlineWidth` reported the literal string `medium`, which no browser does.

### The 1.5px is the device pixel ratio, and the arm was the confound

Four configurations, each asserting `devicePixelRatio` in the same run as the
width:

```
  headless                                dpr 1   3px
  headless, --force-device-scale-factor=1 dpr 1   3px
  headless, --force-device-scale-factor=2 dpr 2   1.5px
  headed                                  dpr 2   1.5px
```

`width × dpr = 3` in all four, and the third row is the one that matters: the
split is the device pixel ratio and not headedness, because a headless arm with
the flag answers the headed number.

**A retraction, and the trap behind it.** An earlier draft of this section said
the flag "never landed" -- that `--force-device-scale-factor` reported
`devicePixelRatio` 1 through `run-expr.mjs` -- and used that to explain why B93's
note called the reading "not a DPR artefact". That was wrong. Re-run on
debugging ports nothing else had used, `run-expr.mjs --chrome-arg
--force-device-scale-factor=2` reports dpr 2, three times out of three, and a
directly launched `--headless=new --force-device-scale-factor=2` reports it four
times out of four. What produced the dpr-1 readings was **a stale Chrome
answering on a reused `--remote-debugging-port`**: several probes had been run
concurrently, the driver's `fetch(/json/version)` loop connects to whatever
answers, and a browser from a previous invocation answers exactly like the one
that was just spawned. `sweep-needs-explicit-port` is the same failure recorded
for the sweep.

So the rule for anything whose answer has dpr in it is not "pass this flag" --
it is **read `devicePixelRatio` back in the same run and check it**, because the
flag can be right and the arm still wrong. The undeclared value is **three device pixels**,
and the `medium` keyword is three CSS pixels — which is why the two disagree at
all. This engine reports `devicePixelRatio` 2 as a fixed part of its device
profile (`Window.getDevicePixelRatio`, and the comment there is about Kasada
binary-searching that number to twenty bits), so 1.5px is the matching answer.

**And the table it was reading from was generated on the wrong arm.**
`webapi/css/chrome_initial_values.zig` carries a `do-not-hand-edit` banner and a
line naming its source: `HeadlessChrome/151.0.0.0`. Every value in it that
resolves against the device pixel ratio is therefore a dpr-1 value, and these
three names are the ones that showed. The undeclared answer was overridden in
`CSSStyleDeclaration` rather than in the generated file.

### The other 689 entries: none of them (B104, 2026-09-04)

That override was the wrong half to fix, and the open question above -- whether
anything else in the table is dpr-dependent -- has an answer now that the
generator pins the persona's scale (`personaScaleFlags`, `cdp.mjs`).

Regenerating both tables at dpr 2 moves **twelve values and no others**: the
eight rule-width names in `chrome_initial_values.zig` (`column-rule-width`,
`row-rule-width`, `rule-width`, `-webkit-column-rule-width` and the four
shorthands that carry a width) and the four inside `hr`'s entry in
`chrome_per_tag_values.zig`, every one of them `3px` to `1.5px`. Two
regenerations agree entry for entry, so the arm is deterministic. `outline` keeps
its `3px`, which is the distinction stated above holding up: a declared `medium`
is three CSS pixels and only the undeclared rule default is three device ones.

So the override in `CSSStyleDeclaration` is gone -- `undeclared` is null for the
rule widths and the recorded value stands on its own. The engine's answer does
not move: measured on the cf-scrapingcourse widget against a dpr-2 arm, all
eight names already read 1.5px, shorthands included, so the join was reaching
the overridden longhand rather than the table's own shorthand entry. What moves
is that the table stops disagreeing with the engine it is the reference for.

After the fix all 22 fixture cases and all nine element cases are identical to
Chrome's, property for property.

## A shorthand has two serialisations, and the list only knew one (B69, 2026-08-30)

`animation` sat on `COMPUTED_JOIN_DECLINED` with a note: "a computed
`animation` reads `none` where the declared form spells all eight components".
The note is true of an element that declares nothing and false of one that
declares an animation, which is the case a page has — so the engine answered
the recorded initial `none` for every animated element on every page.

Nine declaration shapes, measured both ways on Chrome 151 headed
(`scratch/b69/expr-animation-shorthand.js`, `expr-animation-declared.js`):

| declared | computed reads | `el.style.animation` reads |
|---|---|---|
| *(nothing)* | `none` | — |
| `3s linear 1s infinite alternate both running ka` | `3s linear 1s infinite alternate both ka` | `…both running ka` |
| `2s ka` | `2s ka` | `2s ease 0s 1 normal none running ka` |
| `ka` | `ka` | — |
| `3s ka paused` | `3s paused ka` | `3s ease 0s 1 normal none paused ka` |
| `animation-duration: 4s` | `4s` | — |
| `ka 5s ease-in 2s 3 reverse forwards` | `5s ease-in 2s 3 reverse forwards ka` | — |

The two forms differ by exactly one rule: the computed one drops a slot holding
its initial value, the declared one writes all eight. `running` is dropped and
`paused` is kept, which is that same rule and not an exception, and an element
with every slot at its initial joins to nothing and falls through to the
recorded `none`. So the fix is a second `omit` table for the computed join
rather than a change to `chrome_shorthands`, which measured the declared form on
purpose.

**One slot in it is not the declared filler.** The table drops an unset duration
at `auto`; Chrome's *computed* `animation-duration` is `0s` — for an unset
duration, for a name-only longhand, and for an `auto` the page wrote itself
(three shapes, `scratch/b69/expr-anim-dur.js`). This engine's expansion writes
the declared filler into the longhand, so the longhand was reporting `auto`,
which no browser does, and the join printed it. Dropping `auto` in the join
would have hidden that; the longhand is mapped instead.

Eight of the nine shapes are now identical to Chrome's, property for property.
The ninth is the comma-separated case: this engine does not expand
`animation: 1s ka, 2s linear kb` at all, so `animationName` stays `none` where
Chrome reports `ka, kb` — the shorthand happens to read right because the stored
text is answered directly. `background` and `flex-flow` are still on the
declined list, each with a serialisation difference of its own that has not been
measured.

## Two more shorthands the declined list was wrong about (B69, 2026-08-30)

`flex-flow` sat on `COMPUTED_JOIN_DECLINED` beside `animation`, under a note of
the same shape — "a computed `flex-flow` keeps `nowrap` where the declared form
drops it" — and the same error: that describes an element declaring nothing, and
what a page has is an element that declares something. Eleven declaration shapes
on Chrome 151 headed (`scratch/b69/expr-flex-rules.js`):

| declared | `flex` | `flex-flow` |
|---|---|---|
| *(nothing)* | `0 1 auto` | `row nowrap` |
| `flex: 2 3 40px` | `2 3 40px` | `row nowrap` |
| `flex-grow: 7` | `7 1 auto` | `row nowrap` |
| `flex-basis: 30%` | `0 1 30%` | `row nowrap` |
| `flex: 1` | `1 1 0%` | `row nowrap` |
| `flex: none` | `0 0 auto` | `row nowrap` |
| `flex: auto` | `1 1 auto` | `row nowrap` |
| `flex-wrap: wrap` | `0 1 auto` | `row wrap` |
| `flex-direction: column` | `0 1 auto` | `column nowrap` |
| `flex-flow: column wrap` | `0 1 auto` | `column wrap` |
| `flex-flow: wrap` | `0 1 auto` | `row wrap` |

Both computed forms write every component, always. `-webkit-flex` and
`-webkit-flex-flow` mirror them exactly — both spellings name the same
unprefixed longhands in `chrome_shorthands`.

This engine answered `row nowrap` for `flex-flow` on every element, `0 1 auto`
for `-webkit-flex` on every element, and for `flex` it echoed the declared text
(`1`, `none`, `auto`) or the recorded initial when only a longhand was declared.
**All three longhands were already right in all eleven rows**, so a join is the
whole fix — `flex-flow` gets a computed omit list that drops nothing, and `flex`
gets a join of its own because it is `.unmodelled` in `chrome_shorthands` (no
distribution rule was ever measured for its declared form) and so the generic
join never reaches it.

### The suite is flaky right now, and it is not this change

Worth writing down because it cost half an hour of bisecting. On **unmodified
main**, `make test` failed 2 runs out of 4, on a different test each time —
`WebApi: Frames`, `WebApi: CORS response check`, and in a worktree
`WebApi: script async order`. All three are timing- or network-ordering tests,
none reproduces when run alone (`script async order` passed 4/4 in isolation on
the same tree that had just failed it in a full run), and the suite total itself
wobbles between 1570 and 1571 across runs of one tree. So a single red full-suite
run currently proves nothing; re-run it, and check the named test in isolation
before believing it.

## The last two the declined list held, and one Chrome quirk (B69, 2026-08-30)

**`background`.** The note on `COMPUTED_JOIN_DECLINED` is right about the shape
— the computed form puts the layer's colour first and writes every slot, where
the declared form `chrome_shorthands` measured drops the ones at their initial.
What it does not say is that the recorded initial it falls back to is only right
for an element with no background at all; every element that has one reads its
neighbour's answer. Measured on Chrome 151 headed, the order is colour, image,
repeat, attachment, position, `/`, size, origin, clip, and **all nine longhands
were already byte-identical to Chrome's**, so the join is the whole fix.

Multi-layer is left alone on purpose. Chrome joins the layers with `, ` and puts
the colour on the last one, and this engine's per-layer longhands are not ready:
a two-layer `background` leaves `background-size`, `-repeat`, `-attachment`,
`-origin` and `-clip` reading the literal `initial, initial` and the positions
unresolved as `left, right`. The join is taken only when
`background-repeat` has no comma in it — a keyword list with no quoting, so a
comma there is a second layer and nothing else — and a multi-layer element keeps
the old fallback rather than getting a confidently wrong string.

**`timeline-trigger`**, which is not a join at all. Chrome answers `none` on an
element that declares nothing and **the empty string** the moment anything in
the `animation-*` family is declared, whatever the declaration says. Twelve
shapes: `animation-name: none` computes to `none` and still flips it, an
`animation-duration`, `-delay`, `-timeline`, `-play-state`, `-composition` or
`-range-start` each flip it on their own, and `transition: color 2s` and
`opacity: 0.5` leave it alone. So it is the family and not "the element declares
anything". An explicitly declared trigger is reported either way.

That is a Chrome quirk with no spec story behind it, recorded as measured. It
matters here only because `JSON.stringify(getComputedStyle(el))` carries all 736
names and Cloudflare's widget encodes the whole string — and any page with a CSS
animation on the element is in the second row.

### Where the 736 stand

Against a headed Chrome on a fixture whose every box is pinned, the computed
style went 41 differences → 7 over the sessions that worked it, and this one
took it to **3**: `grid-row` and `grid-column` (two-value shorthands this engine
does not expand at all — `grid-area` does, they do not), and
`transform`/`webkitTransform`, which is the running keyframe and a feature
rather than a serialisation.

## `grid-area` expanded and its two siblings did not (B69, 2026-08-30)

The last serialisation difference on the 736-property table was `grid-row` and
`grid-column` reading `auto` on every element that declared one. It looked like
a missing join and it was not: `grid-area` **expands** here — B93 taught it the
grammar, including the rule an omitted `<grid-line>` follows — and its two-line
siblings expand not at all, so all four longhands stayed at `auto` and there was
nothing for a join to read.

Seventeen shapes on Chrome 151 headed, and the rule is `grid-area`'s with two
slots instead of four:

| declared | `grid-row` | start | end |
|---|---|---|---|
| `1 / 3` | `1 / 3` | `1` | `3` |
| `2` | `2` | `2` | `auto` |
| `3 / auto` | `3` | `3` | `auto` |
| `foo` | `foo` | `foo` | `foo` |
| `foo / foo` | `foo` | `foo` | `foo` |
| `foo / bar` | `foo / bar` | `foo` | `bar` |
| **`3 / 3`** | **`3 / 3`** | `3` | `3` |
| `span 2 / span 2` | `span 2 / span 2` | `span 2` | `span 2` |
| `grid-row-end: 4` | `auto / 4` | `auto` | `4` |

An omitted end copies the start when the start is a bare custom ident and is
`auto` otherwise; the join drops the end when it holds what an omitted one would
have held. Those two sentences are the same sentence, which is why `3 / 3` keeps
both halves and `foo / foo` does not — a number is not an ident, so its omitted
form would have been `auto`, and `3` is not `auto`. Only the end is ever
dropped, so `auto / 4` keeps both. The rule holds for longhands declared
directly too: `grid-row-start: foo; grid-row-end: foo` reads `foo`.

`shorthand.zig` already had `gridLineFallback` and `gridAreaJoin`, so this is
`isGridLinePair` plus a two-slot expand and join beside them, registered in the
five places `grid-area` is.

### The 736, end to end

Against a headed Chrome on a fixture whose every box is pinned:

```
  41  where the computed-style track started
   9  when this session picked it up
   4  after the width keywords, the animation and flex and background joins,
      and timeline-trigger
   2  now -- transform and -webkit-transform, which are the running keyframe
```

What is left is not a serialisation. `transform` reads `none` here and a live
matrix in Chrome because the animation is *running*: closing it needs a clock
and keyframe interpolation, which is a feature and has its own plan
(`animation-computed-transform`).

## The four short values are not a measurement of anything the page can see (B95, 2026-08-30)

The Cloudflare widget hands `TextEncoder.encode` four short numbers in a row and
hashes each one, and the third is the only place in the guard's plaintext where
this engine answers something Chrome does not: Chrome sends `0`, this engine
sends `16`. B94 read the values and ruled out three sources; this chapter closes
four more and says what the values are not.

The values, same epoch, both arms:

| | Chrome | this engine |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `5000.266115188599` | `4998.22265625` |
| 2 | `83.9800615310669` | `84` |
| 3 | **`0`** | **`16`** |
| 4 | `0.6387105289554597` | `0.639611171875` |

**They are not invariant, which is the correction B94 needs.** B94 read the same
four doubles in three consecutive runs and concluded from that identity that
they cannot be a timing measurement. The identity is real but it is bounded: an
hour later Chrome answered `5002.609375` / `87.97607231140137` / `0` /
`0.6387295662117005`, and then answered *that* set bit-identically in six more
runs across forty minutes. Two clusters, each internally exact. The instrument
is not what moved them -- B94's own knob, replayed in the later epoch, reports
the later set. This engine's four values did **not** move: the same Debug binary
gives `4998.22265625` / `84` / `16` / `0.639611171875` six hours apart.

**They are not timing, and this is a stronger test than B94's.** B94 burned
150ms per frame inside the widget's `requestAnimationFrame`. This saturated the
whole machine -- six spinning processes, load average from 7 to 11 -- and Chrome
answered the four values bit-identically. A quantity that survives that is not
measured with a clock.

**They are not any number the page hands out.** A knob wrapping every numeric
surface in the widget's realm -- `TextMetrics` (all twelve members), `DOMRect`,
`offset*` / `client*` / `scroll*`, `getBoundingClientRect`, `getComputedStyle`,
`performance.now`, `WebGLRenderingContext.getParameter` and
`getShaderPrecisionFormat`, the audio contexts, `screen`, `SVGGeometryElement`
`getTotalLength` / `getPointAtLength` / `getBBox`, `SVGTextContentElement`, and
twenty-one `Math` functions -- keeps every distinct value it sees and dumps the
set at the fourth encode. The four values are never in it. The pool's *size* at
that moment is 54 in one run and 2 in the next, which is the useful part: the
canvas and WebGL probes are not ordered before these encodes at all, so nothing
they produce can be an input.

**They are not the performance timeline.** The engine-side run-up log (below)
shows the guard reading `performance.mark`, `performance.getEntries` and then
every field of every entry immediately before the encodes, which made the
timeline the last surviving candidate. Dumping Chrome's timeline at exactly that
moment gives six entries -- navigation, visibility-state,
long-animation-frame, two paints, one resource -- and none of their fields is
any of the four values. Those fields also move run to run while the four values
do not.

### The run-up instrument

`Context` already answered "was this member reached, and when first"
(`prop_read`) and "what string did the page encode" (`text_encode`). Neither
answers the question those two raise together: what had the page just read when
it encoded *this*. A guard computing a number from a member it has already read
a hundred times has a `first_seq` far away, so the first-read order says nothing.

So `recentReads` keeps a ring of the members read, newest last, with runs of the
same member collapsed into one slot and a count -- without that collapse sixty
`appendChild` calls in a row fill the whole ring. `recordTextEncode` copies the
ring into any encode of 24 characters or less, and the dump quotes it as
`text encode run-up` lines counting back from the encode. Both scopes have to be
on, and the parser takes at most two `--log-filter-scopes` arguments, so they
share one: `--log-filter-scopes -all --log-filter-scopes +text_encode,+prop_read`.
Driver: `scratch/b95/runup-live.mjs`.

What it says about these four, from the widget realm's whole life: the guard
walks the performance timeline, then builds seventeen SVG elements in a
`<template>`, imports it, appends twenty-one children and removes it -- that is
the Turnstile checkbox drawing itself, not a probe -- and then, with **no
measuring call in between**, does `crypto.subtle` + `TextEncoder.encode` once per
value. The values are computed inside the VM well before they are hashed.

#### Re-confirmed B109, with the loophole closed

Everything above was measured before the persona pins and before the widget
stylesheet's unitless zeros were fixed, so it was re-run on `4911549bb` once the
residual account had closed: same four values, `4998.22265625` / `84` / `16` /
`0.639611171875`, and the same last six reads before every one of them --
`Window.window`, `Window.crypto`, `Window.window`, `Window.crypto`,
`Crypto.subtle`, `TextEncoder.encode`. Two runs agreed hash for hash, while the
oracle's four move between sittings (`5002.609375` in B104, `5000.266115188599`
in B109): **this engine's four are frozen and Chrome's are not.**

The reading above had one loophole: the run-up ring is filled by
`recordPropertyRead`, which only sees members this engine HAS, so "no measuring
call" could have meant "none this engine can see". `runup-live.mjs` now takes
`--scopes`, and the ring fills in any Debug build whether or not `prop_read` is
on, so the second scope is swappable. Run again with
`+text_encode,+unknown_prop`: the widget realm makes **149 unknown-member reads
and not one of them can produce a number** -- `console`, `chrome`,
`SharedArrayBuffer` and `CSS` ten times each (presence probes) and the guard's
own obfuscated globals (`runProgram`, `global`, `xVQL7`, …) twice each. So the
negative is "there is nothing there", not "we cannot see it".

One tempting lead, killed in the same sitting: this engine's first value is an
