exact multiple of 1/256 where B109's oracle value is a multiple of 1/2^20, which
reads like a coarser geometry quantisation -- but B104's oracle value
(`5002.609375`) is a multiple of 1/64, so the granularity is not a property of
the arm. Do not open a plan on it.

### Reading the guard's program, and why that is where this stops

`cf-knob.mjs` records every challenge response but slices the body to 4000
characters, which is exactly what destroys the one document that matters:
`.../new/normal`, ~269KB, carrying a ~247KB inline program. B94's attempt to
lift it from inside the page (chunked through the beacon array) reported nothing
at all. `scratch/b95/dump-normal.mjs` takes it off the wire instead --
`Network.enable`, `Network.getResponseBody` on every challenge request, each
body written whole -- and injects a knob in the same run so a stack read there
names offsets in the document that run saved. Identifiers and offsets are
per-delivery: three runs named the same helper `cA.cT`, `cU.cY` and `bv.bC`.

With the stack limit raised the chain under the encode is legible, and it is a
bytecode VM: one dispatcher (`bg`), a switch of two hundred opcode handlers
reached as `bv.<computed>.<computed> [as run]`, and host helpers like the `bC`
that calls `TextEncoder`. Every frame between the encode and the top is the
interpreter. The logic that computes the four values is in the bytecode, not in
the JavaScript, so reading it statically means writing a disassembler for this
VM -- a different plan, not a next step in this one.

### The byte transplant, and what it leaves standing (B110, 2026-09-04)

The disassembler was never needed, because the question it was going to answer
turned out not to be the question. By B108 six of the fifteen encoded strings
were byte-identical between the arms and **every remaining difference was in two
families** -- three pixel buffers (9216, 8624 x3, 4096) and the four short
computed values -- which are exactly the two families memory records as "not
weighed", from knobs that SUBTRACTED on Chrome. Both propositions could not
hold.

So the fifteen strings were made identical instead of explained. A knob wraps
`TextEncoder.prototype.encode`, keys each argument by `<utf16 length>:<djb2>`,
and encodes the oracle's captured string in its place -- substitution at the one
point where the plaintext is defined, which needs no rasteriser and no
disassembler. `scratch/b110/knobs-b110.mjs`, table in
`scratch/b110/oracle-segments.json`, both taken from the same-window capture in
`tools/fingerprint/scratch/b108/p3`.

Three things had to be proven before the reading counted, and each has its own
run:

* **The content changed.** Under a Debug binary with `+text_encode`
  (`scratch/b110/transplant-live.mjs`), this arm's fifteen segments come out as
  `69:mt6m58 9216:1ly97t5 1024:ard9mt 8624:1m3v0nt x3 30918:t3o0bu 4096:sq54p1
  17:1qum1nx 16:w2taxk 1:3t05 18:vc38ex 15361:3coxr6 x2 22972:1bqvk9l` -- the
  oracle's set, item for item. The engine's `utf16Djb2` was re-implemented in JS
  to compute those targets and checked against four values the engine had
  already printed before it was trusted.
* **The control is a control.** `oracle-bytes-passthru` wraps the same native,
  does the same table lookup, and then encodes the original: its fifteen
  segments are this engine's baseline, unchanged.
* **The knob runs where it matters.** It carries no beacon on purpose -- a
  report is either request-name bytes into the widget's origin (cf's one known
  lever) or an array on the realm's global (which the collector walks) -- so one
  separate run with `--knob oracle-bytes+alive --beacon` proves cf-knob's
  injection executes in `challenges.cloudflare.com/frame`. That run's r2 grew
  from ~4940B to 5026B, which is the pollution being avoided, and it is not in
  the tally.

**The tally: 0/11 served on the transplant arm, 0/11 on the passthru arm, all
twenty-two runs with three rounds away, and a same-window Chrome control taking
its ticket at the end of the series.** Making this engine's payload plaintext
byte-identical to a passing arm's does not move the verdict.

That resolves the fork the other way: neither of the two "not weighed" negatives
was wrong -- **the verdict is not made from the content of these fifteen strings
at all.** What is left standing is everything that is not that content: the
payload's envelope, the VM's execution rather than its output, edge-side session
state, and the one measured difference this never touched -- **r2, which is
4908-4951B here against 4738-4759B on the oracle, the same ~185 bytes recorded in
`cf-r3-is-not-short`.** Read it through fo-plaintext's console channel, never a
wire beacon: the beacon is what pushed r2 to 21751 the last time someone looked.

## Six digits, not six decimals — and the rotation was never exact (B69, 2026-08-30)

`transform` is the last of the 736 computed properties to disagree with Chrome,
and the disagreement everyone was looking at — a running animation's matrix —
turned out to sit on top of two older ones that had nothing to do with
animation.

### The printer

`writeNumber` printed `{d:.6}`: six DECIMAL places. Chrome prints `%g` with
precision 6: six SIGNIFICANT digits, exponent form and all. The two agree
between about 0.1 and 10, which is exactly where the original rule was read off
(`rotate(45deg)` is `0.707107` either way), and disagree everywhere else:

| declared | Chrome | this engine |
|---|---|---|
| `scale(0.000123456789)` | `0.000123457` | `0.000123` |
| `translate(1234567.89px)` | `1.23457e+06` | `1234570` |
| `scale(-0.0000001234)` | `-1.234e-07` | `0` |
| `rotate(1deg)` | `0.0174524` | `0.017452` |
| `scale(12345.6789012)` | `12345.7` | `12345.7` |

And there is no epsilon in it anywhere: a ladder from `scale(1e-6)` to
`scale(1e-17)` prints every rung, `1e-17` included.

### Which is why the right angles had to become exact

`rotate(90deg)` reads `matrix(0, 1, -1, 0, 0, 0)` in Chrome, and this engine's
`@cos` there is `6.123233995736766e-17` — six decimals had been hiding it, and
six significant digits would have printed it. Chrome is not clamping at print
time; it prints `1.74533e-09` for `rotate(89.9999999deg)`. So the rotation
itself is exact at multiples of a right angle, and `cosine`/`sine` in
`transform.zig` now say so, for all four spellings (`deg`, `turn`, `grad`,
`rad`).

### Two rows measured and deliberately not asserted

**Two 45s composing to a right angle.** Chrome gives an exact
`matrix(0, 1, -1, 0, 0, 0)`, this engine `2.22045e-16`. Not the rule above:
Chrome's cosine and sine at 45 degrees are the same double and this engine's
differ in the last bit (`0.7071067811865476` against `0.7071067811865475`), so
`c*c - s*s` cancels there and not here. Matching it means reproducing Blink's
trigonometry, not its serialisation.

**The declared value is already rounded before anything computes with it.**
`rotate(1.5707963267948966rad)` computes to an exact `matrix(0, 1, -1, 0, 0, 0)`
in Chrome and `-0.000004` here — and `el.style.transform` reads back
`rotate(1.5708rad)` on **both**. So Chrome rounds to six significant digits only
on the way out and keeps the full-precision number internally, while this
engine's declaration store keeps the rounded one and every computation
downstream reads it. Same for `rotate(89.9999999deg)`, whose stored angle
becomes exactly `90deg` here. That is a change to the number store rather than
to the transform code, and it is the third defect on `transform-number-format`.

### A note on reading red

`text_measure: plain text is not charged for the emoji table` fails on
**unmodified main** as well, and `WebApi: Window` / `Window scroll` come and go —
the machine was at load average 36 while several sessions ran Chrome. Same
condition the previous chapter records. Check the named test against main before
attributing it to a change.

## A preloaded sheet was fetched twice, on the station's own front page (B95, 2026-08-30)

`www.scrapingcourse.com` — the top document of cf-scrapingcourse — has the pair
every Vite build emits:

```html
<link rel="preload" as="style" href=".../app-DxJb4DfE.css" />
<link rel="stylesheet"          href=".../app-DxJb4DfE.css" />
```

Chrome files **one** resource entry for that pair. This engine filed two, with
different startTimes, so it asked the origin twice — measured on both arms
through `run-expr.mjs --url https://www.scrapingcourse.com/`, which otherwise
agreed URL for URL: fourteen distinct URLs on each arm, fourteen entries on
Chrome and fifteen here. A request count is the loudest kind of wire difference:
it does not need the guard to read a property, only the origin to count lines in
its log. The guard also walks the resource buffer entry by entry — the run-up
log has it reading `entryType`, `name`, `startTime`, `duration`, `transferSize`,
`encodedBodySize`, `nextHopProtocol` and `initiatorType` over every entry
moments before it hashes its four short values.

The dedup that already covered two `<link rel=stylesheet>`s did not cover this
pairing, and could not: `_stylesheet_bodies` holds *completed* bodies, and the
preload is asynchronous, so when the stylesheet link is parsed twenty
milliseconds later the bytes have not landed. The preload also went through
`requestSubresource`, which keeps a prefix and throws the body away.

Two changes, both in `Frame.zig`. A subresource fetched as a stylesheet now
keeps its bytes (bounded by `MAX_STYLESHEET_BYTES`, dropped past it) and files
them in `_stylesheet_bodies` on a 2xx. And `loadExternalStylesheet`, on a cache
miss, looks for an *open* slot for the same URL and waits for it instead of
opening a second one — the loop is `ScriptManager.waitForPreload`'s, evaluation
window marked so a `Target.closeTarget` arriving mid-pump cannot free the frame
this stack holds. Waiting is what Chrome does too: a render-blocking sheet holds
up the parser either way. A preload that fails or was never a stylesheet leaves
nothing behind and the fetch below runs as it always did.

After: fourteen entries on both arms, no duplicate. Regression test:
`preloaded_sheet_is_one_request` in `css/stylesheet_memory_cache.html`, which
also asserts the preload alone still reaches the wire — Chrome fetches `as=style`
and a fix that stopped preloading would pass the count and lose a request.

One trap the test hit first: its polling loop stopped as soon as *one* entry for
the sheet existed, and the synchronous stylesheet fetch always lands before the
asynchronous preload, so it counted one and passed against the unfixed engine.
It waits on a preload-only sheet now. A test that stops at the first sign of the
thing it is counting is not counting.

## A capability listed and never delivered: `long-animation-frame` (B95, 2026-08-30)

`PerformanceObserver.supportedEntryTypes` on this engine listed
`long-animation-frame`, the interface object
`PerformanceLongAnimationFrameTiming` was there with Chrome's exact member list
and order, and `performance.getEntriesByType('long-animation-frame')` answered
`[]` on every page. Chrome files one:

|  | startTime | duration | renderStart | paintTime | presentationTime | scripts |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| www.scrapingcourse.com | 3.5 | 1268.8 | 1264.3 | 1272.3 | 1296 | `[]` |
| the cf widget document | 87.0 | 746.4 | — | — | — | — |

The second row is the one that matters: that is the realm the
cf-scrapingcourse guard runs in, and the engine-side run-up log has it walking
`performance.getEntries()` and reading `entryType`, `name`, `startTime` and
`duration` off every entry moments before it hashes what it sends. A browser
that advertises the type and never produces one is separable by a single
expression, and "claims the capability, never delivers" is the same shape as
the broken-image reading two chapters up.

Nothing here renders, so the entry is pinned to milestones that did happen —
the bargain `PaintTiming` already makes in this file. The frame opens at
`responseStart`, where the bytes began arriving and the parser had work, and
closes at `domComplete`, where the load did; `renderStart` (and
`styleAndLayoutStart`, which Chrome reports as the same instant on a load frame)
is `domInteractive`, where the parser finished and a style pass would begin.
`paintTime` is the end of the frame, which is Chrome's own invariant read off
the entry above — `3.5 + 1268.8 = 1272.3` exactly. `firstUIEventTimestamp`,
`blockingDuration` and `scripts` are what Chrome answers for a load frame: 0, 0
and empty, so no script attribution is modelled.

It is filed only past Chrome's 50ms threshold, which is what makes it an entry
at all — a document that loads in single-digit milliseconds leaves Chrome's
buffer without one too, and that is why the regression test holds its own parser
for 120ms before asserting anything.

**Where it does not reach, measured rather than assumed.** The entry is filed
from navigation milestones, so it only describes the *parse* frame. Read back
out of each realm after the challenge settles
(`scratch/b95/widget-entries.mjs`, Runtime enabled only after the verdict), the
top document now carries `long-animation-frame:92+101` — the fix fires — and the
Cloudflare widget document carries none, because its whole navigation is 80ms
and 80 is under the threshold. Chrome's widget entry is `87.0 + 746.4`: it
brackets the *script* frame the guard runs in, which begins after that document
has loaded and which nothing here models. So the type now exists on a normal
page and still does not exist in the realm the guard reads. Closing that would
mean filing a frame for a long post-load task, which is a second model and a
second set of milestones to justify — not a tweak to this one.

### The second model: a frame that is a turn of the loop (B96, 2026-08-30)

The milestones came first, before the model. `scratch/b96/knob-widget-timeline.js`
is a cf-knob that beacons the widget document's own navigation entry back out of
the widget realm, and it says the widget's load is not slow at all:

| widget document, Chrome 151 | ms |
|---|---|
| `responseStart` | 65.96 |
| `responseEnd` | 79.10 |
| `domComplete` | 85.13 |
| `loadEventEnd` | 85.14 |
| `first-paint` | **779.68** |
| `long-animation-frame` | **89.70 + 686.61** |

So the entry is not derived from the load at all — the load is over in 85ms and
the frame starts 4ms *after* it. What it brackets is in the entry itself:
`scripts: [{ invoker: "DOMWindow.onmessage", invokerType: "event-listener",
startTime: 92.2, duration: 678.7 }]`. One message listener, 678ms of it, long
after the document finished loading. `renderStart` is 771.05 and the first paint
is 779.68, which is why the frame is 686ms long: it ends where the checkbox is
finally drawn.

**Does this engine have such a frame at all?** Not as one task. An instrumented
ReleaseFast build logging every scheduler callback over a live challenge
(`scratch/b96/task-lengths.mjs`) found 78 tasks past 5ms and the longest single
one at **51ms** — six `Worker.receiveMessage` callbacks of 48/41/25/10/51/46ms
where Chrome has one listener of 678. Filing per *task* would have filed
nothing, or one entry by a millisecond. This engine is not blocked the way
Chrome is here; it is faster, and the pre-existing reading that the widget
settles four times sooner says the same thing.

What it does have is the turn of the loop. `Env.runMacrotasks` enters one realm
and drains that realm's queue with nothing scheduled in between, which is the
closest thing here to the interval Chrome calls a frame. Timing that instead,
over the same live challenge, the widget realm ran **two** turns past 50ms —
104ms and 83ms — and the top document ran none (its longest was 19ms). So the
model files where Chrome files and stays quiet where Chrome is quiet, without
anything invented: `startTime` and `duration` are a clock read either side of
the drain, `renderStart`, `paintTime` and `presentationTime` are all the end of
it, because nothing renders and a render pass would begin and end there.

After, read back out of the widget realm with the same
`scratch/b95/widget-entries.mjs` discipline:

| realm | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| top document | `long-animation-frame:114+124` | `long-animation-frame:114+124` |
| widget document | *(none)* | **`long-animation-frame:676+139`** |

The entry type now exists in the realm the guard walks `getEntries()` in. How
many is not fixed — the instrumented run above had two turns past the threshold
and this one filed one — and either way it is shorter than Chrome's single long
frame, because this engine really did do that work in less time. What did not
happen is a ticket.

After, on www.scrapingcourse.com: one entry on each arm, same key order, same
invariants (`paintTime === startTime + duration`, `presentationTime >=
paintTime`, `renderStart` inside the frame, no `scripts`). One honest
difference remains: Chrome's `presentationTime` sits about 23ms past its
`paintTime` — a compositor delay — and this engine's equals it, because
`loadEventEnd` and `domComplete` coincide when nothing presents. Inventing a
delay would be inventing a constant; the paint pair in this engine already
reports `presentationTime === startTime` for the same reason.

## The keyframes were in the document, just not in the cascade (B70, 2026-08-30)

`transform` was the last of the 475 enumerated computed properties to disagree
with Chrome outside the column-rule family. Chrome reports an interpolated
matrix for an animated element; this engine reported `none` — for everything,
including the shapes that have no clock in them at all.

### Why nothing could have resolved it

`StyleManager.parseSheet` skipped `@keyframes` outright, and the comment saying
so was right about the reason: a keyframes rule declares nothing on any element,
so it takes no part in the cascade. The consequence was the part nobody had
followed through. `animation-name` resolves to a rule *by name*, and with no
index there was no name resolution anywhere on the computed-style path — the
rules existed only as CSSOM objects, reachable from `document.styleSheets` and
from nowhere else.

The index now lives beside the cascade rather than inside it, rebuilt with the
rules and fed from all three places a rule arrives: a materialised CSSOM sheet
(off `rule._text`, the way `@media` already was), a `<style>` element's text,
and nested inside `@media` or `@layer`. Going through `document.styleSheets`
from the computed path was the alternative and was not taken: that read
materialises the CSSOM, which is a side effect a style read should not have.

### The clock is held, not read

The first working version read `performance.now()` per property. That is wrong
in a way worth writing down, because it is a tell the old `none` did not have:

| | Chrome 151 | live clock | held clock |
|---|---|---|---|
| read `transform`, burn 250ms, read again | same matrix | **two matrices** | same matrix |
| 10s linear rotation, degrees turned over that burn | 0 | **5.3** | 0 |

A browser sets the document timeline once per rendering frame, and every style
resolution inside that frame sees the same instant. An animation that advances
between two reads of one synchronous script is something no browser does. The
timeline is now sampled once and held on the `Frame`, released where this
engine's `requestAnimationFrame` callbacks run — the timer dispatch, which is
the closest thing it has to a frame boundary.

### Interpolation is per function, not per matrix

`rotate(0deg)` to `rotate(90deg)` halfway is `rotate(45deg)`, not the average of
the two matrices, so the scalars have to survive the parse — `parseFunction`
split into `parseArgs` plus `matrixFor`, and a `ListIterator` both readers
share. A `none` on one side is not a shape mismatch: it stands for the other
side's functions holding their neutral values, which is what makes the common
one-ended `@keyframes spin { 100% { transform: rotate(360deg) } }` interpolate
from zero instead of refusing. Lists of genuinely different shapes — including
`scale(2)` against `scale(2, 3)`, the same transform written two ways — fall to
matrix decomposition in Chrome and are refused here, reporting the interval's
start, which is a value the animation really passes through.

### Twenty-six shapes, all byte-identical

Nine static phases (`scratch/b69/expr-anim-static.js`), thirteen more for the
webkit spellings, `@keyframes` inside `@media`, duplicate names and the
fill/direction corners (`scratch/b70/expr-anim-extra.js`), and four for the
animation declared in a stylesheet rule rather than a style attribute
(`scratch/b70/expr-anim-sheet.js`). Every one identical between headed Chrome
151 and this engine.

One of the thirteen contradicted the guess it was written to confirm.
`animation: 0s linear 0s 2 alternate forwards` on a 0→100px translate reads
`matrix(1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0)`, not `100`: a forwards fill shows the end of the
*last iteration*, and under `alternate` iteration 1 runs backwards, so an even
count finishes where the animation started. The implementation already did
this; the expectation written beside it did not.

The one remaining difference on the 475-name sweep is `transform` itself, and it
cannot be closed: both arms answer a pure rotation matrix with no translation,
sampled at two different instants.

### It did not open anything, and it did not close anything either

cf-scrapingcourse, three runs on the merged ReleaseFast binary: `served=false`
3/3, `r3` still 88–90KB. Consistent with the earlier finding that this station
does not judge collected values.

The full sweep read **19/29** against 22/29 on the two before it, and all three
of the missing stations were DataDome — `dd-datadome`, `dd-leboncoin`,
`dd-hermes`. That is exactly the shape a change-caused regression would have,
and it is not one. Alternating the pre-merge binary (`126dbb122`) against the
merged one (`1d80f94be`) station by station inside one sitting — three rounds,
eighteen runs, alternating arm by arm — **every single run is refused, on both
arms, on all three stations** (`scratch/b70/ab-dd.sh`, log in
`scratch/b70/ab/`). The window closed; the binary did not change. A block of
runs from one arm followed by a block from the other would have said the
opposite, which is the whole reason the arms alternate.

### And the guard's own input is unchanged by it

The sweep is a coarse instrument for this. The fine one is the encoder channel:
`JSON.stringify(getComputedStyle(el))` is one of the fifteen things the widget
encodes, and it is the largest surface any guard in this file reads. Three
readings on the live station, all in one sitting:

| arm | computed-style segment |
|---|---|
| headed Chrome 151 (`report-encodes`, `served=true`) | `len=30918 h=t3o0bu` |
| this engine, merged (`1d80f94be`) | `len=30918 h=t3o0bu` |
| this engine, pre-merge (`126dbb122`) | **`len=30918 h=t3o0bu`** |

Byte-identical to Chrome — and byte-identical **before** the change as well. The
element the widget stringifies is not animated, so its `transform` read `none`
on both arms either way, and this fix does not touch what the guard is handed.
The segment was closed by the computed-style work of the sessions before this
one; B69 measured it at `30902 15ewidm` and it has been Chrome's since some
point between then and `126dbb122`.

Which is the honest shape of the result. Of the nine things the widget encodes,
five are now byte-identical (the widget's own CSS rules, the font probe list,
the two `0|0|0|…` buffers, `readPixels`, and this one). The four that are not
are the three larger pixel buffers — measured not weighed — and the four short
values, which B95 showed are computed inside the guard's bytecode VM rather than
collected from the page at all. There is nothing left on this channel to fix.

## An `about:blank` iframe answers with the viewport, and three things that follow (B70, 2026-08-30)

A probe written for the animation work threw `Cannot read properties of null`
on this engine and not on Chrome: `document.head` is null on the top-level
`about:blank` that `run-expr.mjs` defaults to. Chasing that one line found a
seam nobody had pointed an instrument at, because `about:blank` is not a page
anyone writes — it is the document a guard MAKES, and cf-knob's own
scripted-target list names `page:about:blank`.

The document structure turned out to be fine. Eighteen readings across a
src-less iframe, an explicit `about:blank` iframe and a written-into one agree
on `documentElement`, `head`, `body`, `outerHTML`, `compatMode`, `contentType`,
`characterSet`, `baseURI` and the element count. What did not agree was the
BOXES, and every difference reproduces on a served document with both arms at
`readyState: complete`, so none of it is the `document.write` path
(`scratch/b70/qc/`, eight documents; `scratch/b70/expr-qc-served.js`).

### The rule that swaps with the document's mode

CSSOM View:

> If the element is the root element and the document is **not** in quirks mode,
> or if the element is the HTML body element and the document **is** in quirks
> mode, return the viewport width/height excluding scrollbars.

An `about:blank` document has no doctype, so it is always quirks — and the body
half of that rule was not implemented. In a 300x150 iframe Chrome answers
`body.clientWidth` 300 and this engine answered 284, while
`getComputedStyle(body).width`, `offsetWidth` and `getBoundingClientRect().width`
are 284 **on both arms**. One reading out of four disagreeing is what says it is
the rule and not the layout.

Chrome answers the viewport through everything the body's own box can be:

| body | Chrome `clientWidth` | this engine, before |
|---|---|---|
| bare | 400 | 384 |
| `margin:8px` | 400 | 384 |
| `margin:8px;border:5px solid` | 400 | 384 |
| `margin:8px;width:100px` | 400 | 100 |
| `margin:8px;padding:20px` | 400 | 424 |
| `margin:8px;display:inline` | 400 | 0 |

so the rule is asked before any of the box is measured. It is asked only on
`getClientWidth`/`getClientHeight`, never on `getClientWidthWithCache` —
`offsetWidth` and the resolved computed `width` are built off that one and
Chrome keeps both on the body's real box, which is the whole point of the
divergence.

### `clientTop` and `clientLeft` were a hard-coded zero

The comment said the layout does not apply borders. That had stopped being true:
`borderPx` reads the UA sheet as well as the author cascade, and `offsetWidth`
and `getBoundingClientRect` have carried the border for a while. These two
accessors were what was left behind, and a page sees it in one read — fifteen
shapes measured (`scratch/b70/expr-client-tl.js`), every bordered one wrong.

Each reads its OWN edge: `border-top:6px` alone is `6,0` and `border-left:9px`
alone `0,9`, so neither is half of the `border_x`/`border_y` pair the box model
carries. `display:none` and a non-replaced `display:inline` answer 0 even with a
border declared, while `display:table` answers the border — the test is whether
there is a border box, not which keyword made it.

### A fraction where the IDL says `long`

`getScrollWidth` rounds on its ordinary path and returned `dims.width` straight
for the two root tags, so a `<body>` or `<html>` with a fractional box answered
things like `100.3984375` and `1985.1484375`. `scrollWidth` and `scrollHeight`
are `long` in the IDL: that is not a wrong number, it is an impossible one, and
`Number.isInteger(document.body.scrollWidth)` is a one-expression tell that no
value-matching exercise would ever have produced.

### An existing test was asserting an inference

`frames/iframe_root_box.html` asserted `d.body.clientWidth === 284` under a
comment reading "clientWidth/clientHeight read the same box, so a script that
measures one against the other does not see two different documents." The
citation at the top of that file — headless Chrome 151, `body 284x134` — is
correct and unchanged; it is the computed width. The `clientWidth` line was the
comment's reasoning written down as a measurement. Re-measured on headless
**and** headed Chrome: same body, `width: 284px` and `clientWidth: 300`. They
are meant to differ.

### Two more measured, and deliberately not touched

* **The used border width snaps to the wrong grid.** Chrome snaps to DEVICE
  pixels — at dpr 2, half a CSS pixel — with a floor of one device pixel for a
  non-zero border. `border-width:0.4px` computes to `0.5px` there and `1px`
  here; `3.6px` to `3.5px` there and `3px` here. `offsetWidth` and the bounding
  rect move with it (`0.4px` reads 101 against 102). It decides two of the
  fifteen `clientTop` shapes, which are the two that file does not assert.
* **A bordered root element.** Chrome makes the root's BORDER box the viewport
  and insets the content: a 7px-bordered `<html>` in a 400x200 frame reads
  client 386x186 and offset 400x200. This engine reads client 400x200 and offset
  414x214, adding the border outside the viewport. Same for the top-level body's
  offset box, which Chrome reports as `innerWidth-16` for `margin:8px` and this
  engine reports as the whole viewport — though it gets that case right inside
  an iframe.

Neither is a door: the station work in the chapters above closed the
capability-presence and collected-value levers on cf-scrapingcourse from both
directions. They are named, reproducible, off-site-testable defects on a surface
every guard in this file measures, obtained from a corner nothing had looked at.

### The same corner has a hang in it

Fixing the boxes left four differences on the `about:blank` probe, two of them
the harness (the arms do not share a viewport, so the top document's body and
root numbers are not comparable). The other two are on
`document.open()`/`write`/`close()` — the idiom a guard uses to build itself a
realm — and pulling on them gave six, every one of them spec'd
(`scratch/b70/expr-doc-open.js`, eleven readings, five already identical):

| | Chrome 151 | this engine |
|---|---|---|
| `document.URL` after `open()` | the ENTRY document's URL | `about:blank` |
| ...after `write` | same | `about:blank` |
| ...after `close()` | same | `about:blank` |
| `readyState` after `close()` | `complete` | **`loading`, permanently** |
| iframe `load` fires on `close()` | **1, synchronously** | **0** |
| `document.URL` seen by a script written in | the entry document's URL | `about:blank` |

The third row is the interesting one and it is not a value difference at all.
A guard that writes `iframe.onload = …; doc.write(…); doc.close()` never gets
its callback here. That is the shape of the defect that held ak-macys shut for
six sessions — `decodeAudioData` returning a promise that never settled — and it
is a different KIND of finding from everything the last twenty chapters have
been grinding on, all of which asked whether a number matched.

Filed as `doc-open-into-blank-iframe`, ordered so the hang is closed first.

## scrollWidth counted a stack as a row (B96, 2026-08-30)

`Element.contentWidth` laid every visible in-flow child end to end and added
their widths up, whatever the layout mode. Three 400px block children in a 400px
box therefore answered `scrollWidth: 1200` where Chrome answers 400, and so did
every other arrangement that stacks.

Two things had to be checked before touching it, because the summing had a
stated reason. The first was whether the layout mode could be seen at all: the
comment said no, and it was written before `CSSStyleDeclaration.resolvedDisplay`
existed. It can now.

The second was the reason itself — a page that appends children until
`scrollWidth` passes a threshold, the infinite-marquee idiom, never terminating
if the metric ignores what was just inserted. That one was measured rather than
reasoned about (`probes/expr-b96-scroll-width.js`, Chrome 151 at the persona's
dpr=2, on a real https page with `box-sizing` pinned per box so the page's own
Tailwind reset could not answer for it):

* with **block** children Chrome's loop does not terminate either — fifty
  appends of a 100px div into a 200px box and `scrollWidth` is still 200. The
  summing was defending a shape no page can be written in.
* with the **inline-block strip under `white-space: nowrap`** a marquee actually
  uses, Chrome sums: three appends and `scrollWidth` is 300. That is the case to
  keep, and both engines already agreed on it.

### What names a row

| arrangement (200px parent, three 400px children) | Chrome | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| three block children | 400 | 1200 | 400 |
| ...in a padded box | 410 | 1210 | 410 |
| `white-space: nowrap` + inline-blocks | 1200 | 1200 | 1200 |
| `white-space: pre` + inline-blocks | 1200 | 1200 | 1200 |
| the other four white-space values | 400 | 1200 | 400 |
| `nowrap` + BLOCK children | 400 | 1200 | 400 |
| `nowrap` + one block among inline-blocks | 400 | 1200 | 400 |
| `display: flex` | 1200 | 1200 | 1200 |
| `flex-wrap: wrap` | 400 | 1200 | 400 |
| `flex-direction: column` | 400 | 1200 | 400 |
| `flex-direction: row-reverse` | **200** | 1200 | 200 |
| `display: grid` | 400 | 1200 | 400 |
| `grid-auto-flow: column` (and `column dense`) | 1200 | 1200 | 1200 |
| three floats too wide to share a line | 400 | 1200 | 400 |
| three narrow floats that do share one | 200 | 200 | 200 |

`row-reverse` is the row that contributes nothing: its items overflow off the
LEFT edge, where `scrollWidth` cannot reach.

Two of the branches are asked rather than re-derived. `wrapsText` already
answers "does a line too long for its box break", and it has to be the one
asked: `white-space` is a *shorthand*, so a cascade read under that name finds
nothing at all — the first version of this read it directly, got `null` for every
element, and stacked the marquee strip that should have summed.

### The case that a green filter would have missed

The first version also stacked a wrapping block container outright, and the full
suite caught it as a 30-second watchdog stall in
`src/browser/tests/element/position.html` — a test whose loop doubles its markup
until `scrollWidth` passes twice the track. Chrome terminates that loop on the
seventh doubling (7280 there, 7168 here, asserted step for step), because the
lane's content is `<span>item</span>` repeated with no whitespace between the
spans: one unbreakable run, which overflows rather than wrapping.

So where a line may break is the distinction, not inline-level versus block:
adjacent `inline-block` children are each a break opportunity and wrap, adjacent
inline BOXES with nothing between them are one run and overflow. `.inline_row`
(under `nowrap`) asks for inline-level children; `.unbreakable_run` (a wrapping
block container) asks for inline boxes.

Reading the whole probe back afterwards, **30 of the 32 rows are byte-identical
to Chrome**, up from 14. The two that are not are named rather than folded in:

* `absolute3` — three absolutely positioned children at `left: 0/400/800` answer
  1200 in Chrome and 200 here. `Extent.counts` excludes `.positioned` from both
  extents deliberately, and changing it moves `scrollHeight` too.
* `bodyScrollWidth` — 1920 in Chrome, 1904 here. `<body>` takes its own exit
  above this code.

1583/1583, and the sweep is 22/29 with **no station changed** against the
session's baseline — including dd-datadome and dd-hermes, which an earlier sweep
in this session had shown falling. That fall was DataDome's window, not a
regression: alternating the two arms three rounds each on those two stations
while it was shut, the BASELINE binary passed 1 of 6 and the patched one 0 of 6,
and both were back by the time of this sweep.

## The close that ended nothing, and the document that did not know where it was (B71, 2026-08-30)

B70 filed three divergences in the `document.open()` / `write` / `close()` path
and ordered the hang first. All three are closed. Eleven readings
(`scratch/b70/expr-doc-open.js`, headed Chrome 151 against a ReleaseFast build
of this engine, both arms on the same served page) went from five agreeing to
**eleven agreeing, byte for byte**.

### One early return held all three

`close()` did finish the streaming parser. What it could not do was tell the
frame, because `Frame.documentIsComplete` opens with

```zig
if (self._load_state == .complete) return;
```

and a script-created `about:blank` iframe is `.complete` from the moment it is
created — it has nothing to load. So the completion path was skipped whole:
`readyState` stayed at `loading` forever, no `readystatechange` and no
`DOMContentLoaded` fired, and the frame's `load` event never reached the iframe
element.

That last one is the one that costs a page. The standard way to build yourself
a realm is

```js
iframe.onload = () => { /* the realm is ready */ };
doc.write(...);
doc.close();
```

and the callback on the first line is the only thing the third line could ever
call. It is the same shape as `decodeAudioData` returning a promise that never
settled — the finding that eventually opened ak-macys — and not a value that
failed to match.

The fix is one state: `open()` puts the frame back into `.parsing`, which is
honest, since it is parsing again. Everything downstream then runs for the
second time, in the order Chrome was measured reporting it:

| | Chrome 151 | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| trace, listeners attached after `open()` | `rsc=interactive \| DCL \| rsc=complete` | *(empty)* | `rsc=interactive \| DCL \| rsc=complete` |
| `readyState` after `close()` | `complete` | `loading` | `complete` |
| iframe `load` fired | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| second `close()` | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| two open/write/close cycles | 2 | 0 | 2 |
| window events after `close()` | `doc:DCL \| win:load \| win:pageshow` | *(empty)* | `doc:DCL \| win:load \| win:pageshow` |

A frame that already reported in to its parent has to be allowed to report
again — this parse fires its own load event — but it delays nothing, because the
parent's own load is long over. Both of those are one line each next to the
state change.

One companion was needed. `.parsing` is also the state that means "an inline
script is writing into the document currently being parsed", where a write is
spliced in after the script element instead of streamed. A script-created parser
always streams, so `writeInternal` now says that outright rather than inferring
it from the frame not being in `.parsing`.

### The bridge cannot tell you who is calling

HTML's document open steps set the document's URL to the **entry** document's —
the URL of the document whose script called `open()`, not the one the frame was
loaded from. So a page that writes into its own `about:blank` iframe leaves that
iframe claiming the page's address, on `document.URL`, `document.documentURI`
and `location.href` alike, including to a script written into the document. Ours
said `about:blank` on all three: the realm a guard builds this way was asked
where it is, and answered nowhere.

The first attempt did nothing, and the reason is worth writing down. A bound
method's `*Frame` argument is the **receiver's** frame, not the caller's — for
`iframeDoc.open()` that is the iframe's own frame, which is exactly the
`about:blank` we were trying to replace. An instrumented run said so in one
line: `differ = false, call_url = about:blank`. V8's incumbent context is the
one that knows who is running, and `postMessage` was already using it to name
its `source` window.

The base URL is not part of this and does not move: an `about:blank` child
already inherited its creator's base URL, so relative links in the written
markup already resolved against the parent. A test pins that they still do.

### The referrer, which was not in the plan

Attributing `document.referrer` in the same corner turned up a separate,
pre-existing gap: an `about:blank` iframe reported the empty string, which is
what a document reached by typing its address reports. Chrome reports the
creating document's URL, with or without an explicit `src="about:blank"`.
`about:srcdoc` was measured empty on both arms and stays empty; the
`window.open` case has no reading, because headless Chrome blocks the popup.
`Frame._referrer` feeds `document.referrer` and nothing else, so this moves one
reading and no traffic.

### What is still different, measured

The probe written to check the fix caught something the plan had not named. In
Chrome, listeners registered on the document **before** an implicit `open()` are
gone afterwards; ours survive and fire. HTML's open steps have an explicit
"remove all event listeners registered on document, its Window object, and all
its descendant elements" — and Chrome does all three, plus nulling the
`onXXX` slots:

| dispatch a plain event before / after `open()` | Chrome 151 | this engine |
|---|---|---|
| listener on the document | 1 / 1 | 1 / 2 |
| listener on the window | 1 / 1 | 1 / 2 |
| listener on a descendant element, held by reference | 1 / 1 | 1 / 2 |
| `doc.onclick` after `open()` | `null` | `function` |

This is a behavioural tell, not a value: a guard that hangs a
`readystatechange` handler on the document and then writes into it hears from
us and not from Chrome. Filed as `doc-open-removes-listeners`.

### The door did not move

Two full sweeps back to back on the same route, same build mode, the only
difference being the binary (`results/b71-sweep-base.json`,
`results/b71-sweep-fixed.json`): 19/29 before, 20/29 after, and the one station
that moved was `dd-datadome`. Alternating the two binaries at that station
alone, three rounds each, says what that is worth:

| round | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | challenge | **pass** |
| 2 | challenge | challenge |
| 3 | challenge | challenge |

One pass in four, and DataDome is the family already known to open and close in
windows — B70 spent a three-round alternation proving three DataDome stations
were rejecting BOTH arms at the time. So: 19/29, unchanged.
`cf-scrapingcourse` is still `cf-challenge` and `x-hyatt` is still
`refused-429` in both columns. Three hangs and a wrong address are closed
because they were wrong, not because a guard has admitted anything.

## open() throws the document away, and Chrome throws the listeners away with it (B71, 2026-08-30)

The probe written to check B71's `close()` fix caught something the plan had
not named, which is the only reason it was found: the trace of a written
document showed OUR document's `readystatechange` and `DOMContentLoaded`
listeners firing where Chrome's showed nothing at all. The listeners had been
registered before the implicit `open()`, and Chrome had already removed them.

HTML's document open steps, before anything is parsed:

> Remove all event listeners registered on document, its Window object, and all
> its descendant elements.

We removed none of them. The measurement turns on nothing but the listener
store — register a listener, dispatch a self-made event at it, call `open()`,
dispatch the same event again:

| dispatch before / after `open()` | Chrome 151 | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| listener on the document | 1 / 1 | 1 / 2 | 1 / 1 |
| listener on the window | 1 / 1 | 1 / 2 | 1 / 1 |
| listener on a descendant element, held by reference | 1 / 1 | 1 / 2 | 1 / 1 |
| `doc.onclick` / `win.onresize` / `body.onclick` after `open()` | `null` ×3 | `function` ×3 | `null` ×3 |

The `on*` slots are the same store from the DOM's point of view and Chrome
clears them too, so the removal covers both: `EventManagerBase.lookup` for the
`addEventListener` listeners and `attr_listeners` for the handler functions.

Both stores are keyed by target, so the removal takes a **set** of targets and
walks each store once, rather than walking the stores once per target — a
`document.open()` on a real page would otherwise be quadratic in the node
count. The handler store's matching entries are collected before any of them is
removed, since removing mid-iteration from a hash map is not safe.

What is deliberately NOT in the set is the iframe **element**. Its listeners
live in the parent document, and it is the one the whole idiom is built around:
`iframe.onload = ...; doc.write(...); doc.close()`. A test pins that the load
event still arrives.

### The two stations that moved, and did not

The sweep read 18/29 against 20/29 for the binary without this change, and the
two stations that differed were `dd-datadome` and `px-wayfair`. Alternating the
two binaries at `px-wayfair`, three rounds each, both arms answered
`px-challenge` every time; `dd-datadome` is the station the previous chapter
already showed passing one round in four with the guard's window half shut.
Neither difference is the binary. Both closed doors are where they were.

## matchMedia compared the serialisation, not the query (B96, 2026-08-30)

`window.matchMedia(q)` stores the *canonical* form of `q` — that is what `.media`
reports, and it is right that it does. `matches` then read that stored text
back. The canonical form writes every number to six significant figures, so
every threshold was rounded to six figures before it was ever compared.

x-hyatt's Kasada script reads `devicePixelRatio` eight times and then spends
**314 `(min|max)-resolution: …)` queries binary-searching the same number to
twenty bits**, reading only `.matches` and never `.media`. Its rungs pass the
sixth figure within a dozen steps, and from there on every one of them was being
answered against `2.00000`.

### Where each arm changes its mind

Bisected on both arms rather than sampled, at the persona's dpr=2, on a real
page (`probes/expr-b96-resolution-boundary.js` — it halves the interval the way
the guard does and reports the last matching double):

| crossover | Chrome 151 | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| `min-resolution` dppx | `2.0000001192092896` | `2.000005` | `2.0000001192092896` |
| `min-resolution` dpi | `192.00001144409183` | `192.0005` | `192.00001144409183` |
| `min-width` px | `1920.015625` | `1920.0049438476562` | `1920.015625` |
| `(min-resolution: 75.59055118110236dpcm)` | true | **false** | true |
| the same ratio in dppx, dpi, dpcm | `true,true,true` | `true,true,**false**` | `true,true,true` |

Three findings fell out of the bisection, each measured at two settings before
it went into the engine:

* **A `<resolution>` is a float32.** Chrome's crossover sits exactly where a
  double rounds to the next float — `1 + 2^-23` at dpr 1, `2 + 2^-23` at dpr 2,
  in dppx and in dpi both. Nothing else lands on that number.
* **The unit conversion multiplies by the factor, it does not divide by its
  reciprocal.** Chrome's dpi crossover is `192 + 192 · 2^-24`, and only
  `value * (1/96)` carries that double to exactly `2 + 2^-23`; `value / 96`
  lands one ulp above and answers false where Chrome answers true. A one-ulp
  detail, and it is the difference between matching the boundary and missing it
  by one rung of a twenty-bit search.
* **A `<length>` bound tolerates one 1/64 px unit.** The last matching
  `(min-width: …)` is exactly `innerWidth + 1/64` and the next double does not
  match — at 1920 and at 813, on both axes, and the plain `(width: …)` form
  takes a unit on either side. So the bound is NOT rounded to a float32 either:
  an f32 at 1920 steps by 1/8192 and could not tell those two doubles apart.

Reading the whole probe back afterwards, **40 of its 42 rows are identical to
Chrome**. The two that are not are both `dpcm` crossovers, and they are left
alone deliberately: Chrome's tie there is ±0.005 dppx — five hundred times
ours, the same width at dpr 1 and dpr 2, and not explained by float32, by the
factor, or by the conversion order. Modelling a rounding nobody can account for
would be inventing a constant, so it is recorded instead: `dpcm` is the one
spelling where the two arms still part company, at the fourth significant
figure.

1583/1583.

### The sweep reading, and one thing in it that is not about this change

The sweep came back 21/29 against 22/29, and all three stations that moved are
ones that move on their own: dd-datadome and dd-hermes flipped back to
`datadome-challenge` (they had flipped the other way an hour earlier on an
unchanged binary, and an alternating A/B in the shut window had the BASELINE
passing 1 of 6), and **x-hyatt passed** -- the first time in this file's history.

That last one was chased rather than claimed. `kasada-verdict.mjs` reads
`x-kpsdk-r` off the `/tl` POST, which is the guard's own answer in about ten
seconds instead of the station's pass/refuse at the end of a chain. Twenty-five
alternating pairs, two designs:

| design | base | patched |
|---|---|---|
| base first (15 pairs) | **3 tickets** (`1-B1NUBHs`, `1-B1JbVXI`, `1-B1EFfHU`) | 0 |
| patched first (10 pairs) | 0 | 0 |

Every ticket of the three went to the arm that visited FIRST in its pair, and no
ticket at all was issued during the ten pairs where the patched arm led. So the
open window is what the first design measured, not the binary, and the second
design ran entirely inside a shut one. **No arm-level conclusion is available**
— this change is not shown to cost a ticket and is not shown to win one.

What IS new and belongs to nobody's change: **this engine now gets an x-hyatt
ticket sometimes.** B53 measured 0/3 there and the door map has said "real door,
reference passes and we do not" ever since. Three `x-kpsdk-r: 1-B1…` responses
in one sitting, with `doc=429->200` beside them, say the rate is no longer zero.
Worth re-running the reverse-biased design the next time the window is open.

## The body box did not follow its own margin (B96, 2026-08-30)

`<body>`'s box was the viewport less a hardcoded 16px — the UA stylesheet's
`body { margin: 8px }`, doubled — whatever the page said its margin was. Every
modern page says something else: a Tailwind-style reset opens with
`body { margin: 0 }`, and on www.scrapingcourse.com that put Chrome's body at
1920 against this engine's 1904.

The sixteen pixels are not the interesting part. `getComputedStyle(body).marginLeft`
answered `0px` on both arms — correctly, from the cascade — right next to a box
that had subtracted 8px twice anyway. **A box that does not follow the margin
beside it is a shape no browser produces**, and it is one expression to check:
`body.clientWidth + 2 * parseFloat(getComputedStyle(body).marginLeft) === documentElement.clientWidth`.

Measured on Chrome 151 in one document, setting the margin inline and reading
back (`probes/expr-b96-body-margin.js`), `documentElement.clientWidth -
body.clientWidth`:

| body margin | Chrome | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| as found (`margin: 0` from the page's reset) | 0 | 16 | 0 |
| `0px` | 0 | 16 | 0 |
| `3px` | 6 | 16 | 6 |
| `8px` | 16 | 16 | 16 |
| `20px` | 40 | 16 | 40 |

Twice the margin, every time, and this engine answered 16 for all five.

The fix reads the margin the cascade already holds. The UA's 8px has not gone
anywhere — it is *in* that cascade, which is where `getComputedStyle` was
reading it all along; the box just stopped being the one place with its own copy.
The one wrinkle is that `marginPx` answers 0 for a margin nobody declared, which
is right for an ordinary element and wrong for the one tag whose UA margin is
load-bearing, so `<body>` falls through to the UA sheet in the same order the
computed style resolves in.

Reading the whole body-box probe back: **12 of its 13 rows are Chrome's**, up
from 6. The one left is `box-sizing`, which Chrome computes as `border-box` on
that page and this engine as `content-box` — the reset declares it through
`*, ::before, ::after`, and that is a selector question rather than a box one.
Filed separately.

The sweep read 19/29 against 21/29, and both stations that moved are the ones
that have been moving all evening on unchanged binaries: `dd-leboncoin`, which
an alternating A/B answered `datadome-challenge` 3/3 on BOTH arms minutes later,
and `x-hyatt`, whose ticket window had shut — twenty spaced visits on the
unchanged binary got no `x-kpsdk-r` at all in the same hour. 1583/1583.
## A border is measured in device pixels, and we were counting whole ones (B72, 2026-08-30)

`getComputedStyle(el).borderTopWidth` is a **used** value: not the length the
page wrote, but the width the border is actually drawn at. This engine floored
it to a whole CSS pixel with a floor of one, which is Chrome's rule one grid too
coarse. Chrome floors onto the **device** pixel, with a floor of one device
pixel — half a CSS pixel at the ratio 2 this engine's persona claims.

| declared | Chrome dsf=1 | Chrome dsf=2 | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `0.4px` | `1px` | `0.5px` | `1px` | `0.5px` |
| `0.9px` | `1px` | `0.5px` | `1px` | `0.5px` |
| `1.4px` | `1px` | `1px` | `1px` | `1px` |
| `1.5px` | `1px` | `1.5px` | `1px` | `1.5px` |
| `3.6px` | `3px` | `3.5px` | `3px` | `3.5px` |
| `4.6px` | `4px` | `4.5px` | `4px` | `4.5px` |
| `10.9px` | `10px` | `10.5px` | `10px` | `10.5px` |

The width is not only what the computed style prints. `clientTop` rounds it,
`offsetWidth` and `getBoundingClientRect().width` carry it twice, and all four
move together: `border-width:3.6px` on a 100px box was `3px 3 106 106` here and
is `3.5px 4 107 107` in Chrome. Fifteen of thirty widths differed across the
four readings; all thirty agree now, 32 of 32 cases byte-identical
(`scratch/b72/expr-border-grid.js`).

### The old expectations were a reading taken at the wrong scale factor

`css/computed_border_width.html` asserted `4.6px` → `4px` and cited a Chrome 151
run. That citation was true and the expectation was still wrong: **the run's
scale factor was never written down, and it was dsf=1.** Every one of the old
cells matches the dsf=1 column exactly, which is what says the earlier
measurement was taken there rather than that Chrome changed its mind.

So the engine was announcing `devicePixelRatio: 2` while laying out borders on
the whole CSS pixel — two readings a page gets in one expression. Both tests now
assert `devicePixelRatio` beside the widths: a reading of a device grid taken
without saying which device is a reading of nothing.

`client_top_left.html` had two cases measured and deliberately left unasserted
for exactly this defect (`3.5px` and `3.6px`, Chrome 4 and this engine 3). They
are asserted now, and they are the pair that says `clientTop` rounds a
fractional used width rather than reading a whole one.

### The neighbours were not on the wrong grid — they were on no grid

Pointing the same probe at the rest of the family found something worse.
`outline-width`, `column-rule-width`, `row-rule-width` and
`-webkit-column-rule-width` take a length through a path of their own that
resolved `thin`/`medium`/`thick` and then handed the author's text straight
back: `outline-width:4.6px` computed to `4.6px`, `0.1px` to `0.1px`. Not the
wrong grid — no truncation at all, and a number Chrome cannot print at any scale
factor. Chrome floors all four exactly as it does a border. 24 of 32 readings
differed; all 32 agree now.

`-webkit-text-stroke-width` is measured **not** to snap — `4.6px` stays `4.6px`
at dpr 2 — which fits the scale of its own its keywords already showed
(`0.666667px` / `2px` / `3.33333px`). So the grid is a field on `RuleWidthScale`
and not a property of the family, and the test asserts the stroke's eight
non-snapping readings beside the other four names' 32, so a later change that
snaps everything has something to fail against.

Readings: `scratch/b72/expr-rule-grid.js` and `expr-rule-grid2.js` against
Chrome 151 at `--force-device-scale-factor=2`, `devicePixelRatio` reported in
the same object as the widths (`scratch/b72/ch-rule-dsf2.json`,
`ch-rule2-dsf2.json`).

## The root's box is inside the window, not around it (B72, 2026-08-30)

The root element got the viewport as its **content** box. Everything it wore
then hung outside the window it is laid out in: a `<html style="border:7px
solid">` in a 400x200 frame answered `offsetWidth` 414 — a box wider than the
frame holding it, which no browser can produce.

The `<body>` inherited the mistake twice. It was sized off the *viewport* rather
than off the root's content box, so it stayed 384 wide whatever the root wore;
and it was sized through a **constant 16** rather than its own margin, so
`body{margin:20px}` also stayed 384 where Chrome says 360.

Three rules, measured over eleven served documents at dpr 2 (`scratch/b72/qc/`,
read with `scratch/b72/expr-root-box.js`, Chrome readings in
`ch-rootbox2.json`):

* **the root's content box is the viewport less its own margin, border and
  padding.** A declared `width` still names the content box as anywhere else —
  `width:300px;border:7px` is `offsetWidth` 314, and it still fits inside 400.
* **the body's is the ROOT's content box** less the body's own margin, border
  and padding. `body{margin:0}` is 400 wide, `margin:20px` is 360, and a body
  with `margin:8px;border:4px;padding:6px` is 364 content / 376 client / 384
  offset.
* **`clientWidth` and `scrollWidth` on the scrolling element report the
  WINDOW.** Half of that swap was already here — the `<body>` answers it in
  quirks mode — and the root half had been left out on the reasoning that "an
  undeclared root's box is the viewport anyway". It is. A root with a padding is
  not, and Chrome still answers 400 for a padding box that is really 396.
  `<html style="width:300px">` answers 400 as well, which is the reading that
  says the root reports the window rather than a box that happens to match it.

| reading | Chrome | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| root `border:7px` → `offsetWidth` | 400 | **414** | 400 |
| root `border:7px` → body `clientWidth` | 370 | **384** | 370 |
| root `padding:5px` → root `clientWidth` | 400 | **410** | 400 |
| root `margin:3px` → root `offsetWidth` | 394 | **414** | 394 |
| root `width:300px` → root `scrollWidth` | 400 | **300** | 400 |
| `body{margin:20px}` → body `offsetWidth` | 360 | **384** | 360 |
| quirks root `border:7px` → root `clientWidth` | 386 | **400** | 386 |

Six size readings per document (`clientWidth`, `offsetWidth` and `scrollWidth`
off each root container), eleven documents, so 66 widths and 66 heights.
**The widths go 25/66 identical to 66/66.** Re-running B70's own eight served
quirks/standards documents, they go **36/48 to 47/48** — the one left is a
`display:inline` body's `offsetWidth`, which is ink and not this. On the
TOP-LEVEL document, where
there is no iframe element to take a box from, the twelve width readings across
the two modes go **7/12 identical to 12/12** — including the quirks
`body.scrollWidth` 1904-against-1920 that had been sitting unattributed since
B96 measured it (`scratch/b72/expr-top-box.js`).

`scrollWidth`'s root-container branch was a guard that outlived what it guarded:
it existed because the root box once carried the artificial constants 1920 and
100_000_000, and it dropped the padding every other element adds and answered
the box in the two cases Chrome answers the window.

### The margin half of this was landing at the same time, from B96

The second rule needed the body's own margin where a constant 16 had been, and
`prd/body-box-margin` — the chapter two above this one — was fixing exactly that
on exactly these lines while this branch was open. Both halves are measured and
they agree, so the merge keeps B96's `bodyMarginPx` and this branch's
`containerMarginPx` became two lines: the `<body>` is the one tag whose UA
margin is load-bearing and goes through B96's helper, and `<html>` has no UA
margin and asks `marginPx` like anything else.

Worth naming as a near miss. Two sessions found the same 16px from opposite
ends — B96 from `body.clientWidth` being 1904 where Chrome says 1920 on
scrapingcourse, this one from a bordered root leaving its body 384 wide — and
the halves are only compatible because both were measured rather than reasoned
about. Neither is narrow enough: `marginPx` itself still answers 0 for an
undeclared margin, which is right for an ordinary element, and making it consult
the per-tag table would move margin collapsing and content height for every
element on a page. Nothing measured on either branch asks for that.

### The heights are still wrong, and are deliberately not asserted

Every reading that still differs after this change is a **height** — 44 of the
66 over the eleven documents, where 48 differed before. This engine
stretches an `auto`-height `<html>` and `<body>` to fill the viewport where
Chrome sizes them to their content: `body.offsetHeight` reads 184 in a 200px
frame holding one 20px div where Chrome reads 20, and a document 400px tall
reads the same 184 where Chrome reads 400. The change here moves those numbers
(184 → 170 for a bordered root) without making any of them right.

That is `content-height-memoised-subtree`'s, and it is why
`frames/root_box_edges.html` asserts widths only — asserting the heights would
be pinning this engine's behaviour rather than a browser's. `getScrollHeight`
now says the same thing where it used to cite the guard this change deleted:
the heights are not a swap at all, since Chrome answers the viewport for a short
document and the content for a tall one (200 and 430 for the same frame), so the
reading is `max(viewport, content)` and the content half does not exist yet.

|---|---|---|
| full sweep | **22/29** | **19/29** |

| dd-leboncoin | 0/3 pass | 0/3 pass |
| dd-hermes | 0/3 pass | 0/3 pass |

## One pseudo-element in a list dropped the whole rule (B96, 2026-08-30)

`*, ::before, ::after { box-sizing: border-box; border-width: 0; border-style: solid }`
is the opening line of Tailwind's preflight, and therefore of a large share of
the web. This engine dropped it.

`::before` reached `Parser.pseudoClass`, which strips one colon and then wants an
identifier; it found the second colon and returned `error.InvalidPseudoClass`.
`parseList` propagates that, and `StyleManager.addRawRule` turns a selector error
into a rule that never existed — taking the `*` down with the `::before`. So on
www.scrapingcourse.com every element lost `box-sizing: border-box`: Chrome
computed `border-box` for the body where this engine computed `content-box`, and
a `width:100px;padding:10px;border:5px` box measured 90 there and 120 here.

### Chrome's rule, measured a name at a time

`probes/expr-b96-pseudo-element-list.js` puts each selector in a list beside an
id selector — `#probe, <under test> { letter-spacing: 3px }` — and reads the
property back off `#probe`. `3px` means the rule survived, `normal` means it was
dropped:

| in the list | Chrome |
|---|---|
| `::before` `::after` `::first-line` `::first-letter` | kept |
| `::placeholder` `::marker` `::backdrop` `::selection` | kept |
| `::file-selector-button` `::cue` | kept |
| `::part(x)` `::slotted(x)` | kept |
| `:before` `:after` `:first-line` `:first-letter` (one colon) | kept |
| `::-webkit-scrollbar` **and `::-webkit-nonsense-xyz`** | kept |
| `::-moz-nonsense-xyz` | **dropped** |
| `::totally-unknown-thing` | **dropped** |
| `:totally-unknown-class` | dropped |
| `>>>` | dropped |

So a pseudo-element Chrome knows keeps the list alive and one it does not know
kills it, exactly as an unknown pseudo-class does — and `-webkit-` is a wildcard
where `-moz-` is not. That is the whole specification of the fix, and none of it
was guessed: the `-webkit-` line in particular is the kind of thing a
reasonable implementation gets wrong in both directions.

The compound itself still matches nothing. `#probe::before` sets nothing on
`#probe`, `querySelector('#probe::before')` is null and `matches()` is false —
all three measured on Chrome, all three now true here. A pseudo-element parses
so that its neighbours survive, and for no other reason.

Three probes read back after the change, all against headed Chrome 151 at the
persona's dpr=2 on the same served page:

| probe | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| the pseudo-element list (22 rows) | 13 | **22** |
| where box-sizing comes from (9 rows) | 5 | **9** |
| the body box (13 rows) | 12 | **13** |

The sweep read 20/29 and the one station that moved is `dd-leboncoin`, back to
`pass` from the `datadome-challenge` an alternating A/B had shown it giving BOTH
binaries an hour earlier — the same oscillation, this time in the pleasant
direction. No Cloudflare station moved, and the three closed cf doors are where
they were. 1583/1583.

## The 373 was one stalled page, not 373 failures (B72, 2026-08-31)

`content-height-memoised-subtree` was closed by its third reading: a
per-measurement memo made the nested test pass and the suite **worse** — "373
`ExecutionTerminated`, spread across pages that have nothing to do with layout
(`cookie_store`, `indexeddb`, `url`, `media_devices`)". That number was read as
a cost curve. It is not one.

Re-run with the whole `watchdog stall` line in view, the suite reports:

```
watchdog stalls: 1
      stalled_ms = 30205
ExecutionTerminated: 371
```

**One** stall, 30.2 seconds, in `element/position.html`. Everything after it in
the same binary is collateral — which is exactly why the failures land on
`cookie_store` and `url` and `streams`, pages that have nothing to do with
layout. The 373 and the 371 are the same artefact counted twice, and the real
signal is a single page hanging.

Why that page: `position.html` holds two **marquee loops**, and a marquee loop
is written to run until a metric *grows*.

```js
while (lane.scrollWidth < track.offsetWidth * 2 && guard < 50) {
  lane.innerHTML += lane.innerHTML;
}
```

Seven doublings normally. Any change that stops the metric climbing turns it
into an exponential DOM builder with a guard of 50 — 2^50 nodes. So a layout
change does not have to be *slow* to hang the suite; it only has to make one
number stop moving.

### Four more shapes, all measured, all the same 371

This is `root-container-content-height`, opened because the root containers'
`auto` height is the largest measured box divergence left: on example.com
`getComputedStyle(body).height` is `98.0781px` in Chrome and `756px` here, and
`documentElement.offsetHeight` 396 against 1080. Cloudflare's widget dumps
`getComputedStyle` over the `<body>`, so that number travels in the payload of
every page it challenges.

| shape | suite |
|---|---|
| root containers take their height from `contentHeight` (standards mode only), nothing else changed | **0 ExecutionTerminated**, 1581/1583 |
| …plus the reverted per-child recursion, with `depth` carried so the child's box is measured at `depth + 1` instead of restarting at 0 through `getElementDimensions` | 371 |
| …plus a `contentHeight` memo on the **Frame** (not `call_arena`), held across nested entries by keeping `_layout_depth` up for the whole walk, sentinel before the walk, cleared at 0 | 371 |
| …plus the same memo one level down, on `dimensionsAt` itself | 371 |

Three findings in that table:

* **the cost wall is not at the root.** Asking the root containers for their
  content height is free; the first row is a clean suite. What is not free is
  the per-child recursion, and that is the term B86 reverted.
* **"restarts at depth 0" is not the mechanism.** B86's diagnosis named the
  containing-block walk restarting, and carrying the depth changes nothing.
* **neither is the memo.** B86's stated blocker for a shared memo was that it
  would have to live in `call_arena`, which is released between JS calls —
  `Frame.arena` is the frame's own lifetime and has no such problem, so the memo
  was built and it also changes nothing. Which follows, once the 371 is read
  correctly: the suite was never measuring the memo. It was measuring one hang.

The patches are kept verbatim rather than half-merged:
`probes/b72-depth-carry-attempt.patch` (rows 1–2) and
`probes/b72-memo-attempt.patch` (rows 3–4). The next step is
`content-height-marquee-stall`: find which metric stops growing in
`position.html` and why — note that the loops that hang read **widths** while
the change is to **heights**, so the answer is not obvious and is worth reading
off a log rather than reasoning about.

## Sixty-seven selector constructs, twelve of which deleted rules (B96, 2026-08-31)

The pseudo-element finding above is a special case of a general one:
`parseList` propagates a failure from any compound and `addRawRule` is
`... catch return`, so a construct this engine does not recognise costs the
**whole rule** — every declaration in it, for every element the other selectors
in the list matched. That is worth a sweep rather than one fix at a time.

`probes/expr-b96-selector-constructs.js` puts each construct in a list beside an
id selector — `#probe, <under test> { letter-spacing: 3px }` — and reads the
property back. Sixty-seven constructs, Chrome 151 against this engine:

| dropped here, kept in Chrome | what it is |
|---|---|
| `:nth-child(2n+1 of .a)` | the `of S` clause |
| `:autofill` `:user-valid` `:open` | newer state pseudo-classes |
| `:dir(ltr)` | directionality |
| `:host` `:host(.a)` `:host-context(.a)` | the shadow-host family |
| `*|div` | a namespace-qualified type selector |
| `div:is(&)` | a nesting reference |
| `::highlight(x)` `::view-transition-group(x)` | functional pseudo-elements |

All twelve now parse. Where a match has a cheap definition it is implemented —
`:open` is the attribute, `:dir()` reads the element's own `dir`, and
`:nth-child(An+B of S)` counts only the siblings `S` matches. The rest match
nothing on purpose and say so: nothing here autofills a field or types in one,
a stylesheet here is the document's and never a shadow root's, and there is no
nesting for `&` to resolve. **Parsing is the fix; matching is a bonus** — a
construct that parses costs the page nothing, and one that does not costs it
every declaration in the rule.

Two go the other way and are left alone, asserted as residuals in
`element/selector_constructs.html` rather than quietly:

* `[data-x="y" s]` — Chrome drops the rule, this engine honours the flag.
  Whatever refuses it lives in Chrome's CSS parser; matching that would mean
  rejecting a selector this engine understands.
* `[data-x` unclosed — the `[` swallows the `{ … }` after it, so nothing is left
  to be a declaration block. That is the sheet tokenizer, and CSS Syntax does
  say an unexpected EOF closes every open construct.

Read back: **65 of the 67 rows are Chrome's, up from 53.**

One negative worth recording, because it was the first thing checked and it
would have been the biggest: **the escapes Tailwind generates were already
right.** `.md\:flex`, `.w-1\/2`, `.top-\[13px\]`, `.\!mt-0`, `.bg-black\/50`,
`.data-\[state\=open\]\:block`, the `group-hover\:` and `peer-checked\:` forms,
a `\30 ` unicode escape and an escaped space — twelve shapes, both arms
identical. An earlier version of the probe reported an escape difference and
that was the probe's own double-escaping, not the engine's.

The sweep read 22/29, back to the session's baseline: the two stations that moved
are `dd-datadome` and `dd-hermes`, both swinging back to `pass` from the
`datadome-challenge` they were giving every binary an hour earlier. No
Cloudflare station moved and x-hyatt is still refused. 1583/1583.
### …and then it landed (B72)

The term went in. `contentHeight` asks each child what it holds, bounded by
`MAX_CONTAINING_BLOCK_DEPTH`, and `element/position.html`'s scrollHeight marquee
loop is asserted the way its width-axis sibling already was — it does not
terminate, and Chrome does not terminate it either.

| reading | Chrome | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| wrapper around a 12px div | 12 12 | **0 12** | 12 12 |
| two wrappers deep | 12 12 | **0 0** | 12 12 |
| `overflow:hidden;padding:5px` wrapper | 22 22 | **10 22** | 22 22 |
| 16 levels deep | 12 12 | **0 0** | 12 12 |
| 40 wrappers wide | 480 480 | **0 0** | 480 480 |

B86's own probe agrees: `probes/expr-b86-nested-depth.js` reads twelve at every
level of a 1, 2, 4, 16 and 64-deep chain and 480 for the wide parent, which is
what it was written to check and what it had never once answered. The three
shapes `css/child_box_height.html` measured and deliberately left unasserted are
asserted.

**Cost: a warm suite goes 44s → 46s.** `WebApi: Element` stays out of the
slowest five. (At a guard of 12 rather than 4 the corrected marquee test's own
4096 nodes put it back in at 4.5s — that is the test, not the engine: the same
binary with a guard of 4 reads 1.56s against a 1.35s baseline.)

Four other changes were measured on the way here and **none of them landed**,
because each was measured to change nothing:

* carrying `depth` into the child's box instead of `getElementDimensions`;
* a `contentHeight` memo on the Frame, held across nested entries;
* the same memo one level down on `dimensionsAt`;
* sizing the root containers from their content (that one does something, and
  it is `root-container-content-height`'s, still open — it is why
  `getComputedStyle(body).height` on example.com is still `756px` here against
  Chrome's `98.0781px`).

One caution the bisect turned up the hard way: a blind search-and-replace of
`el.dimensionsAt(frame, true, depth + 1, true)` while stripping the depth
experiment also hit two calls in `inlineInk` that were never part of it — and
the comment above one of them records sixty nested `<span>`s taking the engine
out with a SIGBUS mid-sweep. They were restored and the suite re-run. A bisect
that edits by pattern has to check what else matches the pattern.

## The root containers are as tall as what they hold, and that reading costs a station (B73, 2026-08-31)

`root-container-content-height` had one exec cut left in it, and it is the one
the plan was opened for: an `auto` height on `<html>` or `<body>` was **the
viewport**, so `getComputedStyle(body).height` was a per-document *constant*.
`184px` in a 200px frame for an empty body, for one holding a 20px div and for
one holding a 900px div alike. Cloudflare's widget dumps a whole computed style
off the `<body>`, so that constant travels in every challenge payload — and on
example.com Chrome answers `98.0781px` where this engine answered `756px`.

### What Chrome does, over nineteen served documents

Measured on a headed Chrome 151 at dpr 2, each document in a 400x200 borderless
iframe (`scratch/b73/expr-height-row.js`, readings in
`scratch/b73/ch-support-row.json`, now pinned in
`frames/root_box_heights.html`). Four rules:

* **standards `<body>`**: the height is what it holds, and its children's
  margins *escape* it — `child_margin` holds a 20px div wearing 30px margins and
  the body is 20 tall, not 80. clientHeight/scrollHeight add its padding,
  offsetHeight adds its border, the computed `height` is the content box.
* **standards `<html>`**: the height is the `<body>`'s **margin box**, plus its
  own padding and border for offsetHeight — 36px of computed height and 50 of
  offsetHeight under a 7px border. An empty body gives **8**, not 16: a
  self-collapsing box's own two margins collapse into one.
* **standards, the accessors on `<html>`**: it is the scrolling element, so
  clientHeight is the **viewport** (200 for all nineteen, the mirror of the width
  rule in `frames/root_box_edges.html`) and scrollHeight is the scrolling
  **area** — `max(viewport, the root's border box)`, 200 for every short document
  and 430 for the tall one.
* **quirks**: the `<body>` fills instead, and the swap in `cssomViewport` puts
  the viewport on *its* clientHeight and the root's own box on the root's. A
  quirks body still **grows** past the fill when it holds more —
  `quirks_overflow` is 900 of offsetHeight, not 184 — and both containers grow
  with it.

Two readings deliberately not asserted, measured so the next hop does not have
to: `html,body{height:100%}` is body `200/200/200/200px` and root
`200/200/`**208**`/200px` (the body's margin box hanging 8px past a root that is
exactly the viewport, which needs a scrolling area built from descendant bounds
rather than the root's own border box), and `body{min-height:100vh}` is root
`200/216/216/216px`.

### The change, and the one row it does not reach

Three cuts, all small: leave the height `null` in `dimensionsAt`'s html/body
branch unless the document is quirks; drop the html/body shortcut in
`clientHeightOf` so both containers go through the content pass in **both** modes
(the quirks fill becomes a floor rather than an answer, which is what makes a
quirks body grow); and give the scrolling element the scrolling area in
`getScrollHeight`, taking the same CSSOM swap clientHeight already took.

One more rule fell out of the measurement: **a first child's margin cannot escape
through the root element**, because the root's own margins do not collapse (CSS
2.1 8.3.1). That is the whole of the 16px between the root's height and the
body's.

**Eighteen of the nineteen rows go byte-identical**, from a table that disagreed
everywhere. The nineteenth is `child_margin`, and it is a different defect: an
escaped margin *vanishes* here instead of collapsing into the box that stops it.
Measured on both arms with `scratch/b73/expr-margin-escape-table.js` — 15 shapes,
7 identical, and the plain-div cases agree at one, two and three levels of
nesting, so this is margin collapsing and not the root containers. It is
`escaped-margin-reaches-its-stop`, and it is also the last 32px between our
example.com body height (66px with this change, 756 without) and Chrome's 98.

### And then it costs ak-homedepot

`--only ak-` on the same route, three times: **4/4 on main, 0/4 with the change**.
Every failure is one crash and its tail — `ak-homedepot` takes `timeout:
Runtime.enable` at 55s and the three stations after it time out on
`Page.navigate` (`results/b73-only-ak-*.json`). Alone, homedepot passes in
**38.8s** where main takes **28.4s**, which is a coin flip against a 30-second
CDP timeout, not a pass.

The reason is in `scratch/b73/count-root-reads.mjs`, which hooks the three height
getters on a live page and reports calls and engine time per accessor:

| | calls | engine time |
|---|---|---|
| main, `root:clientHeight` | 117 | **0.3 ms** |
| main, `other:offsetHeight` | 513 | 6166 ms |
| with the change, `root:clientHeight` | 108–143 | **15381 ms** |
| with the change, `root:scrollHeight` | 1 | **7087 ms** |

A homedepot page load reads the root containers' height about 120 times. The
reading was a constant and is now a walk of the whole document, and one walk is
60–140ms there. Note the middle row: the engine *already* spends 6.2 seconds
inside 513 ordinary `offsetHeight` reads on that page, with one single read
measured at **3.9 seconds**. The root containers did not create the cost model;
they are just the biggest subtree in it.

**A memo does not fix it.** Four slots on the Frame (`<html>`/`<body>` times the
two extents) keyed on a new `Page.layout_version` — bumped by `domChanged` and by
`StyleManager.sheetModified`, which between them cover tree mutations, inline
style writes (the declaration syncs itself back through `setAttribute`) and every
stylesheet mutation. On a synthetic page ten reads went 98ms → 0. On homedepot it
changed nothing and the station still failed: a page that is building itself
invalidates between nearly every read. Reverted rather than kept — a cache that
does not hit is a staleness risk with no upside.

### What did come out of it: the ancestor chain was being re-measured per child

`contentHeight` measured every child through `getElementDimensions`, which starts
that child at depth 0; the child then reaches the fill branch in `dimensionsAt`
and re-measures the **whole ancestor chain** to recover a width the walk it is
inside of already had. `dimensionsIn` is `dimensionsAt` told that width.
`CSSStyleDeclaration.containingWidth` already opens with `if (containing.*)
|width| return width;`, so seeding it is enough to delete the walk.

Measured before → after, every value byte-identical:

* five `offsetHeight` reads over a whole served document, three ~2400-node pages
