  (`scratch/b73/expr-subtree-read-cost.js`): 20-deep **81ms → 17**, flat
  **52 → 24**, mixed **60 → 43**;
* homedepot's 510 `offsetHeight` reads: **11.8ms per read → 9.6**, three paired
  runs.

That is `containing-width-carried-down`, and it stands on its own — it is a
general layout-cost fix, it changes no reading, and `--only ak-` is 4/4 with it
(homedepot 26.2s). It is **not** enough to pay for the root-container reading:
with both changes in, homedepot still stalls.

### Where this leaves it

The root-container height work is correct, pinned against Chrome, and **not
merged**. It is kept two ways: as
`probes/b73-root-box-height.patch` (the whole change, including the nineteen-row
`frames/root_box_heights.html` and its ten support fixtures — apply it and the
Chrome table comes with it), and as the branch `prd/standards-root-box-height`
with its worktree left in place. The branch's second commit, `f5d0d211e`, is the
cost work that has since been merged on its own, so a merge of that branch will
have to reconcile it — and `contentHeight` has moved underneath it as well, since
it now returns the escaped margin groups (see the note below this one). The patch
is the cleaner starting point of the two, and `git apply --check` still passes
against it on `c8bedc1a8` — textually only; it has not been built or run since
`contentHeight` changed shape, and that check was deliberately not done in the
main checkout because a peer session building main mid-experiment would compile
the patch by accident. The state at the time it was measured: 18 of 19 rows
byte-identical to Chrome, suite 1583/1583. The nineteenth row, `child_margin`,
is the one the escaped-margin fix below now covers, so a re-measure should read
19 — the residual in the test file has to be dropped for that. What blocks it is not a bug in it — it is that this engine has no
incremental layout, so every height reading pays for its whole subtree, and the
root containers' subtree is the document. The honest next step is not another
memo: it is either making a subtree measurement cheap enough that 120 of them fit
in a page load, or finding a reading that is content-shaped without being a walk.

## An escaped margin was going nowhere (B73, 2026-08-31)

`css/margin_collapse.html` already asserted that a first child's top margin
*escapes* a parent with no edge on that side. What it never asked is where the
margin then **goes**, and the answer is: it keeps escaping, through every
edgeless ancestor, until it reaches one with a border, a padding or a block
formatting context — and there it collapses with whatever margins it meets. That
gap belongs to *that* box.

This engine dropped it at the first parent. Which is invisible in the shape the
old assertions used, because both arms answer 20 for a wrapper holding a 20px div
with 30px margins — Chrome because the margin went further up, this engine
because the margin was gone. The difference shows one level out:

| shape (a 20px block with 30px margins inside it) | Chrome | before |
|---|---|---|
| two edgeless wrappers side by side, in a padded parent | 112 | 42 |
| one edgeless wrapper beside a plain sibling with a 5px margin | 102 | 47 |
| an empty margined box reached through a wrapper, between two blocks | 72 | 42 |
| a self-collapsing first child, then a sibling with a 50px top margin | 72 | 22 |
| an out-of-flow first child, then one with a 30px top margin | 52 | 22 |
| `margin-top` 5, then 40, then 12, three levels deep | 62 | 27 |

Twelve shapes measured on a headed Chrome 151 at dpr 2, through that file's own
harness so the container is the same one the assertions run in
(`scratch/b73/expr-escape-cases.js`, readings in `ch-escape-cases.json`). Six
were already right and stay as the boundary — an edge, a formatting context, and
**text**, because a line box is content and nothing below it can get out. Twelve
of twelve now.

The fix is not a second walk. `contentHeight` reports the two escaped groups
alongside the height, because **the escaped group is exactly the value of `group`
at the moment a pay-out is skipped** — and whether it is skipped is what
`escapes.top` / `escapes.bottom` already decide. The parent joins them into the
run its own margins are in (`MarginGroup.joinGroup`: two runs that adjoin are one
run, so 30 meeting a 10 is 30). The self-collapsing branch joins **both** into
the same group, which is what makes a wrapper whose only content is an empty
margined box read as one gap rather than two.

No extra tree walking, and the measured cost is flat: homedepot's 510
`offsetHeight` reads are 10.0ms each against 9.5–9.7 before, two paired runs.

Residual, stated in the code rather than measured: `marginEscapes` never asks
about `height`, and the spec only lets a *bottom* margin collapse through a box
whose height is `auto`. Every shape here has an auto-height parent, so nothing
above distinguishes the two.

## x-hyatt's ticket comes first, and its rate is too low to test anything with (B74, 2026-08-31)

B96 saw three `x-kpsdk-r` tickets on this engine in one sitting and wrote down
that "x-hyatt now gets a ticket sometimes", with the observation that every
ticket run was `doc=429->200` and every ticketless one was `doc=429` — 59
observations, no exception. Two readings fit that: the ticket *causes* the
recovery, or the edge had already decided before any JS ran and the ticket is
that decision surfacing on the POST. The second would mean the page environment
is not what is being judged at all.

The second is wrong, and the whole line dies on arithmetic rather than on a
missing lead.

### The ticket comes first; the 200 is the reload it permits

Ten alternating pairs, order flipped every round, back to back
(`scratch/b74/rounds.sh` driving `hyatt-tl-timeline.mjs`, per-run timelines in
`scratch/b74/out/`). Chrome took a ticket in **10 of 10**:

| | ticket at | reload request at | document 200 at |
|---|---|---|---|
| median of 10 Chrome runs | 1897ms | ticket + 3ms | 2743ms |
| spread | 1830–2558 | ticket + 1…6 | 2640–4165 |

The reload leaves within six milliseconds of the ticket arriving, every time.
So "ticket" and "429->200" are **one event seen twice**, not two signals whose
correlation means anything. B96's 59-observation co-occurrence is fully spent by
this and carries no further information.

### Nothing before the POST differs between the arms

Across 50 runs of this engine and 10 of Chrome, everything upstream of the POST
is the same shape:

| | this engine (n=50) | Chrome (n=10) |
|---|---|---|
| `x-kpsdk-r` on the 429 document | `1-AA`, all 50 | `1-AA`, all 10 |
| 429 body | 690 bytes, all 50 | 690 bytes, all 10 |
| guard program served | 291 705 – 326 884 B | 293 222 – 316 095 B |
| `/tl` post length | 19 122 – 19 226 | 19 586 – 19 650 |
| `/tl` response | `200 text/plain len=0`, `x-kpsdk-r` absent, all 50 | `200 application/json` len=15, ticket, all 10 |

The 429 carries the same `1-AA` state to both arms and the program sizes
overlap (they are re-randomised per delivery), so **the edge is not pre-judging
at the document request** — the decision happens entirely on the `/tl` POST. The
post-length gap is the already-attributed ~440B one, of which 330B is global
creation order, negated in both directions.

And the one surviving log of a run where *this engine* took a ticket
(`/tmp/b96-hyatt-base-5.log`) reads `tl=200 application/json; charset=utf-8
len=15 cr=true r=1-B1EFfHU`, `doc=429->200`. So there is no third "envelope
rejected" response shape: `text/plain len=0` is a refusal and `json len=15` is a
grant, and **the same binary has been handed both**. Nothing in this client's
content flips it.

### The rate, and why the line closes

Measured today, one hour, same binary (`scratch/b73/lp-rel-escmargin`):

| | tickets |
|---|---|
| Chrome, headed | **10 / 10** |
| this engine, order-balanced alternating rounds | 0 / 10 |
| this engine, single-arm back-to-back burst of 40 | **0 / 40** |

B96's "the ticket favours the first visit of a burst" did not reproduce: this
engine led five of the ten pairs and every one of the forty burst runs, and took
nothing. Cumulatively this engine is about **5 tickets in 157 visits (~3%)**
across three sittings (B84 2/37, B96 3/70, here 0/50) against a reference arm at
90–100%.

**That rate is the finding.** Separating 3% from 6% at α=0.05 and 80% power needs
roughly 750 runs per arm — about 6½ hours of wall clock per arm at 32s a run —
so an engine change that *doubled* our ticket rate is not measurable in any
schedule this file can run. `x-kpsdk-r` remains a good oracle in the one
direction that has resolution: subtracting from Chrome's ~100%, which is what
B84's eight-knob table already used. It is not usable as an A/B judge on our
side, and B96's "worth re-running the reverse-biased design when the window is
open" is not worth running — there is no window to catch, only a low rate.

Two smaller things fell out. Our think time — guard program fully downloaded to
POST sent — is **159–270ms (median 212)** against Chrome's **920–980ms**, tighter
on Chrome's side than load noise explains (±3%, which looks like a timer rather
than work). That reproduces and sharpens B84's timing gap, and B84 already
negated it causally by holding our POST back into Chrome's window; one run here
had a think time of 835ms and still took nothing. And Chrome drops the 429's body
the instant the challenge script reloads, so `Network.getResponseBody` has to be
called on `loadingFinished` rather than after the settle — a deferred read
returns "No resource with given identifier" on exactly the arm that matters.

**What this does to the door map:** x-hyatt stays a real door — the reference arm
walks in and this engine does not. What changes is the instrument, not the
verdict: the row should read *reference ~100%, this engine ~3%, and the ticket
rate cannot referee a change of ours*.

## A percentage in transform threw the declaration away, and every in-flow box's position is still 5px times a node count (B74, 2026-08-31)

Two things came out of asking `transform-number-format` P6 for its ground truth,
and the second is larger than the plan that found it.

### translate(-50%, -50%) computed to none

`parseScalar` in `css/transform.zig` refused a `%` outright, and that refusal
takes the whole declaration -- so nine of nine percentage forms were lost, the
centering idiom included. Measured on a 100x50 `<p>`, Chrome 151 at dpr 2
(`scratch/b74/expr-test-shape-percent.js`), against this engine before the fix:

| declaration | Chrome | before |
|---|---|---|
| `translateX(50%)` | `matrix(1, 0, 0, 1, 50, 0)` | `none` |
| `translate(-50%, -50%)` | `matrix(1, 0, 0, 1, -50, -25)` | `none` |
| `translate(10px, 50%)` | `matrix(1, 0, 0, 1, 10, 25)` | `none` |
| `translate3d(50%, 25%, 10px)` | `matrix3d(…, 50, 12.5, 10, 1)` | `none` |
| `scale(50%)` | `matrix(0.5, 0, 0, 0.5, 0, 0)` | `none` |
| `translateZ(50%)` | `none` | `none` |

The last row is the control that makes the rest a reading rather than a guess:
`translateZ`, `rotate`, `skewX` and `perspective` have no percentage in their
grammar and answer `none` on both engines, so this was not a blanket refusal of
percentages -- it was the absence of the ones that are allowed.

**The basis is the border box, attributed one property at a time.** On the same
100x50 `<p>`, `translate(50%, 50%)` is 50,25; `padding:10px` moves it to 60,35;
`border:5px` to 55,30; both to 65,40; and `box-sizing:border-box` puts it back at
50,25. `transform-origin` has been measuring that same box through
`resolvedOrigin` for a while, so `transformBasis` reads it the same way.

Two boundaries came with it. A **non-replaced inline** element has a box but no
reference box: Chrome answers `matrix(1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0)` for `translate(50%, 50%)`
on a `display:inline` `<p>` whose inline box measures 8x19 -- not 4,9.5 -- while
an `<img>` at the same display *is* transformable and uses its 400x50. And an
element with **no box at all** reports `none` for ANY transform in Chrome,
percentage or not: `display:none` with `translateX(50px)` answered a matrix here,
which was a second defect the display:none row forced out. 27 of 27 readings now
match, against 5 of 27 before -- the five that already agreed being the four
grammar refusals and the display:none row.

### The larger thing: no in-flow box has ever had a position

`out-of-flow-position` fixed absolute and fixed boxes in August and deferred the
rest with a reason: static and relative positions need block stacking, "and the
height half is not done -- without correct heights you cannot stack a correct y".
That premise has since expired. `block-height-from-content`,
`content-height-child-box`, `sibling-margin-collapse`,
`escaped-margin-reaches-its-stop` and `root-container-content-height` all landed.

Measured across fifteen shapes, 27 rows, each child reported as its offset from
its container's border box so the number is independent of the page the probe
runs on (`scratch/b74/expr-inflow-position-matrix.js`):

- **Every box size matches Chrome** -- the collapsed-margin container at 400x70,
  the auto-height line at 18.5, the container after a float at 400x20, the
  inline-block row at 400x34, text-then-block at 400x48.5.
- **26 of 27 positions do not.** The one that does is the absolute row.

Ours are always `5k, 5k`: `calculateDocumentPosition` and
`calculateSiblingPosition` in `Element.zig` have **byte-identical bodies**, both
returning five pixels times a node count, so **every element's x equals its y**.
One expression sees that.

So the inputs are all correct and only the stacking step is missing. What decides
whether it can be built is cost, and that was measured before any of it:

| station | `getBoundingClientRect` calls | ms inside them | geometry reads | mutations | **layout passes a cache would need** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| homedepot | 238 | 6057 | 1 664 | 2 670 | **59** |
| macys | 7 199 | 4131 | 49 055 | 39 398 | **53** |
| sony | 254 | 4276 | 281 | 2 017 | **15** |

Two readings, both from `scratch/b74/count-position-reads.mjs` and
`count-read-clusters.mjs` on a pinned ReleaseFast build. The left half is the
budget: with positions **not** computed, `getBoundingClientRect` alone already
costs four to six seconds against a 30s CDP timeout. The right half is the
architecture: a cached single pass has to recompute only on the first read after
a mutation, and that is 53 passes for macys' 49 055 reads -- a 925x reduction.
Summing preceding siblings per read, which is what the obvious implementation
does, multiplies the four-to-six seconds instead.

That is enough to choose the architecture and not enough to commit to it: the
per-pass cost cannot be extrapolated from an engine that re-walks a subtree per
read, so `layout-pass-cost-prototype` writes a pass that nothing reads from and
times it first. `standards-root-box-height` is the precedent for why that order
matters -- 18 of 19 rows correct and dead on cost.

## The pass is right and 51x too expensive (B75, 2026-08-31)

`layout-pass-cost-prototype` wrote the pass, timed it, and it is dead on cost —
the second entry beside `standards-root-box-height` in the column of things this
engine can compute correctly and cannot afford. Everything below is from
`zig-out-rel-b75` in `.worktrees/layout-pass-cost-prototype` (ReleaseFast,
pinned) and the whole change is kept as
`probes/b75-layout-pass-prototype.patch` plus the branch
`prd/layout-pass-cost-prototype`. It was **not merged**.

### The pass was not a second layout algorithm

`contentHeight` already walks the children in order, pays out the collapsed
margin group in front of each one, and advances a running `total` by the child's
whole box. **That `total` IS the child's offset inside the content box being
filled** — the number `calculateDocumentPosition` has never had. So the pass is a
sink threaded through the walk that exists: hand it the absolute origin of the box
being filled and it can name where every child ends up. An optional parameter and
not a field on the Frame, because the height readers (`clientHeight`,
`scrollHeight`) call the same walk starting at an element whose own origin is
unknown.

Two things the height half gets away with and a position cannot, both isolated on
`scratch/b75/page/index.html` (15 static shapes, 45 boxes, Chrome at device
scale 2, compared by `scratch/b75/compare.mjs`):

* **`<body>`'s UA margin is invisible to the stacking walk.** `verticalMargins`
  asks `marginPx`; only `containerMarginPx` carries the 8px fallback, and it is
  used in exactly one place (the root container's own box). Every box in the table
  was 8px short in x.
* **the root's margin was escaping.** `<html>` has no border or padding, so
  `marginEscapes` let `<body>`'s top margin leave through it instead of landing
  inside — every y 8 short too. The root element's box establishes the initial
  block formatting context and there is nothing outside it for a margin to move:
  Chrome reports `<html>` at 0,0 and `<body>` at 8,8. Neither is observable today,
  because the root's `clientHeight` and `scrollHeight` both short-circuit to the
  viewport before that total is used.

The two are separable in the reading rather than stacked guesses: x depends only
on the first and y on both, and x moved on its own.

**41 of 45 positions came out byte-identical to Chrome.** The four that differ are
four things the walk does not do rather than four it does wrong, each an
independent addition on top of a static position: a relative offset (off by
exactly the declared `7,9`), auto margins (off by exactly `(400-200)/2`), a float,
and an absolute — and the engine already places the last of those correctly
through its own declaration, which is why the walk skips it. Stacking, margin
collapse, container padding, container border, both together, `margin-left`,
nesting, a declared-height container, a padded child and a line of text before a
block are all exact.

### The cost, and where it is

Each row is the warmest of three back-to-back passes over the settled document.
`measured` counts entries into `dimensionsIn` — one per box for a walk that visits
each node once, so the ratio is re-measurement. `sinkless` is the same walk with
the position sink removed.

| page | boxes placed | `measured` | per box | one pass | sinkless | us per measurement |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| synthetic, 800 flat divs | 802 | 804 | **1.0** | 2.3 ms | 2.0 ms | **2.9** |
| sony | 386 | 2 962 | 7.7 | 291 ms | 214 ms | 98 |
| macys | 1 574 | 8 851 | 5.6 | 836 ms | 766 ms | 94 |
| homedepot | 1 125 | 26 739 | **23.8** | **5 265 ms** | 4 880 ms | **197** |

Against the pass counts a cache would need (59 / 53 / 15, measured last chapter)
and the four-to-six seconds `getBoundingClientRect` costs **today**:

| station | 1 pass | x passes | today's rect cost | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| homedepot | 5 265 ms | **311 s** | 6 057 ms | **51x worse** |
| macys | 836 ms | **44.3 s** | 4 131 ms | **11x worse** |
| sony | 291 ms | 4.4 s | 4 276 ms | break-even |

The CDP timeout is 30 seconds and homedepot's whole route already takes about 22.
A cached single pass is not a net win that also buys positions — on the two big
stations it is a net **loss** of one and two orders of magnitude, and on the third
it is a wash. And these are **lower** bounds: the probe blocks the page for six
whole-document walks per tick, so the later ticks measure a starved DOM —
homedepot placed 1 125 boxes where an undisturbed settle has 3 154 elements.

### Three things the readings rule out, and the one they leave

* **not the positions.** The sinkless column is 92-93% of the total. The position
  half is 7% — 385ms of homedepot's 5 265. What is unaffordable is *one pass over
  the document*, which is a fact about the height machinery and predates this
  work.
* **not the algorithm's shape.** On plain markup the pass is flatly linear and
  *inside* the 2-5us per node the plan set as the target: 202 boxes 678us, 402
  1 329, 802 2 646, 1 602 4 662, 3 202 9 196 — 3.4, 3.3, 3.3, 2.9, 2.9 us each,
  five sizes, one shape (`scratch/b75/make-scale-pages.mjs`).
* **not the cascade, and not depth.** 802 boxes under 0, 500, 2 000 and 8 000
  stylesheet rules cost 2 506, 3 198, 2 761 and 2 790us — no trend. And a
  400-deep nest never places more than 65 boxes, because
  `MAX_CONTAINING_BLOCK_DEPTH` is 64, so depth cannot be the term either.

What is left is the per-box cost on real markup: **197us to measure one box on
homedepot against 2.9us on a bare div**, times 23.8 measurements per box. That is
68x on the measurement and 24x on the count, and both are properties of
`dimensionsIn` meeting a real page — percentages, inline runs, replaced elements,
declared sizes in units that need resolving — not of anything the pass added.

So the honest next step is not another pass and not a memo (`b73`'s memo and
`b72`'s two attempts are already in `probes/`). It is making a single box
measurement cheap on real markup, which is the same lever that would pay off the
four-to-six seconds `getBoundingClientRect` costs today whether positions are ever
computed or not. Until that moves, in-flow positions stay at `5k, 5k` — and the
`in-flow-block-position` reading stands: **26 of 27 offsets wrong, every element's
x equal to its y, and one expression sees it.**

## The seven-decimal cut is transform's, not CSS's (B75, 2026-08-31)

`transform` computed from the six-significant-figure print its own store had
already made, so `rotate(1.5707963267948966rad)` was a rotation of `1.5708`
radians. Fixed by keeping the author's text beside the print (merge
`dd0905819`); the rule that decides what "the author's text" means is measured
in `css/transform_number_format.html`'s comment and `transform.dimensionDigits`.
**A `<dimension>` inside a transform keeps at most seven digits after the decimal
point, as WRITTEN; a `<number>` and a `<percentage>` keep all of them, and an
exponent form has no decimals to cut** -- `rotate(1e-9rad)` keeps its `1e-09`
where `rotate(0.000000001rad)`, the same double, comes out `0`.

The obvious follow-up is whether that cut is a fact about CSS numbers, in which
case the length family carries the same defect and
`specified-value-keeps-precision`'s float32 model was only ever measured at large
magnitudes. **It is not.** The discriminating pair `0.000000001px` / `1e-9px`
over twelve length-valued properties -- `outline-offset`, `letter-spacing`,
`word-spacing`, `text-indent`, `border-top-width`, `padding-top`, `margin-top`,
`width`, `perspective`, `flex-basis`, `stroke-width`, `column-gap`
(`scratch/b75/expr-dimension-elsewhere.js`, Chrome 151 at device scale 2) --
answers the SAME thing for both spellings everywhere: `1e-09px` on the nine that
keep a specified number, `0px` on `width` and `border-top-width` (which snap to
the grid) and `0.5px` on `outline-offset` (which rounds to an integer-ish used
value). Zero of twelve show the pair disagreeing.

So `keepsAuthorText` naming `transform` alone is a measurement and not a
narrowing: the cut lives in Blink's parse of a transform function's arguments,
not in its CSS number tokenizer. Nothing else has to change, and a future reader
does not have to re-open it.

## An unexplored channel: how long a geometry read TAKES (B75, 2026-08-31)

Not a finding, a lead with numbers on it -- recorded because it is a *channel*
and not a candidate value, and the chapters above say that is what the two
remaining doors need.

The cost work in this chapter measured the engine's side of a geometry read for
its own sake. Turned round, the same numbers are something a PAGE can read:
anything that brackets `getBoundingClientRect` with `performance.now()` sees how
long this engine takes, and no amount of making the returned NUMBERS match Chrome
changes that.

Both arms on the same 801-box synthetic page, 20 000 calls each
(`scratch/b75/expr-geometry-read-timing.js`; Chrome at device scale 2, and 20 000
rather than 200 because `performance.now()` is coarsened and 200 calls round to
zero on the Chrome side):

| read | Chrome us/call | this engine | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| `getBoundingClientRect` | 0.235 | 8.78 | **37x** |
| `offsetHeight` | 0.115 | 7.51 | **65x** |
| `offsetTop` | 0.230 | 1.69 | 7x |
| `clientWidth` | 0.110 | 2.10 | 19x |
| `getComputedStyle().width` | 0.290 | 3.46 | 12x |
| `nodeName` (control, no layout) | 0.015 | 0.105 | 7x |

**Read the control first.** 7x of every row is general binding and interpreter
overhead, not layout -- so the layout-specific excess is about 5x for a rect and
9x for `offsetHeight`, on flat markup. What makes it worth writing down is that
those two grow with the page while the control does not: on a live homedepot the
same rect read averages **25ms** (238 calls, 6057ms, `count-position-reads.mjs`),
which is five orders of magnitude off the 0.235us above, because `dimensionsIn`
is entered 23.8 times per box there.

What would make this actionable, and what has NOT been done:

  * the Chrome side on a REAL page. The 0.235us is flat synthetic markup; nobody
    has timed Chrome's rect on homedepot, so the honest statement today is "we
    are 5-9x above our own baseline on synthetic markup and unmeasured against
    Chrome on real markup", not "we are 100000x slower";
  * whether either remaining guard times anything. `kasada-collection-map` says
    Kasada reads five faces and does not read performance entries;
    `cf-widget-timing-is-not-a-gate` causally negated a timing difference on cf
    once already -- but that was about us being FASTER than Chrome, which is a
    different claim from a layout read costting milliseconds.

So this is a channel to probe (inject a timing harness into both arms on a live
station -- `chrome-inject-needs-page-enable`, and use a beacon, per
`live-station-probe-beats-example-com`), not a defect to fix. If it turns out to
be nothing, the same numbers still price the layout work: it is the same lever
the layout-pass verdict above names.

## The keyword table's ceiling was the standard, not Chrome (B76, 2026-08-31)

`chrome_keywords.zig` is what this engine will accept as a bare identifier for
each of 682 properties, and it is generated by offering Chrome every candidate
and keeping the pairs Chrome takes. The pool of candidates was every bare
identifier appearing in any mdn-data value syntax -- and the file's own banner
already named the risk in so many words: "a keyword Chrome takes but mdn-data
does not list was never offered to it and would read as rejected here". The
remedy it prescribed was to regenerate against a newer mdn-data.

That remedy cannot work, because the gap is not mdn-data's age. mdn-data
describes the standard, so a property Chrome has and the standard does not is
simply absent from it, and an identifier only that property takes appears in no
syntax at all. Regenerating against mdn-data 3.x would still never offer it.

**How it surfaced.** Not from a property list -- from a station's own
stylesheet. Cloudflare's widget encodes the `cssText` of every rule in its own
sheet into the challenge payload, joined with `|`, and the two arms' plaintext
for that segment differed by exactly 37 characters: Chrome 20696, this engine
20659, same 183 rules. Character-diffing the one rule that differed
(`body, .main-wrapper`) leaves one declaration:

    -webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;

mdn-data 2.24.0 has no `-webkit-font-smoothing` entry, and the string
`antialiased` appears in no syntax in any of its files -- checked, not assumed.
So the keyword was never a candidate, never offered, and read as rejected.

Off the station, on one http page, six readings per value
(`scratch/b76/expr-font-smoothing.js`): 30 readings, **12 differing**, all
twelve belonging to `antialiased` and `subpixel-antialiased`, and differing the
same five ways each -- rule `cssText`, `style=` retention, `setProperty`,
`CSS.supports`, and the computed value. `auto`, `none` and a nonsense sentinel
agreed. That is
`supports-and-inline-retention-are-one-predicate` holding for a sixth time.

### The fix is the pool's ceiling

Blink ships its own list of every CSS value keyword it has,
`third_party/blink/renderer/core/css/css_value_keywords.json5`, and that is the
exact ceiling: a keyword Chrome accepts anywhere cannot be absent from it. The
generator now fetches it (pinned at commit `82774a71a4`, 1165 names, the 28
`-internal-` ones dropped because `CSSValueKeywordsWriter` restricts them to
parser modes an author sheet never uses) and unions it into the pool. Chrome
still decides every pair; only what gets offered changed.

    candidates      1053 -> 1464
    accepted pairs  14046 -> 15103
    keyword kinds added   89
    keyword kinds removed  0

Zero removed is the part worth reading: nothing that used to be accepted stopped
being accepted, so this is strictly the engine becoming less strict, in 1057
places.

**Nine of the 89 are ones real pages use constantly**, and each was a
declaration this engine dropped on the floor:

| keyword | properties | what used it |
|---|---|---|
| `revert-rule` | **all 682** | a cascade keyword Blink has and the standard does not |
| `-webkit-link`, `-webkit-activelink` | 60 each | every colour property |
| `-webkit-fill-available`, `-webkit-min-content`, `-webkit-max-content`, `-webkit-fit-content` | 18 each | the prefixed sizing keywords |
| `-webkit-box`, `-webkit-flex`, `-webkit-inline-box`, `-webkit-inline-flex` | `display` | prefixed flexbox, still in shipped CSS everywhere |
| `antialiased`, `subpixel-antialiased` | `-webkit-font-smoothing` | the one that started this |

`revert-rule` was checked separately before it was allowed to stand, because it
came out of the generator's oracle (`CSSStyleValue.parse`) rather than out of a
declaration, and Typed OM's parser is not the declaration parser. Chrome keeps
it in a rule's `cssText`, retains it from a `style=` attribute and answers
`CSS.supports(prop, 'revert-rule') === true` for `-webkit-box-flex`,
`letter-spacing` and `color` alike (`scratch/b76/expr-revert-rule.js`). It is
left in the per-property lists rather than lifted into `css_wide`: the four
consumers of `css_wide` give a keyword cascade SEMANTICS, and only acceptance
was measured here.

Test: `css/font_smoothing_keywords.html`, red first -- `expected "rule
antialiased = #p { -webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased; letter-spacing: 3px; }"
got "rule antialiased = #p { letter-spacing: 3px; }"` -- and it keeps the
refusal half, so a wider pool cannot quietly become a permissive parser.

**Where else to look.** The same shape applies to every generated table whose
candidate pool comes from the standard rather than from Chrome:
`chrome_arity.zig`, `chrome_keywords.zig`'s sibling value-class tables, and
anything else built by offering mdn-data's vocabulary to Chrome. A table
generated from a pool that cannot contain the answer records a rejection that
never happened.

## The four short values are not weighed, in either direction (B76, 2026-08-31)

B95 left the Cloudflare widget's four short numbers as the one place in the
guard's plaintext where this engine answers something Chrome does not, and
stopped with a verdict on what to do next: "the logic that computes the four
values is in the bytecode, not in the JavaScript, so reading it statically means
writing a disassembler for this VM -- a different plan".

That plan is not needed, because a door does not need to know what a value IS.
It needs to know whether the value is WEIGHED, and that is the one question
`cf-knob.mjs` was built to answer. The same hook that reads the plaintext can
replace it: substitute the four on the arm that holds a ticket and see whether
the ticket survives.

### Both arms, same epoch

`scratch/b76/knobs.mjs`, knob `short4-report` -- `TextEncoder.prototype.encode`,
counting only encodes of 24 characters or less, reporting through the stash on
Chrome (a beacon inside the widget's frame costs Chrome the ticket) and over the
wire on the arm that has no ticket to lose.

| | Chrome, cluster A | Chrome, cluster B | this engine |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `5000.266115188599` | `5002.609375` | `4998.22265625` |
| 2 | `83.9800615310669` | `87.97607231140137` | `84` |
| 3 | **`0`** | **`0`** | **`16`** |
| 4 | `0.6387105289554597` | `0.6387295662117005` | `0.639611171875` |

**Two discrete states, not two epochs, and that is a correction to B95.** B95
saw set A, then set B "an hour later", and read the pair as slow drift. It is
not drift: a day later, six consecutive runs of the same command flipped A -> B
-> B -> B -> B -> B within about four minutes, and set B is byte-identical to
what B95 recorded, verbatim, twenty-four hours earlier. Chrome alternates
between exactly two bit-exact sets. **This engine's four never move at all** --
every reading taken today, on a ReleaseFast binary of current main, is the third
set above, which is also what B69 recorded as `13, 2, 2, 14` characters.

### The Chrome arm, forced to answer ours

`short4-force` overwrites the four slots by position, unconditionally, and
reports what it overwrote -- so the run is validated after the fact rather than
before. Six passes, alternating with the controls in the same window
(`scratch/b76/p2c.sh`, and the first design in `scratch/b76/alt.sh`):

| arm | served |
|---|---|
| `none`, untouched | **11 / 11** |
| all four replaced by ours, first design (index + exact string) | 6 / 6 |
| all four replaced by ours, forced by position, `subs=4` verified per run | 4 / 5 |
| `short4-passthru` -- the same hook installed, nothing substituted | 5 / 6 |

Handing Cloudflare this engine's four answers, including the `16` where Chrome
sends `0`, costs the Chrome arm nothing that the bare hook does not cost it
anyway. The station's own rate is about five in six
(`cf-verdict-is-five-in-six`), and here the hook-only control lost one while the
substitution lost one.

**And one run answers it without any substitution at all.** In `p2c pass4` the
knob reported `short4-force=installed` from `challenges.cloudflare.com/frame`
and then made **zero** encodes of 24 characters or less -- the widget never
computed the four values that run -- and the exchange still ended
`r3:89580B=TICKET`, served. A quantity the guard sometimes does not send cannot
be one Cloudflare requires.

### The other direction

Our arm, the four replaced by Chrome's same-epoch strings, all four
substitutions confirmed in the beacon list: **0 of 5**, `r3` never anything but
`=gen`. Which is what it was before.

So the four values are neither necessary nor sufficient, and their identity is
not worth a disassembler. What a knob cannot exclude is that they are one
feature among many in a score -- but nothing in this file has ever shown
Cloudflare weighing any content of the guard's plaintext, and this was the last
qualitative difference in it.

### Two harness lessons, both of the "reads exactly like nothing happened" kind

* **The first map silently disarmed itself.** It matched on index AND the exact
  string, and the values drift between the two clusters, so a map built one
  minute earlier stops matching and substitutes nothing. `short4-force`
  overwrites by position and reports the overwritten string instead.
* **`sub=` counted out of the wrong line.** `cf-knob`'s summary line truncates
  the beacon list at six entries with an ellipsis, so a driver grepping that
  line reports a lower bound, not a count. It read `subs=2` for a run that
  `--out` showed had substituted all four. Every count in the table above comes
  from the `--out` JSON.

### The plaintext census, re-measured, and the arms' dpr

While the arms were both instrumented, B69's fifteen-encode census was retaken
-- engine side through `Context.recordTextEncode` on a Debug build (nothing in
the realm to find), Chrome side through `report-encodes`, and **Chrome at the
persona's device scale factor**, which is the correction that makes the table
readable: this engine reports `devicePixelRatio` 2 as a fixed part of its device
profile, so a Chrome reference arm at dpr 1 is off by a factor on everything
measured in device pixels (`chrome-arm-needs-persona-dpr`). `cf-knob` builds
Chrome's argv itself, so the flag goes in through a `CHROME` wrapper
(`scratch/b76/bin/chrome-dpr2`).

| segment | Chrome | this engine | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `getImageData` 48x48 | 9216 `1ly97t5` | 9216 `1xof2yz` | content |
| `readPixels` 16x16 | 1024 `ard9mt` | 1024 `ard9mt` | **same** |
| 49x44 buffer, x3 | 8624 `1m3v0nt` | 8624 `101c16` | content |
| WebGPU 32x32 | 4096 `sq54p1` | 4096 `e4lqd` | content |
| `0\|0\|0…`, x2 | 15361 `3coxr6` | 15361 `3coxr6` | **same** |
| `JSON.stringify(getComputedStyle(el))` | 30918 `t3o0bu` | 30918 `t3o0bu` | **same** |
| the widget's own CSS rules | 20696 `ug2ibx` | 20659 `1gin0ur` | 37 characters |
| four short values | 17/16/1/18 | 13/2/2/14 | not weighed, above |
| font probe list | 69 `mt6m58` | 69 `mt6m58` | **same** |

Five of fifteen byte-identical where B69 had two. Two of the three that closed
are worth naming because the record still said they were open:

* **the computed style.** B69 measured this engine 16 characters short of
  Chrome's 30918 and listed 41 disagreeing values behind it. Today, in the
  widget's own realm, the whole 30918-character string is **byte-identical** --
  475 indexed property names and 736 name-to-value pairs, zero differences
  (`scratch/b76/cs-{lp,chrome-dpr2}.txt`). At dpr 1 the Chrome arm differs in
  exactly 8 of the 736, all of them the same defect-that-is-not-one:
  `column-rule-width` and its three aliases answer `3px` undeclared at dpr 1 and
  `1.5px` at dpr 2, which `CSSStyleDeclaration.ruleWidthScale` already records
  as measured. 8 readings x 2 characters is the 16.
* **the font probe list.** B69 had 41 characters against Chrome's 69; both arms
  now spell the same six families.

That leaves the pixel buffers -- right length, wrong content, knob-tested as not
weighed long ago -- and the widget's own stylesheet, 37 characters, which is the
chapter above this one and is now fixed. **The guard's plaintext is very nearly
equal, and the station still refuses us**, which is where
`cfsc-does-not-judge-collected-values` said this would end.

**Re-measured after the keyword fix** (`e31f378d1`, ReleaseFast): the widget's
own stylesheet comes out of this engine at **20696 characters, byte-identical to
Chrome's**, and the off-site probe that found it is 30 readings, 0 differing.
Six of the fifteen encodes now match byte for byte. What is left in the guard's
plaintext is three pixel-buffer families -- right length, wrong content, knob-
tested as not weighed years of chapters ago -- and four short values that this
chapter shows Cloudflare does not weigh. The station is still `served=false`.

## The count that was the only thing saying no (B77, 2026-08-31)

`chrome_keywords.zig` had its candidate pool raised from "the standard" to
"Blink" one chapter ago. The same defect was still live one table over, and this
time it had already been noticed and worked around rather than fixed.

`chrome_arity.one_component` lists 461 property names measured to take no second
component, and the engine reads it as a licence to refuse: `margin-top: 1px 2px`
is thrown away the way Chrome throws it away. A property earns its place there
by refusing **everything the sweep offered it**, which makes the offer the
ceiling — and an offer that never reaches a property's real two-component
grammar reads exactly like Chrome refusing it. Both halves of the offer were
too low:

* the identifier pool was every bare identifier in an mdn-data value syntax, so
  `links` and `tabs` were never paired with anything and
  `scroll-marker-group: after links` read as refused;
* the nineteen generic values carried no **function call**, so
  `clip-path: circle() padding-box`, `shape-outside: circle() border-box` and
  `border-shape: circle() circle()` were never offered either.

The second one was already known, in the sense that matters least. Somebody had
hit it on `transform`, and instead of fixing the sweep they wrote an exemption
into `CSSStyleDeclaration.tooManyComponents` whose comment says it outright:
the sweep "never offered `transform` two of them ... so it reads as
one-component, and `rotate(0deg) scale(1)` was thrown away". Nobody wrote the
same exemption for the other three, so those three stayed broken. **A
hand-written exemption for one victim of a generated table's ceiling is a
sighting of the ceiling, not a fix for it.**

Fixed by widening both halves. The identifier pool now unions Blink's own
`css_value_keywords.json5` (pinned at `82774a71a4`, the same file and pin the
keyword table uses): 1050 → 1461 candidates. `GENERIC` gains sixteen shapes the
nineteen never offered — a function call, a resolution, a frequency, a
dashed-ident, a line-name list, an `an+b`. `var()`, `env()` and `attr()` are
deliberately **not** among them: a declaration holding one parses for every
property there is, so offering one would empty the table rather than widen it.
Attribution, one axis at a time, each a full regeneration:

| offer | one_component | comma_lists | rows moved |
|---|---|---|---|
| as shipped (baseline) | 461 | 111 | reproduces the committed table byte for byte |
| + Blink keyword pool | 460 | 111 | `scroll-marker-group` out |
| + 16 generic shapes | 452 | 115 | `transform`, `-webkit-transform`, `clip-path`, `-webkit-clip-path`, `shape-outside`, `-webkit-shape-outside`, `animation-trigger`, `border-shape` out; 4 comma rows in |
| + `KEYWORD_CAP` 16 → 32 | 452 | 115 | **not one row** — the cap is not a ceiling |

The baseline row is the point of the table: an unmodified regeneration
reproduced the committed file byte for byte, so Chrome had not drifted and every
later diff is the offer's.

`transform` leaves the table, so its exemption had to become a rule: the count
is still answered for it, just explicitly rather than by an accident of the
sweep. `transform: rotate(45deg) 5px` is still refused.

**What it cost, stated rather than hidden.** The count was also the only thing
refusing an *invalid* second component on these four properties, because
`shorthand.refusesLonghand` grades a component only against
`chrome_shorthands.value_classes` — and that table is generated by walking the
longhands of the shorthands the generator probes, so a longhand nothing expands
to, which is what all four of these are, is never graded. Six declarations
Chrome drops are now kept: `clip-path: circle() nonsense`,
`shape-outside: circle() nonsense`, `border-shape: circle() nonsense`,
`border-shape: 1px 2px`, `scroll-marker-group: after nonsense`,
`scroll-marker-group: links after`. Over the shape/box matrix the two arms went
from **34 of 68 readings differing to 9**; over the assertion table, from 16 of
52 to 12. Trading this way round is what the table's own header asks for: a
property wrongly refused "loses a style the page was written with -- the one
kind of wrong these tables exist never to be".

**A rule that looked right and was measured wrong.** The obvious way to keep
those six refusals is to grade the pair's trailing identifier against the
property's keyword list, with an exemption — measured, three sentinel
identifiers, 21 properties — for the ones that take an author's own name there
(`animation: 1s slidein`, `transition: 1s my-prop`). It was built, and it
refused `scroll-marker-group: after links`, which Chrome keeps: the keyword
lists are measured by offering each identifier **alone**, and half of a
two-component grammar routinely does not parse alone at *either* end —
`align-items: first baseline` leads with such a modifier, `after links` trails
with one. Reverted. The residual's only honest fix is measuring value classes
for the longhands no shorthand reaches, which is the third instance of this same
ceiling and is now written down in `shorthand.valueClasses`.

`src/browser/tests/css/arity_pool_ceiling.html`, 24 rows, red before and green
after; the red light named the value (`inline clip-path: circle() padding-box =
(refused)`). Every expectation in it was measured on Chrome 151 first
(`scratch/b77/expr-assertions.js`, 52 readings). Full suite 1595/1595.

**Swept after the merge** (`e6bb70c9c`, ReleaseFast `zig-out-b77`, six groups in
separate processes): **21 of 29 stations pass**, and the eight that do not are
station for station the same eight as before the change — `cf-scrapingcourse`,
`cf-nopecha`, `cf-zeroclover`, `dd-datadome`, `dd-g2`, `dd-saks`,
`dd-allopneus`, `x-hyatt`. One caution for the next reader: the `dd-` group came
back `0/8` on its first run, `timeout: Runtime.enable` on `dd-datadome` and
`timeout: Page.navigate` on the seven behind it. That is
`sweep-timeout-tail-is-one-crash` again, and it was transient rather than a
regression — `dd-datadome` alone answers `datadome-challenge` 2/2 on this build
*and* 2/2 on the previous one, and the other seven all answer normally when run
one at a time.

**None of this opens a door.** It is one more instance of a class: a generated
table whose candidate pool is narrower than Chrome, which records "never asked"
as "Chrome refused". Three instances are now known — `chrome_keywords` (fixed,
B76), `chrome_arity` (fixed here), `chrome_shorthands.value_classes` (open, and
the reason six declarations above are still wrong). `dump-css-units.mjs` is the
counter-example worth copying: it brute-forces all 475 254 alphabetic spellings
up to four letters rather than trusting a list, and has no ceiling at all.

## Half of a gradient's colours were already right (B77, 2026-08-31)

`getComputedStyle` is the surface Cloudflare's collector walks — 736 property
names, read one at a time — so a computed value this engine spells differently
is a reading a guard already has. `background-image` was one of them.

`color: red` computes to `rgb(255, 0, 0)` here, and has for a long time:
`computedColourText` folds a named colour on the computed surface. It takes the
*whole* value, though, and refuses anything carrying a `(`, a `#`, a comma or a
space — because what reaches it as a colour is a bare keyword. So
`background-image: linear-gradient(red, blue)` went straight past it and
computed to itself, where Chrome answers
`linear-gradient(rgb(255, 0, 0), rgb(0, 0, 255))`.

What makes it a gap rather than a design is the other half of the same gradient:
`linear-gradient(#ff0000, #0000ff)` and `linear-gradient(rgb(1, 2, 3), hsl(0,
100%, 50%))` were *already* folded, by `canonicaliseValue`'s token walk, which
folds a hash or a colour call wherever it finds one. Only the bare keyword was
left as written — the one spelling a hand-written stylesheet is most likely to
use.

Two measurements decided the shape of the fix, and both of them ruled out the
obvious implementation:

* **Chrome does not fold at specified time.** `el.style.backgroundImage` reads
  back `linear-gradient(red, blue)` in Chrome, exactly as this engine already
  answered it. Putting the fold in `canonicaliseValue` — where the hash fold
  lives — would have been a fresh divergence on the inline surface to close one
  on the computed surface.
* **Depth is not the rule.** `counter(red)`, `counters(red, ".")`,
  `repeat(2, [red] 1fr)`, `styleset(red)`, `swash(red)` and `url(.../red)` all
  put `red` inside a call, and Chrome folds none of them: there it is a counter
  name, a line name, a feature name, a path. A blanket "an identifier inside a
  call that spells a colour is a colour" would have thrown away six real values
  to fix eleven.

So the walk carries a stack of enclosing function names and folds only inside
the fourteen measured to hold a `<color>`: the six gradient functions, their
four `-webkit-` spellings, `-webkit-gradient`'s inner `from`/`to`/`color-stop`,
and `drop-shadow`. The property is not part of the question — measured,
`linear-gradient(red, blue)` folds under `background-image`, `mask-image`,
`border-image-source` and the `background` shorthand alike.

`src/browser/tests/css/computed_colour_in_function.html`, 25 rows, red before
and green after; every expectation measured on Chrome 151 first
(`scratch/b77/expr-foldassert.js`, `expr-foldwhere.js`, `expr-foldrest.js`). The
eleven that differed were colour-only, and the ten negative controls agreed
before the fix as well as after. Full suite 1596/1596.

One expectation in the test was wrong on the first run and the engine was right:
`url(red)` computes to an absolute URL against the document, and the Chrome
reading had been taken on a `data:` page where there is no document to resolve
against. The control now uses an absolute URL. That is
[[generated-tables-can-be-wrong]] in its third form — a hand-written
expectation, measured on the wrong page.

**Still open in the same family, each needing more than the fold** and so
deliberately not hidden behind it: `image-set(linear-gradient(red, blue) 1x)`
(Chrome also answers `1dppx`), `filter: drop-shadow(0px 0px red)` (Chrome also
reorders the colour to the front and pads to three lengths), `-webkit-gradient`
(Chrome rewrites `left top` to `0% 0%`), the prefixed gradients' inserted
default direction (`-webkit-linear-gradient(red, blue)` gains a `top`),
`color-mix()` and `light-dark()` (evaluated, not folded), `box-shadow` and
`text-shadow` computed shape, and `getComputedStyle(el).webkitTextStroke`, which
this engine answers `undefined` where Chrome answers `1px rgb(255, 0, 0)`.

## The stall is the cascade, and B75's page hid that (B99, 2026-08-31)

`datadome-watchdog-stall` E1 asked whether the 30-second watchdog stall on
dd-datadome was something DataDome waits for. It is not, and it is not
dd-datadome's either. Grepping the top-level `engineLog` of the 252 archived
lightpanda sweeps finds the stall fifteen times across **four** stations
(dd-datadome x7, ak-homedepot x3, ak-kohls x2, ak-expedia x2), and in fourteen of
the fifteen the first station that broke had `first=200` -- the real site had
just been handed over. B98 hunted it on dd-datadome, which serves the real page
in only 23% of 127 runs and closes its window when hammered; **ak-homedepot
serves it in 91% of 64** and does not punish repetition.

### It is not a loop

`Watchdog.zig` fires only when `wait_depth == 0` and nothing has called `touch()`
for 30s, and `touch()` is at the top of `Runner._tick`. So a stall is not "a
condition that never converges" -- it is **one tick, macrotask batch included,
that runs for thirty seconds**.

`sample` on two live stations (ReleaseFast; a Debug build would make the stall
indistinguishable from the build being slow) says where those seconds go. Read
`sample`'s own third section, `Sort by top of stack` -- counting how many lines
of the call graph mention a symbol counts *paths*, not time, and by that measure
`Element.dimensionsIn` looks like the most expensive thing in the engine when its
self time is under five samples. It is the path, not the price.

| self samples | share of the busy thread | symbol |
|---:|---:|---|
| 5923 | 44.4% | `StyleManager.cascadedNamedDeclaration…check` |
| 2067 | 15.5% | `selector.List.matchesPart` |
| 1966 | 14.7% | `selector.List.matches` |
| 1086 | 8.1% | `StyleManager.cascadedDeclaration…check` |

Taking only `StyleManager.cascaded*` and `webapi.selector.*`: **86.9% and 88.7%
of the busy worker thread on ak-homedepot** (two runs), **69.3% on ak-macys**.
Not one number -- the stations differ, and any retelling should carry the station
name with the figure.

So the stall is a product: `getBoundingClientRect` walks the subtree, each node
is asked for ~24 properties, and **every one of those asks re-resolves the
cascade**. `scratch/b99/cascade-cost.mjs` serves its own synthetic page and needs
no station window: 33-36 ns x rules x nodes x reads, flatly linear, and
`--decls 8 --grid 3000x3000x120` reproduces `watchdog stall stalled_ms=30237`
byte-for-byte with the live signature. That is the first deterministic offline
reproduction this stall has had.

### Why B75 ruled the cascade out, and why that reading was the page

`The pass is right and 51x too expensive (B75)` above says, in the list of things
the cost is *not*: "**not the cascade, and not depth.** 802 boxes under 0, 500,
2 000 and 8 000 stylesheet rules cost 2 506, 3 198, 2 761 and 2 790us — no
trend."

Every rule on `scratch/b75/page/scale-css-*.html` ends in `span:nth-child(N)`,
and the body of those pages holds **801 divs and zero spans**. Rules are bucketed
by their rightmost compound, so all 8 000 landed in `tag_rules[span]` and no
element in the document ever reached one of them. The rule count could have been
a million.

`scratch/b99/b75-bucket-artifact.mjs` holds everything else fixed -- same node
count, same rule bodies, same engine -- and changes only that tag:

| rightmost | 0 rules | 500 | 2 000 | 8 000 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `span` (B75's shape) | 2.3 ms | 4.8 | 3.2 | 2.4 |
| `div` (reachable) | 4.9 ms | 485 | 1 935 | **8 381** |

The flat row reproduces B75's reading exactly. **So "not the cascade" was a
property of that page, not of the engine**, and the sentence it supports -- "what
is left is the per-box cost on real markup … properties of `dimensionsIn` meeting
a real page" -- misattributes the cost the chapter correctly measured. The live
sample above is the direct evidence: on homedepot the per-box cost *is* the
cascade.

That matters beyond this stall, because B75 shelved `layout-pass-cost-prototype`
on cost alone, and that prototype fixes a real reading surface: **26 of 27
in-flow offsets wrong, every element's x equal to its y, one expression sees it**.
Its 51x verdict was priced against a term that was misidentified, so it deserves
re-pricing rather than standing as a closed door.

### What moved, and what did not

`cascade-declaration-name-index` (merged) gives each rule a 128-bit filter over
the names it declares, two bits per name, hashed once per read and tested with
one AND. A false positive costs only the scan that used to happen
unconditionally, so it cannot change an answer. Two arms alternated, three rounds,
2 000 rules x 2 000 nodes: **1.00x / 1.54x / 1.92x / 2.46x** at 1 / 4 / 8 / 16
declarations per rule -- the point being that the cost stops tracking the
declaration count at all. On ak-homedepot the `check` self time went 5346 -> 2624
and the cascade share 88.7% -> 79.3%. On the synthetic stall cell it is the
difference between `stalled_ms=30237` and finishing in 26.7 s: **progress, not
headroom.**

Two things it does *not* do, both measured rather than assumed:

* **it does nothing when the rules declare few names.** On the B75-shaped page
  above (two declarations per rule) the mask arm reads 461 / 1 907 / 9 117 ms
  against 485 / 1 935 / 8 381 -- noise. That page's cost is the selector matching
  underneath, 801 divs against 8 000 rules whose ancestor parts match nothing.
  An ancestor filter is the lever there; it is measured but not planned, because
  nobody has yet shown that shape is what a real page looks like.
* **it does not remove the repeated-read factor.** 2 000 x 2 000 costs 425 ms at
  one read and 1 462 ms at ten -- repeats are barely discounted.
  `cascade-per-element-memo` is that lever, and it inherits B73's warning: the
  memo B73 tried died on real pages because the page kept mutating the DOM
  between reads. B73 memoised the geometry, which was the wrong layer, but its
  observation about invalidation applies to the style layer just the same and
  should be measured before that plan writes any code.

### A methodology note worth more than the fix

Three separate benchmark pages in this chapter -- B75's and two of mine -- each
reported "the cascade does not cost anything", and all three were wrong for the
same reason: **the synthetic page's data distribution is itself a premise, and
each of them quietly made the cascade unreachable.** B75's rules were bucketed
under a tag the page did not contain. My first probe declared only `margin-top`,
so `declared_longhands` returned at its first line for nearly every read. My
second made *every* rule declare *every* property the layout reads, so the
name filter could only ever cost -- it measured 7% slower, three rounds
consistent, and I nearly killed a 2x lever on it.

A synthetic benchmark's force comes entirely from resembling real input, and that
resemblance is an assertion to test, not a backdrop. When a synthetic reading is
flat where theory says it should not be, suspect the page before the engine, and
cross-check against a `sample` of a live station -- which is the ground truth for
exactly this class of premise.

## The cache pays where the page does not mutate, and that is most of it (B99, 2026-08-31)

`cascade-per-element-memo` is the second of the two levers the chapter above
named, and the one that carries the repeated-read factor. It is merged.

### The premise B73 left, measured

B73's memo over the height walk died on live pages, and its note reads "页面自己在
建 DOM，几乎每次读之间都失效". Any cross-read cache inherits that objection, so it
was worth one measurement before writing a line of it.
`scratch/b99/mutation-between-reads-sync.mjs` installs a document-start hook that
wraps the mutation entry points **synchronously** — appendChild and friends,
setAttribute and friends, `classList`, and the `className` / `id` / `innerHTML` /
`textContent` setters — plus `getBoundingClientRect` and five layout accessors,
and counts whether anything landed since the previous read. Synchronously,
because a MutationObserver reads optimistic by construction: its callback is a
microtask, so a script doing mutate-read-mutate-read inside one task has not been
told about any of it yet, and every one of those reads counts clean. (The
observer version said 91.2% on homedepot against the synchronous 88.5% — a small
bias, in the direction predicted.)

| station | layout reads | mutations | reads with a mutation since the last | would hit | longest clean run |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| homedepot | 314 | 2 898 | 36 | 88.5% | 87 |
| kohls | 1 943 | 2 066 | 25 | 98.7% | 1 295 |
| macys | **21 695** | 40 094 | 35 | **99.8%** | 19 286 |

So B73's sentence does not survive contact with the number: a real page asks for
its own geometry thousands of times per load — macys 21 695 times — and touches
the document between almost none of those asks. **B73's memo failed because it
was on the wrong layer, not because pages mutate too often**, and that sentence
should stop being quoted as an argument against caching across reads.

### What it moved

`cascadedNamedDeclaration` keeps what it answered per element and property,
misses included, and drops everything when `Page.dom_version` moves or the rules
are rebuilt. Wholesale, because one inserted node changes what `:nth-child`, `+`
and `~` match for elements nobody touched.

| build | cascade+selector share of the busy thread | `cascadedNamedDeclaration` self |
|---|---:|---:|
| main before B99 | 88.7% | 5 393 |
| + name filter | 79.3% | 2 694 |
| + this cache | **33.6%** | **82** |

The synthetic stall cell goes from `stalled_ms=30237`-and-killed to 15 557ms —
half the watchdog rather than three seconds under it. The B75-shaped page (8 000
rules over 801 boxes) goes from 8 381ms to **191**, a shape the name filter could
not touch at all because its rules declare two names.

### And where it does not: the real-station number is a third, not a half

Timing the page's own reads in place on ak-homedepot (`live-read-cost.mjs`, four
samples per arm, arms alternated):

| | mean per read | worst single read | layout total per load |
|---|---|---|---|
| main | ~21 ms | median ~2 500 ms (2 354–4 247) | ~4 580 ms |
| merged | ~15 ms | median ~1 607 ms (1 571–2 572) | ~3 695 ms |

**−29% on the mean, −35% on the worst read** — real, and well short of the
synthetic 2x. The reason is in the table above rather than in the code: the
synthetic page never mutates, homedepot mutates before 36 of its 314 reads, and
every one of those empties the cache. The expensive reads are exactly the ones
that follow a mutation with nothing left to hit.

That prices the next lever, which is **not invalidating wholesale**. It is also
the hard one: a per-element or per-subtree scheme has to account for the
siblings and ancestors whose match changed without being touched, which is the
reason this one is wholesale. Measured, not planned.

### What could not be answered, and the arithmetic saying so

`datadome-watchdog-stall` E4 asks whether dd-datadome's verdict changes once the
stall is fixed. It cannot be answered here, and the numbers are worth writing
down so nobody spends the twenty hours finding out:

* dd-datadome has 83 archived runs with a first status: 59 challenges, 20 passes,
  and 4 where it served `200` and the stall turned the run into an error. Fixing
  the stall moves the pass rate from **24.1% to 28.9%** — 4.8 points. Two
  proportions at 80% power and α=0.05 want **1 343 runs per arm**, about
  20.5 hours each at 55s a run. Same wall as
  `hyatt-now-issues-tickets-sometimes`.
* The obvious cheaper proxy, "how often does a sweep survive", is no better: the
  archived stall rate on ak-homedepot is 3 in 64, and ten runs on the
  **unfixed** build already produced none.

What is verifiable is the margin, because every load yields a reading rather than
waiting on a rare event: the offline repro moved from killed-at-30s to half the
threshold, and the worst real-station read fell by a third. That is the answer
E4 gets.

### One more thing today's sweeps showed, twice

Both A/B pairs ran as blocks — arm A's 29 stations, then arm B's. In both pairs
the **first** arm was handed dd-datadome's real page (`doc=200`, and stalled),
and the **second** got the challenge (`doc=403->200`). Two out of two. The
station hardens against a repeat visit inside a window, so which arm ran first is
a confound, and the striking `6/29 vs 21/29` in both pairs is the stall cascade —
one stall turns the twenty stations after it into errors — not the change.
`antibot-stations-pass-in-windows` already said "只能交替对拍"; the lesson is that
**alternate means per station**, A then B on the same station before moving on,
not per arm.

## The layout pass was never 51x too expensive; the cascade was (B99, 2026-09-01)

`layout-pass-reprice` re-priced the prototype B75 shelved. Its verdict was
"the pass is right and 51x too expensive", and the chapter above already showed
that the cost term it exonerated -- the cascade -- was exonerated by a benchmark
page whose rules were unreachable. This is what the pass costs once the cascade
is actually paid for.

The prototype (`prd/layout-pass-cost-prototype`, two commits, 253 lines) merges
onto today's main with **no conflicts** and the suite stays green, so B75's other
half -- "the pass is right" -- still holds a month and three caches later.

### Three caches, measured one at a time

| station | B75 | + name filter, + cross-read cache | + fixed-property cache | total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| homedepot | 5 265 ms | 2 714 ms | **582 ms** | **9.0x** |
| macys | 836 ms | 314 ms | **40 ms** | **20.9x** |
| sony | 291 ms | 74 ms | **21 ms** | **13.9x** |

Per measured box: homedepot 197 -> 90.8 -> **21.3 us**, macys 94 -> 35.7 ->
**5.2**, sony 98 -> 24.9 -> **7.0**. Node counts match B75's within a few
percent (sony's `placed=386 / measured=2962` is identical), so these are the same
pages doing the same work for less.

The third cache is the one that moved it most, and it was invisible until the
second was in place. Five properties -- `display`, `visibility`, `font-size`,
`font-family`, `text-transform` -- are lifted out of the declaration list into
named fields on the rule and read through `cascadedDeclaration`, a different
function with its own walk. With `cascadedNamedDeclaration` cached they were
what was left: 6.8% of the busy thread themselves and 26.1% underneath in
selector matching on plain main, 17.6% and 65.1% under the prototype. Cached,
ak-homedepot's whole cascade-and-selector family falls from **61.8% of the busy
thread to 1.6%**, and the engine's total self time by 89% -- while building
slightly *more* DOM than the uncached arm (3 351 nodes against 3 254), which is
what says the win is not the page failing to load.

### The denominator moved too, so the ratio is the wrong way to say it

What one layout read costs the page on ak-homedepot, timed in place:

| build | mean | worst single read | layout total per load |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| main before B99 | ~21 ms | ~2 500 ms | ~4 580 ms |
| + first two caches | ~15 ms | ~1 607 ms | ~3 695 ms |
| + fixed-property cache | **~3.1 ms** | **~420 ms** | **~1 130 ms** |

Mean 6.8x, worst read 6x, total 4x. **The worst single read went from two and a
half seconds to four hundred milliseconds**, which is where the watchdog margin
comes from and why the offline stall cell now finishes in half the threshold.

So state the verdict in absolute cost rather than as a ratio, since both sides
fell. Enabling the pass costs `passes needed x one pass` (counts are B75's):

* **sony 15 x 21ms = 0.3 s** -- affordable.
* **macys 53 x 40ms = 2.1 s** -- affordable.
* **homedepot 59 x 582ms = 34 s** -- still fatal on its own; the watchdog is 30.

**"51x too expensive" is dead as a description, but it did not become "ship
it".** It became one remaining term, and a measured one: the pass *count*.
88.5% of homedepot's layout reads sit on a document nothing has mutated since
the previous read, so memoising the pass itself on `Page.dom_version` -- the same
key the cascade caches already use -- puts homedepot at roughly 7 passes,
**4.1 s**. That is the next plan's shape, and until it exists the prototype stays
on `prd/layout-pass-reprice`, unmerged.

Two limits on the numbers above: only homedepot's denominator was re-measured
(macys and sony reuse B75's), and the pass counts 59/53/15 are B75's and were not
re-measured either.

### The in-flow offset tell is no longer blocked by an unknown

`in-flow-block-position`'s reading stands: **26 of 27 offsets wrong, every
element's x equal to its y, and one expression sees it.** What has changed is
that it is no longer waiting on a cost nobody had located. It is waiting on one
named, priced, mechanically-familiar piece of work.

## The last four ways a document answers to a name (B80, 2026-09-01)

`four-name-questions-sweep` closed with four differences left and a ranking by
"can one expression see it". All four are closed now, and the last of them
uncovered something worth more than the four together.

### The two names that were deliberately absent

`CSS.registerProperty` and `CSS.paintWorklet` were left off the CSS namespace
object on the grounds that a present-but-inert name is its own kind of lie, and
the file said what each would have to do to earn its place. Both now do it.

A registration reaches the cascade, and all four of its effects are
page-visible (Chrome 151, `scratch/b80/registered.mjs` and `scratch/b80/q6.js`):

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| enumerated by `getComputedStyle` on every element | absent | yes |
| `<length>` `2em` against a 10px font | absent | `20px` |
| `<color>` `red` | absent | `rgb(255, 0, 0)` |
| `<angle>` `0.5turn` / `<time>` `500ms` / `<resolution>` `96dpi` | absent | `180deg` / `0.5s` / `1dppx` |
| a value that does not parse for the syntax | absent | falls back to the initial value |
| `inherits: false` on a child | absent | the initial value, not the parent's |

The initial value is computed once, at registration, because the spec asks it to
be *computationally independent* -- `initialValue: '2em'` is refused with a
message of its own, which is what makes one stored string enough for every
element. Twelve refusals are Chrome's wording verbatim, including the reading
order: `inherits` is checked before the name, so `{name: 'x', syntax: '*'}`
reports the missing member rather than the bad name.

`CSS.paintWorklet` hands out the `Worklet` Web Audio already had, and the paint
half of `addModule` loads for real: the URL is resolved against the document
base, the module is fetched -- filed as a `script` resource entry the way
Chrome's is -- and compiled, so a module that does not parse rejects with V8's
parse message. Seven settle cases agree with Chrome exactly
(`scratch/b80/addmodule.mjs`), including `AbortError: Unable to load a worklet's
module.` for a 404 and `SyntaxError: 'http://[::' is not a valid URL.` for an
unparseable one. The audio half still rejects everything, and that stays
deliberate: AudioWorkletNode refuses to construct *because* no module loaded, so
a resolved `audioWorklet.addModule` would contradict it. Nothing downstream of a
paint worklet contradicts anything, because nothing rasterises.

### location.valueOf, and the slot that carries the order

`Object.getOwnPropertyNames(location)` opens with `valueOf` in every browser and
did not here. HTML's "create a Location object" steps define it before any IDL
member, which is both why it exists and why it sorts first, and the value has to
be the realm's own `%Object.prototype.valueOf%` -- true per realm, so a child
frame's Location carries the child's.

The source said a template cannot carry a per-context object, which is right.
What it can carry is the *slot*: the template reserves `valueOf` before the
unforgeable members, writable and configurable, and the wrap replaces the value
with the realm's function and Chrome's attribute bits. Redefining an own
property keeps its insertion position, and the position is the whole point.
Five readings agree, in the child realm as well as the page's.

### document.all, and four expectations that came from us

One name reaching more than one element answers an HTMLCollection, not the first
match, and the lookup is one set: any element whose `id` matches plus the
"all"-named kinds whose `name` does, in tree order. Measured over every way two
elements can share a name.

The call form had two bugs beside it. `document.all()` with no argument threw
"invalid argument", and every miss -- absent argument, out-of-range index,
negative index, unknown name -- answered `undefined` where Chrome answers
`null`. **The four `undefined` expectations in the test had been written from
this engine's own answer**, which is the third instance of that failure mode in
this repo's tests and the reason a hand-written expectation gets a probe.

### One row asserted as it is: collections have no identity here

`document.forms === document.forms` is true in Chrome and false here. So are
`images`, `all`, `getElementsByTagName('div')` and `body.children` -- five for
five (`scratch/b80/q9.js`), because every accessor builds a fresh wrapper: the
bridge's identity map keys on the Zig pointer and each call allocates a new one.

That is one expression, it needs no knowledge of the page, and it is *cheaper*
than anything else left in this family -- one change covers five or more
accessors. It is asserted in `document/all_collection.html` as
`same=false (Chrome: true)` rather than skipped, so fixing it turns that row red
instead of leaving it silent.

### [LegacyOverrideBuiltIns], and what it cost

`<form name="title">` makes `document.title` the form in every browser. Thirteen
names measured, covering an accessor, an operation and Object.prototype's own:
all thirteen lose to the form. The handler was `kNonMasking`, so a name any link
of the chain answered never reached it.

Masking it means the ordering question becomes ours to answer, because V8
consults a masking interceptor *before* the own properties while the spec puts
named properties after them, and the vendored V8 C API has no
`HasRealNamedProperty` to ask with (asking through `Object.Has` re-enters the
handler). `location` is the whole list -- the only `[LegacyUnforgeable]` member a
Document has, therefore its only own property -- so the handler declines that one
name, with a comptime check to keep the list honest. The name stays *listed*
either way, because it is a supported property name whether or not it wins.

It also means every property read on `document` enters the getter, so the cost
of the named-object list became the cost of reading `document.body`:

| 2000 reads, 4000-element page | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| settled document (`scratch/b79/named-cost.mjs`) | 2ms | 2ms |
| **during the parse** (`scratch/b80/parse-cost.mjs`) | **1249ms** | **2ms** |

The list is cached against `Page.dom_version`, and the parser does not move that
version -- the previous answer to that was to rebuild per lookup while the
document is loading, which is where the 1249ms comes from and which was
affordable only because most reads did not reach the handler. So the parser now
keeps its own counter, `Page.parser_dom_version`, which the named-object cache
checks alongside the DOM version and nothing else looks at. Chrome is 1ms.

Isolation-checked both ways: with the parser half of the key removed, the list
freezes empty again -- all eight named objects read `undefined` and neither
`getOwnPropertyNames` nor `keys` lists them, which is the bug
`document/named_objects.html`'s first block exists to catch.

### The bug that was underneath: a thrown exception's message is borrowed

Turning the handler masking made `WebApi: TimeRanges` fail with a message no
browser writes: `currentScriptcute 'start' on 'TimeRanges': ...`. Thirteen bytes
of `Failed to exe` replaced by thirteen bytes of `currentScript`.

**It predates all of this.** `DOMException.init` borrows both of its strings, and
a caller that formatted a message -- `TimeRanges`'s bounds sentence -- had it on
the per-call scratch arena. The struct is copied into the context arena when it
becomes a JS object; the strings are not. Measured on main's own binary
(`scratch/b80/q12.js`):

```
first       "Failed to execute 'start' on '"
afterAlloc  "aVeryLongIdNobodyHastart' on '"   <- one getElementById later
afterAlloc2 "currentScriptbodyHastart' on '"   <- one more
```

Masking only made the clobbering allocation land on a path the test suite walks.
And it is not a corner: a guard catches exceptions and reads them back later --
Kasada rejects twenty-five promises in a row on x-hyatt to collect the messages
(README, x-hyatt) -- so what it read here was text no browser produces.

Fixed at the mechanism rather than at the call site. `Local.mapZigInstanceToJs`
already copies a by-value struct into the context arena; a type that borrows
strings now says so with `ownStrings` and takes them along in the same move,
which covers every `init` caller whatever the provenance of what it passed
instead of auditing the fifty that hand over a variable.

**The repro needs a task boundary, and that is why the existing test was green.**
`domexception.html`'s older block churns the arena inside one task and passes:
those three paths go through `Context.fail`, which copies as it throws, and
within one task the arena only bumps forward rather than landing back on the
message's head. Catch in one task, read in the next with one short string
crossing the bridge in between, and it fails -- which is the shape a page uses.
A sentinel proved the same-task rows really ran, so their green was a wrong
repro shape rather than a false green.

### Where the doors are

Unmoved. `19/29` on the merged binary against `20/29` on the pre-merge one, and
the difference is `dd-leboncoin` -- the DataDome column this README has a whole
section about.

That is not an inference from the section. Both binaries were run station by
station over the eight DataDome stations, alternating, twice each in one sitting
(`scratch/b80/dd-ab.sh`, `scratch/b80/dd-{base,new}-{1,2}.json`). Every cell
agrees between the two arms except one, and it is not a disagreement between
them:

```
                base r1   base r2   new r1    new r2
  dd-leboncoin  pass      challenge challenge challenge
  dd-etsy       pass      pass      pass      pass
  dd-seloger    pass      pass      pass      pass
  everything else        identical across all four
```

**The pre-merge binary stopped passing leboncoin between its own two rounds**,
before the merged binary's second round ran. The window closed for the arm that
had it. One pass in eight station-visits is what this vendor looks like from this
address, and `one-sweep-cannot-tell-a-door-from-a-window` is the memory for it.

Every Akamai station, px-wayfair, ks-canadagoose, x-sony, x-zillow and the six
passing Cloudflare stations are unchanged; `cf-scrapingcourse` and `x-hyatt` are
still the two real gaps.

## The last uncached cascade path, and the layout pass clears its budget (B99, 2026-09-01)

`visibility-cascade-cache` is the fourth and last of the caches, and the one that
put the shelved layout pass inside its budget.

### Why it was left out, and why the reason was wrong

`isElementHidden` ran its rule scan **seeded with the element's inline style**, so
the scan pruned against those values and the answer depended on them. That is why
the first three caches skipped it, and with them in place it was what remained:
under the layout-pass prototype a sample of ak-homedepot put it at 16.5% of the
busy thread and the selector matching it drives at 50.8%.

The reading that shaped the fix was that `CSSStyleDeclaration.zig` **never calls
`Frame.domChanged`** — `grep -c` returns 0 — so `el.style.display = 'none'` looked
like a change no `dom_version`-keyed cache could hear about. **That inference was
wrong**, and the experiment that caught it is worth more than the fix: a
deliberately broken variant that cached the whole predicate, inline included, was
run twice. Sharing the `dom_version` invalidation, the inline assertions all
passed; with **no invalidation at all**, four of them went red immediately. So
`dom_version` does move on an inline write — via
`CSSStyleDeclaration.syncStyleAttribute` writing back to the `style` attribute,
which reaches `Attribute.List.putSafe` and `domChanged` one level out of the file
that was grepped.

**A grep over one file answers "does this file contain that call", not "does this
operation invalidate".** The second question is a property of the whole call
stack, and the way to answer it is to switch the invalidation off and see whether
an assertion notices. That same experiment is what showed the four inline
assertions had teeth, rather than assuming it.

So the split stands, but for a different reason than correctness: `ruleHiding`'s
answer takes no `options`, so one entry per element serves every caller, where
caching the predicate would need up to sixteen. It also matches what
`computedDisplay` and `declaredDeclaration` already do — read inline outside the
cache and merge it on top. The refactor landed and the suite ran green **before**
any cache went in, which is what says the two forms are equivalent; the merge
reaches the seeded loop's verdict because `beatenBy` is a total order and max is
associative.

### One document-wide pass, priced four times

| station | B75 | + name filter, cross-read | + fixed properties | + this | µs per measured box |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| homedepot | 5 265 ms | 2 714 ms | 582 ms | **88 ms** | 197 → 90.8 → 21.3 → **3.22** |
| macys | 836 ms | 314 ms | 40 ms | **54 ms** | 94 → 35.7 → 5.2 → **4.64** |
| sony | 291 ms | 74 ms | 21 ms | **8 ms** | 98 → 24.9 → 7.0 → **2.64** |

**3.22 µs a box on homedepot is the plain-markup floor.** The same walk over 800
bare divs costs 3.05 µs a box today and 3.98 over 3 200
(`scratch/b75/page/scale-flat-*.html`, unchanged by any of these caches because
plain markup has no cascade work to save). B75 measured real markup at 197 µs
against that floor's 2.9 — **68x — and attributed it to "`dimensionsIn` meeting a
real page … percentages, inline runs, replaced elements". None of that was it.**
All of it was the cascade being re-resolved, and the gap is now 1.06x.

### The budget, and the gate it opens
