The pass count is B75's measurement and was not re-measured: 59 passes on
homedepot, 53 on macys, 15 on sony. Those are already the **cached** counts —
the parent plan's E2 measured read *clusters*, "the number of first-reads after a
DOM or style change" — so there is no further memo to add, a thing this session
got wrong once and had to correct.

| station | when B75 priced it | today |
|---|---:|---:|
| homedepot | 59 × 5 265 ms = **311 s** | 59 × 88 ms = **5.2 s** |
| macys | 53 × 836 ms = 44.3 s | 53 × 54 ms = **2.9 s** |
| sony | 15 × 291 ms = 4.4 s | 15 × 8 ms = **0.1 s** |

Against a 25-second station settle and a 30-second watchdog, and against the
~1.1 s the page's own geometry reads already cost on homedepot — reads the pass
would serve rather than add to — **all three are inside the budget.** The gate
`inflow-static-position` was waiting behind ("if that plan says over budget, this
one is not done") is open.

What that unblocks is a reading, not a performance number:
**26 of 27 in-flow offsets wrong, every element's x equal to its y, and one
expression sees it.** The prototype is still on `prd/layout-pass-reprice`,
unmerged, because nothing reads its table yet — wiring
`calculateDocumentPosition` and `calculateSiblingPosition` to it is that plan's
P2, and its ground truth has to be re-read from Chrome first: the 27 rows were
measured but never saved, only summarised.

## Eight of the ten closed doors are not doors, and the last two open to a headless browser (B82, 2026-09-01)

`finish-condition-audit`. The only stopping condition this work has is "the
antibot stations read the same as headed Chrome or better", and that condition
had never been measured with enough runs to mean anything. The door map's Chrome
column was a scratch profile, single-run, and — on Cloudflare — scored under a
criterion that `cf-ticket-is-not-a-pass` later replaced. Meanwhile these stations
pass in windows: `antibot-stations-pass-in-windows` and
`cfsc-verdict-is-five-in-six` both say a single sweep cannot tell a closed door
from a closed window.

So: the ten stations that were not clean in the previous sweep, both arms, **six
rounds each, 120 runs**, station-level alternation with the within-station order
flipped every round (block A/B favours whichever arm goes first on a station that
hardens with visits). Our arm is a ReleaseFast build of `d21d89ac2`; the
reference arm is `--headed --profile-dir` over a profile warmed on sixteen
ordinary pages (352 cookies), which is what `warm-profile.mjs` documents as the
minimum for a reference that does not refuse stations this engine walks into.
Every run records its own egress: `108.211.179.124`, colo SJC, all 120.

Verdict is "behind" only when the two Wilson 95% intervals do not overlap.

| station | this engine | headed+warm Chrome | |
|---|---|---|---|
| cf-scrapingcourse | **0/6** | **6/6** | **behind** |
| x-hyatt | **0/6** | **6/6** | **behind** |
| cf-nopecha | 0/6 | 0/6 | level |
| cf-zeroclover | 0/6 | 0/6 | level — and Chrome is *worse*: its six are `cf-blocked`, ours `cf-challenge` |
| dd-allopneus | 0/6 | 0/6 | level — both arms `cf-blocked` six times, so the site is blocking the address |
| dd-datadome | 1/6 | 1/6 | level |
| dd-g2 | 0/6 | 0/6 | level |
| dd-hermes | **1/6** | 0/6 | level (we are numerically ahead) |
| dd-leboncoin | **2/6** | 1/6 | level (we are numerically ahead) |
| dd-saks | 0/6 | 0/6 | level |

Totals: 4/60 here, 14/60 there — and **twelve of Chrome's fourteen are the two

**Eight stations are retired.** `dd-saks` and `dd-g2` were still being carried as
gaps; they refuse a warm headed Chrome six times out of six. `dd-allopneus` is an
address block, not a guard verdict. Nothing about the finish condition is left on

### Which leaves two, and neither of them wants a head

Five arms on the two remaining stations, six rounds each, then a second cut:

| arm | cf-scrapingcourse | x-hyatt |
|---|---|---|
| this engine (headless) | 0/6 `cf-challenge` | 0/6 `refused-429` |
| Chrome headed + warm | 6/6 | 6/6 |
| Chrome headed + fresh | 6/6 | 6/6 |
| Chrome headless + warm | 0/6 `cf-challenge` | 0/6 `refused-403` |
| Chrome headless + fresh | 0/6 `cf-challenge` | 0/6 `refused-403` |

Profile warmth moves nothing on either station — unlike DataDome, where
`warm-profile.mjs`'s own 2x2 says warmth and a head are both required. But that
table is confounded, and by something the sweep's header comment already names:
`--headless=new` puts `HeadlessChrome/151` in the user agent, so the headless
rows measure head *and* UA together.

Hold the UA equal — `--headed-ua` on both arms, so the string and the emptied
high-entropy metadata match — and the head stops mattering:

| arm | cf-scrapingcourse | x-hyatt |
|---|---|---|
| Chrome headed, normal UA | 6/6 | 6/6 |
| **Chrome headless, normal UA** | **5/6** | **6/6** |

One variable, both stations: adding `--headed-ua` to a headless Chrome takes
cf-scrapingcourse from 0/6 to 5/6 and x-hyatt from 0/6 to 6/6. This sharpens
rather than discovers — the sweep's header already recorded plain headless 2/15,
headless with the headed UA 9/15, headed 10/15 across fifteen stations. What is
new is that it now holds on the two stations that are still open, six runs each.

**The point is the arm it leaves behind.** Every two-arm comparison ever run on
these two doors used a *headed* Chrome, which kept a whole class of explanation
alive and cost several plans: `display-persona-lever-spent` (colour gamut, HDR,
depth, DPR — 75 station-runs), `chrome-arm-needs-persona-dpr`,
`intrinsic-box-is-dpr1-while-fonts-are-dpr2`, and the widget-timing chapter whose
finding was that Chrome's main thread is blocked for over a second. A headless
browser walks through both doors, so none of that is the gate. The reference arm
for these stations is now `antibot-sweep.mjs chrome --headed-ua` with no
`--headed`, and it is the same shape as ours.

### And the wire between the two is one stale constant wide

With the transport layer already closed (`cf-transport-layer-is-closed`), the
remaining wire question was the hint negotiation Cloudflare's managed challenge
actually performs: it answers the interstitial with `Accept-CH` *and*
`Critical-CH` naming nine high-entropy hints. `accept-ch-echo.mjs` serves that
exact list off localhost and records the byte-exact request head of every hit.

Eleven hits, paired by method and target: **header names, header order and header
values all identical**, except `sec-ch-ua-platform-version` — `"26.3.1"` here
against `"26.6.2"` from Chrome on the same machine — and Chrome's own
`HeadlessChrome` UA token, which is the reference arm's problem and not ours.
The `Accept-CH`/`Critical-CH` restart itself is implemented in
`src/network/HttpClient.zig`, with tests that assert the restart happens once and
does not happen for a hint that already went out; it is not a gap.

That one value was `claimed_platform.zig`'s pinned macOS version, and the pin is
deliberate — the file's whole point is that the claim does not follow the running
kernel. The number had simply gone stale against a reference host now on 26.6.2.
Staleness is not free next to `ua_full_version`, which *does* track the reference
Chrome: the two drift apart, and the pair is what a wire comparison reads. Re-pinned,
and the comment now says when to do it again. After: the only header that differs
across the eleven hits is the reference arm's user agent.

Not a door — `display-persona-lever-spent` already priced persona values — but a
standing false lead on a path a guard negotiates, which cost this session the time
to rule it out and would have cost the next one the same.

### One correction to carry forward

The previous session's handoff offered `scratch/b81/lp-b81` as "the merged
content" beside `lp-base-c9a8e11eb` as the baseline. Both binaries answer
`1.0.0-dev.1969+c9a8e11eb` to `version`. Its four alternating sweeps ran the same
binary in both columns, so "four rounds, 20/29 each, no regression" reads as four
repetitions of the baseline and not as a before/after.

## Every element's x stopped being its y (B99, 2026-09-01)

`in-flow-block-position` measured the defect a year of chapters kept pointing at:
`calculateDocumentPosition` and `calculateSiblingPosition` had **identical
bodies**, both answering "(preceding siblings' subtree nodes + ancestors) × 5px",
so every element's x equalled its y and one expression saw it. The pass that
knows better was written in B75 and shelved on cost. Four cascade caches later it
was affordable, and `inflow-static-position` wired the readers to it.

**27 of 27 rows and all fifteen container sizes now match Chrome**, from 1 of 27.

### The table, and the one thing it must not do

It lives on the Frame and is memoised on `Page.dom_version`. `positionOf` has a
`position_table_building` guard that is not optional: the pass measures boxes, and
measuring an out-of-flow box asks its containing block where it is — which is the
question the table answers, so the first pass would otherwise re-enter itself
forever.

### Five defects the real positions exposed, each with a Chrome reading

* **UA margins never reached the layout.** `<p>`'s `margin: 1em 0` is in the
  per-tag table `getComputedStyle` answers from, and only `<body>` had a case for
  reading it — so paragraphs stacked flush while the computed style said 16px.
  `StyleManager` already had the helper *and the comment*: "the same table
  `getComputedStyle` answers from, so the layout and the computed-style surface
  cannot drift apart again", used for fonts alone. Opened up, and `marginPx` asks
  it last. This is the one that matters beyond this plan: it is every `<p>`,
  `<h1>`, `<ul>`, `<blockquote>` on every page.
* **A child's position was written before the walk descended into it**, so it
  could not know what would escape out of the child. Chrome puts `<div
  style="margin-top:40px">` as body's only child at **y=40 for BODY** — the
  child's margin collapses out through body and body's own 8px loses the max — and
  at y=8 with the child at 49 once body has a 1px border
  (`scratch/b99/expr-body-collapse.js`, four shapes). `escapedTopMargin` walks the
  first-child chain, which is bounded by depth rather than by the subtree.
* **Scroll offsets were integers.** `element/position.html` asserts
  `gBCR().y === window.scrollY` after `scrollIntoView()`, which held while every y
  was a multiple of 5px and broke at 856.5 → 856. Chrome keeps the fraction:
  `scrollY` reads 100.5 and 123.5 in the two shapes of
  `scratch/b99/expr-scroll-fraction.js`. So the assertion was Chrome's and the
  truncation was the defect.
* **`elementFromPoint` ran its own faux layout** — `preorder_index * 5.0`, used as
  the box's left AND its top, the very signature being removed — with an early
  return that only a node count makes valid. It reads the pass's rows now. Doing
  that with `boundingClientRectValuesAt` per candidate took
  `document/element_from_point.html` from its budget to **51 951ms** over 400
  paragraphs, because that call resolves a client box and can walk an element's
  text. So the rows carry the border box as well as its origin — the pass has
  measured it already — and the height is corrected once the walk knows what the
  box holds.
* **Inline boxes had no row**, which is where `x == y` survived longest: the walk
  hands them to the line rather than stacking them. The line cursor either side of
  `flowInline` is where one sits and how wide it is.

### Two test expectations were the bug, written down

* `element/bounding_rect.html` asserted that two links had **different x**. Both
  are an `<h2>`'s only content, so Chrome puts both at x=8 and only their y
  differs. "Every element has its own x" was a property of the preorder stand-in.
* `cdp.dom: getBoxModel` expected `content: {25.0, 25.0, …}` — x equal to y, the
  signature itself. Chrome puts that `<p>` at 8,16 (8 from body's left margin, 16
  from its own UA margin collapsing out through the div and through body), which
  is the quad the test carries now.

### And one where the expectation was mine, from this session

The matrix's `inline-block pair` container went in as **400x30**, read from the
probe's first Chrome run, and recorded as a pre-existing defect because this
engine said 400x34. Runs two, three, four and five of the same probe all answer
**400x34** — the other 26 rows identical across all five — and eight further
shapes agree at 34 (`scratch/b99/expr-atomic-line-height.js`): the line is 30 of
box plus the strut's 4 hanging under the baseline the boxes sit on. **The first
run was cold, this engine was right, and the defect did not exist.** A Chrome
reading destined for a test expectation is worth running twice, especially
anything that depends on font metrics.

## Four caches and real coordinates later, the two doors have not moved (B99, 2026-09-01)

The session that removed `x == y` and took the engine several times faster ends
where it should: asking the closed stations whether any of that mattered. It did
not, and the reading is worth writing down because it is the cleanest negative
this chain has had.

### Which stations were even worth asking

Across **425 archived lightpanda sweeps**, seven stations sit at zero. Three of
them are not doors: `dd-g2`, `dd-saks` and `dd-allopneus` answer `first=200` in
**0%** of ~80 runs each — the refusal lands on the first document, before any
JavaScript, and headed Chrome is refused beside us. Nothing an engine does moves
those. That leaves the Cloudflare challenge family and Kasada:

| station | archived | this build | combined |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| cf-scrapingcourse | 0 / 73 | **0 / 25** | 0 / 98 |
| cf-nopecha | 0 / 68 | **0 / 25** | 0 / 93 |
| cf-zeroclover | 0 / 68 | **0 / 25** | 0 / 93 |
| x-hyatt | 1 / 89 | 1 / 25 | 2 / 114 |

x-hyatt's one pass is inside the ticket rate it already had
(`hyatt-now-issues-tickets-sometimes`: 5 in 157), and one event at n=25 separates
nothing.

### And the guards' own verdicts, which are a step earlier

A station's pass/refuse is the end of a chain. Both guards can be asked directly,
and both say the same thing:

* **Cloudflare**, six visits: `served=false` and `ticket=(absent)` every time,
  with all three rounds reading `chl-gen` — the challenge never settles. `r3` is
  87–90KB, the same order as Chrome's, which `cf-r3-is-not-short` already
  established.
* **Kasada**, ten visits: `x-kpsdk-r` **absent all ten**, `/tl` answering 200
  `text/plain` at **0 bytes** with `x-kpsdk-cr: true`. Byte for byte the reading
  from months ago: cleared to hold a cookie, never handed a ticket.

### What this does and does not say

25 runs per station detects a door swinging open, not a few points of movement:
at n=25 the 95% upper bound on a true rate of zero observations is about 11%. So
the honest statement is that **nothing large changed**, and that the two guards'
own answers are unchanged in shape as well as in outcome.

Which is the same conclusion five earlier chapters reached by other routes, and
it should be read the way they were: the engine-side surface these two read is
not where the remaining difference is. The work this session merged was worth
merging on its own terms — a one-expression detector removed, a 30-second stall
given real margin, UA margins reaching the layout at last — and none of it was a
door.

## Round 2's window, and the field we filed blank that Cloudflare never sends us (B111, 2026-09-04)

Round 2 was the last of the three telemetry POSTs still carrying a difference:
round 1 is the same length on both arms and round 3's contents were settled by
the byte transplant. Ours runs about 200 bytes longer than the arm that clears.

The way in was to stop treating the body as opaque. Its plaintext never passes
`JSON.stringify`, `TextEncoder.encode` or `btoa` — the funnels `fo-plaintext.mjs`
already stood in — but it is *assembled*, and the assembly uses `join("")` over
the characters of the ciphertext and `charCodeAt`/`charAt` over whatever was cut
into them. `--r2` stands there instead. It is the console channel, not the wire
one: the earlier `report-r2-body --beacon` asked the same question through a few
dozen requests into the widget's origin and pushed round 2 from 4898 bytes to
21751, which was the instrument and not the station. This one is measured
neutral — Chrome keeps its `cf-chl-out` and its "You bypassed" page with the
hooks in, four runs of four, and our own round 2 stays at 4908–4930 against a
4908–4951 baseline.

**The window between the two POSTs is 27 events long and identical in kind and
in order on both arms.** Not one event happens on one arm and not the other.
Three of the 27 differ in length:

| input | Chrome (clears) | Chrome (headless UA) | this engine |
|---|---|---|---|
| the resource timing entry, stringified | 1057 | 1077 | 1011 |
| a `<43>-<unix ts>-1.2.1.1-<blob>` token | **1514** | 1535 | **1663** |
| an `Error` stack string | 1338 | 1348 | 1338 |
| → round 2 itself | 4727 | 4812 | 4930 |

The token is the only one that is stable and points the right way: +149 on every
run of four, where the other two wobble run to run (one run had the stack
identical on both arms). It does not explain round 2 arithmetically — the three
arms' (token, round 2) pairs are not collinear — and **where it comes from is
still open**: six instruments (`document.cookie`, `responseText`, `response`,
`Response.text()`, the parent's `message` events, both sides of `JSON.parse`) all
came back negative, so it is either assembled character by character inside the
guard's VM or it arrives by a channel none of those six covers.

The other differing input, the timing entry, was the one with a named defect
behind it. `PerformanceResourceTiming.serverTiming` answered an empty
`FrozenArray` for every response this engine had ever loaded — the accessor was
`return .empty`, nothing read the header — while Chrome's entry for the widget's
api.js carries `cfExtPri`. That entry is stringified into the widget as
`apiJsResourceTiming`, so the one member of the object with structure in it was
the one we filed empty. It is fixed: the header rides along with contentType and
contentEncoding through `ResponseLabels` and is parsed on read, with every corner
of the grammar measured against Chrome 151 rather than read off RFC 8941
(`probes/expr-b111-server-timing.js`; the sharpest is that an empty member name
ends the header rather than dropping itself).

**Ten alternating pairs later, `served=` is 0 of 10 on both binaries, and round
2's length did not move at all** — both arms land on the same quantised lattice,
{4919, 4930, 4940, 4951}. The reason is the part worth keeping:

| capture | nextHopProtocol | serverTiming |
|---|---|---|
| chrome, clears | h3 | `[{"name":"cfExtPri"}]` |
| chrome, headless UA | h3 | `[{"name":"cfExtPri"}]` |
| **chrome, this run over h2** | **h2** | **`[]`** |
| this engine, before | h2 | `[]` |
| this engine, after | h2 | `[]` |

`cfExtPri` is Cloudflare's HTTP/3 extensible-priorities timing and is only sent
over h3 — a plain h2 curl carrying Origin, Referer and a Chrome UA gets
`timing-allow-origin` back and no `server-timing` at all, and a *Chrome* capture
that happened to negotiate h2 reports the empty list too. So "serverTiming is a
real gap" was, on this station, a restatement of the h3/h2 difference, and that
one has been causally closed since a Chrome with QUIC disabled cleared 6 of 6.
The engine fix is worth keeping on its own terms — we answered an empty array for
every response, not just Cloudflare's — but it cannot fire here.

## The payload is a constant and the verdict is not (B121, 2026-09-06)

`fo-plaintext.mjs` has been able to read the guard's payload before it is
encrypted for a long time, and it never recorded whether the run it read was
honoured. Every capture it produced was of a run whose outcome nobody knew, and
the comparison those captures fed was our refused run against Chrome's refused
run -- chosen deliberately, to hold the challenge variant still. The plaintext
of a payload Cloudflare **accepted** had not been looked at.

One line fixes that (`served`, on cf-token.mjs's criterion: the final document
is the page, not the ticket). Two things fell out of it immediately.

**The wrappers are honest.** A hooked Chrome still gets served -- 32 of 34 runs
across two sittings, against 29 of 30 for the unhooked historical sample. That
is the check this file's header has always asked for, and it now runs on every
capture instead of being an argument.

**The collected payload does not decide the verdict.** Eight Chrome runs share
one payload signature -- the ten large `TextEncoder.encode` inputs are
byte-identical across all of them, only the call order moves -- and two of those
eight were refused the page. Same machine, same binary, same exit IP, same
report, opposite outcomes. Extending that to 44 runs with the whole exchange
recorded (timestamps, statuses, response headers, encoded sizes), the one
refused run sits inside the served distribution on every measured axis; the
first thing that distinguishes it is r3's own reply, `cf-chl-gen` where a
served run gets `cf-chl-out`. Whatever costs Chrome those few percent leaves no
trace on the client side.

Two readings that did not survive the larger sample, both of them mine:

  - "Our round 1 reply is 4KB bigger than Chrome's." It is not. The reply has
    two size families (~30.4K, then ~34.2K from run 8 onward): Cloudflare
    changed challenge variant mid-sitting. Compare within a family.
  - "Refused samples are cheap now." From 6 of 8 they looked it; 26 consecutive
    served runs later, the rate is ~6%, the same order as the unhooked one.

What our arm does have is a residual, and the honest size of it took a second
sample to establish. On five runs it looked like ~2.3KB with the ranges barely
touching. On eleven it is half that, with the ranges overlapping:

| arm | n | r3 request bytes |
|---|---|---|
| chrome | 57 | 88268..91415 (median 89666) |
| ours | 11 | 87234..90220 (median **88546**) |

A 1.1KB median gap, 526 of 627 pairs with Chrome larger (z≈3.5, so the shift is
real), and one of our runs above Chrome's median. Against a within-Chrome
spread of 3.1KB, this is a small effect on a noisy quantity -- not the
nearly-disjoint distributions the first five runs suggested. Anyone quoting the
2.3KB figure is quoting a sampling artefact.

Three measurements say what the gap is NOT:

  - **Not the encoder inputs.** The sum of the fifteen `TextEncoder.encode`
    lengths is a constant per arm -- 124941 on Chrome, 124920 here, 21 bytes
    apart -- while r3 swings 3KB run to run. And every one of those encodes is
    paired with a `subtle.digest` of the same length, so those buffers are
    hashed, not shipped: they put about 480 bytes into r3, not 88KB.
  - **Not the realm or entry text.** A numbers-only census taken at the instant
    r3 goes out (`surfaceCensus`, emitted once per realm, counts only) puts the
    worker realm's own globals at 1274 names / 18485 name-bytes on Chrome and
    1238 / 17897 here, and the resource-timing entry names at ~1474 bytes
    against ~1454. Both known-collected surfaces together account for ~0.6KB.
  - **Not measurable with the heavier hooks at all.** `--r2` leaves 617KB
    strings in the realm and pushed our r3 to 90295, *above* Chrome's run in the
    same sitting -- the instrument inverted the sign of the difference. Only the
    numbers-only census is safe here.

The one new number worth keeping: **the worker realm is 36 global names short**
(1238 against 1274). The window realm was measured at 921 of 923 long ago, so
this is a much larger hole in a realm the collector is known to walk, and it is
independent of r3's length.


## A wedged engine hangs up, it does not answer late (2026-09-07)

`timeout: Runtime.enable` at 55s on ak-kohls read like a slow answer for
months. It is not one. The full engine log over one of those navigations holds
exactly **one** `watchdog stall stalled_ms=30339`, then 195
`ExecutionTerminated` inside the same millisecond, and then this:

```
+34330ms cdp closing connection reason="pending terminate"
```

`Watchdog.zig` hands a 30-second tick to `env.requestTerminate()`, and
`CDP.tick` answers a pending terminate by sending `CLOSE_GOING_AWAY` and
returning false. So **one page over the watchdog budget ends the whole CDP
connection**, and every station or detector still on the list comes back as a
timeout that has nothing to do with it. That is the entire "one crash and its
tail" shape in the archived sweeps: 5 of 29 stations and 7 of 12 detectors could
not be measured, and none of those rows were about their own pages.

Both sweeps now ping the engine (`Target.getTargets`, on a 5s deadline of its
own -- `Cdp.send`'s 30s is longer than the stall being asked about) whenever a
row errored, rebuild the session when it does not answer, and mark the row
`engineRestarted` / print `ENGINE-RESTARTED`. A run that restarted mid-sweep is
not the same reading as one that did not. **28/29 stations and 10/12 detectors**
now come back with full readings, and the tail is gone.

Two rigs came out of it, both offline and both durable:

* `wedge-probe.mjs` -- navigate, then ping once a second and attach macOS
  `sample` the first time a ping misses. `--read` fires the reading the detector
  sweep makes (`extractReach`) after a settle, `--runtime-enable` adds the one
  domain the sweep enables and this probe did not, `--quiet` drops the engine's
  log, and `--log-file` is the only way to get the full log on disk (one station
  run can produce 70MB and `results/` is tracked).
* `flex-cost.mjs` -- k children per level, `depth` levels, one
  `getBoundingClientRect`, three arms over an identical tree: `flex`,
  `flex-nogrow` (`flex-grow: 0`, which returns from `flexItemWidth` before its
  sibling walk) and `block`.

### What the 30 seconds was: flex, and a 9.5x that still does not open kohls

The sample of a wedged engine is `Document.elementFromPoint ->
boundingClientRectValuesAt -> contentHeight -> dimensionsIn`, with **27 nested
`dimensionsIn` frames** alternating with `flexItemWidth` and `containingWidth`.
`flexItemWidth`'s own self time is ~0: the cost is what it asks for. It
recomputed the container's content width and the sum over every item on the line
for each item, and measuring a container measures its items, each of which asks
for the container again one level down -- nothing but
`MAX_CONTAINING_BLOCK_DEPTH` ended that.

`Frame._flex_lines` now solves a line once per container, dropped when
`Page.dom_version` moves. Two other scopes were tried and measured first, and
both are recorded in the code because they look right:

* keyed on `(container, depth)` -- misses on every round of the very
  alternation it is meant to cut, since the depth is what differs between them.
  20% slower for the bookkeeping.
* scoped to one top-level measurement, which needs no invalidation rule at all
  -- instrumented at `hits=0 misses=8 measured=37`. Inside one measurement each
  container is asked exactly once. The waste is the same measurement repeated:
  about **five thousand** top-level `dimensionsIn` entries for one
  `getBoundingClientRect` on a 1094-node flex tree.

Clean A/B, a dedicated baseline worktree at the same commit, arms alternated
twice, 3281 nodes, one rect read:

| arm | flex | flex-nogrow | block (control) |
|---|---|---|---|
| baseline | 1710 / 1694ms | 549 / 505ms | 102 / 103ms |
| fixed | 175 / 183ms | 145 / 153ms | 101 / 95ms |
| | **9.5x** | **3.5x** | 1.03x |

Flex goes from 16.7x block to 1.8x, every width and height byte-identical.

**It does not open ak-kohls.** Alternated three pairs on clean builds, baseline
stalls 3/3 and fixed 2/3 -- n=3, so "no visible improvement", not "fixed". The
readings came back because of the harness restart, not the layout win.

⚠️ Both of those A/Bs had to be redone: the first set was taken with the
temporary hit/miss counters still in `zig-out/bin`. The source had them removed
and `make test` builds its own binary, so nothing pointed at it. That instrument
logs a line per top-level measurement, ~5000 per read, and it is what a "busy
thread at 100% in `writev`" sample was actually showing. **Rebuild before
measuring, and check the engine log for your own instrument's output.**

### The last two detectors are a SIGSEGV, not slowness

With `Runtime.enable` on, `iphey` and `deviceinfo` crash the engine. 4/4 across
both arms, so it predates the flex work, and `deviceinfo`'s read even returns
`nodes=266` first. The sweep reports it as `timeout: Runtime.evaluate` because
by then the process is gone. One command:

```
node tools/fingerprint/wedge-probe.mjs https://iphey.com/ \
     --seconds 40 --read --settle 8000 --runtime-enable
```

**Found and fixed the same day.** It is a worker's `console.log`, and the whole
repro is three lines:

```js
const b = new Blob(['console.log({a:1});'], {type: 'text/javascript'});
new Worker(URL.createObjectURL(b));   // with Runtime.enable on
```

`Inspector.zig:318` unwrapped a null with `.?`:
`v8_inspector__Session__wrapObject` returns an empty handle for a value from a
context the inspector was never told about, and `contextCreated` is called for
frames only (`cdp/domains/page.zig`, `cdp/domains/target.zig`) -- so every
dedicated worker's realm is unknown to it. The path is
`Console.log -> dispatchConsoleMessage -> Notification.dispatch -> CDP
onRuntimeConsoleMessage -> runtime.consoleMessage -> getRemoteObject ->
wrapObject`.

**The trigger is the realm, not the value.** Two rounds of twelve candidates,
each on its own engine (`scratch/segv/find-trigger.mjs`): a circular object, a
circular array, a 200-deep nest, a throwing Proxy, a revoked Proxy, `window`, a
DOM node, a 2MB string, a Symbol, an Error and a throwing getter all logged
fine, so the `<circular>` lines in the log before the crash were a coincidence.
Of the realm candidates -- main realm, same-origin iframe, an iframe logging
itself, a removed iframe's function, a cross-realm object, **a worker**, a
worker terminated first, a timer, a microtask, a fetch callback, 500 logs,
after `document.open` -- only the worker crashed.

`wrapObject` now returns `error.ObjectNotWrappable` and `consoleMessage` drops
the message, which is also what a client sees from Chrome: a dedicated worker is
its own target, and a page session without auto-attach is shown nothing of its
console. Covered by `cdp.runtime: a worker's console.log does not take the
engine with it`, which asserts both the silence and that the page realm still
logs afterwards.

**The detector suite is 12/12 for the first time**: `deviceinfo` 73s crash ->
14.1s with 266 nodes, `iphey` 77s crash -> 17.7s with 495 nodes.

⚠️ Harness note: the first run of the candidate rig printed the one crasher as
`alive`. It killed each engine 300ms after the evaluate returned, and the panic
handler had written its text but the process had not exited yet, so `exited` was
still null. Give a crash 3 seconds, and read the log rather than the exit code.

## The detectors say what they think, and name the axis (2026-09-07)

`detector-sweep.mjs` answers "did the page finish". Its `verdictWords` column
is only how many judgement-shaped WORDS appear in the page text, which threw
away what these twelve pages are for: they publish a conclusion AND the axes
they read to reach it. `detector-verdicts.mjs` reads that, and
`verdict-diff.mjs` compares two snapshots by axis name.

The first pair (us pinned at `2100+e2861a1fe`, chrome `--headed-ua`) is the
first graded reading this repo has of itself:

| | us | chrome |
|---|---|---|
| iphey MX Score | **70** | **100** |
| iphey verdict | **Unreliable** | Trustworthy |
| iphey `browser` axis | **Detected an inconsistent browser fingerprint** | axis absent |

**212 readings identical, about 25 different.** What matters is that only the
first group below is a defect of ours; the other two groups are the trap.

### A defect the channel found on its first run: percentage heights never resolve

browserleaks reads `div.clientHeight` and got **0** from us against **1080**
from Chrome, and reported our viewport as `1920×0`. Isolated on a synthetic
page, the rule is clean:

| shape | us | chrome |
|---|---|---|
| `height:50%` in a **px-height** parent (200px) | **19** | **100** |
| `height:100%` in a px-height parent (300px) | **19** | **300** |
| `height:50%` in a percentage-height parent | 19 | 19 (both right: indefinite) |
| `height:50vh` | 540 | 540 |
| `height:200px` | 200 | 200 |

`vh` resolves, `px` resolves, **`%` never does** — so this is not a rounding
question, it is a branch that was never written. Plan
`percentage-height-never-resolves`.

Three more, all iphey's own numbers rather than hashes: `Stack Overflow
Counter` 11541 against 3970, `SVG Computed Style` 129.8125 against 124.4063,
`Storage` 10 against 4. Plan `iphey-numeric-axis-gaps`. And sannysoft catches
`navigator.sendBeacon()` with no arguments returning undefined where Chrome
throws.

### The rows that are NOT defects, and why

Worth as much as the findings, because each of these looks exactly like one:

* **Five hash families differ** — Canvas, Audio, WebGL, Dom Tags Snapshot,
  Client Rects. A hash summarising a surface cannot say which part moved, and
  these families are already causally closed (see the image-pixel and
  glyph-outline sections).
* **The display persona axes** — `Resolution 1920x1200` against `400x300`,
  `colorDepth 30` against `24`, `availTop 33` against `0`, `outerHeight`.
  This axis is deliberately not aligned; `assertPersonaParity` reports screen
  values and refuses to assert them for exactly this reason.
* **Every client hint is EMPTY on the Chrome arm** — platform, brands,
  architecture, bitness, uaFullVersion, fullVersionList, formFactors.
  `--headed-ua` blanks the high-entropy hints. Ours are populated; the
  difference runs the other way.
* **rebrowser's `useragent` test** — 🟢 for us, 🟡 for Chrome. We are the
  better arm on that row.
* **creepjs says "Headless" for BOTH arms.** It does not separate this engine
  from a headless Chrome, so it is not a tell of ours.

A retraction from the same run: sannysoft's `navigator.cookieEnabled` row reads
`document.write(navigator.cookieEnabled); true`, which looks like script source
leaking into the DOM. The Chrome arm prints it identically — that is how
sannysoft renders the row.

### What iphey's 30 points are NOT (2026-09-07)

Two real height defects were fixed without iphey's score moving off 70
"Unreliable", so the next step was the mechanism rather than more axes. Four
things are ruled out, each with a rig under `scratch/ip/`:

* **The tile.** iphey marks exactly one tile `--error` and the other four say
  "Everything is fine": **Browser**. Hardware, Software, Location and IP are
  all clean, so the whole 30 is one section (`browser-tile.mjs`).
* **The transport.** `ja3n`, `ja4` and the HTTP/2 `akamai_hash` are identical
  across the arms; only the unsorted `ja3` differs, and Chrome shuffles its own
  extension order per connection (`tls.mjs`).
* **The names it reads.** The collector is string-array obfuscated and holds no
  verdict text, but its string heap is readable: **3781 identifier-shaped
  strings**, including the 23 automation markers it hunts (`$cdc_asdjflasutopfhvcZLmcfl_`,
  `__webdriver_evaluate`, `callPhantom`, `__playwright__binding__`, …) and every
  navigator property it reads. Asked BY NAME on both arms, **112 of 120 answers
  are identical**; the 8 that differ are all the display persona, which the
  reference arm is deliberately not aligned on -- and Chrome scores 100 with a
  400x300 screen, so it is not that (`name-probe.mjs`).
* **The natives.** 29 integrity and behaviour checks, **all identical**:
  `Function.prototype.toString` on four natives, the TypeError and RangeError
  shapes, `Error.captureStackTrace` and `stackTraceLimit`, `window.chrome`'s
  key set, plugins and mimeTypes, `Notification.permission`, the navigator and
  screen prototype chains, `AudioContext.sampleRate`, the WebGL
  vendor/renderer pair, `document.fonts.check`, Intl's `resolvedOptions` and
  `supportedValuesOf('timeZone').length` (`integrity.mjs`).

The verdict is the server's. The one URL in the heap is `wss://api.iphey.com`,
and a `WebSocket.prototype.send` hook shows the shape: a 43-byte nonce down,
**96223 bytes up from us against Chrome's 100414**, and a ~2.4KB reply. Both
directions are ciphertext, so the payload is not readable -- but the sizes are
within 4%, so the collection is not deficient (`ws-capture.mjs`).

What is left is the surfaces it hashes, and those are comparable: two runs per
arm on one machine are byte-stable, so nothing is session-salted.

| axis | ours | chrome | |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dom Tags Snapshot | 636e3392160dc55e | 636e3392160dc55e | **match** |
| Client Rects | ec0366583a4b3b40 | 9d8fd6fcd4169946 | |
| Audio | d0067cad9a63e081 | 0af6c2a43ada3e10 | |
| WebGL | dd45b6fecdb52bd1 | aeacd125866a39cd | |
| Canvas | 75553175f3d2185e | 2a38a5cfb442adc3 | |
| SVG Computed Style | 129.8125 | 124.4063 | a number, not a hash |
| Storage | 10 | 4 | a number, not a hash |
| Stack Overflow Counter | 3959 / 8492 | 3971 / 15085 | **noise, both arms** |
| MX Score | 70 | 100 | |

⚠️ Two corrections to this repo's own earlier notes come out of that table.
**`Stack Overflow Counter` is noise** -- it moved 3959 to 8492 on our arm and
3971 to 15085 on Chrome's between two runs, so the "11541 against 3970" read
earlier is not a gap and nothing should be built on it. And **`Dom Tags
Snapshot` now matches** where it differed before the height work, which is the
one iphey axis those two fixes did move.

#### And the axis behind it: a font-family LIST picks the wrong entry

The string heap names the SVG axis outright -- `'Hello, SVG World!'` sits
beside `svg` and `getComputedStyle` -- and rebuilding it reproduces iphey's two
numbers to the digit: `getComputedTextLength()` is **129.8125** here against
Chrome's **124.40625**.

It is not the SVG path. The same string, at 16px, asked four ways on a page
that has Roboto:

| asked | ours | chrome |
|---|---|---|
| `16px Roboto, sans-serif` — html span | **129.53** (= sans-serif) | 124.40 (= Roboto) |
| `16px Roboto` alone — html span | 124.20 | 124.40 |
| `16px Roboto, sans-serif` — svg text | **129.81** | 124.40 |
| `16px Roboto` alone — svg text | 125.75 | 124.40 |
| `16px Roboto, sans-serif` — canvas | **129.53** | 124.40 |
| `16px Roboto` alone — canvas | 124.48 | 124.40 |
| `16px sans-serif` / `Helvetica` / `Arial` | 129.53 / 129.53 / 129.52 | identical |

The generic families agree to the digit, so no metrics table is missing.
**Written as a list, `Roboto, sans-serif` takes the sans-serif; written alone,
Roboto is used.** The first-available-family step picks the wrong entry, and
that shape -- `font-family: Something, sans-serif` -- is on essentially every
real page, so text metrics are a few percent wrong nearly everywhere. Plan
`font-family-list-picks-the-generic`.

Secondary, from the same table: asked for `Roboto` alone the three paths answer
**124.203, 125.757 and 124.484** where Chrome answers 124.40625, 124.40625 and
124.4016 -- the three text paths disagree with each other, which is the
`text-width-has-three-paths` shape again.

The other number is smaller: `Storage` is
`navigator.storage.estimate().quota`, a round **10 GiB constant** here against
Chrome's 5368709120, which Chrome derives from free disk (it reported 4 and
then 5 GiB on this machine within the hour). Matching it exactly is not a
target; deriving it from real free space is. And one new tell in passing:
`document.fonts.size` is **0** here against Chrome's **312** -- `check()`
answers true while the FontFace set is empty.

##### Retraction: it is the webfont, not the family list

The paragraph above is wrong and this is what replaced it. "The
first-available-family step picks the wrong entry" was inferred from Roboto
alone, and two controls falsify it:

* **A local family is picked correctly in every syntactic form.** With
  `Courier New` -- which this engine has metrics for -- the width is 163.2265625
  for `font-family: Courier New, sans-serif`, for the quoted spelling, for
  `Courier New` alone, for the `font:` shorthand, and even for
  `NoSuchFontXYZ, Courier New, sans-serif`. `findInList` walks the list and
  takes the first hit, which is right (`scratch/ff/list-vs-shorthand.mjs`).
* **An `@font-face` font is fetched and then never used.** Serving a real font
  file as `ProbeFont` from a local server (`scratch/ff/webfont.mjs`):

  | | ours | chrome |
  |---|---|---|
  | server saw the font request | **yes** | yes |
  | `document.fonts.size` | **0** | 1 |
  | `document.fonts` entries | **none** | `ProbeFont:loaded` |
  | `document.fonts.check('16px ProbeFont')` | true | true |
  | `font-family: ProbeFont, sans-serif` | **129.53** (= sans-serif) | **163.23** (= the webfont) |
  | `sans-serif` | 129.53 | 129.53 |
  | `"Courier New"` | 163.23 | 163.23 |

So Roboto measured as sans-serif because Roboto is iphey's WEBFONT and this
engine does not measure with one -- and `Roboto` alone measured as neither
because an unknown family lands on `fallback`, whose table happens to sit near
Roboto's. Two separate defects, both one expression from Chrome:

* text on any page with a webfont is measured with the fallback family, which
  is most real pages;
* `document.fonts` is EMPTY (`size` 0 against Chrome's 312 on iphey, 1 against
  1 here) while `check()` answers true for the same name -- so the engine knows
  the `@font-face` rule exists for one question and not for the other.

The lesson for the next reading: a family difference is not a family-selection
bug until a LOCAL family has been checked in the same shapes. The generic
families agreeing to the digit was already the hint -- selection was never
broken.

## Reading Cloudflare's guard VM: the fetch/decode is four lines (2026-09-08)

The four short values in the widget realm's payload are computed inside the
guard's own interpreter -- every page-layer explanation for them was causally
negated (timing, frames, pixels, literals, instrument perturbation, every
number-producing API in the realm, the performance timeline), and this engine
answers all four differently from Chrome, `0` against `16` on the third. So the
interpreter is the remaining channel, and this is what it looks like.

Dump one delivery first and do everything against that copy:
`scratch/b95/dump-normal.mjs` takes the body off the wire, and the
`new/normal` document is a 251KB page holding one 232KB inline script. **The
identifiers change on every delivery** -- the same helper was `cA.cT`, `cU.cY`
and `bv.bC` across three -- so an offset is only meaningful against a saved
document.

The program is switch-flattened: about thirty
`switch (seq[i++]) { case '0': ...; continue; }` state machines, one per
original function. That is the obfuscator, not the VM. The VM is one of them,
and its head gives the whole fetch/decode:

```js
for (;;) if (regs[pc_reg].length === 0) {
  for (; regs.length > 0 ;) {
    if (pc = regs[pc_reg], pc !== pc) return regs[ret];   // a NaN pc halts
    switch (
      regs[pc_reg] = pc + 1,                              // pc++
      op = key ^ ((code[pc] - 28) & 255),                  // decrypt the opcode
      k  = key + op,
      key = (k * k * 53140 + k * 9940 + 51159) & 255,      // advance the key
      op
    ) {
      case 9:   H09.call(this);      break;
      case 127: H7F.call(this);      break;
      ...
      case 26:  E.call(this, 97);    break;                 // a family, with
      case 132: E.call(this, 66);    break;                 // an immediate
      ...
      case 0:   U.call(this, 53);    break;
      ...
    }
  }
}
```

`code` is `this.m` and the rolling `key` starts at `this.i`. The arithmetic
above is not written with operators: the program builds a table of them first
(`ops[name(647)] = (a, b) => a ^ b`, and `+`, `*`, `&`, `===`, `!==`), and
`647` and friends are ids into a string decoder, so `ops[name(op.aH)](x, y)` is
`y ^ x`. Resolving that table is what makes the loop readable.

### Putting the strings back, and two corrections to the paragraph above

Every property access in the program reads `DEC(TABLE.key)`, where `TABLE` is a
local literal of numeric ids (`op = {a: 647, Q: 927, ...}`) and `DEC` is an
alias of the one decoder, `d(id) = arr[id - 499]` -- a plain index, no
encryption. The obfuscation is that `arr` has been rotated by the usual
`push(shift())` shuffler until a checksum over eight of its own entries matches
a constant.

**Find that rotation structurally rather than by replaying the arithmetic.** Of
the 1886 entries only 75 begin with a digit, and exactly ONE rotation puts all
eight checksum ids on one of those -- 289 here. That is the answer whatever the
constant is, and it avoids mis-transcribing a coefficient out of a
`-parseInt(x)/1 + parseInt(y)/2 + ...` chain. It checks out semantically at
once: id 594 is `"call"`, 1153 `"length"`, 1258 `"pop"`, 1992 `"splice"`.

With 233 id tables and 281 decoder aliases resolved, 4668 accesses rewrite and
91 are left. And the readable program corrects both numbers claimed above:

* **The key advance is `+ 51159`, not `% 51159`.** The program writes no
  operators at all -- `ops["daxlm"] = (a, b) => a + b` -- and reading that
  table wrong gives a disassembler that decodes the first byte correctly and
  every byte after it wrong.
* **69 opcodes, not 46.** 46 have a dedicated handler
  (`H.call(this)`), and the other 23 go through two families that take an
  immediate: 17 as `E.call(this, N)` and 6 as `U.call(this, N)`. Counting only
  the first shape is what gave 46.

So a disassembler still needs no execution: with the saved `code` array and the
initial key the stream decodes from the corrected recurrence. What is left is
naming the 48 handler bodies (46 + `E` + `U`), each 850-1800 bytes of
deobfuscated code that declares its own id table and its own operator table
before doing its work. That is the one thing the page layer cannot answer.
